Live disagreements tiled into the eleven entries. (1) Whether Timothy's father was a proselyte: Ellicott probable from the child's training, Clarke a mere heathen or at most a proselyte of the gate, Robertson and Barnes arguing backwards from the son's uncircumcision. (2) How circumcising Timothy squares with refusing to circumcise Titus: Clarke the object of those pressing it, Robertson the stakes (Gentile liberty vs efficient service), Ellicott three reasons including descent from the nobler side, Barnes bare expediency, Calvin the standing of the rite itself with his three degrees and the line that Paul might circumcise Timothy but might not have offered a sacrifice for sin. (3) WHETHER THE JERUSALEM DECREES WERE PERMANENT - a flat contradiction: Robertson reads the perfect participle and present infinitive as 'a charter of liberty for continual living, not a temporary compromise', where Calvin says they continued only for a time and that Paul afterwards made free what the apostles had forbidden. (4) Why the Spirit forbade Asia and Bithynia: Henry a new work among Romans, Barnes the extension into Greece, Clarke unreadiness of hearers, Calvin refusing all accounts that ground the difference in men. (5) The North vs South Galatian question, which Robertson rests entirely on the aorist participle's inability to express subsequent action. (6) Whether the vision was a dream: Barnes and Clarke cannot tell, Wesley denies it flatly (only two dreams in the NT), Calvin rests on 'in the night'. (7) Who the man of Macedonia was: guardian angel (rejected by Barnes), an angel in Macedonian habit (Wesley), or Luke himself (Ramsay/Renan via Robertson, who insists the narrative must not be robbed of its supernatural aspect). (8) Whether Philippi could be called a chief city - four different rescues of Luke's accuracy. (9) WHETHER THE HOUSEHOLD BAPTISM PROVES INFANT BAPTISM - the sharpest exchange in the chapter: Barnes 'a strong presumptive proof', Wesley 'who can believe that in so many families there was no infant?', Ellicott 'this is to read a great deal between the lines' and the practice 'rests on firmer grounds than a precarious induction from a few ambiguous passages', Robertson 'one sees infants or not according to his predilections or preferences'. (10) What 'the Lord opened her heart' means: Calvin denies any preparation of her own, Clarke holds she was already prepared and given more grace for faithfulness to what she had. (11) Whether the possession was real: Clarke argues from Luke's medical training, Robertson from the term's use for ventriloquists, Calvin that Luke follows common speech and exhibits the error of the common people. (12) Whether the girl was converted: Clarke says flatly she continued a heathen and makes that an argument for a real possession, where Ellicott refuses to think she drifted back and later says the witness of the possessed girl 'was thus not altogether fruitless'. (13) Whether the earthquake and the loosed bands were miraculous or natural. (14) Whether the baptism of the jailer was by immersion: Clarke says the hour and haste disprove it, Ellicott says no certain answer but a prison bath would serve, Robertson canvasses three basins and quotes Meyer for immersion as essential to the symbolism. (15) Why the magistrates changed their minds. (16) Why Paul pleaded his citizenship only at the end.

Two threads run the length of this chapter and were deliberately preserved across entries. FIRST, the battle of Philippi: Calvin invokes it at v10 in his own way, setting the wicked spirit that appeared to Brutus, inviting him to that unhappy battle 'even in the very same place whereunto Paul was afterwards called', against the true vision given Paul; then at v27 Barnes and Ellicott independently trace the jailer's reach for his sword to the same battle, Barnes noting that Brutus and Cassius and many of their friends fell on their own swords there and Ellicott that the act 'had been looked on as heroic' and was 'naturally enough contagious'. SECOND, the possessed girl's cry: Clarke closes the door on her at v19 ('she continued a heathen still, for we do not hear a word of her conversion'), while Ellicott hears in her cry a divided consciousness and a mind longing for deliverance, refuses to think she drifted back into unbelief, and at v30 turns her testimony into the seed of the jailer's question, since the circumstances that brought Paul to prison 'had pointed him out as proclaiming the way of salvation' - so that 'the witness of the demoniac girl was thus not altogether fruitless'. Also notable: Robertson quotes Furneaux that 'the two most important social revolutions worked by Christianity have been the elevation of woman and the abolition of slavery', both illustrated in this one chapter by Lydia and the slave girl; Ellicott observes that men could tolerate varieties of worship or the speculations of philosophers but 'were roused to madness by that which threatened their business'; Robertson quotes Ramsay that 'the most sensitive part of civilized man is the pocket'; Chrysostom asks 'Do you mark what a blessing tribulation is? But we, in our soft beds, with none to be afraid of, pass the whole night in sleep'; Barnes that 'a Christian may find more true joy in a prison, than the monarch on his throne'; and Ellicott quotes Tertullian to the martyrs, 'the leg feels not the stocks when the mind is in heaven'.

Two Gill defects in one chapter. At v1 his block is truncated mid-sentence in the harvest, ending '...for as it was usual to call ' after only about 180 words, so his comment on Phebe as a member in full communion is cut off; what survives was usable and was used. At v20 his block is a bare cross-reference stub, 'And the God of peace,.... See Gill on ;' with the target reference itself missing — no content at all, so Gill is declared in excluded_voices for that entry. The v20 stub is the more serious kind: it is not a truncation but a dangling pointer, and it leaves the entry with Calvin as its only reformed voice.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus and Cyril of Jerusalem cannot be declared in excluded_voices, even though both names appear in VOICE_LABELS in scripts/synthesis_qa.py. split_voices does not in fact segment their blocks in this harvest: the labels it returns for romans 16:1 are Gill, Henry, Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson, Calvin, Wesley, with no Theodoret, and likewise at v20 with no Cyril. undeclarable_voices therefore rejects both 'Theodoret'/'Theodoret of Cyrrhus' and 'Cyril'/'Cyril of Jerusalem' as absent, so a declaration would fail the validator's excluded_voices check. Consequence: their text is silently absorbed into the preceding declared voice's segment for usable_source_words. Where their material is unusable — Theodoret's bare verse-echo at v1, Cyril's displaced blocks at v19 and v20 — the only available course is to leave the voice undeclared and simply not use it. Both remain usable and used as tag voices elsewhere in the chapter, per the corpus convention that maps them to eastern-antiochene.

Note 607's fallback clause exercised twice in one key, and this time the fallback was 'keep it where filed' rather than 'move it'. At v21 both Henry and Calvin write past the verse: Henry's block runs on through vv22-23, treating Tertius the amanuensis, Gaius the host, Erastus the chamberlain and Quartus; Calvin's block is almost entirely the doxology of vv25-27, on the glory ascribed to God alone and the mystery hid for many ages. Neither may move, because the rule requires the source to have a key inside the target span and neither has one: Henry's keys are 1, 17, 21, 25 (none at 22 or 23) and Calvin's are 1, 3-7, 11, 16-21 (none at 25, 26 or 27). Each voice's v21-proper material was used and the displaced remainder left where filed. The practical cost is that the vv25-26 and v27 entries have Gill as their only reformed voice, Calvin being absent from those keys entirely.

Three displacements of the eastern voices, of two different kinds. Theodoret lags by one key: his v1 and v2 blocks are bare verse-echoes and his actual comment on Phebe and Cenchrea — the fine remark that the gospel had filled not the towns only but the villages, and raised there a church great enough to have a woman serving as deaconess — sits under v3, where the quoted lemma is Priscilla and Aquila. That one is recoverable, because Theodoret has keys at v1 and v2 and the entry covering vv2-4 contains v2, so the material was used there. Cyril of Jerusalem is displaced outright twice: his v19 block is catechetical matter on Philippians 4 and Isaiah ('rejoice in the Lord alway... shine, shine, O thou new Jerusalem'), and his v20 block discusses 2 Corinthians 4:4 and whether the god of this world blinded the minds of them that believe not. Neither treats any verse of Romans 16, so neither can move anywhere and both are lost. Only his v18 block is apposite, and it is excellent — godliness consists of pious doctrines and virtuous practice, neither acceptable without the other.

Three reported-voice mentions that a naive ghost check flags as ghosts but that are properly grounded. Chrysostom is named in the prose at entries 1, 15 and 22 although he is not a source voice at those keys — but in each case the naming is a report by a voice that IS a source there, and the report is in that voice's own text: at v1 Calvin grants that Origen and Chrysostom considered Phebe a deaconess; at v16 Calvin cites a homily of Chrysostom showing that Christians kissed before partaking of the Supper and then bestowed alms; at v23 Clarke reports that Chrysostom thought Erastus retained the employment as well as the title. The prose attributes each to the reporting voice, and audit-synthesis-quality reports 0 verses with attributions not groundable in any source corpus. Working rule: a scratch ghost-checker that tests only for the presence of a name should not be trusted to distinguish a false attribution from a reported one.

Entry-count predictor holds at 16/16. romans 16 has 26 source keys and 41,436 usable source words, with five keys over 2000 (v1 5573, v17 4441, v21 4992, v25 3379, v27 2465) and 20,586 words in the remainder: 5 + round(20586/2500) = 5 + 8 = 13, and 13 entries is what the chapter took. Drafting overshoot, thirteen entries measured. First drafts ran 645 to 981 words against the 650 ceiling: mean 838, median 849, i.e. about 29 percent over — the worst of any chapter in this run, and worse than genesis 4's 3-30 percent. Every entry needed between two and ten trim rounds. The pattern is clearest where a key carries many short glosses on proper names AND one long connected argument: entries 12 (vv15-16, first draft 922) and 22 (vv22-23, 922) and 27 (981) all had that shape. The three-paragraphs-of-three-voices rule did not hold here because a salutation chapter gives eight or nine voices a sentence each on the same name, so a paragraph that fairly represents the field runs to five or six voices rather than three. Revised working rule for a name-list chapter: cap each paragraph at FIVE voices and give only two of them more than a clause; where a textual or grammatical dispute occupies a paragraph (Ellicott at v27, the apostles question at vv5-7), count it as three voices' worth and admit no others.

CYRIL OF JERUSALEM IS MIXED IN THIS CHAPTER - the first chapter where that is so, and it changes the shape of the defect. GENUINE at keys 16, 17 and 20, where the Catechetical Lectures expound the very verses: Lect. 11.21 quotes 'whether they be thrones, or dominions, or principalities, or powers' and turns Col 1:16 into a creed silencing three heresies; 11.24 on the Only-begotten as Maker of the world fits 1:17 and quotes 'He is before all, and in Him all things consist'; 13.33 quotes Col 1:20 verbatim, 'made peace through the Blood of His Cross, for things in heaven, and things in earth'. RESIDUE at keys 3, 15 and 18. AND KEYS 15 AND 18 CARRY THE SAME BLOCK, identical once markup is normalised (raw strings differ only in whitespace) - Lect. 13.23, the proof out of the Prophets and the spot of Golgotha, foreign to both 1:15 and 1:18. Key 3 is Lect. 6.29 on blinding the thoughts of them that believe not (2Co 4:4), also foreign. So the Cyril defect is PER-BLOCK, not per-chapter: previously he was wholly genuine (acts 13) or wholly residue (1corinthians 10, luke 18, acts 16). Handled with SILENT_BY_ENTRY for the two entries whose Cyril blocks are residue only; the entry containing key 18 also contains the genuine key 20, so Cyril is named there from the genuine material.

ALSO: TERTULLIAN appears once, at key 1, and is residue. It has no bearing on the Colossian salutation. Declared as RESIDUE. This is the FIRST appearance of Tertullian in any chapter of the run; his school would be latin-fathers.

Live disagreements tiled into the eleven entries. (1) Why Paul asserts his apostleship: Gill makes it partly defensive against teachers who insinuated he was no apostle, where ROBERTSON DENIES ANY ATTACK, holding he describes himself only because he is unknown at Colosse, not as in Galatians - and Calvin argues the same way. (2) What makes a saint: Gill denies birth, baptism (which 'neither takes away sin, nor gives grace') and outward reformation and grounds it in election, imputation and the Spirit; CLARKE DISPOSES OF IT IN FIVE WORDS, 'those who professed Christianity'. (3) Whether the salutation named Christ: Ellicott accepts the shorter text and theologises it as an instinctive reluctance to use any phrase that might seem to distinguish Christ's nature from the Godhead, Robertson accepts it and notes it is the only opening benediction lacking the name, CLARKE JUDGES THE EVIDENCE INSUFFICIENT. (4) What hope is doing in v5: Ellicott insists faith and love are KINDLED BY hope rather than leading to it; Calvin warns against perverting the verse to extol the merits of works. (5) Whether Epaphras founded the church and whether he is Epaphroditus: Barnes denies the founding, Ellicott makes him the first evangelist but calls the identification most unlikely, Clarke reports both, with a version that actually reads the longer name. (6) What knowledge is prayed for: Ellicott presses that it is God's WILL and not speculation as to his nature or as to emanations from Deity; Robertson makes the word the keynote of Paul's reply to a false wisdom - 'the cure for these intellectual upstarts is not ignorance, not obscurantism, but more knowledge of the will of God'. (7) WHETHER 'IMAGE' PROVES WHAT THE FATHERS MADE IT PROVE - the sharpest clash in the chapter, and it is in-chapter: Chrysostom's block argues from the title that no angel is ever called image or son while man is called both, and Calvin's block on the same key answers that the ancients, contending with the Arians, insisted on equality and consubstantiality while omitting the chief point, and calls Chrysostom's stress on the term 'excessively weak', set aside by Paul's own use of the word for man. (8) Whether the creation of v16 is the new creation (Gill's three arguments; Barnes). (9) Whether 'before all things' means dignity or pre-existence. (10) What headship means: Calvin grants the root-and-members metaphor elsewhere but holds Paul here speaks chiefly of GOVERNMENT. (11) Who is the subject of 'it pleased', the word Father being absent from the Greek: four different answers. (12) Why 'the body of his flesh': Ellicott supposes without ascribing polemical intention that the philosophy depreciating the body was in Paul's mind, Robertson says plainly it is against incipient Docetism. (13) What the condition of v23 threatens: Gill's final perseverance, Barnes's flat 'impossible to be saved unless we continue', against Ellicott's 'if, as I presume; if, as I trust' and Robertson's condition assumed fulfilled. (14) What filling up the afflictions of Christ means - five distinct answers. (15) WHICH COMES FIRST, WARNING OR TEACHING: Ellicott makes teaching the instruction of those already warned; WESLEY REVERSES IT OUTRIGHT, 'we teach the ignorant, and admonish them that are already taught'; Robertson divides by subject instead.

The controversy behind the epistle is named by four commentators in three different idioms, and the entries were tiled to keep them together. CYRIL, writing in the fourth century, turns Col 1:16 into a creed and silences three parties with it: 'Silenced be every heresy which brings in different creators and makers of the world; silenced the tongue which blasphemes the Christ the Son of God; let them be silenced who say that the sun is the Christ, for He is the sun's Creator, not the sun which we see. Silenced be they who say that the world is the workmanship of Angels, who wish to steal away the dignity of the Only-begotten.' ROBERTSON names the same target in modern dress at v13 ('a full and final answer to the Gnostic depreciation of Jesus Christ by speculative philosophy and to all modern efforts after a reduced picture of Christ'), at v17 ('the Gnostic philosophy that matter is evil and was created by a remote aeon is thus swept away'), at v19 ('the Gnostics distributed the divine powers among various aeons. Paul gathers them all up in Christ'), at v22 (against incipient Docetism) and at v28 (against 'intellectual exclusiveness'). ELLICOTT names it at v17 (the Demiurgus), v22 (the idea that Jesus Christ had not come in the flesh) and v28 (the speculators in mystic knowledge). CALVIN names no school but describes the mechanism at v12: 'there is nothing that Satan so much endeavors to accomplish as to bring on mists with the view of obscuring Christ, because he knows, that by this means the way is opened up for every kind of falsehood. This, therefore, is the only means of retaining, as well as restoring pure doctrine - to place Christ before the view such as he is with all his blessings.' Other notable single-voice material: Robertson's 'the permanence of the universe rests, then, on Christ far more than on gravity. It is a Christo-centric universe'; his baseball figure at v24, that it is now Paul's turn at the bat, Christ having had his turn, the grandest of all; and 'the preacher is an expert on the word of God by profession'. Wesley's 'power detains reluctant captives, a kingdom cherishes willing subjects', and 'he is the cement, as well as support, of the universe. And is he less than the supreme God?' Cyril's dilemma at v20, that either God in his truth must destroy all men or in his loving-kindness cancel the sentence, and the wisdom of God preserving both. Chrysostom's rule at v15, that where the meanness is great the Scripture boldly asserts the honour but where the nature is higher it forbears.

Progressive through Leviticus 19 and all three distinct - no repetition signature here. Declared via the chapter-wide RESIDUE set; all three entries carry excl=['Jamieson'].

Chrome at the chapter tail, SIXTEENTH confirmation and THIRTEENTH consecutive Ellicott carrier. Ellicott's block at key 26 measures 1036 words, of which 992 are the site nav/footer chrome; the marker is the previous-chapter nav string 'Numbers Num 7 Numbers Num'. Who officiated at the cleansing of the Levites is a flat contradiction between two sources. Ellicott (v5): 'As Moses had already officiated in the consecration of the priests, so now, notwithstanding the fact that Aaron and his sons were already consecrated, he is commanded to officiate at the cleansing of the Levites.' Calvin (v5) makes the opposite one of three ways God checked Levitical presumption: 'by desiring that they should not be initiated by Moses, but by Aaron.' Gill (v7) sides with Calvin: 'the cleansing of the Levites was the work of Aaron, either by himself or by his order.' The text supports both - Moses is the addressee of the imperatives, Aaron the one who waves them in v11 - and the entry states the split rather than resolving it.

Two further live disagreements. (1) The water of purifying: Clarke and Wesley identify it with the water made from the ashes of the red heifer of Num 19 and both conclude the ordinance must have been instituted earlier than it is described, Wesley generalising that 'such kind of transplacings of passages being frequent in scripture'; Ellicott denies that any explanation of the particular water is given, thinks the reference probably to the brazen laver, and notes that the ashes reading would require the sin-offering of v8 to have been sacrificed BEFORE the sprinkling of v7 - a sequence problem the others do not see. (2) The age of entry, 25 here against 30 in ch. 4: Clarke refers to his own earlier reconciliation, Keil argues from the heading and closing formula that this law governs the standing service and so never conflicted, and Ellicott lays out three possibilities (a post-Canaan rule in force until David lowered it to 20; a later direction displaced in the narrative; or lighter duties from 25 and onerous from 30) and settles on none.

Coverage shape of numbers 8. Henry appears at ONLY TWO keys, 1 and 5, but his key-5 block is 2,208 words and covers the whole chapter through v25 - so puritan-evangelical is present in entries 1 and 2 and absent from entries 3-6 by source, not by choice. Keil is capped at 200w at seven keys (6, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 21, 24) and every one of those blocks is majority verse quotation with a sentence or two of real comment at the tail; the cap truncates him mid-word at key 6 ('i.e., in'). Calvin is absent from entries 3 (8-11) entirely. Clarke's chapter-closing block at key 26 (318w) is the longest homiletic excursus in the chapter and is where the Antinomianism warning sits.

Numbers 8 is a rabbinic-citation chapter for Gill: Aben Ezra four times (the tribes mixed before Sinai; the night lamp-lighting; atonement preceding the presentation; the ancient men of v26), Chaskuni once (the doubled 'given' as the twofold giving, first to the Lord then to Aaron), Jarchi twice (the doubled 'given' as the two services of bearing the vessels and of the temple song; the older Levites returning to shutting doors, singing and loading wagons - which Gill rejects as 'too burdensome'), and the anonymous 'wise men' on the age of the bullock. Gill's open dissent from Jarchi is the notable item: he reports the authority and then declines part of it.

Fidelity self-grade, all six entries. Every claim in every entry is traceable to a named block in data/commentary/cow/numbers/8.json; no voice is named who is not present in that entry's span; no school appears in prose that is absent from its tags dict. JFB stride bug, sixteenth confirmation, and the first with an internal duplicate. All three JFB blocks in exodus 20 are commentary on Exodus 8, the plague of frogs: v5 describes the frogs alighting on every vessel of food and the wicker bowls used in Egypt, while v11 and v17 are BYTE-IDENTICAL to each other, both giving the god Ptha represented with a frog's head, Pharaoh's promise to let Israel go if Moses would intercede, and his hardening when he saw there was a respite (Ex 8:15). The donor is Exodus 8 — an EARLIER CHAPTER OF THE SAME BOOK, which fits the revised rule that the donor is an earlier position in the commentary volume (Exodus being long enough that the donor stays inside it, as with acts 23, genesis 50 and genesis 4). None of it treats any verse of Exodus 20, so JFB is unusable at all three keys and is declared in excluded_voices at entries 4, 9 and 17. New sub-observation worth watching: the duplication of one donor block across two different keys means the stride is not always a clean one-to-one displacement.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, ten for ten on voice and position — Ellicott, at v26, the chapter's last commented key — but in a NEW FORM that the earlier nine did not take. Here the boilerplate does not terminate the blob: it is sandwiched inside Ellicott's segment, which runs to 1043 words of which only about fifty are genuine ('Neither shalt thou go up by steps... Thus it would seem that Solomon's altar had steps'). After that comes the full StudyLight site chrome — devotional titles, Site Tools, Manage My Preferences, the copyright block — and then inline JavaScript, a nav-accordion script with vfAccInit and a DOMContentLoaded handler. Genuine Calvin and Wesley text follows AFTER the junk, because Ellicott is not the last voice in this key's segment order. Refinement of the rule: the tail attaches to ELLICOTT's block at the chapter's last commented key, and whether it terminates the blob depends only on whether Ellicott happens to sit last in that key's segment order. Practical consequence: usable_source_words overcounts v26 by roughly a thousand words.

Note 607's fallback clause fired five times in one chapter, the heaviest concentration yet, and the pattern is now clear enough to state as a rule of the harvest. In a chapter whose sections are commandments, the expository voices write one long block per SECTION and file it under the section's first verse, so the block routinely overruns the key it is filed under. Henry does it three times: his v3 block runs through vv4-11 (second, third and fourth commandments), his v12 block through vv13-14, his v22 block through vv24-26. Wesley does it at v3 (running through vv4-6) and at v8 (through vv9-11). Keil does it at v9 (his block is almost entirely the Fifth Word, i.e. v12) and at v14 (running through vv15-18). Of these seven overruns only ONE was recoverable: Keil's altar material, filed at v23 but treating vv24-25, could move because Keil has a key at 25 inside that span — and moving it both improved the entry and removed an exclusion. The other six could not move, because Henry's keys are only 1, 3, 12, 18, 22 and Wesley has none at 4-6 or 9-11, so each voice's section-material stays filed where it is and the overrun is lost. Henry has 5 keys in a 26-key chapter and loses most of his substance this way.

A third Gill defect of the kind noted at romans 16. Gill's v11 block is a bare truncated verse fragment — 'For in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, the sea,' and nothing more, cut off mid-clause with no comment attached. Unlike the romans 16:20 stub this is not a dangling cross-reference but a plain truncation of the lemma itself. Gill's other 25 keys in the chapter are intact and substantial, so this is isolated damage rather than a systematic thinning; the entry covering vv9-11 drew its reformed voice from Gill's v9 and v10 blocks instead.

Entry-count predictor holds at 17/17. exodus 20 has 26 source keys and 45,323 usable source words, with six keys over 2000 (v1 6017, v3 2933, v4 2336, v8 3574, v12 5967, v26 2892) and 21,604 words in the remainder: 6 + round(21604/2500) = 6 + 9 = 15, and 15 entries is what the chapter took. Two keys over 4500 — v1 and v12 — each became its own entry as the tiling rule requires. The chapter has no gaps: all 26 keys are present and consecutive. Worth recording that the predictor survived a chapter where the natural sense-units (the ten commandments) cut across the word budget: the fourth commandment spans vv8-11 but v8 alone is 3574 words, so it had to be split into v8 and vv9-11, and the second spans vv4-6 but had to be split at v5. The predictor is indifferent to sense-units and was right anyway.

Drafting overshoot, fifteen entries measured, and the picture is unchanged from romans 16. First drafts ran 623 to 1053 words against the 650 ceiling: mean 889, median 897, about 37 percent over — worse than romans 16's 29 percent and the worst of the run so far. Only one entry (v2, on a thin 844-word key) came in under the ceiling first time. The five-voices-per-paragraph rule recorded after romans 16 did not help here, because exodus 20 has only eight voices and the problem is different: each commandment attracts a long principled argument from Calvin, a long list of particulars from Clarke, and a long comparative note from Ellicott, so a paragraph with three voices in it is already 300 words. Revised working rule for a law chapter: allow ONE voice per paragraph to run at length and hold the other two to a single clause each; where two voices both argue at length on the same question — Calvin and Clarke on the sabbath's continuing obligation, Ellicott and Calvin on images — give them a paragraph to themselves and admit no third.

JFB stride bug, seventeenth confirmed instance. Both JFB blocks in this chapter are displaced from Exodus 6: the v5 block is the genealogy passage authenticating the descent of Moses and Aaron, and the v11 block is a ten-word fragment on a kinship term ('The Septuagint and Syriac versions render it "his cousin."'). Neither comments on Exodus 18. Both declared in excluded_voices; JFB is unusable in this chapter.

Keil and Delitzsch blocks at v7, v14 and v26 contain nothing but the reproduced KJV text of a run of verses, with no commentary attached. Note 607 fallback fired twice. Henry has only three keys in the chapter (1, 7, 13) and writes one block per section: his v7 block expounds vv7-12 and his v13 block expounds vv13-18. Drafting overshoot again, and worse than at exodus 20: first drafts ran 620-1196 on the QA count against a 650 ceiling, mean about 800. The vv19-23 entry drafted at 1196 and had to be rewritten from scratch rather than trimmed. Cause here is a third pattern, distinct from romans 16 (many voices glossing one name) and exodus 20 (three voices each arguing at length): a single long advice-speech that every voice comments on in full, so Calvin, Ellicott, Clarke and Wesley each supply a complete parallel treatment of the same six clauses. Working rule for advice or speech chapters: pick ONE voice to carry each clause and cite the others only where they differ.

Jamieson stride-6 residue, THIRTY-FIRST consecutive chapter, and the FIRST GAPPED RUN recorded. Chrome, SEVENTEENTH confirmation and FOURTEENTH consecutive Ellicott carrier - and the first time in the run that it lands on a key that is NOT the chapter's last verse. The chrome attaches to Ellicott's LAST block in the chapter, not to the chapter's last key: Ellicott is absent from keys 28 and 29, so his final block is at 27 while the chapter runs to 29. This is decisive confirmation of the rule inferred at joshua 6 - the carrier is the voice's last block, and the coincidence with the chapter's last verse in earlier chapters was incidental. Real usable source for romans 2 is 52,995 words, not the 53,987 the sizer reports.

Romans 2 is the widest-voiced chapter of the run so far: TWELVE distinct voices and all FIVE schools, with three patristic voices all GENUINE and on-passage. Theodoret of Cyrrhus appears at 28 of 29 keys (his commentary on the Pauline epistles), quoting the verse and then commenting - several of his blocks are pure verse quotation with no comment (keys 15, 23, 28). John Chrysostom appears once, at key 17, from Homily V on Romans, exactly on 'thou art called a Jew'. Cyril of Jerusalem appears once, at key 16, from Catechetical Lecture 15 on the judgment of secrets - genuinely apposite to Rom 2:16. This is the FIRST chapter in which Cyril of Jerusalem is genuine at his only key; he has previously been wholly residue (1co 10, luke 18, acts 16) or mixed (colossians 1). Matthew Henry appears at only two keys, 17 and 25, and Albert Barnes and A.T. Robertson appear at nearly every key.

Two textual disagreements that span centuries and are visible inside the sources themselves. (1) v17 'Behold' vs 'But if': Ellicott calls the Authorised reading a corrupt one, a decisive consensus of the best MSS having ei de, and finds the answering clause in the question of v21 with the 'therefore' there merely resumptive. Calvin had seen the same variant and DECLINED it - it would meet his approbation were it generally received, but the greater part of the MSS was then opposed, the whole difference being one letter, and the difficulty with the conditional is that no corresponding clause can be found. Calvin's own block then carries an EDITORIAL SEQUEL correcting him: 'Griesbach has since found a majority of MSS in favor of this reading, and has adopted it.' Wesley prints the conditional. (2) v24, the source of the quotation: Calvin argues for EZEKIEL 36:20 against Isaiah 52:5, on the ground that Isaiah contains no reproofs of the people whereas that chapter of Ezekiel is full of them; Ellicott and Robertson both refer it to the LXX of Isaiah 52:5, Ellicott noting that the original sense concerns the dishonouring of God's name by the enslavement of his people; Wesley's block is the bare Isaiah reference.

Four further live disagreements in romans 2. (1) v6, judgment by works against justification by faith: Ellicott raises the problem explicitly and answers it by distinguishing two elements in Pauline theology and two points of view - the classification of mankind by its fruits, and the individual before his Judge who can claim nothing; Calvin answers it only by denying that reward proves merit, 'an absurd inference'. (2) v12, whether any heathen may be saved: Barnes refuses to soften it, insisting Paul gives no intimation of their salvation and that the apostles evidently believed the great mass would be destroyed; Clarke appeals to the true light that lighteth every man and denies the Gentiles come under the same rule. (3) v16, what the verse connects to: Calvin's block records that Jerome, Chrysostom and Theophylact joined it to v15 while almost all modern critics join it to v12; Barnes and Ellicott take the modern side, Wesley alone keeps the patristic connection. (4) v20, who the 'foolish' and 'babes' are: Wesley and Clarke say they are the GENTILES, these being the titles the Jews commonly gave them; Gill says they are the COMMON PEOPLE AMONG THE JEWS who did not know the law, 'instructor' being the usual title of their own doctors. (5) v26, whether the law-keeping Gentile is real: Gill and Robertson say the case is hypothetical, Clarke takes it as real.

Cross-citation between voices inside the catena, and editorial layers inside single blocks. (a) Barnes at romans 2:2 cites CALVIN BY NAME - 'The design of the apostle here, says Calvin, is to take away the subterfuges of the hypocrite' - the first instance recorded in this run of one catena voice quoting another. (b) Calvin's blocks at 2:8, 2:16, 2:17 and 2:19 each carry a LATER EDITOR'S NOTE embedded in the same block and indistinguishable from Calvin's own text: at 2:8 the editor answers Calvin's complaint of irregularity by invoking Bishop Lowth on Hebrew parallelism and says 'All the anomalies, noticed by Calvin instantly vanish' when the passage is set out in lines; at 2:16 the editor reports the patristic-versus-modern division on what the verse connects to; at 2:17 the editor supplies Griesbach's later manuscript count against Calvin's textual judgement; at 2:19 the editor notes what 'Calvin has pas[sed]' over. Any synthesis of a Calvin block in Romans must treat the block as a composite of Calvin plus a nineteenth-century editor.

Fidelity self-grade, all eight entries. Every claim is traceable to a named block in data/commentary/cow/romans/2.json; no voice is named outside its span; no school appears in prose that is absent from its tags dict. Word counts: 1 = 650; 2-5 = 649; 6-9 = 648; 10-13 = 649; 14-16 = 649; 17-20 = 649; 21-24 = 648; 25-29 = 647. All within the 350-650 window; the tiling covers 1-29 exactly. Jamieson is declared residue chapter-wide and excluded from entries 3, 4 and 7. One lint catch worth recording: entry 5 originally named Chrysostom in reporting Calvin's list of fathers on the connection of 2:16, but Chrysostom's block sits at key 17, outside that span, so the build flagged NAMED BUT NOT SOURCED HERE and the prose was reworded to 'Jerome, Theophylact and other fathers'. The full list is retained in the entry's debate text. The sharpest disagreements - the 'Behold/But if' variant, the Isaiah/Ezekiel attribution, who the 'foolish' are, and whether the law-keeping Gentile is real - are stated as unresolved rather than harmonised.

JFB stride bug, eighteenth confirmed chapter, and the second total case after romans 16. All four JFB blocks in this chapter are displaced from Galatians: v3 and the rest carry Galatians 3:27 and 4:1-16 material (baptism as the toga virilis, the heir under age, Paul's 'be as I am'). None comments on James. All four declared in excluded_voices; JFB is unusable in this chapter.

Cyril of Jerusalem's single block in this chapter, filed at v1, is his catechetical exposition of 2 Corinthians 4:4 on the blinding of unbelievers' thoughts — wholly unrelated to James 2:1. It is NOT declarable in excluded_voices: undeclarable_voices rejects the name, exactly as at romans 16 with Theodoret and Cyril (note 798), because split_voices does not segment his block in this harvest. Left undeclared and unused.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, fifteenth confirmed instance, again attached to Ellicott and again at the chapter's last commented key. Ellicott's genuine note ends with the Alford quotation; the site chrome, CSS and commentary menu follow, inflating usable_source_words for v26 by roughly a thousand words.

Note 607 fallback fired three times. Henry has only three keys in the chapter (1, 8, 14) and writes one block per section: the v1 block runs through v7, the v8 block through v13, and the v14 block through the Paul-James reconciliation. He has no key inside any of those spans, so all three stay in the entries they are filed under. Drafting overshoot, fourth distinct cause. First drafts here ran 640-1050 against the 650 ceiling, mean about 870, roughly 35 percent over. The cause is neither romans 16's many-short-glosses nor exodus 20's three-long-arguments nor exodus 18's parallel-speech pattern: james 2 carries SEVEN voices at every key (Gill, Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson, Barnes, Calvin, Wesley all appear at 20+ of the 26 keys), so even a one-clause mention of each fills a paragraph before any argument is stated. Working rule for a full-bench chapter: name at most FOUR voices per paragraph and let the other three appear elsewhere in the entry, rather than closing each paragraph with a roll-call.

Caught a live ghost in the pre-flight: Ellicott quotes 'the Greek, John the Golden Mouthed' on mercy, and I attributed the passage to Chrysostom by name. Chrysostom has no block in this chapter, so the ghost detector flagged it. Rewritten as 'a Greek father'. General rule: when one commentator quotes a second by an epithet rather than a name, resolving the epithet manufactures a voice the span does not contain.

Jamieson stride-6 residue, THIRTY-SECOND consecutive chapter, and the LONGEST CLEAN RUN yet recorded: keys 2, 8, 14, 20, 26, 32 - offset 2, SIX members, no gap. The previous record was five clean members (acts 16 had seven but with the run reaching the chapter end; colossians 1 had five; romans 2 had three with a gap). Every block is JOHN 14-16 material, the Farewell Discourse, and the run is progressive: the warnings and encouragements just given; unbelief as the root of sin; the Spirit speaking not from himself but what he hears; the joy of the world at not seeing him; the dispensation of the Spirit; and the promise of plainness yet to come. All six distinct - no repetition signature. Declared via the chapter-wide RESIDUE set; six of the eleven entries carry excl=['Jamieson'].

Cyril of Jerusalem residue in acts 15, with the repetition signature, AND a validator collision worth recording. Eight keys - 11, 18, 20, 26, 28, 29, 35, 36 - all Catechetical Lectures 16-17 on the Holy Spirit, none of them commenting on Acts 15. Keys 20, 28 and 29 carry the SAME block (Lect. 16.29, 'This Holy Spirit, who in unison with Father and Son has established the New Covenant'); keys 35 and 36 carry the same block as each other (17.34). Key 28 is the trap: 'it seemed good to the Holy Ghost and to us' looks apposite to a lecture on the Spirit, but the block there is the recycled 16.29, identical to 20 and 29, so the fit is accidental. VALIDATOR COLLISION: declaring him via excluded_voices FAILS validate-synthesis.py five times over, because synthesis_qa.VOICE_LABELS carries the SHORT form 'Cyril' and _LABEL_RE requires a colon immediately after it, so the actual head 'Cyril of Jerusalem:' matches nothing and the validator reports the declared block as absent. He had to be dropped silently instead. This is the SAME VOICE_LABELS defect first recorded nine batches ago; it now blocks a legitimate declaration rather than merely permitting a silent drop.

Chrome, EIGHTEENTH confirmation and FIFTEENTH consecutive Ellicott carrier. Ellicott's block at key 41 measures 1099 words, of which 992 are the site nav/footer chrome; the marker is the previous-chapter nav string 'Acts Act 14 Acts Act'. Genuine Ellicott payload is 107 words. Here the carrier key IS the chapter's last verse, unlike romans 2 where Ellicott's last block fell at 27 while the chapter ran to 29 - which confirms again that the rule is the voice's LAST BLOCK, with coincidence at the chapter end when the voice happens to run that far. Real usable source for acts 15 is 77,559 words, not the 78,551 the sizer reports.

JOHN LIGHTFOOT IS GENUINE AND EXACTLY ON PASSAGE in acts 15 - the first time in this run. Four keys, 7, 16, 17 and 20, each commenting on that very verse: 15:7 'a good while ago' (aph hemeron archaion), read as an allusion to the promise of the keys; 15:16 'I will build again the tabernacle of David', with the rabbinic exchange between Rab Nachman and R. Isaac on when 'Bar Naphli', the son of the fallen, will come; 15:17 'that the residue of men might seek', with the argument that James must have spoken in Hebrew, that is Syriac; 15:20 'that they abstain from pollutions of idols', with the four-fold analysis of the decree and the attack on the Nicolaitans. This directly answers the standing owner item 'Lightfoot off-by-one-chapter and off-by-five-keys': his misalignment is NOT systematic across the corpus. Chapters should be checked individually rather than assumed defective.

The Petrine-primacy thread runs through four entries of acts 15 and is the chapter's dominant polemic, argued from four different facts. (1) v13, the ORDER OF SPEECHES: Chrysostom infers that James was bishop and therefore speaks last; Clarke that he was president of the council and alone pronounced the definitive sentence, which he would not have done had Peter been head; Ellicott that James's position is one of pre-eminence, no one speaking after him; Barnes that the transaction shows Peter had no such authority as the Papists pretend, since otherwise his opinion would have been followed without debate. (2) v14, the TITLE: Clarke notes that James does not give Peter even the title he received from our Lord. (3) v19, the FORMULA 'my sentence is': Clarke and Robertson find real authority in it (Robertson calls James President of the Conference), while Gill and Barnes deny that James assumed any authority to settle the case and Ellicott stands between, allowing the tone while denying a decree. (4) v23, the DRAFTING: Wesley argues that the decree is drawn up according to James's proposal and not Peter's, so the Church of that day had no conception of Peter's primacy. Also live at v13: WHICH JAMES - Barnes says James the Less son of Alpheus, Ellicott says the brother of the Lord, Calvin reports the old writers who make him the disciple surnamed Justus and Oblias.

Five further live disagreements in acts 15. (1) v6, WHO SAT: Clarke and Calvin confine the council to apostles and elders as the lawful judges, Barnes, Gill and Robertson hold the whole church was convened, and Ellicott goes furthest, saying the laity were present and gave their vote and that the right to approve involves the power to reject. (2) v21, WHAT THE MOSES CLAUSE IS FOR: Ellicott, Clarke, Wesley, Barnes and Gill all take it as the reason for writing to Gentiles and not to Jews, who hear the law weekly; Robertson turns it into the reason the four things are named at all; and Calvin says flatly the place 'hath been badly expounded, and drawn into a contrary sense', his own reading being that ceremonies cannot be abolished at the first dash and concord must be redeemed for a time - 'it was meet that the old ceremonies should be buried with some honor'. (3) v28, WHETHER THE DECREE STANDS: Wesley says all four were necessary for that time but the first was repealed by the same Spirit, as 1 Corinthians shows; Clarke says failure to keep them would be sin against the Spirit who commanded them. (4) v34, WHETHER SILAS'S STAYING IS TEXT: Barnes, Clarke, Robertson and Ellicott all reject the verse on manuscript evidence, Ellicott adding that a copyist supplied it to explain v40; Gill alone treats it as text and explains Silas's change of mind. (5) v39, WHOSE THE SHARPNESS WAS: Wesley denies anything in the text implies it was on both sides and says Paul maintained the right with love; Robertson says the son of consolation lost his temper.

Coverage shape of acts 15, the widest chapter of the run by voice count. TWELVE voices, all FIVE schools. Matthew Henry appears at only five keys (1, 6, 7, 22, 36) but with enormous blocks - 2,597, 4,951, 306, 3,892 and 2,893 words - each covering a large stretch of the chapter, so puritan-evangelical is carried by Henry in entries 1, 3, 8 and 10 and by Lightfoot in entries 3, 6 and 7. Chrysostom is genuine at three keys (1, 13, 35), from the Homilies on Acts and exactly on passage. Cyril of Jerusalem is residue at eight. A.T. Robertson and Albert Barnes appear at nearly every key and carry the grammatical-historical school throughout. Notably ABSENT from the whole chapter: Keil, Theodoret, Jamieson as a genuine voice. The chapter also carries the run's densest concentration of named modern scholars inside the blocks - Ramsay, Lightfoot (cited BY Robertson, distinct from the Lightfoot voice), Mill, Griesbach, Westcott and Hort, Hackett, Knobel's successor Milligan - which makes several entries as much a report of nineteenth-century criticism as of the text.

Fidelity self-grade, all eleven entries. Every claim is traceable to a named block in data/commentary/cow/acts/15.json; no voice is named outside its span; no school appears in prose that is absent from its tags dict. Word counts: 1 = 646; 2-5 = 650; 6-7 = 647; 8-10 = 650; 11-14 = 645; 15-19 = 649; 20-21 = 649; 22-24 = 647; 25-30 = 647; 31-36 = 645; 37-41 = 649. All within the 350-650 window; the tiling covers 1-41 exactly. Jamieson is declared residue chapter-wide and excluded from the six entries where he appears. Cyril of Jerusalem is residue too but had to be dropped silently rather than declared, because the validator cannot match the head 'Cyril of Jerusalem:' against its short label 'Cyril' - recorded separately as a source-defect. The chapter's sharpest disagreements - who sat in the council, whether Peter had primacy, what the Moses clause is for, whether Silas's staying is text, and whose the sharpness was in the quarrel - are all stated as unresolved rather than harmonised.

JFB stride bug, nineteenth confirmed chapter. All four JFB blocks here are displaced from Numbers 18 and are the same material repeated: the division of the sacred office between priests and Levites, the Levites given as gifts, the stranger who intrudes put to death, and the priests' perquisites out of the votive offerings. The v2 and v8 blocks are byte-identical, as at exodus 20. None comments on Deuteronomy 7; all four declared in excluded_voices, so JFB is unusable in this chapter.

Note 607 fallback twice. Henry has only two keys in the chapter (1 and 12) and writes one block per section: the v1 block covers vv1-5 and the v12 block runs to the end, taking in vv16 and 25-26. He has no key inside 2-5 or 17-26, so both stay where filed — which means the entry at vv12-16 carries his comment on the graven images of vv25-26. This is now the standard shape for Henry in an OT chapter and no longer worth a separate note unless the recovery clause fires.

No StudyLight boilerplate tail in this chapter: the last commented key (v26) ends with Keil's bare verse text and Gill's note, and Ellicott has no block there at all. That is consistent with the fifteen confirmed instances rather than against them — the tail attaches to Ellicott's block, so where Ellicott does not comment on the chapter's last key there is nothing for it to attach to. Worth recording as the first negative case observed.

JFB stride bug, 20th confirmed instance and the second in Exodus. Both JFB blocks in this chapter are displaced Genesis 46 material: key 6 carries the count of the seventy who went down to Egypt and Stephen's seventy-five, key 12 carries Joseph's chariot going up to meet Jacob and the contrast between chariots and wagons. Neither touches Exodus 7. Both declared in excluded_voices; split_voices segments them, so both are declarable.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, 16th positive instance. Attached to the Ellicott block at v25, the chapter's last commented key, exactly as at romans 16 and james 2 — site chrome, menu CSS and commentary-list text run on after the comment. Deuteronomy 7 supplied the first negative case (no Ellicott block at the last key, no tail); this chapter is the rule again.

Note 607 fallback fired twice. Henry has only keys 1, 8 and 14 in this chapter. His key-8 block treats the magicians of vv10-12, but he has no key inside the 10-13 span, so that material stayed in the vv6-9 entry where it is filed. His key-14 block treats the whole first plague through v21, and again there is no Henry key in 15-18 or 19-21, so the three heads (dreadful, righteous, significant) and the water-into-wine comparison stayed in the v14 entry. Wesley's v10 and v20 blocks are near-verbatim Henry; the shared material was written once, under Henry at v14, and Wesley's distinctive lines (every creature is to us what he makes it; it is sin that turns our waters into blood) carried the vv19-21 entry.

Keil declared excluded at two entries for a different reason from the stride bug. His blocks at keys 15 and 23 are pure verse-text dumps (the AV text of the following verses with no comment attached); the actual exposition sits in his blocks at keys 8, 9 and 14. split_voices segments both, so both are declarable, and both were declared rather than mined for content that is not there.

Drafting overshoot again, cause five. All eight drafts came in 670-840 against the 650 ceiling. Here the driver was neither many short glosses nor voices arguing at length but SOURCE ENUMERATIONS that resist compression: Clarke's ten-plague chronology, his transcribed traveller's encomium on Nile water, Ellicott's catalogue of the Egyptian water system, Clarke's four reasons for permitting the contest. Each is a list whose items are individually cheap and collectively expensive, and trimming prose around them does not help. Working rule: when a block is a list, decide up front how many items the entry can afford and drop the rest at draft time rather than trimming them one word at a time afterwards.

Jamieson stride-6 residue, THIRTY-THIRD consecutive chapter: keys 4, 10, 22, 28 - offset 4, four members, no gap. Repetition signature AT THE HEAD of the run, as at joshua 6: keys 4 and 10 carry the IDENTICAL block (267 words on the position of Reuben's camp and its attendant tribes, Numbers 2 material). Keys 22 and 28 are distinct and later - the consecration of Aaron's four sons (Numbers 3) and the sacrificial sense of the Hebrew for 'bring near' (Numbers 8). So the run repeats its first block once, then advances. Declared via the chapter-wide RESIDUE set; four of the seven entries carry excl=['Jamieson'].

Chrome, NINETEENTH confirmation and SIXTEENTH consecutive Ellicott carrier. Ellicott's block at key 28 measures 1041 words, of which 992 are the site nav/footer chrome; the marker is the previous-chapter nav string 'Numbers Num 22 Numbers Num'. Genuine Ellicott payload is 49 words, on Mount Peor as a peak of the northern Abarim looking over the face of Jeshimon. Ellicott is absent from keys 29 and 30, so key 28 is his LAST block though the chapter runs to 30 - the same pattern as romans 2 and the opposite of acts 15, confirming yet again that the carrier is the voice's last block and not the chapter's last verse. Real usable source for numbers 23 is 22,090 words, not the 23,082 the sizer reports.

Three sharp disagreements in numbers 23, one of them a direct collision between two voices in the catena. (1) v21, 'He hath not beheld iniquity in Jacob' - FOUR incompatible answers. Gill takes it of NON-IMPUTATION: not that there was no sin nor any observed, but that God did not mark it in strict justice. Wesley narrows the term: not such iniquity as in the Canaanites, which God punishes with utter destruction. Clarke calls the passage difficult and offers two escapes, referring the words to the PATRIARCH Jacob rather than the nation ('a nobler character, Abraham excepted, is not to be found in history'), or taking the two Hebrew words in their commoner senses of trouble and afflictive labour, so the verse promises protection rather than pronouncing on character. CALVIN EXPLICITLY REJECTS GILL'S ANSWER: 'Some reply feebly, that it was not seen, because God did not impute it' - his own reading grounds the saying in adoption and sanctifying grace, 'as Jerusalem was the holy city and the royal abode of God, though it was a den of thieves'. (2) v23, 'no enchantment against Jacob': Calvin sets out three readings and prefers the third, that no divination AVAILS AGAINST Israel; Ellicott adopts the FIRST, that there is no augury IN Jacob because they had no need of it, and quotes Hengstenberg applying it to the Church of all ages. Clarke and Gill side with Calvin's third. (3) v22, the reem: Clarke argues at length that no single-horned animal can be meant, since Moses gives Joseph the plural 'horns of a reem', and settles on the rhinoceros or wild bull; Keil simply renders 'buffalo'.

Numbers 23 has an internal structural feature worth recording: the chapter narrates THREE attempts to curse, and the commentators give a DIFFERENT reason for each change of station. The first station is explained by Ellicott and Wesley in flatly contradictory terms - Ellicott renders the place a bare or barren height, since heathen augurs chose elevated places with an extensive prospect, while Wesley says the word 'properly signifies the plain' (v3). The second change (v13) is explained optically: Clarke and Wesley by Balaam's nerve, Henry by the strategy of showing only a despicable part, and CALVIN by the art itself - superstitious persons 'imagine that there is some magical power in the sight, as if the eyes contributed partly to the efficacy of their incantations', which he says profane writers show was a commonly received opinion. The third change (v27) is explained by Gill on a wholly different principle - not the view but the religion of the place: 'if not better for the view of the people, yet a more religious place, on which account the king hoped for success.' Ellicott also tracks Balak's own naming of God across the chapter: JEHOVAH at v17, ELOHIM at v27.

An editorial layer inside a Calvin block, hostile to Calvin himself. At numbers 23:10 the Calvin block carries a note reporting Cornelius a Lapide contrasting the happy deaths of those he deemed righteous with the deaths of those he counted enemies of the Church, and listing CALVIN among the latter: 'Calvin, excruciated, according to Beza, by divers diseases, was in addition preyed upon by lice, as Jerome Bolsec, a physician of Lyons, and formerly his disciple, reports in his Life, ch. 22. Hence observe, that those who persecute the Church, were, by God's just judgment, eaten by worms. Such was the case with Huneric, Herod, Antiochus, the emperors Maximinianus and Arnulphus, and Calvin.' This is the second kind of editorial contamination recorded in Calvin blocks - romans 2 carried a nineteenth-century editor CORRECTING Calvin (Griesbach, Lowth), and numbers 23 carries a Counter-Reformation polemic ATTACKING him, both embedded in the block and typographically indistinguishable from Calvin's own text. Any synthesis of a Calvin block must be read as a composite.

Fidelity self-grade, all seven entries. Every claim is traceable to a named block in data/commentary/cow/numbers/23.json; no voice is named outside its span; no school appears in prose that is absent from its tags dict. Word counts: 1-3 = 650; 4-8 = 647; 9-12 = 650; 13-17 = 648; 18-21 = 650; 22-24 = 649; 25-30 = 586. All within the 350-650 window; the tiling covers 1-30 exactly. The last entry is deliberately shorter because its span carries only 1,504 real source words, the thinnest in the chapter. Jamieson is declared residue chapter-wide and excluded from the four entries where he appears. Matthew Henry supplies puritan-evangelical in entries 1, 3 and 4 only, being present at just three keys (1, 11, 13); entries 5, 6 and 7 therefore carry three schools rather than four, by source and not by choice. The chapter's sharpest disagreements - the iniquity not beheld, the sense of the enchantment clause, the identity of the reem, and whether Balaam went up a height or down to the plain - are stated as unresolved rather than harmonised, and Calvin's explicit dismissal of Gill's answer as feeble is reported as such.

Jamieson stride-6 residue, THIRTY-FOURTH chapter confirmed. Jamieson blocks appear at keys 2 and 26 only, offset 2, on a five-slot skeleton 2/[8]/[14]/[20]/26 -- THREE GAPS, the most heavily gapped run recorded to date (previous worst: romans 2, one gap in four slots). Both blocks are off-passage: key 26 carries a warning against 'the introduction of any heathen superstition or forms of worship different from those which I have appointed', citing Deut 12:32 / Num 15:39 / Matt 15:9, plus a note that the ancient dispensation was 'only a temporary economy' -- i.e. residue from the Numbers 32 / Deuteronomy region, not Joshua 7. Declared in excluded_voices on entries 1-5 and 24-26. The stride-6 pattern now holds across 34 chapters with offsets 0/2/4 observed; gapping is common and is not evidence against the stride.

Chrome tail, TWENTIETH confirmation and SEVENTEENTH CONSECUTIVE Ellicott carrier. Key 24 Ellicott block measures 1465 words, of which the last 992 are the standard chrome boilerplate; genuine Ellicott content is 473 words. As in romans 2 (key 27) and numbers 23 (key 28), the carrier key is NOT the chapter's last verse -- Ellicott has no block at 25 or 26, so the chrome attaches to his LAST block in the chapter, wherever that falls. That rule is now confirmed four times. Chapter reported 27,494 usable source words; real total is 26,502.

EDITORIAL LAYER inside the Calvin block at key 24, third instance recorded and the most extensive. After Calvin's own argument closes ('if they were reprobate, then condemnation could not be premature'), the block continues in a different voice: 'These admirable remarks are well fitted to satisfy every candid mind...' It then names and refutes Grotius for holding that Achan alone died, and quotes-and-mocks the article 'Achan' in the Cyclopaedia of Biblical Literature ('as the writer appears both to have invented it, and to plume himself on the invention'). This is the 19th-century Calvin Translation Society editor, not Calvin, and is typographically indistinguishable from Calvin's text. Compare romans 2 (editor CORRECTING Calvin via Griesbach and Lowth) and numbers 23:10 (a Lapide ATTACKING Calvin). The synthesis attributes to Calvin only what precedes the break.

The chapter's sharpest division is whether Achan's children died with him, and it is a THREE-WAY split with textual evidence on one side only. Clarke (key 25, 705w -- his longest single block in this chapter) argues NO, from the Hebrew pronouns (stoned HIM, burnt THEM, after they had stoned THEM), then canvasses seven witnesses: Vulgate and Septuagint and Syriac and Anglo-Saxon speak only of Achan and his goods, Targum matches the Hebrew, the ARABIC ALONE names the children, and two De Rossi manuscripts read 'him' for 'them'. He concludes 'while Justice required his life, Mercy was extended to the salvation of his soul.' Ellicott argues YES on the logic of herem -- the cattle were not accomplices and perished, so complicity need not be asserted at all -- and says only that Achan's future state 'is in the hands of the Judge who doeth judgment; no mercy to his crime on earth was possible.' Wesley argues YES on three independent grounds including probable complicity ('as the Jewish doctors affirm') and Achan's age (fifth from Judah, so grown children). Calvin argues YES but refuses to justify it, retreating to incomprehensible counsel.

CALVIN'S POSITION SHIFTS WITHIN THE CHAPTER, and he says so himself. At v1 he attempts a real explanation of why the whole nation bore one man's guilt. At v10 he refers back to that discussion and withdraws from it: the judgment of God 'had hidden reasons, into which, though it may perhaps be lawful to inquire soberly, it is not lawful to search with prying curiosity.' At v24, facing the children's deaths, he retreats further still -- 'What here remains for us, but to acknowledge our weakness and submit to his incomprehensible counsel?' Three positions on one question inside one chapter, in order of increasing severity of the case. Separately at v10 he splits the rebuke of Joshua four ways against Clarke (no reprehension at all), Gill (encouragement), and Henry (God called the mourning enough): Calvin says God reprimands not the prostration but the excess, and refers the censure to the FUTURE rather than the past.

SAME PROOF-TEXT, OPPOSITE CONCLUSIONS: at v14 Clarke and Ellicott both appeal to the election of Saul (1 Sam 10:20-21) to settle how Achan was discovered, and reach contrary results. Clarke: 'if the lot was used in the one case it was doubtless used in the other also, as the procedure in the main was entirely similar.' Ellicott: 'The parallel passage -- viz., the selection of King Saul from the tribes of Israel -- shows that the oracle of God was consulted. They inquired, and the Lord answered.' Wesley sides with the lot. Also at this span: Clarke reports Kennicott's collation showing the EXECUTION of the command has 'man by man' twice and drops 'by households', with six Hebrew copies and the Syriac preserving labbottim -- while Keil, facing the same verse, calls the LXX/Vulgate/seven-MSS plural 'a conjecture rather than the original reading', and Wesley harmonises with no emendation at all. Three distinct methods on one corruption.

HENRY'S BLOCK AT KEY 16 IS SECTIONAL, covering vv16-26 (4,014 words, 99 percent of that key). It contains his treatment of the arraignment (v19), confession (vv20-21), conviction (vv22-23), condemnation (v25), execution and the valley of Achor (v26) -- all of which lie OUTSIDE the 14-18 entry that sources it, and none of which is sourced in the 19-23 or 24-26 entries. Consequence for the fidelity rule: Henry may be named only in the 14-18 entry, and only for his on-span material (the lot proceeding gradually, Judah the guilty tribe, Achan's silence). This is the same 'named but not sourced here' trap that fired on romans 2 s14 with Chrysostom. Sectional commentators (Henry especially) need this check on every chapter where their block sits at a section head.

Fidelity self-grade, joshua 7, six entries, all six verse-by-verse checked against the catena. Word counts 650/650/650/649/650/650, all inside the 350-650 window. Tiling 1-5 / 6-9 / 10-13 / 14-18 / 19-23 / 24-26 tiles vv1-26 exactly. Every claim in every entry traces to a block inside that entry's own span: no voice is named outside the span that sources it (checked specifically for Henry, whose sectional block at key 16 discusses vv19-26; his material there is used ONLY in the 14-18 entry and only for on-span content). Jamieson declared in excluded_voices on entries 1 and 6 (keys 2 and 26), both blocks being off-passage residue. No voice attributed a position it does not hold: Clarke's denial that the children died, Ellicott's contrary reading, and Calvin's refusal to justify are each kept distinct. The editorial layer inside the Calvin block at key 24 (Grotius, the Cyclopaedia of Biblical Literature) is attributed to no one. Ellicott's 992-word chrome tail at key 24 was excluded before drafting.

JFB stride bug, 21st confirmed instance — and the first with TWO DIFFERENT DONORS in one chapter. JFB has only two blocks here and neither touches Joshua 7: key 2 carries the allotment of Sihon's territory to Reuben, Gad and half Manasseh (Numbers 32 / Joshua 13 material, Arnon to Gilead, Bashan), while key 26 carries a homily on not adding to or omitting from the appointed forms of worship (Deuteronomy 12:32 / Numbers 15:39). Every earlier case had all displaced blocks drawn from a single donor chapter; this one does not, so the bug is not simply a fixed-offset read into one neighbouring file. Both declared in excluded_voices.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, 17th instance, and it REFINES the rule. Previous cases all landed on the chapter's LAST commented key; here it lands on key 24, with keys 25 and 26 still carrying Gill, Clarke, Wesley and JFB blocks after it. What key 24 is, is Ellicott's LAST block in the chapter (his keys stop at 24). So the correct statement is: the tail attaches to the end of Ellicott's final block, which usually but not always coincides with the chapter's last commented key. The deuteronomy 7 negative case (no Ellicott block at the last key, no tail) fits this refined form exactly.

Note 607 fallback fired twice, both times on Henry, who has only keys 1, 6, 10 and 16 in this chapter. His key-1 block runs on into the sending of the three thousand to Ai (vv2-3), but he has no key inside the 2-5 span, so the culpable-security material stayed in the v1 entry. His key-16 block is far larger: it covers the discovery by lot, the arraignment, the confession and the conviction, i.e. vv16-23, and he has no key in either 17-20 or 21-23, so all of it stayed in the v16 entry. That made v16 a two-voice entry (Gill and Henry only) carrying material the neighbouring entries also treat from other sources — the eye/heart/hiding progression appears under Henry at v16 and under Clarke and Wesley at v21, which is not duplication because the sources are independent, but the two were deliberately written to different emphases (Henry moral, Clarke numbered with the James parallel).

A genuine three-way disagreement worth preserving in the tags: were Achan's children executed? Clarke argues at length from the Hebrew (stoned HIM singular, burned THEM plural), from the versions (only the Arabic names the children; the Latin, Greek and Syriac refer the burning to his goods), from two De Rossi MSS reading the singular, and from Deuteronomy 24:16, that the man alone died and the children were brought out only to see and fear. Ellicott holds all were destroyed together on the herem logic and Joshua 22:20. Wesley defends the execution as just, arguing the children were probably grown and privy. Calvin assumes it and refuses to explain it away. Both entries carry the debate; the Clarke position is filed at v25 where his textual argument sits, and the Ellicott/Wesley positions at v24.

JFB stride bug, 22nd confirmed instance. Both JFB blocks in this chapter are displaced Numbers 31 material — key 12 carries the Midianite war and the seduction at Baal-peor, key 18 the partial destruction of Midian and the tribes absent on their pastoral wanderings. Neither touches Deuteronomy 27. Single donor here, unlike joshua 7 where the two blocks came from different donors. Declared in excluded_voices at the vv12-18 entry.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, 18th instance, on Ellicott at key 26 — which is both the chapter's last commented key and Ellicott's last block, so it fits the refined rule recorded at joshua 7 without discriminating between the two forms.

Gill declared excluded at the v1 entry, and the reason is worth recording because it is a new one. His key-1 block is not displaced and not boilerplate: it is the bare lemma ('And Moses, with the elders of Israel, commanded the people,') with no comment attached at all. Naming him would have meant inventing an attribution, so he was declared excluded instead. undeclarable_voices accepts it, since split_voices does segment the empty block. Distinguish this case in future from the stride bug (wrong content) and from the Keil verse-dump case at exodus 7 (AV text of following verses with no comment): here there is no text at all beyond the catchword.

Jamieson stride-6 residue, THIRTY-FIFTH chapter. Keys 2/8/14/20/26, offset 2, FIVE MEMBERS AND NO GAPS -- the second-longest clean run recorded, after acts 15's six. Every block is 1 Corinthians 15 material: the first-fruits and the Passover-sabbath dating of the resurrection (key 2), the end of the mediatorial kingdom (key 8), Bengel's gradation from those baptized at the point of death (key 14), the folly of denying a fact of revelation because we do not know the how, with Ezekiel 37:3 (key 20), and the suitability of bodies to their species, De Wette and Estius and 'I believe in the resurrection of the flesh' (key 26). Declared in excluded_voices on five of the six entries. Note the irony: the residue is 1 Cor 15 on the resurrection, dropped into a chapter whose central error is that the resurrection is past already -- a topical matcher would find these blocks highly plausible, which is exactly why they must be checked by provenance and not by subject.

Chrome tail, TWENTY-FIRST confirmation and EIGHTEENTH CONSECUTIVE Ellicott carrier. Key 26 Ellicott block measures 1257 words, of which the last 995 are chrome (StudyLight footer, copyright statement, sub-menu CSS, then inline JavaScript); genuine Ellicott is 262 words. Marker string for this chapter: '2 Timothy 2Ti 1 2 Timothy 2Ti'. Carrier is the chapter's last verse here. Chapter reported 36,629 usable source words; real total is 35,634. SEPARATE COINCIDENCE WORTH NOT MISREADING: Adam Clarke's block at the same key 26 is exactly 992 words -- the same length as the chrome measured in joshua 7 and elsewhere -- but it is entirely GENUINE (the Greek of v26, then Wiclif 1378, Coverdale 1535 and other English versions set side by side, then the Korah reading). Length alone is not a chrome test; the marker string is.

PATRISTIC PROVENANCE IS PER-VOICE, NOT PER-CHAPTER: this chapter carries Chrysostom and Cyril of Jerusalem side by side, one genuine and one residue. CHRYSOSTOM (keys 1, 11, 20) is exactly on-passage at all three: the shipwrecked master and the wounded general on 'be strong in the grace' (v1), the objector who asks 'when I live, I die, and when I die, I live?' on the faithful saying (v11), and 'in a great house there are not only vessels of gold and silver' (v20). His Homilies on 2 Timothy are the actual source. CYRIL OF JERUSALEM (keys 2, 8) is Catechetical Lecture material: key 2 is the three children in the furnace and the power of repentance to quench fire, which has nothing to do with committing the deposit to faithful men; key 8 is the argument that the Virgin was of David's family, which shares the phrase 'seed of David' with v8 but is not comment on the verse. Treated as SILENT rather than declared, because of the VOICE_LABELS defect. Taken with the acts 15 finding that Lightfoot was genuine there, the rule is now firm: check each patristic voice in each chapter; neither 'the fathers are always residue' nor the reverse holds.

CHRYSOSTOM AND GILL CONTRADICT EACH OTHER BY NAME on what the great house of v20 is. Chrysostom: 'he speaks not of the Church only, but of the world at large. For think not, I pray, that he means it of the Church' -- he needs the wider reading because he is answering the perplexity why the wicked are suffered to remain undestroyed. Gill, arguing the same verse: 'by this great house, in the application of the simile, is not meant the world, as some think' -- he needs the narrower reading because his point is that it should not distress anyone to find wicked men inside the church. Each states the other's position as the view to be rejected. Clarke, Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Wesley all side with Gill. This is the first recorded instance in the corpus of a Greek father and a Reformed commentator each explicitly naming and rejecting the other's reading of the same figure.

COMFORT OR SEVERITY at v13, 'if we believe not, yet he abideth faithful' -- a five-way split and the sharpest doctrinal division in the chapter. Wesley reads pure comfort: 'though some believe not, God will make good all his promises to them that do believe.' Ellicott denies this in the strongest terms available to him: 'Those who have understood these words as containing soothing, comforting voices for the sinner, for the faithless Christian who has left his first love, are gravely mistaken. The passage is one of distinct severity -- may even be termed one of the sternest in the Book of Life; for it tells how it is impossible even for the pitiful Redeemer to forgive in the future life.' Barnes agrees and turns it against a caricature of his own tradition: 'Let no one then suppose that, because he is elected, he is safe, if he lives in sin... if that were the doctrine of election, it would deserve all the opprobrium that has ever been heaped upon it.' Clarke: 'as true to his threatenings as to his promises.' Gill and Henry hold both senses at once, faithful to the threatening and faithful to the promise. Note that the wesleyan-arminian school is itself split here, Wesley comforting and Clarke threatening.

FOUR METAPHORS FOR ONE WORD at v15, 'rightly dividing' (orthotomeo). (1) Clarke reports the common view, that it alludes to the priests dividing the sacrificial victim down the spine so that half the spinal marrow lay each side of the backbone -- and rejects it flatly: 'probably nothing was much farther from the apostle's thoughts than this view, which is now commonly taken', adding that the scrupulous division was not an original Jewish ordinance. (2) Ellicott: laying out a road (Prov 3:6 LXX) or drawing a furrow. (3) Robertson reports Theodoret for the furrow and Parry for a stone mason cutting stones straight, then offers (4) his own: 'Since Paul was a tent-maker and knew how to cut straight the rough camel-hair cloth, why not let that be the metaphor? Certainly plenty of exegesis is crooked enough (crazy-quilt patterns) to call for careful cutting to set it straight.' Separately Ellicott resists Alford and Huther-Meyer, who held the sense of cutting was already lost by Paul's day, as 'premature', granting only that Clement of Alexandria uses the noun for orthodoxy in the third century, and suggesting Paul's own use gave the word a fresh starting-point.

Gill 200-word cap fires FIVE TIMES in this chapter, at keys 7, 8, 13, 19 and 20 -- each block truncated mid-sentence at exactly 202 words including the head. Examples: key 13 breaks at 'and his salvation is an everlasting and unchangeable one; nor'; key 19 at 'this stands sure upon t'; key 20 at 'and is a very large one, and f'. Keil-and-Delitzsch blocks show the same 200-word cap in OT chapters, so the defect is source-wide and not voice-specific. Standing owner item: a re-fetch of the capped tree. In this chapter the cap cost real content -- Gill's completion of the great-house argument at key 20 is exactly where he denies the world-reading that Chrysostom asserts, and the sentence is cut off mid-clause.

Fidelity self-grade, 2timothy 2, six entries, every verse checked against the catena. Word counts 650/650/650/634/650/650, all inside the 350-650 window. Tiling 1-2 / 3-7 / 8-13 / 14-18 / 19-21 / 22-26 tiles vv1-26 exactly. Ten voices appear in the chapter (Chrysostom, Cyril of Jerusalem, Gill, Henry, Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson, Calvin, Wesley, Jamieson); every claim traces to a block inside its own entry's span. Two sectional-block traps were checked explicitly: Henry's key-1 block covers vv1-7, so he is named in the 1-2 entry only for v1-2 material and NOT in the 3-7 entry, where his block is not sourced; Calvin appears only at key 1 and so is named only in the first entry. Jamieson declared in excluded_voices on entries 1, 8, 14, 19 and 22 (keys 2/8/14/20/26), all 1 Corinthians 15 residue. Cyril of Jerusalem dropped silently at keys 2 and 8, since the VOICE_LABELS short form makes a correct declaration impossible. Ellicott's 995-word chrome tail at key 26 was excluded before drafting; Clarke's coincidentally 992-word block at the same key is genuine and was used.

JFB stride bug, 23rd confirmed instance. All three JFB blocks in this chapter are displaced Deuteronomy 27 / Joshua 8 material — key 9 on whether the stones carried the Decalogue or the blessings and curses, key 15 on the unhewn stones and the peace offerings, key 21 on the tribes ranged on Gerizim and Ebal with the ceremony of Amen. None touches Judges 7. Single donor, like deuteronomy 27 and unlike joshua 7. Worth noting for whoever tracks this: the donor here is the very chapter landed in the previous batch, so the same displaced text has now been seen from both ends — as the target in deuteronomy 27 and as the intruder here. Declared in excluded_voices at the vv9-15 and vv20-22 entries.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, 19th instance, on Ellicott at key 25 — the chapter's last key and also Ellicott's last block, so it fits the refined rule from joshua 7 without discriminating between its two forms.

Two disagreements worth preserving in the tags. (1) The water test: were the 300 lappers the brave or the timid? Josephus and Theodoret make the kneelers brave and the lappers cowards, Theodoret finding the divine aid precisely in God's choosing the most fearful; Ben Gersom and Ellicott read the lappers as the self-controlled; Keil states flatly they were not the cowardly or indolent; Gill sets both readings side by side and declines to decide. (2) The war-cry at v18: the word for 'sword' is absent from the Hebrew here though present at v20. Clarke holds it genuine, citing the Chaldee, Syriac, Arabic and eight collated MSS; Ellicott holds it better omitted, the phrase being literally 'for Jehovah and for Gideon'; Henry independently reads it without the word.

Note 607 fallback fired once, and one near-duplication was avoided. Henry has keys 1, 9, 16 and 23; his key-1 block runs on into the reduction of the army at vv2-3, and since he has no key inside the 2-8 span that material stayed in the v1 entry, which is why entry 1 carries the whole winnowing. Separately, Wesley is not a voice in this chapter at all, so the usual Henry/Wesley near-verbatim overlap did not arise; but Henry's key-16 block and Ellicott's key-16 note both describe the men being shown what to do at the signal, and these were deliberately given different emphases (Henry christological, Ellicott mechanical) rather than merged.

JFB stride bug, 24th confirmed instance, and a new variant of the repeat pattern. All three JFB blocks in this chapter are displaced Numbers 6 Nazarite material, so the donor is single. Keys 18 and 24 are BYTE-IDENTICAL to each other (the definition of a Nazarite, the three abstinences from wine, the razor and the dead body, with the reasons); key 30 is a DIFFERENT portion of the same donor chapter (cutting the hair at the end of a limited vow, bringing it to the sanctuary door, the wave of the shoulder and the cake). Previous cases were either all-identical (exodus 20, deuteronomy 7) or all-distinct (romans 16, james 2); this is the first partial repeat — two identical plus one distinct, all from one donor. Key 30 has no other voice at all, so excluding JFB leaves it empty and the vv30-31 entry rests on key 31 alone.
