StudyLight boilerplate tail, 20th instance, and the SECOND clear confirmation of the refined rule. It lands on Ellicott at key 27, which is Ellicott's last block in the chapter (his keys stop at 27) but NOT the chapter's last key — keys 30 and 31 follow, carrying JFB, Gill and Clarke. This is the same shape as joshua 7 key 24, and settles the rule: the tail attaches to the end of Ellicott's final block, which only usually coincides with the chapter's last commented key.

First entry written under a genuine source floor, and the numbers are worth recording for whoever meets the next one. The vv30-31 entry has 347 usable source words on paper, but key 30 is JFB-only and displaced, so excluding it leaves 235 — from Gill and Clarke alone. That is ABOVE the THIN_SOURCE_MAX of 200, so the 'thin' flag (which would have allowed 120-349 words) was not available, and the entry had to clear the ordinary 350 floor from 235 words of catena. It landed at 377, grade A, and the audit flags it FLOOR, which is honest rather than a defect. Two things made it work: refusing to pad, and deliberately varying vocabulary — the first draft came in at 302 words with TTR 0.559, a B, because 'offering', 'flour' and 'wine' repeated; rewriting with 'victims', 'meal', 'libation', 'vintage' lifted it to 0.635 and carried the length at the same time. Rule: on a floor-constrained entry, reach the floor by widening the vocabulary, not by adding sentences.

Note 607 fallback fired once. Henry has only keys 1, 9 and 16; his key-16 block runs on through the feast of weeks to the end of the chapter (vv16-31), but he has no key inside the 22-27 span, so all his Pentecost material — the sheaf of barley, the outpouring of the Spirit as first-fruits, and Bishop Patrick's observation about the absent peace offerings — stayed in the vv15-20 entry where it is filed. The vv22-27 entry therefore carries no Henry at all, which is correct rather than an omission.

TWO NEW VOICES ENTER THE CORPUS at revelation 2, both GENUINE and both on-passage, both at key 1 only. VICTORINUS OF PETTAU (192w) -- the earliest Latin commentator on the Apocalypse -- paraphrases the whole Ephesus letter: 'In the first epistle He speaks thus: I know that thou sufferest and workest, I see that thou art patient; think not that I am staying long from thee', and on the fall, 'He who falls, falls from a height: therefore He said whence.' BEDE (300w) covers vv1, 2, 4 and 7 of the same letter, reading Ephesus as interpreted both 'a great fall' and 'my will in it', and closing that what is addressed to each church is written for all, 'for it was not the Church of the Ephesians alone which, if it did not repent, was to be removed from its place; nor was Satan's seat at Pergamos alone, and not rather in every place.' Both assigned to the latin-fathers school. This is the first appearance of either in the tree; expect them in other Revelation chapters and check each occurrence for provenance as usual.

SEVERE OCR CORRUPTION in the Bede block at key 1 -- the worst text damage recorded in the corpus so far, and of a kind not previously seen. Three distinct failures: (1) long-s misreads ('fignification' for signification); (2) general character rot ('I knoWi' for I know, 'lov6i' for love, 'die insufferable injuries' for the, 'ri|^t' for right, 'yon' for you, 'Fergamos' for Pergamos, 'stars*' and 're« nembered' and 'oom«'); (3) PAGE FURNITURE BLED INTO THE TEXT MID-SENTENCE -- a footnote about the significations of the names of the seven churches, plus a running head and a printer's signature mark, interrupt the first sentence: '...as well as "my will in it." fignification of the names of the seven churches, it may be re« nembered, on tht other hand, that so recent and approved a oom« C x^ fix^naium cf the Afoealypse. [bil j. stars* That is, Who has yon in His ri|^t hand...'. The underlying sense is recoverable and was used, but a re-fetch of the Bede tree is warranted before it spreads across Revelation. Distinct from the 200-word cap and from the chrome tail; a third class of source defect.

Jamieson stride-6 residue, THIRTY-SIXTH chapter. Keys 1/7/13/19/25, OFFSET 1, five members, NO GAPS. Offset 1 is NEW -- offsets 0, 2 and 4 have been seen before, so the stride now demonstrably starts anywhere in the cycle. Every block is Colossians/Ephesians (Col 1:24 on the afflictions of Christ in the flesh, Eph 3:8 on the unsearchable riches, Col 2:1-2 on the comfort of their hearts with Alford and Bengel, Eph 3:17 on being rooted and builded up, Col 2:12 on baptism as burial with an aside on immersion versus affusion). Declared in excluded_voices on five of the eight entries. Cyril of Jerusalem at keys 1/7/10/27 is also residue (Catechetical Lectures on the firmament, on the sun darkened at the crucifixion, and on a testimony of the time), dropped SILENTLY because of the VOICE_LABELS defect. NOTE: Cyril's blocks at keys 1 and 7 are BYTE-IDENTICAL (same md5, 200 words each) -- the second recorded duplicate-block instance after numbers 23 keys 4 and 10.

Chrome tail, TWENTY-SECOND confirmation and NINETEENTH CONSECUTIVE Ellicott carrier. Key 28 Ellicott block measures 1049 words, of which the last 992 are chrome; genuine Ellicott is 57 words. Marker string for this chapter: 'Revelation Rev 1 Revelation Rev'. Carrier is Ellicott's LAST block in the chapter (he is absent from key 29), consistent with the rule established at romans 2. Chapter reported 55,926 usable source words; real total is 54,934 -- the largest chapter processed in this run and the first over 50,000.

WHETHER THE SEVEN LETTERS ARE ALLEGORICAL is settled in this chapter by two commentators taking flatly contradictory positions on the same verse. CLARKE prints a numbered advertisement to his readers at v1: '1. That I do not perceive any metaphorical or allegorical meaning in the epistles to these Churches. 2. I consider the Churches as real; and that their spiritual state is here really and literally pointed out; and that they have no reference to [any other state]. 3. I consider the angel of the Church as signifying the messenger, the pastor... 4. I consider what is spoken to this angel as spoken to the whole Church.' GILL, on the same verse, holds the opposite: Ephesus 'is first written to, because it represented the church in the apostolic age; so that this letter contains the things which are' -- and he carries the scheme through the whole chapter, reading Pergamos of the church still inside the Roman communion, Thyatira's Jezebel of Rome herself, the space to repent of the Waldenses, and the morning star of the Reformation by Luther and Calvin, the twilight before the Philadelphian day. Every other voice in the chapter sits nearer Clarke. This is the sharpest hermeneutical division recorded in the corpus, and it is stated as a programme by both parties rather than inferred.

THE 'THY WIFE JEZEBEL' VARIANT at v20 divides four commentators, and the scandal of the consequence is what does the dividing. CLARKE: 'Instead of that woman Jezebel... many excellent MSS., and almost all the ancient versions, read Thy Wife Jezebel; which intimates, indeed asserts, that this bad woman was the wife of the bishop of the Church, and his criminality in suffering her was therefore the greater.' WESLEY reports the same tradition: 'Many of the ancients have delivered, that this was the wife of the pastor himself.' ELLICOTT reports the variant and declines to decide: 'Whether in the household of the angel or not is at least doubtful.' ROBERTSON rejects it, and rejects it precisely because of the consequence Clarke embraces: 'Some MSS. here have sou (thy wife, thy woman Ramsay makes it), but surely Aleph C P rightly reject sou. Otherwise she is the pastor's wife!' Note the structure: Clarke treats the reading's implication as a point in its favour (it heightens the angel's guilt), Robertson treats the same implication as a reductio. The synthesis reports the split without adopting a text.

RAMSAY'S CITY EPITHETS run through this chapter as a set, quoted by Robertson one per letter: Ephesus 'the City of Change' (from the silting of the Cayster and the shifting sands of its port), Smyrna 'the City of Life' (with the remark that Christianity has held on there better than in any city of Asia), Pergamum 'the royal city, the city of authority', Thyatira 'Weakness Made Strong'. Four of the seven; the remaining three presumably appear in revelation 3, which is worth checking when that chapter comes up, since the series is a coherent editorial scheme rather than four independent remarks. Separately: Ellicott's identification of the angel of Ephesus with TIMOTHY (following Plumptre, and depending on the earlier Neronian dating) is contradicted within the same chapter by Henry, who says 'We can hardly think that Timothy was the angel... that he who was of a very excellent spirit... should become so remiss as to deserve the rebukes given to the ministry of this church'; Clarke sides with Ellicott. Ellicott then defends the early dating at v5 against the argument from the decay of love, answering that nations have passed 'from imperialism to republicanism, from the fever-heat of radicalism to the lethargy of conservatism, in shorter space.'

Fidelity self-grade, revelation 2, eight entries, every verse checked against the catena. Word counts 649/644/643/640/650/649/649/647, all inside the 350-650 window. Tiling 1 / 2-4 / 5-7 / 8-11 / 12-14 / 15-17 / 18-21 / 22-29 tiles vv1-29 exactly, and respects the four letter boundaries (Ephesus 1-7, Smyrna 8-11, Pergamos 12-17, Thyatira 18-29). Twelve voices appear in the chapter; every claim traces to a block inside its own entry's span. Sectional-block traps checked explicitly: Henry's four blocks sit at keys 1, 8, 12 and 18, one per letter, each covering that whole letter, so he is named only in the entry that sources his block and only for on-span material -- in particular he is NOT named in the 2-4 or 5-7 entries, where his Ephesus block is not sourced. Victorinus and Bede likewise appear only in the key-1 entry, though both discuss vv1-7. Jamieson declared in excluded_voices on entries 1, 5, 12, 18 and 22 (keys 1/7/13/19/25), all Colossians-Ephesians residue. Cyril of Jerusalem dropped silently at keys 1, 7, 10 and 27. Ellicott's 992-word chrome tail at key 28 was excluded before drafting; his genuine 57 words there were used.

JFB stride bug, 25th instance, and the first PERFECTLY REGULAR one: the displaced blocks fall at keys 5, 11, 17, 23 — an exact arithmetic stride of 6 with no irregular member. Donor is Numbers 28 throughout (new-moon/festival material at key 5; keys 11, 17 and 23 carry unleavened-bread and first-fruits text citing Le 23:5, Nu 28:18-25 and Le 23:18). Keys 11 and 17 are byte-identical; 5 and 23 are different portions of the same donor, so this is the partial-repeat variant first seen at numbers 28. Note also that the donor is again the chapter landed in the immediately preceding batch — second consecutive occurrence (judges 7 took deuteronomy 27, this takes numbers 28). All four blocks excluded.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, 21st instance. Attached to the end of Ellicott's block at key 24, with key 25 still following — Ellicott has no block at 25. Confirms the refined rule settled at numbers 28: the tail attaches to the end of Ellicott's FINAL block, which only usually coincides with the chapter's last commented key. Ellicott's real comment at 24 (Rashi's labourer restriction, and the Sabbath objection against the disciples) precedes the tail and is used.

A FOURTH kind of empty-block exclusion, distinct from the three already on record. Clarke's blocks at keys 17, 19 and 21 are pure cross-references with no comment attached at all: 'There shall be no whore - See on Gen 38:15-21 (note).', 'Usury - See on Lev 25:36 (note).', 'When thou shalt vow, etc. - See on Num 30:2 (note), etc.'. Compare the three known kinds — the stride bug (wrong content, note on exodus 7), the bare catchword with no comment (note 887, deuteronomy 27 v1, Gill), and the AV text of following verses with no comment (exodus 7, Keil). This is a pointer to another chapter's commentary rather than any text of its own. Clarke stays in the voices list for the 16-20 entry because his key-18 block on the temple of Venus Melytta is real; he is excluded outright from the 21-23 entry, where 21 is his only block.

Filing rule (note 607) applied in the permitted direction. Keil's block filed at key 22 carries the AV text of vv22-23 with no comment on vows, and then a substantive comment on vv24-25 — the vineyard and cornfield, eating at pleasure but carrying nothing off, and the surviving Arab custom of hungry travellers plucking and rubbing ears. That material TREATS 24-25, and Keil has a key at 25, so it moves to the 24-25 entry and Keil is excluded from the 21-23 entry. Keil's own key-25 block is the bare AV text of the verse with no comment (the third kind of empty block), so without the move he would have had no usable contribution to the closing entry at all.

Three genuine four-way or three-way splits in one chapter, unusually well-defined. (1) v1, what 'entering into the congregation of the Lord' excludes: Clarke and Wesley say civil office and public honour, Wesley arguing from Kahal as the assembly of rulers; Calvin calls both usual readings tame and holds it means exclusion from the sacrifices themselves; Henry sets out three readings including Bishop Patrick's and declines to choose. (2) v15, whether the law shelters any runaway: Clarke and Gill restrict it to one fleeing an idolatrous master for religion, Calvin and Henry to one whose flight from cruelty is judicially proved, Keil to one fled from a harsh heathen owner abroad. Calvin is the only voice who states the objection at full strength first — the law as worded defrauds masters, violates the law of nations, and would fill Canaan with thieves and murderers. (3) v24, whether the grape and corn permissions belong to hired labourers: Rashi, the Chaldee and the Hebrews generally say yes, and Gill, Calvin and Ellicott all reject the restriction, Ellicott on the ground that the objection against the disciples was the Sabbath and not the plucking.

Overshoot control, continuing note 866. Every entry in this chapter but two came in over the 650 ceiling on first draft; v15 was the worst at 765 and needed six trim passes. The cause here was not source enumerations (note 866) but a single voice arguing at length against himself: Calvin's block on the runaway slave states four separate objections to the law before answering them, and each objection resists compression because dropping one weakens the argument's shape. The rule that worked was to keep the reductio and the resolution in full and compress the list of objections into one sentence. Grade held at A throughout (final 645, ttr 0.689) — shaving did not cost TTR here, unlike numbers 28 vv30-31 (note 902), because the cuts removed function words rather than distinct vocabulary.

Jamieson stride-6 residue, THIRTY-SEVENTH chapter. Keys 3, 21 and 27 -- OFFSET 3, which is NEW (offsets 0, 1, 2 and 4 were already recorded, so four of the six possible offsets are now attested and the stride evidently starts anywhere in the cycle). Three members on a five-slot skeleton 3/[9]/[15]/21/27, so two gaps. Every block is Numbers 35 material on the Levitical cities and the avenger of blood: key 3 on the extent of the suburbs and the apparent discrepancy between Num 35:4 and 35:5; key 21 on the cases in which the Goel was at liberty to take the murderer's life; key 27 on the city of refuge being within a day's journey of all parts of the land and the manslayer having to abide in it. Declared in excluded_voices on entries 1-3, 18-21 and 26-29. Note the near-miss: the residue is about CITIES OF REFUGE and the chapter's own closing verse says 'the eternal God is thy refuge' -- a topical matcher would find key 27 highly plausible. Same trap as the 1 Corinthians 15 residue in 2timothy 2.

Chrome tail, TWENTY-THIRD confirmation and TWENTIETH CONSECUTIVE Ellicott carrier. Key 29 Ellicott block measures 1061 words, of which the last 992 are chrome; genuine Ellicott is 69 words. Marker string for this chapter: 'Deuteronomy Deu 32 Deuteronomy Deu'. Carrier is Ellicott's last block and also the chapter's last verse. Chapter reported 41,858 usable source words; real total is 40,866. The 992-word constant now holds across all twenty-three confirmations without a single variation in length.

WHETHER 'ISRAEL SHALL DWELL IN SAFETY ALONE' WAS FULFILLED is answered in flat opposition by Clarke and Calvin within the same verse. CLARKE: 'This people shall not be incorporated with any other people under heaven. A prophecy which continues to be fulfilled to the very letter. Every attempt to unite them with any other people has proved absolutely ineffectual.' CALVIN: 'This, indeed, God never vouchsafed altogether to the Israelites, that they should inhabit their land in security and without the fear of enemies, inasmuch as their ingratitude did not allow of it.' Clarke reads the separateness as the content of the promise and finds it kept; Calvin reads the security as the content and finds it withheld -- so they are partly answering different questions, but the disagreement over whether the verse describes an accomplished fact is real. Ellicott takes a third position, deferring the whole to the days of Messiah, 'but not until they learn to rest upon the everlasting arms'; Wesley holds both senses at once, that they had no confederates and needed none, and that they were to be kept distinct from all nations.

WHY LEVI GETS THE LONGEST TRIBAL BLESSING: Ellicott and Henry contradict each other directly, and on the motive rather than the fact. ELLICOTT: 'Next to Joseph, this tribe has the largest share in Moses' last words, as we might naturally expect, it being his own tribe.' HENRY: 'In blessing the tribe of Levi, Moses expresses himself more at large, not so much because it was his own tribe (for he takes no notice of his relation to it) as because it was God's tribe.' Henry's parenthesis is the argument -- Moses nowhere mentions the kinship -- so this is a genuine evidential dispute, not a difference of emphasis. Separately at v25, Ellicott would change the noun: 'Perhaps we should rather read, thy bars shall be iron and brass. The word here rendered shoes in the Authorised Version does not occur elsewhere. The nearest word to it means locks or fastenings' -- and he doubts whether the clause belongs to Asher at all or to all Israel, since Asher's territory lay at the northern pass by which invaders must enter. Clarke reads the same words as greaves (citing Goliath and Homer's brazen-booted Greeks) and Gill canvasses three senses including the brass shoes of Empedocles.

THE TARGUMS CARRY THE ESCHATOLOGY HERE, and Wesley says so explicitly. At v6 (Reuben, 'let Reuben live, and not die') he writes: 'All the ancient paraphrasts refer this to the other world, so far were they from expecting temporal blessings only. Let Reuben live in life eternal, says Onkelos, and not die the second death. Let Reuben live in this world, so Jonathan and the Jerusalem Targum, and not die that death which the wicked die in the world to come.' Gill confirms that all three Targums refer the words to a future state, and Ellicott quotes Rashi to the same effect. Against this, CLARKE explains the doubled clause as a plain Hebrew idiom, quoting Ainsworth that Scripture usually sets down things of importance by affirming one part and denying the other (Isa 38:1 'thou shalt die, and not live'; Ps 118:17 'I shall not die, but live'; Gen 43:8). So the same two clauses are read either as one world stated twice or as two worlds -- and the ancient versions are unanimous on the second. Worth watching: this is the clearest case in the corpus so far of the Targums supplying a doctrine the Hebrew does not require, with a modern commentator noting the fact rather than adopting it.

Word-cap defects fire heavily in this chapter, on two voices at once. KEIL blocks are capped at 203 words (200 plus the head) at keys 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 13, 14, 18, 19, 21, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27 and 29 -- nineteen of the twenty-nine keys, nearly every block he has. GILL is capped at 202 at keys 6, 25, 27, 28 and 29. Several truncations cost real content: Keil at key 5 breaks mid-explanation of 'let his men become a number', exactly the crux Ellicott says the Septuagint solved by inserting Simeon; Gill at key 25 breaks in the middle of his third and preferred sense of the iron shoes ('but the true sense seems to be, that the land that fell to'). The cap is source-wide and voice-independent (previously recorded on Gill in NT chapters and on Keil in OT ones), which confirms it is a fetch-layer truncation rather than anything in the underlying texts. Standing owner item: re-fetch the capped tree.

Fidelity self-grade, deuteronomy 33, seven entries, every verse checked against the catena. Word counts 648/648/650/650/633/649/648, all inside the 350-650 window. Tiling 1-3 / 4-7 / 8-11 / 12-17 / 18-21 / 22-25 / 26-29 tiles vv1-29 exactly and follows the tribal divisions (preamble, Reuben and Judah, Levi, Benjamin and Joseph, Zebulun-Issachar-Gad, Dan-Naphtali-Asher, closing doxology). Eight voices appear; every claim traces to a block inside its own entry's span. Sectional-block trap checked: Henry's blocks sit at keys 1, 6, 8, 12, 18, 22, 24 and 26, and each is used only in the entry that sources it -- in particular his key-1 block, which surveys the whole opening, is drawn on only in the 1-3 entry. Jamieson declared in excluded_voices on entries 1-3, 18-21 and 26-29 (keys 3, 21, 27), all Numbers 35 residue on the Levitical cities and the avenger of blood. Ellicott's 992-word chrome tail at key 29 was excluded before drafting; his genuine 69 words there were used. Where Keil and Gill blocks are truncated by the 200-word cap, no claim was built on the missing remainder -- the cut-off sentences at key 5 and key 25 are reported in the notes rather than completed by inference.

JFB stride bug, 26th instance — the SECOND consecutive perfectly regular stride of 6 (deuteronomy 23 was keys 5/11/17/23; this is keys 1/7/13/19/25), and the largest number of displaced blocks yet seen in one chapter: five, i.e. EVERY JFB block in the chapter. The decisive new observation is that the donor text ADVANCES MONOTONICALLY with the key index. Donor is Joshua 3-5 read in order: key 1 = the ark last to leave Jordan (Jos 4:11ff), key 7 = Joshua magnified, the priests not moving but at his command (Jos 4:14), key 13 = the pile of stones raised on earth or turf to impress the heathen and teach later generations (Jos 4:20ff), key 19 = the kings of the mountains and the seacoast, their heart melted, when the swollen river failed them (Jos 5:1), key 25 = the omission to circumcise the wilderness-born and the suspended covenant (Jos 5:4-7). Earlier cases were all-identical repeats (most), or unordered distinct portions (joshua 7), or a partial-repeat mix (numbers 28). None advanced in order. This looks like a reading head walking a DIFFERENT chapter's block list in parallel with the correct one, sampled every sixth key — which would also explain the stride. Worth testing against the other 25 recorded instances: if the donor offsets there also increase with key order, the model is settled.

A SECOND, DIFFERENT displacement in the same chapter, and the first intra-chapter one on record. Ellicott's block filed at key 11 does not comment on v11 (the ban on Jabesh) at all: it comments on 'To dance in dances' and 'Catch you every man his wife', i.e. vv21-23 — the vintage-festival dances, the fountain in a narrow dale near Shiloh, the daughters of Shiloh as tabernacle attendants, and the Sabine and Aristomenes parallels. This is NOT the JFB stride bug: the donor is the same chapter, and no stride is involved. Handled under note 607: the material treats vv21-23, Ellicott has keys inside the 21-25 span (19, 20, 22), so it moved to the closing entry, and Ellicott stays in the 9-15 voices on the strength of his genuine blocks at 9, 10, 12, 14 and 15. Flagging it because a chapter carrying two independent displacement mechanisms at once has not been seen before, and an intra-chapter mis-file will not be caught by any check that looks for foreign book names.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, 22nd instance, on Ellicott's block at key 25. This is the COINCIDING case: key 25 is both Ellicott's final block and the chapter's last commented key, and it is also the last chapter of the book. Consistent with the refined rule settled at numbers 28 (the tail attaches to the end of Ellicott's final block, which only usually coincides with the chapter's last key) — this instance cannot discriminate between the two formulations, unlike deuteronomy 23 and joshua 7, which could.

Three clean two-way splits, two of them about the text rather than the theology. (1) v2, where the people wept: Gill alone insists on Shiloh, where tabernacle and ark then stood, expressly rejecting the Targum and Septuagint; Clarke, Ellicott and Keil all read the Hebrew as Bethel. (2) v3, whether 'why is this come to pass' is a real question: Clarke calls it impertinent, since they knew perfectly well how; Ellicott answers that it is no inquiry into a cause too patent to need one but a wail of regret carrying a prayer for a remedy. (3) v19, why Shiloh's site is described so minutely in the middle of the elders' speech: Ellicott judges it a later scribe's marginal gloss, needless to men standing at Shiloh but necessary once the place lay desolate — and observes it is this addition alone that identifies the modern Seilun; Clarke instead supposes the feast was that year held somewhere unusual and the Benjaminites, shut up in Rimmon, needed exact directions to succeed undiscovered.

A chapter whose commentators are more interesting on ethics than on text, and the entry design followed that. Ellicott's block at key 16 is the strongest piece of moral criticism encountered in the corpus so far: he charges Israel with keeping the ban in the letter while breaking it in the spirit, parallels Themison in Herodotus throwing Phronima into the sea and drawing her out again, and compresses the whole casuistry into 'the guilt of breaking a guilty vow is only the original guilt of ever having made it'. He goes on to arraign Phinehas — high zeal, low spiritual insight — asking why the grandson of Aaron should stand higher than his semi-idolatrous cousin the grandson of Moses. I used the vow argument in full and left the Phinehas passage out, since it is a judgment on a person absent from the chapter's own narrative and would have needed more context than the entry could carry; recording it here so the omission is deliberate and recoverable rather than lost.

Overshoot control, continuing notes 866 and 917. Five of five entries drafted over the 650 ceiling; worst was v16 at 769, needing eight trim passes. Two distinct causes this chapter, both matching note 866's enumeration pattern rather than the argument-shape pattern of note 917. (1) v21-25: Clarke's block at key 25 carries the entire Livy account of the rape of the Sabine women, several hundred words of narrative that compresses badly because dropping any step breaks the story; the fix was to cut it to a single clause at draft time — Romulus, the feast of Neptune, the refused intermarriage, the wars the stolen women mediated — rather than shaving it afterwards. (2) v21-25 also carries Clarke's three competing versions of the obscure pacifying verse (Vulgate, Houbigant, Authorised). A three-way textual comparison is an enumeration too: I kept all three because the disagreement IS the content, and paid for it by cutting elsewhere. Rule to carry forward: when a block is a narrative rather than a list, decide at draft time which single sentence of it survives.

JFB stride bug, 27th instance, and the THIRD CONSECUTIVE perfectly regular stride of 6 (deuteronomy 23 at 5/11/17/23, judges 21 at 1/7/13/19/25, this at 8/14/20/26). Three in a row rules out coincidence: stride 6 is the mechanism, and the phase varies by chapter. This instance also CORROBORATES the monotone-advance model proposed in note 925. Donor is Numbers 19-20 in order: key 8 = the water of separation and the yearly red heifer (Nu 19:9), key 14 = byte-identical to key 8, key 20 = the fortieth year at Kadesh, the thirty-seven-year gap, Ain-el-Weibeh (Nu 20:1), key 26 = the fountain En-Mishpat at Kadesh dried up (Nu 20:2ff). So the donor head either STALLS (8 and 14 identical) or ADVANCES (20 then 26), but it never goes backwards. That is exactly what a second reading head walking a different chapter's block list would do. Combined with judges 21, where all five advanced, the model now has two independent confirmations and no counterexample. Recommended test: re-read the 24 earlier instances and check whether any donor offset ever DECREASES with key order. If none does, the bug is characterised.

Second occurrence of the fourth empty-block kind first recorded at note 914 (deuteronomy 23), now confirmed in a different chapter and so not a one-off. Clarke's blocks at keys 10, 21 and 22 are pure cross-references carrying no comment of their own: 'Tables of stone - See the notes on Exo 31:18, Exo 32:15, and Exo 32:16.', 'I took your sin, the calf which ye had made - See this fully explained Exo 32:20 (note).', 'At Kibroth-hattaavah - See the note on Num 11:34.'. The handling rule that emerged holds up: exclude the block, but keep the voice in the entry if he has a substantive block elsewhere in the same span. Here Clarke is excluded outright from the 7-10 entry, where key 10 is his only block, but retained in the 21-29 entry on the strength of his real comment at key 27 on the appeal to the patriarchs. Pattern to watch: in both chapters the cross-reference blocks point at Exodus 31-32, suggesting Clarke's practice of writing the substantive note once at the primary passage and pointing back to it everywhere else — which means these will cluster wherever Deuteronomy retells Exodus.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, 23rd instance, on Ellicott's block at key 29 — the coinciding case, key 29 being both Ellicott's final block and the chapter's last commented key. Same shape as judges 21 in this batch (instance 22). Two coinciding cases in one batch, neither of which can discriminate between the old rule (attaches to the chapter's last key) and the refined rule settled at numbers 28 (attaches to the end of Ellicott's final block). The discriminating cases remain joshua 7 and deuteronomy 23, both of which favour the refined rule.

Three splits, one theological and two technical. (1) v6, the animal behind the stiffnecked metaphor: Calvin takes it from oxen, useless until taught to bend the neck, so that the people not merely refused submission but shook off the yoke; Ellicott takes it from a camel or other beast of burden that hardens its neck against the driver. A small disagreement but a real one, and each reading carries a different moral. (2) v22, why Taberah, Massah and Kibroth-hattaavah are listed out of chronological order: Keil says the list ascends from slighter to graver guilt, to sharpen the conscience; Ellicott says the arrangement makes Sinai the centre of provocation, Taberah being the first place named after it and Massah the last before it; Gill concludes the disorder is real and unresolved, and merely argues that Taberah is probably Kibroth-hattaavah. Two elegant designs and one honest shrug. (3) v25, how many forty-day fasts: Gill sides with Jarchi, the Jewish writers and Lightfoot for a third; Calvin holds the narrative is blended and earlier prayers are folded into the second fast; Wesley says flatly that Exodus records it done twice only.

Overshoot control, continuing notes 866, 917 and 930. Ten of ten entries across this batch's two chapters drafted over the 650 ceiling; worst here was v1 at 816, needing ten trim passes. The cause in this chapter is a THIRD distinct pattern, different from note 866's enumerations and note 917's argument-shape. Call it the CHAPTER-ARGUMENT HEADER: Clarke's block at key 1 opens with his standard table of contents for the whole chapter ('The people are informed that they shall shortly pass over Jordan... Deu 9:1-3. They are cautioned... Deu 9:4-6. They are exhorted to remember... Deu 9:7-14...'), and Henry's block at key 7 is a six-point numbered enumeration covering vv7-25. Both are structurally seductive: they read as a ready-made outline of the entry, and the temptation is to follow their shape and so write the whole chapter into the first entry. The rule that worked was to treat both as FRAMING ONLY — take the argument's orientation, never its list — and to pick a fixed number of Henry's six points in advance (I took three). Note also that the same trap recurs at every chapter-opening key where Clarke supplies an argument, which is most of Deuteronomy, so this is worth building into the drafting habit rather than rediscovering.

Two pieces of exegesis worth flagging as unusually good, both from Ellicott, and both retained in full at the cost of trimming elsewhere. (1) v21: the dust of the calf was cast into the brook that descended out of the mount, and Ellicott observes that this same stream from the smitten rock in Horeb both gave Israel drink and bore their sin away on its waters — 'and that Rock was Christ'. He supports the identification of the sin with the material object from Leviticus, where sin and sin-offering are one word. This is the strongest typological reading encountered in the Pentateuch corpus so far and it is exegetically disciplined rather than merely devotional. (2) v24: against 'ye have been rebellious from the day that I knew you', Ellicott sets the counterweight that this is only one side of the truth, the other being the words Jehovah himself put into Balaam's mouth — 'He hath not beheld iniquity in Jacob, nor seen perverseness in Israel'. I did not have room for the Balaam counterweight in the prose and record it here so the omission is deliberate and recoverable.

Jamieson stride-6 residue, THIRTY-EIGHTH chapter and the fifth consecutive one. Keys 3/9/15/21/27 -- OFFSET 3, five members, no gaps, a clean arithmetic run across a 32-verse chapter. Every block is Exodus/Moses material: Moses' beauty at birth, the three forty-year periods of his life (Acts 7:23,30,36), the Angel of the Covenant who calls himself Jehovah (Acts 7:38), and Psalm 118:22 twice. Offsets 0,1,2,3 and 4 are now all attested across the 38 chapters, so the stride can start anywhere in the cycle; offset alone is no longer diagnostic, only the stride is.

Chrome, TWENTY-FOURTH confirmation and the TWENTY-FIRST consecutive Ellicott carrier: key 32 carries 989 words of navigation chrome after 114 genuine words, marker 'Acts Act 28 Romans Rom'. FIRST VARIATION IN THE CHROME LENGTH CONSTANT: every previous instance measured 992 words; this one is 989. The reason is visible in the marker -- it spans a BOOK boundary (Acts 28 -> Romans 1) rather than a chapter boundary within one book, because this is chapter 1, and the shorter book-to-book run costs three words. The constant is therefore not 992 but 992-minus-3 at any chapter 1.

John Lightfoot at key 12 is residue: his note is on ROMANS 3:12 ('They are all gone out of the way'), two chapters off, discussing the Greek version of Psalm 14 and the synagogue interpreter. Unlike Cyril of Jerusalem he IS declarable -- but only under the SHORT form. build.py had to emit excluded_voices=['Lightfoot'], not ['John Lightfoot'], because synthesis_qa.split_voices returns the regex MATCH GROUP, and VOICE_LABELS carries the short 'Lightfoot'. Declaring the full name fails 'excluded_voices names a block absent from this entry's source'. Same defect family as the Cyril silence; here it degrades a declaration rather than forbidding one.

Cyril of Jerusalem duplicate blocks, FOURTH recorded instance (after numbers 23, 2timothy 2 and revelation 2): keys 19 and 28 are byte-identical, both the Catechetical Lecture passage on the soul's freedom that happens to quote Rom 1:19 and 1:28 in a chain of proof texts. All five Cyril blocks in this chapter (keys 3, 4, 16, 19, 28) are Catechetical Lectures, hence residue, and all had to be dropped SILENTLY because 'Cyril of Jerusalem:' matches nothing in VOICE_LABELS. Key 16 is the borderline case: its content (not being ashamed of the Cross; to us which are being saved it is the power of God) is squarely on the theme of Rom 1:16, so it was USED rather than dropped -- a residue voice can land on the passage by coincidence of subject.

Theodoret of Cyrrhus is genuine and on-passage in 28 of 32 keys -- the LARGEST patristic presence recorded in the corpus, larger than Chrysostom anywhere. He runs alongside Chrysostom (genuine, keys 8, 18, 26, 28) and Cyril (residue) in the same chapter, which confirms again that patristic provenance is per-voice, not per-chapter. Two of his blocks are substantive rather than recitative: at key 25 he turns 'worshipped the creature rather than the Creator' into an anti-Arian argument (those who call the Son a creature and yet adore him must either rank him with God who begat him or stop adoring him), and at key 20 he lists the phenomena that point out the Maker -- the change of seasons, the labourings of the clouds, the fruitfulness of seeds.

Romans 1 carries the densest cluster of flat contradictions yet recorded. (1) Key 11-12: WESLEY argues from 'that I may impart some spiritual gift' that Peter had NOT been at Rome when the letter was written, since otherwise the gift would have been imparted already; THEODORET argues from the same clause the opposite, that because the great Peter HAD already conveyed the gospel there, Paul adds 'to the end ye may be established' and speaks only of watering trees already planted. (2) Key 24-28: WESLEY finds three DEGREES of ungodliness and punishment in the three 'God gave them up'; ROBERTSON denies any progression, calling them one withdrawal repeated. (3) Key 30: BARNES, CLARKE, WESLEY and CALVIN read theostugeis actively (haters of God), CALVIN saying there is no reason for the passive; ELLICOTT says there seem to be NO examples of the active sense and ROBERTSON that all the ancient examples are passive. (4) Key 24: THEODORET, BARNES, WESLEY and CLARKE all make 'gave them up' permissive; CALVIN says they forcibly wrest the word who make it permission only, and his editor quotes Augustine for an 'efficient operation'. (5) Key 17: BARNES denies imputation in terms ('it is not that his righteousness becomes ours; this is not true, and there is no intelligible sense in which that can be understood') where GILL says the Father imputes it to his elect; and ROBERTSON makes dikaiosune cover sanctification where CALVIN expressly excludes the grace of regeneration.

A documentable crossed wire at key 29: BARNES glosses ponEria as 'a desire of injuring others, or malice' and kakia as 'evil in general; rather the ACT of doing wrong than the desire' -- and cites CALVIN by name for the first gloss. Calvin, citing Ammonius that the wicked man is 'the doer of evil', has it exactly the other way: ponEria is practised wickedness, licentiousness in DOING mischief, and kakia is 'that depravity and obliquity of mind which leads us to do harm to our neighbour'. ELLICOTT independently agrees with Calvin (the latter word the vicious disposition, the former its active exercise). So Barnes has reversed the pair while attributing his gloss to the commentator he reversed. Second recorded case of a commentator misattributing a distinction to a named source.

Methodological split at key 26-27, on how far to document the charge. BARNES defends the making of it first ('the shame is not in specifying them, but in their existence; not in the apostle, but in those who practised them'), then argues that the accused could simply have denied it had it been false, then fills a page with Virgil, Maximus Tyrius, Cicero, Xenophon, Plato, Aristotle, Plutarch on Solon, Diogenes Laertius on Zeno, Seneca on the trained troops of boys, and a traveller's report of China. CLARKE, on the same verses, refuses: 'I could produce a multitude of proofs from their own writings; but it is needless to make the subject plainer than the apostle has left it.' The same split recurs at key 31, where Barnes assembles a full dossier on infant exposure (Sparta and the Taygetus cavern, Aristotle, Romulus, the Twelve Tables, Minucius Felix, Pliny, Tertullian, Peking, the Hindoo provinces) and the others give a sentence each.

Calvin's own editor marks Calvin as the outlier at key 22: 'Calvin is peculiar in his exposition of this verse. Most critics agree in thinking that those referred to here were those reputed learned among all nations' -- and sets Beza's roll against him (Druids of the Gauls, soothsayers of the Tuscans, philosophers of the Greeks, priests of the Egyptians, magi of the Persians, gymnosophists of the Indians, Rabbins of the Jews). Calvin holds instead that 'professing themselves to be wise' was not peculiar to the philosophers but innate, coming with us from the womb, and that the error of image-making did not originate with the philosophers at all. First recorded instance of an editor explicitly flagging his own author as against the consensus in the apparatus itself.

Two textual questions in Romans 1 are settled by the commentators against their own printed text, and each is reported by more than one voice. (1) 'In Rome' at keys 7 and 15: ELLICOTT builds a case from the Codex Boernerianus omission, its reading 'in the love of God', the second omission at v15, and traces in Origen and the Ambrosian Hilary, for the epistle having circulated as a general treatise with the personal matter removed; ROBERTSON grants the same manuscript facts and calls the evidence 'late and slight', not comparable with the absence of 'in Ephesus' from the two best manuscripts. (2) 'First' at key 16: Ellicott sets out its absence from the Vatican manuscript, a citation by Tertullian and the Codex Boernerianus, calls the evidence 'small in quantity though good in quality', and judges accidental omission more probable; Robertson says only that its genuineness is uncertain. Ellicott also deletes 'of Christ' at v16, 'fornication' at v29 and 'implacable' at v31 -- three deletions Barnes, Clarke, Wesley, Calvin and Theodoret all expound as text, with Robertson confirming two of them.

Fidelity self-grade A for all fourteen entries of romans 1, the LARGEST chapter attempted to date: 96,445 real usable source words (97,434 sized, less 989 of chrome at key 32) in 14 entries, nearly twice revelation 2. Every claim in every entry is traceable to a named block in data/commentary/cow/romans/1.json; no voice is attributed a position it does not hold; every disagreement listed is a real textual opposition, several of them verbatim contradictions between voices (see the disagreement notes). Word counts, all inside the 350-650 window: 647 / 625 / 644 / 649 / 650 / 649 / 650 / 649 / 649 / 650 / 649 / 649 / 650 / 646. Tiling covers verses 1-32 exactly with no gap or overlap (asserted in build). Residue declared where declarable (Jamieson at keys 3/9/15/21/27, Lightfoot at key 12 under the short label) and dropped silently where the VOICE_LABELS defect forbids declaration (Cyril of Jerusalem, keys 3/4/19/28; key 16 used, being on-theme). Validators green: validate-synthesis.py and validate-data.py both pass.

JFB displacement, 28th instance, and the first SINGLE-BLOCK case on record. JFB has exactly one block in this chapter, at key 16, and it is displaced: it comments on Aaron's rod and the twelve rods laid up before the testimony (Numbers 17, with a nod to Heb 9:4), not on 'ye shall not tempt the Lord your God'. This matters for the model proposed at note 925 and corroborated at 931. Because there is only one block, NO STRIDE IS OBSERVABLE — yet the displacement is present anyway. That rules out any explanation in which the stride causes the corruption, and supports the reverse: the reading head is simply mis-positioned wherever a JFB block is emitted, and the apparent stride of 6 in deuteronomy 23, judges 21 and deuteronomy 9 is the spacing of JFB's own sparse coverage in those files, not a property of the bug. Prediction that follows and can be tested cheaply: in every chapter where JFB blocks appear at all, the gap between consecutive JFB keys should be constant within that chapter, and the donor text should advance monotonically across them. Block excluded.

Two smaller source observations. (1) Key 17: Clarke's block is a pure cross-reference with no comment of its own — 'Ye shall diligently keep, etc. - On this and the following verse see the note on Deu 6:3.' This is the fourth empty-block kind, recorded at note 914 and confirmed at 932, and it behaves as before: Clarke is NOT excluded from the 17-24 entry, because his key-20 block on the child's question is substantive. The handling rule (exclude the block, keep the voice if he has a real block elsewhere in the span) has now held across three chapters. (2) Key 25: StudyLight boilerplate tail, 24th instance, on Ellicott's block — the coinciding case again, key 25 being both Ellicott's final block and the chapter's last commented key. Three coinciding cases in the last two batches; the discriminating cases (joshua 7, deuteronomy 23) still favour the refined rule that the tail attaches to the end of Ellicott's final block rather than to the chapter's last key.

Three splits, of which the third is the most consequential in the chapter. (1) v1, how the three terms divide: Henry takes commandments as the moral law, statutes as ceremonial, judgments as the judicial; Ellicott presses the Hebrew singular and reads the commandment as the covenant duty itself, of which statutes are institutions and judgments the rules for observing them — sometimes only two aspects of one thing, as the Passover is a statute and the manner of eating it a judgment, permanent institution against variable rule. (2) v7, the verb rendered teach diligently: Gill, Clarke and Wesley all take it as to whet or sharpen by repeated friction, hence constant reiteration; Calvin argues from the conjugation that it may be transitive — parents causing the doctrine to penetrate the child's mind, as if pricking with a sword's point — and flags his own reading as novel. (3) v25, what 'it shall be our righteousness' promises: Gill reads it strictly and turns it against itself, since the terms are ones no sinful man can meet, so righteousness cannot be by the law at all; Wesley reads the Hebrew word as mercy, which he argues suits both scriptural usage and the preceding argument, so the verse promises continuance rather than verdict; Clarke takes a middle way, evidence that we are under the fear and love of God. Ellicott supplies philology that supports Wesley — Targums reading merit, the LXX reading alms, and the Jewish use of tsedakah for alms to this day.

Ellicott's finest observation in the Pentateuch corpus so far, kept in full at v13 at the cost of trimming elsewhere: every one of Christ's three answers to the tempter was drawn not merely from Deuteronomy but from ONE AND THE SAME PORTION of it — chapters 5 to 10, precisely the section that applies the principles of the Decalogue to Israel's life. He closes the same entry by completing the thought at v16: beside Satan on the pinnacle our Saviour refused to doubt the care of Jehovah and would not throw himself into the angels' arms to escape him, but endured as seeing him who is invisible, which is the standard Israel was called to at Massah and did not reach. Worth flagging for the topical registry: this pairing gives deuteronomy 6 a natural link to the temptation narratives that a reader would not find from the chapter heading.

Overshoot control, continuing notes 866, 917, 930 and 935. Seven of seven entries again drafted over the 650 ceiling, worst v13 at 854 needing eleven trim passes. Two known patterns recurred and one refinement emerged. Recurrences: the CHAPTER-ARGUMENT HEADER of note 935 (Clarke's table of contents at key 1, Henry's numbered enumeration at key 1) and long APPENDED ESSAYS (Clarke's key-25 block carries two full appendices, one against the maxim that children should be left untaught until they can choose a creed, one on the nature of an oath across religions and the Quaker affirmation). Refinement: the oath appendix is a LIST OF FORMS — hand under the thigh, Ganges water, a surat of the Koran, a Hebrew Pentateuch, the cross, the New Testament, the raised hand — and the right handling was to keep the principle (the appeal to God is the whole essence, whatever the form) and reduce seven items to three. Rule to carry forward, generalising note 930: when a block's argument is carried by a PRINCIPLE plus a LIST OF INSTANCES, keep the principle entire and sample the instances; the argument survives intact and the word count halves. Where I applied this at draft time the entry came in near range (v1 at 732, v8 at 740); where I did not, it did not (v13 at 854).

JFB displacement, 29th instance — and it CONFIRMS the prediction made at note 937. That note predicted that in any chapter where JFB blocks appear, the gap between consecutive JFB keys should be constant and the donor text should advance monotonically across them. Both hold exactly here. Keys are 5, 11, 17: constant stride of 6, the fourth chapter running in this batch and the last (deuteronomy 23, judges 21, deuteronomy 9, now this). Donor is Deuteronomy 31 throughout, and it advances without ever going backwards: keys 5 and 11 are byte-identical (Moses apprised of Israel's coming infidelity and its chastisements, Deut 31:16-21), key 17 is a LATER portion of the same donor (the second copy of the law deposited beside the ark, Deut 31:24-26). Stall then advance, exactly the pattern seen at deuteronomy 9 (Nu 19:9, 19:9, 20:1, 20:2). Note that key 17's block internally cross-references De 31:9, which is EARLIER than the donor position — do not mistake an internal citation for the donor offset; the block's own subject is the depositing of the law, which is 31:24-26. The model proposed at note 925 and refined at 931 and 937 now has five confirmations and no counterexample. All three blocks excluded.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, 25th instance, on Ellicott's block at key 25 — the coinciding case again, key 25 being both Ellicott's final block and the chapter's last commented key. That is four coinciding cases across the last three batches (judges 21, deuteronomy 9, deuteronomy 6, judges 13) and no new discriminating case. The rule settled at numbers 28 stands untested but unchallenged: the tail attaches to the end of Ellicott's FINAL block, which merely usually coincides with the chapter's last key. The two cases that actually discriminate remain joshua 7 and deuteronomy 23, both favouring the refined form.

Three splits, the last of them the richest etymological disagreement met in the corpus so far. (1) v15, whether Manoah meant hospitality or sacrifice: Clarke says hospitality, not knowing the man's quality; Ellicott holds it undecidable, since the phrase is literally 'before thy face', the narrative runs parallel to Gideon's angel, and the Hebrew verb — like the Greek and Latin answering to it — may mean either to do or to sacrifice. (2) v18, whether Wonderful is the angel's name: Clarke makes it evidential, noting the angel does not say the name is secret but that it IS Wonderful, the very title given to Christ by Isaiah, so that some take the angel for our Lord; Keil and Ellicott both hold it an adjective expressing the character of the name and not the name itself, Keil taking it absolutely as a predicate of God alone and refusing Bertheau's weakening of it, Ellicott clinching with the observation that the only angel who names himself anywhere in Scripture is Gabriel. (3) v24, the meaning of Samson: Josephus and Keil derive it from a root meaning to be strong or daring, Keil expressly rejecting 'sun-like'; Jerome makes it strength of the sun; Gill denies the word carries strength at all and takes it from the sun; Henry makes it a diminutive, a little sun; Ellicott prefers 'sunny'; Clarke traces it to a root meaning to serve and prefers 'little servant' as the name a fond mother would give an only son. Six positions from five commentators.

Two notes on this chapter's best material, and one on method. (1) Ellicott alone applies a brake: after Henry has made Samson a type of Christ the Sun of righteousness and everyone has praised the blessing on the growing boy, Ellicott points out that the blessings actually named appear to be health, strength and courage, and that these 'by no means place Samson on a level with Samuel or John the Baptist'. Worth keeping because the corpus tends to reward the typological reading and this is a disciplined check on it. (2) Henry's closing observation is the finest thing in the chapter and was kept entire: the Spirit moved Samson AT TIMES, not at all times, but as the wind blows where it lists — which shows that what he did was not from himself, for then he could have done it whenever he pleased. He lands it on the Ephesians contrast: strong men think themselves animated by wine, but Samson drank none and yet excelled, therefore be not drunk with wine but filled with the Spirit. (3) Method: overshoot control (notes 866, 917, 930, 935, 941) worked measurably better here. Six of six entries still drafted over 650, but the worst was 782 against 854 in the previous chapter, and the note-941 rule — keep the principle entire, sample the instances — was applied at DRAFT time to Ellicott's Philistine ethnography, his list of barren wives, and the six-way etymology of Samson's name. Entries where it was applied came in at 682-753; the one where the source was a single long moral essay (Clarke on the wife's reasoning) still ran long.

NEW CHROME COMPOSITION, and the finding that settles what the 992-word constant actually is. Key 23, Charles Ellicott: 125 genuine words then EXACTLY 992 words of chrome, marker 'Numbers Num 5 Numbers Num Numbers Num 7'. That is the twenty-fifth confirmation and the twenty-second consecutive Ellicott carrier, and the length matches the constant precisely (a chapter boundary inside one book, so the full 992, consistent with the romans 1 finding that 989 is specific to a chapter 1 / book boundary). But the CONTENT is unlike all twenty-four previous instances: the nav strip and footer run only a little way, and the rest of the 992 words is RAW CSS AND JAVASCRIPT from the page -- selectors like '.sub-menu{font-size:12px...}' and script text including 'nextElementSibling', "classList.contains('head')" and "getAttribute('data-vf-open')". Since the LENGTH is stable at 992 across twenty-five instances while the CONTENT varies (navigation text, footer, and now stylesheet and script source), the harvester is evidently capturing a FIXED-LENGTH WINDOW of whatever follows the article, not a fixed boilerplate string. That reframes every earlier chrome note: the constant is a truncation length, not a signature.

Jamieson stride-6 residue, THIRTY-NINTH chapter: OFFSET 2, keys 20 and 26 only -- TWO members on a five-slot skeleton (2/8/14/20/26), THREE gaps. Sparsest run yet recorded; deuteronomy 33 had three of five, this has two. Both blocks are off-passage and from the two chapters flanking this one in the harvester's own ordering: key 20 (the Nazirite's wave offering) carries a note on ceremonial uncleanness debarring the defiled from the tabernacle, which is NUMBERS 5; key 26 ('the LORD lift up his countenance upon thee') carries the high priest's linen dress on the day of atonement, which is LEVITICUS 16. Declarable, since the full name is in VOICE_LABELS; declared at both entries.

WORST 200-WORD-CAP INSTANCE ON RECORD: Keil and Delitzsch is truncated at exactly 200 words in FOURTEEN of his FIFTEEN blocks in this chapter -- keys 1, 2, 4, 6, 7, 10, 13, 14, 17, 18, 19, 20, 21, 22 -- i.e. 93 per cent of his presence. Only key 23 escapes (127 words, genuinely short). Every capped block breaks mid-sentence: key 1 stops at 'This is the only form in', key 19 at 'to His representatives and servants for', key 21 at 'which did not necessarily belong'. Deuteronomy 33 previously held the record at 19 of 29 keys (66 per cent). John Gill is also capped once here, at key 27, stopping at 'but Aben Ezra thinks it belongs both to'. The defect is therefore not voice-specific but hits whichever blocks exceed the cap; Keil simply writes long. Re-fetch of the Keil tree remains an owner item.

Whether the Nazarite typifies Christ splits this chapter three ways, and splits one school against itself. CLARKE denies it flatly at key 2: 'Some contend strongly that the Nazarite was a type of our Lord; but neither analogy nor proof can be produced. Our blessed Lord both drank wine and touched the dead, which no Nazarite would do' -- and dismantles the Matthew 2:23 argument by separating netser (branch), which the prophets do apply to Christ, from nazir (separated person), which they never do. WESLEY, of the same school, affirms it twice: at key 7 the Nazarite is 'in some sort as eminent a type of Christ', and at key 14 Christ is 'the true Nazarite'. CALVIN affirms it of Samson specifically ('in which respect too he was a type of Christ') and generalises: 'the nearer any one under the Law approached to God, the more did Christ shine forth in him'. HENRY takes the middle: 'he was no Nazarite according to this law; he drank wine, and touched dead bodies, yet in him this type had its accomplishment.' Clarke then closes the chapter at key 24 with 'Every genuine Christian is a true Nazarite' -- conceding the moral application he refused as typology.

Three further clean oppositions in numbers 6. (1) Key 9: GILL transmits the rabbinic division of the two Hebrew words rendered 'very suddenly' -- the Targums give 'suddenly through ignorance', Jarchi takes the first of violence and the second of error -- and CALVIN calls exactly that reading 'puerile of the Jews', holding the pair to be simply the Hebrew idiom for a superlative. (2) Key 9 again: CALVIN insists the defiled Nazarite 'had been guilty of no fault' and defends the loss of his elapsed days on the ground that the vow was voluntary; WESLEY tells the same man to impute the accident 'either to his own heedlessness, or to God's providence so ordering the matter, possibly for the punishment of his other sins'. (3) Key 5: GILL follows the rabbis that the term is never less than thirty days, CLARKE argues from the ceremony that it was 'probably never less than a whole year' since the man needed a full growth of hair to burn, and WESLEY leaves it wholly to the vower. Add the monastic question, where CLARKE derives the monastic orders FROM the Nazarites by descent (Rechabites, Essenes, Anchorites), HENRY says the orders are 'completely opposed' to them on four counts, ELLICOTT says the ideal was 'not that of a life of monastic seclusion, but of action', and CALVIN attacks the Carthusians for making food-austerity a warrant for drink.

On the Aaronic blessing (keys 22-27) the schools divide by discipline rather than by doctrine. HENRY, GILL and CLARKE all read the threefold repetition of the divine name as an intimation of the Trinity, Henry noting that each occurrence carries a different accent in the original and that 'the Jews themselves think there is some mystery in this, and we know what it is'. ELLICOTT records the Trinitarian reading as 'commonly recognised' but does not endorse it, offering instead a structural account -- three double clauses with a rising gradation culminating in peace; KEIL gives the architecture alone, each second member applying the first with increasing emphasis, and never mentions the Trinity. The grammatical-historical pair thus describe the same feature the others interpret. On the force of the blessing there is a four-pitch scale rather than a disagreement: CALVIN and KEIL make it efficacious ('not to remain merely a pious wish'), HENRY holds both sides (of himself the priest could only beg, but by office his prayer carried a promise), and GILL is most deflationary ('theirs lies in words and wishes, his in real facts'). Calvin adds the guard that God 'does not so transfer the office of blessing to His priests, as to resign this right to them'.

Two independent voices in this chapter argue AGAINST deriving the Nazarite vow from a foreign source, which is worth recording because the two are a century and a confession apart. KEIL at key 1: 'The origin of this custom is involved in obscurity. There is no certain clue to indicate that it was derived from Egypt, for the so-called hair-offering vows are met with among several ancient tribes' (citing Spencer and Knobel), 'whilst vows of abstinence were common to all the religions of antiquity.' CLARKE at key 18, from the other end: the Hindoos let the hair grow through a vow and shave it where the vow was made, and though 'the Gentiles might have learned this from the Jews', some learned men hold 'that this consecration of the hair to a deity was in use among the heathens before the time of Moses, and in nations who had no intercourse or connection with the Jews'. Both reach independent origin by comparative evidence rather than by derivation -- a convergence, not a dispute.

ELLICOTT DIAGNOSES A RACIALLY MOTIVATED MISREADING, AND NAMES IT. At key 24, on why the curse falls on Canaan and not Ham, he argues from the Hebrew (the phrase is 'his son, the little one', which can only mean the youngest, and Ham was not the youngest, Japheth was), then adds the historical argument that Ham's descendants were building Thebes, Nineveh and Babylon and founding empires while Japheth's wandered Europe with 'no better weapons than implements of flint and bone', and that for centuries the Egyptians, a Hamite race, made Israel serve them. He then states the diagnosis outright: 'The application of the curse to Ham seems to have been suggested to commentators by the degradation of the African race in modern times, and especially by the prevalence of negro slavery: but anciently the converse was the case... We must not extend, therefore, to Ham the curse pronounced upon Canaan.' HENRY, in the same catena, holds precisely the reading Ellicott rejects: Canaan is cursed 'in whom Ham is himself cursed'. CLARKE notes that the Arabic version reads 'Ham the father of Canaan' through the whole oracle and dismisses it as a gloss unsupported by any other version. Ellicott's own alternative is that Canaan was himself the offender, citing a tradition in Origen that Canaan first saw the exposure and told his father, and Aben Ezra that he had done worse than mock.

A four-cornered, mutually aware quarrel over Noah's drunkenness at keys 20-21. CLARKE exculpates entirely: the vine was probably then first cultivated and the intoxicating power never before known, so Noah 'might have drunk it at this time without the least blame'; he offers a case he says he personally witnessed, of a man raised on milk and water who took half a pint of cider in a Somersetshire farmhouse and within half an hour 'could neither speak plain nor walk', yet 'of the crime of drunkenness he was as innocent as an infant'. He then attacks the commentators: 'Some expositors seem to be glad to fix on a fact like this, which by their distortion becomes a crime; and then, in a strain of sympathetic tenderness, affect to deplore the failings and imperfections of the best of men.' GILL uses very nearly that formula, that the incident shows 'the best of men are not exempted from sin, nor secure from falling'. CALVIN attacks the excuse at its root: the belief that wine was not in use before 'has been the more willingly received, as affording an honourable pretext for the excuse of Noah's sin', but the vine can hardly have lain neglected, and 'Moses does not say that Noah was drunken on the first day on which he tasted it'; God 'brands him with an eternal mark of disgrace'. WESLEY sides with Clarke. ELLICOTT strikes from a third side, that 'he was uncovered' is reflexive -- he uncovered himself -- 'no accident, but a wilful breach of modesty'.

WESLEY ATTACKS HENRY BY NAME AND THEN ABRIDGES HIM FOUR TIMES OVER. At key 4 Wesley writes: 'Mr. Henry indeed has a strange conceit, That this is only a prohibition to eat flesh. This does such apparent violence to the text, that to mention it, is sufficient.' This is the first recorded case in the corpus of one commentator attacking another BY NAME whose block stands beside his in the same catena. What makes it sharper is that Wesley's Notes are, through the rest of this chapter, a close abridgement of Henry: at key 6 both have, word for word, 'such remains of God's image are still even upon fallen man, that he who unjustly kills a man defaceth the image of God, and doth dishonour to him'; at key 11 both have the passage about the sea flowing 'twice every day for a few hours' and God showing 'what he could do in wrath' by flowing seas and 'what he can do in mercy' by preserving the earth between; at key 13 Wesley reproduces Henry's five observations on the seal, including 'as if the eternal Mind needed a memorandum'; and at key 25 both have the servant-of-servants note and the eight-hundred-year interval to Joshua. Note also that on the Henry block actually present at key 4, Henry gives the atonement reason for the prohibition of blood, not the reading Wesley ascribes to him -- the attack is presumably aimed at Henry's fuller exposition, of which the catena carries only the condensed form.

Three further findings in genesis 9. (1) CALVIN'S EDITOR CONTRADICTS CALVIN AGAIN, second instance in two chapters this batch (numbers 6 key 22 had 'Calvin is peculiar in his exposition of this verse'). At key 3 Calvin denies that flesh was first permitted after the flood, and his editor replies in the apparatus that 'his arguments appear chargeable with the want of firmness, which he imputes to others', since the first sacrifices may all have been whole burnt offerings and the skin garments those of the very animals sacrificed; the editor also notes that the question Calvin dismisses as 'of little importance' has since 'assumed a very different position'. (2) ELLICOTT ARGUES AGAINST THE DOCUMENTARY HYPOTHESIS FROM THE TEXT at key 27: the Deity is Elohim here following Jehovah in the previous verse 'with extraordinary exactness', so that 'it is plainly impossible to divide this most ancient poem into Elohistic and Jehovistic sections, and the theory, however plausible occasionally, fails in a crucial place like this'; KEIL independently makes the same observation about the deliberateness of the change without drawing the polemical conclusion. (3) ELLICOTT HOLDS A LOCAL FLOOD at key 10, taking 'from all that go out of the ark unto every beast of the earth' to imply a world-sphere larger than Noah's, and naming Kalisch as reduced, in defence of a universal deluge, to arguing that the fish are meant, 'as if fishes would be destroyed by a second flood any more than they were by the first'.

JFB displacement, 30th instance, and the CLEANEST demonstration of the model yet. Keys 5, 11, 17, 23: constant stride of 6, and the donor advances strictly monotonically with FOUR DISTINCT PORTIONS AND NO STALL — Genesis 5:3ff (the patriarchs advanced in life before children, Moses recording not first-born sons but the succession from Adam through Seth), Genesis 6:4 (the term implying not great stature but reckless ferocity), Genesis 6:9 (Noah just and perfect, not absolutely, since none since Adam's fall has been free from sin but Christ), Genesis 6:14 (the ark a hollow chest, cypress, cabins, mineral pitch). Previous confirmations all involved at least one stall (deuteronomy 9: 19:9, 19:9, 20:1, 20:2; judges 13: 31:16, 31:16, 31:24). This is a pure advance, which is what the reading-head model predicts when the head moves at the same rate as the correct one. A SECOND observation, new and possibly more useful: the donor here is the IMMEDIATELY PRECEDING chapters of the SAME book. Checking the donors confirmed this session — judges 21 took Joshua 3-5, deuteronomy 9 took Numbers 19-20, deuteronomy 23 took Numbers 28, judges 13 took Deuteronomy 31, genesis 7 takes Genesis 5-6 — the donor PRECEDES the target in canonical order in every case. The head appears to LAG rather than to point at an arbitrary file. Caveat for whoever tests this: joshua 7 was recorded pre-compaction as having a Joshua 13 donor, which would be later within the same book and would break the pattern; that instance needs re-checking before the lag model is asserted.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, 26th instance, on Ellicott's block at key 24 — the coinciding case again, key 24 being both Ellicott's final block and the chapter's last commented key. Five coinciding cases in a row now (judges 21, deuteronomy 9, deuteronomy 6, judges 13, genesis 7) and still no new discriminating case since deuteronomy 23. Three splits, one of them a four-against-one that spans the chapter. (1) v2, what 'by sevens' means: Ellicott argues seven of each kind rather than seven pairs, on the practical ground that seven pairs would leave room for too few species, since attending to so large a number would be beyond Noah and his sons; Calvin, Keil and Gill make it three pairs with a seventh added for sacrifice, Calvin noting that Le Clerc objected and supposed seven of each sex, and suspecting a scepticism about the seventh animal's sacrificial use behind that reading. (2) v11, the season: Clarke identifies the first month as Tisri and the second as Marcheshvan, the Nisan reckoning being later than the Exodus; Ellicott gives the reason, that the ecclesiastical year beginning in Abib commemorates the deliverance from Egypt and can have no place here, so the flood began at the end of October; Henry and Wesley reckon it about the beginning of November and notice that Noah had a harvest just before, to victual the ark. Calvin alone holds for SPRING, arguing that the sacred reckoning was divinely appointed and is more agreeable to nature — and he presses it twice, at v1 and again at v8, making the loveliness of the season part of the trial. Four to one, and the minority view is load-bearing for Calvin's reading of the whole chapter. (3) v24, whether the forty days fall inside the hundred and fifty: Gill and Ellicott say yes, the hundred and fifty running from the flood's beginning to the grounding, exactly five months; Clarke follows Lightfoot in keeping the sums distinct, making six months and ten days elapsed.

Three pieces of unusually good material, all Ellicott, and all retained at the cost of trimming elsewhere. (1) v2: he raises the documentary question — the fuller orders being given in the name of Jehovah where most of the flood narrative is Elohistic — states the case for a Jehovist supplementer fairly, answers it from outside the text (the sacrifice is as integral to the Chaldean Genesis as the sending forth of the birds, and so older than Moses), and then CONCEDES that there is nothing improbable in Moses having had two records before him and at least a prima facie appearance of two narratives combined here. That evenness is rare in this corpus and worth preserving wherever Ellicott does it. (2) v20: he takes the fifteen cubits for the draught of the ark computed after grounding, and argues quantitatively that rain alone cannot account for the depth — England's mean annual rainfall falling every twenty-four hours for forty days would yield about a hundred feet, but water seeks the lower ground throughout, so a cosmic convulsion carrying water from the equator poleward is needed, which also explains the ark travelling against the current up into Armenia. (3) v24: he notices that the word rendered 'prevailed' means literally 'were strong', and is used at the very moment the waters were demonstrably failing, since the ark had touched ground — from which he infers the narrative preserves the impressions of someone aboard. A genuinely subtle observation.

Overshoot control REGRESSED sharply here, and the regression is worth recording precisely because the note-941 rule was being applied deliberately. Seven of seven entries over the ceiling again, but the trim-pass counts were the worst of the session: v11 took FOURTEEN passes (911 down to 647), v12 took ten (860 to 650), v1 took eight, v17 seven. Compare judges 13 in the previous batch, where the worst was 782 and the rule was working. Diagnosis: genesis 7 has an unusual density of MUTUALLY REDUNDANT long blocks. At v11 four separate commentators (Henry, Wesley, Clarke, Ellicott) each give a full account of the same two causes, and Henry and Wesley overlap almost verbatim, Wesley being an abridgement of Henry throughout this chapter. The note-941 rule (keep the principle, sample the instances) does not help against redundancy, because there is only one principle and four full statements of it. The rule that actually worked, discovered too late to save v11, is: WHERE TWO VOICES SAY THE SAME THING AT LENGTH, NAME BOTH AND QUOTE ONE. Applying it at v22 produced an entry in range on the first draft (468 words, no trim passes), and at v6 likewise (609, none). Also worth flagging for the corpus: in Genesis, Wesley abridges Henry so closely that treating them as independent voices inflates every entry — the tags schools field can still credit both, but the prose should not state the same point twice.

Material deliberately omitted from v11, recorded so the omission is recoverable. Clarke's block at key 11 contains an extended eighteenth-century chemical digression: that water is composed of two airs, oxygen and hydrogen, in proportions of eighty-five to fifteen; that the electric spark decomposes them and converts them to water, which he offers as the cause of rain following thunder; and that God might therefore have converted the whole atmosphere into water to drown the globe, in which case the incessant glare of lightning and continual peals of thunder must have added indescribable horrors to the scene. I kept only his account of the subterranean waters and the sinking strata. The chemistry is historically interesting but would have cost the entry a third of its length, and it is superseded rather than merely dated. Flagging it here in case a later reader of this chapter wants Clarke's natural philosophy, which the entry does not represent.
