Intra-catena citation, four instances in one chapter -- commentators quoting each other while the quoted man's own block stands in the same catena. (1) Key 2: Clarke transcribes Wesley's note on predestination IN FULL, saying 'the Rev. J. Wesley has an excellent note here which I will copy out for the benefit of those of my readers who may not have his works at hand' -- and Wesley's block stands a few inches down the same page. (2) Key 10: Ellicott quotes Calvin BY NAME and with approval ('Calvin rightly says: when he states that the prophets inquired and examined, this refers not to their writings or teaching, but to the private longing with which each was fired') -- and Calvin's block in this catena says precisely that. (3) Key 8: Ellicott quotes the hymn 'A charge to keep I have' -- Charles Wesley -- while John Wesley's block stands in the same entry. (4) Key 12: Ellicott quotes two more Charles Wesley stanzas on angels searching the mystery in vain. Compare the genesis 9 finding, where Wesley attacked Henry by name while abridging him elsewhere in the same chapter. The pattern is now firm: these commentators are in conversation with each other, and the catena silently reassembles that conversation.

Five-position election controversy at 1:2, the densest single-verse disagreement in the chapter. Gill: eternal election of these persons both to grace and to glory, known to the apostle not by revelation but by a judgment of charity. Barnes: the election is real, but a man has evidence of it only so far as he is renewed by the Spirit and has holiness of heart and life, AND NO FARTHER -- no one can go up to heaven and inspect the book of life. Ellicott: refuses both escapes -- it is 'an evasion of the difficulty' to say they were elect only in the mass, since the election was individual and personal, and YET for all their election they are not certain of salvation, the title implying no more than that God has put them into the visible Church. Clarke: corporate only, arguing with Lardner and Macknight that if the letter had been directed to persons elected to eternal life no one could have received it, since none could be sure of his election till he arrived in heaven. Wesley: a full set-piece against predestination -- denies foreknowledge in the strict sense (there is no more foreknowledge than afterknowledge with God), reduces true predestination to three propositions, and lays four numbered charges against any other, that it is cruel respect of persons and mere creature partiality, that it contradicts the universal offers of grace, that it makes probation meaningless, and that it is of fatal consequence since all men are ready on slight grounds to fancy themselves of the elect number.

The Jew-or-Gentile question about the readers runs as a single argument across five widely separated keys, and one commentator carries it. At 1:1 Barnes catalogues the parties (native Jews on Eusebius, Jerome, Grotius, Beza, Mill and Cave; Gentiles on Procopius, Cassiodorus and Wetstein) and does not decide; Ellicott decides for dispersed Jews and holds Palestine, not heaven, is the home contrasted, while Robertson holds the reverse, that heaven is our native country. At 1:14 Ellicott states the strongest case AGAINST his own view -- that the letter assumes its readers lived in ignorance and vice, which is 'contended, with much plausibility' to make them Gentiles -- and answers it in four steps. At 1:18 he settles it from the word 'tradition', which in the New Testament means something sedulously taught and handed down as an heirloom and so cannot describe a sensual life learned by example, whereas among the Jews it governed how a cup was washed: 'the readers of this Letter were certainly Jews by birth.' He then asks whether the Apostle of the Circumcision would dare call Judaism a vain conversation and an Egyptian bondage, and answers from Acts 15:10. At 1:23 'not of corruptible seed' becomes 'not of the seed of Abraham, but of the seed of God', an argument against Jewish arrogance toward Gentile converts. At 1:24 the whole Isaiah quotation is read as proclaiming the equality of Jew and Gentile, with the omitted words 'surely the people is grass' carrying the point. Robertson meanwhile says at 1:18 that 'the reference here seems mainly to Gentiles' and Clarke holds both nations wedded to inherited vanities. Calvin faces the same difficulty at 1:14 and answers by another road entirely: the Jews were blind in the midst of light, having a veil over the eyes so that they did not see Christ in the Law.

Outliers of unusual character in this chapter. (1) Key 25: Clarke appends to his comment an ~1,100-word treatise on the chemistry and physics of GOLD -- specific gravity 19.3, a cubic foot weighing 1,348 lbs, one grain divisible into two million visible parts, one pound sufficient to gild a wire 25,000 miles long -- and turns it into an apologetic: gold survives any culinary fire but is volatilised in the focus of a powerful burning glass, 'this is but a late discovery, and previously to it a philosopher would have ridiculed St. Peter for saying, gold that perisheth.' An early-nineteenth-century laboratory report offered as vindication of a scriptural adjective, attached to a verse eighteen verses away from the phrase it defends. (2) Key 11: Ellicott makes the verse the most striking in the New Testament on prophetic inspiration and sets it between Montanism, which he illustrates from Montanus himself ('Lo, man is as a lyre, and I am as that which strikes the chords: the man is unconscious, and I alone wake'), and the opposite error that Isaiah saw Mary and Jesus as plainly as we do; he then quotes Keble on the Greek poets. In the same block he forbids the verse to be used for the pre-existence of Christ or the procession of the Spirit from the Son, on the ground that 'Christ' always marks the office and not the person -- while Barnes says in his block on the same verse that 'it is clear from this passage that Christ must have had an existence before his incarnation.' (3) Key 12: Barnes leaves exegesis for astronomy, describing Saturn's diameter, its 22,000 mph motion and its rings, as fields of eternal study for holy minds. (4) Key 12 and key 25: Ellicott twice invokes the Tubingen school, first that Peter's concurrence with Paul refutes their theory of divergence 'only the Tubingen school reject the Epistle on the ground that it makes the Apostles too harmonious', and then as the chapter's closing line, 'Well may the Tubingen school wish to disprove the genuineness of this Epistle!'

Fidelity self-grade A for all thirteen entries of 1peter 1. Every proposition in every prose block is traceable to a named commentator's block at a verse inside that entry's range; no voice is named who is not sourced in that entry; no scripture reference appears unlinked; the two residue voices (Jamieson at keys 1/7/13/19/25, Cyril at keys 3/11/12/17/20/25) are excluded or silently dropped and contribute nothing. Word counts, all inside the 350-650 window: key 1 = 649; key 2 = 649; key 3 = 640; keys 4-5 = 645; keys 6-7 = 636; keys 8-9 = 642; keys 10-11 = 647; key 12 = 645; key 13 = 614; keys 14-16 = 643; keys 17-18 = 649; keys 19-21 = 650; keys 22-25 = 647. Total 8,356 words of synthesis over 91,763 words of real usable source (92,757 reported, less 994 of chrome), a compression of about 11 to 1. Thirteen entries tile verses 1-25 exactly. Every first draft ran over the ceiling and required between two and five trim passes; key 12 needed four, from 787 down to 645.

Chrome measured on the Ellicott block at key 40: 992 words / 24,947 characters appended after 153 words of genuine comment, nav strip 'Acts Act 20 Acts Act Acts Act 22'. Usable source is therefore 58,970 words, not the 59,962 the sizer reports. FIFTH measurement, and it confirms the character-window finding filed on 1peter 1 (which corrected the earlier, wrong romans 1 note): 1peter 1 = 24,951 chars; genesis 9 = 24,953; numbers 6 = 24,952; romans 1 = 24,949; acts 21 = 24,947. Spread across five instances is now 7 characters, against a word spread of 992-994 explained entirely by nav-strip tokenisation. The capture is a fixed-length character grab of whatever follows the article; the payload has been CSS and JavaScript source in every instance since numbers 6.

Jamieson stride-6 residue, FORTY-SECOND chapter. Keys 2, 8, 20, 26, 32, 38 -- offset 2, SIX members, no gaps. This is the SECOND CONSECUTIVE chapter in which the residue is a MONOTONIC WALK rather than a scatter, and here the walk runs in canonical order right up to the book being commented on: key 2 = Luke 24 (the meal after the resurrection), key 8 = John 21:23 (John alone surviving the destruction of Jerusalem), key 20 = Acts 1:3 (the primary evidence of the resurrection), key 26 = Acts 1:9 (Lu 24:50-53, taken up while they looked), key 32 = Acts 1:14 (the days of expectant prayer), key 38 = Acts 1:14 AGAIN, the identical 79-word block repeated verbatim. The duplication at the tail is new and diagnostic: the pointer appears to walk forward through a neighbouring commentary at a fixed stride and then STALL, re-emitting the last block it reached. Taken with the Gal 6:8 -> 6:13 -> 6:18 -> Eph 1:3 -> Eph 1:8 walk in 1peter 1, this is strong evidence that the misalignment is a single index advancing through the wrong text, not random substitution. All six blocks excluded.

Voice inventory anomalies in this chapter. (1) John Chrysostom is GENUINE here, not residue: two large blocks (keys 18 and 39, 1,277 and 1,192 words) from the Homilies on Acts, expounding this very chapter. This is the first genuine patristic voice I have met in the COW catena, and it carries the eastern-antiochene school into entries 18-19 and 35-40. It exposes the VOICE_LABELS defect from the other side: the short form 'Chrysostom' in scripts/synthesis_qa.py works fine for USING him in prose, but would fail if he ever needed declaring in excluded_voices. (2) Cyril of Jerusalem is residue as usual (keys 1, 13, 25, 40 -- Catechetical Lectures on Barnabas at Antioch, on Moses, on the Spirit and the New Covenant, and on the Mysteries), dropped SILENTLY because 'Cyril of Jerusalem:' matches nothing in VOICE_LABELS. Seventeen batches now. (3) Matthew Henry is again MIXED: his block at key 19 is from the CONCISE commentary ('How watchful should we be against prejudices!', 'it would be hard to defend Paul from the charge of giving way too much'), while his blocks at keys 1, 8, 15 and 27 are from the full Exposition. This is the second book in which I have found the two works merged under one voice name without a marker -- the first was 1peter 1 key 17. It matters exegetically here, because the Concise Henry passes a much harsher verdict on Paul's compliance than the Exposition anywhere does.

The chapter's spine: whether Paul was right to take the vow at James's suggestion. Eight positions, and the two Wesleyan voices are flatly opposed to each other. WESLEY condemns it outright -- could Paul follow such advice 'in godly sincerity'? was it not 'too great a deference to be paid to any mere men'? He should have answered plainly 'I do not keep the Mosaic law; neither need any of you', since Peter did not and God had commanded him not to; and the compliance 'seemed to flow not out of spiritual but carnal wisdom; seeming to be what he really was not: making as if he believed the law still in force.' CLARKE, same school, confesses 'it is exceedingly difficult to account for the conduct of James and the elders, and of Paul... There seems to have been something in this transaction which we do not fully understand', reports the charge that it was 'the greatest error of his life' and 'a virtual denial of Christ' with his subsequent imprisonment read as 'a judgment of God upon him', and answers that no sacred writer ever censured it and Paul himself reflects on it with comfort. HENRY (Concise) says it would be hard to defend Paul from giving way too much, and that 'integrity and uprightness will be more likely to preserve us than insincere compliances.' CHRYSOSTOM defends without reserve: Paul 'complied, and did all: for in fact thus was it expedient', and bearing the expenses made it 'a step open to no suspicion.' BARNES vindicates in four steps against the infidel charge of double-dealing, concluding 'He violated none of the dictates of honesty and truth.' CALVIN denies dissimulation but grants the charge of being 'too easily entreated' has 'more colour', refuses the reading that the ensuing trouble was punishment, and turns the passage against the 'false Nicodemites' who plead Paul's example to cover conformity to Popery. ELLICOTT calls it 'so wisely planned in the interests of peace.' ROBERTSON answers Furneaux, who 'calls it a compromise and a failure. I do not so see it', arguing the aim was not to conciliate the Judaizers but to break their hold on the deluded thousands, and that it worked, since the explosion came from a different set of enemies entirely.

Two further within-school splits, both between Wesley and Clarke, on top of the vow. (1) At 21:4 and 21:12, whether the Spirit's warning bound Paul: WESLEY says 'St. Paul knew that this prediction had the force of a command. They did not know this'; CLARKE says the exact reverse, that 'they all understood the prophecy to be conditional and contingent; and that it was in Paul's power to turn the scale', and at 21:14 that 'every one saw that he had power to go, or not to go.' Clarke drives it home with a comparison no one else makes: 'This was a similar case to that of David in Keilah. David prevented the threatened evil by leaving Keilah: Paul fell into it by going to Jerusalem' -- which implies the outcome was avoidable. (2) At 21:21, whether the charge against Paul was true: WESLEY says it was -- 'And so undoubtedly he did. And so he wrote to all the Churches in Galatia' -- and breaks out, 'Amazing! that they did not know this! Or, that if they did, they did not openly testify it at all hazards, to every Jewish convert in Jerusalem!' CLARKE says the information 'was incorrect', that Paul 'had not yet said to any Jew, forsake Moses'; BARNES calls it 'incorrect and slanderous'; ROBERTSON says the elders 'do not believe this false charge.' ELLICOTT takes a middle position worth recording on its own: false as a personal accusation, but 'fanaticism is sometimes clear-sighted in its bitterness', since once circumcision was declared nothing 'it ceased to have a raison d'etre', and 'If a Jew had asked, Why then should I circumcise my child? it would not have been easy to return a satisfying answer.'

Four findings of method rather than doctrine. (1) ARCHAEOLOGY OVERTAKES THE COMMENTARY. At 21:28 Clarke, writing before the discovery, knows the temple barrier inscription only from Josephus. Ellicott and Robertson can both quote the STONE, each citing the slab found and deciphered by Clermont-Ganneau and published in 1871, Robertson adding that it had been built into the wall of a mosque on the Via Dolorosa; Ellicott gives the full text. Two commentators independently reaching for the same excavation report, sixty years after the third had to argue from a literary source alone. (2) FOUR SOLUTIONS TO A NUMERICAL CRUX at 21:38, Luke's four thousand against Josephus's thirty thousand -- and GILL alone supplies the cause by noting that JOSEPHUS GIVES BOTH FIGURES HIMSELF in different places. Ellicott rejects Josephus ('his statistics, in such cases, are never to be relied on'); Robertson takes Lysias to mean the armed core of the larger mob; Clarke offers a harmony (26,000 melted away before Olivet) AND reports Dean Aldridge's palaeographic conjecture that a copyist mistook Greek delta (four) for lambda (thirty), supported by the argument that 600 casualties is no proportion to 30,000 but a fair one to 4,000. Calvin adds a fourth line, refuting the identification of the man with Theudas. (3) FOUR SOURCE-CRITICAL CONJECTURES ABOUT LUKE in one chapter: Ellicott at 21:8 imagines Luke learning from Philip 'all, or nearly all, that we find in the first eleven chapters of this book'; Robertson at the same verse supposes Luke 'did, take notes from Philip and his daughters'; Ellicott at 21:16 makes Mnason one of the eye-witnesses 'from the beginning' whom Luke names as his informants; Robertson at 21:18 argues from the fullness of the report that Luke was present and gathering first-hand material. (4) A UNANIMOUS TEXTUAL VERDICT IGNORED: at 21:8 Ellicott, Barnes, Clarke and Robertson all report that 'we that were of Paul's company' is no part of the text -- yet Gill expounds it as genuine and names the seven men, and Henry builds a homiletical reflection on it, that 'those that travel together through this world will separate at death, and then it will appear who are of Paul's company and who are not.' A commonplace resting on an interpolation.

Outliers worth keeping from acts 21. (1) At 21:9 the four prophesying daughters draw FIVE distinct positions on women speaking: Ellicott makes them a recognised order answering to the widows, cites the catacomb inscriptions and Pliny's letter to Trajan, and argues that Paul 'was therefore open to the teachings of experience' and modified his judgment later, adding that 'the very prohibition proves that the practice was common'; Robertson finds the prohibitions hard to reconcile with the permission and 'wonders if there was not something known to Paul about special conditions in Corinth and Ephesus that he has not told', concluding that 'the whole problem is difficult and calls for restraint and reverence' and noting that 'today in our Sunday schools the women do most of the actual teaching'; Calvin, holding women bear no public office, has them prophesying 'at home, or in some private place, without the common assembly'; Clarke asks 'If Philip's daughters might be prophetesses, why not teachers?'; Gill takes from the verse only that Philip was married, 'which may be observed against the Papists.' (2) At 21:23 Ellicott alone observes from Hegesippus that JAMES HIMSELF lived under the Nazarite rule -- 'No razor came upon his head, and he drank neither wine nor strong drink' -- so the advice came from a man bound by the same vow. (3) At 21:29 Barnes and Robertson independently turn the mob's bad inference into a moral: Barnes, 'If men would state facts as they are, no small part of the slanderous accusations against others would cease'; Robertson, 'This is the way of the mob-mind in all ages. Many an innocent man has been rushed to his death by the fury of a lynching party.' (4) The chapter closes on two fine strokes: Chrysostom asking 'What spectacle could be equal to this, to see Paul, bound with two chains, and haranguing the people!', and Ellicott noting that many in that crowd had not seen Paul act in public since the day, twenty-five years before, when 'he had kept the garments of those who were stoning Stephen' -- and that he now stood accused of the self-same crimes before a mob as frenzied as the one he had then led. Set beside Gill's aside at 21:28 that Paul was 'little of stature, and weak in body', Robertson's verdict that 'Paul's stature and words reach heroic proportions on this occasion' lands hard.

Fidelity self-grade A for all ten entries of acts 21. Every proposition in every prose block is traceable to a named commentator's block at a verse inside that entry's range; no voice is named who is not sourced in that entry; no scripture reference appears unlinked; the residue voices (Jamieson at keys 2/8/20/26/32/38, Cyril at keys 1/13/25/40) are excluded or silently dropped and contribute nothing, while Chrysostom at keys 18 and 39 is genuine and used. Word counts, all inside the 350-650 window: verses 1-6 = 642; 7-9 = 636; 10-14 = 621; 15-17 = 637; 18-19 = 649; 20-22 = 636; 23-26 = 649; 27-28 = 650; 29-34 = 648; 35-40 = 647. Total 6,415 words of synthesis over 58,970 words of real usable source (59,962 reported, less 992 of chrome), a compression of about 9 to 1. Ten entries tile verses 1-40 exactly. Entry 18-19 carries all five schools at once, the first time the eastern-antiochene school has been genuinely represented rather than dropped as residue. Every first draft ran over the ceiling; entries 23-26 and 27-28 each needed a full prose rewrite rather than incremental trimming, 23-26 coming down from 863 words.

JFB stride bug, 33rd confirmation, and a NEW VARIANT that cuts against my own deuteronomy 6 conclusion. Four blocks at keys 6/12/18/24 — a perfect stride of six — all from Numbers 32 (Reuben and Gad and the trans-Jordan grant; key 24 is the town list, Dibon and Aroer on the Arnon). What is new: the blocks at 6, 12 and 18 are BYTE-IDENTICAL, the same 244-word passage emitted three times, not three successive portions of the donor. Every prior confirmation had the donor position either advancing or stalling once; a triple identical emission has not been seen before. Key 6's copy also begins mid-sentence ('with sincerity and zeal'), so the head is parked mid-block in the donor, which is what the reading-head model predicts. But at deuteronomy 6 I argued from a lone displaced block that the apparent stride was merely the spacing of JFB's own sparse coverage and not a step the corruption takes. A perfectly regular stride of six emitting the same text three times is hard to explain that way, and I am recording it as evidence against that conclusion rather than folding it in. Donor precedes target canonically — ninth confirmation of the lag model. All four excluded.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, instance 28, on Ellicott's key-29 block. Seventh consecutive chapter in which Ellicott's final block coincides with the chapter's last key, so it still fails to discriminate between the two candidate rules. Worth saying plainly: the refined rule from numbers 28 has now gone seven chapters without a test, and I would not treat it as confirmed.

Two bare cross-references in the same key: Clarke's key-5 block is 'Your clothes are not waxen old - See on Deu 8:4' and Ellicott's is the four words 'See on Deuteronomy 8:4.' The pattern noted at deuteronomy 23 and 9 holds and is now seen in a second commentator — these cluster where Deuteronomy retells earlier material, because the substantive note was written once at the primary passage. Both voices have substantive blocks elsewhere in the 2-9 span, so under the established rule the blocks are passed over and the voices kept; nothing is recorded in excluded_voices.

Three separate voices spill across entry boundaries here, and in every case the filing rule keeps the material where it was filed because the voice has no key inside the target span. Henry's key-1 block runs through vv1-9, and he has no key in 2-9. Henry's and Calvin's key-10 blocks both run through vv11-15, and neither has a key in 11-16. Keil's key-25 block treats v29, and he has no key at 29. Chapters where one commentator writes a running exposition rather than verse notes will do this systematically, and the effect is to load the entry at the START of the run — which is why entry 10 here carries the whole parties-to-the-covenant argument.

Length control across eight entries: three landed in range on the first draft (637, 552, 633 after one pass) and the rest overshot by 20 to 85 words. The overshoots cluster exactly where the chapter offers a long single-voice argument that resists the note-969 treatment — Calvin on the heart not given, Calvin on the root and the drunkard, Calvin on the secret things — because there is no second voice saying the same thing at length to compress against. Note 969 works on redundancy; it does nothing for a chapter whose bulk is one commentator being thorough alone. Where that is the shape, the discipline has to be selection at the outline stage: choose the two or three moves of the argument to carry and drop the rest before drafting, not after.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, instance 29 — and the FIRST DISCRIMINATING CASE in seven chapters. The tail attaches to Ellicott's key-39 block. Ellicott has no block at keys 40 or 41, so 39 is his final block, but it is NOT the chapter's last key: the chapter runs on to 41. The tail followed Ellicott, not the chapter. This confirms the refined rule proposed at numbers 28 — the tail attaches to the end of Ellicott's final block — and falsifies the competing rule that it attaches to the chapter's last key. Every case since deuteronomy 23 had the two coinciding; this one separates them cleanly.

A SECOND and distinct boilerplate tail, from a different source, found in the same chapter. Gill's key-41 block ends with sacred-texts navigation furniture: 'Next: Numbers Chapter 16 Sacred Texts | Bible << Previous: John Gill's Exposition of the Entire Bible: Numbers: Numb... Index Next: ...'. This is not the StudyLight tail and does not look like it — it is short, it names the scrape source, and it attaches to Gill rather than Ellicott. Worth checking whether it appears at the end of Gill's final block in other chapters; if so there are two independent tail defects in the corpus, keyed to two different commentators, and only one of them has been tracked so far.

JFB stride bug, 34th confirmation. Three blocks at keys 11, 29 and 41, all displaced, all from Leviticus 24-25: key 11 is the note on offences of a social nature punished through the judges, keys 29 and 41 are the Jubilee and the sabbatic year with the sixth year's triple yield. Donor advances monotonically and precedes the target canonically — tenth confirmation of the lag model. But the spacing is 18 then 12, which is IRREGULAR, and that matters: deuteronomy 29 in this same batch had a perfect stride of six with three byte-identical emissions, and I recorded it there as evidence for a fixed stride. This chapter cuts the other way in the same run. Two chapters, opposite evidence, no resolution — the honest position is that the stride is not yet explained, and neither the fixed-stride nor the sparse-coverage account fits both cases.

A new sub-kind of empty block, and a rule change it forces. Clarke's key-1 block is nothing but his chapter argument — the running table of contents for the whole chapter, verse ranges and summaries, with no comment on verse 1 itself. I have been treating that header as a drafting hazard (it reads as a ready-made outline and drives overshoot, per notes 917 and 930); it is also an EMPTY BLOCK by the established test, since it contains no comment of the commentator's own on the verse it is filed under. Because entry 1 here is the single key 1, Clarke has no substantive block in the span, so he is excluded outright. His key-20 block is the familiar bare cross-reference and is the only Clarke block in the 17-21 span, so he is excluded there too. Two exclusions of the same commentator in one chapter, on two different empty-block kinds.

Second chapter in this batch showing the running-commentary spill described for deuteronomy 29, and it behaves identically. Henry writes exposition by pericope rather than by verse, so his key-1 block covers vv1-21, his key-30 block covers vv30-36, and in both cases he has no key inside the span the material actually treats, so it stays where filed. Keil's key-31 block likewise runs into v32, but Keil DOES have a key at 33, so that material could move and did. The rule is working, but the effect is worth stating plainly: for commentators of Henry's type the entry at the head of a run carries the argument for the whole run, and entries later in the run lose him entirely.

Length control, second chapter of the batch: five of seven entries landed in range on the first draft (593, 626, 464, 627, 606, 640 — six of seven, in fact), and only the last needed trimming, by 64 words. That is a marked improvement on deuteronomy 29 earlier in the same run, where five of eight overshot. The difference is what note 998 predicted: numbers 15 is a chapter of many short competing notes rather than a few long single-voice arguments, so the note-969 compression has something to work on in nearly every paragraph. The one entry that overshot, the tassels, is the one where Calvin, Clarke and Henry each develop a separate long argument that does not overlap with the others.

Chrome measurement six, and the first non-terminal instance. The StudyLight nav/CSS chrome falls at key 23 on Charles Ellicott, after 177 genuine words, and runs 992 words / 24,949 characters, ending mid-token in the same JS fragment as every previous case (...('data-vf-open')==='1';}for(var i=0;i). The six measurements now stand at 1peter 1 key 25 (994w/24,951), genesis 9 key 29 (992/24,953), numbers 6 key 23 (992/24,952), romans 1 key 32 (992/24,949), acts 21 key 40 (992/24,947) and exodus 2 key 23 (992/24,949): a character spread of 7, the word variation being entirely nav-strip tokenisation. What is new here is the position. In all five earlier chapters the chrome fell on the last block of the last key and so truncated nothing. In exodus 2 it falls mid-chapter, and Calvin and Wesley follow it cleanly at the same key, so the fetcher is not simply appending page furniture at the end of a chapter fetch but can splice it into the middle of a key. Ellicott's genuine comment on 2:23 survives (the regnal-length argument for Thothmes III or Rameses II) but anything he wrote on 2:24-25 is gone.

Jamieson, Fausset and Brown residue, chapter 43 of the misalignment. Exodus 2 carries exactly ONE Jamieson block, at key 10, and its content is Genesis 43 (Jacob committing his sons to God as they go down to Egypt) — nothing to do with Pharaoh's daughter naming Moses. Excluded from entry 5-10. A single member gives no stride to test, so this chapter neither confirms nor breaks the stride-6 pattern established in the two preceding chapters (1peter 1: keys 1,7,13,19,25, five members walking monotonically Gal 6:8 to Eph 1:8; acts 21: keys 2,8,20,26,32,38, six members walking Luke 24 to Acts 1:14 with the last block repeated verbatim). Worth recording anyway as a data point that the residue can be a single stranded block rather than a series.

The 200-word fetch cap truncates Keil and Delitzsch throughout exodus 2. Keil is the OT-set replacement for Barnes/Robertson and appears at twelve keys here; every one of his blocks is cut at exactly 200 words, and because Keil's format prefixes the full verse text before the comment, several blocks are almost entirely verse quotation with one or two sentences of exposition surviving. Key 17 spends its whole allowance printing 2:17-21 and yields only the note that hô'îl means voluit and that the Midian life was still a banishment; key 22 prints 2:22-23 and is cut mid-sentence in the middle of the Baumgarten argument about which Pharaoh died. Same defect flagged in genesis 9 and numbers 6. A re-fetch at a higher cap would materially improve every OT chapter's grammatical-historical school coverage.

Calvin alone censures Moses's parents, twice, against a unanimous chorus of praise. On the ark (2:3) Ellicott, Gill, Henry, Clarke and Wesley all read the bulrush chest as careful and even ingenious contrivance, and Henry and Wesley make it an act of faith on the strength of Hebrews 11:23; Calvin says their timidity 'cannot advisedly be excused', and presses the comparison that the dams of brute beasts do better by their young than these parents did by theirs. On the child's beauty (2:2) the same five take the goodliness of the child as the ground and warrant of their faith; Calvin says that if they were moved to preserve him because he was beautiful, this 'deservedly detracts from the praise' of that faith, since faith should not depend on the appearance of its object. This is the sharpest single-voice minority in the chapter and it runs across two verses, so it is not a passing remark.

Two disagreements at once on the name Moses, and Calvin's unintended-witness reading. (a) Philology: Ellicott and Keil derive the name from the Egyptian (mesu, 'child' or 'born of', as in Thothmes, Ahmes), Ellicott adding that the princess would naturally have named him in her own tongue and that the Hebrew explanation is an accommodation; Clarke argues for the Hebrew mashah, 'to draw out', on the ground that the princess had been long enough among the Hebrews to know the language, and Gill and Henry follow the Hebrew without argument. (b) Calvin ignores the etymology entirely and reads the naming as testimony extorted from an unwilling witness: in giving the child a name that records his rescue from the water, the princess 'bear[s] loud and public testimony to the very thing which she would have preferred to conceal', so that God moved her tongue as he afterwards moved the tongue of Balaam's ass. The three readings do not conflict on the facts; they conflict on what the verse is FOR.

The killing of the Egyptian: Ellicott alone condemns it, and the two who defend it hardest also fence the defence. Ellicott says the Jewish commentators gloss the act over or eulogise it as heroical, but it was clearly the deed of a hasty and undisciplined spirit — the offence did not deserve death, and had it done so Moses had neither legal office nor divine call to make himself an executioner — so that by this one wrong act he put it out of his power to help his brethren for forty years, and he collects the bill at 2:14, where the sting of the rejoinder lies not in the day's interposition but in the previous day's blow. Against him: Calvin holds on Stephen's authority that Moses knew himself divinely appointed avenger and was armed by God's command; Clarke supplies a ground nobody else has, that the Egyptian had probably killed the Hebrew, so that the Noahide precept justified him; Wesley and Henry say shortly that he acted by special warrant from heaven. But Calvin at once forbids the inference (private persons are by no means countenanced by this example, the sword of vengeance belonging to the judges, and if these fail the innocent 'all we can do is to murmur') and refuses to call the act perfect (the looking about and the secret blow show his faith was weak, so the Apostle's praise must not be read as praise of something perfect); Wesley makes the same reservation in a parenthesis, that the warrant 'makes not a precedent in ordinary cases'. Gill reads the same glance the opposite way, as arguing no consciousness of evil but only care for his own preservation.

Ellicott builds four arguments for Mosaic authorship out of incidental detail in this one chapter, all of the same form — the narrative says something an outsider would not have thought to say. (1) At 2:1 the father's name is omitted where any later writer would have supplied Amram from the genealogy. (2) At 2:12 Moses hid the body 'in the sand', not 'in the ground', which fits the sand creeping up to the cultivated land east of the Delta and is what a man who dug the grave would remember. (3) At 2:19 Reuel's daughters say 'an Egyptian delivered us', where any other author would have written 'a man' or 'a stranger' — the mistake is one Moses would remember being made about him. (4) Also at 2:19, 'and also drew water enough for us' presupposes that the shepherds had already consumed some of the maidens' water, an unexplained detail that only makes sense from inside the scene. No other voice in the catena argues authorship from incidental detail at all; Clarke's only contribution in that direction is the report that some suppose Moses wrote Job, and Genesis, during the Midian years.

Matthew Henry Concise spliced onto Exposition, now in a third book and twice in one chapter. Keys 16 and 23 both carry the full Exposition and then, with no break or marker, the corresponding Concise paragraph, which restates the same material in compressed form and adds matter the Exposition does not have — at key 23 the Concise closes with an evangelistic appeal ('Take courage then, ye who, conscious of guilt and thraldom, are looking to Him for deliverance... Come unto me, all ye that labour') that has no counterpart in the Exposition. Previously logged at 1peter 1 key 17 and acts 21 key 19, where it mattered exegetically because the Concise passed a harsher verdict on Paul's compliance than the Exposition anywhere did. Here the two agree in substance, so the only cost is double-counting Henry's weight in the word budget, but the pattern is now established across three books and both testaments and should be handled in the fetcher rather than per chapter.

Four independent chronologies for the death of the king, reached by four different methods. Ellicott argues from regnal length: Moses was eighty at the Exodus and forty at the flight, so the Pharaoh he fled must have reigned above forty years, and only Thothmes III and Rameses II did so between the start of the eighteenth dynasty and the close of the nineteenth. Clarke names candidates on authority — Usher for Ramesses Miamun (whose son Amenophis drowned in the Red Sea), Abul Farajius for Amenophis himself as the author of the edict — and dates the death about forty years after the flight from Stephen. Gill sets Eusebius (Orus, then Acenchres and Achoris) against Usher (the same king throughout, dead in the sixty-seventh year of his reign, Moses then sixty), and adds the general caution that Scripture often puts close together what was done at a considerable distance. Calvin argues from probability alone, with no king-lists: the tyrant of chapter 1 cannot have lived to this point, since he would have reigned above eighty years, 'which is not usual', so one or more kings intervened — which is also Wesley's bare supposition. Four methods, four answers, and none of the four engages the others' evidence.

Calvin grades the Midianite religion instead of sorting it, and in doing so contradicts Ellicott flatly. Ellicott says without qualification that the Midianites, as descendants of Abraham by Keturah, worshipped the true God and seem at this time to have been a religious people, citing Reuel's name ('friend of God'), Jethro's sacrifices 'for God', and the elders eating bread with him 'before God'. Calvin reaches the opposite starting point — Melchizedek was the only priest of the living God in Abraham's day, Abraham himself was drawn out of a family sunk in idolatry, and it is plain from other passages that the Midianites were joined to idols — and yet cannot make Jethro an idolater, since Moses would not have married into a house 'defiled by foul unrighteousness'. His resolution is a graded verdict rather than a binary one: 'there is some difference between idolatry and the impure worship of God, corrupted in some respects', so the Midianites 'had not entirely departed from the principles of His religion, although they had contracted some defilement from the stinking puddles of error which had gradually crept in'. Worth flagging as a rare case where a commentator explicitly refuses the true-worship/false-worship binary the rest of the catena assumes.

Fidelity self-grade A for all six entries of exodus 2. Tiling covers 1-25 exactly with no gaps or overlaps: 1-4 (649w), 5-10 (647w), 11-12 (648w), 13-15 (647w), 16-22 (649w), 23-25 (650w) — all inside the 350-650 window. Voice coverage: entries 1, 11, 16 and 23 name all seven live OT voices (Gill, Henry, Clarke, Ellicott, Calvin, Wesley, Keil and Delitzsch); entry 5 names seven with Jamieson excluded as Genesis 43 residue; entry 13 names the five that actually appear at 13-15 (Gill, Clarke, Ellicott, Calvin, Wesley — no Henry and no Keil block falls in that range). Every proposition in the prose is traceable to a named block in data/commentary/cow/exodus/2.json; where a voice is reported as alone in a view (Ellicott on the killing, Calvin on the parents, Calvin on the graded Midianite religion) the claim was checked against every other block in the range before being written. Real usable source words after deducting the 992-word chrome at key 23: 27,990 across six entries. No entry names a voice not present in its own verse range, and no block present in a range goes unused except the excluded Jamieson residue.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, instance 30, and the SECOND discriminating case in two chapters. The tail attaches to Ellicott's key-24 block. Ellicott has no block at key 25, so 24 is his final block, while the chapter's last key is 25. As at numbers 15, the tail followed Ellicott and not the chapter end. Two independent confirmations back to back, after seven chapters in which the two candidates always coincided. The numbers 28 rule can now be treated as established: the StudyLight tail attaches to the end of Ellicott's final block in the chapter, wherever that falls.

Second confirmation of the Gill tail flagged at numbers 15. Gill's key-25 block ends with sacred-texts navigation furniture: 'Next: Exodus Chapter 20 Sacred Texts | Bible << Previous: John Gill's Exposition of the Entire Bible: Exodus: Exodu... Index Next: ...'. Same shape as the numbers 15 instance, same commentator, different book. This is now a confirmed second tail defect, independent of the StudyLight one and keyed to Gill rather than Ellicott. Here it sits at the end of Gill's final block, which is also the chapter's last key, so this instance does not discriminate between the two candidate rules for the Gill tail; that question is still open and needs a chapter where Gill stops before the last key — which will be rare, since Gill has a block at every key in most chapters.

JFB stride bug, 35th confirmation, and the first SAME-BOOK case. Four blocks at keys 1, 7, 13 and 19 — again a perfect stride of six — all displaced, and all from Exodus 7: the demonstration of supremacy over Egypt, the rods of Moses and the court officials, Pharaoh concluding the magicians had matched Aaron, and the river turned to blood with the fish destroyed. Donor position advances monotonically, and the donor precedes the target within the SAME book, which is new; every previous verified case had the donor in a different and earlier book. The lag model therefore holds in a stronger form than stated: what matters is canonical position, not book boundaries (11th confirmation). Key 1's block is also truncated at the head, beginning mid-thought, consistent with the reading-head model. On the stride question, this is a second perfect six after deuteronomy 29, against the irregular 18-then-12 of numbers 15; recent evidence now runs two to one for regularity, but numbers 15 is not explained away and the question stays open.

Refinement of note 1010. At numbers 15 I found Clarke's key-1 chapter-argument header standing alone with no verse comment, and treated it as a new kind of empty block. Here the same header appears at key 1 but is FOLLOWED by substantive comment on the third month, on the phrase 'the same day', and on the name of the mountain. So the header is not itself an empty-block marker: it prefaces real comment as often as it stands alone, and the test has to be applied to what follows it, not to its presence. Clarke is kept as a voice here. The drafting hazard the header poses is unchanged either way.

Wesley abridges Henry three times in this one chapter — at key 1 on the fifty days and the mountain, at keys 11 and 12 on the bounds and the two intimations, and at key 16 on the whole sermon-staging of the theophany, in places almost word for word. This is the densest concentration of the pattern I have seen in a single chapter, and it creates a specific hazard for the tiling: Henry's key-9 block and Wesley's key-10 block cover the same ground but fall in different entries under the span '9-10', while Henry's key-16 and Wesley's key-16 fall in the same one. Where a Henry-Wesley pair straddles an entry boundary, the material must be used once and the other entry left to its remaining voices, or the same sentences appear twice in the chapter under two different attributions.

Length control regressed sharply here: four of nine entries needed three or more trim passes, and entry 1 took four passes to come down from 717. The diagnosis from note 998 fits exactly — this chapter's bulk is Calvin and Henry each developing long arguments alone, with Ellicott adding a third independent long note, and note 969 has nothing to compress where three voices are each saying something different at length. The passes that actually worked were structural, not lexical: dropping whole subordinate ideas (Clarke's Jupiter medals, the Sinai place-names, Ellicott's veil analogy) moved 20 to 45 words each, where sentence-level tightening moved two or three. Recording the working rule: when an entry overshoots by more than about forty words, stop shaving and cut a whole idea instead.

JFB stride bug, 36th confirmation. Three blocks at keys 5, 17 and 23, all displaced, all from Deuteronomy 1-2: the presumptuous attempt to go up after the spies and the repulse by the Amorites and Amalekites, the passage along Edom's border and buying meat and water for money, and Elath and Ezion-geber with the Emims and Horims. Donor advances monotonically and Deuteronomy precedes Joshua canonically — twelfth confirmation of the lag model. The spacing is 12 then 6, IRREGULAR. That matters for the stride question: within this batch, exodus 19 gave a perfect six and joshua 4 gives an irregular gap, exactly as deuteronomy 29 and numbers 15 did in the previous batch. Four recent chapters, two regular and two irregular. My deuteronomy 29 note treated the perfect stride plus byte-identical emissions as evidence for a fixed step; that reading cannot be sustained across all four, and the honest position remains that the spacing is unexplained.

Bearing on the outstanding joshua 7 caveat. I have been carrying an unresolved note from before compaction that joshua 7 was seen to have a Joshua 13 donor, which would break the lag model by putting the donor AFTER the target. Joshua 4's donor is Deuteronomy 1-2, the immediately preceding book, which is consistent with the model but does not settle joshua 7 either way. Recording explicitly that the joshua 7 case still needs an actual re-read of its JFB blocks rather than inference from neighbouring chapters, and that it remains the only reported counter-example to the lag model in thirty-six confirmations.

Clarke's chapter-argument header standing alone again, exactly as at numbers 15 key 1: his key-1 block here is nothing but the running summary of the whole chapter, verse ranges and all, with no comment on verse 1 itself. Since entry 1 is the single key 1, he has no substantive block in the span and is excluded. Taken with the exodus 19 case, where the same header was followed by real comment on the third month and the name of the mountain, the pattern is now clear: Clarke opens a chapter with his argument, and whether that block is empty depends entirely on whether he then goes on to the verse. The test must be applied to what follows the header, never to the header itself — and where the first key stands alone as its own entry, the exclusion is common enough to expect.

A cross-entry duplication hazard caught in drafting, worth recording as a rule. Gill at key 9 and Henry at key 20 independently make the same striking connection — that the stones John the Baptist pointed at when he said God could raise up children of these stones may be these very stones, Bethabara being the house of passage. Those keys fall in different entries (2-9 and 19-24), so nothing in the tiling or the validators would have caught the repetition; only noticing it while writing prevented the same conceit appearing twice in one chapter under two attributions. Same hazard as the Henry-Wesley pairs at exodus 19, but harder to see, since here the two voices arrive at the point independently rather than one abridging the other. Worth a habit: when a striking image appears in one entry, check whether any other voice in the chapter reaches it too.

Two commentators give incompatible totals for the eastern tribes without either acknowledging the other. Ellicott works from the last census and reaches a hundred and ten thousand five hundred and eighty for the two and a half tribes (Reuben 43,730; Gad 40,500; half Manasseh 26,350), concluding that more than half stayed behind. Gill states flatly that a hundred and thirty thousand were liable. Clarke, on a third basis, puts those who stayed at seventy thousand five hundred and eighty. Calvin says only that the forty thousand were a third or thereabouts. Presented in the entry as the disagreement it is rather than harmonised, since no source in the catena resolves it.

Length control recovered sharply from exodus 19 in the same batch: five of six entries landed in range on the first draft (593, 590, 629, 417 and one at 644 after a single light pass), and only the last entry needed real trimming, by 61 words in two passes. The difference from exodus 19 is the one note 998 predicts — joshua 4 is a chapter of many short competing notes with two long voices rather than three or four long ones, so there is redundancy for note 969 to work on. The note-1018 rule also held: in the one entry that overshot, cutting two whole clauses moved 28 words where the preceding sentence-level pass had moved 4.

DECISIVE on the Jamieson misalignment: stride 6 confirmed, and the pointer stall caught in the act. Numbers 24 carries Jamieson, Fausset and Brown at keys 3, 9, 15 and 21 — stride 6, offset 3, four members, the cleanest arithmetic yet seen. The content settles the mechanism. Key 3 carries Jamieson on NUMBERS 3 (the consecration of Levi as substitutes for the first-born, Num 3:12-13). Keys 9, 15 and 21 then carry the SAME block repeated BYTE-IDENTICALLY three times (Num 3:15, the Levite census counted from a month old). So the index advanced exactly once and then stalled, re-emitting its last block at every subsequent stride position. This is the same stall observed at the tail of acts 21 (Acts 1:14 repeated once), but here it is sustained across three consecutive members, which rules out coincidence. Combined with the two monotonic walks already logged (1peter 1: Gal 6:8 to Eph 1:8 across five members; acts 21: Luke 24 to Acts 1:14 across six), the picture is now: a single index walking a wrong region of the Jamieson tree at a fixed stride of 6, sometimes advancing and sometimes stalling. Chapter 44 of the misalignment. The re-fetch is worth doing and the mechanism is now specific enough to test against.

Chrome measurement seven, and a CORRECTION to the character figures in the six earlier chrome notes. Measured consistently — from the nav strip that begins the block to the next <strong> voice head — the chrome in numbers 24 (key 25, inside the Charles Ellicott block) is 992 words, 30,341 characters, 126 newlines. Re-measuring exodus 2 the same way gives 992 words, 30,341 characters, 126 newlines: BYTE-IDENTICAL. The '24,9xx chars' figures recorded for 1peter 1, genesis 9, numbers 6, romans 1, acts 21 and exodus 2 were measured from a later offset and understate the block; the earlier claim of a 'character spread of 7' across measurements should be read as an artefact of inconsistent slicing, not as real variation. The correct statement is that the chrome is a fixed, invariant 30,341-character payload. Also: this is the SECOND consecutive chapter in which the chrome is NON-TERMINAL — it lands mid-key on Ellicott, and John Wesley follows it cleanly at the same key 25, so Ellicott's comment on 24:25 survives but anything he wrote after it in that block is lost. A smaller nav tail ('Next: Numbers Chapter 25 Sacred Texts | Bible ...') also trails Gill's block at the same key, as it did in exodus 2; that one is only about twenty words and does not distort the budget.

Clarke's seventeen-point rehabilitation of Balaam, against the whole rest of the catena. At 24:25 Adam Clarke closes the Balaam cycle with seventeen numbered propositions arguing that 'the badness of this man's character has been very far overrated' and that 'it does not appear that he was either a hypocrite, false prophet, or a sorcerer in the common acceptation of the term, and that he risked even life itself in following and fulfilling the will of the Lord.' His grounds: Balaam knew and worshipped the true God; was a true prophet in the habit of receiving oracles; used no spells, necromancy or evocation of spirits even in view of the camp; sought God's will by the means God himself prescribed (supplication, prayer, sacrifice of clean beasts); told Balak everything God said although he knew it would enrage him; and refused rewards 'even of the most extensive kind'. He allows only covetousness, and even that with the parenthesis '(and who thinks this a sin?)'. On the fatal counsel of Numbers 31:16 and Revelation 2:14 he proposes that it may have been no more than advice 'to form alliances with this people, especially through the medium of matrimonial connections; and seeing they could not conquer them, to endeavor to make them their friends' — a bad doctrine, he grants, but not the deliberate snare tradition assumes; and he lays the ultimate blame on Israel, since it was the Moabitish women and not Balaam who called the people to sacrifice, so that to fall at so slight an invitation 'argued great degeneracy'. This runs against Calvin at every point in the chapter (the coaxing of God by delusive means, the servile self-excuse, the man forcibly drawn where he was unwilling to go) and against Henry, who reads the preface as vain-glory and the parting advice as soliciting hell. Notable as the sharpest single-voice revisionism met in this catena so far, and it is argued rather than asserted.

The word shethum ('whose eyes are open') divides the catena five ways, and Clarke presses the point twice. (1) Clarke argues flatly for SHUT, since the following verse uses a different verb (galah) for opening, and reads it as Balaam's own confession that he had once been unable to see even the angel in his path, 'once I was blind, but now I see'; at 24:15 he returns to it, calling it strange that our version renders the word open 'when the very sound of the word expresses the sense', praising the Vulgate's cujus obturatus est oculus, and blaming the Targum for a false paraphrase that most versions then followed. (2) Wesley glosses 'who had his eyes shut, but now open'. (3) Keil renders 'the man with closed eye' without argument. (4) Henry reports both readings and turns the ambiguity homiletically: many have their eyes open who have not their hearts open. (5) Ellicott declines to decide, noting the form occurs nowhere else in Scripture and that if the root is identified with satham it means to close, but that the next verse settles the sense either way, Balaam being in an ecstasy with the outer eye shut and the inner preternaturally opened. (6) Calvin rejects BOTH standard options — the pluperfect 'had his eyes closed' as too poor (it merely recalls that his ass saw more clearly than he did) and 'whose eye was open' as unnatural — and proposes a third sense, that the eyes were HIDDEN, 'because in their secret vision they have more than human power', citing the same root at Psalm 51:6 for hidden wisdom. Calvin also passes on from Jarchi the report that some Hebrews inferred from this verse that Balaam was blind in one eye.

Calvin and Keil take exactly opposite sides of the same two options on 'Amalek was the first of the nations', and each dismisses the other's view by name or in substance. Keil rejects priority in age, power and celebrity — naming Knobel as holding it — on the ground that 'this Bedouin tribe, which descended from a grandson of Esau, was surpassed by many other nations' in all three respects, and refers the title instead to Amalek as the first heathen nation to open the conflict of the nations against Israel. Calvin calls that very reading 'poor and unsatisfactory' and finds instead an indirect rebuke of Amalekite pride: they claimed precedence over other nations on the score of antiquity, 'as if they had been created together with the sun and moon', so that the phrase is ironical and makes a pointed comparison between the boasted origin and the slaughter awaiting them at the end. Clarke sides with the antiquity reading ('the most ancient and most powerful of all the nations or states then within the view of Balaam'). Ellicott alone weighs the philology: reshith more often denotes priority in time and its counterpart aharith (latter end) supports that, while the earlier reference to Amalekite kings favours rank, and he allows that both may be intended. Wesley reports both without deciding and adds that the defeat of Amalek was 'an earnest and firstfruit of the large harvest of victories' to come.

Four voices identify the Kenites with Midian and Keil refutes all four from Old Testament usage. Wesley: the kindred of Jethro, but specifically the part 'mingled with the Amalekites and Midianites', not those dwelling with Israel, to whom the words do not apply. Gill: expressly NOT the family of Jethro (against Aben Ezra, Jarchi and Abendana), since those were not a people by themselves but encamped with Israel and went into Canaan, later remaining with Judah as Rechabites; he allows only a distinct people of the same original stock settled near and afterwards among the Amalekites. Clarke, following Dr Dodd: Kenites and Midianites are the same, or at least confederate tribes, since Jethro is called a priest of Midian in Exodus and a Kenite in Judges; but Clarke also notes the difficulty that the Midianites here lived close to the Dead Sea, far from Jethro's Midian near Horeb, and suggests a migrated colony. Calvin: 'By the Kenites I understand the Midianites', and it is 'altogether unreasonable' to refer the name to Jethro's descendants, since barely forty years had passed since Jethro left his son with Moses and his was one small family, whereas a people already celebrated is in view; Calvin assigns the breaking of their power to Gideon's three hundred. Against all of them, Keil argues that the Old Testament knows no Kenites whatever except those who went to Canaan with Hobab, so that the distinction between Canaanitish and Midianitish Kenites (Michaelis, Hengstenberg) has no sufficient ground, and 'the hypothesis that by the Kenites we are to understand the Midianites is as unfounded as' the rest. A rare case of the grammatical-historical school arguing from exhaustive lexical survey against a consensus of the other three schools.

Clarke denies at 24:19 the very connections Ellicott and Henry build at 24:17, and his argument against Bar-cochba is a good one. On 24:17 Ellicott collects the external evidence for a messianic reading — both Targums, Ibn Ezra's report that many interpret of the Messiah, the pretender under Adrian taking the name Bar-cochab ('son of a star'), and the Magi's 'we have seen his star in the East' — and Henry supplies a transmission mechanism for the last, that Balaam was one of the children of the east and a tradition preserved in that country may have set the wise men looking. Two verses later Clarke denies all of it: 'I cannot think that the meteoric star which guided the wise men of the east to Bethlehem can be intended here; nor do I think that Peter refers to this prophecy when he calls Christ the day star; nor that Revelation 2:28... nor Revelation 22:16... refers at all to this prophecy of Balaam. Nor do I think that the false Christ who rose in the time of Adrian, and who called himself Barcochab... did refer to this prophecy.' His ground against Bar-cochba is logical rather than assertive: 'the Son of the star is not The Star that should arise, but at the utmost a descendant; and then, to vindicate his right to the Jewish throne, he must show that the person who was called the star... had actually reigned before him' — that is, the title as chosen would defeat the claim it was meant to support. In place of the messianic-star chain Clarke offers only that stars were general titles of royalty among the Asiatics, illustrating with Roxana (Persian Roushen, splendour) and Esther (Persian Sitareh, whence our word star).

Calvin and Gill independently reach the same obscure historical anchor for 'ships from the coast of Chittim'. Both note that Chittim is used generally of Greece but transferred by Scripture to Italy, and both settle the ambiguity by the same event: the Roman embassy that stopped Antiochus. Calvin, on Daniel 11:30, says the ships of Chittim there 'must be taken for those of Italy or Rome... because the angel there predicts that the ships of Chittim would come, which should overcome, and render frustrate the efforts of Antiochus; which was plainly brought to pass by the mission of Popilius' — the famous circle drawn in the sand at Eleusis in 168 BC. Gill reaches it from the other end, through the Targums (Jonathan reads Italy, the Jerusalem Targum reads the Roman legions), and puts it memorably: 'ships from Cittim design Romans in Grecian ships; for in such were the Roman ambassadors carried, who distressed Antiochus, king of Syria'. Both then conclude that Greeks and Romans are together intended here. Ellicott independently notes that the Vulgate renders the verse Venient in trieribus de Italia and identifies the Kittim with the Romans at Daniel 11:30; Wesley says the name means Macedonia sometimes, Italy sometimes, 'and sometimes both, as in this place'; Clarke reports Calmet contending strongly for Macedonia alone but follows Ainsworth in allowing both. A four-way convergence on a single second-century BC diplomatic incident is unusual enough to record.

Two source-critical remarks worth keeping. (1) Ellicott, at 24:24, raises a question no other voice in the catena asks: 'There is no evidence as to the manner in which Balaam's prophecies came into the hands of the Israelites. It is possible that he may have communicated them to Moses, in the expectation of receiving from him the reward which he had failed to obtain from Balak, or, if captured, in the hope of thereby saving his life.' A rare instance of a nineteenth-century commentator in this set asking how a text got where it is rather than only what it means. (2) Keil, at 24:25, makes a small grammatical point with large consequences: the Hebrew says only that Balaam 'turned towards his place', not that he returned to it (the construction differs from the one that would mean return), 'so that the question, whether he did so, must be determined from other circumstances'. Ellicott independently reaches the same caution — Balaam probably set out intending to go home, but the sequel shows he stayed among the Midianites and perished with them — and Gill allows that he may have reached Mesopotamia and come back again, citing Chaskuni. Clarke and Wesley say he intended Mesopotamia and settled among the Midianites instead. So the whole set treats the chapter's last clause as leaving the question open, which is unusual restraint.

Matthew Henry Concise spliced onto Exposition, now in a fourth book. Numbers 24 carries Henry at only three keys (1, 10 and 15), and at keys 1 and 10 the block contains the full Exposition followed with no break or marker by the corresponding Concise paragraph, restating the same material in compressed form. Previously logged at 1peter 1 key 17, acts 21 key 19, and exodus 2 keys 16 and 23. The pattern now spans four books and both testaments, and in this chapter as in exodus 2 it occurs twice within one chapter. Cost here is only double-counted weight in the word budget, since the two agree in substance; but in acts 21 the Concise passed a materially harsher verdict than the Exposition, so the splice is not always harmless. Belongs in the fetcher, not in per-chapter handling.

Fidelity self-grade A for all six entries of numbers 24. Tiling covers 1-25 exactly, no gaps or overlaps: 1-3 (648w), 4-9 (650w), 10-14 (650w), 15-17 (648w), 18-21 (650w), 22-25 (650w) — all inside the 350-650 window. Voice coverage: entries 1, 10 and 15 name all seven live OT voices (Gill, Henry, Clarke, Ellicott, Calvin, Wesley, Keil and Delitzsch); entries 4-9, 18-21 and 22-25 name the six that actually appear in those ranges, Henry having blocks only at keys 1, 10 and 15. Jamieson excluded as residue at entries 1-3, 4-9, 15-17 and 18-21 (keys 3, 9, 15, 21). Every proposition in the prose is traceable to a named block in data/commentary/cow/numbers/24.json; where a voice is reported as standing alone or against the rest (Keil on the Kenites, Calvin against Keil on Amalek, Clarke on the star chain and on Balaam's character) the claim was checked against every other block in the range before being written. Real usable source words after deducting the 992-word chrome at key 25 and the Jamieson residue: 22,300 across six entries, from a gross size of 24,532.

JFB stride bug, 37th confirmation, and the SECOND same-book case after exodus 19. Only two blocks, at keys 4 and 22, both displaced and both from Genesis 19: key 4 is the two angels at Sodom and the gate as the eastern market and seat of justice, key 22 is Lot lingering and the angels' friendly urgency. Donor advances (19:1 then 19:15-17) and precedes the target within the same book — thirteenth confirmation of the lag model, which now holds in eleven different books and twice within a single book. On the stride question this chapter is silent by construction: two blocks eighteen keys apart cannot distinguish a fixed step from JFB's own sparse coverage, the same limitation recorded at deuteronomy 6. Both excluded.

A disagreement the tiling separated, worth recording because no validator would surface it. Gill's key-3 block opens by assuming the command came in a dream or vision of the night, and Henry assumes the same; Keil's key-2 block denies it flatly — 'not in a vision of the night, however, of which there is not a syllable in the text.' Those keys fall in adjacent but different entries, so the two sides never meet in the prose. I carried Gill's assumption in entry 3 without attributing a counter-position, since Keil is not a voice in that entry. Same class of hazard as the joshua 4 duplication (note 1033), but the inverse: there the risk was saying one thing twice, here it is presenting one side of a dispute as settled because the other side is filed one entry away. Both argue for reading the whole chapter's blocks before tiling, not just the span in hand.

Clarke's chapter-argument header appears again at key 1 and is FOLLOWED by substantive comment, on the emphatic Hebrew of 'God did tempt Abraham', on the Septuagint and Symmachus, and on the Targum of Jonathan. So Clarke is kept here. Across four chapters the tally is now two empty (numbers 15, joshua 4) and two substantive (exodus 19, genesis 22), which confirms note 1032's rule and shows the split is close to even — the header is no predictor either way, and the test has to be applied every time to what follows it.

Wesley abridges Henry four times in this chapter — at key 1 on the trial and the tempting, at key 2 on the ladder of the command, at key 3 on the steps of obedience, and at keys 13 and 14 on the ram and Jehovah-jireh. That is denser than the three instances at exodus 19 (note 1017), and here the pairs straddle entry boundaries in a way that needed watching: Henry's key-1 block runs through v2 while Wesley's key-2 block carries the same material filed one key later, and Henry's key-11 block runs through vv13-14 where Wesley's key-13 and key-14 blocks carry it again. In both cases I used the material once, in the entry where the second voice is filed, and left the earlier entry to its other content. The rule that worked: when a Henry-Wesley pair straddles a boundary, place the shared material in the LATER entry, since that is where the abridging voice is filed and where the verses it treats actually fall.

Length control on the largest chapter of the batch: four of nine entries needed trimming, but only one needed more than a single pass, and every successful cut was structural rather than lexical, per note 1018. The cuts that moved the needle were whole discarded ideas — Calvin's James guard at entry 1 (43 words), Clarke's Jupiter-medals digression's genesis-22 analogue in entry 4, Henry's thousands-and-millions moral at entry 15 (35 words). Sentence-level tightening again moved two or three words at a time and was not worth the passes. Also worth recording: on a chapter this dense I cut ideas at the OUTLINE stage for entries 4, 15 and 19 before drafting, and those three came in at 633, 611 and 573 with no trim passes at all. Pre-emptive selection beats post-hoc trimming, which is what note 998 was reaching for.

JFB stride bug, 38th confirmation, and the largest single-chapter cluster yet: SEVEN displaced blocks, at keys 6, 12, 24, 48, 54, 60 and 72, all from 1 Chronicles 3-4. Key 6 is the sons of David and Amnon's expectations; key 12 the eleven sons born at Jerusalem; key 24 the dislocated text after Jeconiah with Davidson's proposed rearrangement; key 48 Caleb's grandfather the Kenezite; key 54 Bithiah the daughter of Pharaoh; key 60 the potters of Netaim and Gedera; key 72 the Simeonite cities David assigned to Judah. Donor position advances monotonically through 1 Chronicles 3:1 to 4:31, and 1 Chronicles precedes Nehemiah canonically — fourteenth confirmation of the lag model. Spacing is 6, 12, 24, 6, 6, 12, which is irregular, but note that this chapter's scrape keys are themselves sparse, so the gaps may be an artefact of where JFB has any block at all.

NOT ATTEMPTED — blocked, and I am recording why rather than starting it. Nehemiah 7 is the register of returning exiles: 22 scrape keys across 73 verses, 5,367 usable source words, and no contiguity, so under the tiling rule it must be written as single-key entries with no ranges (the convention already used at ezra 2 and 1chronicles 1, which have one entry per source key and declare no pericopes). Sixteen of the 22 keys fall under 200 source words and would need the thin-verse exemption. That much is merely laborious. The blocker is what the JFB exclusions leave behind. Keys 12, 24, 48 and 60 contain NOTHING BUT a displaced JFB block, so once it is excluded they have zero usable source words and no entry can honestly be written for them at all. Key 54 is left with twelve words after exclusion — a note that some of Kennicott's and De Rossi's manuscripts read Mehira for Mehida — against a thin floor of 120 prose words. Keys 34 (16 words, distinguishing one Elam from another), 19 (24 words, a variant reading of a number) and 33 (49 words, on the word 'other' before Nebo) are in the same position. Key 8 is itself a bare cross-reference of the Clarke kind, saying that since the chapter is almost identical to Ezra 2 nothing need be added and the reader is referred there. Nine of 22 entries therefore cannot be written without manufacturing filler, which is precisely what the thin exemption exists to prevent (see the note above THIN_SOURCE_MAX in validate-synthesis.py and docs/plans/cow-synthesis-quality-audit.md). This needs an owner decision of the same kind numbers 31 is waiting on: either the chapter is dropped from the repair queue, or its four JFB-only keys are allowed to be omitted outright, or a lower floor is defined for register chapters. Nothing was written to the data tree; the pick is released.

JFB stride bug, 39th confirmation, and the THIRD same-book case after exodus 19 and genesis 22. A single block at key 1, on the broad-tailed Eastern sheep whose tail weighs fifteen pounds and upwards and which usually bled on the Jewish altars — that is Leviticus 3:9, the fat tail of the peace offering, displaced into Leviticus 21. Donor precedes target within the same book; fifteenth confirmation of the lag model. With only one block, no stride can be inferred, the same limitation recorded at deuteronomy 6 and genesis 22. Excluded.

Clarke's chapter-argument header at key 1, followed by substantive comment on the priests not assisting at a laying-out. Running tally across five chapters: substantive at exodus 19, genesis 22 and leviticus 21; empty at numbers 15 and joshua 4. Three to two, close to even, which is what note 1049 predicted and confirms that the header carries no information about whether the block is usable — the test has to be applied every time to what follows it.

A live disagreement between two commentators about whether the chapter's own rule still binds, worth flagging because it is unusually direct. Clarke on the blemishes says 'Let no man say this is a part of the Mosaic law, and we are not bound by it. It is an eternal law, founded on reason, propriety, common sense, and absolute necessity,' and at verse 20 turns it on his own communion — formerly the Church of England was cautious about admitting men with gross personal defects, 'but now we find the hump-backed, the jolt-headed, bandy-legged, club-footed, one-eyed, etc., priests even of her high places. Why do our prelates ordain such?' Henry, at the same verses, says the reverse in as many words: under the gospel the blemished may thank God they are not thereby excluded from the ministry, since 'there is many a healthful beautiful soul lodged in a crazy deformed body,' and the disqualifying blemish now is a reigning vice. Carried as a debate rather than harmonised. Also recorded because the two positions sit in different entries under the tiling (16-19 and 20-24) — Henry has no key past 16, so his side had to be stated in the earlier entry and Clarke's outburst in the later one, and a reader of only one entry sees only one side. Third instance of the hazard noted at joshua 4 and genesis 22.

Three commentators give three different totals for the disqualifying blemishes, none acknowledging the others: Clarke a hundred and twenty on Ainsworth's authority, itemised by body part; Gill a hundred and forty; Ellicott a hundred and forty-two, from the second-Temple registers. Presented as the disagreement it is. Ellicott also preserves the procedure behind his figure — a chamber in the Temple court where the Sanhedrin examined every priest, the rejected putting on black and going away in silence while the accepted put on white and feasted, and the rejected then being employed to select wood sound enough for the altar. That last detail is the kind of thing the catena carries and nothing else in the corpus does.

Jamieson stride-6 confirmed a FOURTH time, and a THIRD monotonic walk — this one in the New Testament. 1 Corinthians 11 carries Jamieson, Fausset and Brown at keys 2, 8, 14, 20, 26 and 32: stride 6, offset 2, six members. The content is a monotonic walk through ACTS 22, Paul's defence on the stairs, in canonical order: key 8 = Acts 22:3 (brought up at the feet of Gamaliel, 'the strictest form of traditional Judaism', 'a zealot'); key 14 = Acts 22:8 ('the Nazarene'); key 20 = the covenant clause; key 26 = Acts 22:17-18 (the temple vision, 'after his conversion he kept up his connection with the temple as before'); key 32 = Acts 22:22 (the fury at the mention of a mission to the Gentiles, and the protection of the Roman officer). Key 2 is a 26-word fragment. The tally is now: 1peter 1 (five members, Gal 6:8 to Eph 1:8), acts 21 (six members, Luke 24 to Acts 1:14 with the last block repeated), numbers 24 (four members, Numbers 3 with the block repeated byte-identically three times), and now 1corinthians 11 (six members, Acts 22 throughout). Four chapters, one stride, three walks and one stall. Note that acts 21's residue walked ACTS 1 while this chapter's walks ACTS 22 — the wrong region differs per chapter, so the pointer is not parked at a fixed global offset. Chapter 45 of the misalignment.

Three DIFFERENT residue mechanisms in one chapter, plus the eighth chrome measurement. (1) TERTULLIAN at key 1 is Against Marcion book 5 on 1 CORINTHIANS 15, the resurrection of the body — right epistle, wrong chapter. A chapter misfile, not a stride walk. Declarable, since VOICE_LABELS carries 'Tertullian' as an exact full name; declared in excluded_voices on entry 1-3. (2) CYRIL OF JERUSALEM at key 3 is Catechetical Lecture 13, on the Cross and Golgotha — nothing to do with 'the head of every man is Christ'. This one CANNOT be declared, because VOICE_LABELS carries the short form 'Cyril' and the regex requires 'Cyril' immediately followed by a colon, which never matches the head 'Cyril of Jerusalem:'. Dropped SILENTLY, as the defect requires. (3) Cyril at keys 23 AND 24 is genuine (Mystagogical Catechesis 4, on the Eucharist, quoting 1 Cor 11:23 directly) but key 24 repeats key 23 BYTE-IDENTICALLY — a duplicate, not a misfile. It was left in place since Cyril is used in that entry and the only cost is a small inflation of the measured source. (4) CHROME: key 34, inside the Charles Ellicott block, 995 words / 30,497 chars / 126 newlines, cutting Ellicott off immediately after 'They are quite general, whenever I come'. The newline count is identical to the exodus 2 and numbers 24 measurements (126); the character count differs by 156 because the nav strip carries the book name, and '1 Corinthians  1Co  10 ...' is longer than 'Numbers  Num  23 ...'. So the CSS/JS payload is invariant and only the nav strip varies with book-name length. THIRD consecutive non-terminal chrome: A.T. Robertson follows it cleanly at the same key.

THE VOICE_LABELS DEFECT IS NOW MEASURABLE, and this chapter is the strongest case yet for fixing it. 1 Corinthians 11 carries four voices outside the standard eight: Tertullian (key 1), Cyril of Jerusalem (3, 23, 24), John Chrysostom (2, 17, 28) and John Lightfoot (thirteen keys). Against the VOICE_LABELS regex in scripts/synthesis_qa.py these behave in three different ways. 'Tertullian' is listed as an exact full name and the head is exactly 'Tertullian:', so it matches and can be declared. 'Chrysostom', 'Lightfoot' and 'Robertson' are listed as SHORT forms, but because the regex looks for the label followed by a colon, and the heads are 'John Chrysostom:', 'John Lightfoot:' and 'A.T. Robertson:', the short form still matches the tail of the full head — so these three work by accident. 'Cyril' is the one that breaks: the head is 'Cyril of Jerusalem:', where the label is followed by ' of Jerusalem' and not by a colon, so the regex never matches and the voice can never be declared in excluded_voices. That is the whole defect, stated precisely: it is not that short forms are used, but that ONE short form happens to be a prefix of a longer name rather than a suffix. The fix is one line — replace 'Cyril' with 'Cyril of Jerusalem' in VOICE_LABELS, or make the regex tolerate an intervening qualifier. Until then every Cyril residue block must be dropped silently and cannot be audited. Twenty-one batches old and now blocking real work: this chapter had a genuine Cyril at two keys and a residue Cyril at a third, and only the silent drop could distinguish them.

Four voices independently reconstruct the Corinthian abuse, and they split two against two on its cause. CHRYSOSTOM, nearest in time, describes an institution decaying from within: as the first three thousand had all things common, an outflowing of that communion descended to later believers, who opened their tables on stated days so that after the communion of the Mysteries all went to a common entertainment, the rich bringing provisions and inviting the destitute; the corruption came from the party spirit, which is why Paul had put his own name at the head of the I-am-of-Paul list, to tear the custom up by the root.
