CALVIN follows him on the origin but adds external evidence — Tertullian for the antiquity of the agape, and Pliny's letter to Trajan reporting that the Bithynian Christians said they used to depart and reassemble to take an innocent repast in common — and adds his own conjecture that the agape derived from the sacrificial feasts of Jews and Gentiles alike, Christians correcting the faults while keeping a resemblance. Against this, CLARKE and LIGHTFOOT independently reconstruct a DOCTRINAL corruption: false teachers made the Corinthians keep the Supper exactly as the Jews kept the passover, so the sacrament became an appendix to an ordinary meal. Lightfoot presses it furthest, arguing at 11:26 that the Passover haggadah was a set declaration of the deliverance from Egypt and that the Judaizers kept that declaration in the Eucharist 'as if the Eucharist were instituted and superadded only for that commemoration', and again at 11:29 that they 'would see nothing of the body of Christ in the Eucharist, or of his death, their eyes being too intent upon the commemoration of the Passover', so that 'they retained the old leaven of Judaism in this new Passover'; at 11:33 he denies that 'tarry one for another' sanctions those paschal ante-suppers. Clarke reaches the same picture and calls them 'mongrel Christians'. Two independent English commentators, a century apart, converging on a Judaizing reconstruction that neither Greek father nor Genevan reformer entertained.

The chapter's central crux divides the catena on BOTH of its clauses, and Ellicott calls them perhaps the two most difficult passages in the New Testament. On POWER ON HER HEAD: Ellicott and Lightfoot agree, independently and against everyone else, that the Greek word always denotes a power one holds oneself and never a power exercised over one — Lightfoot saying it is so in Matthew, John and 'elsewhere a thousand times', Ellicott calling this the fatal objection to the received view and citing Paul's own repeated use in this epistle. Ellicott then identifies the power with the woman's long hair, her glory, noting that Callistratus twice uses the word of an abundance of hair and that Samson would give it force for Jewish readers, and finding it eminently Pauline to call the badge of subordination a power. Against them Calvin, Clarke and Robertson take the word as metonymy for the token of ANOTHER'S authority, Calvin citing the figure directly, Clarke citing Theophylact and Photius, Robertson conceding that as we see it the veil is more a sign of subjection than of authority. On BECAUSE OF THE ANGELS there are five answers: Wesley, Robertson and Clarke (following Pearce) take them for holy angels present in worship, Robertson adding that the angels themselves veil their faces before Jehovah and Clarke supporting the Jewish notion from Ecclesiastes, from the charge before the elect angels, and from Agrippa's oration in Josephus; Calvin knows and rejects as 'too forced' the view that ministers are meant, since Malachi calls priests angels; LIGHTFOOT says that if the power is a veil then the angels are DEVILS, so called in this same epistle; and ELLICOTT refers the phrase to the fall of the angels in Genesis 6, where the Greek has angeloi, arguing that Paul uses the legend as an argument with those who believed it without endorsing it, and against Meyer keeps them good angels, since the point is that they should not be tempted. Clarke reports a sixth view, Lightfoot's own, that the angels are the paranymphs who sought out spouses — which the truncated Lightfoot block in this catena does not reach.

Ellicott argues in four numbered steps that the body not discerned is THE CHURCH, and no one else in the catena reaches that reading. Dropping the words 'the Lord's' as unsupported by manuscript evidence, he argues: (1) the verb means to arrive at a right estimate of the character or quality of a thing; (2) the fault Paul condemns is that the Corinthians treated these gatherings as opportunities for individual indulgence and not as Church assemblies, failing to estimate the meetings as corporate and themselves as members rather than isolated individuals; (3) referring the words to a physical presence 'is to divorce them violently from their surroundings', and would make the practical remedy given at 11:33-34 no remedy at all, besides which, if the physical body were meant, both 'the Lord's' and 'and the blood' would surely have been added, since non-recognition of the blood would be as great an offence; (4) Paul never uses 'body' of Christ's physical body without clear indication, whereas 'the Body' for the Church is frequent and occurs a few verses earlier on this very subject. Against this: LIGHTFOOT makes it an act of the understanding, a true judgment of the nature and signification of the sacrament, and identifies the offenders as the Judaizers; CLARKE agrees with Lightfoot; ROBERTSON keeps to the verb (our 'discriminate') and says the eating probes the heart; GILL, BARNES and WESLEY take it as putting a right difference between this bread and common food; and CYRIL, at 11:23, stands at the far end — since Christ himself said 'this is my Body', 'who shall dare to doubt any longer?' Set against Ellicott's gloss on the same words, that to those who first heard them they implied 'not that a physical presence was about to be perpetuated, but rather that there was now something for them which would in after ages console them for a physical absence', this is the sharpest cross-school opposition in the chapter, and it runs between a fourth-century catechist and a nineteenth-century Anglican on the same clause.

Three textual observations in this chapter carry confessional freight, and two of the commentators say so outright. (1) At 11:24 Ellicott and Robertson agree that 'broken' is no part of the text — Ellicott saying the insertion of 'take, eat' was probably made to produce verbal identity with Matthew and 'broken' added as explanatory, Robertson that the received reading is clearly not genuine, that Luke's 'given' carries the real idea, and making the theological point that 'the body of Jesus was not broken. The bread was broken, but not the body of Jesus.' (2) At 11:27 Ellicott states that the entire weight of manuscript evidence favours 'or' rather than 'and', and adds the charge that the conjunction 'was probably retained in the English version lest the disjunctive or might seem to favour the practice of receiving in one kind only' — an accusation of confessional motive against the translators, and one that lands directly on Calvin's argument two verses earlier that to distribute the bread without the cup is to mutilate Christ's institution, that obeying half a command is to make sport of it, and that the plea that Christ spoke only to the Apostles is 'exceedingly childish' since Paul here addresses men and women indiscriminately. (3) At 11:29 Ellicott removes both 'unworthily' and 'the Lord's', Robertson agreeing on the former. The three readings together shift the verse away from every use that later controversy made of it, and the two who press them hardest are the two grammarians.

Ellicott is doing something in this chapter that the rest of the catena does not attempt, and it is worth recording as a whole. (a) At 11:4 he observes that Paul's ruling reverses the practice he was raised in, since the Jewish man prayed veiled in the Tallith to confess his unworthiness to look on God, and credits him with 'a profound insight into human nature... how an external symbol would infallibly tend to modify doctrine', so that keeping the custom might have hindered the recognition of every soul's direct communication with the Father. (b) At 11:16 he draws two general morals: that as with slavery, Christianity did not efface recognised social arrangements by sudden revolution but leavened the world gradually, coming 'not to unsex woman, but to raise, dignify, and ennoble her as woman — to abolish for ever her real wrongs, but not to yield to a revolutionary clamour for imaginary rights'; and that the temporary application of the rule has been universally kept while the eternal principle behind it has been forgotten, which he takes as evidence of the wisdom that withheld the apostolic writers from laying down minute directions for worship, 'for men would, in a servile obedience to rules, have soon and completely forgotten the living principles on which they were based.' (c) At 11:18 he turns an exegetical difficulty into method: 'this is not a treatise, but a letter, and not only a letter, but an answer to a letter,' so that if we had the letter it replies to, much that puzzles us would be plain. (d) At 11:23 he mounts an evidential argument nobody else makes — if the Betrayal and Crucifixion are not historical, how is the existence of the Eucharistic feast to be accounted for, in an epistle whose authenticity has never been disputed, among Jews who spoke of the wine they drank as blood; a conspiracy like Catiline's might have chosen such a symbol, but 'such a band of men as the early Christians certainly could not of their own thought have made such a choice'; and 'Christendom was not an afterthought of the Apostles, but the forethought of the Lord.' Four distinct kinds of argument — psychological, sociological, methodological and evidential — in one chapter from one voice.

Lightfoot is a NEW voice for this loop, genuine, and capped at 200 words throughout — with OCR damage on top. John Lightfoot's Horae Hebraicae et Talmudicae appears at thirteen keys in 1 Corinthians 11 and is genuine at twelve of them (key 3 is residue, commenting on 1 Cor 12:3 on calling Jesus accursed). School mapping follows the established convention found in existing NT tags files: puritan-evangelical, five prior hits against one stray. Two defects: (1) EVERY substantial Lightfoot block is cut at exactly 200 words, the same fetch cap that truncates Keil throughout the Old Testament chapters. Because Lightfoot's method is to quote a rabbinic source at length before drawing his conclusion, the cap frequently removes the conclusion — most damagingly at key 10, where the block breaks off just as he begins 'if I were of opinion that the apostle treated here of public assemblies only, I would render his words to this sense', so that his actual proposal is lost, and Clarke's report elsewhere in the same catena of Lightfoot's paranymph reading has nothing in the Lightfoot block to check it against. (2) OCR DAMAGE: the Hebrew and Greek in these blocks is badly mangled (key 25 opens 'MIND NT VN What* is giving? Behold, all my goods are given to N.', which is a garbled Hebrew citation), and ligatures and quotation marks are corrupted throughout ('ὦ veil' for 'a veil', 'Hwercitations' for 'Exercitations'). Same class of damage as the Bede OCR item already on the owner list. A re-fetch at a higher cap would recover a great deal here: Lightfoot is the only voice in this catena supplying rabbinic parallels, and his reconstruction of the Corinthian fault as Judaizing is one of the chapter's substantive contributions.

Fidelity self-grade A for all ten entries of 1corinthians 11. Tiling covers 1-34 exactly, no gaps or overlaps: 1-3 (647w), 4-6 (650w), 7-10 (645w), 11-16 (650w), 17-19 (650w), 20-22 (603w), 23-24 (646w), 25-26 (641w), 27-29 (650w), 30-34 (645w) — all inside the 350-650 window. Voice coverage: entries 1-3 and 23-24 name all ten voices present in range (Gill, Henry, Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson, Calvin, Wesley, Lightfoot and, respectively, Chrysostom and Cyril); entries 17-19 and 27-29 name nine including Chrysostom; the remaining six name the eight that actually appear. Five schools are represented across the chapter: reformed, puritan-evangelical, wesleyan-arminian, grammatical-historical and eastern-antiochene. Exclusions: Jamieson declared on entries 1-3, 7-10, 11-16, 20-22, 25-26 and 30-34; Tertullian declared on entry 1-3; Cyril at key 3 dropped SILENTLY because the VOICE_LABELS regex cannot match the head 'Cyril of Jerusalem:'. Every proposition in the prose is traceable to a named block in data/commentary/cow/1corinthians/11.json; where a voice is reported as standing alone or against the rest (Ellicott and Lightfoot on exousia, Ellicott on the body as the Church, Lightfoot on the angels as devils, Cyril against Ellicott on presence, Robertson against Ellicott on Luke's dependence) the claim was checked against every other block in the range before being written. Gross size 70,342 usable source words; real usable after deducting the 995-word chrome at key 34 and the Jamieson residue is 67,924, the largest chapter attempted in this loop.

JFB displacement, 40th confirmation, and a new sub-kind. Both JFB blocks in this chapter are FRAGMENTS rather than whole displaced passages. Key 11 is 17 words beginning mid-sentence — 'from the excesses incident to camp life, as well as from habits of personal neglect and impurity' — which belongs to no clause in Judges 4 and reads like the tail of a comment on Numbers 31:19-24 or a Nazirite passage. Key 23 is five words, a bare cross-reference, '(See on Nu 30:2)', and Numbers 30 (vows) has nothing to do with Jabin being subdued. Every previous confirmation (33 chapters) has been a substantial block lifted whole from a donor chapter; this is the first where the displaced material is truncated to a stub. Both keys carry other voices, so both exclusions are clean and the entries lose nothing.

Two source blocks in this chapter end mid-word, independent of the JFB problem. Henry at key 17 stops at 'Lastly, We must suppose she kept her tent as q' — cut off inside a word. Keil at key 21 stops at 'even though there can be no doubt that Jael acted under the influence of religious enthusiasm for the' — cut off before the object. Both are the LAST sentence of an otherwise complete and long block, so the truncation is at the tail of the scrape rather than the head. This differs from the JFB displacement, where the fragment begins mid-sentence. Worth watching whether tail-truncation clusters in the same chapters as head-truncation.

Clarke's chapter-argument header tally, now seven chapters. Judges 4 key 1 carries the header followed by SUBSTANTIVE comment — 'When Ehud was dead - Why not when Shamgar was dead? Does this not intimate that Shamgar was not reckoned in the number of the judges?' That takes the running tally to five substantive against two empty (numbers 15 and joshua 4 stood alone). Close enough to even that the header carries no predictive information at all: it must be read past every time, and Clarke kept or dropped on what follows it, never on the header's presence.

Fourth instance of the tiling hazard the validators cannot catch, and the costliest yet. Henry has only four keys in this chapter — 1, 4, 10, 17 — and his key-10 block runs on through vv12-15, carrying the richest devotional material in the chapter (Deborah's 'this is the day', 'Has not the Lord gone out before thee? Darest not thou follow when thou hast God himself for thy leader?', and the reflection on God crossing hands to put the head on the woman's shoulders). Under the filing rule that material cannot move to the 12-16 entry, because Henry has no key inside that span. The result is that the battle entry (vv12-16) has no puritan-evangelical school at all, while the muster entry carries Henry material about verses it does not cover and therefore cannot use. Previous instances (joshua 4, genesis 22, leviticus 21) were arguments split across a boundary; this one is a whole school silently absent from the chapter's central pericope. The rule is right — moving it would ground prose in a source the entry does not contain — but the cost should be visible, and it argues again for reading the whole catena before fixing the tiling, since a boundary one verse earlier (11-16 instead of 12-16) would not have helped either.

The sharpest multi-sided moral disagreement met so far, and it is staged rather than resolved. On whether Jael was divinely directed: Gill affirms an impulse upon her spirit which its own effect proved to be of God, since it bred not malice but zeal for God's glory; Ellicott calls that assumption, made in order to defend an act of assassination peculiarly terrible and peculiarly treacherous, unwarrantable to the last degree, and tells those who adopt it not to press such private interpretations on others; Keil grants the religious enthusiasm and still denies that either the prophecy of 4:9 or the praise of 5:24 makes the act morally justified. On the verdict itself, Clarke draws a ten-count indictment — breach of a treaty made with sacrifice and oath, breach of hospitality he says she was bound to defend at the hazard of her own life, deliberate and unprovoked murder — and then refuses to give a verdict: I will not justify, I dare not absolutely condemn. Ellicott adds the structural answer to the argument from silence (ancient narrative marks disapproval by a single casual adjective, as Homer does) and rebukes Bishop Wordsworth by name for reading 4:23 as making the work of Jael the work of God. All four positions were carried into the tags as debates at keys 21 and 23 with holders named, and the prose states no side as settled — the leviticus 21 lesson applied deliberately rather than after the fact.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, 31st instance: attached to Ellicott's final block at key 24, which is also the chapter's last key — so non-discriminating, like the seven before numbers 15. The numbers 28 rule (the tail attaches to the end of Ellicott's final block, wherever that falls) still rests on the two discriminating cases, numbers 15 and exodus 19. Gill's separate sacred-texts navigation tail did not appear in this chapter at all, so its attachment rule remains untested.

Length control, eight entries: 645, 644, 639, 558, 641, 646, 647, 644. Five needed a trim pass and all five cuts were structural (note 1018), never lexical: the Delphi-Bees etymology, the Marathon comparison, Henry's broken-reed and idol reflection, the Maccabee-Martel etymology, and a three-voice pile-up on one Hebrew idiom compressed to one voice. The one entry that came in without a trim (vv10-11, 558) was the one where I cut at the outline stage — note 1051 — dropping Ellicott's nine-poles tent description, the Sigar em-Messiah tree, the LXX oak-of-the-covetous and Ewald's swamp before writing a word. The pattern holds across three chapters now: pre-cutting produces a first draft under 600, post-cutting produces a first draft at 670-750 and costs two passes. A new wrinkle appeared at vv4-5: the voices list is derived from source presence, so an entry can pass every validator while listing a voice the prose never names. Keil was listed at key 5 and unused, because his key-5 block's only substantive sentence treats v6. I added a Keil clause grounded in his own transition (her seat securing rights at home, the summons securing them abroad) rather than leaving the badge unsupported. Worth a standing check: after assembling, confirm every name in tags.voices actually appears in that entry's prose.

JAMIESON MISALIGNMENT, FIFTH STRIDE-6 CONFIRMATION AND FOURTH MONOTONIC WALK. Jamieson appears at keys 3, 9, 15, 21 -- stride 6, offset 3, four members, exactly the numbers 24 pattern. Unlike numbers 24 (which advanced once then stalled on byte-identical blocks), this one WALKS monotonically through 2 CORINTHIANS 2-3: key 3 = 2 Cor 2:10, key 9 = 2 Cor 2:15, key 15 = 2 Cor 3:1-2 (letters of recommendation, 'Christians lives are the only religious books the world reads'), key 21 = 2 Cor 3:6-7 (the ministration of death engraven on stones). Running tally of confirmed stride-6 Jamieson residue: 1peter 1 (offset 1, walks Gal 6 to Eph 1), acts 21 (offset 2, walks Luke 24 to Acts 1), numbers 24 (offset 3, Numbers 3, stalled), 1corinthians 11 (offset 2, walks Acts 22), philemon 1 (offset 3, walks 2 Cor 2-3). The wrong region DIFFERS PER CHAPTER, so the pointer is not parked at a fixed global offset. All four Jamieson blocks excluded and declared as residue.

CYRIL OF JERUSALEM RESIDUE AT KEY 25, AND IT POINTS INTO THE SAME WRONG REGION AS THE JAMIESON WALK. The single Cyril block in this chapter is Catechetical Lectures material on 2 Cor 4:4, the god of this world blinding the minds of them that believe not -- nothing to do with Philemon 25. Note the coincidence: the Jamieson walk in this same file runs 2 Cor 2:10 -> 3:7, and the Cyril misfile lands at 2 Cor 4:4, just past the end of that walk. Two INDEPENDENT residue voices in one chapter pointing into the same wrong book and adjacent regions. Dropped SILENTLY rather than declared, because the VOICE_LABELS defect (see separate note) makes 'Cyril of Jerusalem' undeclarable.

VOICE_LABELS SHORT-FORM DEFECT, STILL OPEN, NOW BLOCKING FOR THE SECOND CHAPTER. scripts/synthesis_qa.py builds _LABEL_RE from the VOICE_LABELS short forms joined and followed by \s*:. 'Chrysostom', 'Lightfoot' and 'Robertson' work only by accident, being SUFFIXES of the heads 'John Chrysostom:', 'John Lightfoot:', 'A.T. Robertson:'. 'Cyril' cannot work, because it is a PREFIX of 'Cyril of Jerusalem:' and is followed by ' of Jerusalem', never a colon. One-line fix: list 'Cyril of Jerusalem' instead of 'Cyril', or allow an intervening qualifier before the colon. Until then any chapter with a Cyril of Jerusalem block cannot declare it and must drop it silently. Twenty-two batches open.

NO CHROME AT ALL -- FIRST IN NINE MEASUREMENTS. Every previously measured chapter carried an invariant StudyLight chrome block of 992-995 words / 30,341-30,497 chars / 126 newlines (char count varying only with book-name length in the nav strip). philemon 1 has none anywhere in the file. Since the chrome has appeared in three consecutive non-terminal chapters (exodus 2, numbers 24, 1corinthians 11) and is absent here, its presence is not a function of position in the corpus.

CALVIN RUNS OFF THE END OF THE EPISTLE AT KEY 24. The Calvin block at verse 24 ends his Philemon commentary correctly (the warning drawn from Demas), then prints 'END OF THE COMMENTARIES ON THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON' and continues straight into a translation of Calvin's version of 1 TIMOTHY, running through 1 Tim 1 and into 1 Tim 2:6 before the block is cut. Roughly 500 of the 656 words at that key are 1 Timothy text, not Philemon commentary. Only the opening on Demas was used.

MATTHEW HENRY IS CONCISE THROUGHOUT AND IS SPLICED ACROSS THE WHOLE LETTER. Henry appears at only four keys (1, 8, 15, 23) and every block is Henry's Concise, not the Exposition; the block at key 15 in fact summarises the entire epistle rather than verses 15-16. This is the fifth book in which Matthew Henry Concise has been found spliced in where the Exposition is expected.

CHRYSOSTOM IS GENUINE HERE. Unlike the Cyril block, the three Chrysostom blocks (keys 1, 4, 17) are real Homilies on Philemon and align with their verses. Key 17 is the best of them: he observes that no procedure is so apt to gain a hearing as not to ask everything at once, and that the mention of the injury is held back to the very last, using 'if he hath wronged thee' rather than 'if he hath stolen', so confessing the offence as the wrong of a friend against a friend rather than of a servant.

THE CENTRAL DISPUTE OF THE CHAPTER: WHETHER ONESIMUS WAS A SLAVE AT ALL, AND WHETHER THE LETTER SANCTIONS SLAVERY. Barnes argues at length (a 1,800-word note at v16 and a 3,300-word closing essay at v25) that the word rendered servant means a servant of any kind, that all the evidence Onesimus was a slave lies in that one word, that the mention of owing suggests a man able to hold property, and that in any case Paul neither forced nor advised the return and never asked that he be received as a slave; he adds the Hebrew law of Deut 23:15 forbidding the return of an escaped servant. Robertson answers flatly, 'So it has to be here. So it should be always', and elsewhere calls 'receive him as myself' the death-knell of human slavery. Clarke and Calvin simply assume the slave status -- Clarke stating that the Christian religion never cancels any civil relations, Calvin that the authority of masters is not taken away and Philemon is only asked to forgive and restore. Ellicott takes a third path, granting the status but locating in v16 the principle he calls absolutely destructive of the condition of slavery.

TWO COMMENTATORS INDEPENDENTLY REACH FOR THE SAME PAIR OF CLASSICAL PARALLELS, AND CLARKE FOLLOWS ONE TO ITS OUTCOME. Barnes at v17 points to Horace, Epistles i.9, the recommendation of Septimius to Claudius Nero, as a plea strongly resembling this one; Clarke prints that letter in full with a translation, judges it written with much art but greatly exceeded by Paul, and then points beyond it to Pliny's letter to Sabinianus on behalf of a freedman. Barnes prints that Pliny letter in full at v25. Clarke goes one step further than Barnes and prints the SECOND Pliny letter (Epistles ix.24), in which Sabinianus is thanked for having actually forgiven the man -- so the parallel case is carried through to its result, which the Philemon record does not give us.

CALVIN ON PRAYER AND FREE GRACE, DRAWN FROM AN INCIDENTAL PHRASE. On 'through your prayers I shall be given unto you' (v22) Calvin notes that what believers obtain through their prayers is said to be GIVEN to them, and infers that our prayers, though not unsuccessful, have no power through their own merit, since what is yielded to them is of free grace. He also concedes squarely that we do not know whether Paul was ever released, and that there is no absurdity even if he was disappointed of a hope about God's temporal kindness, since he kept his mind in suspense until the result declared the will of God.

CALVIN RAISES THE OBVIOUS OBJECTION TO PAUL'S BOND. On 'put that on mine account, I will repay it' (vv18-19) Calvin asks how a man who without the aid of the churches had not the means of living sparingly and frugally could promise to pay money, and calls the promise amidst such poverty ridiculous if taken literally; he concludes that without irony, by an indirect figure, Paul is asking Philemon to blot out and cancel the account, since he who claims the whole man as his property need not trouble about paying money. Ellicott and Robertson take the opposite line -- Ellicott calls it a regular bond couched in legal form and infers that Paul had money he could rightly call his own, most likely the Philippian offerings, and Robertson calls it a collectable promissory note and notes how many of the papyri concern debts.

BARNES USES PHILEMON 18 AGAINST THE IMPUTATION OF ADAM'S SIN. The verb rendered 'put that on mine account' occurs elsewhere in the New Testament only at Rom 5:13, where it is rendered 'imputed', and Barnes builds a numbered argument on the coincidence: Onesimus and not Paul did the wrong; Paul was never blameworthy for it and no possible supposition could make it right to charge it on him; he VOLUNTARILY assumed it, and only that consent made him answerable. He then applies the principle directly -- God 'reckons things as they are', does not hold men blameworthy for the sin of Adam, and this case must not be adduced to prove that Adam's sin is charged on his posterity; it demonstrates one point only, that a man who voluntarily takes a wrong upon himself may be held responsible for it.

ELLICOTT ON THE RARITY OF THE WORD 'PARTNER'. In the singular and in absolute use, unconnected with explanatory words, the title is found nowhere else in the New Testament except at 2 Cor 8:23, where Titus is called Paul's partner and fellow helper, and even there the context ties it to the collection of alms. Ellicott therefore refuses to read it as general Christian fellowship -- which he says would require some such addition as 'in Christ' and would not justify the strength of the personal appeal -- and argues for a particular bond, noting that Philemon, though Paul's own convert, is addressed not as a son but as a brother.

THE PLAY ON THE NAME ONESIMUS RUNS THREE TIMES AND ITS HISTORY IS DISPUTED. It appears at v11 (useless / useful), at v20 (let me have profit of thee), and by implication in the whole appeal. Ellicott says the name means useful or profitable though formed from a different root than the words used at v11, that it is hardly possible not to see a play, and adds -- curiously enough -- that the OLD GREEK COMMENTATORS DO NOT NOTICE IT. That is testable against this very file: Chrysostom is present at keys 1, 4 and 17 and indeed never remarks on the pun. At v20 Ellicott paraphrases, 'May I find thee, as I have found him, a true Onesimus', and Clarke calls it an evident paronomasia.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, philemon 1, seven entries, all in window. 1-3 = 644w, 8 voices. 4-7 = 650w, 7 voices. 8-9 = 649w, 6 voices. 10-14 = 648w, 6 voices. 15-16 = 641w, 7 voices. 17-19 = 645w, 7 voices. 20-25 = 650w, 7 voices. Every claim traced to a named block in data/commentary/cow/philemon/1.json before writing. Exclusions: all four Jamieson blocks (keys 3, 9, 15, 21) declared as residue; the single Cyril of Jerusalem block (key 25) dropped silently for the VOICE_LABELS defect; roughly 500 words of 1 Timothy text at key 24 ignored as spillover. Real usable source after exclusions 45,451 words against a gross 46,763. No Wesley, no Keil, no Barnes-free entries. Chrysostom used only where genuine.

Keil is truncated at exactly 200 words in SIXTEEN of his seventeen blocks in this chapter — keys 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, 10, 13, 16, 18, 19, 20, 22, 24, 25 all land on 200 exactly, and only key 27 (51 words) falls under the cap and is therefore complete. Gill's key-1 block is also exactly 200 while every other Gill block in the chapter runs between 17 and 160, so the cap caught him only where his material was long. Henry (2662, 2520, 2206), Clarke (up to 1680) and Ellicott (up to 1096) are untouched, so this is not a uniform per-block limit but something that bit two sources. Every capped block therefore ends mid-sentence, and in Keil's case the cut usually falls just after his own quotation of the verse text, so a substantial part of what survives is bare scripture rather than comment. The chapter is still writable — the material before each cut is usable and I quoted nothing across a truncation point — but the size command's 22,952 usable source words overstates what is actually there, and a chapter whose bulk is Keil would not be. Worth a check across other 1samuel chapters before one of them is picked.

JFB displacement, 41st confirmation, and the cleanest instance in the corpus. All FIVE JFB blocks in this chapter come from Joshua 8 — the feigned flight from Ai and the men of Bethel, the uplifted spear and the ambush, the twenty miles to Ebal, and the reading of the law on the plaster at Ebal and Gerizim. They sit at keys 4, 10, 16, 22 and 28: a perfect stride of six that runs clean to the chapter's last key, the third perfect-stride case after deuteronomy 29 and exodus 19. Keys 10 and 16 are BYTE-IDENTICAL, the same 107-word passage emitted twice, which is the second repeat case after deuteronomy 29's byte-identical triple. Key 28 is also truncated mid-word (memory would often revert to the s). JFB was excluded from all five keys; every one of them carries other voices, so the exclusions cost the chapter nothing. Note that the donor here is Joshua 8 while the host is 1 Samuel 1 — a lag of roughly one book plus Judges and Ruth, which is consistent with the reading-head model but not with any fixed canonical offset, since judges 4's donor was three chapters back in the same book.

The Henry-has-only-three-keys hazard, met twice in one batch. Henry appears at keys 1, 9 and 19 only — and those are the chapter's three largest keys (5187, 3320, 2515), because each is a section header carrying a long run-ahead over the verses that follow. Key 1 runs over vv1-8, key 9 over vv9-18, key 19 over vv19-23. Under the filing rule none of that can move, since Henry has no key inside the 2-8, 10-14, 15-18 or 20-23 spans, so five of the eight entries have no puritan-evangelical school at all. Judges 4 showed the same shape one chapter earlier (Henry at 1, 4, 10, 17). The pattern is now clear enough to predict: when a voice's key count is far below the others and its keys coincide with the chapter's largest, that voice is a section-header source and will be absent from most entries no matter how the chapter is tiled. Two consequences worth acting on. First, check the key-count profile before tiling, not after — it tells you which schools will be thin where. Second, the entry that DOES hold the header must carry the run-ahead material only so far as it bears on its own verses; at key 19 I used Henry on the early worship, the remembering and the name, and deliberately left his material on the weaning unused, since those verses belong to an entry he cannot reach.

Two structural features of a chapter-1 pick, both new to this corpus. First, the opening key carries the BOOK preface rather than comment on the verse: of key 1's 5,187 words, Clarke spends 1,680 on a synopsis of the whole book and its authorship and Keil's 200 surviving words are the Introduction to the Books of Samuel, so the material actually about Ramathaim-zophim is only Gill, Ellicott, Wesley and Henry's opening. This turned out to be an advantage rather than a loss, because Clarke's claim that these books are properly a continuation of Judges runs straight into Ellicott's insistence that the opening formula signifies no such thing — a genuine debate that only exists because both wrote prefaces. Second, the StudyLight tail (32nd instance) attached to Ellicott's key-28 block, which is also the chapter's last key, so this instance is non-discriminating like the seven before numbers 15; the numbers 28 rule still rests on the two discriminating cases.

Two four-way disagreements in the closing verses, both staged rather than resolved. On what word Elkanah prays the Lord to establish, no antecedent is recorded anywhere in the narrative, so each voice supplies one: Keil takes it to be Eli's blessing, which the parents might regard after the birth as a promise from Jehovah himself, and expressly rejects the Rabbinic alternative; Ellicott records that alternative in Rashi's form (a voice from heaven foretelling a just one named Samuel, after which every mother named her son Samuel and, seeing his actions, said this was not he) and offers Bunsen's plainer sense to those who decline it; Wesley refers the word to Hannah's own vow; Clarke reads it as a father's prayer that the child be preserved and made a blessing to Israel. On whether the closing words should be rendered lent to the Lord, Clarke defends the received translation from the grammar, the root for asking signifying to lend in one conjugation, with the Vulgate, Septuagint and Syriac all following the double sense; Ellicott calls the rendering flatly false; Keil traces the error to a false rendering in the Greek and says Jehovah had not lent the son to Hannah at all; Wesley keeps the word and turns it devotional, that whatever we give to God is lent to him in the sense that he will certainly repay it. Both went into the tags as debates with holders named, and the prose states no side as settled.

Length control across two chapters this batch, sixteen entries. 1samuel 1 came in at 641, 637, 636, 647, 633, 619, 648, 649 and judges 4 at 645, 644, 639, 558, 641, 646, 647, 644. Thirteen of the sixteen needed a trim pass; every cut was structural (note 1018), none lexical. The overshoot on 1samuel was worse than on judges — first drafts at 800, 747, 740, 726, 725, 707, 706 — and the reason is identifiable: this chapter has six voices where judges 4 had four effectively, and six voices on a short verse means six positions to place rather than four, so the outline-stage cutting that note 1051 recommends has to be much more aggressive than it feels safe to be while drafting. The rule I would state now is that the pre-cut should scale with the VOICE COUNT, not the source-word count: at six voices, plan to drop roughly one idea per voice before writing, not one or two from the entry as a whole. The standing check added at judges 4 — that every name in tags.voices actually appears in the entry's prose — caught nothing this time, having been applied during drafting rather than after; it is worth keeping as a drafting habit rather than a post-hoc check.

JFB displacement, 42nd confirmation, and the first case where the DONOR ADVANCES IN LOCKSTEP with the host key. All four JFB blocks are displaced and all four sit at a perfect stride of six: key 3, key 9, key 15, key 21. Their donors advance monotonically through the source text as the host key advances. Key 3 is a 13-word fragment glossing kesitah — literally lambs, probably a coin with the figure of a lamb on it — which belongs to Genesis 33:19. Key 9 is Genesis 34:1-4, Dinah going out and Shechem's attachment to her. Key 15 is Genesis 34 further on, Hamor and Shechem seeming to act honestly but neither expressing regret nor restoring Dinah. Key 21 is Genesis 34 further still, the circumcision demanded of the Shechemites as a cloak to cover a diabolical design, and it is truncated mid-sentence. So the reading head is at Gen 33:19 when the host is at 40:3 and has moved steadily into and through Genesis 34 by the time the host reaches 40:21. Every previous case established only that displaced blocks appear at intervals; this one shows the donor position is a monotonic function of the host position within a single chapter. Fourth same-book case. All four blocks excluded; every one of those keys carries other voices, so the exclusions cost nothing.

The 200-word truncation cap is NOT confined to 1samuel 1 — it recurs here, which makes it a corpus-wide scraper defect rather than a one-chapter accident. In genesis 40, Keil is capped at exactly 200 words in six of his seven blocks (keys 2, 6, 9, 10, 13, 17; only key 21, at 51 words, falls under the cap and is complete), and Gill is capped at exactly 200 in two of twenty-three (keys 1 and 5, his two longest; every other Gill block runs between 17 and 200). Henry (up to 1141), Clarke (up to 314), Ellicott (up to 1046), Calvin (up to 733) and Wesley (up to 162) are all untouched. That is the same signature as 1samuel 1: Keil almost entirely capped, Gill capped only where he ran long, everyone else free. Two chapters from different books and different testaments show it, so the cap should be assumed present wherever Keil appears. Practical consequence for picking: the size command counts capped words as usable, so it overstates any chapter whose bulk is Keil, and a chapter that looks writable on its word count may not be.

An editor's footnote is spliced into the body of Calvin's key-16 block, ahead of Calvin's own words. The block opens with a quotation attributed to 'Egypt and the Books of Moses, p. 27' about wicker baskets on the Egyptian monuments and the perfection of the baking art, then breaks off with a stray em-dash and begins Calvin's actual comment mid-sentence ('He does not care respecting the skill and fidelity of Joseph...'). The same pattern appears in Calvin's key-12 block, where a long editorial note about the white tablet and the nail is embedded in the middle of his comment on lifting up the head. Anything drawn from those passages would be attributed to Calvin by the fidelity check, since it is inside his blob, while in fact belonging to his editor. I left both untouched. Worth watching in other Calvin chapters: his blocks in this edition carry editorial apparatus inline, and the fidelity gate cannot tell it apart from the commentator's own voice.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, 33rd instance, and the THIRD DISCRIMINATING CASE — it confirms the numbers 28 rule again. Ellicott's keys in this chapter are 1, 8, 11, 15, 19 and 20, so his final block is at key 20 while the chapter runs to key 23; the tail attaches to the end of that key-20 block, not to the chapter's last key. That matches numbers 15 and exodus 19, the only two previous cases where the two could be told apart, and the rule can now be stated with reasonable confidence: the StudyLight tail attaches to the end of Ellicott's final block, wherever in the chapter that falls. Separately, Gill's own sacred-texts navigation tail (Next: Genesis Chapter 41 Sacred Texts | Bible - Previous: John Gill's Exposition...) appears at key 23. Gill's last block IS the chapter's last key here, so this instance is non-discriminating and his tail's attachment rule remains untested — it still needs a chapter where Gill stops before the last key.

The sharpest named collision between two voices met so far, and it sits inside a single entry. On Genesis 40:23 Henry reports with approval the parallel between Joseph and Christ — Joseph's two fellow-prisoners answering to the two thieves, one saved and one condemned, and the butler forgetting the man who said remember me where the thief who said remember me was not forgotten — attributing it to Lightfoot from Broughton. Clarke, commenting on the same verse, attacks precisely that reading by name of its type: many commentators have seen in every circumstance of Joseph's history a parallel to our blessed Lord; he believes God never designed such parallels, is astonished to find comparatively grave and judicious men trifling in this way and forcing the features of truth into the most distorted anamorphosis, warns that we should beware how we attribute designs to God that he never had, and calls the mischief done by this system really incalculable, since it furnishes infidels with pretexts to scoff at all spirituality. Unlike the leviticus 21 and joshua 4 cases, where the two halves of a disagreement fell in different entries and could not be set against each other, both blocks are filed at keys inside the same span, so the prose could stage the quarrel directly and the tags carry it as a debate with both holders named. This is the shape a tiling should aim for: check before fixing boundaries whether a chapter's live disagreement can be kept in one entry.

The Henry-Wesley abridgement pattern is total in this chapter, and for once it costs nothing. Wesley has six keys (1, 4, 6, 8, 14, 20) and Henry three (1, 5, 20); at every one of Wesley's keys his comment is a compression of Henry's, sometimes word for word — the opening (we should not have had this story of Pharaoh's butler and baker recorded in scripture if it had not been serviceable to Joseph's preferment; the world stands for the sake of the church) is byte-for-byte identical apart from punctuation, and the sadness comment at key 6 and the modesty comment at key 14 are near-verbatim. What makes this chapter different from exodus 19 and genesis 22, where the pair straddled entry boundaries, is that here the duplication is USEFUL. Henry's key-1 block runs ahead over vv1-8 and carries his remark about Joseph not reflecting on his brothers who sold him, which belongs to v15 and therefore could not be used in the vv1-4 entry that holds it. Wesley's key-14 block reproduces exactly that remark, and key 14 sits inside the vv9-15 span, so the material reached its proper entry through the abridging voice after the original voice could not carry it there. Working rule to add: when a section-header voice's run-ahead is stranded by the filing rule, check whether an abridging voice repeats it at a key inside the target span — the abridgement can rescue the material legitimately.

Length control, five entries: 640, 644, 647, 644, 635, all grade A, none over 650 on either tokenizer. Every one needed trimming and the first drafts were the worst of the run — 818, 804, 785, 702, 662 — which is consistent with the voice-count rule recorded at 1samuel 1 (note 1080) and sharpens it. This chapter carries SEVEN voices in three of its five entries, the most yet, and the overshoot scaled with that almost exactly: the seven-voice entries drafted at 785-818, the six-voice entry at 702, the five-voice entry at 662. Since the entries are all capped at 650 regardless, the practical rule is that the per-voice budget is what shrinks: at four voices each voice can have three ideas, at seven each can have one and a half. I drafted as though each voice deserved a full hearing and then cut back, which cost two to four trim passes per entry. The correction for next time is to allocate before drafting — divide 600 words by the voice count, and write to that quota per voice rather than per paragraph. Note also that all five cuts that actually moved the needle were whole ideas dropped (Clarke's Smithfield polemic, Ellicott's Egyptian palm idiom nearly, Calvin's birthday passage, Henry's Nebuchadnezzar caution, Gill's catalogue custom), while lexical tightening across three passes on entry 5 moved only 16 words in total. Note 1018 continues to hold without exception.

JFB displacement, 43rd confirmation, and the strongest single piece of evidence yet for the reading-head model: the donor stream is CONTINUOUS ACROSS CHAPTER BOUNDARIES. In genesis 39 the three JFB blocks sit at keys 3, 9 and 21 — strides of 6 and 12, both multiples of six — and their donors advance monotonically: key 3 is Genesis 32:32 (the sinew that shrank and the Jewish custom of extracting it), key 9 is Genesis 33:4 (Esau's sudden embrace, the enmity of twenty years vanishing), key 21 is Genesis 33:16-17 (Jacob's intended route round the Dead Sea to Seir). Now set that beside genesis 40, landed earlier in this same batch, whose four JFB blocks at keys 3, 9, 15 and 21 draw on Genesis 33:19, 34:1-4, 34:8-12 and 34:14-24. Laid end to end the donor positions run 32:32, 33:4, 33:16, then 33:19, 34:1, 34:8, 34:14 — a single monotonic sweep that does not reset when the host chapter changes. Whatever process produces these blocks is reading forward through Genesis at its own pace while the host text advances independently, and the two are sampled together at a fixed stride. This also predicts something checkable: a chapter picked between these two in canonical order should show donors between 33:16 and 33:19, and chapters after genesis 40 should show donors past Genesis 34. Fifth same-book case. All three blocks excluded here; every affected key carries other voices.

Third chapter confirming the 200-word truncation cap, with the same signature as 1samuel 1 and genesis 40: Keil capped at exactly 200 in five of six blocks (keys 2, 7, 11, 14, 20; only key 22, at 111 words, is under the cap and complete), Gill capped at exactly 200 in two of twenty-three (keys 1 and 6, his longest), and Henry (up to 1771), Clarke (542), Calvin (953) and Wesley (88) untouched. Three chapters across two books now show it. Treat the cap as a fixed property of the scrape wherever Keil appears, and discount his contribution when sizing a chapter. Separately, the editor's-footnote defect first recorded at genesis 40 (note 1098) recurs in this chapter three times, all in Calvin: his key-7 block opens with a long quotation from Egypt and the Books of Moses p. 25 on Egyptian marital morals before Calvin's own words begin mid-sentence; his key-11 block carries an embedded Greek gloss on the word epitasis and a French translator's note; his key-19 block ends with another p. 26 quotation on Egyptian women's freedom. Anything drawn from those passages would pass the fidelity check as Calvin's, since it sits inside his blob. I used none of them. The pattern is now clearly editorial apparatus inlined throughout this edition of Calvin, not a one-off.

Henry's blocks in this corpus splice two different works together, and the seam is visible. His key-13 block runs the Exposition through to the end and then, without any marker, restates the same material in the compressed sentences of the Concise commentary — Joseph's mistress, having tried in vain to make him a guilty man, endeavoured to be avenged on him; those that have broken the bonds of modesty will never be held by the bonds of truth — which had already appeared verbatim a few lines earlier. His key-19 block does the same, closing with a Concise-style paragraph that repeats the prison material and then adds a Christological application absent from the Exposition. The same doubling appeared at 1samuel 1 key 1. The practical hazard is that a block which looks like sustained argument is partly a summary of itself, so a writer drawing on the tail may unknowingly restate what he has already used from the head, and the corpus templating check would see the repetition as the synthesis writer's fault rather than the source's. Read Henry's long blocks to the end before drafting, and treat the final paragraph as a possible duplicate rather than new material.

Second confirmation, in consecutive chapters, that an abridging voice can rescue material the filing rule strands. Henry has only four keys here (1, 7, 13, 19), all of them section headers with long run-aheads, so five of the chapter's verses lie in entries he cannot reach. His key-19 block carries the best material on the imprisonment — that Potiphar likely chose that prison because it was the worst, where the irons entered into the soul, but God designed it to pave the way to Joseph's enlargement, and that God despises not his prisoners and can raise up friends where they are least expected. All of that treats vv20-23, and Henry has no key there. Wesley's key-20 and key-21 blocks reproduce it almost word for word, and both keys sit inside the 20-23 span, so the material reached its proper entry through the abridgement while the original stayed where it was filed. The same thing happened at genesis 40, where Wesley's key-14 block rescued Henry's stranded remark about Joseph not reflecting on the brothers who sold him. Two consecutive chapters make this a reliable technique rather than a lucky accident: when a section-header voice's run-ahead is stranded, search the abridging voice's keys inside the target span before giving the material up. Note also the corollary hazard — if the material is used in BOTH entries, once from the original and once from the abridgement, the corpus templating check will see the near-duplicate and blame the writer.

Length control, five entries: 646, 646, 649, 589, 642, all grade A. First drafts came in at 795, 743, 742, 589, 719 — the same seven-and-six-voice overshoot as genesis 40, and the vv16-19 entry, which has only THREE voices (Gill, Henry, Calvin), landed at 589 on the first attempt with no trim pass at all. That is now a clean natural experiment across two chapters and eleven entries: three voices drafts in range, five drafts about 70 over, six about 90 over, seven about 150 over. The relationship is close enough to linear that the per-voice quota rule from note 1102 can be stated as a number — roughly 600 divided by the voice count is the budget each voice actually gets, and drafting at more than that guarantees a trim pass per extra voice. Every effective cut this chapter was again a whole idea dropped (Clarke's forty court ladies and the oranges, Calvin's vain-pretexts passage on reputation, Calvin's rare-virtue clause, Wesley's prisoners sentence, Henry's detestable-wickedness line); across five entries the lexical passes moved single-digit word counts while the structural cuts moved 45-105 each. Note 1018 holds at eleven chapters without a counterexample.

JAMIESON MISALIGNMENT, SIXTH STRIDE-6 CONFIRMATION, FIFTH MONOTONIC WALK, AND A NEW OFFSET. Jamieson appears at keys 6, 12, 18, 24 -- stride 6, and for the first time OFFSET 0 (the keys are the exact multiples of six). Four members, and a monotonic walk through 1 CORINTHIANS 9-10: key 6 = 1 Cor 9:24 (the Isthmian games and the foot race), key 12 = 1 Cor 10:1 (the chapter heading and the fathers under the cloud), key 18 = 1 Cor 10:6 (the lusting after flesh in the wilderness), key 24 = 1 Cor 10:11 (the ends of the ages). Running tally of confirmed stride-6 Jamieson residue with offsets: 1peter 1 (offset 1, Gal 6 to Eph 1), acts 21 (offset 2, Luke 24 to Acts 1), numbers 24 (offset 3, Numbers 3, stalled), 1corinthians 11 (offset 2, Acts 22), philemon 1 (offset 3, 2 Cor 2-3), 1thessalonians 5 (offset 0, 1 Cor 9-10). Offsets 0, 1, 2, 3 have now all been observed, and the wrong region still differs per chapter. All four blocks excluded and declared.

THE CYRIL RESIDUE IS A SINGLE STUCK FRAGMENT DEPOSITED ACROSS BOOKS -- BYTE-IDENTICAL PROOF. The Cyril of Jerusalem blocks at 1thessalonians 5 keys 23 AND 28 are byte-identical to each other (1,075 characters) and byte-identical to the Cyril block found at philemon 1 key 25 in the previous batch: the Catechetical Lecture on 2 Cor 4:4, 'He blinded the thoughts of them that believe not.' The same fragment therefore lands twice in one chapter and again in a different book. This kills the hypothesis that the Cyril misfiling is per-chapter noise; it is one fragment being re-deposited. Key 5 is a separate misfile, Cyril on 1 John 3:10 and John 1:12 (sonship by choice and not by nature, with Judas and Paul as the proofs) -- a topical near-miss on 'children of light', not commentary on 1 Thess 5:5. All three dropped SILENTLY.

VOICE_LABELS DEFECT NOW SUPPRESSES A GENUINE BLOCK AS WELL AS RESIDUE. Confirmed again by reading scripts/synthesis_qa.py lines 138-145: _LABEL_RE joins the VOICE_LABELS short forms with a trailing \s*: -- so 'Chrysostom', 'Lightfoot' and 'Robertson' match only because they are SUFFIXES of the heads 'John Chrysostom:', 'John Lightfoot:' and 'A.T. Robertson:', while 'Cyril' can never match because it is a PREFIX of 'Cyril of Jerusalem:' and is followed by ' of Jerusalem', never a colon. Two consequences seen in this chapter. (1) The three residue blocks cannot be declared and had to be dropped silently. (2) A GENUINE Cyril block at key 21 is equally invisible to split_voices, so its words are silently attributed to whichever voice precedes it and no exclusion accounting can ever see it. One-line fix: list 'Cyril of Jerusalem' instead of 'Cyril', or permit an intervening qualifier before the colon. Twenty-three batches open.

CYRIL AT KEY 21 IS GENUINE AND QUOTES THE VERSE. Unlike the three misfiled blocks, the Cyril of Jerusalem block at key 21 quotes 1 Thess 5:21-22 verbatim inside a catechetical exhortation: 'Be an approved banker, holding fast that which is good, abstaining from every form of evil,' set among 'Make thou thy fold with the sheep: flee from the wolves: depart not from the Church... learn to distinguish the pastures of doctrine.' Used in the synthesis for entry 20-22. Chrysostom at keys 1, 12 and 19 is likewise genuine, from the Homilies on 1 Thessalonians.

CHROME FOUND AGAIN, AND FOR THE FIRST TIME SWALLOWED INSIDE A VOICE BLOCK. The Charles Ellicott block at key 28 measures 1,008 words, of which only about fifteen are real commentary ('The grace. -- St Paul's autograph to conclude the letter'). Everything after that is the StudyLight footer, a CSS blob, and 221 words of raw JavaScript (the verse-popup script, beginning '(function('). Measured from the 'Footnotes:' marker the chrome is 984 words / 30,366 raw characters / 126 NEWLINES -- squarely on the invariant established over the previous measurements (992-995 words, 30,341-30,497 chars, 126 newlines). Two things are new: the chrome is TERMINAL here (last key of the chapter) where the previous three instances were non-terminal, and it is INSIDE a voice block rather than standing free, so it is silently credited to Ellicott. Tenth measurement overall; philemon 1, measured last batch, had none at all. Real usable source for this chapter is therefore about 44,324 words, not the 45,308 that a naive count after voice exclusions gives.

CALVIN RUNS PAST THE END OF THE BOOK AGAIN -- SECOND CONSECUTIVE CHAPTER, SAME SHAPE. The Calvin block at key 27 (832 words) closes his 1 Thessalonians commentary correctly, then prints 'END OF THE COMMENTARY ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS' and continues into his DEDICATORY EPISTLE to the physician Benedict Textor (Geneva, 1st July 1550, mentioning the death of his wife) and then into THE ARGUMENT ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS. Roughly 600 of the 832 words are not commentary on 1 Thess 5:27. This is the same defect found last batch at philemon 1 key 24, where Calvin ran on into 1 Timothy. In BOTH cases the run-on sits at the LAST key where Calvin appears in the book (he is absent from philemon 25 and from 1 Thess 5:28), which suggests the scrape takes Calvin's text to the end of the file rather than to the end of the chapter. Worth checking every book-final Calvin block in the tree.

TRICHOTOMY AT 5:23 -- A FIVE-WAY DISAGREEMENT, THE SHARPEST IN THE CHAPTER. Ellicott calls the verse Paul's fullest and most scientific psychology, not a rhetorical piling up of words: spirit apprehends intuitively and survives death; soul is intellect, affection and will and belongs to the lower nature, so that in the twofold division the soul is reckoned with the body. Clarke sets out three parts flatly, with the spirit as the immortal principle and source of life to body and soul. Calvin accepts three terms but redistributes them, spirit being reason and soul being will and the affections, and rejects as making the prayer absurd the reading that takes spirit for vital motion and soul for the renewed part. Robertson denies that the verse settles anything: 'Not necessarily trichotomy as opposed to dichotomy,' and reads a prayer for the man as an undivided whole. WESLEY DENIES TRICHOTOMY OUTRIGHT on a dilemma -- only soul and body are natural constituents, the spirit being adventitious and given to Christians only, for the soul 'is either matter or not matter: there is no medium. But if it is matter, it is part of the body: if not matter, it coincides with the Spirit.' Barnes treats the division as popular language and declines to say whether Paul sanctions it.

WHETHER ENTIRE SANCTIFICATION IS ATTAINABLE IN THIS LIFE, AT 5:23. Clarke states the Wesleyan position directly: the whole man may be so sanctified as to be preserved blameless till the coming of Christ, 'and thus we learn that the sanctification is not to take place in, at, or after death,' adding that he who can believe will find this thing also possible to him. Barnes rebuts it in a sentence at the same verse: 'A prayer for perfect sanctification, however, should not be adduced as a proof that it is in fact attained in the present life.' Henry stands with Barnes, that the best are sanctified but in part while in this world, though we should press towards complete sanctification. Ellicott sidesteps by rendering 'sanctify you WHOLE' rather than wholly -- the idea being that no part is left unsanctified, not that the work is finished.

WHO IS APPOINTED TO WRATH, AT 5:9. Gill reads the verse as it stands and infers vessels of wrath fitted for destruction, of old ordained to condemnation, so that our exemption is distinguishing grace. Clarke answers at length that the appointed are the JEWS AS A NATION, appointed not from eternity nor from any remote time but from the moment they finally rejected the gospel -- which is why the apostles were commanded to begin at Jerusalem -- and insists that 'even this appointment to wrath does not signify eternal damnation', since many may have turned to the Lord who smote them during the siege. Wesley glosses it in one line, of the obstinately impenitent. Ellicott refers it to a mysterious moment of God's eternal counsels and then says something neither party would: 'we ourselves are the only persons that can defeat God's predestinations.'

WHETHER SALVATION IS EARNED OR RECEIVED, AT 5:9. On the word rendered 'obtaining', Ellicott presses it to mean acquire by one's own efforts, and concludes that 'God does not predestinate men to salvation without laborious acquisition on their part', though the price can be paid only through union with Christ. Calvin takes the same word the opposite way: 'Paul, undoubtedly, does not mean that God has called us, that we may procure salvation for ourselves, but that we may obtain it, as it has been acquired for us by Christ.' Robertson notes only that the noun may be passive (God's possession) or active (obtaining) and prefers the active.

THE FALL OF JERUSALEM READING AT 5:1-3. Clarke stands alone in referring the times and seasons chiefly to the destruction of the Jewish commonwealth, appealing to his own note on the same two words in Acts 1:7, and reads 'peace and safety' as the state of the Jewish people when the Romans came against them, refusing every overture, with the sudden destruction as the storming of the city, the burning of the temple, the massacre of hundreds of thousands and the dispersion of the rest. Gill, Henry, Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Calvin all take the day of the Lord as the return to judgment. Clarke reads the whole chapter through that lens, which also drives his reading of 5:9.

WHAT IS FORBIDDEN AT 5:22 -- FOUR POSITIONS ON 'ALL APPEARANCE OF EVIL'. Gill, Barnes and Clarke read it of the APPEARANCE of evil, Barnes building a long rule for doubtful practices (dress, amusements, the opera, the ball-room, games of hazard) and Clarke warning against driving morality so near the bounds of evil that weak persons believe we touch it. Ellicott says flatly that 'this translation cannot stand' and renders it 'hold yourselves aloof from every evil kind' -- of whatever you may be testing. Robertson supports 'class or kind' from the papyri, granting that the word naturally means look or appearance but denying that it would mean semblance as opposed to reality. Calvin rejects BOTH the universal reading and the subdivision reading (calling the latter 'an exceedingly gross blunder') and applies it to doctrine in which falsity has not been proved but a suspicion of lurking poison remains: from such we suspend our step rather than reject outright.

AN INTERNAL DISSENT INSIDE THE ELLICOTT COMMENTARY. At 5:23 the note on where the soul is reckoned in the twofold division adds, in parenthesis, 'not, probably, as Bishop Ellicott says on our present passage, as part of the spirit, but as part of the body'. The contributor is therefore contradicting Charles Ellicott, the bishop whose name the commentary bears, on the very verse. First instance of a signed-commentary contributor dissenting from the editor found in this corpus.

BOTH BARNES AND CLARKE END THE BOOK ON AN ANTI-PAPAL READING OF 5:27. Barnes suggests the Holy Spirit foresaw that the withholding of Scripture 'would be defended by cardinals, and popes, and councils' and made this injunction to counteract it, noting that Paul dwells more on the great apostasy in the Thessalonian letters than anywhere else. Clarke's closing essay is longer and hotter, identifying the prohibition of Scripture to the people with 'the mystery of iniquity which then began to work', and ending with a striking concession -- that a genuine Protestant will wish Rome 'not her destruction, but her reformation', and that she has in her own hands the means of her own regeneration. Calvin at the same verse says those who forbid the people to read the writings of Paul are 'more refractory than even devils themselves', since they are unmoved by so strict an adjuration. Ellicott adds the critical history: Baur read the adjuration as the mark of a forger seeking authority, while Wordsworth answered that the constant public recitation is a guarantee of the Epistle's integrity.

CLARKE'S EDITION-CORRECTING DATELINES NOW SEEN IN TWO BOOKS ONE BATCH APART. His note at 1 Thess 5:28 ends 'Finished correcting for a new edition, on the shortest day of 1831. - A. C.'; the Philemon note landed last batch ended 'Finished correcting for a new edition, Dec. 23, 1831.' The two datelines are two days apart and place the Thessalonians revision immediately before the Philemon one, so the scrape preserves the order in which Clarke worked through the epistles in that revision.

BARNES ON FREE INQUIRY AT 5:21, THE LARGEST CLAIM HE MAKES IN THE CHAPTER. Taking the verb from the assayer, whose trial was made by fire, he argues that Christianity does not require men to disregard their reason, does not make it a duty to receive all that synods and councils have decreed, and is 'more than any other form of religion, the friend of free inquiry'; we are to examine every opinion 'no matter by whom held; by what councils ordained; by what venerableness of antiquity sustained', to be subjected to no pains or penalties for not believing what we do not perceive to be true, and then to hold what we have found true though it cost a martyr's death. Calvin reaches the same practical end from the opposite direction, inferring that the spirit of discrimination must be conferred on believers, since otherwise 'prove all things' would have been said in vain, and declaring that heaven and earth may be commingled rather than that prophecy should cease.

CHRYSOSTOM'S TWO BEST PASSAGES. At 5:12 he explains why the ruler's office is harder than the physician's or the father's: both may give pain and keep their standing, the one because the patient's friends are on his side and the other by nature and by law, whereas whoever the priest reproves 'is sure to cease from being thankful, and to become an enemy'; and a man cut off from the public prayers grieves not at the loss of the blessing but at the public disgrace, 'we do not shudder at, do not dread, the thing itself.' At 5:19 he works the lamp of the Spirit into a rule for the tongue: the eye and ear are the lamp's opening and the mouth is its door, so that when a man reviles you, opening your mouth 'adds force to the wind', whereas if two doors stand opposite and you shut one there is no draught and the blast is spent.

MATTHEW HENRY IS EXPOSITION PLUS CONCISE, SPLICED END TO END, AT EVERY KEY. Henry appears at only six keys (1, 6, 11, 12, 16, 23) with blocks of 1,000-1,565 words, and each one carries the full Exposition followed by the Concise restating the same material in shorter form -- at key 1 the Concise paragraph begins 'It is needless or useless to ask about the particular time of Christ's coming' after the Exposition has already said it. This differs from the splice seen in earlier books, where Concise REPLACED the Exposition; here both are present and the block is close to double length. Sixth book in which the Henry text is found spliced.

THE 200-WORD CAP BITES HARD ON GILL IN THIS CHAPTER. Gill's block is truncated at exactly 200 words at eight of the twenty-eight keys (5, 11, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 23), and Wesley is cut at 201 and 207 at keys 16 and 23. In every case the sentence stops mid-clause. Gill is the voice most often truncated in the NT files, as Keil is in the OT ones; the re-fetch item already standing for Keil and Lightfoot should include him.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, 1thessalonians 5, seven entries, all in window. 1-3 = 648w, 8 voices. 4-7 = 641w, 8 voices. 8-11 = 629w, 8 voices. 12-15 = 650w, 9 voices. 16-19 = 649w, 9 voices. 20-22 = 650w, 8 voices. 23-28 = 649w, 8 voices. Every claim traced to a named block in data/commentary/cow/1thessalonians/5.json before writing. Exclusions: all four Jamieson blocks (keys 6, 12, 18, 24) declared as residue; three Cyril of Jerusalem blocks (keys 5, 23, 28) dropped silently for the VOICE_LABELS defect, while the genuine Cyril block at key 21 was used; about 600 words of 2 Thessalonians front matter at key 27 ignored as Calvin spillover; about 984 words of StudyLight footer, CSS and JavaScript inside the Ellicott block at key 28 ignored as chrome. Gross usable 47,050; after voice exclusions 45,308; after chrome and spillover about 44,324. No entry rests on a single school.

JFB displacement, 44th confirmation, and the case that turns the pattern into a QUANTITATIVE LAW. Both blocks here are displaced and sit at a stride of six: key 13 is Genesis 45:14-15 (Joseph embracing Benjamin and his brothers, forgiveness demonstrated more fully than by words), key 19 is Genesis 45:16-20 (Pharaoh inviting Jacob's family into Egypt and providing for their removal). The donor advances with the host, as at genesis 39 and 40. But exodus 5 also breaks the guess I made last batch, that the donor stream is a single continuous sweep across the corpus: genesis 40's donors ended at Genesis 34, and exodus 5's begin at Genesis 45, so the stream is not one unbroken read. Working the numbers instead: convert host and donor to canonical chapter positions (Genesis 1 = 1, Exodus 1 = 51, and so on) and take the ratio donor/host across every case recorded so far — genesis 22 (22 -> 19), genesis 39 (39 -> 33), genesis 40 (40 -> 34), exodus 5 (55 -> 45), exodus 19 (69 -> 57), leviticus 21 (111 -> 93), numbers 15 (132 -> 114), deuteronomy 29 (182 -> 149), joshua 4 (191 -> 154), nehemiah 7 (420 -> 341). The ratios are 0.864, 0.846, 0.850, 0.818, 0.826, 0.838, 0.864, 0.819, 0.806, 0.812 — mean 0.834, spread 0.806 to 0.864, across host positions ranging from 22 to 420. That is a twenty-fold range in host position holding a ratio steady to within plus or minus four per cent. The donor is not at a fixed lag from the host; it is at a fixed FRACTION of the host's canonical position, as though a second index advanced through the same corpus at about five-sixths of the rate. The lag therefore grows with position: three chapters back at Genesis 22, seventy-nine back at Nehemiah 7. This is testable in advance, and I am testing it on the next chapter of this batch.

Fourth chapter confirming the 200-word truncation cap, same signature again: Keil capped at exactly 200 in ten of eleven blocks, Gill in two of twenty-three (his two longest), and Henry (up to 1066), Clarke (493), Ellicott (1102), Calvin (711) and Wesley (186) untouched. Four chapters across three books now. A consequence showed up here for the first time in a way that affected the writing: Keil's block at key 22 is nothing but the two verses quoted, the cap having cut it off before any comment began, so the entry covering vv22-23 had a voice present in the source with nothing to say. I excluded him there rather than pad his badge with prose he does not support. Worth adding to the standing checks: after building the voices list, look for blocks that are pure verse quotation, since the cap can leave a Keil block with no comment at all, and a voice listed on a badge should have said something.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, 34th instance, and the FOURTH DISCRIMINATING CASE. Ellicott's keys in this chapter run 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 20, 21, 22, so his final block is at key 22 while the chapter runs to key 23; the tail attached to the end of that key-22 block, not to the chapter's last key. With numbers 15, exodus 19 and genesis 40 that makes four independent discriminating cases and no counterexamples, so the numbers 28 rule can now be treated as settled: the StudyLight tail attaches to the end of Ellicott's final block, wherever in the chapter that falls. Gill's separate sacred-texts navigation tail did not appear here at all, and its attachment rule is still untested.

Third, fourth and fifth confirmations of the abridgement-rescue pattern, all inside one chapter, which settles it as a technique. Henry has only four keys here (1, 3, 10, 15), every one a section header with a long run-ahead, so most of the chapter falls in entries he cannot reach. Three times his stranded material was recoverable through Wesley, whose keys sit inside the target spans: Henry's key-3 block carries the observation that the cities they built were witnesses the people were not idle, which belongs to vv6-9, and Wesley repeats it at key 8, inside that span; Henry's key-15 block carries the rebuke that the officers should have humbled themselves before God rather than fly in the face of their best friends, which belongs to vv19-21, and Wesley repeats it at key 21; and the same block carries the whole expostulation passage on vv22-23 — is this God's coming down to deliver Israel? must I who hoped to be a blessing become a scourge? — which Wesley repeats almost verbatim at key 22. In every case the material reached its proper entry through the abridging voice while the original stayed where it was filed. Five confirmations now across three chapters. The check is cheap and should be standard: when a section-header voice's run-ahead is stranded, list the abridging voice's keys and see whether any fall inside the target span.

Two clean disagreements in this chapter, one of which the text itself settles a few verses later. First, who the taskmasters and officers were. Clarke, Wesley and Ellicott all make the taskmasters Egyptians and the officers Hebrews, Ellicott adding a third grade above both, the lords of service, and describing the officers as scribes who kept the tale of the bricks. Calvin dissents and takes BOTH ranks to have been drawn from the children of Israel, reasoning that in so great a multitude some might have evaded Egyptian overseers, whereas Israelites set over their own people would know them too familiarly for any to escape. What makes this worth recording is that Gill settles it from the text at verse 14, where the officers are described as men whom Pharaoh's taskmasters had set over the people — which shows both that the ranks were distinct and that the upper was Egyptian and the lower Israelite. The disagreement and its resolution fall in different entries (vv6-9 and vv10-14), so the tags carry the dispute at the first and Gill's textual settlement at the second. Second, whether the officers' reproach of Moses and Aaron is excusable, which produced the widest spread of opinion I have met on a single clause: Clarke is lenient (the afflicted must be allowed the privilege of complaining, and the considerate will hear such words with indulgence), Calvin severe (it sprang from unbelief, measuring God's favour by immediate success, and is not free from the charge of ingratitude), Wesley intermediate (they should have humbled themselves before God), and Gill deliberately balanced (a prediction or an imprecation, and if not wicked at least imprudent). All four holders are named in the tags at key 19.

Length control, seven entries: 633, 650, 631, 649, 644, 645, 650, all grade A. First drafts were 769, 724, 730, 752, 687, 711, 755 — an average overshoot of about 95 words on entries carrying six or seven voices, which is exactly what note 1107 predicts and no better than last batch. The per-voice quota was known going in and I still drafted over it every time, which suggests the rule needs to bite at the outline stage rather than at the drafting stage: writing 600 divided by seven is not a target one hits by writing carefully, it is a target one hits by deciding in advance which single idea each voice contributes and refusing the second. The evidence that this works is in the entries themselves — vv15-18, with five voices, drafted at 687 and needed one pass, while the seven-voice entries needed two or three. Every effective cut was again a whole idea (Calvin on access to kings, Clarke on preserving the word Jehovah, Ellicott's three-grade hierarchy compressed, Henry's cruel-instruments observation, Calvin's counsel-of-tyrants passage, Clarke's literal rendering of the last clause); the lexical passes moved four to ten words each and were not worth the time. Note 1018 now holds across thirteen chapters.

INVESTIGATED AND REJECTED, not attempted; nothing written to the data tree. Exodus 39 sizes at 7091 usable source words across 23 keys, which looks comfortable, but the keys are non-contiguous (1,2,3, 6-10, 23-25, 27-30, 32-34, 37-39, 41, 43) and the size command counts material that cannot be used. Breaking it into the runs a span may legally cover: 1-3 has 2021 words and is writable; 32-34 has 1876 and is writable; 43 has 2120 and is writable. The rest fails. Run 6-10 nominally holds 140 words, but key 9 is JFB-only and displaced, so after exclusion it has ZERO usable source and no entry can cover it; the other four keys are bare cross-references in their entirety — Onyx stones, possibly the Egyptian pebble, see Exodus 25:7; Stones for a memorial, see Note on Exodus 28:12; Breastplate, see Exodus 28:15; And they set in it four rows of stones, see the notes on Exodus 28:17 — 56 words of pointer with no comment attached. Run 37-39 counts 372 words, which is above the 200-word thin threshold and so would have the thin exemption refused, yet its real content is 74 words (Clarke on the candlestick and Ellicott on the lamps of arrangement), because Keil's 200 words there are pure verse quotation, cut off by the truncation cap before any comment began, and key 39 is JFB-displaced. Key 41 is the same trap: 240 nominal words, above the thin threshold, of which 178 are Keil quoting verses 41 and 42 verbatim and 57 are a single real note from Ellicott about the absent conjunction. Runs 23-25 and 27-30 are thin-eligible and just barely writable on one substantive block each (Clarke on the habergeon, Clarke on the holy crown and the Persepolis tiaras), but three of the eight runs cannot be written at all without inventing content. The root cause is structural and worth stating: Exodus 39 executes the instructions given in Exodus 28, so the commentators mostly decline to comment twice and point back instead. A chapter whose catena is predominantly cross-references has no distillable commentary, and no word count will reveal that. Requesting an owner decision of the same class as numbers 31 and nehemiah 7.

THE JFB DONOR LAW PREDICTED THIS CHAPTER CORRECTLY, OUT OF SAMPLE. Before profiling exodus 39 I computed from the ten previously recorded cases that the donor sits at a fixed fraction of the host's canonical chapter position, mean ratio 0.834 with a spread of 0.806 to 0.864, and predicted that exodus 39 (canonical position 89) would draw its displaced blocks from position about 74, that is Exodus 24, with a plausible window of Exodus 21 to 27. The chapter has three JFB blocks and all three fall inside that window. Key 9 is the golden candlestick, a lamp bearer with seven branches worked into knobs and flowers, and it cites its own source explicitly as Exodus 25:32-36. Key 33 is the coarse goats-hair curtains, one more in number than the others and extending a yard lower on each side, which is Exodus 26:7-13. Key 39 is the boards that formed the walls, the five cross bars and the middle bar reaching from end to end, which is Exodus 26:15-28. Canonical positions 75, 76 and 76 against a predicted 74, giving ratios of 0.843, 0.854 and 0.854 — all inside the previously observed band and close to its mean. The spacing is also consistent with the stride of six, keys 9, 33 and 39 differing by 24 and 6, with the intermediate keys simply absent from this chapter. This is the 45th confirmation of the displacement and the first successful advance prediction of the donor. The anomaly is no longer a catalogue of instances but a rule with a parameter: donor position is approximately five-sixths of host position, which also explains why the lag looked erratic when measured in chapters (three at Genesis 22, seventy-nine at Nehemiah 7) while being constant as a proportion.

JFB displacement, 45th confirmation, and a SECOND SUCCESSFUL ADVANCE PREDICTION in the same batch. Exodus 33 sits at canonical position 83, so the ratio law recorded at exodus 5 (donor position is about 0.834 of host position) predicted a donor near position 69, that is Exodus 19-20, before I looked. Both JFB blocks fall there. Key 14 reads They were eye and ear witnesses of the awful emblems of the Deity's descent, but they perceived not the Deity Himself, which is Exodus 20:18-21 and has nothing to do with My presence shall go with thee.
