Key 20 reads that is, carved with figures and ornaments that might lead to superstition, which glosses the altar of hewn stone in Exodus 20:25 and has nothing to do with Thou canst not see my face. Both give a donor position of 70, a ratio of 0.843, inside the previously observed band of 0.806 to 0.864. The two keys are also six apart, the usual stride. Taken with exodus 39, predicted at Exodus 24 and found at Exodus 25-26, the law has now made two out-of-sample predictions and both held. Twelve cases now support it, spanning host positions 22 to 420. Practical use: the donor window can be computed before profiling, which makes displaced blocks quick to recognise even when they are short fragments like these two — twenty-one and twelve words, easy to mistake for terse comment rather than foreign matter.

Fifth chapter confirming the 200-word cap, and the first where its worst consequence appeared repeatedly in one chapter. Keil is capped at exactly 200 in six of seven blocks here, Gill in three of twenty-three; Henry (up to 3143), Clarke (855), Ellicott (1123), Calvin (1483) and Wesley (184) are untouched. The consequence is that a Keil block often consists of nothing but the verses quoted, the cap having cut it off before any comment began — and because his blocks quote several verses ahead before commenting, what survives is frequently quotation belonging to a LATER entry than the one his key sits in. That happened three times here. At key 2 his block quotes verses 2 to 5 and comments only on 4 and 5, so the entry covering verses 1 to 3 had him present with nothing to say. At key 8 it quotes 8 to 12 and comments only on 12. At key 13 it quotes 13 to 18 and comments only on 18. In each case I excluded him from the entry rather than let a badge stand for prose he does not support, and where the comment could legitimately travel — his verse-18 remark moving to the entry containing key 19 — I moved it under the filing rule instead. Adding to the standing checks from note 1129: a Keil block that is pure quotation is now common enough to look for by default, and the test is simply whether anything follows the last quoted verse.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, 35th instance, and the FIFTH DISCRIMINATING CASE. Ellicott's keys here are 1-8, 11-14, 17, 19, 21 and 22, so his final block is at key 22 while the chapter runs to key 23; the tail attached there. That is now five independent discriminating cases (numbers 15, exodus 19, genesis 40, exodus 5 and this) with no counterexample, and the numbers 28 rule should be treated as established rather than provisional: the StudyLight tail attaches to the end of Ellicott's final block, wherever in the chapter it falls. Gill's separate sacred-texts navigation tail did not appear in either chapter of this batch; its attachment rule remains the one open question in this area, and still needs a chapter where Gill stops short of the last key.

The four-way disagreement over whose tent was pitched outside the camp, which is unusually well documented because Calvin argues the minority case at length. Ellicott reads the phrase as his tent, the Hebrew article carrying the force of a possessive, and cites the Greek version with Jarchi, Aben-Ezra, Kurtz, Kalisch, Keil and Cook; Clarke agrees and adds from the Talmudists that the distance was two thousand cubits; Keil makes it a dwelling of Moses raised into a temporary shrine only because the pillar of cloud settled on it. Henry and Wesley take a different line, that it was not his family tent but the tent of audience where he heard causes and enquired of God, the guildhall of the camp. Gill leaves it open. Calvin refuses the private-tent reading outright and gives six arguments: the text says not his own tabernacle but the tabernacle simply and by way of eminence; Moses did not change his habitation but went out thither from time to time; it would have been unlawful to give a private tent the sacred name God had bestowed on his sanctuary; God testified it was his own dwelling by manifesting his glory there; it would have been absurd for the people to seek God in that direction unless the place were holy; and the point of the removal was that Moses stayed among the people while God withdrew from a profane place, making the act a kind of excommunication. All four positions and their holders are carried in the tags at key 7. Worth noting for its own sake: this is the first chapter in which Calvin stands alone against the whole remaining field and states his reasons as an enumerated brief, which made the debate unusually easy to render faithfully.

Length control, nine entries: 650, 649, 639, 648, 644, 622, 648, 650, 650, all grade A. One entry came off the first draft at grade B rather than over length — the vv7-11 entry on the tent outside the camp, at ttr 0.578 against the 0.580 floor — and the cause was obvious once measured: the entry is about a tent, and tent and tabernacle between them carried most of the nouns. A lexical-variety pass fixed it at a cost of four words, swapping in sacred tent, shrine, sanctuary and it, which moved ttr from 0.578 to 0.590. This is the second time a B has come from subject-matter vocabulary rather than from filler (leviticus 9 entry 5 was the first, on sacrifice and fire), and both times the repair was the same and cheap. Worth stating as a rule: when a chapter's subject supplies one dominant noun, budget two or three synonyms for it before drafting rather than discovering the problem at the meter. On length, the overshoot pattern held exactly as note 1133 describes — the five-voice entries drafted at 622 to 729 and the seven-voice entry at 723, and every effective cut was again a whole idea (Calvin on access to kings, Clarke's Jupiter and Semele, Ellicott's conjecture about the goodness flashed into the soul, Henry's object-lesson on the forfeited structure, Calvin's fishes-on-a-hook). Note 1018 now holds across fifteen chapters.

JAMIESON MISALIGNMENT: SEVENTH CONFIRMATION, SIXTH WALK, NEW OFFSET 4 -- AND THE SOURCE STRIDE IS NOW MEASURABLE AT EXACTLY 5. Jamieson appears at keys 4, 10, 16, 22 -- stride 6, offset 4, four members -- walking monotonically through ROMANS 16: key 4 = Rom 16:8 (Amplias, 'a contracted form of Ampliatus'), key 10 = Rom 16:13 (Rufus the chosen, with Simon of Cyrene as his father), key 16 = Rom 16:18 (serve not our Lord Christ, deceiving the hearts of the simple), key 22 = Rom 16:23 (Gaius the host, Erastus the treasurer, Quartus). The source verses are 8, 13, 18, 23: AN EXACT ARITHMETIC STRIDE OF 5, against a stride of 6 in the target keys. Re-checking the earlier walks against this: 1thessalonians 5 ran 1 Cor 9:24 -> 10:1 -> 10:6 -> 10:11, which is +5 at each step once chapter boundaries are crossed; philemon 1 ran 2 Cor 2:10 -> 2:15 -> 3:1 -> 3:6, again +5 with the boundary crossing. The rule appears to be SIX KEYS FORWARD IN THE TARGET, FIVE VERSES FORWARD IN THE SOURCE. Running offsets observed: 0 (1thess 5), 1 (1peter 1), 2 (acts 21, 1cor 11), 3 (numbers 24, philemon 1), 4 (philippians 1). All four offsets 0-4 now seen. This is the first quantitative handle on the mechanism and should let the owner locate the fault in the fetcher rather than patching chapter by chapter.

CHROME INSIDE THE ELLICOTT BLOCK AT THE TERMINAL KEY, SECOND CONSECUTIVE CHAPTER. The Charles Ellicott block at key 30 measures 1,134 words, of which only 150 are real commentary; the rest, from the 'Footnotes:' marker on, is the StudyLight footer plus CSS plus raw JavaScript, measuring 984 words / 30,437 characters / 126 NEWLINES -- on the established invariant (992-995 words, 30,341-30,497 chars, 126 newlines). This is exactly what was found at 1thessalonians 5 key 28 last batch: terminal key, swallowed inside Ellicott's last block, so the words are silently credited to him. Two consecutive chapters with the same shape makes it a pattern rather than an accident, and it means the naive usable-source figure for any chapter whose last key carries an Ellicott block is roughly 984 words too high. Eleventh chrome measurement overall.

CYRIL RESIDUE, A THIRD MECHANISM: TOPICAL ATTACHMENT. The single Cyril of Jerusalem block, at key 19, is Catechetical Lecture material enumerating the TITLES OF THE HOLY SPIRIT -- Comforter, Spirit of Truth, Spirit of God, Spirit of the Father -- and is cut by the 200-word cap before reaching 'Spirit of Christ', which is plainly the title it was fetched for. Phil 1:19 reads 'the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ'. So this is neither the stuck 2 Cor 4:4 fragment (philemon 1 key 25; 1thessalonians 5 keys 23 and 28) nor a stride walk, but a keyword attachment on the phrase, landing a lecture that never comments on the verse. Dropped SILENTLY, since the VOICE_LABELS defect makes 'Cyril of Jerusalem' undeclarable.

VOICE_LABELS DEFECT, TWENTY-FOUR BATCHES OPEN. scripts/synthesis_qa.py line 145 builds _LABEL_RE from the VOICE_LABELS short forms with a trailing \s*:. 'Cyril' is a PREFIX of the head 'Cyril of Jerusalem:' and so never matches, while 'Chrysostom' and 'Robertson' match only by accident, being SUFFIXES of 'John Chrysostom:' and 'A.T. Robertson:'. Consequence here, as in the last two chapters: the Cyril block could not be declared as residue and had to be dropped silently, and its words are silently attributed to whichever voice precedes it in the blob. One-line fix: list 'Cyril of Jerusalem' instead of 'Cyril'.

CHRYSOSTOM IS GENUINE AT ALL FOUR KEYS, AND KEY 22 IS THE BEST PASSAGE IN THE CHAPTER. The Chrysostom blocks at keys 1, 8, 18 and 22 are all real Homilies on Philippians. At key 22 he refuses to accept the apostle's hesitation between life and death and presses him with a series of comparisons: what trader whose vessel is full of untold wealth, when he may run into port, would prefer to be still at sea? what wrestler, when he might be crowned, would choose to contend? what general, who might be quit of war with trophies and refresh himself in the palace, would choose still to stand in battle array? He prefaces it with an unusual confession -- 'We all shudder at death, I am wont to say, some by reason of our many sins, of whom I too am one, others from love of life, and cowardice, of whom may I never be one.'

THE PRAETORIUM AT 1:13 -- A FIVE-WAY DISAGREEMENT. Barnes argues at length for the emperor's palace, on three grounds (provincial usage for the chief magistrate's residence, an ancient report that the Roman palace was so called, and the greetings from Caesar's household at 4:22), while noting that Bloomfield and Rosenmuller prefer the praetorian camp. Clarke takes the palace. Calvin names it the hall and palace of Nero and supports it with a long antiquarian excursus deriving praetorium from the general's tent. Ellicott lays out palace, attached barrack, and camp outside the walls, observes that all the ancient commentators take the first but that it agrees badly with Acts 28:16-30 (Paul in his own hired house), and follows Lightfoot in taking the word for a BODY OF MEN, the praetorian guard, noting that 'in all other places' is really 'to all the rest'. Robertson agrees with the guard (ten thousand picked soldiers) but reports Mommsen and Ramsay for the judicial authorities of the imperial court.

CALVIN BREAKS WITH ALL PRECEDING INTERPRETERS AT 1:21. On 'to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain' he writes: 'Interpreters have hitherto, in my opinion, given a wrong rendering and exposition to this passage; for they make this distinction, that Christ was life to Paul, and death was gain. I, on the other hand, make Christ the subject of discourse in BOTH clauses' -- supplying the preposition, which he says the Greeks leave to be understood, so that Christ is gain to him in life and in death alike. He argues the sense is fuller, since Christ alone makes us happy in death and in life. Clarke independently reads it the same way ('Whether I live or die, Christ is gain to me') and Henry reports 'To me, living and dying, Christ is gain' as an alternative. Against them, Barnes takes it of a single purpose of life, Ellicott of the whole concrete state of life lived in Christ, and Robertson says living is coextensive with Christ.

WHAT SALVATION MEANS AT 1:19, WITH BARNES NAMING CLARKE AS AN OPPONENT. Clarke takes it of temporal safety and release, arguing the Romans would see that a man proclaiming a prince whose kingdom was not of this world could be no enemy to Caesar. Barnes rejects that view and names Clarke, with Koppe and Rosenmuller, as holding it, on the ground that Paul was not certain of release and could not have expected release from 'the supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ'. Ellicott takes the word as safety, shown either in life by release or in death by coming home to Christ. Calvin says flatly that what follows shows he is not speaking of the safety of the body. Wesley reads a higher degree of glory. Robertson takes it of release, reports that Lightfoot takes it of eternal salvation because verse 20 suits that better, and asks whether Paul carried both conceptions in the word. Direct in-text naming of one commentator by another is rare in this corpus.

WHETHER PAUL'S CONFIDENCE AT 1:25 WAS FULFILLED, AND WHAT KIND OF KNOWLEDGE IT WAS -- SIX POSITIONS, ONE OF THEM LIMITING APOSTOLIC INSPIRATION. Clarke states as fact that after two years in bonds at Rome he was released. Wesley calls it 'a prophetic notice given him while he was writing this' and says 'doubtless he did see them after this confinement'. Gill denies both: not a certain knowledge from revelation but a conjectural knowledge from the present state of things, and 'of this there is no sufficient proof'. Barnes agrees the ground was neither revelation nor intelligence from the palace but his belief that his life was needful, and warns that 'know' is not to be pressed as absolute since 1:27 and 2:17 admit a doubt. ELLICOTT GOES FURTHEST: the same word is used at Acts 20:25 of a conviction which 'so far as we can follow out the history, was not verified', and he concludes that 'the apostolic inspiration, like the apostolic power of miracle, was a gift relative to the apostolic work, not necessarily extending beyond it.' Calvin answers the objection by a rule -- the saints hold a sure persuasion only where they have a sure token from God, and expect everything else conditionally.

BISHOPS AND DEACONS AT 1:1 -- FIVE COMMENTATORS, ONE CONCLUSION, ONE RESERVATION. Henry says the apostle acknowledges but two orders and that the same titles, qualifications and acts of office are everywhere ascribed to bishops and presbyters alike (citing Dr Hammond). Clarke calls the question how one city could have several bishops a waste of paper, dismisses the answer that Philippi was a metropolitan see as 'the extravagance of trifling', and says 'I believe no such officer is meant as we now term bishop'. Robertson notes that in the second century the word came to mean one superior to elders (Ignatius) 'but not so in the N.T.'. Wesley says the names were used promiscuously in the first ages. Calvin concedes that order requires one presiding -- but 'of particular bodies, not of whole provinces, much less of the whole world' -- and says the later restriction of the name 'originated in a human custom, and rests on no Scripture authority', from which corruption one man 'under the pretext of a new appellation, usurped dominion over the others'. Ellicott alone adds a reservation: granting the indifferent use of the titles, he holds it 'in no way weakens' the historical development of the Episcopate early in the second century, probably under the sanction of St John.

BARNES'S CHAPTER INTRODUCTION IS 4,485 WORDS AND IS THE LARGEST SINGLE BLOCK MET IN THE CORPUS SO FAR. It gives the topography and history of Philippi (named from Philip, formerly Crenides from its springs, the Thasian gold and silver mines, the road from Asia to Europe), the battle in which Cassius killed himself and Brutus wept over him as 'the last of the Romans', and then refuses to let that be the reason the town is remembered: 'Philippi was the first place in Europe where the gospel was preached; and this fact invests the place with more interest and importance than it derives from the battle fought there.' He adds a contemporary note, that two American missionaries visited the ruins in May 1834, saw what might have been the forum where Paul and Silas were beaten, and found the road from Neapolis still paved throughout.

CALVIN QUOTES HIS OWN VERSE, AND NAMES A CONTEMPORARY HE DESPISES. At 1:7 he cites Tertullian's saying that the blood of the martyrs is the seed of the Church and adds that he imitated it himself in a Latin poem, quoting two lines of his own composition. At 1:18 he says that when he heard 'that impure dog Carolus was scattering the seeds of pure doctrine at Avignon and elsewhere, we gave thanks to God because he had made use of that most profligate and worthless villain for his glory' -- but sets a limit at once: 'though Paul rejoiced in the advancement of the gospel, yet, had the matter been in his hand, he would never have ordained such persons as ministers.' Both are unusually personal for a commentary and worth flagging for any future reader of the synthesis.

MATTHEW HENRY IS EXPOSITION PLUS CONCISE AT EVERY KEY, SEVENTH BOOK. Henry appears at eight keys (1, 3, 7, 8, 9, 12, 21, 27) with blocks running to 2,011 words, and each carries the full Exposition followed by the Concise restating the same material. The block at key 12 covers verses 12-20 and the block at key 21 covers 21-26, so Henry's coverage is by paragraph rather than by verse, which leaves several keys (2, 4, 5, 6, 10, 11, 13-20, 22-26, 28-30) with no Henry at all.

THE 200-WORD CAP BITES ON GILL AT NINE KEYS. Gill is truncated at exactly 200 words at keys 1, 5, 7, 9, 10, 11, 15, 17, 19, 27, always mid-clause. Combined with the same finding at 1thessalonians 5 (eight keys), Gill is now clearly the voice most often lost to the cap in the NT files. The standing re-fetch item for Keil and Lightfoot should be widened to include him.

TWO INDEPENDENT NOTES ON THE LIMITS OF WHAT THE TEXT WILL BEAR AT 1:22. Ellicott calls the Authorised rendering of 'if I live in the flesh, this is the fruit of my labour' inaccurate and 'perhaps a gloss to soften the difficulty of the original', and says the construction 'is clearly broken by emotion or absorption in thought' and can only be supplied by conjecture. Robertson notes there is no word for 'if' in the Greek at all, and that the verb rendered 'I wot not' elsewhere means to make known, so that 'I do not declare what I shall choose' makes perfectly good sense. Barnes reports the renderings of Coverdale, Luther, Koppe, Rosenmuller and Calvin, grants the thought is valuable, and doubts it can be got out of the Greek.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, philippians 1, nine entries, all in window. 1-2 = 650w, 9 voices. 3-6 = 650w, 8. 7-8 = 649w, 9. 9-11 = 649w, 8. 12-14 = 643w, 8. 15-18 = 648w, 8. 19-21 = 649w, 8. 22-26 = 649w, 8. 27-30 = 643w, 8. Every claim traced to a named block in data/commentary/cow/philippians/1.json before writing. Exclusions: all four Jamieson blocks (keys 4, 10, 16, 22) declared as residue; the single Cyril of Jerusalem block (key 19) dropped silently for the VOICE_LABELS defect; about 984 words of StudyLight footer, CSS and JavaScript inside the Ellicott block at key 30 ignored as chrome. Gross usable 61,018; after voice exclusions and chrome about 58,944 by the build's own count, of which the chrome removal accounts for 984. No entry rests on a single school; the largest single source block in the chapter, Barnes's 4,485-word introduction, was used only for entry 1-2.

JFB displacement, 46th confirmation, and a THIRD SUCCESSFUL ADVANCE PREDICTION. Leviticus 24 sits at canonical position 114, so the ratio law recorded at exodus 5 predicted a donor near position 95 — Leviticus 5, with a working window of Leviticus 2 to 8 — before I looked at the chapter. There is a single JFB block, at key 5, and it is Leviticus 6:24-30 entire: the law of the sin offering, the fat and inwards washed and salted and burnt on the altar, the rest of the carcass belonging to the officiating priest and eaten only within the tabernacle precincts by members of a priestly family, the earthen vessel broken because porous and the metallic pan scoured because the flesh had made it too sacred for common use. Donor position 96 against a predicted 95, a ratio of 0.842 where the ten-case mean was 0.834 and the observed band 0.806 to 0.864. The block is wholly foreign to its host, since Leviticus 24:5 is the baking of the twelve shewbread cakes and has no slain victim in it at all. That is now three advance predictions in two batches — exodus 39 (predicted Exodus 24, found Exodus 25-26), exodus 33 (predicted Exodus 20, found Exodus 20), and this — and thirteen cases supporting the law overall. A practical note on method: with only one displaced block in the chapter there was no stride to check, so the ratio was the only test available, and it was enough. That is the first time the law has done work no other signal could have done.

A new unusable-block category to sit beside the bare-quotation one from note 1137: the BARE CROSS-REFERENCE. Leviticus 24 repeats material given in Exodus, and Clarke responds by pointing back rather than commenting again, so three of his eleven blocks here are nothing but pointers — key 1 is the chapter argument alone, key 2 is Pure oil olive, see every thing relative to this ordinance explained on Exodus 27:20-21, key 5 is See the whole account of the shew-bread in the notes on Exodus 25:30, and key 20 is This is a repetition of the lex talionis, which see explained Exodus 21:24. None of these says anything about the verse it sits under. I excluded Clarke from the first two entries on that ground, exactly as I have been excluding Keil where the 200-word cap leaves nothing but quoted verses, and the result is that entries 1 and 5-9 carry four voices instead of five while losing nothing real. This is the same defect that made exodus 39 unwritable (note 1134), but at a survivable scale: there the cross-references were the whole catena for several runs, whereas here they are one voice out of six. The generalisation worth recording is that a chapter which re-enacts earlier legislation will have a systematically thinner catena than its word count suggests, because the commentators decline to comment twice — and the thinning falls hardest on Clarke, who cross-references most freely.

StudyLight boilerplate tail, 36th instance, non-discriminating: Ellicott's last block is at key 23, which is also the chapter's last key, so this instance cannot distinguish the two rules and the numbers 28 rule stands where the five discriminating cases left it. Gill's separate sacred-texts navigation tail also appears at key 23, and it is likewise his last block and the chapter's last key, so it too tells us nothing new. That open question — where Gill's tail attaches when he stops short of the final key — has now gone eight chapters without a test case, and it may be that Gill simply always runs to the end of a chapter, in which case the question is unanswerable rather than merely unanswered. Worth checking directly some time: if Gill's key list is coextensive with the chapter's in every chapter examined so far, the rule cannot be established and the search should stop.

Three clean disagreements in one chapter, and the middle one is a rare case of a voice reading a law as being about somebody else's god. First, how the shewbread lay: Wesley says flatly that the two rows were not one loaf above another but one beside another, and argues it from the incense set upon each, while Ellicott renders the word piles and describes the twelve as stacked one upon another in two heaps laid across the board, overhanging it at either side. Second, and most interesting, whose god is meant by whosoever curseth his God. Ellicott takes it of the heathen's own deity, reasoning that since the criminal who occasioned the law was an Egyptian, provision is made first for Gentiles sojourning in Israel who still profess their own faith, so that such a man is left to his co-religionists to punish and Israel is not to interfere; Clarke, Wesley and Calvin all take it of the true God, Calvin making the verse the guard of the third commandment. Third, whether like for like is literal: Gill will not have breach for breach and eye for eye taken strictly at all, understanding the price or value of them in a pecuniary way, while Calvin defends the rule as it stands, arguing that without it an accomplished villain could maim his brother and then laugh at both the man and the Law, and answering the charge of injustice by noting that God does not command an eye for an eye until he has restricted it to injuries knowingly and wilfully inflicted. All three are carried in the tags with holders named. Worth noting how the third pairs with the second: Calvin, who is severest on the blasphemy law, is also the one who extends the equality clause furthest, holding that God takes the whole human race under his protection because he created all men after his own image.

Length control, six entries: 630, 648, 650, 643, 647, 647, all grade A. One entry drafted in range on the first attempt — the vv1-4 entry at 630 — and it is the only four-voice entry in the chapter, which is now the fourth consecutive confirmation of the voice-count relation from notes 1102, 1107, 1133 and 1140. The rest drafted at 828, 888, 734, 845 and 794 on five and six voices. A second grade-B-from-vocabulary case appeared and was fixed the same way as the two before it: the shewbread entry came off the first draft at ttr 0.587, because cakes, table, piles and frankincense carried nearly all the nouns in a passage about nothing else. Swapping in loaves, board and stacks, and cutting the geometry of the projecting handbreadths, moved it to 0.614 while also taking off the length. That is three instances now — leviticus 9 on sacrifice and fire, exodus 33 on tent and tabernacle, and this — and the rule can be stated firmly: where a chapter's subject supplies one dominant noun, choose two or three synonyms BEFORE drafting, because the meter will otherwise catch it after the work is done. Every effective length cut was again a whole idea (Ellicott's three golden moulds, the three possible placements of the incense bowls, the eight priestly perquisites, Clarke's Kennicott and De Rossi manuscript evidence, Calvin's second objection to the lex talionis, Jarchi's distinction about the wounded beast). Note 1018 holds across sixteen chapters.

JFB displacement, ratio-law prediction MISSED. Host numbers 9 = canonical chapter position 126; the law derived over ten cases (donor_pos/host_pos, mean 0.834, band 0.806-0.864) predicted a donor near Leviticus 15, window 12-18. The two JFB blocks here, at keys 7 and 13 (stride 6, as usual), are Leviticus 19:23 (fruit trees not to bear in their earliest years, to be regarded as uncircumcised) and Leviticus 19:30. Leviticus 19 is canonical position 109, giving a ratio of 0.865 -- one thousandth above the prior band maximum, and one chapter outside the predicted window. Recording it as a miss rather than widening the band after the fact: the law places the donor at a fixed FRACTION of host position rather than a fixed lag, and that much still holds, but its usable precision is about plus or minus 0.03 x host, which at this position is roughly four chapters. Fourth out-of-sample test; running record three hits (exodus 39, exodus 33, leviticus 24) and one miss.

200-word truncation cap, seventh chapter with the identical signature: Keil capped at exactly 200 words in 8 of his 9 blocks, Gill only where he ran long, no other voice touched. Worst consequence again at key 2, where Keil's block is cut off inside his quotation of vv2-6 before any comment begins, so the key holds pure verse text and his only real comment falls on v6, outside the entry the key sits in -- Keil therefore excluded from entry 1-5. Both JFB blocks (keys 7 and 13) are displaced Leviticus 19 material and are excluded as well; both keys carry other voices, so the exclusions cost nothing.

StudyLight tail rule, sixth discriminating case and still no counterexample: the site boilerplate (nav CSS, copyright, commentary list) is attached to the end of Ellicott's final block, which here is key 22, while the chapter's last key is 23. Gill's separate sacred-texts tail ('Next: Numbers Chapter 10 Sacred Texts') sits at key 23, which is both Gill's last block and the chapter's last key, so this chapter is again NOT discriminating for the Gill tail -- nine chapters now without one, consistent with the possibility that Gill always runs to the chapter's last key and the question is unanswerable from within the corpus.

Editorial footnotes inlined inside Calvin's blocks again, and here they are unusually dangerous. Key 18 carries the editor's apparatus on sacraments spliced mid-sentence into Calvin's argument, complete with Latin quotations from Augustine and volume-and-page citations; key 19 carries an editor's note reporting Dathe, Malvenda and 'other ancient commentators' as ADOPTING the very opinion Calvin is rejecting in the surrounding sentences, plus a Vulgate citation and, at the very end, the line 'They also serve, who only stand, and wait' attributed in the footnote to Milton's sonnet on his blindness. A reader distilling the block without noticing the seams would credit Calvin with Milton's line and with the position he explicitly refuses. The fidelity gate cannot see the difference, since the footnote sits inside the Calvin span.

Ellicott and Wesley divide on what the cloud covered, and each states the other's position as the thing to be denied. Ellicott renders 'the tabernacle of the tent of the testimony' as the tabernacle BELONGING TO the tent, and argues from the older narrative -- Moses could not enter the tent of meeting because the cloud abode upon it, with no part of the structure singled out -- that there is no sufficient ground for confining the cloud to the chamber where the two tables were kept. Wesley reads the same phrase as 'the tabernacle ABOVE the tent of the testimony', i.e. precisely that part in which the ark stood, 'for there the cloudy pillar stood'. Recorded as a debate in the tags rather than harmonised.

Length control, sixteenth-plus confirmation of note 1018 and no improvement to report. All five entries overshot on first draft (669, 772, 693, 768, 831 against a 650 ceiling) despite the quota being known before a word was written. Structural cuts -- dropping a whole named idea, e.g. Houbigant's rejoinder to Clarke on the papyrus leaves, Jarchi's remark on asking Moses before Aaron, Calvin's argument that the paschal lamb was a true victim -- moved 26 to 65 words each; lexical shaving moved 4 to 12. Entry 19 needed four passes because I tried shaving before cutting on the last 30 words. The lesson stands: draft to the quota, and when over, cut ideas first. Two entries (15 and 19) landed at 648 and 645, which is tighter to the ceiling than is comfortable.

Abridgement-rescue in the reverse direction, a sixth confirmation with a new wrinkle. Henry holds keys only at 1 and 15, so his long run-ahead at key 15 -- 'this is repeated again and again, because it was a constant miracle... mentioned long after by David, and by the people of God after their captivity... the guidance of this cloud is spoken of as signifying the guidance of the Blessed Spirit' -- would have been stranded when the material's proper home is the closing entry 19-23. Wesley carries the same material at key 21, inside that span, so it reaches the last entry legitimately through the abridging voice rather than through Henry. Previous cases all ran the other way (Wesley's key rescuing Henry's material for an earlier entry); this is the first where the abridgement carried Henry's material FORWARD past his own last key.

LIGHTFOOT RESIDUE IS A CLEAN CHAPTER MISFILE WITH THE VERSE INDEX PRESERVED -- THE SHARPEST DEFECT SIGNATURE FOUND SO FAR. John Lightfoot appears at keys 1, 15, 19, 23, 24, 27 of acts 11, and every block is his Horae Hebraicae on ACTS 2. Critically, five of the six land on THE SAME VERSE NUMBER IN THE WRONG CHAPTER: key 15 = Acts 2:15 ('It is but the third hour of the day'), key 19 = Acts 2:19 (the pillaring smoke), key 23 = Acts 2:23 ('delivered by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God'), key 24 = Acts 2:24 ('having loosed the pains of death'), key 27 = Acts 2:27 ('Thou wilt not leave my soul in hell'). Only key 1 breaks the pattern, carrying Acts 2:13 (the mockers saying they are full of new wine). This is categorically different from the Jamieson stride: for Lightfoot the VERSE selector is right and the CHAPTER selector is wrong. Whoever fixes the fetcher should be able to test that hypothesis directly against any other chapter carrying Lightfoot blocks. All six declared as residue.

CORRECTION TO MY OWN PREVIOUS NOTE: THE JAMIESON SOURCE STRIDE IS NOT AN EXACT 5. Last batch (philippians 1) I inferred from Romans 16:8/13/18/23 that the rule was six keys forward in the target and exactly five verses forward in the source, and said the earlier walks fitted. This chapter breaks it. Jamieson here is at keys 3, 9, 15, 21, 27 -- stride 6, offset 3, FIVE members, the eighth stride-6 confirmation -- walking JOHN 12-13, but the anchors are 12:37-41 (the block carries its own range label '37-41'), 12:44, 12:44 AGAIN (keys 9 and 15 are byte-identical, a stall), 13:3, and 13:6. Counting continuously through John 12 (50 verses) the distinct positions are 37, 44, 53, 56: gaps of 7, then 0 at the stall, then 9, then 3. The +5 I reported was probably an artefact of pinning range-comments to a single verse; JFB blocks routinely cover verse ranges, so the anchor is imprecise by several verses either way. The stride of 6 IN THE TARGET KEYS remains exact and is now confirmed eight times; the source stride should be treated as irregular until it can be measured against blocks that carry their own range labels, as the one at key 3 does.

CHROME INSIDE THE ELLICOTT BLOCK AT THE TERMINAL KEY, THIRD CONSECUTIVE CHAPTER. Key 30, Charles Ellicott: block of 1,253 words of which 269 are real commentary, the remainder being the StudyLight footer, CSS and JavaScript, measuring 984 words / 30,326 characters / 126 NEWLINES. Identical in shape to 1thessalonians 5 key 28 and philippians 1 key 30. Three consecutive chapters establishes it: when the last key of a chapter carries an Ellicott block, roughly 984 words of chrome are silently credited to him and the naive usable-source figure is that much too high. Twelfth chrome measurement.

CYRIL RESIDUE: EIGHT BLOCKS, ONE OF THEM GENUINE, AND A NEW DUPLICATE PAIR. Cyril of Jerusalem appears at keys 12, 15, 16, 17, 21, 23, 24, 26 -- the most Cyril blocks yet seen in one chapter. Keys 12 and 15 are BYTE-IDENTICAL (Catechetical Lecture 17.27, Peter healing Aeneas at Lydda and raising Tabitha at Joppa). Keys 16, 17, 21, 23 and 24 are unrelated catechetical material (Phil 4:4; Acts 5:12; Isa 11:2; the Epistles of Paul; the name of Jesus). Key 26 IS ON POINT: Catechetical Lecture 16.28, 'And in Antioch also, a most renowned city of Syria, when the preaching of Christ took effect, Barnabas was sent hence as far as Antioch to help on the good work, being a good man and full of the Holy Ghost' -- which is the subject matter of this very pericope, and it was used. The seven others dropped SILENTLY, since the VOICE_LABELS defect makes 'Cyril of Jerusalem' undeclarable.

VOICE_LABELS DEFECT, TWENTY-FIVE BATCHES OPEN. scripts/synthesis_qa.py line 145: _LABEL_RE joins the VOICE_LABELS short forms with a trailing \s*:, so 'Cyril' can never match the head 'Cyril of Jerusalem:'. Note that 'Lightfoot' DOES work, being a suffix of 'John Lightfoot:' -- which is why the six Lightfoot residue blocks in this chapter could be declared while the seven Cyril ones had to be dropped silently. The asymmetry is itself a demonstration of the bug. One-line fix: list 'Cyril of Jerusalem' instead of 'Cyril'.

CLARKE'S CHAPTER ARGUMENT AT KEY 1 HAS ITS CROSS-REFERENCES REWRITTEN TO ROMANS 8. Clarke's summary of Acts 11 at key 1 reads 'He defends himself by relating at large the whole business concerning Cornelius, Rom 8:4-17. His defense is accepted... Rom 8:18. An account of the proceedings of those who were scattered abroad... Rom 8:19-21' and so on through Rom 8:30. Every reference should be to Acts 11 and the verse numbers are correct; only the book and chapter have been replaced. This is a THIRD distinct flavour of the same underlying fault seen in the Lightfoot blocks -- verse index preserved, book and chapter wrong -- and it appears here inside a reference-tagging layer rather than in block selection.

WHETHER THE WORD WAS SPOKEN TO GREEKS OR GRECIAN JEWS AT 11:20 -- A SIX-WAY SPLIT ON READING AND SENSE. Clarke reports that Hellenes rests on a long list of versions and fathers, that Griesbach admitted it to the text and few critics doubt it, and argues that otherwise the verse does again what was already done. Robertson calls Hellenes 'undoubtedly the correct reading' and rests on the presence of kai, which makes no sense otherwise. Ellicott finds the manuscripts nearly balanced (B and D for Hellenistae, A for Hellenes), notes that the Sinaitic reads the incomprehensible 'Evangelistae', which so far as it goes tells for Hellenistae, and then decides for Hellenes on internal evidence in a numbered four-point argument. Barnes and Calvin BOTH KEEP THE OTHER READING and yet expound it of Gentiles -- Calvin on the ground that the Jews already mentioned were partly of Cyprus, which counted as part of Greece, so Luke must be marking a further class, 'this contrariety doth cause me to expound it of the Gentiles'. Henry alone holds out for Hellenist Jews, citing Lightfoot for the view that they were so called at Antioch as Jews of the corporation of a Syrogrecian city.

WHO GAVE THE NAME CHRISTIAN AT 11:26. Clarke argues from the verb chrematisai, which in the New Testament means to appoint or warn by divine direction (Matt 2:12; Luke 2:26; Acts 10:22), that the name is FROM GOD and was most likely given through Saul and Barnabas, and calls it 'the highest character which any human being can bear upon earth'. Barnes canvasses the same senses, concedes the divine-communication sense is the most usual, and yet inclines the other way, since had the apostles conferred it the record would have said so rather than merely that they were called. Robertson holds the Gentiles must have given it, since the Jews would not use Christos of them and called them Galileans or Nazarenes. Calvin sidesteps: there were Christians at Jerusalem and Samaria before this, since to be a disciple of Christ is to be a Christian, but when they began plainly to be called what they were, the name served to set forth Christ's glory.

PERSEVERANCE AT 11:23, WITH CLARKE AT HIS MOST POLEMICAL. On Barnabas exhorting them to cleave to the Lord with purpose of heart, Clarke writes: 'God gave them the grace... it was their business to use this. If they did not, the gift would be resumed... It is absurd to talk of being children of God, and of absolute, final perseverance, when the soul has lost its spiritual union... if he ever had the salvation of God, he has lost it; he is fallen from grace; nor is there a word in the book of God, fairly and honestly understood, that says such a person shall absolutely and unavoidably arise from his fall.' Barnes reads the same phrase as a settled plan formed at conversion without which there can be no evidence of piety; Ellicott, more mildly, that man's will can frustrate grace and its co-operation in firm resolve was needed. Robertson notes only that the glow of first enthusiasm often passes after a revival.

WHAT WITHSTANDING GOD MEANS AT 11:17 -- WESLEY AND CALVIN TURN THE SAME WORDS AGAINST OPPOSITE TARGETS. Wesley: 'And who are we that we should withstand God? Particularly by laying down rules of Christian communion which exclude any whom he has admitted into the Church of the first born... O that all Church governors would consider how bold an usurpation this is on the authority of the supreme Lord of the Church!' Calvin, at the same verse: 'we do not only resist God by striving against him, but also by lingering... he which doth not receive those whom God offereth, and shutteth the gate which God openeth, he hindereth the work of God so much as in him lieth; as we say at this day, that those men make war against God who are set against the baptizing of infants', adding that magistrates who should assist the martyrs and instead stop their mouths resist in the same manner. Two of the most quotable applications in the chapter, pointing in opposite directions.

WHO THE ELDERS WERE AT 11:30, WITH BARNES NAMING CALVIN. Barnes notes this is the first mention of elders in the Christian church, doubts the synagogue elders can be meant, and inclines to think no office is denoted at all but simply the aged and prudent members entrusted with the distribution; he adds 'Calvin supposes that the apostles were particularly intended. But this is not probable.' Clarke offers a third account, that they were probably those who first believed, reports a division of the primitive disciples into eye-witnesses, firstfruits and successors, and inclines to the deacons.

FOUR VOICES INDEPENDENTLY MAKE 11:2 AN ARGUMENT AGAINST THE PAPACY. Barnes: the fact that Peter was called to account 'shows conclusively that the apostles and early Christians did not regard Peter as having any particular supremacy... If Peter had been regarded as having the authority which the Roman Catholics claim for him, they would have submitted at once.' Clarke: the primitive church at Jerusalem 'had no conception of St. Peter's supremacy... this absurd dream is every where refuted in the New Testament.' Robertson ends his note 'It is plain that Peter was not regarded as any kind of pope or overlord.' Henry: 'so far were they from looking upon him as infallible, or as the supreme head of the church', and notes that Peter himself 'does not insist upon his being the chief of the apostles, for he was far from the thought of that supremacy which his pretended successors claim.' Calvin alone does not take the opening, being occupied instead with identifying the objectors.

CHRYSOSTOM'S SINGLE BLOCK COVERS THE WHOLE SECOND HALF OF THE CHAPTER AND CONTAINS THE BEST PASSAGE IN IT. His one block sits at key 19 (1,290 words) and comments continuously on verses 19-30, which means it can only be used in the entry containing verse 19. Two things in it are worth preserving. On the dispersion: 'If they had made it their express study how best to establish the Church, they would have done no other thing than this - they dispersed the teachers.' On Barnabas going to fetch Saul, an unrestrained encomium: 'He came to the athletic wrestler, the general fit to lead armies, the champion of single combat, the lion - I am at a loss for words, say what I will - the hunting-dog, killer of lions, bull of strength, lamp of brightness, mouth sufficing for a world.'

MATTHEW HENRY IS PARAGRAPH-BLOCKED, NOT VERSE-BLOCKED, AND CARRIES BOTH EXPOSITION AND CONCISE. Henry appears at only four keys (1, 19, 25, 27) with blocks of 3,495, 3,955, 200 and 1,782 words. The block at key 1 covers verses 1-18 and the one at key 19 covers 19-30, so twenty-six of the thirty keys have no Henry at all; the 200-word block at key 25 is Concise only. Eighth book in which the Henry text is found spliced or mis-scoped.

ROBERTSON DRAWS A CHRISTOLOGICAL ARGUMENT FROM 11:21. 'The hand of the Lord' is an Old Testament phrase for the hand of Jehovah, while 'turned unto the Lord' in the same verse refers to the Lord Jesus of verse 20 -- 'clearly showing that the early disciples put Jesus on a par with Jehovah. His deity was not a late development read back into the early history.' At the same verse the three-way split on what the hand of the Lord means: Chrysostom takes it of miracles, Clarke of the energy of God accompanying the preaching, and Henry expressly prefers the power of grace on the heart 'because many saw the miracles who were not converted'.

THE 200-WORD CAP BITES ON GILL, LIGHTFOOT AND CYRIL. Gill is truncated at exactly 200 words at key 28; Lightfoot at keys 15, 23, 24 and 27; Cyril at keys 16, 21, 23 and 24. In each case the block stops mid-sentence. The standing re-fetch item should note that the cap now demonstrably truncates the two voices whose blocks are ALSO misfiled, so a re-fetch would need to fix both faults at once to be worth doing.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, acts 11, eight entries, all in window. 1-3 = 646w, 7 voices. 4-15 = 642w, 6. 16-18 = 648w, 7. 19-21 = 649w, 9. 22-24 = 648w, 6. 25-26 = 624w, 9. 27-28 = 634w, 8. 29-30 = 630w, 7. Eight rather than the seven the entry-count guide suggests, because verses 25-26 carry the naming of the Christians, which could not be compressed into a joint entry with 22-24 without losing the four-way disagreement over who gave the name. Every claim traced to a named block in data/commentary/cow/acts/11.json before writing. Exclusions: six John Lightfoot blocks (keys 1, 15, 19, 23, 24, 27) and five Jamieson blocks (keys 3, 9, 15, 21, 27) declared as residue; seven Cyril of Jerusalem blocks dropped silently, the eighth (key 26) used as genuine; about 984 words of chrome inside the Ellicott block at key 30 ignored. Gross usable 42,946; after all exclusions 38,987 by the build's own count.

JFB displacement: FIRST NT HOST, and the ratio law holds when positions are reckoned WITHIN THE NT rather than across the whole canon. Five JFB blocks here, at keys 2, 8, 14, 20, 26 -- stride 6, the same stride seen at numbers 9 -- and all five are Acts 3 material marching forward: keys 2 and 8 carry the same block on Acts 3:1-4 (Peter and John going up at the hour of prayer), key 14 is Acts 3:12 (the might and merit of the cure not due to us), key 20 is Acts 3:17 (will not break the bruised reed, ye did it through ignorance), key 26 is Acts 3:22-23 (that Prophet, on pain of being cut off). A continuous donor sweep, not a repeat. Whole-canon positions give donor 1021 / host 1042 = 0.980, far outside the band; NT-internal positions (Matthew 28 + Mark 16 + Luke 24 + John 21 = 89 preceding chapters) give Acts 3 = 92 and Acts 24 = 113, ratio 0.814, inside the 0.806-0.864 band derived from ten OT cases. The implication is that the defect is an offset in the source's own file ordering and that OT and NT are indexed separately, which is why the fraction rather than the lag is constant. Fifth out-of-sample test; record now four hits (exodus 39, exodus 33, leviticus 24, acts 24) and one miss (numbers 9).

Two displacement kinds met in one chapter, and they need different handling. (a) JFB's five blocks are the familiar cross-book defect and were excluded. (b) Calvin's key-21 block is displaced WITHIN the chapter: it is filed under verse 21 but discusses Drusilla's parentage, her betrothal to Epiphanis, Felix's use of Simon the Cyprian to entice her away, and Paul's later refusal to be silent about Christ -- all of which treats vv24-25. Under the filing rule this material could move, because Calvin holds key 23, inside the 23-24 span; so it was used there rather than dropped, and Calvin still carries entry 19-21 through his substantive key-19 comment on the absent accusers. Chrysostom is the mirror case: he holds ONE key in the chapter, 22, and his block runs on through vv23-27 and into chapter 25. Having no key anywhere else, his run-ahead cannot move, so his verse-22 and verse-23 material was used in the entry where it is filed and the rest left unused. Worth stating as a rule: a run-ahead is rescuable only if the voice holds a key inside the target span, which is why single-key patristic voices lose most of their material.

Chapter shape and tiling. 27 keys contiguous, 45,976 usable source words -- 1.55x the entry-count predictor's usual load and over the batch threshold, so this chapter was the whole batch. Ten voices, an unusually deep NT bench: Gill, Barnes and Robertson at all 27 keys, Clarke 23, Ellicott 22, Calvin 18, Wesley 15, JFB 5 (all displaced), Henry 3, Chrysostom 1. Henry's three keys (1, 10, 22) are section headers running 4,433 words at the longest, so nearly all his material for vv2-9 and vv11-21 is stranded: Wesley, his abridger, holds keys 2 and 4 but nothing in 5-9, so only part could be rescued. Three keys individually exceed the 4,500-word split threshold (1 at 5,333, 10 at 5,949, 22 at 6,613) and had to stand as single-verse entries, which no tiling can avoid. Final tiling 1 | 2-4 | 5-9 | 10 | 11-13 | 14-15 | 16-18 | 19-21 | 22 | 23-24 | 25 | 26 | 27 = 13 entries, exactly matching the keys-over-2000 + round(remaining/2500) predictor.

Three live disagreements recorded rather than harmonised. (1) At verse 8 Ellicott suspects the invitation to examine is a technical term and that Tertullus was proposing the prisoner be put to the question by scourging or other torture, keeping back the fact of his citizenship; Robertson answers flatly that torture was out of the question for a Roman citizen and the word means only hearing what Paul had to say. (2) At verse 22 the commentators split on the grammar with a real consequence: Barnes (with Beza, Grotius and Doddridge), Clarke (with Wakefield and Calmet) and Wesley read the knowledge as still to be acquired -- after I have been more accurately informed -- while Henry, Ellicott and Robertson take Felix to have known the Way already and to have deferred anyway, which makes the adjournment cynical rather than cautious. (3) At verse 25 Clarke reports Bishop Pearce's view that Felix trembled for his domestic peace, fearing Drusilla would be moved, and rejects it; Barnes and Calvin take the fear as ordinary conviction of sin. Note also a smaller one at verse 17, where Ellicott dates the absence at four years, Robertson at several, and Gill at five and twenty since the conversion -- which bears directly on what many years meant in Paul's compliment at verse 10.

Two source-shape facts worth recording for NT chapters. (1) The 200-word truncation cap that dominates the OT catena is essentially ABSENT here: Gill is capped at exactly 200 in only 2 of his 27 blocks and no other voice is capped at all, with Barnes running to 1,703 words, Chrysostom to 1,506, Ellicott to 1,339 and Henry to 4,433. Whatever produces the cap in the OT sources is not operating on this NT set, which is why an NT chapter of the same verse count carries three times the words. (2) The StudyLight tail sits at the end of Ellicott's final block as always, but here that block is key 27, which is also the chapter's last key, so acts 24 is NOT a discriminating case for the tail rule. Gill's separate sacred-texts tail does not appear in this chapter at all.

Length control on a thirteen-entry chapter, and the discipline got worse rather than better. Every one of the thirteen entries overshot on first draft, by 20 to 269 words against the 650 ceiling, and the mean number of trim passes was five; entry 5-9 took six and entries 22 and 25 took seven each. Structural cuts again moved 20 to 95 words apiece while lexical shaving moved 2 to 12, exactly as note 1018 has said for seventeen chapters. Two new failure modes surfaced here that are worth naming. First, on a chapter with ten voices the four-voices-per-paragraph rule silently drops a voice: entry 16-18 was drafted without Gill and entry 2-4 without him too, both caught only by the two-way voice check, and both had to be repaired by adding a sentence and trimming forty words to pay for it. On a deep bench the check must be run before trimming, not after. Second, chasing the last ten words produced one genuinely damaged sentence -- a cut left Barnes credited with a remark whose referent had been deleted -- which was caught on re-read and rewritten. Landing thirteen entries between 640 and 650 words is not a virtue; it means every entry was drafted a hundred words too long.

BLOCKER: OUT-OF-RANGE KEY 55 IN A 24-VERSE CHAPTER STOPS THE CHAPTER FROM LANDING. data/commentary/cow/1corinthians/16.json carries a key "55" holding John Lightfoot's Horae Hebraicae on 1 COR 15:55 ('O death, where is thy sting'). 1 Corinthians 16 has twenty-four verses. This is the chapter-misfile mechanism reported from acts 11 caught in the act: the fetcher wrote a NEIGHBOURING CHAPTER'S note into this file AT ITS OWN VERSE NUMBER, and because 55 exceeds the chapter length it produced a key that cannot exist here rather than colliding silently with a real one. WHY IT BLOCKS: validate-synthesis.py derives the chapter's verse set straight from the source keys (QA.coverage_problems builds  from source_keys), so key 55 counts as a verse that the pericopes must cover; any chapter that has an out-of-range scrape key AND declares pericope ranges therefore fails 'pericopes tile the chapter'. The validator's own comment anticipates this class of defect -- it cites the documented 2 Chronicles 27 key '16' holding Matthew Henry on chapter 28 -- and says such keys are 'recorded as advisories by --coverage rather than failures here', but that exemption does not reach the coverage check when ranges are declared. I did NOT edit the source file to work around it: deleting the key would destroy the evidence and would touch the tree the owner's hourly sync writes. The chapter is written and in window but has not been landed. OWNER DECISION NEEDED: either drop key 55 from the source file, or teach coverage_problems to ignore source keys greater than the chapter's verse count.

LIGHTFOOT IS OTHERWISE GENUINE IN THIS CHAPTER, WHICH SHARPENS THE ACTS 11 FINDING. Keys 5, 8, 10, 19 and 22 carry Lightfoot's Horae on 1 Cor 16:5, 16:8, 16:10, 16:19 and 16:22 and are real commentary on those verses; only key 1 (1 Cor 15 material on the Lord becoming man) and the out-of-range key 55 are residue. So the fault is not that Lightfoot's whole contribution is misfiled, as at acts 11 where all six blocks were Acts 2: it is that stray blocks from the NEIGHBOURING chapter are carried into the file at their own verse numbers alongside the chapter's genuine material. Two of his genuine blocks are themselves arguments against the printed subscription -- at key 5 he makes the translation of one clause 'the whole hinge of the controversy' and argues for Ephesus over Philippi, and at key 10 he says the man who added the underwriting was 'deceived again' into thinking Timothy carried the letter.

JAMIESON: NINTH STRIDE-6 CONFIRMATION, WALKING ACTS 26-27. Keys 1, 7, 13, 19 -- stride 6, offset 1, four members. Key 1 is JFB on Acts 26:25 (Paul's reply to Festus, 'Can anything surpass this reply, for readiness, self-possession, calm dignity?'); key 7 is a six-word fragment; key 13 is Acts 27:2-6 (the ship of Adramyttium, the centurion expecting to find another bound for Italy); key 19 is Acts 27:7 (contrary winds, Cnidus, the island of Coos). Offset 1 has now been seen twice (1peter 1 and here). Consistent with the correction filed last batch: the stride of 6 in the TARGET KEYS is exact and repeatable; the source anchors are approximate because JFB blocks comment on ranges.

THE STUCK CYRIL FRAGMENT REACHES A THIRD BOOK. The Cyril of Jerusalem block at key 23 is byte-identical (1,075 characters) to the blocks at philemon 1 key 25 and at 1thessalonians 5 keys 23 and 28 -- the Catechetical Lecture on 2 Cor 4:4, 'if some are right in their interpretation... he blinded the thoughts of them that believe not'. Fourth occurrence, third book, and the second time it has landed on key 23 specifically. Key 10 is separate unrelated catechetical material. KEY 20 IS GENUINE and was used: Cyril on the kiss of peace, 'Then the Deacon cries aloud, Receive ye one another; and let us kiss one another', which is exactly 1 Cor 16:20. All residue dropped silently, since the VOICE_LABELS defect leaves 'Cyril of Jerusalem' undeclarable.

CHROME INSIDE THE ELLICOTT BLOCK AT THE TERMINAL KEY, FOURTH CONSECUTIVE CHAPTER. Key 24, Charles Ellicott: block of 1,081 words of which 97 are real commentary; the rest is the StudyLight footer, CSS and JavaScript, measuring 984 words / 30,249 characters / 126 NEWLINES. Identical in shape to 1thessalonians 5 key 28, philippians 1 key 30 and acts 11 key 30. Four consecutive chapters. Thirteenth chrome measurement.

EDITORIAL APPARATUS SWALLOWED INTO THE CALVIN BLOCKS AT THREE SEPARATE KEYS. (1) Key 5: Calvin's discussion of where the epistle was written breaks off mid-sentence into a verbatim quotation of ADAM CLARKE's note on the same question ('St. Paul was now at Ephesus; for almost all allow, in opposition to the [subscription]...') attributed only as '-- Dr.'. This is the second instance of a Clarke-inside-Calvin splice; the first was at 1thessalonians 5:14. (2) Key 20: of a 1,051-word Calvin block, the great bulk is an editor's anti-Roman excursus on the mass, quoting 'Lectures on Popery (London, 1836)' and Calvin's own note on Rom 16:16 and a third writer's Annotations; only the closing sentences are Calvin on 1 Cor 16:20. (3) Key 22: the block drifts into a Latin epitaph for HENRY BULLINGER with an English verse translation, which is Calvin Translation Society front matter, not commentary on Anathema Maranatha. In all three cases the editorial matter is silently credited to Calvin and inflates his usable-source count.

WHERE THE MONEY WAS TO BE LAID BY, AT 16:2 -- ELLICOTT DISSENTS BY NAME. Barnes renders 'lay by him in store' as 'Let him lay up at home', and Robertson 'By himself, in his home'. Henry agrees and thinks the arrangement made for the sake of the poorer sort, who were to lay by weekly 'and not bring in to the common treasury, that by this means their contributions might be easy to themselves, and yet grow into a fund'. Ellicott dissents explicitly: 'I cannot think with Stanley and others that the Apostle means that each was to lay by in his own house, and not in some general treasury,' arguing from the stated object that the money be ready in bulk when Paul arrived, which private hoards would not secure. Clarke takes a middle course: each cast up his week's earnings and brought the sum on the first day to the common box, which he identifies with the synagogue's alms-purse.

WHAT THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK PROVES, AT 16:2. Barnes builds a numbered argument that the choice of the day is proof it was observed as holy time at Corinth and, since the same order went to Galatia, that the observance was general and rested on apostolic authority. Clarke calls it 'a strong argument for the keeping of the Christian Sabbath' and adds that Paul is following the rule of the synagogue, where collections were made on the sabbath so the poor should not be kept from coming. Ellicott is more cautious: the Greek is 'on one of the sabbaths', a Hebraism for the day after the sabbath, and the name 'the Lord's Day' does not yet occur, appearing first at Rev 1:10. CALVIN TURNS IT THE OTHER WAY: the day 'puts us in mind of our Christian liberty' precisely because it is not tied to the shadows of the law, though believers have always had a certain day of rest, 'not as if the worship of God consisted in idleness, but because it is of importance for the common harmony'; and where Paul forbids distinguishing days (Gal 4:10) he means with a view to religion, not to polity.

WHERE THE COMMA BELONGS AT 16:3. Read with the comma after 'letters', the Corinthians accredit their own delegates by letters of their own; read with it after 'approve', Paul sends them with letters of his. Barnes names Macknight and Doddridge for the first and Griesbach, Locke, Rosenmuller, Bloomfield, Beza, Grotius and Whitby for the second, prefers the second as according better with the design of the passage, and reports that Mill doubted whether the construction is possible in Greek. Ellicott and Robertson adopt the second without argument. CLARKE ESCAPES ALTOGETHER by reading the verb as a future perfect ('whom ye shall HAVE approved', with Bishop Pearce) and referring the letters to ones the Corinthians had already sent him. Robertson closes with a fact awkward for everybody: no name from Corinth occurs in the list of those who actually travelled with Paul (Acts 20:4).

WHAT THE THREE MEN SUPPLIED, AT 16:17 -- ROBERTSON DECLARES IT UNDECIDABLE. 'That which was lacking on your part they supplied' will bear either 'these filled up my lack of you' or 'these filled up your lack of me'; Robertson says 'Either makes perfectly good sense and both were true. Which Paul meant we cannot tell.' Clarke offers the same pair in other terms, either fuller communications than the letter carried or contributions towards Paul's support. Henry takes the first and builds on it, that report had made the Corinthians' cause worse than it was and these men did a good office by truly stating the facts.

FIVE VOICES AGREE AGAINST THE PRINTED SUBSCRIPTION, AND BARNES CALLS IT FALSE. The subscription in the English Bibles says the epistle was written from Philippi. Lightfoot rests the whole controversy on the translation of one clause and argues for Ephesus; Clarke says 'almost all allow, in opposition to the subscription, that it was written from Ephesus' and thinks verse 8 puts it past question; Ellicott calls the subscription 'an incorrect statement' arising from a misrepresentation of the very words; Calvin reports the common opinion for Philippi and prefers Ephesus; Gill and Henry both argue from the greeting sent by the churches of Asia rather than of Macedonia. Barnes goes furthest, at 16:24: the subscription 'was evidently written by some other hand than that of Paul, and has no claim to be regarded as inspired... in this instance, the subscription is evidently in its main statement false.' Lightfoot at key 10 adds that the same subscriber was 'deceived again' into supposing Timothy carried the letter.

HENRY ON THE LIMITS OF INSPIRATION, AT 16:7. On 'if the Lord permit' he argues that the apostles 'did not know thereby how God would dispose of them', and that this purpose cannot have been formed by revelation: 'had it been such he could not have spoken of it in this manner. A purpose formed thus in him must have been the purpose of God, signified to him by his Spirit; and could he say he would come to Corinth upon this view only, if God permit, that is, that he would execute God's own purpose concerning himself, with God's permission?' He concludes it was 'a common purpose, formed in his own spirit'. This is the same question Ellicott raised at Phil 1:25 last batch, reached from the opposite direction and by a different commentator.

HENRY'S BEST LINE IN THE CHAPTER, AT 16:14. On 'let all your things be done with charity', following immediately on 'quit you like men, be strong': 'When the apostle would have us play the man for our faith or religion, he puts in a caution against playing the devil for it... There is a great difference between constancy and cruelty, between Christian firmness and feverish wrath and transport. Christianity never appears to so much advantage as when the charity of Christians is most conspicuous.'

TWO ANCIENT AND ONE MODERN PARALLEL FOR ANATHEMA MARANATHA. Clarke lists the three Jewish forms of excommunication -- niddui (simple exclusion for thirty days), cherem (inflicted on one who had borne the first, with dire execrations but still leaving room for repentance) and shammatha (the direst, cutting off all hope of reconciliation) -- and transcribes from an old manuscript a form of the cherem anathematizing a man 'in both houses of judgment... among the seraphim and ophanim... by all the congregations of the great and the small'. Lightfoot works the Hebrew term through its three scriptural senses. BARNES REACHES INSTEAD FOR A TRAVELLER'S ANECDOTE: a pretended saint in Egypt, set ashore short of his destination, stood on the bank cursing and stamping and crying at every word 'Shar Ulah!' -- may God send and do justice -- which Barnes glosses as 'to punish you adequately is out of my power: I remit you to the vengeance of God', and asks whether that is not the import of the phrase. Ellicott denies any connection between the two words and prints them as two sentences.

CYRIL'S GENUINE BLOCK DESCRIBES THE KISS AS PERFORMED, AT 16:20. 'Then the Deacon cries aloud, Receive ye one another; and let us kiss one another. Think not that this kiss is of the same character with those given in public by common friends... this kiss blends souls one with another, and courts entire forgiveness for them... The kiss therefore is reconciliation, and for this reason holy.' Set beside it, Ellicott's history of the practice -- given up in the Latin Church in the thirteenth century, still used in the Greek Church on great occasions such as Easter Day -- and Robertson's note that in the synagogue men kissed men and women women, and that the custom seems never to have been promiscuous between the sexes.

Terminal scrape chrome inside the Ellicott block, FIFTH consecutive chapter (1thessalonians 5 k28, philippians 1 k30, acts 11 k30, 1corinthians 16 k24, judges 2 k22). Keil and Delitzsch truncated at exactly 200 words at ALL ELEVEN keys where he appears in this chapter. Every block stops mid-sentence. Adds to the standing 200-word cap re-fetch item: the cap is per-block and total, so a K&D block that opens by quoting two full verses (as at keys 17 and 21 here) can spend most of its budget on the text before any comment survives.
