BEDE APPEARS IN THIS CHAPTER, and confirms the standing OCR defect. Revelation 18 carries a Bede block at key 1 (300 words), the first time Bede has been a usable voice in this run. It is genuine and apt commentary on Revelation 18 -- the angel understood as the Lord incarnate or the doctors of the Church, Babylon as the city of the devil, and a fine gloss that he calls those rich in sins who by an infelicitous traffic exchange their souls for temporal abundance, since excess of luxuries makes poor instead of rich. Two things to record. First, like Matthew Henry's blocks, it is a SECTION exposition, not a verse comment: the single block filed under key 1 runs numbered notes on verses 1, 2, 3, 4, 6 and 7, so it spans well past the entry it sits in. Second, it confirms the Bede/Lightfoot OCR item already on the owner's re-fetch list. The block carries unescaped HTML entities rendered as literal text (" and '' appear inline) and clear OCR corruption: 'madces' for 'makes', 'frotn' for 'from', 'tempc^ral' for 'temporal', and stray carets before quotation marks. The text is usable but the entity noise and the corrupt words would show to a reader if any Bede block were ever surfaced verbatim. Bede is mapped to the latin-fathers school in this chapter's build, and he is visible to split_voices since VOICE_LABELS lists the bare surname 'Bede' -- unlike 'Cyril', which is a prefix of the real head and therefore invisible.

The live disputes in revelation 18, all carried into the entry tags. (1) WHAT BABYLON IS, and whether the prophecy is yet fulfilled: Clarke is the dissenting voice and says so twice. At v2 he lists Rome pagan, Rome papal and Jerusalem without choosing; at v8 he asks 'of what city is this spoken?' and answers that Rome pagan was never so treated since Alaric and Totilas burnt only parts of it, that Rome papal has not been so treated either, and that the description is true of Jerusalem, which is not generally thought to be intended; at v24 he concludes there is no city to which all these things are yet applicable and the prophecy must remain to be fulfilled. Barnes goes the other way and argues at length that Rome may literally be burnt, canvassing Jewish and early Christian expectation. Gill, Wesley and Henry assume the papal application throughout. Bede allegorises to the city of the devil and looks for no city at all. (2) WHETHER THE CARGO LIST IS LITERAL: Gill argues sharply that it cannot be, since goods that do not sell in one city sell in another and the ruin of commerce in one place is often the rise of it in another, so all these things will be merchandised somewhere to the end of the world; Robertson treats it as documentary, counts twenty-nine items of import into the port of Rome and cites Galen, Pliny and Aristides; Barnes treats it as scene-setting; Clarke twice abandons his own comment for Bishop Bale's item-by-item Reformation polemic. (3) BODIES AND SOULS OF MEN at v13: Robertson holds the first word means simply bodies, treated as livestock alongside the horses and chariots, and suggests the following conjunction be rendered 'even' so the two phrases are one; Barnes reports Stuart's narrower reading that it means grooms; Wesley keeps them apart and makes souls of men the most gainful merchandise of all at Rome. (4) WORN OR SOLD at v16: Barnes takes the city as personified and clothed in the finery, Clarke denies it on lexical grounds from Kypke, that the verb means to abound or be laden with, so these are trade goods not ornaments. (5) THE TEXT AT v17: Barnes and Clarke both prefer 'one who sails to a place' (a coaster) over the received 'all the company in ships', Clarke explaining that before the compass every voyage was performed within sight of land; Robertson declines Nestle's further conjecture of 'sea' for 'place'. (6) HOW FAR THE BLOOD-GUILT REACHES at v24: Barnes takes it nearly literally, Ellicott denies the literal sense expressly and grounds the charge in the tendency of her principles, Wesley piles up statistics and then concedes they may be overcharged. (7) A DATING ARGUMENT at v20 raised by Ellicott alone: because the verse names apostles in heaven, some have inferred the twelve were all dead before the Apocalypse was written and therefore John did not write it; Ellicott answers that the verse states nothing about who has passed into heaven and is simply a summons to all who fought on their Lord's side.

Fidelity self-grade, revelation 18, six entries tiling 1-24. Word counts: 1-3 644w (8 voices), 4-8 644w (6), 9-11 649w (7), 12-14 647w (7), 15-20 647w (7), 21-24 650w (6). All within the 350-650 window. Every claim in every entry is attributed to a named voice and traceable to that voice's block for the verses in range; no verse in 1-24 is uncovered. NO CALVIN in this chapter, since he wrote no commentary on Revelation; the reformed school is carried by Gill alone throughout, and Bede supplies a latin-fathers entry at 1-3, the first in this run. Positions I disagree with are stated in the voice's own terms and not softened: Clarke's flat refusal of the whole application at v8 and v24, Barnes's argument that Rome may literally burn, Gill's mystical turn on the cinnamon to the licensed brothels of Rome and their revenues, Wesley's Inquisition statistics with his own concession that they may be overcharged, and Robertson's excursus from sorcery to modern quackery and faith-healers. Two summarising decisions are recorded rather than concealed: Clarke's very long Bishop Bale quotations at k11 and k12 (507 and 640 words of Reformation polemic against the mass, relics and clerical wares) are reported as what they are and sampled rather than reproduced at length, and Barnes's chapter-level REMARKS at k24 are used only for the blood-guilt point. DECLARED DEVIATIONS: (a) Jamieson is in RESIDUE for the whole chapter, its three blocks belonging to 1 Timothy 2, and is declared as excluded_voices on the three affected entries. (b) The Cyril blocks at keys 3 and 9 (stuck fragment C, byte-identical to each other and irrelevant to this chapter) are dropped WITHOUT an excluded_voices declaration. This is forced, not chosen: the VOICE_LABELS list in scripts/synthesis_qa.py contains the bare string 'Cyril', which is a PREFIX of the real head 'Cyril of Jerusalem:', so the regex never matches and undeclarable_voices rejects both 'Cyril' and 'Cyril of Jerusalem'. CORPUS-WIDE: KEIL AND DELITZSCH IS TRUNCATED AT 200 WORDS IN 93% OF ITS BLOCKS. Measured across every file in data/commentary/cow/: K&D has 10,472 blocks, of which 9,727 (92.9%) are EXACTLY 200 words, and ZERO exceed 200 — maximum observed is exactly 200. That is a hard cap applied at scrape time, not natural block length. For comparison, every other witness routinely runs far longer: Matthew Henry to 14,242 words, Adam Clarke to 10,884, John Calvin to 7,841, Wesley to 7,153, Barnes to 5,044, JFB to 4,647, Ellicott to 2,667. The cap is not global — it bites K&D almost universally and NOBODY else at that rate, except John Gill, who shows a suspicious spike of 2,756 blocks at exactly 200 words (9.3%) while only 798 of his blocks exceed 200 and his max is 695; that pattern suggests a subset of Gill's chapters came through the same capped scrape path. WHY IT MATTERS DISPROPORTIONATELY: K&D is the principal Old Testament commentary in this corpus, and the remaining generate queue is entirely OT (419 chapters). Every one of those chapters will be written against a K&D cut off mid-sentence. WORSE: K&D's blocks characteristically OPEN by quoting the raw lemma for a range of verses, so the 200-word budget is often consumed entirely by scripture text and the exposition is truncated away before it starts — see the deuteronomy 16 note of the same date, where keys 2, 10, 14, 17 and 19 are all lemma-plus-fragment and key 2 is 200 words of pure verse text with no commentary at all. OWNER ACTION: this is a re-scrape question, not something a writer can work around.

REFINEMENT of my earlier deuteronomy 16 note this same date about K&D blocks being 'systematically offset'. The observation stands but the DIAGNOSIS was wrong, and the corrected cause is more useful. I described K&D's blocks as lemma dumps whose commentary was displaced forward into the next pericope. The real mechanism is the corpus-wide 200-word truncation cap on K&D (see the separate corpus-wide note of this date: 9,727 of 10,472 K&D blocks are exactly 200 words and none exceed it). K&D characteristically opens a block by quoting the lemma for several verses; the cap then cuts the block at word 200, so what survives is the verse text plus whatever commentary happened to begin before the cap — which is why the surviving fragment always seems to be about the NEXT section rather than the filed one. It is truncation, not displacement. Practical consequence is unchanged (check what K&D's block actually treats before trusting its key), but the fix is different: this is repaired by re-scraping K&D without the cap, not by relocating material.

JFB DISPLACEMENT LAW — TENTH DATUM, but a WEAK one, and I want the next reader to treat it as weak. JFB appears at only two keys, 8 and 14: one interval of 6, phase 2. Two terms establish a single interval, not a run, so this chapter corroborates the stride without independently confirming it the way a three- or four-term sequence does. Running record: acts 24 (2/8/14/20/26), acts 3 (4/10/16/22), james 1 (1/7/13/19/25), 1john 3 (6/12/18/24), ephesians 1 (4/10/16/22), romans 4 (4/10/16/22), luke 1 (26/32/38/62/74), 1corinthians 16 (1/7/13/19), deuteronomy 16 (2/8/14), exodus 3 (8/14). Ten for ten on stride; phase still varies freely. Both blocks here are displaced and the donor march is again strictly forward, this time through GENESIS 43-44 (Joseph's brothers): v8 = Gen 43:34 (the double mess, Benjamin's portion five times as much, 'drank freely'), v14 = Gen 44:2 (the silver cup missing from the governor's house, the messenger sent to search them). MATTHEW HENRY'S KEYS MARK HIS SECTION HEADS — THIRD CHAPTER CONFIRMING IT, and the cleanest instance yet. Henry appears at only 4 of 22 keys: 1, 7, 11, 16. Those are exactly the first verses of the chapter's four natural divisions — vv1-6 the burning bush, 7-10 the commission, 11-15 the objections and the Name, 16-22 the instructions — and his block at each key expounds the whole section beneath it. The rule now looks reliable enough to USE: where Henry's key count is far below the other witnesses, his key list hands you the commentator's own pericope boundaries before you make any tiling decision. Exodus 3 was tiled on exactly that basis, subdividing only where one of Henry's sections exceeded ~4500 source words (1-6 split into 1 | 2-3 | 4-6; 11-15 into 11-12 | 13-15; 16-22 into 16-17 | 18-20 | 21-22). The filing rule still binds — Henry's section material may only be used in the entry keyed at his own verse.

K&D 200-WORD TRUNCATION, WORKED EXAMPLE — and a warning that the damage is recoverable here only by luck. Every K&D block in this chapter is exactly 200 words except key 22 (45). See the corpus-wide note of this date: 9,727 of 10,472 K&D blocks corpus-wide are exactly 200 words and none exceed it. What the cap does in practice is visible here key by key. K&D opens a block by quoting the lemma for several verses, so the cap eats the exposition: key 3 = lemma vv3-6 plus a fragment on v6; key 8 = lemma vv8-9 plus a fragment on v11 ('he had learned humility in the school of Midian'); key 12 = lemma vv12-13 plus a fragment on v13; key 14 = lemma vv14-15 plus a fragment on v16; key 17 = lemma vv17-18 plus a seven-word stub on v21; key 22 = 45 words of PURE LEMMA with no commentary at all. Only keys 1, 2 and 7 are on-verse and intact enough to use directly. THE LUCK: because K&D's keys happen to fall one inside each successive span of this tiling, every displaced fragment could be legitimately relocated under the filing rule — key 8's fragment into entry 11-12 (K&D has key 12 there), key 12's into 13-15 (key 14), key 14's into 16-17 (key 17). That will NOT generally hold. Where it does not, the material is simply lost. K&D is declared in excluded_voices at entry 21-22, where key 22 is lemma-only and key 17's surviving stub says nothing.

END-OF-CHAPTER RESIDUE: FIFTH SIGHTING, FIVE FOR FIVE ON THE FINAL VERSE. Ellicott's block at key 22 — the last verse of the chapter — ends in StudyLight navigation, copyright boilerplate and ~2KB of raw CSS ('.sub-menu{font-size:12px...'). Running record, all on a chapter's maximum key: luke 1:80, romans 4:25, 1corinthians 16:24, deuteronomy 16:22, exodus 3:22 — five chapters, five books, both testaments. Deuteronomy 16:22 also showed GILL carrying scrape navigation on the same key, so it is not an Ellicott-specific fault but a property of the last key in a chapter. The scrub is mechanical: for each chapter's maximum key, cut from the first CSS selector, from 'Footnotes: Copyright Statement', or from the 'Next:'/'Previous:' navigation marker.

THE LIVE DISPUTES IN THIS CHAPTER, several of them unusually sharp. (1) v11 — why the man who once killed an Egyptian now hesitates. Henry calls it a fluctuation of temper, 'good men are not always alike bold and zealous'. Calvin flatly reverses the valuation: the hesitation is 'the excuse of modesty... not only free from blame but worthy of praise', and the EARLIER boldness was the fault, Moses having 'advanced hastily at first, not having sufficiently considered his own powers'. K&D side with Calvin in a phrase — he 'had learned humility in the school of Midian'. (2) v12 — is the worship on the mountain the sign? Clarke: 'This was NOT the sign.' Ellicott: it is precisely the sign, and there is nothing odd in that, since it accords with the divine economy to give tokens 'which are future, and appeal to faith only'. Flatly contradictory. (3) v13 — why would the people ask God's name? Clarke and Ellicott explain it by Egypt (they had 'drank deep into the Egyptian superstitions'; every god in a polytheism has a name). K&D and Calvin both refuse the Egyptian explanation, K&D because the fathers' name 'cannot have vanished entirely from the memory of the people', Calvin because it is incredible that the prophet had forgotten the God he served. (4) v16 — did an enslaved people keep any government? Clarke: 'not likely the Hebrews were permitted to have any regular government at this time.' Ellicott, citing Rosenmuller, infers from this very verse that they DID enjoy internal organisation and native government. (5) v19 — 'no, not by a mighty hand'. Clarke says the received rendering is a 'palpable contradiction' and takes the negative particle as 'unless/except' (so: not until he sees the hand stretched out), citing Becke's Bible 1549, the Vulgate's nisi and the LXX. Ellicott renders it 'not EVEN under a mighty hand' — the exact opposite. Calvin notes only that 'interpreters differ'.

TWO APOLOGETIC SET-PIECES worth flagging, three centuries apart and on the same kind of evidence. (a) v4 — Ellicott takes the Hebrew 'when JEHOVAH saw, ELOHIM called' as decisive against the documentary hypothesis: 'The German theory of two authors of Exodus, one Jehovistic and the other Elohistic, is completely refuted by this passage; for it is impossible to ascribe one clause of a sentence to one author, and the next to another.' Compare Calvin at v1, who makes the Horeb/Sinai double name answer 'certain modern cavillers, who have argued, at least, against the identity of the author of the Pentateuch'. Two commentators, centuries apart, both defending Mosaic authorship from an alternation of names inside one chapter. (b) v22 — the spoiling of the Egyptians is met two quite different ways. Clarke and Gill answer it as UNPAID WAGES (Clarke: 'if accounts were fairly balanced, Egypt would be found still in considerable arrears to Israel'). Calvin knows that defence, grants that their labour deserved recompense, and judges it too small a ground; his own answer is divine ownership — 'let us see what every one's property is. Who will boast that he has anything, except what is given him by God?' — with the guard that this does not make God arbitrary, 'because His will is the most certain rule of perfect equity'. Note also that Clarke, Wesley, Ellicott and Calvin are unanimous that 'borrow' is a mistranslation, Clarke observing that the common English version 'is almost the sole transgressor' among ancient and modern versions alike, having copied Becke's Bible of 1549.

All 9 entries self-graded A. Every entry 350-650 on both counters, 0 flags in every category, mean TTR 0.658, mean zip 0.463. Two-way voice check ran clean before assembly (0 declared-but-unnamed, 0 excluded-but-named); every declared exclusion names a block present inside its own span. LENGTH CONTROL WAS BAD HERE and I want it recorded honestly: first drafts ran 758, 783, 819, 821, 823, 824 and 941 words against a 650 ceiling, and every entry needed between two and five trim passes — far worse than 1corinthians 16, where 17 of 24 landed first-pass. The cause is not the four-voices-per-paragraph rule, which held; it is that exodus 3 pairs very large spans (2548-4301 source words) with six or seven substantial voices per span, so the material genuinely exceeds what 650 words can hold and the drafting error is in deciding what to LEAVE OUT before writing rather than trimming after. One entry (13-15) first drafted at 913 words also came back grade B on TTR 0.580; a compact rewrite rather than incremental trimming fixed both length and TTR at once. RULE FOR NEXT TIME: when a span exceeds ~2500 source words with 6+ voices, pick the three or four strands the entry will carry BEFORE drafting and discard the rest deliberately.

SCRAPE RESIDUE RULE CORRECTED — it follows ELLICOTT'S LAST BLOCK, not the chapter's last verse. Joshua 11 has 23 keys; the junk is at key 22, NOT key 23, and key 23 is clean. Ellicott's key-22 block is 1021 words of which only about 30 are real commentary ('Goliath of Gath and his gigantic relatives seem to have been a part of this remnant'); the remaining ~990 are StudyLight navigation, copyright boilerplate, CSS — and, new this time, RAW JAVASCRIPT (a study-desk widget binder, 'var d2=ref.getAttribute...'). Ellicott simply has no block at key 23, so the furniture attached to the last block he does have. That reconciles all five earlier sightings (luke 1:80, romans 4:25, 1corinthians 16:24, deuteronomy 16:22, exodus 3:22), where Ellicott happened to be present on the final verse and the two rules coincided. Sixth sighting overall. NOTE ALSO that deuteronomy 16:22 showed GILL carrying navigation residue on the same key, so the general rule is: the last block of a given commentator's scraped page carries whatever page furniture followed it. A scrub should therefore key on the LAST BLOCK PER COMMENTATOR PER CHAPTER, not on the chapter's maximum verse key, and must strip JS as well as CSS: cut from the first CSS selector, from 'Footnotes: Copyright Statement', from a 'Next:'/'Previous:' navigation marker, or from the first JavaScript token.

HENRY'S KEYS MARK HIS SECTION HEADS — FOURTH CONFIRMATION, and it drove the tiling. Henry appears at only 3 of 23 keys: 1, 10, 15, which are the heads of the chapter's three natural divisions (vv1-9 the northern coalition and Merom, 10-14 Hazor and the cities, 15-23 the summary of the conquest). Prior confirmations: 1corinthians 16 (1/5/10/13/19), deuteronomy 16 (1/18), exodus 3 (1/7/11/16). I tiled on that basis and subdivided only where a section exceeded ~4500 source words. ONE DEPARTURE WORTH RECORDING: v15 was NOT given its own entry even though Henry heads a section there, because key 15 is Gill 22 words + Henry 1599 words — a single-voice entry. It was merged into 15-18 instead, which brought seven voices to the span. The rule gives you the boundaries; it does not follow that every boundary should become an entry edge.

JFB DISPLACEMENT LAW — FIRST PARTIAL BREAK IN THE DISPLACEMENT PATTERN, though the stride holds. JFB sits at keys 17 and 23: interval of 6, phase 5. As in exodus 3 this is only TWO terms, so it corroborates the stride without independently confirming a run. The new fact is that the two blocks behave DIFFERENTLY. Key 17 is displaced as usual — 17 words on 'the directions given for the instruction of their children', which is Deuteronomy material and has nothing to do with Joshua's northern campaign; excluded at entry 15-18. But key 23 is 234 words of GENUINE, ON-CHAPTER commentary: the theological defence of the herem ('This relentless doom of extermination... cannot be reconciled with the attributes of the divine character, except on the assumption that their gross idolatry and enormous wickedness left no reasonable hope of their repentance'), plus the Eber-usurpation argument and the prudential reading of the ban on alliances. It is used as a declared voice at entry 23 and carries that entry. So through eleven chapters the stride-6 spacing has never failed, but this is the first chapter in which a stride block was NOT displaced. Running record of phases: acts 24 (2/8/14/20/26), acts 3 (4/10/16/22), james 1 (1/7/13/19/25), 1john 3 (6/12/18/24), ephesians 1 (4/10/16/22), romans 4 (4/10/16/22), luke 1 (26/32/38/62/74), 1corinthians 16 (1/7/13/19), deuteronomy 16 (2/8/14), exodus 3 (8/14), joshua 11 (17/23).

K&D 200-WORD TRUNCATION — second worked example, and this time the damage is NOT fully recoverable. Ten of eleven K&D blocks here are exactly 200 words (key 22 is 66). Per key: 2, 3, 4, 7, 8 are on-verse and usable; 11 is essentially all lemma (vv11-16 quoted); 22 is 66 words of PURE LEMMA -> K&D excluded at entry 21-22. TWO PIECES ARE LOST OUTRIGHT, which exodus 3 was lucky enough to avoid. Key 5 is lemma vv5-6 plus commentary on V6 (the emphatic pronoun before the verb, 'I will provide for...'), but K&D has NO key at 6, so under the filing rule it cannot be moved and simply cannot be used. Key 10 is lemma v10 plus a genuinely useful note on V13 ('the singular upon their hill is to be taken as distributive: standing, now as then, each upon its hill'), but K&D has no key at 12, 13 or 14, so that too is lost — and it would have been the fourth voice in a three-way dispute about what 'stood still in their strength' means. Only key 17's tail (on vv19-20, the hardening) could be relocated, because K&D has key 19 inside that span. So the recoverability of truncated K&D material depends entirely on whether K&D happens to hold a key in the destination span, and here it failed twice.

THE LIVE DISPUTES. (1) v13 — what 'the cities that stood still in their strength' means, THREE readings. Walls not demolished when taken (Gill, from Kimchi and Jarchi; Wesley, 'with their fence, walls or bulwarks'). Built on mounds or hills (Ellicott literally, with the Vulgate; Clarke prefers this on the practical ground that hill cities could be held cheaply as places of refuge, and notes it makes 'Jerusalem shall be builded on her own heap' read as 'on her own hill'). Or cities that stayed NEUTRAL — Clarke reports this reading and declines it, Ellicott adopts it as his own judgement ('those who remained absolutely neutral in the war'). (2) vv19-20 — the hardest question in the chapter, and a genuine four-way. CALVIN states the objection against himself: Moses forbade any league with these nations, so peace was not available; 'had they made a hundred attempts to avoid war, they must nevertheless have perished', and it seems unjust to blame men acting under compulsion. He notes the SEPTUAGINT evaded the problem by rendering the verse without the peace clause at all. GILL answers with the Jewish tradition that Joshua sent three offers on first landing (flee, make peace, or fight) and all chose war. K&D shut that door: 'It cannot be inferred from this, that if the Canaanites had received the Israelites amicably, God would have withdrawn His command to destroy them.' CLARKE relocates the guilt earlier — they had sinned against all the light they had, and their refusal of peace was the PROOF of wilful idolatry, not its cause. ELLICOTT reads the hardening as evidence for the defence: it 'goes to prove... that the conquest of Canaan was not intended to be a massacre of the unresisting inhabitants'. (3) vv16/21 — composition. CLARKE takes 'the mountain of Israel' as proof of post-Joshua editing, 'incontestable evidence that several notes have been added to this book since the days of Joshua'. CALVIN denies any mountain of that name is meant at all, reading an antithesis between the hill country of the ten tribes and that of Judah. WESLEY answers Clarke directly at v21: it does not follow, and even a later clause added by Ezra is unnecessary, since Judah's pre-eminence was already visible in Joshua's own day. (4) v9 — whether 'houghed' means disabled or killed: Clarke says killed outright, Wesley says hamstrung and unfit for war, Ellicott says we cannot be certain.

Jamieson stride-6, SEVENTEENTH confirmation. JOHN LIGHTFOOT APPEARS IN THIS CHAPTER, and the OCR damage is severe enough to destroy exactly what makes him worth having. Lightfoot supplies genuine Horae Hebraicae material at keys 1, 3, 13, 21 and 27, and it is apt and useful: Paul saw the Lord twice, at Damascus and in the Jerusalem trance, and alone among the apostles saw him after the ascension (k1); the necessity of the apology was the accusation of taking maintenance from heathen churches (k3); among those who wrought in holy things without serving at the altar were the men who picked the worms out of the altar wood, blemished men unfit to minister there but nourished from the consecrated things, from tract Shekalim, with the further point from tract Tamid that none but the king might sit within the court, so the verb means besieging rather than sitting at the altar (k13); the question whether those without law are the Sadducees or the heathen (k21); and the Hebrew equivalences for approved and not approved (k27). THE DAMAGE: the Hebrew is destroyed outright, surviving only as Latin-letter garbage -- 'WW5', 'D5', 'WW', 'DVT MS oyonnan', 'bape'. The Greek is mangled: 'Tots' for the article in 'Tots anomois', 'pocedpevovtes' for the participle, ligature breaks such as 'adoki- mos' and 'preach- ing' and 'cast- away' and 'con- cerning'. HTML entities appear as literal text throughout (" and &). Since Lightfoot's whole contribution is rabbinic citation, the OCR has removed the evidence and left only the assertions. This confirms and sharpens the standing Lightfoot/Bede re-fetch item: a re-fetch is not cosmetic here, it is the difference between a citable voice and an uncitable one. Note that VOICE_LABELS contains the bare surname 'Lightfoot', which works only because it is a SUFFIX of the real head 'John Lightfoot:' -- the same accident that saves 'Chrysostom' and 'Robertson' and fails for 'Cyril'.

A FIFTH DISTINCT CYRIL FRAGMENT, and it is the first one that is unambiguously apt. Key 22 carries a Cyril of Jerusalem block of 200 words, 1,047 chars, md5 97dca4e2be49, opening 'But the Saviour comes in various forms to each man for his profit. For to those who have need of gladness He becomes a Vine; and to those who want to enter in He stands as a Door; and to those who need to offer up their prayers He stands a mediating High Priest.' It goes on: 'He is made all things to all men, remaining in His own nature what He is.' The catechetical lecture is applying the very phrase of 1 Corinthians 9:22 to CHRIST rather than to Paul -- an inversion of the text that is genuinely illuminating and directly on the verse it is filed under. It was therefore USED, not silenced. Running tally of distinct Cyril fragments: A, the 2 Cor 4:4 blinded-thoughts block (1,070 chars, faf6f21d5467), five occurrences across philemon 1, 1thessalonians 5 twice, 1corinthians 16 and 2corinthians 11; B, the two-names block (1,097 chars, 763fd91d7fb4), hebrews 7 k17 and k21; C, the raise-our-thoughts-higher-than-the-Jews block (1,039 chars, 1a11faff4532), revelation 18 k3 and k9; D, the two-comings-from-Malachi block (1,099 chars, 0617aea8ae3f), revelation 18 k12; E, this one. EVERY ONE OF THE FIVE IS EXACTLY 200 WORDS as the dumper reports it, and all five fall between 1,039 and 1,097 chars. That is now five independent samples supporting a fixed truncation at the scrape rather than natural block boundaries -- worth checking against the Cyril source tree directly.

TERMINAL ELLICOTT CHROME -- TWELFTH CONSECUTIVE CHAPTER. The Charles Ellicott block at 1corinthians 9:27 is 1,348 words, of which about 350 are commentary; the remaining roughly 1,000 words are the same page dump logged at revelation 18: terminal navigation ('1 Corinthians 1Co 8 ... 1Co 10 Footnotes:'), the StudyLight copyright footer crediting BibleSupport.com, raw CSS, site menus and devotional lists, and raw JavaScript including DOMContentLoaded handlers and a navigation-accordion IIFE referencing study-desk.html. Eleven of the twelve cannot separate 'last verse key' from 'last Ellicott block' because they coincide; judges 2 alone separates them and favours LAST ELLICOTT BLOCK. The navigation label is chapter-relative (prev/next chapter), confirming it is the page's own chapter navigation. A general fix should cut at the string 'Copyright Statement These files are public domain', which has now been present in every instance across twelve chapters; the per-chapter cut markers currently hand-set in each scratchpad dump.py are a workaround, not a fix. ALSO at key 27: Albert Barnes (1,523w) and Adam Clarke (1,743w) carry chapter-level end matter rather than comment on the verse -- SEVENTH consecutive chapter for that defect, and the sizer still counts every word of it.

The live disputes in 1corinthians 9. (1) THE SISTER WHO IS A WIFE, v5: Gill calls it a Hebraism answering to the sister-spouse of the Canticles and rejects the reading that makes her a rich woman ministering of her substance, since that would relieve the churches of the very charge Paul claims; Ellicott dismisses the same Roman reading as inadmissible because the appeal to Peter settles it, and records that the practice growing out of that misapprehension was condemned at the first council of Nicaea; Henry argues from the word for power, which implies authority to require attendance such as no man has over any but a wife or servant; Clarke takes it as decisive against clerical celibacy while noting Clement said the apostles carried their wives not as wives but as sisters; Calvin reports and denies Eusebius's inference that Paul was married and had left his wife somewhere. (2) CLARKE AGAINST REPROBATION, v9: from 'doth God take care for oxen' Clarke argues that God could not reprobate an ox since he careth for oxen and surely cannot reprobate a man, and to the reply that a man has sinned and an ox cannot he answers that the decree is supposed to be from eternity and a man can no more sin before he exists than an ox can when he exists. Ellicott meanwhile enters the opposite caution, that the words must not be read as denying divine regard for the brute creation, which runs through the Mosaic law and appears in the closing question of Jonah. (3) THE TEXT AT v10: Clarke reports that the best MSS give simply 'in hope of partaking' and quotes Bishop Pearce that the longer words are superfluous if not wrong, Griesbach having removed them; CALVIN DESCRIBES THE SAME VARIANT, SAYS HE WOULD PREFER THE SHORTER WERE HE AT LIBERTY TO CHOOSE, AND THEN DECLINES TO FOLLOW HIS OWN PREFERENCE because most Greek manuscripts agree in the other and the meaning is unaffected -- a commentator refusing his own conjecture, worth recording as a method. (4) WHO IS WITHOUT LAW, v21: Lightfoot asks whether the Sadducees or the heathen are meant, tells his reader to inquire, and confesses that how Paul could conform to the heathen is not easy to judge; CLARKE NAMES LIGHTFOOT AND REFUSES HIM on two grounds, that Paul could expect no success among men who denied the resurrection and that among the heathen he might appear as one who was not a Jew. This is the only place in the run so far where two voices in the same catena argue with each other by name. (5) WHO THE WEAK ARE, v22: Gill and Barnes take them for weak Christians; Ellicott says we can scarcely read it so, since the whole passage treats of classes outside the Church, and makes it the weak points rather than the strong points of Jews, proselytes and Gentiles. (6) THE GOSPEL OR THE PRIZE, v23: Clarke proposes that the word we translate the gospel should here be rendered the prize or reward; Robertson reads the compound the other way, that Paul does not wish to enjoy the gospel just by himself. (7) HOW FAR THE RACE HOLDS, v24: Clarke, Calvin, Wesley and Henry all state that only one won there while all may win here, Henry adding that there should nevertheless be a noble emulation; CHRYSOSTOM ALONE GUARDS THE OTHER FLANK, warning expressly that the words are not to be taken as though only one out of many would be saved, far from it. (8) THE BUFFETED BODY, v27: Clarke takes the body itself for the enemy to be mortified by abstinence and severe labour; Gill denies expressly that watchings, fastings, whipping, scourging or lying on the bare ground are meant, making it the body of sin; Ellicott insists the language is figurative throughout and concerns the appetites; Robertson denies the Gnostic premise that Paul thought his body evil; Calvin notes the ancient monks obeyed it literally and still missed the main thing. (9) WHAT A CASTAWAY PROVES, v27: Wesley presses the verse into a full doctrine of conditional election, that believers are elected to privileges which if abused leave those very elect persons reprobate, and names Paul as the instance; Ellicott corrects the rendering, that the Greek means one who has not behaved according to the prescribed regulations rather than a castaway.

Fidelity self-grade, 1corinthians 9, nine entries tiling 1-27. Word counts: 1-2 649w (10 voices), 3-6 641w (9), 7-9 649w (7), 10-12 650w (7), 13-15 650w (10), 16-18 650w (7), 19-22 649w (10), 23-25 649w (9), 26-27 650w (8). All within the 350-650 window. Every claim in every entry is attributed to a named voice and traceable to that voice's block for the verses in range; no verse in 1-27 is uncovered. This is the widest voice list of the run: Chrysostom, Cyril, Gill, Calvin, Henry, LIGHTFOOT (first appearance as a usable voice), Clarke, Wesley, Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson, across five schools. Lightfoot is mapped to puritan-evangelical alongside Henry. Positions I disagree with are stated in the voice's own terms and not softened: Clarke's use of the muzzled ox against the decree of reprobation, Wesley's full doctrine of conditional election at the last verse with Paul named as an instance, Gill's flat denial that any bodily austerity is meant, Clarke's proposal to render 'the gospel' as 'the prize', and Chrysostom's warning against a soteriological misreading of the race. Two summarising decisions are recorded rather than concealed: Barnes's and Clarke's chapter-level end matter at k27 (1,523 and 1,743 words) is used only for the points that bear on the verse, and Clarke's long Epictetus quotation is compressed rather than reproduced entire. DECLARED DEVIATIONS: Jamieson is in RESIDUE for the whole chapter, its four blocks belonging to Acts 20-21, and is declared as excluded_voices on the four affected entries. NO UNDECLARABLE DROPS THIS CHAPTER -- the single Cyril block at k22 was genuinely apt and was used, so the VOICE_LABELS prefix defect did not bite here as it did at 2corinthians 11, hebrews 7 and revelation 18. The defect remains unfixed and will bite again on the next chapter where a Cyril block must be dropped; the one-line fix is to list 'Cyril of Jerusalem' instead of 'Cyril' in scripts/synthesis_qa.py.

Exodus 13 fidelity self-grade: A on all ten entries, no flags, no FLOOR, no TMPL, mean TTR 0.627 / zip 0.449. Length discipline held better than any chapter this run: 8 of 10 entries first-pass in range. The two overshoots were both the pillar entries — 21 came in at 734 and needed five separate cuts to reach 648, and it is the entry where the three-strand rule (note 1339) was hardest to apply, because seven voices speak at key 21 and four of them independently identify the Lord with Christ. Recording the working fix: where several voices agree on a single identification, compress them into ONE clause naming all of them rather than giving each its own sentence — that alone saved about 60 words.

JFB displacement, twelfth chapter and the strongest run yet: Exodus 13 carries FOUR displaced JFB terms at keys 4, 10, 16 and 22 — stride 6, phase 4. Every one of the four is off-chapter and the donor march runs strictly forward through Exodus 2: key 4 = Ex 2:5 (Pharaoh's daughter bathing, the crocodile enclosure in the sacred stream), key 10 = Ex 2:9-10 (Jochebed parting with Moses the second time, the naming by the princess), key 16 = Ex 2:15-16 (the flight in the second year of Thothmes I, Midian on the eastern shore of the gulf, Dahab-Madian), key 22 = Ex 2:16 (the 'prince of Midian' gloss and the shepherdesses). All four declared in excluded_voices. Stride 6 has now held in twelve of twelve chapters; phase continues to vary freely.

Henry's keys mark his own section heads — SIXTH confirmation. Exodus 13 has Henry at 1, 11, 17 and 21, which are exactly his four section divisions (firstborn law; firstlings and catechising; the choice of the way; the pillar). No span in the final tiling crosses a Henry boundary. The rule is now reliable enough to seed tiling before any other analysis, with the caveat already recorded at Joshua 11: it gives candidate boundaries, not final entry edges.

K&D truncation — a counter-example that sharpens the corpus-wide finding. Exodus 13 has eleven K&D keys, ten of them exactly 200 words (the cap) and one, key 22, at 45 words. Key 22 is therefore the rare uncapped K&D block, and its 45 words are real exposition after the lemma: 'This sign of the presence of God did not depart from Israel so long as the people continued in the wilderness.' Contrast Joshua 11, where the short K&D block was junk. Practical rule: a K&D block UNDER 200 words has ended naturally and is usable to its last word; a block AT exactly 200 has been cut mid-exposition and whatever it was about to say is lost.

Two K&D losses in Exodus 13 that the filing rule cannot repair. K&D's key-4 block spends its 200-word budget quoting the lemmas of vv 4-8 and reaches genuine exposition only at v8 (the elliptical relative in 'because of that which Jehovah did to me', with the completion supplied from the context); v8 falls in span 5-8, where K&D has no key, so it cannot be relocated. Likewise K&D's key-16 block quotes v16 and then expounds v17 (the Philistine road, the anxious 'lest' after 'said'); v17 is its own span and K&D has no key there. Both dropped. By contrast K&D's key-12 note on v15 DID relocate legitimately into entry 13-16, because K&D has key 16 inside that span.

Calvin loss at Exodus 13. His key-8 block ends by expounding v9 — the comparison of the passover to the ring on the finger and the ornament bound on the forehead, constantly seen. v9 falls in span 9-10, where Calvin has no key, so the material could not move and was dropped. Worth noting because it removes the one Reformed voice from the four-way phylactery dispute at vv9-10, leaving Gill to carry that side alone.

Residue, seventh sighting, and the type is stable. Ellicott's key-22 block is 1,011 words of which roughly 27 are real commentary ('He took not away. —Comp. …The cloud probably disappeared at Abel-shittim'); the remainder is StudyLight chrome — footer links, copyright text, then raw CSS. This is again the LAST Ellicott block on the chapter's scraped page, confirming the corrected rule (residue follows the last block of a given commentator's page, not the chapter's last verse). Ellicott remained usable at 22 after the real 27 words were extracted.

Four-way dispute at vv9-10 on the sign upon the hand, the best-documented in the chapter. Gill: figurative only, and he presses the argument that a literal phylactery 'could be of no use to answer the end next mentioned', that the Lord's law may be in thy mouth. Wesley: proverbial, things never out of our thoughts — one sentence. K&D: the words presuppose a real custom of mnemonic bands (a bracelet at the wrist, a band on the forehead) but are NOT traceable to heathen branding of soldiers and slaves, and are then used figuratively. Ellicott: the practice is real, ancient, and defensible — a similar custom prevailed in Egypt (Wilkinson), and adopting an Egyptian custom purged of superstition is quite in the spirit of the Mosaic institutions, substituting the words of the Law for the magic charms of sorcerers. Clarke stands apart by not arguing at all: he simply documents the tephillin in full technical detail (the four portions, thirty verses, four compartments for the head and one rolled column for the hand). Ellicott alone concedes the split verdict at v16 — this passage might be metaphorical, but the Deuteronomy commands 'seem to have been intended, and were certainly understood, literally.'

Duration of the pillar — a five-way spread at v22 worth recording because every witness answers and no two agree exactly. Clarke: nobody agrees; probably Succoth (perhaps Rameses) to the Jordan opposite Jericho, after which the ark led; others say Mount Hor and Aaron's death. Gill and Wesley: to the borders of Canaan, the ark taking over at the crossing. Ellicott: most precise of all — probably Abel-shittim. K&D: no terminus, only the principle, that the sign did not depart so long as the people continued in the wilderness. Clarke alone converts the dispute into doctrine (miracle granted while necessary, withdrawn when the canon was complete), which is why his is the strand the entry carries.

Jamieson stride-6, EIGHTEENTH confirmation, and the FIRST WITH A VARIABLE TARGET STRIDE. Keys 9, 21, 27, 33, 45 and 51 carry blocks belonging to LUKE 13 running into LUKE 14: the tower in Siloam (k9, on Lu 13:4), the synagogue ruler and 'how the faithful and true Witness tears off the masks which men wear' (k21, on Lu 13:14-16), the mustard seed and the leaven (k27, on Lu 13:18-21), 'who will strive, while entrance is practicable' (k33, on Lu 13:24), the reference to Mt 23:37 for O Jerusalem (k45, on Lu 13:34-35), and the man with the dropsy (k51, on Lu 14:3-6). All six keys are congruent to 3 mod 6, so the arithmetic is intact, BUT THE STRIDE IS NOT CONSTANT: the target gaps run 12, 6, 6, 12, 6, and slots 15 and 39 are genuinely EMPTY -- verified, neither key carries a Jamieson block at all. This is the first observed instance of the sequence skipping slots. The reason appears on the source side. Source verses are 13:4, 13:14, 13:18, 13:24, 13:34, 14:3, giving source gaps of roughly 10, 4, 6, 10, 4. Set beside the target gaps of 12, 6, 6, 12, 6, the correspondence is close and consistent: where the source jumps about ten verses the target jumps twelve, where the source jumps four to six the target jumps six. THE TARGET STRIDE TRACKS THE SOURCE GAP, ROUNDED UP TO A MULTIPLE OF SIX. Every previous chapter had a constant target stride of 6 with an irregular source stride, which looked like a fixed-period insertion; this chapter shows the period is not fixed but quantised, and that the empty slots correspond to larger jumps in the source rather than to random loss. That is a materially different mechanism from the one the earlier seventeen chapters suggested, and it is worth re-examining the earlier data for chapters where a stride slot was assumed absent. Updated offset tally: offset 0 - 1thessalonians 5, romans 14; offset 1 - 1peter 1, 1corinthians 16, judges 2, hebrews 7; offset 2 - acts 21, 1corinthians 11; offset 3 - numbers 24, philemon 1, acts 11, acts 17, philippians 2, revelation 18, luke 24; offset 4 - philippians 1, 2corinthians 11, 1corinthians 9. OFFSET 5 STILL NEVER OBSERVED. NOTE: luke 24 was NOT synthesized in this batch; see the accompanying observation note for why.

CATENA AUREA INLINE ATTRIBUTIONS ARE LOST FROM THE HEAD STRUCTURE. luke 24 carries a Catena Aurea layer, and at seven keys (1, 13, 25, 36, 41, 45, 50) the catena runs SEVERAL FATHERS TOGETHER UNDER A SINGLE strong-tag head. The head names only the FIRST author of the run; every subsequent author is marked inside the block text by a bare all-caps abbreviation -- 'AMBROSE;', 'AUG.', 'CHRYS.', 'CYRIL;', 'BEDE;', 'THEOPHYL.', 'EUSEBIUS.', 'GREG.', 'GLOSS.', 'ORIGEN.'. Example: the block headed Bede at key 1 is 924 words of which the back half is Ambrose; the block headed Theophylact at key 1 contains Theophylact, then Chrysostom, then Cyril, then Eusebius; the block headed Ambrose at key 1 contains Ambrose, then Augustine, then Bede. Counts across the chapter: 65 inline markers, and 22 author-instances whose text sits in a key where that author is NOT among the heads. Broken out: Augustine 6, Chrysostom 4, Bede 4, Gregory 2, Cyril 2, Ambrose 1, Eusebius 1, Theophylact 1, Gloss 1. WHY THIS MATTERS BEYOND TIDINESS: (a) ORIGEN appears twice in the chapter as an inline marker and NEVER ONCE as a head, so Origen is present in the corpus and invisible to every tool that reads the head structure -- the sizer, the validators, the school tagging and the voice lists all behave as though he is not there; (b) any synthesis that names a father from inline-attributed text will be flagged NAMED BUT NOT SOURCED HERE by the chapter lint, since the lint builds its head set from strong tags only, which pushes the writer toward either silence or misattribution to the head author; (c) usable_source_words is unaffected but the per-voice accounting is wrong at seven keys. SUGGESTED FIX, in order of value: teach the block splitter to treat the inline all-caps markers as secondary heads, which would recover Origen and correct the attribution of about 22 passages in this chapter alone. Other Catena chapters in the Gospels are very likely affected the same way and should be checked before any of them is synthesized. luke 24 was NOT synthesized in this batch.

WHY LUKE 24 WAS PICKED BUT NOT SYNTHESIZED IN THIS BATCH, and what the next worker inherits. The picker offered luke 24 and the sizer returned 64,720 usable source words across 53 keys, the second largest chapter offered in this run after acts 17. At the standing entry-count formula that is twelve entries. Before drafting I did the structural survey, which turned up two things that made the setup materially heavier than any previous chapter and are filed separately: the Jamieson stride here is VARIABLE rather than fixed, and the Catena Aurea layer runs several fathers together under one head so that inline attributions are invisible to the lint. The chapter also carries twenty-six distinct voice labels, twelve of them new to this build and needing school mappings, and a NAME COLLISION between a bare 'Cyril' head at keys 1 and 41 and a 'Cyril of Jerusalem' head at ten keys, the two co-occurring at both of the bare-Cyril keys. In a catena on Luke the bare Cyril is Cyril of Alexandria, whose Commentary on Luke is the chief Greek source, so the two must be given distinct prose labels or the name check will confuse them. I stopped at that point rather than begin drafting, on the standing rule that a chapter one cannot finish must not be started: this session had already carried three full chapters since its last compaction and twelve entries of this density was not a job I judged I could complete without the prose degrading. Nothing is abandoned in the queue's sense -- no data file was written, no verse was stamped, and the working tree is clean, so luke 24 remains unclaimed and the next worker picks it up whole. WHAT IS ALREADY DONE AND SHOULD NOT BE REDONE: the source survey above; the Jamieson identification, keys 9, 21, 27, 33, 45, 51 carrying Luke 13 into Luke 14; the catena inline-marker census; and a working tiling of twelve entries balanced by source weight, namely 1-4, 5-12, 13-14, 15-20, 21-26, 27-31, 32-35, 36-38, 39-43, 44-46, 47-49, 50-53. Keys 1, 13, 36, 45 and 50 carry the oversized section blocks (5,375 / 9,939 / 7,834 / 2,980 / 4,187 words) and the tiling above isolates them deliberately. RECOMMENDATION: fix the catena block splitter before luke 24 or any other Gospel Catena chapter is attempted, since without it roughly twenty-two passages in this chapter cannot be attributed correctly and Origen cannot be attributed at all.

JFB displacement, THIRTEENTH chapter, and the pattern is now as firm as anything in the corpus. Deuteronomy 18 carries three displaced JFB terms at keys 6, 12 and 18 — stride 6, phase 6. All three are off-chapter and the donor is a single continuous passage, Numbers 26 (the second census): key 6 = the design of the new census after a lapse of thirty-eight years; key 12 = the principal households, Reuben diminished by Korah's conspiracy; key 18 = the tribe pre-eminent in the guilt of Baal-peor, greatly reduced, with the reflection on God's justice and faithfulness. All three declared in excluded_voices. Stride 6 has held in thirteen of thirteen chapters.

Henry's keys mark his own section heads — SEVENTH confirmation, and the cleanest yet. Deuteronomy 18 has Henry at exactly 1, 9 and 15, which are the chapter's three natural divisions (the priests' portion; the Canaanite abominations; the promised prophet). Henry appears at no other key. The tiling was built on those three boundaries and nothing had to be moved afterwards. Note that Henry's blocks here are enormous — 1,059 / 843 / 2,161 words — so his keys are not merely markers but carry the bulk of the section's exposition.

K&D truncation: the sub-200 rule from Exodus 13 needs one qualification. Deuteronomy 18 has twelve K&D keys, eleven of them exactly 200 words (the corpus cap) and one, key 22, at 45. By the Exodus 13 rule a sub-200 block has ended naturally and is usable to its last word — but key 22 here is PURE LEMMA, the text of v22 and nothing else. The reason is that K&D's actual exposition of vv21-22 (the false prophet discovered by non-fulfilment; the occurrence of what was predicted made the criterion of true prophecy, and not signs and wonders) sits back at key 17, displaced backward. Corrected rule: a sub-200 K&D block has ended naturally, but it may still be empty of exposition if that exposition was displaced to an earlier key — check the preceding K&D block before writing the voice off.

K&D loss at Deuteronomy 18, and a distinction worth recording about when displaced material may be used where it is filed. K&D's key-16 block ends by expounding vv19-20 (the instructions on behaviour towards the prophets, given in the name of the Lord for emphasis; whoever did not hearken, of him the Lord would require it). vv19-20 fall in span 18-21, where K&D has no key, so the material could not relocate — and it was DROPPED rather than used at entry 16-17, because it is plain exposition of vv19-20 and entry 18-21 covers those verses with other voices. Contrast the case at entry 12-14, where K&D's remark WAS used in the entry it is filed under: there the material is an argument about the JUNCTION between v14 and v15 ('when Moses thus attaches to the prohibition the promise, it is evident from this connection alone...'), which is v14 commentary as much as v15. The working distinction: displaced-forward material that expounds the next verse is dropped; displaced-forward material that argues about the seam between this verse and the next stays.

Residue, EIGHTH sighting. Ellicott's key-22 block is 1,031 words of which about 35 are real ('If the thing follow not... one form of our Lord's test for all prophets, By their fruits ye shall know them'); the rest is StudyLight chrome — chapter navigation, copyright text, then CSS, then raw JavaScript (an accordion initialiser). Again the LAST Ellicott block on the chapter's scraped page, consistent with the corrected rule. This is the second sighting of the JavaScript variant after Joshua 11, so the residue now has two established forms and both terminate an Ellicott page.

The chapter's central dispute, and the sharpest three-way split in the corpus so far: who is 'a prophet like unto me'? Gill: a single person, and he rules the alternatives out by name — not Joshua (Aben Ezra), not Jeremiah (Baal Haturim), not David, not a succession (Jarchi) — because a single person only is spoken of and there is a dissimilitude between Moses and any one of the prophets and all of them in succession; it is the Messiah. Clarke, Wesley: the same, Clarke citing Ainsworth's argument from the closing chapter of Deuteronomy that there arose not a prophet in Israel like unto Moses, so the promise cannot be of the ordinary prophets. Henry: BOTH, holding that a succession may be included but that the promise is primarily of Christ and is the clearest promise of him in all the law of Moses. Calvin ALONE takes the singular for a plural: the word is used for a number of prophets, since Moses is treating of the continual manner of the Church's government and not of what God would do within a short time — and he explicitly rejects the Christ-alone reading as 'not at all more correct' than the Joshua/Jeremiah restriction, on the ground that God's intention was to leave the Jews no excuse for turning aside to familiar spirits. K&D would have sided with Calvin (the promise 'neither relates to one particular prophet, nor directly and exclusively to the Messiah') but his statement of it survives only at key 14.

A second, quieter disagreement at vv9-11 on whether the forbidden arts were real. Gill, Clarke and Wesley describe the practices as impostures dressed in technical vocabulary; Calvin traces them to a natural desire after knowledge that God himself implanted, perverted by the devil's machinations, which makes them a corruption of something good rather than mere fraud; Ellicott goes furthest, noting that four of the practices are ascribed to king Manasseh and adding flatly that 'it is hardly possible that all of them were mere imposture and deceit.' Henry stands at the other pole, calling the arts senseless and absurd, and yet insists their remains survive where Christ's religion is professed, ascribing that survival to the powers and policies of the rulers of the darkness of this world.

Deuteronomy 18 fidelity self-grade: A on all ten entries, no flags, no FLOOR, no TMPL, mean TTR 0.640 / zip 0.453. Length discipline was WORSE than Exodus 13, not better: only 2 of 10 entries came in under 650 first-pass (entry 3 at 564 and entry 22 at 647), and four drafts landed above 800 (entry 10 at 921, entry 15 at 991, entry 12 at 874, entry 6 at 866). Diagnosis: the three-strand rule (note 1339) controls how many topics an entry carries, but not how many WORDS each strand gets, and on a chapter where five or six voices speak at every key each strand quietly grows to 300. Working fix for the next chapter: before drafting, assign each of the three paragraphs an explicit word budget summing to about 600, and write to it — the trimming passes cost far more effort than budgeting would have.

Two source defects in genesis 48, both familiar. (1) JAMIESON RESIDUE AT KEY 4, A SINGLE MEMBER. The 62-word block is on GENESIS 41:16, Joseph before Pharaoh -- 'disclaiming all merit, he ascribed whatever gifts or sagacity he possessed to the divine source of all wisdom' -- and has nothing to do with 48:4. Source verse 16, target key 4. Because there is only ONE Jamieson block in the whole chapter there is no gap to measure and no stride can be derived, so this chapter can neither confirm nor contradict the stride-6 pattern; it is recorded only as a single-member instance of the same residue family, and as a reminder that the pattern's evidence base consists of chapters carrying three or more members. Jamieson is in RESIDUE here and declared as excluded_voices on the 1-7 entry. (2) TERMINAL ELLICOTT CHROME AT KEY 22 -- THIRTEENTH CONSECUTIVE CHAPTER. The Ellicott block is 1,463 words of which 476 are commentary and roughly 987 are page furniture: the terminal navigation ('Genesis Gen 47 Genesis Gen ...'), the StudyLight copyright footer, raw CSS and raw JavaScript, exactly as at 1corinthians 9 and revelation 18. Sequence now: 1thessalonians 5 k28, philippians 1 k30, acts 11 k30, 1corinthians 16 k24, judges 2 k22, romans 14 k23, acts 17 k34, philippians 2 k30, 2corinthians 11 k33, hebrews 7 k28, revelation 18 k24, 1corinthians 9 k27, genesis 48 k22. Twelve of the thirteen cannot separate 'last verse key' from 'last Ellicott block' because they coincide; judges 2 alone separates them and favours LAST ELLICOTT BLOCK. The cut string 'Copyright Statement These files are public domain' has now been present in all thirteen instances and remains the right general fix.

The live disputes in genesis 48. (1) WHETHER THE QUESTION 'WHO ARE THESE?' IS A REAL ONE, v8: Gill and Clarke read it from the blindness, that Jacob saw two figures but could not distinguish them until brought near; Ellicott takes it as a formal turn rather than a failure of sight, the solemn addressing of the discourse to those about to be invested with patriarchal rank; CALVIN DOUBTS THE SEQUENCE ALTOGETHER, holding that Jacob had inquired about the youths before naming them his heirs and that the narrative has placed the question after the event it preceded. (2) WHO PERFORMED THE ACT OF REVERENCE, v12: Ellicott reports that the Samaritan, Syriac and Septuagint treat the Hebrew verb as a contracted plural, which many moderns follow and which would make Manasseh and Ephraim the ones who bowed, but judges the pronoun favours the singular and the sense equally satisfactory either way. (3) WHAT 'GUIDING HIS HANDS WITTINGLY' MEANS, v14: the Septuagint, Syriac and Vulgate render it 'placing his hands crosswise' while Onkelos supports the received text; Ellicott allows some philological support for the three chief versions though it must rest mainly on their own authority, which is however very great. (4) HOW THE PROPHECY OF EPHRAIM'S GREATNESS WAS FULFILLED, v19 -- THE MOST INSTRUCTIVE DISPUTE IN THE CHAPTER, because the two witnesses cite DIFFERENT CENSUSES and neither notices the other. Ellicott takes the final numbering on the plains of Moab, where Manasseh had 52,700 and Ephraim only 32,500, so that on the figures the greatness went the wrong way, and explains the outcome by the division of Manasseh across the Jordan, by Joshua being an Ephraimite, and by the ark being placed in an Ephraimite town; he adds the comparison that Joshua after the conquest must have held a position like General Washington's after American independence. Wesley takes the wilderness mustering, where Ephraim WAS the more numerous and had the standard of that squadron, and agrees with Ellicott only on the division of Manasseh. Both are correct about their own census -- Ephraim was larger at the first numbering and smaller at the second -- and the apparent contradiction is an artefact of which census each chose. A reader given only one of the two would draw the wrong conclusion about the prophecy. (5) THE PORTION TAKEN WITH SWORD AND BOW, v22, a five-way spread. Wesley: purchased, then dispossessed by the Amorites, then retaken by force. Calvin: only a tent-place was bought, as the price shows, so the gift takes in the much larger common land of the city; and he rules out the reading that sword and bow stand figuratively for prayer and supplication as 'still more improbable'. Ellicott: Shechem was strictly a Hivite town, but Amorite may be used loosely or to give the exploit greater glory. Gill: denies the premises outright, that it was taken neither from the Amorite nor by sword and bow. CLARKE REFUSES TO ANSWER, and the refusal is the best thing in the entry: many attempts have been made to explain the verse and all have hitherto been fruitless, the words were no doubt well understood by Joseph and probably allude to some transaction not now on record, and it is much safer to confess our ignorance than to hazard conjecture after conjecture. Gill and Ellicott independently refuse the obvious candidate, the sack of the city by Simeon and Levi, on the ground that Jacob condemns that exploit in the very next chapter.

Fidelity self-grade, genesis 48, five entries tiling 1-22. Word counts: 1-7 646w (7 voices), 8-12 648w (7), 13-16 648w (6), 17-21 646w (6), 22 648w (5). All within the 350-650 window. Every claim in every entry is attributed to a named voice and traceable to that voice's block for the verses in range; no verse in 1-22 is uncovered. Voices: Gill, Calvin, Henry, Clarke, Wesley, Ellicott and KEIL AND DELITZSCH, the last new to this build and mapped to grammatical-historical per the standing voice-to-school map. The final entry covers a single verse, which the entry-count formula supports (22 keys and 19,002 words give five entries) and which the material justifies, since verse 22 carries a self-contained crux with five distinct answers. Positions I disagree with are stated in the voice's own terms and not softened: Clarke's argument from the patriarchs' composure to their belief in the immortality of the soul, Clarke's attack on Delaney for praising Joseph's prostration, Calvin's warning against those who 'hew out dry and perforated cisterns in seeking causes of divine adoption', Gill's flat denial that the portion was taken from the Amorite or by sword and bow, and Wesley's account of divine freedom, which lands close to Calvin's from the opposite camp. ONE SUMMARISING DECISION recorded rather than concealed: at verse 16 all four voices who touch the Angel identify him with Christ, and rather than flatten that into a single agreed reading the entry sets out their four distinct arguments -- Gill from the works predicated, Clarke from the word Goel and the law of the redeeming kinsman, Calvin from the divine worship offered, Wesley by assertion -- because the convergence is more informative than the conclusion. DECLARED DEVIATION: Jamieson is in RESIDUE for the whole chapter, its single block belonging to Genesis 41, and is declared as excluded_voices on the 1-7 entry. No undeclarable drops this chapter.

JFB displacement, FOURTEENTH chapter, and the first NT epistle in the run to show it. 1 Timothy 5 carries four displaced JFB terms at keys 4, 10, 16 and 22 — stride 6, phase 4. All four are off-chapter and the donor is a single continuous passage, 1 Corinthians 14: key 4 = revelation/prophesying/knowledge/doctrine corresponding pairs, key 10 = 'a foreigner… one speaking a foreign language', key 16 = 'I will pray with the understanding' and the unlearned man's Amen, key 22 = the law quotation from Isaiah 28 about other tongues. All four declared in excluded_voices. Stride 6 has now held in fourteen of fourteen chapters, across OT narrative, OT law, Gospels, Acts and now the Pastorals — the defect is in the scrape, not in any book.

Henry's keys mark his own section heads — EIGHTH confirmation, with one qualification new to this chapter. Henry appears at 1, 3, 9 and 17, but the blocks are wildly uneven: 318, 1804, 120 and 2052 words. The 1804 and 2052 blocks are true section heads (widows; elders), key 1 is the chapter opening, and key 9 at 120 words is a FRAGMENT, not a head — it reads as a stray paragraph of Henry's concise commentary rather than his exposition. Refinement to the rule: Henry's keys mark section heads when the block is large; a short Henry block (under ~200 words) may be a fragment and should not be given a tiling boundary on its own.

Gill truncation in 1 Timothy 5, and a second, worse scrape defect. Gill's blocks at keys 1, 3 and 17 are all exactly 200 words — the same cap already documented for K&D and suspected for Gill corpus-wide. Worse: Gill's key-18 block is the single word 'In', and his key-19 block is 12 words. Wesley's key-18 block is 'Deut 25:4' — two words, a bare cross-reference with no comment. So on v18 (the ox and the labourer) BOTH Gill and Wesley are effectively absent from the corpus, and the verse had to be carried by Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson alone. Worth checking whether one-to-three-word blocks occur elsewhere; they are a distinct defect from the 200-word cap and would be easy to detect corpus-wide.

Residue, NINTH sighting, and the first where the real content dominates. Ellicott's key-25 block is 1,518 words, of which roughly 200 are genuine and substantial commentary on the hidden good works, followed by an 'EXCURSUS' heading, then StudyLight chrome, then raw JavaScript. Every previous sighting had a tiny real fragment (27-35 words) buried in junk; here the junk is appended to a full-length note. Rule holds — it is again the LAST Ellicott block on the chapter's scraped page — but the practical lesson is that block length is no guide to whether residue is present: a long Ellicott block at the chapter's end still needs the tail inspected.

Calvin is present at ONE key only in this whole chapter (key 1, 259 words) and absent from the other twenty-four; Cyril of Jerusalem appears once, at key 23, capped at exactly 200 words. Chrysostom appears three times (keys 8, 11, 21) with no stride pattern, and his blocks read as genuine on-verse homily material. The Calvin gap is the notable one: his commentary on the Pastorals exists, so a single 259-word block across a 25-verse chapter looks like a scrape gap rather than an authorial silence. Flagging for the owner — if other NT chapters show the same one-key Calvin pattern, the Calvin fetch for that corpus may have failed.

Two disputes about the widows' roll that the chapter never settles. First, what the enrolment IS: Gill argues it is simply the list of widows relieved by the church and explicitly rejects the deaconess reading (with the Arabic version against him); Wesley and Clarke take it as admission to the female diaconate; Ellicott reconstructs 'an official band of workers… a distinct order, formally entered on the Church's list'; Robertson agrees there was church work attached. Second, what 'the wife of one man' requires: Clarke lists three readings (conjugal fidelity; one husband at a time; never married more than once) and prefers the first on the authority of the Greek fathers; Robertson takes the third flatly; Wesley takes the widest, 'whether with one or more persons successively'. Both disputes are live and none of the six voices concedes.

The chapter's sharpest philological split, on the verb at v11. Barnes protests that the English 'wax wanton' conveys a thought by no means in the original and does injustice to the apostle AND to the younger widows — in the Greek there is no idea of lasciviousness or lewdness, and 'wanton' in 1611 meant roving in gaiety or sport. Clarke agrees on the sense but derives it differently, from words meaning to remove and the rein, a metaphor from a pampered horse whose rein has been taken away. Robertson goes straight the other way and glosses it 'to feel the impulse of sexual desire', recording Souter's 'exercise youthful vigour against Christ'. The same three-way pattern recurs at 'having damnation' (Ellicott and Barnes both insisting on judgment rather than damnation) and at the laying on of hands in v22 (Gill: ordination only; Ellicott: ordination plus absolution of penitents; Robertson: undecidable, 'suits either situation, or both').

1 Timothy 5 fidelity self-grade: A on all twelve entries, no flags, no FLOOR, no TMPL, mean TTR 0.648 / zip 0.454. Length discipline improved but is still the main cost. Note 1365's fix (explicit paragraph budgets) was applied from entry 3 onward and worked: entry 1, drafted before the fix, came in at 855 and took eleven trim passes; entries drafted after it averaged about 720 first-pass and most took two or three. The further refinement that actually moved the number was capping each paragraph at THREE voices rather than trying to give all seven or eight a sentence — at roughly 30 words a sentence, an eight-voice entry cannot come in under 720 if every voice speaks in every paragraph. Recommended rule for the next NT chapter, where six to eight voices per key is normal: three paragraphs, three voices each, about 65 words per voice, and let each voice speak once in the entry rather than once per paragraph.

JFB displacement, FIFTEENTH chapter, and the subtlest instance yet. Genesis 8 carries two displaced JFB terms at keys 4 and 10 — stride 6, phase 4, holding again. What is new is that the donor is the IMMEDIATELY PRECEDING chapter, Genesis 7, so the displaced text is about the same flood and reads as plausibly on-chapter to a careless eye. Key 4 comments on a repeated announcement of the flood, citing the doubled dream of Genesis 41 as parallel — that is Genesis 7:4, not the ark resting on Ararat. Key 10 says 'The ark was finished; and Noah now, in the spirit of implicit faith… waited for directions from God' — that is Genesis 7:5, not the second sending of the dove. Both excluded. Practical warning for future chapters: where the donor is adjacent, the usual test (obviously wrong subject matter) fails, and the displacement must be caught by asking what verse the comment would be answering.

K&D in Genesis 8 is present at four keys and contributes real exposition at exactly ONE place, all of it displaced. Keys 2, 7 and 14 are capped at exactly 200 words (the corpus-wide cap) and keys 2 and 14 spend the whole budget transcribing the lemmas of the following verses; key 21 is 77 words and, like 1 Timothy 5 key 22, is PURE LEMMA — the sub-200 block that has ended naturally but says nothing. The only usable K&D material is the raven exposition at the tail of key 2, which treats vv6-7 and was relocated into the 6-12 entry because K&D has key 7 inside that span. K&D was therefore declared in excluded_voices at entries 1, 13 and 21. Note the widened use of excluded_voices: previously it named displaced/off-chapter material only; here it names blocks that are present in source but carry no exposition at all. The validator accepts this (it only requires the named block to exist), and declaring it puts the loss in the data rather than only in a note.

K&D loss at Genesis 8 that could not be repaired. The key-14 block spends its 200 words on the lemmas of vv14-20 and reaches genuine exposition only at v20 — 'The first thing which Noah did, was to build an altar for burnt sacrifice, to thank the Lord' — which is cut off by the cap mid-sentence. v20 is its own span and K&D has no key there, so the material could not be relocated and was dropped. This is the third chapter running where K&D's only real contribution sits past the cap in a block whose budget was consumed by lemma quotation.

Residue, TENTH sighting. Ellicott's key-22 block runs long and is genuine for most of its length — the six-seasons refutation and the account of the great alternations — before breaking into StudyLight chrome and then raw JavaScript. Consistent with the corrected rule (residue terminates a commentator's scraped page, and this is Ellicott's last block on Genesis 8). Second confirmation of the 1 Timothy 5 lesson that block length is no guide: a long Ellicott block at a chapter's end still needs its tail inspected.

How many seasons the closing verse names is a clean three-way split, and it cuts across the usual school lines. Clarke alone reads six divisions, takes them for the actual postdiluvian seasons of Armenia where Noah then was, and supports the reading from the Targum of Jonathan and the Coptic calendar. Ellicott calls the six-season reading untenable and refutes it agriculturally — Palestine itself has two seed times, winter crops sown in October and November, summer crops in January and February — reading the verse instead as the great alternations on which the earth's well-being depends. Calvin reaches Ellicott's conclusion by a different route, that the Jews erroneously divide the year into six parts whereas Moses, by setting summer against winter, divides it popularly into two. So the Reformed and grammatical-historical voices agree against the Wesleyan one, which is the reverse of the alignment on most disputed points in this corpus.

Whether the raven returned is disputed on the Hebrew, and the corpus is unusually unanimous against the popular reading. Clarke: the common supposition that the raven flew off and was seen no more is a meaning the Hebrew will not bear, since the words are 'going forth and returning'; and it must be allowed, since the bird could not have kept the wing twenty-one days. K&D and Wesley read it the same way — it returned but was never taken back in. Ellicott agrees and adds a mechanism, that Noah retained the raven's mate and so had security for its return each night to its old perch. Ellicott alone reports the contrary tradition (the Chaldean Genesis, many commentators, and the ancient versions), that the raven did not return, having found abundant food in the floating dead bodies. Calvin and Gill supply the same reason for choosing the bird — it feeds on carrion, so if the earth were dry the smell of carcasses would keep it away, and its return was therefore itself the report.

Genesis 8 fidelity self-grade: A on all eight entries, no flags, no FLOOR, no TMPL. One entry needed a second pass for a different reason than usual: entry 13 (the chronology of the drying) first came back grade B on BOTH diversity measures, TTR 0.554 and compression 0.403, because a chapter-dating entry is inherently full of repeated numerals and date formulas ('month', 'days', 'seventeenth', 'hundred and fifty'). The fix was not trimming but restructuring — replacing Ellicott's spelled-out table with his two conclusions, and stating the 354/365 arithmetic once instead of three times. New rule worth keeping: for any entry whose material is mostly dates or numbers, expect the diversity gates rather than the length gate to bite, and plan to state each figure ONCE across the whole entry. On length, the per-paragraph draft-and-measure method (write one paragraph, count it, then write the next) was adopted from entry 4 onward and is a clear improvement on note 1373's rule alone: entry 1, drafted whole, came in at 865 and took ten passes; entry 4, the first drafted paragraph by paragraph, came in at 608 first time and needed none.

A SECOND CHROME FAMILY, PREVIOUSLY UNRECORDED, AND A CORRECTION TO HOW I HAVE BEEN DESCRIBING THE FIRST. Deuteronomy 24 contains NO StudyLight footer at all -- Charles Ellicott's blocks stop at key 16, six keys short of the chapter end, and I first recorded the chapter as having no chrome anywhere. THAT WAS WRONG, because I searched only for the StudyLight marker 'Copyright Statement'. Key 22, the LAST key, carries chrome of a different kind inside the JOHN GILL block: sacred-texts.com navigation, 31 words, reading 'Next: Deuteronomy Chapter 25 Sacred Texts | Bible << Previous: John Gill's Exposition of the Entire Bible: Deuteronomy: ... Index Next: ...'. A sweep of the first 400 chapter files found this sacred-texts tail at the LAST KEY of 43 of them, always inside Gill. It is far smaller per instance than the StudyLight family (31 words against roughly 1,000) but it is a distinct defect with a distinct marker and a distinct source site. WHAT THIS DOES TO THE THIRTEEN-CHAPTER STUDYLIGHT SERIES. I have been recording that series as 'chrome inside the terminal Ellicott block' and citing judges 2 as the one case separating 'last verse key' from 'last Ellicott block' in favour of Ellicott. Verified afresh: in judges 2 the last key is 23, Ellicott's last block is at 22, and the chrome is at 22 -- so it does follow Ellicott there. But deuteronomy 24 shows Ellicott's last block WITHOUT chrome when it sits six keys short of the end, while the last key gets chrome from another voice entirely. Taken together the two families point at a simpler mechanism than 'Ellicott attracts chrome': CHROME ATTACHES TO WHICHEVER VOICE'S BLOCK SITS LAST AT OR NEAR THE CHAPTER'S LAST KEY, and the marker text is determined by the site that voice was scraped from -- StudyLight for Ellicott, sacred-texts for Gill. The apparent Ellicott association across thirteen chapters is an artefact of Ellicott usually being the last block at the last key in those chapters. TESTABLE PREDICTION: a chapter whose last key carries neither Ellicott nor Gill should show either no chrome or a third marker belonging to whichever site that voice came from. CONSEQUENCE FOR THE FIX: cutting on 'Copyright Statement These files are public domain' alone will miss the sacred-texts family entirely. The splitter needs a marker set, not a single string, and the sacred-texts tail should be cut on 'Sacred Texts | Bible' or on the 'Next: <Book> Chapter <n>' pattern.
