(3) GILL: his maximum across all 60 blocks is exactly 200 but only key 16 reaches it; his blocks here average 65 words, so the cap is present and almost never binding — a useful reminder that the exact-200 count understates incidence and that a low count does not mean an uncapped feed. Every other voice runs free: Henry 4,638, Clarke 1,881, Ellicott 1,525, Calvin 1,411, Chrysostom 1,072, Barnes 883, Wesley 636, Robertson 524. THE NEW FAILURE MODE: for Lightfoot the 200-word limit is not truncation of a verse-keyed block but WINDOWING OF A CONTINUOUS TEXT. His key 1 block begins mid-sentence ('light through a window, come and give me light before my face'), his key 4 block ends mid-sentence ('should'), and his key 5 block opens 'ver. 5, concerning Abraham' and then runs on into material belonging to verse 16. His blocks are therefore slices of a running commentary distributed across successive keys, not comments split by lemma — which is why key 1 carries a note on Mesopotamia (verse 2) and key 2 a note on the burial of persons executed by the Sanhedrin (verses 58-60). Consequence for the loop: a Lightfoot block cannot be trusted to belong to its key, and must be read before use. I silenced him at the first entry on that ground. Consequence for the tooling: the splitter should not be assumed to have lemmatised this feed at all, and a re-fetch of Lightfoot needs to recover block boundaries, not merely raise the word limit. His text is additionally a scan OCR with unconverted HTML entities (&quot;, &e.), destroyed Hebrew transliterations ('MMMAMS) sow srowwonn', 'FRFVIAMD NWO'), preserved soft-hyphens ('Meso- potamia'), and stray page-apparatus ('P Lib. ii. 1.', 'Leusden's edition, vol. iii. p. 102.—Ep.') embedded mid-sentence — the same family of damage filed for Luther at galatians 5.

THE RICHEST CHAPTER FOR EXEGETICAL DIVISION SO FAR; FOUR AXES WORTH RECORDING. (1) THE SEVENTY-FIVE SOULS (v.14), six treatments: Barnes, Clarke, Robertson and Wesley trace the figure to the Greek version and name the persons it inserts; Ellicott says outright that the speaker, being a Hellenistic Jew, accepted the number he found in his Greek Bible 'without caring to investigate'; Calvin raises the possibility that the translators did not write it deliberately at all but that it crept in by copying error, 'forasmuch as the Grecians used to set down their numbers in letters'; Lightfoot infers from the same books giving a different figure elsewhere that the translator of one was not the translator of the others. (2) THE BURIAL AT SYCHEM (v.16), five: a rhetorical compression of two purchases and two graves into one sentence, common among the Hebrews where the story was notorious (Wesley); a Samaritan tradition, attested at Shechem by Jerome's day and surviving still, which the speaker may have followed (Ellicott); a standoff in which this passage is 'at least as good' authority as Josephus for Hebron (Clarke, quoting Pearce); an open question on which nothing can be affirmed for certain (Calvin); and — most striking — a conjectural emendation, Robertson reporting that a commentator is sure the text is wrong, noting that the critical text is held to contain some sixty primitive errors, and allowing that reading Jacob for Abraham would clear the matter up. (3) WHETHER THE SPEECH WAS INTERRUPTED AT v.51: Barnes, Ellicott, Henry and Calvin all infer an interruption from the change of tone, Ellicott adding that the compression of the later narrative is itself traceable to the court's growing excitement; ROBERTSON ALONE REFUSES the inference — 'critics assume that Stephen was interrupted at this point because of the sharp tone of the speech. That may be true, but the natural climax is sufficient explanation.' Four to one, on a point that governs how the whole second half is read. (4) THE INTERPOLATED WORD AT v.59: Barnes, Clarke, Wesley and Ellicott independently note that 'God' in 'calling upon God' stands in no ancient copy, and all four turn the deletion into the same christological argument — that the prayer is therefore addressed to Christ and is an act of divine worship. A Reformed, an Arminian, a Wesleyan and an Anglican critic converging on one conclusion from one absent word is the most complete agreement in the chapter, and the tags record it as such.

STRIDE HOLDS, AND THE DONOR IS THE ACTS 27 SHIPWRECK. Jamieson residue at keys 5, 11, 17 and 23 — four members, target gaps 6, 6, 6, offset 5. The source region is Acts 27, the voyage and wreck: k5 comments on the boat taken aboard under the lee of Clauda ('small southwest of Crete, now called Gonzo; about twenty-three miles to leeward ... the boat had been towed between twenty and thirty miles after the gale sprang up' [Smith]), k11 on the long abstinence ('the hardships which the crew endured during a gale of such continuance, and their exhaustion from laboring at the pumps and hunger, may be imagined, but are not described'), k17 on the fourteenth night ('from the time they left Fair Havens ... drifting the Adriatic, that sea which lies between Greece and Italy ... no doubt from the peculiar sound of the breakers'), and k23 on lowering the boat ('already lowered. let the boat drift away'). Source verses run roughly 27:16, 27:21, 27:27, 27:32 — gaps of about 5, 6 and 5 against target gaps of 6, 6, 6, the same quantising the series has shown throughout. Two things worth adding to the file. (1) The blocks here are TINY — 64, 57, 44 and 8 words, 173 in total, against the 5,083 words of residue in revelation 16 and the 4,648-word block that turned out to be an editorial introduction. Residue size therefore varies by two orders of magnitude across chapters, which means the defect is invisible to any size-based heuristic and must be found positionally. (2) The 8-word block at key 23 is small enough that split_voices returns None for its name in some paths, so a residue detector that filters on a parsed voice name will miss it. Any inverse-map work should treat a Jamieson block as suspect by POSITION first and only then look at content. This is my 26th chapter confirming the residue and the second (after revelation 16) where I could name the donor verses individually.

FRONT MATTER AT THE FIRST KEY, CHROME AT THE LAST, AND A FOREIGN FATHER INSIDE WESLEY. Three defects, all positional, and the first is new. (1) BARNES'S KEY-1 BLOCK IS 3,326 WORDS, OF WHICH THE FIRST 2,730 ARE THE EPISTLE'S INTRODUCTION — 'The Second Epistle of PAUL THE APOSTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS INTRODUCTION I. THE DESIGN OF THE SECOND EPISTLE ...' — and only the last 596 words, beginning at the marker 'Verse 1.', are comment on the verse. This is the mirror image of the terminal-chrome rule: on the FIRST chapter of a book, the commentator's front matter attaches to the chapter-INITIAL block, exactly as the scrape's navigation furniture attaches to the terminal one. It is also the same class of defect as the Jamieson block at revelation 16 key 20, which was the editorial introduction to the Pastoral Epistles: the scrape does not distinguish front matter from verse comment anywhere. Practical rule for any first chapter: seek the 'Verse N.' marker inside a long Barnes block before using a word of it, and expect the sizer to overstate usable words by a couple of thousand. (2) ELLICOTT'S TERMINAL BLOCK AT KEY 24 is 2,317 words of which 1,425 are StudyLight chrome — and the payload here is different from the previous four sightings: not the copyright-and-links footer alone but inline JavaScript, 'document.addEventListener("DOMContentLoaded" ...' and a menu accordion, preceded by a navigation strip ('Additional Features Bulletin Insert Font Resources ... ESV KJV NAS NIV NLT NRS WEB'). Fifth sighting of Ellicott terminal chrome; first with executable script in it. (3) A 350-WORD PASSAGE OF TERTULLIAN AGAINST MARCION IS INLINED INSIDE WESLEY'S KEY-1 BLOCK, immediately after Wesley's 19 genuine words on 'Timotheus our brother'. Tertullian is in VOICE_LABELS, so split_voices does separate it and it can be — and here is — declared under excluded_voices; but g15_per.py does not carry him in its roster, so the structure mapper silently folds his 350 words into Wesley's count and reports Wesley at 369 words when his real contribution is 19. Corpus incidence of Tertullian: 60 blocks across 43 files (luke 37, galatians 6, 1corinthians 6, colossians 4, 2corinthians 2). Like Bede at revelation 16, this is a real if small feed that the working roster does not know about, and it needs the same owner decision. (4) Minor, for completeness: Gill is capped at exactly 200 words in 3 of his 24 blocks (keys 8, 21, 22) and 200 is his maximum across the chapter, so the NT-tree cap is present here too, though it bites far less than in hebrews 13.

CYRIL: THE PROOF-TEXT RULE PAYS OFF, AND FOR ONCE A BLOCK IS USABLE. Three Cyril blocks in this chapter, and applying the rule established at ephesians 5 and revelation 16 — a Cyril block is usable only if it quotes the target verse — sorts them cleanly. Key 3 carries a catechetical section on the blinding of unbelievers' thoughts, which is exposition of the FOURTH chapter of this epistle and never touches the third verse: arbitrary, set aside. Key 14 carries the section on the name Ecclesia and the first scriptural use of the word 'assemble', which touches nothing here: arbitrary, set aside. But key 22 quotes the target verse verbatim in the course of proving that Paul was full of the Holy Ghost — 'But He who sealed us for this very purpose is God, who gave us the earnest of the Spirit' — so it IS exposition of this verse in the only sense the Cyril column ever offers, and it is used, declared, and given an eastern-antiochene school summary. This is the first chapter in my series where the rule has admitted a Cyril block rather than excluding one, which is worth recording because it shows the rule is discriminating and not merely a way of dropping an inconvenient column. THE VALIDATOR GAP CUTS BOTH WAYS AND IS NOW DEMONSTRATED. Because synthesis_qa.VOICE_LABELS carries the short form 'Cyril' and _LABEL_RE requires a colon immediately after it, while the catena writes 'Cyril of Jerusalem:', split_voices returns no Cyril block anywhere in this chapter — the per-key dump above lists Chrysostom, Gill, Henry, Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson, Calvin, Wesley, Tertullian and Jamieson, and no Cyril at all. The consequence is asymmetric and worth stating plainly: excluded_voices IS checked against split_voices, so the two arbitrary blocks cannot be declared and must go in outliers; voices is NOT checked, so the one genuinely usable block CAN be declared without objection. The corpus therefore accepts a Cyril attribution it cannot verify and rejects a Cyril exclusion it cannot see. The one-line fix — adding 'Cyril of Jerusalem' to VOICE_LABELS ahead of 'Cyril', or letting the regex tolerate the qualifier — closes both halves at once and should precede any audit of column coverage.

FOUR REAL DIVISIONS, AND ONE OF THEM IS A COMMENTATOR REFUSING TO PAPER OVER PAUL. (1) VERSE 23, CHRYSOSTOM AGAINST THE HARMONISERS, and the sharpest thing in the chapter. He states the contradiction as a contradiction: 'What sayest thou, O blessed Paul? To spare them thou camest not to Corinth? Surely thou presentest us with something of a contradiction. For a little above thou saidst that thou therefore camest not, because thou purposest not according to the flesh nor art thine own master, but art led about every where by the authority of the Spirit ... But here thou sayest it was thine own act.' He then canvasses three solutions — that the Spirit itself urged the motive of sparing; that a different visit is meant; or that after the second epistle the Spirit no longer forbade and Paul stayed away voluntarily — and prefers the last, with the Spirit forbidding first and Paul concurring afterwards on his own conviction. No other voice in the chapter registers the tension at all; Barnes and Clarke go straight to Paley's reconstruction and Calvin to the reproach. Recorded in the debate list with all three of Chrysostom's options preserved. (2) VERSE 8, THE TROUBLE IN ASIA, six positions and no resolution: the Demetrius riot (Wesley, Calvin, and Barnes's majority report); not that but the fighting with beasts, since Paul never entered the theatre and so ran no risk justifying the words (Whitby and Macknight, as reported by Barnes); the Jews lying in wait (Semler, as reported by Barnes); a persecution recorded nowhere (Clarke); BODILY ILLNESS rather than any peril, on the ground that the phrase is unlocalised where Paul localises real perils, and that 'the language is obviously more vividly descriptive of the collapse of illness than of any peril' since he 'could hardly have despaired of life during the tumult' (Ellicott); and simple agnosticism (Robertson). Ellicott's is the minority reading and much the best argued; it also drives his medical reading of the rare word for 'sentence' at verse 9 as a physician's prognosis, with a second suggestion from Hippocrates that it means a virulent secretion, i.e. 'we had the symptoms of a fatal disease in us'. (3) VERSE 15, THE ITINERARY. Ellicott, Barnes, Gill and Robertson reconstruct Corinth-first (Ephesus to Corinth by sea, then Macedonia, then Corinth again, then Jerusalem); Clarke reconstructs Macedonia-first with Corinth on the return, reading 'by you' to mean that Paul would sail up the Aegean leaving Corinth to the west, and rejecting the Achaia-outward reading on the geographical ground that Achaia 'was out of his way considerably, and he could scarcely go through Achaia without passing close by Corinth'. Since the whole charge of fickleness turns on which leg was dropped, this is not a trivial divergence. (4) VERSE 24, HOW FAR AN APOSTLE MAY CLAIM DOMINION OVER FAITH. Clarke and Barnes concede a real dominion — the right to prescribe articles of belief and forbid contrary doctrine, 'essential to them as apostles' — while denying it was ever exercised in a lordly manner; Ellicott and Robertson make the clause a half-apology and a rhetorical self-correction, the readers having a standing-ground independent of Paul; Gill and Calvin read it as a disclaimer of tyrannical power. Clarke then extends his half of it into a Reformation polemic against those who claimed the right without apostolic warrant, which is where the chapter's most quotable sentence sits: 'Did they succeed? Yes, for a time; and that time was a time of thick darkness; a darkness that might be felt.'

THE CALVIN COLUMN INLINES ITS TRANSLATOR'S FOOTNOTES, SIXTH BOOK CONFIRMING. Every substantial Calvin block in this chapter carries editorial matter run into the body text with no separator: French glosses of the translator's own renderings ('Des martyres et afflictions des fideles', 'Qu'il ha certain espoir', 'Vaines et caduques', 'Es-tu si insupportable, et si orgueilleux?') and English annotations with trailing attributions. The English ones are the dangerous kind, because they read as Calvin's own prose. Three specimens from this chapter alone: at verse 8, a long passage signed 'Burgesse on 2 Corinthians 1, pp. 269, 270, 278' distinguishing a burden exceeding heavy from one above strength and illustrating it with Samson carrying off the gates of Gaza; at verse 5, a note on the present participle of comforting, 'that doth never cease to do it, that never withdraweth his consolations ... as the devil is called ho peirazon', signed to a page of another commentary; and at verse 15, a bibliographic note reporting that 'Most modern Commentators explain the charin ... but the ancient Commentators, and some modern ones, as Wolf and Schleus, for charan', with the Tyndale, Cranmer and Geneva renderings. THE CLEANEST DEMONSTRATION IS AT VERSE 12. Calvin's block there contains a 90-word passage on the verb anastrepho — 'a continual coming back again to the point from which he set out; a circulation; beginning, continuing, and ending everything to the glory of God ... acting in reference to God, as the planets do in reference to the sun, deriving all their light, heat, and motion from him; and incessantly and regularly revolving round him. Thus acted Paul: thus acted the primitive Christians' — which is word-for-word ADAM CLARKE'S, and Clarke's own block at the same key contains the identical sentences. Two voices in the same catena key carrying the same text, one of them as an unmarked footnote inside the other. I attributed it to Clarke in the prose, which is demonstrably right; but a reader or a tool working from the Calvin column alone would attribute it to Calvin. THE STANDING CONSEQUENCE, now confirmed across deuteronomy 19, ephesians 3, 2corinthians 5, ephesians 5 and this chapter: apparent agreement between the reformed voice and another school may be transmission rather than convergence, and any automated agreement metric computed over the Calvin column is measuring the translator as much as Calvin. Practical rule when drafting: never credit Calvin with a sentence that names a modern authority, cites page numbers, or reads in nineteenth-century English.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, all 11 entries, all grade A. Source: 24 catena keys, 58,117 usable words as the sizer reported them, of which roughly 4,678 (8.0 percent) is not commentary on this chapter at all — 2,730 words of epistle introduction under Barnes at key 1, 1,425 words of StudyLight chrome inside Ellicott's key-24 block, 350 words of Tertullian against Marcion inlined in Wesley's key-1 block, and 173 words of Jamieson residue at keys 5, 11, 17 and 23. Henry comments by section, so his key-7 block covers verses 7 through 11 and his key-15 block covers 15 through 19; I used only the material falling inside each entry's own range and did NOT name him in entries 8, 10, 17, 19, 21 or 23, where he has no head. A CORRECTION TO THE ACTS 7 NOTE, AND TWO MORE DISCRIMINATING GAPS. (1) CORRECTION. At acts 7 I recorded that Cyril's two byte-identical blocks sat 36 keys apart and called that six times the stride. This chapter has another Cyril duplicate — keys 8 and 16 are byte-identical (md5 1eb83aa281), an exposition of 2 Corinthians 4:4 on the blinding of unbelievers, filed under neither verse — and the distance is EIGHT keys, not a multiple of six. The multiple-of-six relation at acts 7 was therefore coincidence, and I withdraw that part of the note. What stands is the substantive finding: verbatim repetition of a block occurs in more than one voice's feed, it is a property of the emitter rather than of the Jamieson scrape, and its spacing is NOT tied to the six-key stride. (2) JAMIESON residue here at keys 4, 10 and 16 — offset 4, target gaps 6 and 6. Source region Ephesians 4, and each block all but dates itself by citing its own neighbourhood: k4 comments on the tossing to and fro and refers to Eph 4:13 as the positive counterpart, so it is on Eph 4:14; k10 glosses hardening with a reference to Eph 4:18, so it is on 4:19; k16 opposes the new man to the old man 'which is to be put off (Ep 4:22)', so it is on 4:24. Source gaps 5 and 5 against target gaps 6 and 6 — two more gaps, neither of them 6 in the source, both quantising up. Running total of discriminating gaps across the series: ephesians 4 five, deuteronomy 14 four, hebrews 13 three, deuteronomy 15 three, 2peter 1 two, plus the corpus-scale single-class result (748 of 748) and the byte-exact zero-advance repetitions at acts 7.

THREE DOCTRINAL CRUXES, EACH DIVIDING THE VOICES ALONG CONFESSIONAL LINES, AND ONE OF THEM NAMED AS SUCH. (1) VERSE 10, 'make your calling and election sure' — four accounts. Calvin makes the surety evidential: a good conscience and integrity of life answering to the profession is one proof that we have really been elected and not called in vain, and he notes that calling is named first though election is prior and weightier. Barnes reads it as assurance, the appeal resting on the uncertainty low attainment throws over a man's own salvation. Clarke reverses the order outright, making election the being chosen as God's people IN CONSEQUENCE of obeying the heavenly calling, and holds both forfeitable unless the graces are added. Wesley states the same conditionality with an edge — 'O cast not away these inestimable benefits! If ye are thus diligent to make your election firm, ye shall never finally fall.' Ellicott stands between with a definition rather than a doctrine, calling and election being two aspects of one fact. The same verse also carries a variant, the inserted 'by means of your works', which Calvin rejects as unauthorised and unnecessary while Ellicott rejects its authority and accepts its sense — opposite verdicts on one reading. (2) VERSE 19, 'a more sure word of prophecy' — five positions on one comparative. Henry takes it at face value and holds prophecy the stronger of the two proofs, outweighing the vision on the mount. Robertson calls precisely that view 'less likely'. Clarke settles it lexically, proving from five New Testament passages that the adjective means confirmed, so the transfiguration confirmed the prophecies rather than being weighed against them; Wesley and Ellicott agree. Barnes catalogues the constructions, including Luther's simple removal of the comparative, and Gill sets out the alternatives and finds all of them unsatisfactory. Calvin closes off the escape of reading the comparative as a positive. Ellicott, having chosen a rendering, still admits the sense of the sentence is 'not quite clear'. (3) VERSES 20-21, 'private interpretation'. Barnes concedes the phrase has caused as much diversity 'as perhaps any phrase in the New Testament' with no agreement reached. ROBERTSON DECIDES IT AND NAMES THE PARTY HE DECIDES AGAINST: 'Peter is not here warning against personal interpretation of prophecy as the Roman Catholics say, but against the folly of upstart prophets with no impulse from God' — the first time in this series a commentator has framed an exegetical choice explicitly as a confessional one. Clarke reaches the same result from the noun's second sense, impulse. Calvin reports the reader-side reading as the one almost everyone gives and calls its doctrine true. A fourth division follows immediately at verse 21: Clarke has the prophets 'carried away out of themselves and out of the whole region of human knowledge', not knowing the intent of their own words, and Wesley says they were 'purely passive'; Calvin expressly denies it — they were not bereaved of mind 'as the Gentiles imagined their prophets to have been', but dared announce nothing of their own. All four are recorded in the entries' debate lists.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, all 8 entries. Source: 62,584 usable words after the chrome cut (63,894 as the sizer reported), across 21 catena keys and 10 voices. Every proposition in every entry is traceable to a named block inside that entry's own verse range; no voice is named in an entry where it has no head. Deliberate omissions, none of which changes any reported position: the long introductions to the epistle under key 1 (Barnes 4,351 words and Clarke 4,141, both largely on the canonical history) are used only for what they say about the authorship question and the name; Clarke's account of the Greek mysteries at key 16 is compressed to the one point that bears on the word for eyewitness; Calvin's French editorial glosses are not reproduced; Barnes's extended practical applications are given by one instance each. NOTE ON APPARATUS INSIDE A VOICE: Calvin's key 3 block contains an editorial paragraph written in the third person about Calvin himself ('Our version and Calvin seem to connect this verse with the foregoing... Others, perhaps more correctly, view this verse as connected with...'), so the block mixes the commentator with his English editor. Nothing from that paragraph is attributed to Calvin in the prose. 27TH CONFIRMATION, AND THE DONOR IS ACTS 18 — PAUL AT CORINTH. Jamieson residue at keys 2, 8, 14 and 20 — four members, target gaps 6, 6, 6, offset 2. The source region is Acts 18, and every member is identifiable from its content: k2 is on 18:1, describing Corinth ('rebuilt by Julius Caesar on the isthmus between the Aegean and Ionian Seas; the capital of the Roman province of Achaia ... owing to the banishment of the Jews from Rome by Claudius Caesar'); k8 is on 18:9, the night vision ('these signal successes were stirring up the wrath of the unbelieving Jews ... He is reassured, however, from above'); k14 is on 18:12, Gallio ('the proconsul ... He was brother to the celebrated philosopher Seneca, the tutor of Nero, who passed sentence of death on both'); k20 is on 18:19, Ephesus ('the capital of the Roman province of Asia ... Aquila and Priscilla'). Source gaps 8, 3 and 7 against target gaps 6, 6, 6 — three more discriminating gaps, not one of them equal to the stride, all quantising to it. THE COINCIDENCE IS WORTH FLAGGING SO IT IS NOT MISTAKEN FOR A MECHANISM: the donor here is the Acts narrative of Paul's founding of the very church this epistle addresses, which looks meaningful and is not. Across my series the donors have been 2 Thessalonians 3 (into revelation 16), Acts 27 (into 2corinthians 1) and now Acts 18 (into 1corinthians 4). A thematically apt donor and a wildly inapt one arise from the same blind pointer, so donor identity carries no information about the target and must never be used to guess a target's correct content. Running total: 27 chapters confirming the residue, and the third in which the donor verses could be named individually. Block sizes here are 93, 43, 27 and 121 words — again tiny, as at 2corinthians 1 and unlike revelation 16's 4,648-word block, reinforcing that the defect must be found positionally rather than by size.

FRONT MATTER AT THE FIRST KEY AND CHROME AT THE LAST, BOTH CONFIRMED AGAIN — AND THE FIRST-KEY RULE GENERALISES. At 2corinthians 1 I recorded that Barnes's key-1 block carried 2,730 words of EPISTLE introduction before reaching the verse. This chapter shows the pattern is not confined to a book's opening chapter: here at 1corinthians 4, BOTH Barnes and Clarke open their key-1 blocks with the CHAPTER ARGUMENT. Barnes begins '1st Corinthians CHAPTER 4 THIS chapter is a continuation of the subject discussed in those which go before ... The proper division would have been at verse 6', and runs through a precis of all twenty-one verses before commenting on the first. Clarke's key-1 block opens with a verse-by-verse table of contents ('Ministers should be esteemed by their flocks as the stewards of God ... 1Cor 4:1, 2. Precipitate and premature judgments condemned, 1Cor 4:3-5 ...'). So the rule is: whatever front matter a printed commentary places before a unit — book introduction for chapter 1, chapter argument for every chapter — is swept into the CHAPTER-INITIAL catena key, exactly as scrape navigation furniture is swept into the chapter-TERMINAL one. The two are mirror images of the same boundary failure, and a chapter has both. TERMINAL END, this chapter: Ellicott's key-21 block is 2,054 words of which 1,820 are StudyLight chrome — seventh sighting, and the largest proportion yet at 89 percent. Barnes's key-21 block is 1,853 words of which 1,632 are his REMARKS ON 1st CORINTHIANS CHAPTER 4, an end-of-chapter essay rather than comment on verse 21; Clarke's terminal block does the same thing with his own end-of-chapter notes. So the terminal key carries THREE kinds of overflow at once here — scrape chrome, and two commentators' end-of-chapter matter. PRACTICAL RULES, now firm: (1) on any chapter, look for the verse marker inside the first Barnes or Clarke block before using a word of it; (2) on any chapter, treat the last key's longest block as chrome or end-matter until proved otherwise; (3) the sizer's usable-word count overstates by the sum of both, here by roughly 3,500 words or 7.8 percent of the reported 44,908.

A METHOD ERROR OF MINE, CAUGHT IN TIME: NEVER JUDGE A CYRIL BLOCK FROM ITS OPENING. Applying the rule established at ephesians 5 and revelation 16 — a Cyril block is usable only if it quotes the target verse — I inspected the two Cyril blocks in this chapter by reading their first 400 characters, which is how I have screened them in every previous chapter. Key 15 opened by quoting its verse verbatim and was accepted. Key 9 opened 'If any man receive not Baptism, he hath not salvation; except only Martyrs, who even without the water receive the kingdom', which is catechesis on baptism and touches nothing in this chapter, so I provisionally marked it arbitrary and planned to set it aside in outliers. THAT WAS WRONG. Reading the whole block when I came to draft the entry, the target verse appears near the end: 'And the Martyrs confess, by being made a spectacle unto the world, and to Angels, and to men' — which is 1 Corinthians 4:9 quoted exactly, and is the point the whole paragraph is travelling toward. The block IS exposition of this verse in the only sense the Cyril column ever offers, and it is used and declared. WHY THE ERROR IS STRUCTURAL AND NOT CARELESS. The Cyril column is a proof-text index: a catechetical section is filed at every verse it quotes. The quotation is therefore located wherever the argument happens to reach it, which for a section of any length is usually NOT the opening — Cyril states a thesis first and adduces the proof text afterwards. Screening on the opening is thus biased precisely against the blocks that are genuine. CORRECTED RULE, which supersedes the screening practice implied in notes 1506, 1519 and 1524: search the WHOLE Cyril block for the target verse before judging it, and expect the quotation late. I have not gone back over the earlier chapters, so the exclusions recorded at ephesians 3 key 5, ephesians 5 keys 20/23/33, revelation 16 keys 14/18 and 2corinthians 1 keys 3/14 were all screened by the flawed method and at least some may be wrong. Those chapters are landed and I am not proposing to disturb them, but the corpus-wide count of usable Cyril blocks is very likely an UNDERCOUNT for two independent reasons now — the VOICE_LABELS mismatch that hides the blocks from split_voices, and this screening bias. Both should be fixed before anyone audits that column.

THREE REAL DIVISIONS, ONE OF THEM A COMMENTATOR DISOWNING THE DOCTRINE HIS OWN TRADITION BUILT ON THE VERSE. (1) VERSE 7, AND CLARKE AGAINST EVERYONE. 'Who maketh thee to differ' is the verse Augustine built predestination on — Robertson records that 'ten years before the challenge of Pelagius, the study of St. Paul's writings, and especially of this verse and of Ro 9:16, had crystallized in his mind the distinctively Augustinian doctrines of man's total depravity, of irresistible grace, and of absolute predestination.' Henry, Barnes and Wesley all take it as the general maxim that nothing we have is our own. Calvin takes it to church order. CLARKE ALONE READS IT NARROWLY, as addressed to one puffed-up teacher at Corinth — 'didst thou not receive it from myself or some other of my fellow helpers who first preached the Gospel at Corinth?' — and then does something rare in the corpus: he states that the general doctrine others draw from it 'is true in itself, though it does not appear to me to be any part of the apostle's meaning in this place', while warning against 'many religious people, who imagine that they have been eternal objects of God's favor, and that others have been eternal objects of his hate, for no reason that they can show for either the one, or the other.' A voice conceding a doctrine's truth while denying it this proof text is worth more than another vote either way. (2) VERSE 8, WHETHER THE IRONY IS IRONY. Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Calvin all take the three clauses as sarcasm — Barnes defending the device itself as showing 'that there may be occasions when irony may be proper, though it should be rare.' Clarke first prints Whitby's straightforward paraphrase, in which the Corinthians really are full and rich and reigning without needing Paul, and then dissents from it in his own voice: 'I am of opinion that the apostle here intends a strong irony.' Both readings are preserved in the entry's debate list. (3) VERSE 6, WHY THESE NAMES. Locke (as Barnes reports) holds nobody had actually been made head of a party and the names are illustrative; Barnes, Clarke and Bishop Pearce argue from greater to less; Ellicott makes it delicacy toward Cephas's admirers; Calvin says those attached to Paul never started parties at all. Gill enters the flat correction that matters: 'it is certain, from his way of arguing and reasoning, that these are not fictitious names, but they were really divided.' (4) A SMALLER ONE WORTH THE FILE: where this chapter should begin. Barnes and Clarke both say the division is wrong and it should start at verse 6, Clarke adding that chapter 3 should have ended at verse 5. Calvin, at the other end, says whoever divided the epistles 'ought to have made this the beginning of the chapter' — meaning verse 21. Three commentators independently judging the received chapter break wrong, and disagreeing about which way to move it.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, all 9 entries, all grade A. Source: 21 catena keys, 44,908 usable words as the sizer reported them, of which roughly 3,500 (7.8 percent) is not comment on the verses at all — about 1,820 words of StudyLight chrome inside Ellicott's key-21 block, about 1,632 words of Barnes's end-of-chapter REMARKS in the same key, Clarke's end-of-chapter notes in the same key, the chapter arguments opening Barnes's and Clarke's key-1 blocks, and 284 words of Jamieson residue at keys 2, 8, 14 and 20. Word counts, all inside the 350-650 window: 1-2 = 639, 3-5 = 646, 6-7 = 646, 8-9 = 648, 10-11 = 649, 12-13 = 650, 14-16 = 640, 17-18 = 647, 19-21 = 650. Type-token ratios 0.648 to 0.697, zip ratios 0.444 to 0.474, so every entry clears the A threshold on both axes with margin. TILING: nine entries over twenty-one verses, cut at the argument's joints — stewards and fidelity (1-2), the three tribunals (3-5), the figure and the question about differing (6-7), the irony and the arena (8-9), the triple contrast and the hardships (10-11), the labour and the offscouring (12-13), father not tutor (14-16), the sending of Timothy (17-18), and the promised visit with the rod (19-21). Coverage_problems returns empty. VOICE COVERAGE: Gill, Barnes and Calvin at all 21 keys; Clarke, Robertson and Wesley at 20; Ellicott 19; Henry 4 (keys 1, 7, 14, 17); Chrysostom 4 (keys 3, 6, 10, 17); Jamieson 4 (all residue, all declared excluded); Cyril 2 (keys 9 and 15, BOTH quoting their target verses and both used — see the note on my corrected screening method). HEAD PLACEMENT shaped several entries: Henry comments by section, so I named him only in entries 1, 6, 14 and 17 and kept him out of 3, 8, 10, 12 and 19 where he has no head; Chrysostom likewise appears only in 3, 6, 10 and 17. Where a voice was quoted INSIDE another's block — Chrysostom on insatiable piety quoted by Ellicott at key 8, Whitby and Bishop Pearce quoted by Clarke, Locke and Grotius and Bloomfield reported by Barnes, Lightfoot and Robertson-and-Plummer and Marcus Aurelius quoted by Robertson — I attributed the quotation to the reporting voice, or credited the source as reported, and never listed the quoted party among the entry's voices. DELIBERATE OMISSIONS, none of which changes a reported position: Henry's key-7 block of 2,559 words and key-1 block of 1,996 are used only for the material inside each entry's range; Barnes's key-21 REMARKS and Clarke's end-of-chapter notes are not drawn on at all; Clarke's rabbinic parable of the orphan girl at key 15 is dropped because the catena truncates it before its point; Calvin's repeated expansions on ministerial fidelity are compressed to one statement each. TRUNCATION CARRIED IN THE NOTES AND NOT ATTRIBUTED TO ANY COMMENTATOR IN THE PROSE: Gill capped at exactly 200 words at keys 7, 15 and 20, with 200 his maximum across the chapter, and Chrysostom capped at 200 at key 3. At key 20 the cap cuts Gill off in the middle of his elimination argument, before he says what the kingdom of God positively is; I reported only the eliminations that survive and attributed no conclusion to him. NOTE FOR THE CAP FILE: Gill caps at 200 here and at 2corinthians 1, but at 201 in genesis 2 and hebrews 13, so the boundary is not a fixed constant per voice; it appears to differ by feed or by scrape run, and de-truncation work should not assume one value.

Fidelity self-grade, all six entries. 1-7 639w, 8-11 632w, 12-14 576w, 15-17 627w, 18-21 643w, 22 631w; all in the 350-650 window, six entries tiling keys 1-22 with no gap in the source. Every named voice is sourced at a key inside its own range and no voice with a block in range is left unnamed. Positions I could not verify against a second witness are attributed to the voice that states them (Shuckford via Clarke, Lightfoot via Gill and via the editor printed inside Calvin, Abenezra and Augustine via Keil, Origen via Clarke) rather than asserted. Nothing is drawn from the Jamieson block at key 3, which is declared as excluded residue.

Keil and Delitzsch is capped at exactly 200 words in all ten of its blocks in this chapter - 10/10, 100 percent, the second Exodus chapter to score 100 percent after exodus 27 at 8/8. Running OT total is now 58 of 63 measured Keil blocks at exactly 200 across seven chapters. The cap is mid-sentence: the k18 block breaks off at the bare Hebrew form 'lahem for lahen' with the argument unfinished, and the k19 and k21 blocks recover the lost text only because each restarts from an earlier verse and overruns forward. Keil remains on the OT re-fetch list; this chapter is the strongest single case for it.

Chrome at the last key in two different voices, from two different sources. Gill k22 carries a trailing site-navigation tail (129 raw words down to 98 usable); Ellicott k22 carries a much larger one, a run of volume and chapter labels, 1318 raw words down to 334 usable. Gill carried no tail at all at exodus 27, so the presence of chrome is not a property of the voice or of the book - the per-voice provenance map has to be built per chapter, not per book.

Editor's apparatus printed inside a voice block, again. The Calvin block at k21 opens with three sentences of third-person commentary about Calvin - 'The accuracy of Calvin's criticism is undeniable', a survey of the LXX and Geneva Bible glosses, a Lightfoot citation, a Poole quotation, and the verdict 'The balance of comments appears to favor Calvin's solution' - before Calvin's own text begins at 'It is not at all my opinion'. The k18 Calvin block does the same, opening with two Lightfoot references including 'In opposition to Calvin, he considers them to have been Egyptian women', and carries scattered Latin and French variant readings mid-sentence. Nothing from those paragraphs is attributed to Calvin in the synthesis. Same family as 2peter 1 k3 and hebrews 13 k24, and it now looks like a standing property of this Calvin feed rather than an accident of one volume.

Two voices quote the same third source with the same words, by different routes. Gill at k20 reports that some think the midwives 'made a glorious confession of their faith', crediting Dr Lightfoot 'who takes the midwives to be Egyptians'. The editorial matter inside the Calvin block at k18 cites Lightfoot's dissertation by its actual heading, 'The words of the Hebrew Midwives not a lie, but a glorious confession of their faith', and notes that 'In opposition to Calvin, he considers them to have been Egyptian women'. Gill's sentence is a compression of that heading plus its author's position. Agreement between two voices here is inheritance from a common source, not independent convergence - the same question the prevalence field raises for the Wesley/Henry overlaps.

The sharpest disagreement in the chapter is whether the midwives lied and what God rewarded. Clarke denies there was any lie or even prevarication and defends the answer as a fact stated in the face of danger; Wesley sees no reason to doubt its truth; Ellicott calls it probably true but not the whole truth, a half truth taken as refuge by women who lacked the courage of their convictions; Keil calls it a deception that succeeded, then quotes Augustine that God rewarded the kindness and not the falsehood; Calvin convicts them of two vices and holds flatly that they lied and sinned, rejecting the category of the serviceable lie because whatever is opposed to the nature of God is sinful. Gill sets out both readings and chooses neither. The second axis follows from it: who received the houses and who built them - the midwives (Keil, Wesley, Ellicott), the Israelites by God's hand (Calvin, and Clarke at the end), or the Israelites by Pharaoh's, on Shuckford's repunctuation reported by Clarke.

Wesley abridges Henry twice inside a single chapter, the first time that has happened in this run. At the seventy souls Wesley reproduces Henry's turn about the number of the nations, and at the death of Joseph he carries Henry's 'All that knew him loved him... but when he was dead he was soon forgotten' with only cosmetic change. Running count of Wesley/Henry near-verbatim overlaps is now eight instances across the chapters synthesized in this run, with one counter-case at 1samuel 6. Two in one chapter strengthens the case that the tags' prevalence field should down-weight agreement traceable to a common source.

Keil and Clarke contradict each other on the span of the chapter's events and neither shows any sign of knowing the other's figure. Working from the same two termini - the death of Joseph and the birth of Moses - Keil's reckoning gives roughly 360 years and Clarke's roughly 145. The gap is not a difference of interpretation about a disputed word but a different chronology carried in silently from each writer's own system, and a reader consulting both would have no way to see which assumption produced which number.

Jamieson has exactly one block in this chapter, 36 words at k3, and it is not commentary on Exodus 1. With only a single member there is no run and therefore no residue class to measure, so this chapter contributes nothing to the mod-6 stride finding either way; it is declared as excluded residue rather than silenced, since a reader would otherwise be told nothing was withheld when something was. Consistent with the corpus finding that the Jamieson tree is displaced rather than duplicated.

Fidelity self-grade, all eight entries. 1-3 581w, 6-10 140w thin, 23-25 223w thin, 27-30 262w thin, 32-34 610w, 37-39 360w, 41 358w, 43 572w. The chapter's source keys are gappy - 1,2,3,6,7,8,9,10,23,24,25,27,28,29,30,32,33,34,37,38,39,41,43 - so the eight entries are the eight contiguous runs and the tiling is forced, not chosen. Three entries are thin against a measured source of 56, 130 and 176 usable words. Two entries sit deliberately at the bottom of the full window because their runs measure 274 and 235 usable words, just above the 200-word thin ceiling; both are written short rather than padded to the target. Every named voice is sourced at a key inside its own range.

NEW DEFECT FAMILY: the Matthew Henry feed splices the Concise commentary onto the tail of the Exposition block, and the join is detectable by a change in scripture-reference style. Both Henry blocks in this chapter show it. At k1 the Exposition body cites 'Rev. vii. 13, 15' and 'Rev. xix. 8' in roman numerals, then the block continues into a condensed restatement of its own second half citing 'Re 19:8' in the arabic short form. At k32 the same thing happens: the body cites '2 Chron. xxix. 36' and 'Rev.'-style refs, and the appended tail cites 'Col 2:9' and 'Re 21:3'. The tail is not additional comment - it is the same argument compressed, so a reader gets the material twice and a word-count sizer counts it twice. The style shift gives a clean programmatic signature for a corpus-wide scan: a Henry block containing both a roman-numeral verse reference and an arabic short-form reference.

Dittography inside the Henry k1 block, independent of the Concise splice: 'girded himself with the curious girdle of resolution, to go through with his undertaking - charged himself with the curious girdle of resolution, to go through with his undertaking - charged himself with all God's spiritual Israel'. The clause 'the curious girdle of resolution, to go through with his undertaking - charged himself with' is repeated verbatim, so the sentence reads as though Christ girded and charged himself with the same girdle twice. This is a duplication inside a single block rather than across keys, which is a different failure from the cross-key repetition recorded at acts 7 and 2peter 1.

Jamieson stride, seven hundred and forty-ninth chapter with no exception. Three blocks, at keys 9, 33 and 39, all congruent to 3 mod 6. None of the three is on Exodus 39: k9 is on the lampstand and cites Exodus 25:32-36 in its own text, k33 is on the goats' hair curtains of Exodus 26:7-13, k39 is on the boards and bars of Exodus 26:15-30. The source therefore lags the target by roughly thirteen chapters here, the same direction as the Numbers displacement and a smaller lag, which is what a monotone drift in position predicts - Exodus 39 sits earlier in the corpus than Numbers 1, and its lag is correspondingly shorter than the seventeen chapters measured there. Jamieson's genuine commentary on Exodus 39 is not in this file and I did not find it elsewhere.

The 200-word cap, and the mechanism that partly hides it. Keil 3 of 4 blocks at exactly 200 (k2, k33, k38); the fourth, k41, runs 178 and stops of its own accord. Gill 2 of 5 at exactly 200 (k2, k43), and the k43 block breaks off mid-quotation of Jarchi at the words 'and the', losing the second half of a blessing formula. Two observations that qualify earlier notes. First, Keil's k2 block is 200 words of the biblical text of Exodus 39:2-9 and contains no comment at all - the cap was reached before any comment began, so the block holds a head and conveys nothing, the same shape as the name-stripped Gill block at deuteronomy 14 k21 that the GHOST check cannot catch. It is silenced here rather than declared, since nothing is being withheld. Second, Keil's k41 block is the CONTINUATION of his k38 block and repeats about 130 of its 200 words verbatim before going on to new material. That overlap is why any of his comment survives at all, and it is also why the sizer over-reports: those 130 words are counted twice. Running OT total for Keil at exactly 200 is now 61 of 67 across eight chapters.

Wesley abridges Henry three more times in this chapter, bringing the running count to eleven instances. At k1 Wesley reproduces Henry's 'Those that wear robes of honour must look upon them as clothes of service' paragraph and the whole high-priest typology that follows it. At k32 he reproduces Henry's account of the five months and the three reasons for the despatch, keeping 'The workmen were taught of God, and so were kept from making blunders, which would have retarded them' almost word for word. At k43 he reproduces Henry's k32 section on the blessing - 'He not only praised them, but prayed for them: he blessed them as one having authority' and the whole argument about wages, the manna and the raiment that waxed not old. The k43 case is the first cross-key instance recorded: Wesley's block under one key abridges Henry's block filed under a different key eleven verses earlier, so a per-key comparison would have missed it.

A countable disagreement about the chapter's own structure. Calvin at k1 says the clause 'as the Lord commanded Moses' is repeated seven times and that the repetition is meant to awaken attention. Henry at k1 says there are six paragraphs closing that way and lists their verses - 5, 7, 21, 26, 29, 31. Neither refers to the other and neither shows any sign that the count is in dispute. The chapter as it stands carries the refrain more often than either figure, so both men are counting something narrower than every occurrence, and they are not counting the same thing. Recorded because it is the rare case where two voices contradict each other on a fact a reader can check in ten seconds, and the synthesis has to report both rather than adjudicate.

Clarke refuses an inference Ellicott draws from the same verse. On the gold beaten into plates and cut into wires, Ellicott says the method is 'nowhere else mentioned' and 'implies a ruder state of the art of metallurgy than we should have expected'. Clarke says he 'cannot suppose that the Israelites had not then the art of making gold thread, as they possessed several ornamental arts much more difficult', and explains the beaten plates by the requirements of the figure instead. This is a clean instance of the same datum read as evidence of capability by one voice and of incapacity by the other, with the disagreement resting entirely on a prior estimate of what the people could do.

Two entries in this chapter sit just above the thin ceiling and are worth flagging as a rule-boundary case rather than a defect. The run 37-39 measures 274 usable source words after the Jamieson residue is excluded, and the isolated key 41 measures 235; both are above THIN_SOURCE_MAX of 200, so both must reach the 350-word floor. Each is written at 360 and 358 words respectively, which is an expansion of about 1.3x and 1.5x against its source. Nothing is invented - the disagreement over 'the lamps to be set in order' and Ellicott's argument about the missing conjunction genuinely carry that much - but the shape is worth recording, because a gappy chapter forces short runs into their own entries and the floor then bites hardest exactly where the source is thinnest. If the owner ever revisits the window, the case for scaling the floor to the span's source rather than stepping it at 200 is strongest here.

Chrome, one family and one voice only. Ellicott k43 carries 985 words of book-and-chapter navigation tail, 1032 raw down to 47 usable - a run of labels of the form 'Exodus Exo 38 Exodus Exo ...'. No other voice carries a tail anywhere in this chapter, which is the opposite pattern from exodus 1, where Gill and Ellicott both carried one at the last key. Together the two chapters confirm that chrome is per voice per chapter and cannot be predicted from the book: the same Ellicott feed carries a tail at the last key of both chapters, but the same Gill feed carries one at exodus 1 k22 and none at exodus 39 k43. Also worth noting for the sizer: the raw span figure for key 43 is 2112 usable words by the current measure, against about 1127 once the tail is cut, so the sizer is 87 percent high on that key - a larger error than the 26 percent recorded at hebrews 13.

Editor's apparatus inside a Calvin block again, third chapter running. The k32 block carries an interpolated gloss mid-sentence - a French phrase with its English translation and a dangling attribution mark - inside Calvin's sentence about the mouth of the witness, and closes with a bare misfiled chapter marker reading 'Exodus 24'. The gloss is a translator's variant reading, not Calvin's text, and the trailing marker points at the wrong chapter entirely. Same family as exodus 1 k18 and k21, 2peter 1 k3 and hebrews 13 k24. On the evidence now standing it is a property of this Calvin feed rather than an accident of any one volume, and any Calvin re-fetch has to strip apparatus rather than merely raise a cap.

28TH CONFIRMATION, DONOR EXODUS 33-34, AND A THREE-MEMBER RESIDUE WITH A DOUBLE GAP. Jamieson residue at keys 2, 14 and 20 — only three members this time, with target gaps of 12 and 6, both multiples of the stride, so the run is 2, (8 missing), 14, 20 at offset 2. The source region is the golden-calf aftermath in Exodus 33-34, and each block is identifiable: k2 is on the cloud descending at the tent entrance and Moses as mediator ('when he appeared as their mediator, when he repaired from day to day to intercede for them, that welcome token of assurance was given that his advocacy prevailed'), which is Exodus 33:9; k14 is on Moses seeing the divine glory ('This is one of the most mysterious scenes described in the Bible ... The face, hand, back parts, are to be understood figuratively'), which is Exodus 33:23; k20 is on the second tables ('God having been reconciled to repentant Israel, through the earnest intercession, the successful mediation of Moses ... Now, Moses was to prepare the stone tables, and God was only to retrace the characters'), which is Exodus 34:1. TWO THINGS THIS CHAPTER ADDS. (1) THE MISSING MEMBER. A stride-6 run through this chapter's 20 keys with offset 2 predicts members at 2, 8, 14 and 20; key 8 has no Jamieson block at all. So the residue can be SPARSE — a member can simply be absent — which means counting members is not a safe way to test the stride, and a chapter with two members twelve apart is as much evidence as one with four members six apart. Any corpus-scale re-test should check residue classes mod 6, not gaps between consecutive members. (2) THE DONOR CROSSES A CHAPTER BOUNDARY AGAIN. Exodus 33 has 23 verses, so the step from 33:23 to 34:1 is a single record in a flat sequence but looks like a wild jump in book/chapter/verse terms. This is the same behaviour recorded at revelation 16, where the pointer ran off the end of 2 Thessalonians into the next book's front matter. Source gaps here are about 14 and 1 against target gaps of 12 and 6 — again quantising, and again meaningless unless computed over the concatenated record stream. Donors seen so far in my series: 2 Thessalonians 3 and the Pastorals introduction (into revelation 16), Acts 27 (into 2corinthians 1), Acts 18 (into 1corinthians 4), Exodus 33-34 (into leviticus 10).

THE 200-WORD CAP DESTROYS A WHOLE COLUMN HERE, AND THE FIRST/LAST KEY RULES HOLD IN A THIRD BOOK. (1) KEIL AND DELITZSCH IS EFFECTIVELY UNUSABLE IN THIS CHAPTER. He has seven blocks and SIX of them stand at exactly 200 words (keys 2, 5, 7, 8, 9, 13), with 200 as his maximum anywhere. That would be ordinary truncation, except for what fills the allowance: the Keil column prefixes each block with the FULL TEXT of the verses it is about, so the cap is spent on lemma before any exposition begins. At key 13 the entire 200 words are the quoted text of verses 13 through 17 and not one word of comment survives; the same is true of the 12-word block at key 20. I therefore declared Keil silent — not excluded, since the blocks are genuine and not foreign — in the entries covering keys 13 and 20, and used him only where comment survived the cap (keys 2, 5, 7, 8, 9). THIS IS A DIFFERENT AND WORSE FAILURE MODE THAN PLAIN TRUNCATION, and it is systematic rather than accidental: any Keil block whose lemma runs long is guaranteed to be empty of commentary. Since Keil is the OT tree's principal critical voice, and since the cap and the lemma-prefix habit are both properties of the feed rather than of the chapter, a large fraction of Keil's corpus-wide contribution may be lemma only. That is worth measuring before anyone treats Keil coverage counts as coverage of Keil's commentary. (2) FRONT MATTER AT THE FIRST KEY, third book confirming: Clarke's key-1 block opens with the chapter argument, a verse-by-verse table of contents ('Nadab and Abihu offer strange fire before the Lord, and are destroyed, Lev 10:1-5. Aaron and his family forbidden to mourn for them, Lev 10:6, 7 ...') before reaching a word of comment. Recorded previously for Barnes at 2corinthians 1 (epistle introduction) and for Barnes and Clarke at 1corinthians 4 (chapter argument); the rule generalises across books and testaments. (3) CHROME AT THE LAST KEY, eighth sighting: Ellicott's key-20 block is 1,372 words of which 1,238 — ninety percent — are StudyLight navigation and boilerplate. (4) Gill capped at exactly 200 at keys 16 and 20, with 200 his maximum, so the NT-value cap appears here in an OT book; taken with genesis 2 and hebrews 13 at 201 and 2corinthians 1 and 1corinthians 4 at 200, the cap is not constant per voice or per testament and must be measured per file.

FOUR DIVISIONS, AND ONE OF THEM IS A CONFESSION THAT SCRIPTURE QUOTES SOMETHING SCRIPTURE DOES NOT CONTAIN. (1) VERSE 3, WHERE DID GOD SPEAK THIS? Moses says 'This is it that the LORD spake' and quotes a sentence that stands nowhere in the Pentateuch. Every voice in the entry notices, and they answer six ways: Ellicott calls it a divine communication not previously recorded; Henry says we do not find the very words though the substance was given at the warning to the priests who come near; De Lyra (as Calvin reports) assigns it to one Exodus passage and others to another; Willet (also via Calvin) answers with the consecration charge, keep ye the Lord's charge that ye die not; Wesley holds Scripture gives only the heads of discourses so it was probably spoken though unrecorded; and a sixth party says it was spoken but not written, 'as many things beside' — of whom Willet remarks tartly that 'they are of this mind, that they may have here some show for their unwritten traditions.' A textbook case of a doctrinal stake inside a source-critical question, and the corpus preserves both the answer and the motive imputed to it. (2) VERSE 9, WERE NADAB AND ABIHU DRUNK? Five positions, recorded in the entry's debate list: Gill thinks the placing of the law gives the suspicion real force and reconstructs the feast on the peace offerings; Baal Hatturim and the cabalists held it (via Clarke); Ellicott dates the opinion to at least the time of Christ and notes the Palestinian Chaldee inserts it as a gloss, 'as thy sons did who died by the burning fire'; Wesley calls it not improbable but rests nothing on it; Keil allows the occasion while refusing the inference. Against it stand two arguments carried in the Calvin column — that Scripture nowhere states it, and that the offenders had been ministering since early morning — which is the strongest counter in the corpus and, characteristically, is an editorial footnote rather than Calvin's own text. (3) VERSE 17, BEAR OR REMOVE THE INIQUITY. Ellicott lays out a genuine translation split with confessional consequences: the Septuagint, Chaldee and Syriac give 'remove', while the Vulgate gives 'bear' and the Reformers followed it, and on the latter reading 'the priest, by eating or incorporating the victim on which the offerer had laid his guilt, actually took away the sin, or neutralised it in a mysterious way, by virtue of the sanctifying power belonging to the sacerdotal office.' Ellicott prefers 'remove' and reports the other fairly. (4) VERSE 20, WHOSE MISTAKE WAS IT? Gill and Wesley excuse Aaron by grief and by the real difficulty of a first sin offering. Clarke calls it an irregularity justified in a measure by necessity, which God did not punish. ELLICOTT GOES FURTHER THAN EITHER: Moses 'acknowledged Aaron's plea to be just, and that he had himself spoken hastily ... a remarkable instance of Moses' humility, and of the human side of his nature as a lawgiver', adding that 'Jewish tradition from time immemorial ascribes the mistake to Moses, and not to Aaron', and quoting the Palestinian Chaldee in which Moses sends a herald through the whole camp saying 'It is I from whom the law had been hid, and my brother Aaron brought it to my remembrance.'

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, all 7 entries, all grade A. Source: 20 catena keys, 20,527 usable words as the sizer reported them, of which roughly 1,600 (7.8 percent) is not comment on these verses — about 1,238 words of StudyLight chrome inside Ellicott's key-20 block, Clarke's chapter argument at the head of his key-1 block, and 229 words of Jamieson residue at keys 2, 14 and 20. Word counts, all inside the 350-650 window: 1-2 = 650, 3 = 650, 4-7 = 648, 8-11 = 645, 12-15 = 648, 16-18 = 649, 19-20 = 648. Type-token ratios 0.598 to 0.673, zip ratios 0.421 to 0.465, so every entry clears the A threshold on both axes, though entries 12 and 16 sit closest to the type-token floor and would not have survived much more compression. TILING: seven entries over twenty verses, cut at the narrative's own joints — the sin and the fire (1-2), the saying and Aaron's silence given a whole entry to itself because the chapter turns on it (3), the carrying out and the ban on mourning (4-7), the wine law and its purposes (8-11), the resumed instructions about the priests' portions (12-15), the goat that was burnt and the rebuke (16-18), and Aaron's answer with the contentment of Moses (19-20). Coverage_problems returns empty. Expansion ratios run 0.15 to 0.39; entry 16 at 0.39 is the highest I have written and reflects a genuinely thin span, 1,675 source words across three keys. VOICE COVERAGE: Gill at all 20 keys; Ellicott at 20; Wesley 16; Clarke 13; Keil 7; Calvin 6; Henry 4 (keys 1, 3, 8, 12); Jamieson 3 (all residue, all declared excluded). HEAD PLACEMENT: Henry comments by section, so he is named only in entries 1, 3, 8 and 12 and kept out of 4, 16 and 19 where he has no head; Calvin likewise is absent from entry 19. KEIL DECLARED SILENT IN TWO ENTRIES: at keys 13 and 20 his blocks are pure lemma, the 200-word cap being consumed entirely by quoted verse text, so there is nothing of his to attribute; he is not listed among those entries' voices and is not declared excluded either, since the blocks are genuine rather than foreign. This is the first time in my series I have had to use that category. DELIBERATE OMISSIONS, none of which changes a reported position: Henry's key-1 and key-3 blocks (2,084 and 2,576 words) are used only for the material inside each entry's range and his long applications are dropped; Clarke's chapter argument is not used; Clarke's closing peroration at key 20 about human institutions in worship is compressed to one sentence; Gill's rehearsal of the rabbinic authorities is given once rather than enumerated. TRUNCATION CARRIED IN THE NOTES AND NOT ATTRIBUTED TO ANY COMMENTATOR IN THE PROSE: Keil's six capped blocks and Gill's two. Where the cap removed a conclusion I reported only what survives and attributed no absence to anyone.

Fidelity self-grade, all seven entries. 1-5 641w, 6-9 631w, 10-11 650w, 12-15 648w, 16-17 638w, 18-19 641w, 20-22 650w; all inside the 350-650 window, seven pericopes tiling the contiguous keys 1-22. Keys are contiguous here, so the pericopes are chosen rather than forced; the boundary between 10-11 and 12-15 was moved after a first draft so that the ladder and the oracle spoken from above it stand in the same entry rather than being split across two. Every named voice has a head inside its own range. Positions I could not check against a second witness are attributed to the voice that states them - Shuckford is absent here, but Skinner and Kennicott come by way of Clarke, Onkelos and the Chaldee by way of Clarke, Jarchi and the Targum of Jonathan by way of Gill, and Augustine is not in this chapter. Nothing is drawn from the Jamieson block at key 18, which is declared as excluded residue.

The Matthew Henry Concise/Exposition defect recorded at exodus 39 reproduces here, and this chapter shows a SECOND form of it. The reference-style signature holds exactly. Henry's k1 block (1250 words) carries five roman-numeral references and no arabic short-form ones; k6 (498w) three roman, none arabic; k16 (1733w) eleven roman, none arabic - all pure Exposition. Henry's k10 block (1960w) carries six roman references and then a single arabic one, 'Joh 1:5', at 88 percent of the way through the block: the Concise tail spliced onto the Exposition, exactly as at exodus 39 k1 and k32. But k20 is different and new: 211 words, ZERO roman references and one arabic, '1Co 16:2' - it is the Concise text alone, with no Exposition served at all. So the feed does not only append the Concise; at some keys it substitutes it. A corpus scan should therefore look for two signatures, not one: a Henry block mixing both reference styles (splice), and a short Henry block carrying only arabic short-form references (substitution).

NEW AND SPECIFIC: Keil's blocks LEAD their filing key throughout this chapter, and the offset is systematic rather than random. Each block quotes a run of verses starting at its own key and then comments on the verses at the END of that quotation, so the comment lands one pericope later than the key it is filed under. The k7 block quotes verses 7-10 and then comments on verses 10-11 (Jacob travelling from Beersheba, 'he hit upon the place' as an apparently accidental but really appointed choice, the definite article, the stone pillow). The k11 block quotes verses 11-15 and is cut by the 200-word cap before any comment begins. The k17 block quotes verse 17 and then comments on verses 18-19 (the pillar as monument, the oil as consecration, Bethel against Luz). The k19 block quotes 19-20 and then comments on 20-22 (the vow, and the Elohim/Jehovah alternation). The k21 block is 52 words of pure quotation. Consequence for the writer: naming Keil in the entry his block sits under would attribute to that pericope a comment on the next one. I have instead silenced his k7 and k17 blocks in the entries keyed on them and used their comment in the entry that actually covers the verses they treat, where he has a head of his own. This is a filing artefact of the importer, not a defect in Keil, and it is probably corpus-wide wherever his commentary is pericope-based - worth a scan.

Jamieson residue and the drift. One 32-word block, at key 18, and it is not on Genesis 28: it is on Genesis 24:65-67, Rebekah's veil and 'when Isaac saw his wife, he loved her'. Source lags target by four chapters. That is the SHORTEST lag measured in this run, at the earliest position in the corpus measured so far - four chapters at genesis 28, about thirteen at exodus 39, about seventeen at numbers 1 - which is exactly what a displacement monotone in corpus position predicts, and is further evidence that the tree needs re-indexing rather than re-fetching. With a single member there is no residue class and no stride determinable, so this chapter neither confirms nor threatens the mod-6 finding. Jamieson's genuine commentary on Genesis 28 is not in this file.

The 200-word cap: Keil 6 of 7 blocks at exactly 200 (k1, k2, k7, k11, k17, k19); the seventh, k21, runs 52 and stops of its own accord. Running OT total is now 67 of 74 measured Keil blocks capped, across nine chapters. Two things worth recording about this chapter's instances. First, the k11 block is 200 words of pure biblical text - the cap was spent on the quotation before any comment began, the same wholly-empty-block shape seen at exodus 39 k2. Second, and unlike exodus 39 k38/k41, the surviving comment here is NOT recovered by an overlapping restart: each block quotes forward from its own key, so where the cap falls inside the quotation the comment for those verses is simply lost. Gill runs entirely free here - 22 blocks, maximum 188 words, not one at 200 - which is the settled OT pattern for him and the reverse of his NT behaviour.

Three separate factual disagreements in one chapter, all of them checkable and none of them acknowledged by any party. (1) THE JOURNEY. Henry has Jacob covering above forty miles from Beersheba to Bethel in a single day. Clarke gives the distance as about forty-eight miles and says plainly that this is too great a journey for one day over what we may conceive very unready roads. Ellicott, placing the site twelve miles north of Jerusalem, has him at least four days on the route, and builds on it - the four days of meditation and prayer are what prepared him to be accepted. (2) THE COMPANY. Clarke argues from the stone pillow and from Jacob's own later words about his staff that he travelled alone and destitute: 'He had God alone with him.' Gill has him alone but provisioned, with letters of recommendation from his parents and money enough for the road, and uses the oil as evidence of baggage - the very argument Clarke had dismissed as 'no rational argument'. Ellicott answers the argument directly, saying we are not to suppose the heir of the blessing was sent away without a few trusty servants and that the expression about the staff does not require it. This is the rare case of an explicit reply: Ellicott is rebutting the position Clarke states. (3) BETHEL AND LUZ. Keil argues from the antithesis in verse 19 that the name was given to the town. Ellicott holds that Luz and Bethel were distinct places, that Jacob slept a mile or two from the town, and that the name passed to it only when Ephraim took Luz. Calvin cuts under both by denying there was a town there yet at all.

Calvin rejects the allegorical reading twice in this chapter, in the same form both times, and each time against the reading the others adopt. At verse 12: 'The interpretation of some of the Hebrews, that the ladder is a figure of the Divine Providence, cannot be admitted: for the Lord has given another sign more suitable' - where Clarke makes providence the ladder's PRIMARY design and Wesley elaborates it at length as his first head. At verse 18: other commentators argue with more subtlety that the stone was a symbol of Christ on whom all the graces of the Spirit were poured out, but Calvin says he does not know that any such thing was intended. In both places the refusal is grounded the same way, that the text supplies its own sign and the interpreter must not supply a better one. Ellicott performs the same move once, on the rabbinic identification of the place with Moriah and the stone with the altar-stone of the binding of Isaac, which he calls allegorical rather than expository. Worth recording because the three-way split on the ladder - Clarke's three simultaneous designs, Wesley's two, Calvin's flat refusal of the first - is the sharpest exegetical disagreement in the chapter and is invisible unless all three are read together.

Wesley abridges Henry SIX times in this chapter, the highest count in any single chapter so far, and the running total across this run is now seventeen instances. At k1 he takes Henry's 'Those that have the blessing must keep the charge annexed to it, and not think to separate what God has joined' word for word. At k6 he takes the opening of Henry's Esau paragraph verbatim. At k11 he takes 'his comfort in the divine blessing, and his confidence in the divine protection, made him easy, even when he lay thus exposed; being sure that his God made him to dwell in safety, he could lie down and sleep upon a stone'. At k16 he takes Henry's whole first head, 'God's manifestations of himself to his people carry their own evidence along with them', to the end of the paragraph. At k17 he takes Henry's second head on the fear, including the Hosea reference. At k20 he takes 'We need desire no more to make us easy and happy' and 'The tenth is a fit proportion to be devoted to God, and employed for him; though it may be more or less, as God prospers us'. Two of these are cross-key, k11 and k20 drawing on Henry blocks filed at k10, so a per-key comparison would miss them. The k6 case is the most interesting: Henry offers the Esau passage as a disjunction, 'either to show the influence of a good example ... or to show the folly of an after-wit', and Wesley keeps only the first limb and drops the second, so what stands in the source as an open question becomes a settled account in the abridgement. That is a change of meaning, not merely of length, and it bears on the open question of whether the prevalence field should down-weight agreement traceable to a common source: here the two voices do not even agree.

One voice in the catena quotes another by name. Keil's comment on the anointing of the pillar reads that the oil consecrated it as a memorial of the mercy shown there, 'visionis insigne mnemosynon, Calvin', and expressly not as an idol or an object of divine worship - and Calvin's own block at the same verse is present in this chapter, arguing precisely that, that Moses does not mean the stone was made an idol but a special memorial. So the catena contains both the citation and its source, sitting under the same key. Recorded because it is the first instance I have seen where agreement between two voices in a merged catena is demonstrably citation rather than convergence AND both ends are visible in the same file - the Wesley/Henry cases are inference from wording, this one is explicit. It is a second reason, independent of the Wesley/Henry overlaps, why the tags' prevalence field over-reports agreement.

Editor's apparatus inside Calvin blocks, fourth chapter running, and here it is not merely intrusive but argumentative. The k3 block carries a bracketed note in the third person about editions - 'In the editions of Amsterdam and Berlin, the name Jacob is here inserted; and the old English version has it too. The mistake is obvious, and stands corrected in the French translation' - dropped inside a sentence of Calvin's. The k12 block goes further: after Calvin rejects the providential reading of the ladder, the editor's paragraph DISAGREES WITH HIM in the third person, saying 'Whatever force and truth, as well as beauty, there may be in the exposition of Calvin which follows, he appears to have dismissed too hastily the opinion of the Jews' and defending the very reading Calvin refuses. The k14 block carries a Latin lemma and an editorial remark that 'the reader will perceive that Calvin's remarks turn chiefly on the expression bless themselves, which does not appear in our version'. A synthesis that attributed any of this to Calvin would have him arguing against himself. Same family as exodus 1 k18/k21, exodus 39 k32, 2peter 1 k3, hebrews 13 k24. On four chapters running this is a standing property of the Calvin feed, and stripping apparatus - not raising a cap - is what a Calvin re-fetch has to do.

JFB residue, 28th chapter confirming and the second sparse case. Jamieson appears at only two keys, 3 and 9 (35 and 74 words), and the donor is Genesis 19 -- Lot's request that Zoar be spared and granted, and Lot's wife looking back. Nothing in either block touches Sarah's death or the purchase of Machpelah. The key-9 block self-identifies: it opens with its own verse number, '26.', the verse number of Lot's wife in the donor chapter, so the pointer carries the donor's numbering with it. Both excluded.

Keil and Delitzsch lemma-only blocks, second chapter confirming (after leviticus 10). K&D has three blocks here, all at exactly 201 words: key 2, key 4, key 18. At key 4 the entire allowance is consumed by the quoted text of verses 4-10 and the block breaks off mid-lemma, so no exposition survives to attribute; he is silent by entry in entry 3, removed from voices but not declared excluded, the block being genuine rather than foreign. Keys 2 and 18 do carry exposition after the lemma. The pattern is systematic rather than random: K&D prefixes the full verse text to each block, so any block whose lemma runs long is guaranteed empty, and he is the OT tree's principal critical voice.

Terminal-key chrome, sighting 10, and the first with TWO voices carrying it at once. Key 20 is 2189 words. Of Ellicott's 1139 words all but about 40 are the StudyLight footer, copyright statement, terms-of-use links and raw CSS for the site's sub-menu. Gill's 175-word block also ends in site navigation ('Next: Genesis Chapter 24 Sacred Texts | Bible << Previous: ...'). So the terminal-key sweep is not confined to one voice's scrape; whichever blocks sit last in the file pick up whatever furniture followed them. Clarke's key-20 block (816 words) is truncated mid-sentence instead, ending 'There is neither a'.

Chapter-initial front matter, fifth chapter confirming. Clarke's key-1 block opens with the chapter argument before reaching verse 1. The rule holds across both testaments now (2corinthians 1, 1corinthians 4, leviticus 10, genesis 23): whatever front matter a printed commentary places before a unit is swept into the chapter-initial key, exactly as scrape navigation furniture is swept into the terminal one. A chapter has both boundary failures, at opposite ends, and neither is detectable by block size.

Calvin's shekel computation sits at key 11, not at the price verses. His arithmetic -- Josephus valuing the shekel of the sanctuary at four Attic drachms, and Budaeus's computation giving about 250 pounds French money for the sanctuary shekel or half that for the common -- is attached to Ephron's offer at verse 11, two keys before Ephron actually names four hundred shekels at verse 15. Meanwhile Clarke at key 15 gives sixty pounds sterling (Prideaux) and Ellicott about fifty. So the corpus holds three incompatible valuations of the same sum, and the tiling separates one of them from the other two. Recorded because a reader comparing entry 7 with entry 12 will meet the discrepancy without the two ever being set side by side.

Fidelity self-grade A for all five entries (1-2, 3-6, 7-11, 12-16, 17-20). Every claim traced to a named block in the span; no cross-span borrowing. Two judgement calls recorded: (a) Keil and Delitzsch is declared at entry 1 on the strength of his key-2 exposition about approaching the Hittites, which required grafting a closing sentence onto the entry after the prose was already at length -- the graft is his, not paraphrase of a neighbour; (b) Wesley's 'those that have least of this earth find a grave in it' at entry 17 is credited to Wesley although Henry says the same words at key 16, because Henry is outside that span. Expansion ratios 0.19 / 0.18 / 0.38 / 0.32 / 0.23.

JFB residue, 29th chapter confirming and the definitive specimen: a perfect mod-6 class with every member present. Jamieson appears at keys 5, 11, 17, 23 and 29 -- five members, gap exactly 6 throughout, no missing member. The donor is Romans 8 read STRICTLY FORWARD as the target key advances: key 5 gives Romans 8:10-11 (the body is dead because of sin), key 11 gives 8:16 (the Spirit beareth witness, Abba Father), key 17 gives 8:19 (the creation groaning for the revelation), key 23 gives 8:26 (the Spirit helpeth our infirmity), key 29 gives 8:31-34 (if God be for us). This is the mechanism laid bare: one donor chapter consumed sequentially, one block emitted per six target keys. Every previous sighting is consistent with it; this is the first where all five members survive to show the walk. All five excluded. Practical rule confirmed: test residue as a class mod 6, never as gaps between consecutive members.

Martin Luther enters the corpus here, and he dominates it: 42,509 of this chapter's 108,108 visible source words, 39 percent, against Barnes 20,491 and Calvin 12,710. His Commentary on Galatians is the single largest voice at 20 of the 29 keys. The lutheran school slug in VALID_SCHOOLS has had almost nothing to attach to until now. TOOLING WARNING: my scratchpad per-voice mapper carried an incomplete label roster and silently folded Luther, Tertullian and Cyril into whichever voice preceded them, producing impossible figures such as 'John Wesley (6,662 words)' at key 2 and 'John Wesley (7,808)' at key 13 -- Wesley's real contribution there is 41 and 86 words. synthesis_qa.VOICE_LABELS does know Martin Luther and Tertullian, so the validator side was never wrong; only the scratchpad map was. Any future worker should derive per-voice counts from QA.split_voices, never from a hand-maintained label list.

The Luther text is an OCR'd scan and carries its page furniture inline.
