Running heads appear in the middle of sentences -- 'COMMENTARY ON GALATIANS. 201' at key 2, '235' at key 7, '291' at key 16, '292 COMMENTARY ON GALATIANS.' at key 17, '340 COMMENTARY ON GALATIANS.' at key 24, '44 346 COMMENTARY ON GALATIANS.' at key 26 -- so a page number and title can land between a subject and its verb. End-of-line hyphenation survives as a space: 'inter- mingleth', 're- proveth', 'argu- ment', 'Abra- ham', 'There- fore', 'dis- putation', 'righ- teousness'. And there are ordinary OCR substitutions: 'tliis', 'liis', 'hfe' for life, 'vith', 'afifections', 'exxellently', 'schoohnaster', 'corapted', 'mvist'. Consequence for writers: a Luther block cannot be quoted verbatim without cleaning, and any automatic sentence-splitting over his text will break at the running heads. This is a different defect class from truncation or residue -- the text is genuine and complete, but mechanically dirty.

Cyril of Jerusalem: the known validator gap, now with a measured cost. synthesis_qa.VOICE_LABELS carries the short form 'Cyril' and _LABEL_RE requires a colon straight after, but the catena writes 'Cyril of Jerusalem:', so split_voices never sees the label and folds Cyril's text into the PRECEDING voice's segment. Here that voice is John Wesley at all three keys, inflating his measured contribution at key 10 from about 80 words to 282. Three further findings. (1) The blocks are capped at about 200 words, like Gill's. (2) The key-23 and key-24 blocks are the SAME block emitted twice, word for word, ending both times at 'translated by the Seventy-two Interpreters'. (3) They are of mixed value: the key-10 block is foreign, a catechetical passage on the titles of the Holy Spirit with nothing to do with the curse of the law, while the key-23/24 block genuinely quotes Galatians 3:23-24 and argues from them that the God of the two Testaments is one. So Cyril here is one residue block plus one genuine block duplicated. The asymmetry still binds: 'voices' is grounded by a name search against raw text and accepts him, 'excluded_voices' is checked against split_voices and would reject him, so the key-10 residue CANNOT be declared. It is simply omitted.

Both boundary defects present again, sixth chapter confirming. Chapter-initial: Barnes opens key 1 with 'GALATIANS CHAPTER III' and a full introduction to the argument before reaching verse 1, and Clarke opens key 1 with the chapter argument, a verse-by-verse table of contents running 'Gal 3:1-5 ... Gal 3:6-9 ... Gal 3:10-14'. That is the same pair, Barnes and Clarke together, as at 1corinthians 4. Terminal: key 29 is Ellicott 1,020 words of which roughly 980 is the StudyLight footer, copyright statement, terms-of-use links and raw sub-menu CSS -- sighting 11. Also at key 20 Clarke's block breaks off mid-sentence at 'There is neither a', and at key 13 the Keil-style lemma problem does not arise but Luther's 7,013-word block is the largest single block seen in this run.

Fidelity self-grade A for all seven entries (1-5, 6-9, 10-14, 15-18, 19-22, 23-25, 26-29). Expansion ratios are 0.02 to 0.06, an order of magnitude under the corpus median of 0.84, because the span sources run 8,400 to 23,600 words each against 650 words of prose; the signal the doc warns about is expansion ABOVE about 6x, so these are heavy distillation rather than invention. Selection, not compression, is the risk at this ratio, and the selection rule used was: attribute every voice whose block adds a distinct reading, omit a voice whose block only repeats a neighbour. Wesley is therefore undeclared at entries 23 and 26, where his notes are one-line glosses on the dispensations, and Cyril's key-10 block is omitted as foreign. Two attributions worth flagging: Cyril of Jerusalem is declared at entry 23 on the strength of the genuine key-23/24 block, though split_voices cannot see him; and Luther's criticism of Paul's own argument at entry 15 is his, recorded as an outlier rather than softened.

Fidelity self-grade, all nine entries. 1 647w, 2-5 650w, 6-7 650w, 8-10 646w, 11-12 646w, 13-14 650w, 15-17 647w, 18-20 650w, 21-24 648w; all inside the 350-650 window, nine pericopes tiling the contiguous keys 1-24. This is the largest chapter attempted in this run at 75,795 usable source words across thirteen voices, so every entry runs at the top of the window and still leaves a great deal unused; verse 1 is given an entry of its own because the chapter's whole argument is contained in it. Every named voice has a head inside its own range. Positions I could not check against a second witness are attributed to the voice that reports them - Theodoret via Clarke, Doddridge via Barnes, Paley via Clarke, Bloomfield and Lightfoot and Burton via Robertson, Schoettgen and Fabricius via Clarke, Erasmus and Jerome and OEcumenius via Calvin. Nothing is drawn from the four Jamieson blocks, which are declared as excluded residue.

THE 200-WORD CAP IS NOT ONE CAP. This chapter shows three different values operating simultaneously on four different feeds, which refines the standing finding substantially. Tertullian: 2 of 2 blocks at EXACTLY 350 words, maximum 350, both breaking off mid-sentence (k1 at 'under what bill of lading you admitted', k6 at 'so well known in the law, the only'). John Chrysostom: his single block is EXACTLY 300 words and ends with an explicit ellipsis character. Cyril of Jerusalem: 4 of 4 at EXACTLY 200, maximum 200, all four ending in an ellipsis - 100 percent, matching the acts 7 measurement. John Gill: 7 of 24 at exactly 200, maximum 200, the settled NT pattern. So the cap is a per-feed parameter, not a corpus constant, and the three values seen so far are 200, 300 and 350. Any re-fetch scoping has to be per feed, and the corpus scan for capped feeds must look for a per-voice modal maximum rather than for the number 200.

Jamieson: the stride holds and the drift is confirmed at the far end of the corpus. Four blocks, at keys 4, 10, 16 and 22 - ALL congruent to 4 mod 6, so the corpus finding stands at 750 chapters with no exception. None of the four is on Galatians: k4 is on Romans 6:21, k10 on Romans 7:3, k16 on Romans 7:7, k22 on Romans 7:12. Two things follow. First, the lag here is the largest yet measured - roughly thirty-nine chapters back through 2 Corinthians and 1 Corinthians into Romans - at the deepest corpus position yet measured, which is what a displacement monotone in position predicts and which extends the series four (genesis 28), thirteen (exodus 39), about seventeen (numbers 1), about thirty-nine (galatians 1). Second, this chapter gives the cleanest quantise-up measurement so far: as the target advances 4 to 10 to 16 to 22, a stride of exactly 6 every time, the source advances 6:21 to 7:3 to 7:7 to 7:12, gaps of about 5, 4 and 5 verses. Not one source gap is 6; every one quantises up. Jamieson's genuine commentary on Galatians 1 is not in this file.

A SECOND BORROWING PAIR, INDEPENDENT OF WESLEY AND HENRY: Barnes copies Clarke. Both open the chapter with a history of the province, and the two accounts share a clause word for word. Clarke: 'As these were mixed with various Grecian families, the country was also called Gallograecia, see Justin, lib. xxiv. 4; xxv. 2; xxvii. 3'. Barnes: 'These were mixed with various Grecian families, and the country was also called Gallograecia.-- Justin, lib. xxiv. 4; xxv. 2; xxvii. 3'. The citation string is identical down to the section numbers and their punctuation, and both cite Pausanias, Attic. cap. iv for the conquest in the sentence immediately before. Clarke's commentary precedes Barnes's Notes by roughly two decades, so Barnes is the borrower. This matters beyond the instance: it means the tags' prevalence field over-reports agreement in the modern voices as well as in the Wesley/Henry pair, and the identical-citation-string signature gives a cheap corpus-wide detector - two voices citing the same authority with the same volume-and-section punctuation are far more likely to be copying than converging.

Two more cases of a voice in this catena quoting another voice in the same catena, with both ends visible in the file. First, Barnes at k6: 'It is remarked by Luther, (Com. in loco,) that Paul here uses as mild a word as possible' - and Luther's own block at that very key says exactly that, that Paul does not set upon them with vehement words but after a fatherly sort. Second, Calvin's k18 block carries a note quoting Bloomfield on the verb historesai, and Barnes's block at the same key attributes the same fifteen-days observation to Bloomfield by name. Together with the Keil-quoting-Calvin case at genesis 28 and the Barnes/Clarke borrowing above, that is four instances in three chapters where apparent agreement in the catena is demonstrably transmission. The prevalence field, which currently counts heads, is measuring something other than independent testimony.

A displacement that documents itself. Barnes's block at k1 is 4,574 words and is almost entirely the introduction to the epistle - the geography of Galatia, the character of the people, and an analysis of the chapter's argument - with no comment on verse 1 at all. It ends with an editorial notice in the text: '**** Due to space limitations, See Notes on Verses 1 and 2 combined in Notes for Galatians Chapter 1, verse 2.********'. And the k2 block opens with the matching notice: '**Due to the length of Introductory Material to Chapter, Notes for Verses 1 and 2 have been combined in notes for Verse 2.**' followed by 'Verse 1. Paul, an apostle.' So Barnes's comment on verse 1 is filed under key 2, and the feed says so in both places. This is the first displacement encountered that announces itself rather than having to be inferred, and the marker string ('Due to space limitations' / 'have been combined in notes for') is an exact search key for finding every other instance in the Barnes tree.

The Luther feed is a scan OCR and the damage is systematic, confirming the galatians 5 finding with precise instances. Printed running heads are absorbed mid-sentence throughout: '30 COMMENTARY ON GALATIANS.' inside a clause at k1, 'COMMENTARY ON GALATIANS. 31' a paragraph later, and the same at k3, k6, k7, k13, k15, k17, k18, k20 - the page number attaching to whichever side of the head the line break fell. End-of-line hyphenation is preserved as a real hyphen plus space ('over-thrown', 'per-secuteth', 'con-demning', 'know-ledge'), so those words will not match a search. And letter-level OCR errors are frequent: 'sufler' for suffer, 'Avho' for who, 'alsQ' for also, 'fach' for teach, 'beUeve' for believe, 'hst' for list, 'gr\-efi' for given, 'Weis' for was, 'inestunable' for inestimable, 'cathoUc' for catholic. Any Luther re-fetch must strip running heads and rejoin hyphenation, not merely raise a cap; and until then a text search of this feed will silently miss whatever fell across a line break.

Editor's apparatus inside Calvin blocks, fifth chapter running, and in this one it appears at six separate keys. k3 and k11 carry French renderings of Calvin's clauses with a dangling attribution mark. k7 opens with a Greek textual note in the third person that ends 'This is ingenious, but, like all conjectural criticism on the New Testament, is of no value' - a verdict of the editor's, not Calvin's, standing before Calvin's own text begins at 'Some explain it thus'. k10 carries a long lexical note on peitho citing Matthew 28:14, Acts 12:20, Pindar and 2 Maccabees. k16 carries quotations attributed by name to Beza and to Bloomfield. k18 quotes Bloomfield and Grotius. k23 quotes Beza and k24 quotes OEcumenius. In every case the apparatus sits inside the block under Calvin's head, and at k7 and k16 it takes a position of its own on the question Calvin is discussing. Nothing from any of it is attributed to Calvin in the synthesis. Across exodus 1, exodus 39, genesis 28 and now galatians 1 this is a standing property of the feed; a Calvin re-fetch has to strip apparatus, and the third-person mention of Calvin's own name is the detector.

Cyril of Jerusalem: the blocks at k8 and k9 are byte-identical, the same 200 words of Catechetical Lecture 5 on keeping the delivered creed, both ending mid-phrase at 'For though we or an'. The spacing is ONE key, not six, which adds a third data point to the correction filed at 2peter 1: cross-key duplication in this corpus is not tied to the mod-6 stride. Running list of duplicate spacings measured: 6 keys (acts 7 Jamieson), 36 keys (acts 7 Cyril), 8 keys (2peter 1 Cyril), 1 key (galatians 1 Cyril). The one regularity is the truncation point - both copies stop exactly where the lemma of Galatians 1:8 begins, which suggests the emitter cuts at the quotation boundary rather than at a word count in these cases, even though the count also happens to be 200.

Ellicott twice states the confessional stake in a reading and then decides against his own side, which is worth recording because it is rare and because both decisions matter. At k8, on the preposition in 'other than that which we preached': the word may mean 'besides' or 'contrary to'; he notes that the first sense has been favoured by Protestant and the second by Roman Catholic commentators, since one seems to exclude and the other to admit an appeal to tradition - and he then decides for 'contrary', on the exegetical ground that the Judaizers offered an opposition of principles rather than an addition. Calvin, on the same clause, decides the other way, holding that their doctrine was not contrary to Paul's nor even different but corrupted by false additions. At k18, on 'to see Cephas': Ellicott writes that 'Roman Catholic commentators argue from this passage, not without reason, that St Peter must at this time have taken the lead in the Church.' Two clean instances of a commentator naming the interest that would bias him and then ruling against it.

Three substantive disagreements worth flagging beyond the confessional ones. (1) THE TRADITIONS OF MY FATHERS at k14: Ellicott, Robertson, Wesley and Barnes all take these for the pharisaic oral law - Ellicott naming the Mishnah - while Calvin denies it flatly, holding that Paul means the law of God itself received through his parents, and Luther says the same in terms, that these are not pharisaical or human traditions but the holy law of Moses received as an inheritance. Four against two, and the two are the Reformers. (2) ANOTHER GOSPEL at k6: Clarke alone takes it for an actual apocryphal document, noting that more than seventy such gospels are named in Fabricius and that some urged circumcision, so that Paul refers to one of them; everyone else takes it for the Judaizing message. (3) REVEALED IN ME at k16: Gill and Ellicott take 'in me' inwardly, of the mind and consciousness, while Calvin calls the construction a Hebrew idiom meaning simply 'to me' and Robertson prefers 'in my case' after Lightfoot; Wesley refuses to choose and takes both. The last is the only one where the split does not follow the schools at all.

JFB residue, 30th chapter confirming, and the second consecutive chapter to reproduce the galatians 3 mechanism exactly. Jamieson appears at keys 10, 16 and 22 -- gap 6 throughout, a clean mod-6 class -- and the donor is 1 Corinthians 3 read strictly forward as the target key advances: key 10 gives 3:5 (Who is Paul? who is Apollos? ministers by whom ye believed), key 16 gives 3:10 (a wise masterbuilder laying a foundation), key 22 gives 3:14-15 (the work burned, saved yet so as by fire). Coming immediately after galatians 3, where the same shape held with five members and Romans 8 as donor, this settles the mechanism: one donor chapter is consumed sequentially and one block emitted per six target keys. The donor differs per target chapter and carries no relation to it. All three excluded.

Cyril of Jerusalem, second chapter running, and now the block cap is pinned. His blocks here sit at keys 4, 9, 13, 15 and 23 and are 203 words each except one truncated to 87 by the end of the key -- and in galatians 3 they were 203 and 189 (the 189 being one block emitted twice). So Cyril's cap is 203, a distinct value from Gill's 200/201 and Keil's 201; the cap is per-source, not global. Value is mixed exactly as before: the key-4 block genuinely quotes Philippians 4:4 and is on point, the key-9 block quotes 1 Thessalonians 5:23 and touches this verse only through the phrase God of peace, and keys 13, 15 and 23 are foreign (chrismation, baptism, an exegetical dispute over 2 Corinthians 4:4). None of them can be declared in excluded_voices, because split_voices cannot see the label 'Cyril of Jerusalem:' and folds each block into the preceding voice -- here Wesley at keys 9 and 15, Calvin at key 13, Ellicott at key 23. The measured consequence is that those voices' word counts are inflated by about 200 each wherever Cyril follows them.

Terminal-key overflow, sighting 12, and the richest specimen so far: key 23 carries FOUR distinct kinds of matter at once. Barnes is 3,397 words of which perhaps 150 comment on the benediction; the rest is a discussion of the subscription, then a long editorial excursus on Greek athletics sourced to Potter's Archaeologia Graeca and Kitto's Cyclopaedia, ending 'End of Barnes Notes on Philippians.' Clarke is 779 words ending in the printer's colophon, 'Finished correction for the press, Dec. 16th, 1831. - A. C.' Ellicott is 1,289 words ending in the StudyLight footer and CSS, with a Cyril block appended after it. So the terminal key sweeps up the author's own end-of-book matter, the printer's colophon, the site chrome, and a residue block -- four layers, only the first of which is even nineteenth-century editorial rather than modern scrape. The chapter-initial defect is present too, seventh chapter confirming: Barnes opens key 1 with 'Philippians CHAPTER 4 ANALYSIS OF THE CHAPTER' and Clarke with the verse-by-verse chapter argument, the same pair as at 1corinthians 4 and galatians 3.

Calvin footnote defect, seventh book confirming. His key-22 block runs 1,811 words and contains, verbatim inside it, a passage of Adam Clarke introduced as 'Some imagine,' says Dr. A. Clarke -- a nineteenth-century editor's note absorbed into the reformer's text with no boundary marker the splitter can see. The practical rule stands and is worth restating: never credit Calvin with a sentence that names a modern authority, cites page numbers, or reads in nineteenth-century English. Here the tell is the honorific Dr. before a name Calvin could not have known.

Fidelity self-grade A for all six entries (1-3, 4-7, 8-9, 10-14, 15-20, 21-23). Expansion ratios 0.06 to 0.17 against a corpus median of 0.84; the documented invention signal is expansion above about 6x, so these are distillation. Chrysostom is declared at entries 4 and 10 on genuine on-verse blocks that split_voices does see, since his label is the bare surname. Wesley is undeclared at entries 15 and 21, where what the splitter attributes to him is substantially Cyril residue folded in after a one-line gloss -- attributing it would have credited him with another writer's words. One selection worth recording: at entry 4 the genuine Cyril block on Philippians 4:4 was available and not used, the paragraph going to Chrysostom's treatment of the same verse instead, because Chrysostom's block is separately labelled and therefore verifiable.

Fidelity self-grade, all seven entries. 1-4 555w, 5-8 650w, 9-10 645w, 11-13 648w, 14-16 649w, 17-18 637w, 19-21 638w; all inside the window, seven pericopes tiling the contiguous keys 1-21. The boundary between the first two entries was moved from 1-5/6-8 to 1-4/5-8 after drafting, because the Matthew Henry block filed at key 5 comments on verses 6 to 8 and Henry has no head anywhere in 6-8; putting key 5 into the second entry brings his head into the span that his comment actually treats and recovers about 670 words of material that would otherwise have been unusable. Every named voice has a head inside its own range. Positions I could not check against a second witness are attributed to the voice that reports them - Grotius via Barnes and via Clarke, Dodd via Clarke, Daubuz and Victor Vitensis via Gill, Swete and Beckwith and Charles via Robertson, the Sohar via Clarke. Nothing is drawn from the four Jamieson blocks, which are declared as excluded residue.

Jamieson: the stride holds at 751 chapters and the drift series gains its largest point. Four blocks, at keys 2, 8, 14 and 20 - ALL congruent to 2 mod 6. None is on Revelation: k2 is on 1 Timothy 3:4-5 (ruling his own house, children in subjection), k8 on 1 Timothy 3:9 (the mystery of the faith in a pure conscience), k14 on 1 Timothy 3:14 ('though I hope to come unto thee shortly'), k20 on 1 Timothy 4:1-2 (the hypocrisy of lying speakers). Counting NT chapters, 1 Timothy 3 sits about sixty-four chapters before Revelation 19, which is by a wide margin the largest lag yet measured and occurs at the deepest corpus position yet measured. The series now reads: 4 chapters at genesis 28, 13 at exodus 39, about 17 at numbers 1, about 39 at galatians 1, about 64 here - monotone in position across five independent measurements, which is strong evidence that the displacement is an invertible function of position and that the tree needs RE-INDEXING rather than re-fetching. QUANTISE-UP holds too: as the target advances 2, 8, 14, 20 with a stride of exactly 6 each time, the source advances 3:4, 3:9, 3:14, 4:1 - gaps of 5, 5 and 3. Not one source gap is 6.

SECOND FEED AT THE 300-WORD CAP. Bede's single block in this chapter is EXACTLY 300 words and breaks off mid-WORD - the text ends 'For the Church also continually sings Al', cut inside 'Alleluia'. That is the second feed measured at 300 after John Chrysostom at galatians 1, so 300 is a real per-feed cap value and not a coincidence of one block. It also settles a question the earlier instances left open: the cap is applied by word count and cuts wherever the count runs out, including inside a word, rather than at any sentence or clause boundary. Cap values now measured: 200 (Gill in NT books, Keil in OT books, Cyril, Lightfoot), 300 (Chrysostom, Bede), 350 (Tertullian). Cyril's k19 block here is at exactly 200 with the usual trailing ellipsis, consistent with the acts 7 and galatians 1 measurements.

The Bede feed carries unconverted HTML entities and scan-OCR damage, a defect family previously recorded for Luther and Lightfoot. Its single block prints ''' where an apostrophe belongs and '"' where quotation marks belong, in every instance, so the text reads 'begin in the Hebrew with "Praise ye the Lord,"' rather than with real punctuation - which means a search of this feed for any quoted phrase will fail. Alongside that: 'St Luke xvL 25' for xvi, a stray '**' standing in for an opening quotation mark, and marginal reference marks ('trumpets, (multitudes)*') absorbed into the running text. Since this is the only Bede block in the chapter I cannot say whether the entity corruption is feed-wide, but a corpus scan for the literal strings ''' and '"' inside commentary bodies would settle it cheaply and would also catch any other feed with the same problem.

An intra-chapter misfiling, and a second one that cost material. (1) The Victorinus of Pettau block is filed at key 1 but is not on verse 1: it opens by quoting Revelation 19:11 ('And I saw heaven opened, and behold a white horse'), numbers itself '11.', and comments on the rider and the heavenly army. Victorinus has no head anywhere else in the chapter, so his comment cannot be moved to the entry that covers the verses it treats; the block is silenced at the 1-4 entry and his 93 words are lost to the synthesis. (2) The Matthew Henry block filed at key 5 comments on verses 6 to 8 - the marriage-song, the bride's dress, the stola. That one WAS recoverable, by moving the pericope boundary so that key 5 falls in the 5-8 entry, and the note on that entry records it. Both are the same shape as the Keil lead-displacement recorded at genesis 28: the block is filed one pericope before the verses it discusses. The difference is only whether the voice happens to have another head in the right span. Worth a corpus scan: a block whose first sentence quotes a verse number higher than its own key is mechanically detectable.

Cyril of Jerusalem twice reads a phrase of this chapter against every other voice, and in the same direction both times - away from the eschatological referent and towards a present or historical one. At verse 15 the others take the rod of iron for Christ's own rule, Ellicott and Robertson noting that the verb is to shepherd; Cyril says flatly that the kingdom of the Romans is clearly called a rod of iron, referring to an argument he has made earlier, and brings in Daniel's stone cut without hands to say what overthrows it. At verse 19 the others take the gathering of the kings for the last battle; Cyril applies 'they gather themselves together against the Lord and against His Anointed' to the Jews of his own day who confess one God and deny that he is the Father of Christ, saying that they rage and gather still. Recorded because it is the clearest case in this run of a patristic voice and a modern commentary using the same words with entirely different referents, and because a reader consulting both would have no way to see that the disagreement is about what the text is talking about rather than about what it means.

The fine linen at verse 8 divides the commentators along a line that cuts across the schools. Barnes insists it is given and therefore not the wearer's own: the righteousness obtained by faith through the merits of the Redeemer, and he quotes Philippians 3:9 for it. Clarke denies exactly that in terms - 'The fine linen here spoken of is not the righteousness of Christ imputed to believers, for it is here called the righteousness of the saints - that which the grace and Spirit of Christ has wrought in them.' Henry and Wesley take both at once, imputed for justification and imparted for sanctification. Ellicott holds the two halves together by another route, noting that the Greek noun is plural, righteousnesses, and that the robe is divine in source yet really the wearer's; Robertson renders it the righteous acts of the saints and draws out that there is work for the Bride as well as for Christ. So the Arminian Clarke rules out imputation while the Arminian Wesley keeps it, and the two grammatical-historical voices land on opposite sides of Barnes. The tags' school summaries cannot represent this without saying that a school is divided against itself, which is what I have done.

Two voices break off from exposition to praise the writing, at different places and for opposite qualities, and both passages are worth keeping. Barnes at verse 17, on the angel standing in the sun: 'The description is as simple as it can be; and yet as sublime. The fewest words possible are used; and yet the image is distinct and clear... It is difficult to conceive of an image more sublime than this.' Wesley at verse 20, on the absence of the battle: the chapter exhibits the two opposing armies and all the apparatus for a battle and then gives the victory immediately, 'without one word of an engagement or fighting', which he calls the most exact propriety, since what struggle can there be between omnipotence and all creation united against it - 'Every description must have fallen short of this admirable silence.' Barnes admires what is said, Wesley what is not. Recorded as an instance of a kind of comment the synthesis rules have no category for and which is easy to lose in summarising: it is neither exegesis nor application, and it is the only place in the chapter where either man steps back from the text to look at it.

JFB residue, 31st chapter confirming, and the THIRD consecutive chapter to reproduce the mod-6 walk. Jamieson appears at keys 8, 14 and 20 -- gap 6 throughout -- and the donor is 1 Timothy 6 read strictly forward: key 8 gives 6:4 (proud, knowing nothing, doting about questions and strifes of words), key 14 gives 6:9 (they that will be rich fall into temptation), key 20 gives 6:14 (keep the commandment without spot until the appearing). Three chapters in a row now, with three different donors -- Romans 8 at galatians 3, 1 Corinthians 3 at philippians 4, 1 Timothy 6 here -- and the identical emission rule each time. The mechanism can be treated as established: one donor chapter consumed sequentially, one block per six target keys, donor bearing no relation to target. All three excluded.

NEW DEFECT CLASS: unreadable OCR. Bede's block at key 1 is 300 words of which roughly the first 40 percent is not English at all but mangled character soup with HTML entities left in -- 'rtvdr. th'te rhrCT 6riifei)^idx'flbws*i'the'inidst t3f the dty' is the opening, which is trying to say something about the river flowing in the midst of the city. The rest of the block recovers and is perfectly legible: the twelve months intimating all the time of life, the cross bearing fruit through the doctrine of the twelve apostles, and the leaves read as a perpetual song. A page running head is embedded mid-block too ('Explanation of the Apocalypse. [bk. iii.]'), as in the Luther scan at galatians 3. This is distinct from truncation, residue and chrome: the text is the right text, in the right place, on the right verse, and simply cannot be read. Bede is declared for entry 1 on the legible portion only; nothing was paraphrased out of the corrupt half. Any de-truncation or cleanup pass should treat entity-laden character soup as its own category, since a length check will not catch it and a voice check will pass it.

Boundary overflow attaches to SECTION edges, not only chapter edges -- a refinement of the rule recorded at genesis 23 and philippians 4. Barnes proves it twice inside this one chapter: his key-5 block is 2,341 words, most of it 'REMARKS ON CHAP. XXI., XXII. 1--5' appended after the verse comment, and his key-6 block opens with 'ANALYSIS OF CHAPTER XXII. 6--20' before reaching the verse. So the same author's front matter and back matter both land mid-chapter, at whichever key begins or ends a printed section. Clarke's key-1 block is the ordinary chapter argument, eighth chapter confirming that pattern. Terminal key 21 is sighting 13 and adds a first: Ellicott's 1,421 words end not in CSS or footer text but in a live JavaScript block -- fetch calls, DOMParser, querySelectorAll, event binding -- so executable page script is now inside the commentary corpus. Wesley's 784 words at the same key carry his whole chronological table of the book's contents plus a Cyril block, and Clarke's 640 carry a dispute about the dating of the Apocalypse.

Fidelity self-grade A for all five entries (1-5, 6-9, 10-15, 16-17, 18-21). Expansion ratios 0.07 to 0.18 against a corpus median of 0.84; the invention signal is expansion above about 6x, so these are distillation. Bede is declared at entry 1 for the legible half of a badly OCR-corrupted block, and nothing was drawn from the unreadable half. Calvin is absent from this chapter entirely, as he wrote no commentary on Revelation, so the reformed school rests on Gill alone throughout. Cyril of Jerusalem residue is present at keys 1, 2 and 21, folded into Wesley by the splitter as at galatians 3 and philippians 4, and again cannot be declared excluded; none of it was used. Entry 10 was extended after first draft because verse 15 fell inside its range and had not been reached in the prose.

MAJOR FINDING, corpus-wide: Wesley's Old Testament Notes reproduce Matthew Henry verbatim, so Henry and Wesley are NOT two independent witnesses on OT chapters. Measured on this chapter with difflib against the catena itself: at key 1, 281 of Wesley's 417 words (67 percent) are shared with Henry's block, including a single unbroken run of 31 words -- 'We have here the call by which Abram was removed out of the land of his nativity into the land of promise...'. At key 4 the overlap is 43 percent of Wesley, at key 6 it is 59 percent, at key 10 it is 19 percent. This is not a scrape defect; Wesley's Notes are historically an abridgement of Henry and Poole. But the consequence for this pipeline is severe and silent: the SCHOOL map puts Henry in puritan-evangelical and Wesley in wesleyan-arminian, so wherever both are declared on an OT chapter the prevalence machinery reports two schools agreeing when there is one source. Worse, a writer paraphrasing both will produce sentences of the form 'Henry and Wesley say the same thing in the same words' as though that were a convergence of witnesses -- I wrote exactly such a sentence at genesis 23 entry 1 before understanding this. Recommended rule going forward: on any OT chapter where Henry and Wesley both have blocks at the same key, diff them before attributing, and credit the point to Henry alone unless Wesley's block adds something Henry's does not contain. Applied here: Wesley is undeclared at entry 6, where his whole contribution at key 6 is Henry's sentence, and his key-4 note was likewise not used.

Calvin footnote defect, ninth book confirming, and two variants of placement in one chapter. At key 1 the interpolation is INSIDE Calvin's block and refers to Calvin in the third person: 'Many learned commentators, Dr A. Clarke among the number, suppose this to have been a second call from God... But the objections adduced by Calvin against such an interpretation are of great weight.' That is the sharpest specimen yet, since the text names Calvin as someone else, and names Adam Clarke, who is another voice in the same catena -- so a synthesis could unwittingly have Calvin cite Clarke. At key 15 the placement is different again: the editorial footnote comes FIRST, at the head of the block, quoting Taylor and citing Hengstenberg's Egypt and the Books of Moses p. 199 on whether Egyptian women went unveiled, before any of Calvin's own words appear. Previous sightings had the interpolation inline or appended; head-of-block is new. The screening rule holds and can be stated more sharply: in a Calvin block, any sentence naming a post-Reformation authority, giving a page number, or speaking of Calvin in the third person is editorial.

Two smaller defects. JFB residue at key 11 only, 18 words, donor Genesis 10 ('In the general division of the earth, the countries of Armenia, Mesopotamia, and Syria, fell to his descendants' -- the table of nations, Shem's line). A single member, so no mod-6 class can be tested here; recorded because the three preceding chapters each carried a clean three- or five-member class, and a lone 18-word member shows the same pointer can also fire once and tiny, far below any size heuristic. Excluded. Separately, Keil and Delitzsch is lemma-only at key 16: all 127 words are the quoted text of verses 16 to 20 with no exposition, so he is silent by entry at entry 14 -- removed from voices but not declared excluded, the block being genuine rather than foreign. He is usable at keys 1, 2, 5, 7, 8, 9 and 11, where exposition survives the 200-word cap. Third chapter confirming that K&D's habit of prefixing full verse text guarantees empty blocks whenever the lemma runs long.

Fidelity self-grade A for all five entries (1-3, 4-5, 6-9, 10-13, 14-20). Expansion ratios 0.07 to 0.20 against a corpus median of 0.84; the invention signal is expansion above about 6x, so these are distillation. The Henry/Wesley duplication governed the attribution throughout: Wesley is declared only where his block carries something Henry's does not, and is left undeclared at entry 6 because his whole key-6 contribution is a sentence of Henry's. One draft error caught and corrected before landing: the first version of entry 6 read 'Henry finds... and Wesley adds that he could not have ground to pitch his tent on but by their permission', which is precisely the false-corroboration the duplication produces -- that clause is Henry's, and the sentence now credits it to Henry alone. Clarke's chapter argument occupies the head of key 1, ninth chapter confirming the chapter-initial pattern, and was not used.

THE MOST SERIOUS ATTRIBUTION DEFECT FOUND IN THIS RUN. The patristic feed for this chapter is not a set of single-voice blocks at all: it is the Catena Aurea, chopped into runs and headed by whichever father happened to open each run, with the other fathers' extracts left inside the block under inline capitalised attributions. The block headed 'Theophylact' at k1 contains, after two sentences of Theophylact, extracts marked 'CYRIL.' and 'ORIGEN;'. The block headed 'Ambrose' at k1 contains 'CYRIL;', 'GREG.', 'ORIGEN;' and 'BASIL;'. The block headed 'Basil' at k1 contains 'AMBROSE;'. The same holds at k5, k9, k14, k22, k28, k31, k38 and k42. Consequences. (1) Voice attribution in this feed is correct ONLY for the opening extract of each block; everything after the first inline capital belongs to somebody else. (2) The head names are not a list of the voices present: 'GREG.', 'TITUS BOST.' and 'GREEK EX.' appear inline and have no head anywhere in the chapter, so their material cannot be attributed at all under the current tooling. (3) The writer's rule I adopted, and which I recommend as the standing one until the feed is fixed, is to use an inline extract only where that father ALSO has a head somewhere inside the entry's span; otherwise the material is unusable. I lost Chrysostom's comment on the fever at k38 to exactly this rule. A corpus scan for a capitalised proper name followed by a period or semicolon inside a commentary body would find every affected block.

The same catena splitter cuts a father's name in half. The block at k9 is headed 'Maxim' and its body begins with the two characters 'US;' - that is, the catena's 'MAXIMUS;' was split so that 'Maxim' became the block head and 'US;' the first word of the text. This is direct evidence for the mechanism proposed in the note above: the importer is scanning for a capitalised token and treating it as a head, with no check that the token is a complete name. The same chapter also carries 'Athan' as a head, which is the catena's own abbreviation and therefore innocent, and both 'Cyril' and 'Cyril of Jerusalem' and 'Cyril of Alexandria' as three separate heads - which is the VOICE_LABELS prefix bug already filed against scripts/synthesis_qa.py, appearing here in its worst form, since a bare match on 'Cyril' hits all three. My build had to use a negative lookahead to keep them apart.

Fidelity self-grade, all eleven entries. 1-4 642w, 5-8 649w, 9-10 584w, 12-13 489w, 14-15 619w, 16-21 649w, 22-27 649w, 28-30 646w, 31-37 655w wait 648w, 38-41 575w, 42-44 492w; all inside the window. Key 11 is ABSENT from the source, so no entry may span it and the temptation is forced into two runs, 1-10 and 12-13; I split the first further at 1-4 and 5-8 because ten keys carried fifteen heads. This is the largest chapter in the run by voice count - twenty-four distinct heads - and the entries name up to fourteen voices each, so every voice gets a sentence or two and no more. Attribution rule used throughout: an inline catena extract is attributed to the father the catena names, and used only where that father has a head inside the entry's own span. Nothing is drawn from the four Jamieson blocks, declared as excluded residue.

Empty-marker blocks at scale. Albert Barnes carries the literal sentence 'No entry from BARNES for this verse' followed only by a marginal cross-reference at keys 4, 6, 8, 10, 12, 31, 33, 34, 36, 38, 41 and 43 - twelve of his thirty-three blocks in this chapter, more than a third. John Wesley's blocks at k4, k8, k10, k12, k27, k38 and k42 are bare scripture references with no comment at all ('De 8:3.', 'Mr 1:35.'). These are empty markers rather than withheld commentary, so I have silenced them rather than declaring them as excluded_voices; but they matter for two reasons. First, they inflate every head count and every word count taken from head presence, including the sizer. Second, the GHOST check treats a head with no usable content exactly like a head with content, so an entry that happens to span only empty Barnes markers forces the writer either to name a voice that says nothing or to silence him by hand. A cheap fix would be to teach the tooling the literal string 'No entry from' and a body consisting solely of a scripture reference.

Correction to the fidelity note filed immediately above: the word count for the 31-37 entry is garbled there, reading '655w wait 648w'. The figure as landed is 648 words. The other ten counts in that note are correct as given.

Jamieson: 752 chapters, no exception. Four blocks, at keys 3, 9, 21 and 27 - all congruent to 3 mod 6. None is on Luke 4: k3 is on the parable of the fig tree from the Olivet discourse, k9 on the same discourse ('Take ye heed, watch and pray'), k21 on Judas holding the bag in John 12, k27 on the thirty pieces of silver in Matthew 26. Note that these four are NOT drawn from one continuous stretch of a single book, unlike every previous chapter measured, where the residue came from a single run of consecutive source verses. Here the sources jump between the Olivet discourse, John and Matthew. That is the first residue set in this run that is not internally consecutive, and it should be recorded against the monotone-drift model: either the model needs a term for the Gospels' parallel material, or these four blocks come from a harmony rather than from a continuous commentary. Worth checking before the re-indexing decision is scoped, since an invertible displacement is the whole basis of that proposal.

Chrome, and the largest single tail measured in this run. The Ellicott block at k44, the last key of the chapter, runs 997 words raw and 7 words usable - a tail of 990 words, or 99.3 percent of the block. The surviving comment is the whole of his note: 'He preached. - Literally, was preaching.' Compare the 985-word Ellicott tail at the last key of revelation 19 and the 984-word tail at the last key of exodus 1: three chapters in three different books, all Ellicott, all at the final key, all between 984 and 990 words. That consistency is itself informative - it suggests a fixed block of navigation matter appended to the last Ellicott block of every chapter, which would be removable by a single rule rather than by per-chapter markers. Also worth noting for the sizer: this chapter's reported 51,720 usable source words include those 990.

Three disagreements in this chapter are worth keeping. (1) THE ORDER OF THE TEMPTATIONS, raised four times by five voices with five positions: Gill holds Matthew's order the true one which Luke neglects without contradicting, and argues it from Matthew's connecting words; Clarke agrees that the kingdoms stand last in Matthew and that nothing can have followed; Lightfoot merely records that the pinnacle is second in Matthew and third here; Augustine says it is uncertain which came first and that it matters little provided all took place; Robertson refuses to choose and characterises both, Luke's order being geographical (wilderness, mountain, Jerusalem) and Matthew's climactic (hunger, nervous dread, ambition), with a climax in Luke's too (sense, man, God). (2) HOW THE KINGDOMS WERE SHOWN: Theophylact states against the commoner view that they were shown in visible form; Robertson calls the panorama mental while allowing a visible Satan; Ellicott makes it the ecstatic compression of images characteristic of the soul in vision. (3) WHETHER THE PASSAGE AT NAZARETH WAS APPOINTED: Ellicott and Clarke take it for the lesson of the day, Ellicott adding that in the modern Jewish calendar the chapter is the second lesson for the day of Atonement; Calvin denies it, holding that a liberty of choice was allowed and Christ chose deliberately; Wesley says he opened upon it by particular providence.

Two moderns rebuke the fathers on the same point, and one of the rebuked is a voice in this very chapter. On 'the acceptable year of the Lord' Ellicott writes that 'a somewhat slavish literalism' led some of the Fathers to infer that our Lord's ministry lasted a single year, and Robertson names Clement of Alexandria and Origen as having argued it, adding that this is to turn figures into fact. Origen has four blocks in this chapter and is one of the voices the synthesis draws on. The catena does not carry his one-year argument here, so the charge cannot be checked against the text in front of me, and I have therefore reported it as Robertson's attribution rather than as Origen's position - naming Robertson's two Alexandrians without using Origen's name, which would also have tripped the sourcing check, since he has no head in the entry where the rebuke falls. Recorded because it is a case where the merged catena puts a father and his modern critic in the same chapter without putting them in the same entry, so a reader of either entry alone would not know the other existed.

A clean chapter, and worth recording as the negative control against a long run of defective ones. Deuteronomy 20 has 20 keys and 12,483 usable source words with NO Jamieson residue at all (Jamieson is entirely absent from the chapter), no Cyril, no terminal-key chrome, no chapter-initial front matter beyond Clarke's ordinary chapter argument at key 1, and no lemma-only Keil and Delitzsch block -- all nine of his blocks carry exposition after the quoted verses, which is the first chapter in this run where that is true of every one. Two things likely explain it: the chapter is short, and its voice set is small and entirely nineteenth-century-or-earlier with no patristic feed. The absence of Jamieson is the most interesting part, since three consecutive chapters before this one carried clean mod-6 residue classes. Whatever emits the donor blocks did not fire here at all, which means the defect is not a universal property of the scrape but something that fires per chapter.

Calvin footnote defect, tenth book confirming, here as Latin scholia. Three of his blocks carry editorial matter that is plainly not his: at key 10 a note on the Roman fetiales with citations to Livy 4:30 and 38:45, Varro L.L. 4:15 and Dionysius 2:72, plus French glosses ('Les herauts d'armes'); at key 12 an untranslated Cicero quotation with the citation 'Cic, de Off. 1:11'; at key 19 further French renderings interleaved with the text. The French glosses are the translator's, the Latin citations the editor's. The screening rule stands and now has a third tell to add to the two already recorded: besides naming a post-Reformation authority and speaking of Calvin in the third person, an untranslated classical quotation with a modern-style volume-and-section citation is editorial. None of this material was attributed to Calvin in the synthesis; his own point at key 10, that the equity behind heralds was implanted in all nations, is his and was used.

Fidelity self-grade A for all five entries (1-4, 5-9, 10-15, 16-18, 19-20). Expansion ratios 0.16 to 0.67, notably higher than recent chapters because the source is small; entry 16 at 0.67 is the highest ratio in this run and still well under the corpus median of 0.84 and far under the ~6x invention signal, its span carrying only 828 source words. Henry is undeclared at entries 5, 16 and 19 because he has no block at those keys, and Wesley is undeclared at entries 1 and 10 for the same reason -- so the Henry/Wesley duplication recorded at genesis 12 could not distort this chapter, since the two never appear at the same key. One judgement worth flagging: entry 16 handles the ban on the Canaanite nations, where Clarke argues at length that the sentence fell on the nations' political existence rather than on every life, Gill reports the proselyte exception, and Keil and Delitzsch keep the strict sense. All three positions are given as their holders state them, including Calvin's concession at entry 10 that the law allowed the Jews more than was justly lawful, which is his own judgement on the text and is recorded as an outlier rather than softened.

JFB residue, 33rd chapter confirming, fourth mod-6 class in five chapters, and the second donor seen to cross its own chapter boundary. Jamieson appears at keys 3, 9 and 15 -- gap 6 throughout -- and the donor is 1 Corinthians read strictly forward ACROSS the 11/12 boundary: key 3 gives 11:27 (guilty of the body and blood; the and/or variant and the Romanist argument for communion in one kind), key 9 gives 11:32 (chastening, citing Revelation 3:19 and Hebrews 12:8), key 15 gives 12:2 (ye were Gentiles carried away unto dumb idols). Donors so far: Romans 8 at galatians 3, 1 Corinthians 3 at philippians 4, 1 Timothy 6 at revelation 22, Genesis 10 at genesis 12 (single member), and now 1 Corinthians 11-12 here. Note the pleasing accident that revelation 22's donor was 1 Timothy 6 while 1timothy 1 is itself a target -- the donor set and the target set overlap, so the pointer is not reading from some separate reserve of text but from the same corpus. All three excluded.

Chapter-initial front matter, tenth chapter confirming and by far the largest instance: key 1 runs 11,880 words of which roughly 8,000 are book introduction. Barnes contributes 4,740 words beginning 'THE FIRST EPISTLE OF PAUL TO TIMOTHY. INTRODUCTION. I. NOTICES OF THE LIFE OF TIMOTHY' and NEVER REACHES verse 1 at all -- the block ends mid-introduction with the sentence 'The remainder of this note is continued in note on 1 Timothy 1:2'. Clarke contributes 4,110 words of essay on identifying Timothy and dating the epistle, reaching his verse comment only in the last ~180 words. Calvin's block opens with the running title 'COMMENTARIES ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO TIMOTHY CHAPTER 1'. NEW SUB-PATTERN, and a useful one: when the front matter is long enough it consumes the whole chapter-initial block and the verse commentary is DISPLACED INTO THE NEXT KEY. Barnes's actual notes on verses 1 and 2 sit at the end of key 2, after 1,400 further words of introduction, and key 2 opens 'Continuation of Note from 1 Timothy 1:1. Material for Verse 2 is at end of this material.' The source signposts the displacement in plain English at both ends, which means it is programmatically detectable: a block containing 'remainder of this note is continued' or 'Continuation of Note from' marks a spilled boundary.

Fidelity self-grade A for all six entries (1-2, 3-7, 8-11, 12-14, 15-17, 18-20). Expansion ratios 0.04 to 0.10 against a corpus median of 0.84 -- low because the source runs 48,090 words, some 8,000 of which are unusable front matter. Chrysostom is declared at five of the six entries on genuine homily material that split_voices sees under his bare surname. Calvin appears only at entry 1, having just 312 words in the whole chapter. One correction made before landing: the first draft of entry 3 read that Barnes and Clarke agree those who swerved never had what they missed; in fact that is Barnes's point alone, Clarke says they aimed and missed, and Ellicott reads the verb as meaning they had once been in the right direction and failed to keep in it. The sentence now gives Barnes and Ellicott as opposed readings, which is what the sources support, and the disagreement is recorded as a debate.

Fidelity self-grade, all seven entries. 1-3 643w (Bede, Gill, Henry, Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson, Wesley); 4-6 642w (Gill, Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson, Wesley); 7-9 649w (same six, Jamieson excluded); 10-12 634w (same six); 13-15 649w (Gill, Henry, Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson, Wesley, Jamieson excluded); 16-19 635w (Gill, Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson); 20-21 627w (Gill, Barnes, Clarke, Robertson, Jamieson excluded). Every claim traced to a head inside its own span; no inline catena extracts used. Chapter source 40,228 usable words over 21 contiguous keys.

JAMIESON STRIDE: 753 chapters, still no exception. All three Jamieson blocks in revelation 9 sit at keys 9, 15 and 21 — every one congruent to 3 mod 6, target stride exactly 6. Residue sources are 1 Thessalonians: k9 is 1Th 3:1-5, k15 is 1Th 3:10 (opens 'See on 1Th 2:9'), k21 is the 1Th 4:1-18 section header. Source gaps 5 then ~8; quantise-up holds at k9-k15, and the k15-k21 pair is the widest source gap measured to date. Lag from revelation 9 back to 1 Thessalonians is ~62 chapters, sitting just under the ~64 measured at revelation 19 and consistent with drift being monotone in corpus position. Note that the residue for BOTH revelation chapters measured so far lands in the Pauline letters, and both land in adjacent epistles.

BEDE AT EXACTLY 300, third occurrence. The single Bede block in this chapter (k1) is exactly 300 words, matching revelation 19 (where it cut mid-word inside 'Alleluia') and galatians 1 (Chrysostom 300). The 300 cap is now confirmed across two books for the Bede feed specifically. The same block carries HTML-entity corruption and OCR damage: literal ''' and '"' sequences left unresolved, plus 'ispoken briefly^', 'v/'' and 'It For even the elect *' with a stray guillemet. Bede belongs on the re-fetch list on both counts.

VICTORINUS MISFILED AT k1 FOR THE SECOND CHAPTER RUNNING. Same signature as revelation 19: exactly one Victorinus of Pettau block in the chapter, always filed at key 1, always commenting on other verses — here it opens by quoting Revelation 9:13-14, the sixth trumpet and the angels at the Euphrates, twelve verses downstream of its filing key. Two chapters, two identical displacements, one block each. This looks like a whole-chapter Victorinus note being attached to the chapter's first verse key rather than a per-verse feed. SILENCED rather than declared: an excluded_voices entry would tell the reader something was withheld, when in fact nothing about verses 1-3 was ever there.

INTERPRETIVE FREE-FOR-ALL ON THE FALLEN STAR, the widest spread of identifications recorded in a single entry so far. Wesley: a good angel of the invisible world, the falling meaning only swiftness. Ellicott: an evil power, argued from the perfect participle, from the Lucifer emblem in Isaiah and from Christ's saying about Satan as lightning — a good angel 'seems hardly possible'. Robertson: same, from the tense alone. Henry: an eminent bishop, or Boniface III, made universal bishop by a usurping emperor 'as the reward of his flattery'. Gill: Mahomet and the publishing of the Alcoran. Clarke reports the field with visible impatience and includes 'Signior Pastorini professes to believe that Luther is intended!' — the exclamation mark is his. Six mutually exclusive readings of one figure, and the only agreement is between the two grammarians, who reach it by grammar rather than by history.

TWO COMMENTATORS DISSENTING FROM THEIR OWN SIDE, both Clarke, in the same chapter. (a) At v15 he lays out the arithmetic of the hour/day/month/year in full — 24 hours to a day, 4 weeks to a month, 12 months to a year — and then refuses to perform the sum, referring those who read the divisions as prophetic periods elsewhere, 'not professing to discuss such uncertainties'. Wesley, on the same verse, performs exactly that sum and gets 212 years; Clarke elsewhere gets 150 for the five months where Wesley gets 79. Same rule, incompatible totals, from writers of the same school. (b) At v21 he gives the complete anti-Roman identification of sorceries, fornication and thefts, then withdraws his assent: 'it is going too far to say that this is the true interpretation. And yet to express any doubt on this subject is with some little else than heresy.' This is the second instance of the pattern first noted at Ellicott in galatians 1 — a commentator naming the confessional stake and deciding against his own side. Worth a corpus scan for the phrase-shape 'it is going too far to say'.

BARNES MULTI-PART NOTE ARTIFACT, new marker string. The Barnes block at k21 opens with the literal line 'This is part 2 of 4 Parts of the Note for Revelation 9:20-21.' and k12 opens 'Continuation of Barnes Notes on Revelation 9:11'. These are feed-level splitting artifacts, not authorial text, and they join the galatians 1 marker ('**** Due to space limitations, See Notes on Verses 1 and 2 combined...'). Three distinct Barnes splice markers now collected; add 'This is part N of M Parts of the Note' and 'Continuation of Barnes Notes on' to the corpus scan alongside the space-limitations string. Practical effect here: a single Barnes note on vv.20-21 is spread over two keys and the sizer counts it twice.

BARNES ARGUES HIMSELF INTO A CORNER AND SAYS SO. Building the Turkish identification of the sixth trumpet, he notes that the reckoning by 'two myriads of myriads' matches the Turkman toman, and cites Gibbon's own phrase 'the myriads of Turkish horse'. Then: 'if it were supposed that John was writing after the event, this would be the language which he would be likely to employ — for this is nearly the identical language employed by the historian Gibbon.' He offers as evidence of fulfilment a resemblance that would equally follow from vaticinium ex eventu, and states the alternative without noticing that it undercuts him. Ellicott, on the same number, draws the opposite conclusion — that its bewildering size 'might have been sufficient to keep interpreters from looking for some slavishly literal fulfilment'.

JFB residue, 34th chapter confirming, fifth mod-6 class in six chapters, and the largest membership yet at four. Jamieson appears at keys 3, 9, 15 and 21 -- gap 6 throughout -- and the donor is Ephesians read strictly forward ACROSS the 2/3 boundary: key 3 gives 2:9 (not of works, lest any man should boast), key 9 gives 2:14 (he is our peace, who hath made both one), key 15 gives 2:19 (no more strangers and foreigners but fellowcitizens), key 21 gives 3:1 (Paul the prisoner of Jesus Christ), the last block opening with Jamieson's own structural note that the first chapter treated the Father's office, the second the Son's, and this the Spirit's -- which is his headnote to Ephesians 3 and fixes the donor location beyond doubt. Donor list now: Romans 8, 1 Corinthians 3, 1 Timothy 6, Genesis 10, 1 Corinthians 11-12, Ephesians 2-3. Three of the six cross the donor's own chapter boundary, so the walk is by continuous text and not by chapter. All four excluded.

A textual variant with doctrinal weight, and the corpus splits by date rather than by school. At verse 15 the received text reads 'sanctify the Lord God in your hearts'; Ellicott states that the true reading is 'sanctify the Lord the Christ' without a shadow of doubt, and Robertson independently gives 'Christ as Lord' as the correct text against the Textus Receptus. Ellicott then builds an argument on it: the words in Isaiah 8:13 name Jehovah Sabaoth, so a Jew like Peter could not have transferred them to a man he had known familiarly unless the church's doctrine states a fact. Barnes and Clarke, working from the older text, never see the question -- Clarke instead spends his space asking how God can be 'sanctified' at all, since to sanctify is to make holy. The split is not reformed against grammatical-historical but pre-critical against post-critical: the two commentators with access to the nineteenth-century apparatus agree against the two without it. Worth recording because a synthesis that simply harmonised the four voices here would silently suppress the strongest christological argument in the chapter.

Fidelity self-grade A for all six entries (1-4, 5-7, 8-12, 13-17, 18-20, 21-22). Expansion ratios 0.04 to 0.07 against a corpus median of 0.84 -- the source runs 69,987 words, the largest chapter landed in this run after galatians 3. Two spans required deliberate restraint rather than compression. At entry 1 the question whether ornament is forbidden absolutely has five distinct positions ranging from Wesley's flat prohibition to Barnes's defence of ornament in principle, and all five are given as their holders state them rather than averaged. At entry 18, the spirits in prison, the corpus openly disagrees and one voice reports Luther's admission that he did not know what the passage means; the entry says so instead of choosing. Gill is present but undeclared at entry 5 and Wesley at entry 13, in both cases because their blocks there only restate what a neighbour says at greater length. Cyril of Jerusalem residue is folded into Wesley at key 21 by the splitter, as in the three preceding chapters, and again could not be declared excluded; none of it was used.

Fidelity self-grade, all six entries. 1-3 649w (Gill, Henry, Clarke, Ellicott, Calvin, Wesley, Keil); 4-6 642w (Gill, Keil, Clarke, Ellicott, Calvin, Wesley); 7-9 601w (same six); 10-12 617w (Gill, Henry, Ellicott, Calvin, Wesley, Keil; Jamieson excluded); 13-16 579w (Gill, Wesley, Clarke, Ellicott, Calvin); 17-20 551w (Gill, Calvin, Clarke, Ellicott; Jamieson excluded, Keil silenced). Every claim traced to a head inside its own span. Chapter source 17,715 usable words over 20 contiguous keys, but see the separate note on the Ellicott k20 tail: roughly 1,000 of those words are navigation chrome and raw JavaScript, so the true usable figure is nearer 16,700.

JAMIESON STRIDE — FIRST WHOLE-BOOK SCAN, AND IT IS CLEAN. Rather than measure one chapter, I scanned every Deuteronomy chapter in the cow tree for Jamieson keys. 33 chapters carry them, and in EVERY ONE the keys form a single residue class mod 6 with no exception: deut 28 has eleven keys (3,9,15,21,27,33,39,45,51,57,63), all congruent to 3; deut 4 has seven, all congruent to 4; deut 32 has seven, all congruent to 2. Sample sizes up to eleven, 33 chapters, zero violations. This is much stronger evidence than the one-chapter-at-a-time accumulation, and it matters for the re-indexing decision: within a chapter the target keys are a strict arithmetic progression of common difference 6, so the displacement is invertible per chapter once the source anchor of the first key is identified. deuteronomy 8 itself has keys 11 and 17, both congruent to 5, with residue from Leviticus (k11 on reserving holy things, k17 on the deputy high priest and the sin offering led outside the camp, citing Le 4:17). NOTE A COMPLICATION: the lag here is roughly 67 chapters (Deut 8 is canonical chapter 161, Lev 4 is 94), which does NOT fit the monotone-in-corpus-position model built from genesis 28 (lag 4), exodus 39 (13), numbers 1 (17), galatians 1 (39), revelation 19 (64) and revelation 9 (62). At canonical position 161 that model predicts a lag near 20, not 67. Either the drift is not monotone, or Deuteronomy's Jamieson tree carries its own offset. The stride finding is unaffected; the drift model needs revisiting before it is relied on.

ELLICOTT END-OF-CHAPTER TAIL, WORST INSTANCE YET: RAW JAVASCRIPT IN THE BLOCK. The Ellicott block at k20 is 1037 words of which only about the first 50 are commentary. The remainder is the navigation tail already recorded at exodus 1 k22 (984w), revelation 19 k43 (985w) and luke 4 k44 (990w) — chapter links, copyright statement, terms of use, dead-link notice — but this time it continues into executable page script: a click-binding IIFE building study-desk URLs (_bindClick, getAttribute('data-vt'), '/study-desk.html?q1='), and an accordion initialiser operating on getElementById('navigation'). Previous measurements stopped at the copyright boilerplate; this one shows the scraper captured the page's inline <script> as well. That raises the priority of the single removable rule: it is not only inflating the sizer, it is putting JavaScript source into a commentary corpus. Detector suggestion: the string 'Copyright Statement These files are public domain' already marks the boundary in every instance measured, and everything after it can be dropped.

ATTRIBUTED BORROWING, THE CLEAN COUNTERPART TO BARNES-COPIES-CLARKE. At v5 Keil glosses the verb for chastening as 'to admonish, chasten, educate; like paideuein' and then quotes, by name, 'It includes everything belonging to a proper education (Calvin)'. Calvin's own block on the same verse is present in this chapter and makes exactly that argument: the verb 'is taken by some in too restricted a sense for to chastise, whereas it comprehends the whole process of a proper education.' So we have the source and the borrower side by side in one chapter, three centuries and two confessions apart, with the debt openly acknowledged. This is the honest form of what galatians 1 showed dishonestly (Barnes reproducing Clarke's Galatia history with an identical citation string and no acknowledgment). Both cases bear on the same question already raised for the tags: the prevalence field counts Keil and Calvin here as two independent voices agreeing, when on this point they are one voice cited twice. If prevalence is ever down-weighted for transmission, attributed borrowing like this is the easiest case to detect — search for a voice name appearing inside another voice's block.

CALVIN EDITOR'S APPARATUS, SIXTH CHAPTER RUNNING, AND THE WORST FORM SO FAR. The Calvin block at k11 has a translator's footnote spliced inline into the body, mid-sentence, in untranslated Latin and Greek: Calvin writes 'Moses will hereafter speak in his Song of the rebelliousness of this people,' and the sentence is then interrupted by 'LXX. autem pro eo (Jeshurun) substituerunt ho egapemenos ... fatente etiam Steucho, se nescire a quo verbo id nomen duci possit si Dilectum significat, -- C.'s own translation of the word is The beloved, waxen fat, and grown thick, kicked.' before resuming 'It was needful, then, that a restraint should be put...'. The same block also carries visibly damaged text: 'he warns them to themselves (for he uses this word for to from that impious ingratitude' has lost a phrase. Elsewhere in the chapter the apparatus appears as bare page references ('See note on Deuteronomy 11:2, p. 383') and as harmony cross-references ('The passage which I have interwoven from Deuteronomy 11'), which are Calvin's arrangement rather than corruption and should be kept. The footnote splices are not. Detector: a Latin clause beginning 'LXX. autem' or a dash followed by "C.'s own translation".

SUSPECTED REFERENCE ERROR, NOT ACTED ON. Ellicott at v15 lists the occurrences of challamish (flint) as 'Deuteronomy 32:13, Job 28:9, Psalms 114:8 (an allusion to this passage), and Isaiah 1:7'. The first three are right. Isaiah 1:7 is about the country being desolate and burned with fire; the flint verse in Isaiah is 50:7, 'I have set my face like a flint'. This looks like a digit dropped either by Ellicott or by the feed, but I have not checked a print edition and did not use the reference in the prose, so it is filed as suspected rather than confirmed. Worth including in any pass that verifies scripture citations inside commentary blocks against the text they claim to cite -- that check would be cheap and would catch this whole class.

JFB residue, 35th chapter confirming, sixth mod-6 class in seven chapters. Jamieson appears at keys 2, 8, 14 and 20 -- gap 6 throughout -- and the donor is John 13 walked strictly forward: key 2 gives 13:12 (Know ye what I have done to you? -- 'the question was put merely to summon their attention'), key 8 gives 13:17-18 (happy are ye if ye do them; he that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel, with the note that the beatitude is on no supposition applicable to Judas), key 14 gives 13:23 (the disciple whom Jesus loved reclining next to him -- 'thus modestly does our Evangelist denote himself'), key 20 gives 13:27-30 (the successive steps by which Judas reached the climax of his guilt). Donor list now: Romans 8, 1 Corinthians 3, 1 Timothy 6, Genesis 10, 1 Corinthians 11-12, Ephesians 2-3, John 13. All four excluded.

A SECOND, DISTINCT RESIDUE MECHANISM: John Lightfoot, and it is not mod-6. He has six blocks in this chapter and they split cleanly by content. On-verse at keys 2 ('He killed James with the sword', with the rabbinic list of the four deaths delivered to the Sanhedrim), 20 ('Because their country was nourished by the king's country', with Ezekiel 27:17 on Judah trading wheat with Tyre) and 23 ('And he was eaten of worms', comparing Josephus). FOREIGN at keys 1, 12 and 13, where the material is all from ACTS 13 -- the commissioning and imposition of hands, the deputy Sergius Paulus (anthupatos), and 'They came to Perga in Pamphylia' with Strabo on the river Cestrus. So the donor here is the IMMEDIATELY FOLLOWING CHAPTER, not an unrelated book, and the members do not form an arithmetic class (keys 1, 12, 13 with gaps 11 and 1). This is the first residue in 35 chapters that is neither mod-6 nor a boundary sweep, and the first where one voice is simultaneously genuine and foreign in the same chapter. Practical consequence: a voice cannot be classified as residue or genuine at chapter level; it must be judged block by block. Lightfoot's text is also OCR-damaged in the same way as Bede at revelation 22, with Hebrew and Greek reduced to character soup ('mop stoning; MID NW burning; AW Killing'), so the rabbinic citations are unusable even where the surrounding English is readable.

TOOLING TRAP, caught by the validator and worth recording so the next worker does not lose a run to it. A voice may need TWO DIFFERENT SPELLINGS depending on which tags field it goes in. The corpus convention for the voices list is the full name 'John Lightfoot' (see mark 15), and ungrounded_voices accepts it because it searches the raw source pool by name keys. But excluded_voices is checked by undeclarable_voices, which does an exact lowercased match against the names split_voices returns -- and synthesis_qa.VOICE_LABELS carries only the bare surname 'Lightfoot'. Declaring 'John Lightfoot' in excluded_voices therefore fails the validator with 'names a block absent from this entry's source', even though the block is plainly there. My own pre-flight check missed it because I had written a loose substring test; the validator caught it. The rule: excluded_voices must use the exact string from VOICE_LABELS, voices may use the fuller corpus form. The same trap is latent for every VOICE_LABELS entry that is a bare surname or short form -- Robertson, Chrysostom, Cyril, Bede, Augustine, Origen, Basil, Tertullian, Theodoret, Victorinus, Gregory, Leo.

Fidelity self-grade A for all six entries (1-5, 6-11, 12-17, 18-19, 20-23, 24-25). Expansion ratios 0.04 to 0.28 against a corpus median of 0.84. Lightfoot is declared at entries 1 and 20, where his blocks are on-verse, and excluded at entry 12, where they carry Acts 13 material; he is neither declared nor excluded at entry 6, where the only mention of his name in the prose is Ellicott citing him, so he appears there as a reported critic in a debate rather than as a witness. Chrysostom is declared only at entry 18; his 1,131 words at key 1 were read and not used, the entry having no room once the historical identification of Herod was set out. Henry is undeclared at entries 1 and 24, where he has no block. One judgement recorded: at entry 18 Chrysostom asks why God let the guards die and answers it, which is the only place in the chapter where a commentator questions the justice of the narrative rather than explaining it; his answer is given as he gives it.

Fidelity self-grade, all eight entries. 1-3 645w (10 voices: Chrysostom, Gill, Henry, Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson, Calvin, Wesley, Cyril); 4-6 649w (9, Jamieson excluded); 7-9 649w (7); 10-12 643w (9, Jamieson excluded); 13-15 646w (8); 16-18 644w (8, Jamieson excluded); 19-21 645w (8); 22-24 649w (7, Jamieson excluded, Cyril silenced). Every claim traced to a head inside its own span. TWO DELIBERATE OMISSIONS, both from misfiled Ellicott blocks — see the separate note: his block at k1 is the section header on 6:10-17 and his block at k2 is his comment on v18, self-labelled '(18)'. I did not use either, since using them would have put content from one pericope inside another; the material at k2 is consequently missing from the 16-18 entry, where it belongs. Chapter sized at 55,550 usable words, but roughly 6,900 of that is chrome at k24 alone (see notes), so the true figure is nearer 48,600.

ELLICOTT MISFILED AT THE HEAD OF THE CHAPTER — TWO BLOCKS, ONE VACATING ITS PROPER KEY. Checked every Ellicott block in the chapter against its key. k3 through k24 are correctly aligned. But k1 is not a comment on v1 at all: it is his section header on 6:10-17 ('In Ephesians 6:10-17. St. Paul sums up his practical exhortation in that magnificent description...'), which belongs at k10. And k2 is his comment on VERSE 18, carrying the verse number in its own text: '(18) Praying always with all prayer and Supplication.' There is no Ellicott block at k18, so this is not a shift — it is two blocks displaced to the front of the chapter, one of which left its proper key empty. Attribution is certain (the block labels itself), so the filing is recoverable: k1's content should move to k10 and k2's to k18. Distinct from the Victorinus pattern (one block per chapter, always at k1, always about other verses) in that here the displaced material has a demonstrable home. Worth a corpus scan for Ellicott blocks whose first characters are a parenthesised verse number that disagrees with their key.

CALVIN'S BACK MATTER DUMPED INTO THE LAST VERSE — A NEW AND LARGE CHROME FAMILY. The Calvin block at k24 is 5,928 words. Only the first ~230 comment on v24 (the sense of en aphtharsia, following Erasmus). The remaining ~5,700 are CALVIN'S OWN TRANSLATION OF THE BIBLICAL TEXT of Galatians and Ephesians, printed complete as the volume's back matter, with his French alternative renderings inline as footnotes ('Par grace, ou, en la grace de Christ'). The dump runs Galatians 1 through 6 and Ephesians 1 through 4 at least. This is not navigation chrome and not an editor's apparatus — it is an entire biblical text mis-scoped into one commentary block, and it is the largest single non-content payload measured anywhere in the corpus. Detector: the run begins after the genuine comment with continuous scripture prose and no exposition; the French gloss pattern (a quoted French phrase followed by its English) recurs every few hundred words. Practical effect: the sizer over-reports this chapter by about 5,700 words from this block alone.

ELLICOTT END-OF-BOOK TAIL: NOW CSS AS WELL AS JAVASCRIPT. The Ellicott block at k24 is 1,175 words: genuine comment on the salutation for roughly the first 200, then a RAW CSS STYLESHEET (.int-s-button, .lex-search-div, media queries) followed by the JavaScript bundle already recorded at deuteronomy 8 k20 — the verse_popups.cgi fetch, the scriptRef click binder, the accordion initialiser. deuteronomy 8 showed the end-of-CHAPTER tail reaching into script; this is the end-of-BOOK tail and it is larger, carrying the page's stylesheet too. Running series for the same feed: exodus 1 k22 984w, revelation 19 k43 985w, luke 4 k44 990w, deuteronomy 8 k20 1037w, ephesians 6 k24 1175w. The boundary marker 'Copyright Statement These files are public domain' holds in every instance; everything after it can be dropped. NOTE the contrast at the same key: Clarke's 1,065-word block here is genuine throughout — the versional subscriptions, his judgment that subscriptions were 'added in a much later age, and generally by unskillful hands', and his colophon 'Finished the correction for a new edition, Dec. 15th, 1831.' Length alone does not identify chrome.

JAMIESON STRIDE: four keys, perfect progression, and the NT drift model survives where Deuteronomy broke it. The four Jamieson blocks sit at keys 6, 12, 18 and 24 — an exact arithmetic progression of difference 6, all congruent to 0 mod 6. Residue is Romans 15-16: k6 is Rom 15:18 ('I will not dare to go beyond what Christ hath wrought by me'), k18 is Rom 15:32 ('with you refresh myself'), k24 is Rom 16:3 (Prisca, 'the wife is here named before the husband'). LAG: ephesians 6 is canonical chapter 1103 and Romans 15 is 1061, a lag of 42 — which sits right beside the galatians 1 measurement (position 1092, lag ~39) and continues the monotone NT series through revelation (1103/42, 1197/62, 1207/64). That matters because deuteronomy 8 did NOT fit: position 161 with a lag of 67 where the model predicts ~20. With ephesians 6 confirming the NT progression, the deuteronomy outlier is better explained as that book's tree carrying its own offset than as the drift being non-monotone. Recommend the owner treat the drift as monotone WITHIN a tree and check for per-book or per-testament offsets before scoping the re-indexing.

CYRIL OF JERUSALEM IS A TOPICAL FLORILEGIUM, NOT A COMMENTARY, AND IT DUPLICATES. Seven Cyril blocks in this chapter, but only FIVE distinct texts: k1 and k3 are byte-identical (193w, on honouring parents), and k17 and k18 are byte-identical (200w, on the subsistence of the Holy Ghost). The others are matched to their keys by catchword rather than by exposition — k11 is the baptismal chrism because the verse says 'put on'; k16 is faith stopping the lions' mouths because the verse says 'shield of faith'; k24 is a eucharistic passage from the Catechetical Lectures that comments on nothing in the closing benediction at all. This is a different mechanism from the Catena Aurea splitting defect: there the attribution was wrong; here the attribution is right and the ASSIGNMENT is decorative. Two consequences for the tooling: duplicate blocks inflate both the head count and the sizer, and GHOST cannot distinguish a florilegium match from a real comment. Cyril's cap is the same 200 measured at galatians 1 (4 of 4); three of his seven here sit at exactly 200. I silenced the k24 block for the 22-24 entry on the standing rule for blocks that comment on nothing in their span.

THE SLAVERY PASSAGE: FIVE POSITIONS, AND ONE COMMENTATOR ARGUING AGAINST HIS OWN TEXT'S MISUSE. Clarke: 'In heathen countries slavery was in some sort excusable; among Christians it is an enormity and a crime for which perdition has scarcely an adequate state of punishment' — and in the same block, that a Christian slave was bound to serve faithfully the man whose money bought him, 'howsoever illegal that traffic may be considered.' Barnes is the most remarkable. At v7 he forbids the master two inferences: that a pious slave's submission means the slave thinks him right, and that religion's command of obedience means religion approves the master — 'It does this no more than it sanctioned the conduct of Nero and Mary, because religion required [the martyrs to submit].' At v8: 'Religion does not approve of slavery. It is the friend of human rights.' At v6 he turns the command against eyeservice into a structural indictment: a hired freeman may be trusted out of sight, a slave may not, which is why drivers are necessary, and only religion removes the need — 'the extensive prevalence of true religion would set the slave at liberty.' Then at v19, expounding a request for prayer, he breaks off to count: 'not far from ten thousand prisoners... not far from three millions of slaves' in his own country. Ellicott locates the limit in the phrase 'according to the flesh' and credits the abolition to a conception logically worked out; Chrysostom says slavery is 'nothing but a name'; Henry expects it 'rooted out by the influence of Christianity'; Calvin describes the institution exactly and warns servants that the gospel procured them no carnal freedom. Filed because the entry could only carry the summary: the primary sources here are worth reading whole.

CALVIN EDITOR'S APPARATUS, SEVENTH CHAPTER RUNNING — THREE INSTANCES IN ONE CHAPTER. Same defect recorded at deuteronomy 8: translator's footnotes spliced inline into the body, mid-sentence.
