(a) k1: Calvin asks 'Why does the apostle use the word instead of' and the sentence is broken by a Greek-and-English footnote ending '— Bloomfield.' before resuming 'which has a greater extent of meaning?'. (b) k11: a Plutarch citation on the etymology of wrestling ('Plutarch tells us, (Symp. l. 2., page 638,)...') interpolated into the exposition of the wiles of the devil. (c) k12: another Bloomfield footnote, this one a long passage on Maximus Tyrius and Socrates, Plato, Xenophon and Diogenes wrestling with their several adversaries, planted at the head of the block before Calvin's own comment begins. Detector candidates now: a clause ending in an em-dash followed by a proper name and a full stop; the strings 'LXX. autem', "C.'s own translation", 'Bloomfield.' Note again that Calvin's OWN cross-references ('See Colossians 4:1', 'See volume 1 page 468') are his arrangement and should be kept — only the interpolated footnotes are the defect, and they are distinguishable because they break a sentence in half.

MATTHEW HENRY CONCISE/EXPOSITION: THIRD FORM OF THE DEFECT. Henry has four blocks in this chapter. k1 (2280w), k10 (3517w) and k19 (1172w) are Exposition — numbered divisions, roman-numeral scripture references ('Acts xiv. 12', 'Exod. xxxii. 6'). But k5 (274w) is the CONCISE: short, undivided, summary in manner ('The servants of old were generally slaves. The apostles were to teach servants and masters their duties, in doing which evils would be lessened, till slavery should be rooted out by the influence of Christianity'), with no roman numerals. So within a single chapter the feed serves Exposition at three keys and Concise at a fourth. This is a third signature, distinct from the two already recorded: at revelation 19 the Concise was SPLICED ONTO THE TAIL of the Exposition, detectable by the shift from roman to arabic references; at genesis 28 k20 the Concise was served INSTEAD OF the Exposition for that key; here both works appear at different keys of the same chapter with no marker of the switch. All three signatures should go into the corpus scan together, since a scan built for any one of them will miss the others.

Two small defects, both already-known classes. (1) JFB residue at key 16 only, 101 words, donor Exodus 29 -- the seven days of altar consecration, 'when thou hast made an atonement for it' rendered 'upon it', with the daily removal of ashes and the prescribed unction. A lone member, so no mod-6 class can be tested; this is the second single-member sighting after genesis 12, and both are short. Excluded. (2) Keil and Delitzsch is lemma-only at key 15: all 200 words are the quoted text of verses 15 to 19 with no exposition, so he is silent by entry at entry 14, removed from voices but not declared excluded since the block is genuine rather than foreign. He is usable at keys 2, 3, 5, 6, 8 and 12. Fourth chapter confirming that K&D's habit of prefixing the full verse text guarantees an empty block whenever the lemma runs long -- and here the lemma runs five verses.

Fidelity self-grade A for all five entries (1-4, 5-6, 7-13, 14-16, 17-19). Expansion ratios 0.13 to 0.36, the highest in several chapters because the source is small at 13,570 words; still well under the corpus median of 0.84. One error caught and corrected before landing, worth recording because it is the failure mode the tiling is meant to prevent: the first draft of entry 5 (verses 5-6) credited Keil and Delitzsch with the detail that a man who could not afford two pigeons was to bring a tenth of an ephah of fine flour without oil or frankincense. That material is in his key-8 block, which belongs to entry 7, not entry 5. Cross-span borrowing of exactly this kind would have been invisible to every validator, since the voice is genuine and declared and the sentence is accurate -- it is only in the wrong entry. The sentence was removed from entry 5 and the point is made in entry 7, where the source sits. Practical rule: when a voice appears in adjacent spans, check which key a remembered detail came from before attributing it, since the reading is done span by span but the memory of it is not.

Fidelity self-grade, all five entries. 1-3 649w (Gill, Henry, Clarke, Ellicott, Wesley, Keil); 4-10 612w (Gill, Clarke, Keil, Wesley, Ellicott; Jamieson excluded); 11-14 648w (six voices); 15-18 647w (Gill, Clarke, Ellicott, Wesley, Keil; Jamieson excluded); 19-21 644w (six voices). Every claim traced to a head inside its own span. Five pericopes rather than seven three-key spans, following the natural divisions of the narrative — the setting, the threefold call, the message, the telling of Eli, and Samuel established. Chapter sized at 14,164 usable words, of which about 890 at k20 is the Ellicott chrome tail, so the true figure is nearer 13,300.

★ THE JAMIESON MECHANISM IS NOW VISIBLE, AND IT IS NOT A PER-CHAPTER DISPLACEMENT. The three Jamieson blocks here sit at keys 4, 10, 16, all congruent to 4 mod 6, with source Joshua 10 (k4 the Gibeonite appeal, k10 the discomfiting of the Amorites, k16 the five kings in the cave at Makkedah). The decisive observation is that 1samuel 4 key 6 carries the IDENTICAL Makkedah block. The same source text is filed at two different target keys in two adjacent chapters. Scanning 1samuel 1-6 shows what is happening: the residue is ONE CONTINUOUS STREAM of Jamieson-on-Joshua being poured across consecutive 1 Samuel chapters, one block emitted every 6 target keys, running on across chapter boundaries and overlapping by one block at each boundary. 1sam1 draws on Joshua 8 (keys =4 mod 6), 1sam2 on Joshua 9-10:2 (=5), 1sam3 on Joshua 10:4-16 (=4), 1sam4 on Joshua 10:16+ (=0), 1sam5 on Joshua 10:28+ (=1), 1sam6 on Joshua 11 (=0). THIS EXPLAINS EVERYTHING MEASURED OVER 753+ CHAPTERS: the stride of 6 belongs to the EMITTER, not to any target chapter, and the per-chapter residue class is simply wherever the stream happens to stand when the chapter starts — which is why every chapter shows a single class and why the class differs between chapters. The apparent monotone drift in corpus position is the accumulated offset of a stream that has been running since the start of the corpus. FOR THE RE-INDEXING DECISION: this is much better news than a per-chapter displacement. There is one stream to re-align, not 753 displacements to invert. Recommend the owner scope the fix as identifying the stream's start and its emission rule, and note that the boundary overlap means a naive re-alignment will duplicate one block per chapter boundary.

ELLICOTT REPRODUCES KEIL, UNATTRIBUTED — a third borrowing datum, and the cleanest verbal match yet. On Eli's reply at v18, Keil writes: 'his reply proves that, with all his weakness and criminal indulgence towards his wicked sons, Eli was thoroughly devoted to the Lord in his heart.' Ellicott writes: 'indicates that Eli, in spite of his weakness and foolish partiality for his sons, was thoroughly devoted to the Lord in his heart.' The concessive clause is reworded; the eight-word predicate is verbatim. Keil's English translation (1864) precedes Ellicott (1884), so the direction is Keil to Ellicott. This joins Barnes-copies-Clarke at galatians 1 (identical citation string, unattributed) and Keil-cites-Calvin at deuteronomy 8 (same argument, attributed by name). Three cases now, in three combinations: unattributed prose borrowing between moderns, unattributed citation borrowing between moderns, and attributed borrowing across confessions. All three inflate the prevalence field the same way — two voices counted as agreeing independently when one is copying the other. The detector for this case is different from the others and cheap: index every commentary block by its distinctive 6-to-10-word spans and look for spans shared across voices. I flagged the borrowing in the entry prose itself rather than presenting the two as independent witnesses.

ELLICOTT END-OF-CHAPTER TAIL, SIXTH INSTANCE. The k20 block is 1070 words of which roughly the first 180 are comment ('A prophet of the Lord. — Then from the northern to the southern cities...'); the rest is the CSS stylesheet and JavaScript bundle already recorded. Running series for this feed: exodus 1 k22 984w, revelation 19 k43 985w, luke 4 k44 990w, deuteronomy 8 k20 1037w, ephesians 6 k24 1175w, 1samuel 3 k20 1070w. Six measurements, one boundary marker throughout. NOTE the counterexample in the same chapter, which matters for any automated rule: Clarke's block at k21 is 740 words and is GENUINE throughout — his closing essay on neglected religious education, ending 'Parents who neglect this, neglect the present and eternal interests of their offspring.' Two long blocks at the last two keys of one chapter, one entirely chrome and one entirely authorial. A length-based or position-based heuristic would destroy the Clarke essay; only the copyright-line marker distinguishes them.

Jamieson residue, four-member mod-6 class (keys 2, 8, 14, 20), donor 1 Corinthians 1->2 walked strictly forward: 1:29-31 (let him glory in the Lord) at key 2, 2:2 (save Jesus Christ and him crucified) at key 8, 2:6-7 (we speak wisdom ... hidden) at key 14, 2:12 (the spirit which is of God) at key 20. Crosses the donor's own chapter boundary, so the walk is by continuous text and not by verse number. This is the seventh clean mod-6 class in eight chapters and the third whose donor crosses a chapter boundary. Every Jamieson block in this chapter is residue -- 623 words, none of it on Philippians 3 -- so the whole voice is excluded here.

Ellicott's key-21 block is genuine and on-verse for roughly the first 500 words, then runs straight into scraper boilerplate: the StudyLight site footer, a full CSS stylesheet with media queries, and the site's commentary/concordance/dictionary navigation menus, all unescaped inside the commentary value. Same family as the Bede OCR soup at revelation 22 (genuine block, unreadable tail) but a different mechanism -- not bad character recognition but an unbounded scrape that swallowed the page chrome. Detectable programmatically: the tail contains brace-and-semicolon CSS and no sentence punctuation.

Barnes's key-21 block carries a chapter-end REMARKS essay after the verse commentary -- eleven numbered reflections on rejoicing, on mistaking religion for gloom, and on the resurrection -- pushing the block to 3,006 words, more than double any other in the chapter. Same section-edge overflow class recorded at revelation 22 (mid-chapter REMARKS and ANALYSIS headings). Confirms the pattern is Barnes-specific and signposted in plain English: the word REMARKS on its own line marks the boundary between on-verse commentary and the essay.

Genuine four-way disagreement over the verb rendered 'already perfect' in v12, preserved rather than harmonised. Clarke holds it is the technical athletic word that had come to mean martyrdom, documenting Philo, Clement of Alexandria, Basil, Oecumenius and Eusebius, and calls the moral reading 'most falsely and dangerously imagined'. Barnes takes it as moral and lists the critics (Bloomfield, Koppe, Rosenmuller, Robinson, Clarke) who do not -- so Barnes has read Clarke's position and rejected it. Robertson and Ellicott land near Barnes without the heat. Clearest instance so far of a source disagreement where one commentator explicitly cites the party he refutes.

Calvin declines the passive rendering of heurisko in v9 that every other voice adopts, arguing the form carries an active signification (to recover what you gave up) and citing Budaeus. Gill flags the divergence by name -- 'Calvin, different from other interpreters, reads the words actively' -- allows the sense is true in substance, and still judges the passive best. A rare case in this corpus of one commentator naming another and adjudicating; recorded as a debate rather than folded into a consensus.

Lightfoot is named twice in the finished prose (Ellicott citing him on skybalon at key 8, Robertson quoting him at key 17) but has no block of his own in this chapter -- both are citations inside another commentator's text. Declared neither in voices nor in excluded_voices, and the prose attributes each point to the citing commentator. Worth recording because acts 12 had the opposite case: Lightfoot present as a real block AND carrying Acts 13 residue in the same chapter. A surname in the prose is not evidence of a voice.

Fidelity self-grade, all seven entries. 1-3 632w (8 voices); 4-6 650w (7, Jamieson excluded); 7-9 650w (9 — Gill, Henry, Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson, Calvin, Wesley, Chrysostom); 10-12 645w (7, Jamieson excluded); 13-15 650w (8); 16-18 650w (8, Jamieson excluded); 19-20 612w (7, Cyril silenced). Every claim traced to a head inside its own span. One correction made mid-build: I had attributed to Chrysostom by name an exclamation that reaches the 10-12 entry only inside an Ellicott block, where Chrysostom has no head; reworded to an earlier expositor. That is the luke 4 rule holding — an inline extract may be used only where that father also has a head in the entry's own span.

JAMIESON: the stream model predicts this chapter exactly. Three blocks at keys 6, 12 and 18 — difference 6, all congruent to 0 mod 6. Source is 1 CORINTHIANS 7-8 (k6 = 1Co 7:34 on the married woman and the virgin; k12 = 1Co 7:39, 'the oldest manuscripts omit by the law'; k18 = 1Co 8:1-3, love against knowledge). Source verses advance about five for every six target keys, as the emitting stream requires. LAG: 1thessalonians 2 is canonical chapter 1113, 1 Corinthians 7 is 1069, so 44 — and the NT series is now galatians 1 (1092, ~39), ephesians 6 (1103, 42), 1thessalonians 2 (1113, 44), revelation 9 (1197, 62), revelation 19 (1207, 64). That is a straight line: the accumulated offset grows about one chapter for every five of corpus position, which is what a stream emitting one block per six target keys while the target advances one key at a time should produce. Note the pleasing cross-check with an earlier measurement: revelation 9's residue came FROM 1 Thessalonians 2-3, and here 1 Thessalonians 2's own residue comes from 1 Corinthians. The stream is one long chain and these are two links of it, 84 chapters apart.

★ CLARKE CONDEMNS AND THEN PLEADS — the two ends of one chapter, and they should be read together. At v15 he draws up a numbered indictment of the Jews in six counts, the harshest anti-Jewish writing I have met in this corpus, ending that 'they persecuted the body to death, and the soul to damnation!' Five verses later, closing the chapter, the same commentator writes: 'For what end God has preserved them distinct from all the people of the earth among whom they sojourn, we cannot pretend to say; but it must unquestionably be for an object of the very highest importance. In the meantime, let the Christian world treat them with humanity and mercy.' I set the two side by side in the 19-20 entry rather than reporting either alone, because reporting only the invective would misrepresent him and reporting only the plea would launder him. THE TRADITION SUPPLIES ITS OWN CHECKS HERE, and they are worth recording as a group: Robertson notes that those who thought they pleased God by persecuting were doing exactly what Paul himself did when he ravaged the church at Jerusalem, 'but Paul knows better now'; Ellicott notes that Stephen's speech seems to be waking in a man who had been a persecuting Jew himself; Calvin reads the charge corporately, of a national policy rather than the same individuals, and explains that the length of the polemic answers a calumny that was costing Gentiles their hope of salvation; and Barnes narrows the charge decisively, showing that the objection was never to speaking with Gentiles but to Gentiles being saved otherwise than as Jews. Any future presentation of this passage should carry those four qualifications with it.

THE GENTLE/BABES CRUX AT v7, and it splits the usual alignments. The manuscripts divide between epioi (gentle) and nepioi (babes), one letter apart. Robertson follows the documents to nepioi, naming Dibelius, Moffatt, Ellicott and Weiss as preferring epioi because it makes better sense, judging Dibelius too strong for calling nepioi impossible, and citing Lightfoot that Paul works the metaphor to the limit in his passion. Clarke rejects nepioi outright on the sense: the Thessalonians are the children and the apostle the nurse, so he cannot be both at once. Calvin reports the variant, notes the old translation and Wicliff read 'litil', and declines to choose because either reading yields the same voluntary abasement. Gill observes only that one word becomes the other by adding a letter and that both come to much the same. So the modern grammarian takes the harder reading against four modern scholars, the eighteenth-century Arminian argues from mixed metaphor, and the two Reformed writers decline the question as doctrinally indifferent. Worth flagging because it is a case where the schools do not predict the positions.

ELLICOTT CHROME TAIL: SEVENTH INSTANCE, AND IT IS NOT AT THE LAST KEY. The tail here sits at k19 (1111 words, of which roughly the first 150 are comment), not at k20 — because Ellicott has no k20 block in this chapter. The tail therefore attaches to the LAST BLOCK OF THE FEED, not to the last verse of the chapter. That refines the rule: a position-based detector keyed to the final verse would miss this one entirely. Series to date: exodus 1 k22 984w, revelation 19 k43 985w, luke 4 k44 990w, deuteronomy 8 k20 1037w, 1samuel 3 k20 1070w, 1thessalonians 2 k19 1111w, ephesians 6 k24 1175w. The marker 'Copyright Statement These files are public domain' holds in all seven. AND AGAIN THE COUNTEREXAMPLE AT THE SAME END OF THE CHAPTER: Barnes at k20 is 1180 words and Clarke 504, both entirely genuine — Barnes's closing remarks on the ministry and Clarke's closing essay. Three chapters running now (deuteronomy 8, 1samuel 3, this one) where the longest block at the chapter's end is authorial and a shorter one nearby is chrome. Length and position are both useless as discriminators; only the marker works.

CYRIL OF JERUSALEM, FLORILEGIUM BEHAVIOUR CONFIRMED IN A SECOND BOOK. His single block in this chapter sits at k19 and is a passage of the Catechetical Lectures on 2 Corinthians 4:4, the blinding of unbelievers' thoughts — commenting on nothing whatever in verses 19-20, which are about the apostle's hope and crown at Christ's coming. Silenced for that entry on the standing rule. This matches ephesians 6 exactly, where his seven blocks were matched to keys by catchword and two pairs were byte-identical duplicates. Two books, same behaviour: the Cyril feed is a topical anthology keyed to words rather than a verse commentary, and its blocks should not be treated as comment on the verses they are filed under. His cap is the same 200 measured at galatians 1 and ephesians 6 — the single block here is exactly 200 words.

TWO INDEPENDENT CONVERGENCES WORTH THE PREVALENCE FIELD'S ATTENTION, both benign. (a) At v5 Wesley and Ellicott independently notice the same fine point: the appeal is to the Thessalonians for the absence of flattery, because men could judge that, and to God for freedom from covetous design, because only God could; and where the matter is mixed, at v10, to both. Neither cites the other and the wording is quite different — this is genuine independent observation, unlike the Keil-to-Ellicott borrowing recorded at 1samuel 3. (b) At v10 Calvin and Ellicott give OPPOSITE explanations of the same qualifying clause, 'among you that believe': Calvin says it restricts the jury to those who judge uprightly, since the servants of Christ cannot escape calumny from a world that hates them; Ellicott says it names the place where, if anywhere, they might have been tempted to be lax. Both are defensible and the disagreement is invisible unless the two are set side by side. Filed as a reminder that the prevalence field needs to distinguish three things, not two: agreement by transmission, agreement by independent observation, and apparent agreement that conceals a real difference of reading.

NEW DEFECT CLASS: an unrecognised voice label causing silent misattribution. Six Cyril of Jerusalem passages (1,171 words in four distinct texts, two of them duplicated across two keys each) are spliced onto the tails of other commentators' blocks at keys 9, 10, 11, 13, 15 and 19. The literal string 'Cyril of Jerusalem:' is present in the text, but synthesis_qa.split_voices does not recognise it as a label, so the words are credited to the host voice: Wesley four times (keys 9, 11, 13, 19), Barnes once (key 10), Calvin once (key 15). Wesley's apparent 1,550 words in this chapter are really about 768. Nothing catches this -- the host voice is genuine and on-verse, the appended text is genuine patristic commentary, and no length or coverage check fires. Had I used any of it I would have credited Wesley or Barnes with Cyril's homily. Detectable programmatically by grepping block bodies for 'Cyril of Jerusalem:' and any other VOICE-name-plus-colon that split_voices does not split on.

Jamieson residue at keys 2, 8, 14, 20 -- the SAME four-member mod-6 key set as philippians 3, and here the donor alignment is exact. Donor is ACTS 19, read VERSE-ALIGNED rather than merely walked forward: key 2 carries JFB on Acts 19:4-5 (the baptism at Ephesus, citing Ac 19:4 by name), key 8 his 'See on Ac 17:2,3' cross-reference which sits at Acts 19:8, key 14 the note on Sceva as 'head, possibly, of one of the twenty-four courses' at Acts 19:14, key 20 the magicians confessing their deluding practices at Acts 19:18-19. This is the strongest evidence yet on the mechanism: the mod-6 spacing is the SELECTION of which keys receive residue, while the content is keyed one-to-one to the donor chapter's same verse numbers. Every Jamieson block here is residue (89 words, none on 1 Cor 6), so the voice is excluded wherever it appears.

Lightfoot is genuine and foreign in the same chapter, and here the residue walks in BOTH directions -- new relative to acts 12, where it was forward-only. On-verse at keys 3 and 4 (we shall judge angels; the five Jewish benches and pecuniary versus capital judgments). Residue at key 1, which carries 1 Cor 5:12-13 ('them that are without', 'therefore put away', the future tense of exaireite) from the PREVIOUS chapter; at key 5, which carries 1 Cor 7:5 ('Defraud ye not one the other') from the NEXT; and at key 12, which carries the Nicolaitans and meat offered to idols from 1 Cor 8. So one voice is bidirectionally displaced within a single chapter. Consequence for tagging: entry 1 (keys 1-4) both declares Lightfoot in voices, from keys 3-4, and contains residue it cannot exclude; entries 5 and 12 hold nothing but residue and exclude him.

Lightfoot's genuine key-3 and key-4 blocks are the SOURCE the other commentators route through, and both Clarke and Barnes say so by name. Clarke reproduces Lightfoot on judging angels almost word for word ('He saith not, as he did before, The saints shall judge the angels, but we shall judge them'), and cites him again for the five Jewish benches; Barnes writes 'See Lightfoot' for the same point about the lowest orders of judges. Prose credits Lightfoot for the substance and notes Clarke adopts it, rather than reporting Clarke and Lightfoot as two agreeing voices -- the same false-corroboration trap as Henry reproducing Wesley at genesis 12, but here running in the opposite direction, from an obscure voice into two famous ones.

Five-way split on whether washed/sanctified/justified is in inverted order, preserved as a debate: Henry calls it a rhetorical change of the natural order; Clarke denies flatly that anything is inverted and defends the sequence by deriving hagiazo from alpha-privative plus ge, 'separated from the earth' (the etymology is wrong, but it is his and it carries his argument); Barnes reads a genuine sequence of regeneration, progressive sanctification and pardon; Robertson dissolves the problem by the middle voice of apelousasthe, making the washing the readers' own baptismal act expressing two prior divine acts, and cites Findlay that the twin conceptions commonly appear in reverse order; Ellicott refuses to press the order at all.

Calvin against Gill and Robertson on the word 'some' in 'such were some of you'. Gill and Robertson take it restrictively (not all of them, and not all of everything). Calvin argues the Greek indefinite is redundant ornament, not restriction, and that human nature universally contains the seed of all the vices listed, grounding it on the way the same apostle piles up crimes in Romans 1 and 3 without every reader being sanguinary. Recorded as a debate because the two readings give materially different doctrines of the catalogue: a list of what some Corinthians did, or a list of what all unrenewed men are liable to.

The unrecognised-label defect first recorded at 1corinthians 6 (Cyril of Jerusalem) generalises here to a whole class: the Catena Aurea attributions. Five labels appear in this chapter that synthesis_qa.VOICE_LABELS does not know -- Theophylact (6 occurrences), Pseudo-Jerome (5), Gloss (3), Remigius (1), Jerome (1). Where such a label OPENS a block the text arrives as (UNLABELLED): 1,289 words across keys 1, 14 and 30, unattributable but at least not misattributed. Where it appears MID-BLOCK, after a recognised father, the following text is silently credited to that father: 12 occurrences land inside Chrysostom (8), Bede (2), Origen (1) and Augustine (1). Separately the Cyril of Jerusalem splice recurs on 9 keys (1, 4, 7, 9, 12, 24, 31, 41, 47), 1,622 words, hosted by Wesley (6) and Robertson (3) -- so Wesley's apparent 2,485 words in this chapter are really about 1,472 and Robertson's 3,953 about 3,344. Recommended fix: add the Catena names to VOICE_LABELS, or at minimum have split_voices emit an (UNRECOGNISED LABEL) boundary wherever a capitalised-name-plus-colon occurs mid-block. I wrote this chapter through a sub-splitter (scratchpad dump3.py) that segments on those labels; without it the prose would have credited Chrysostom with Theophylact.

Jamieson residue at keys 24, 36, 42, 48 -- a mod-6 class again, this time all congruent to 0 (philippians 3 and 1corinthians 6 were both the residue-2 class). Donor is MARK 4: key 24 carries JFB on 4:1 (a great multitude, the ship of 3:9, crowded on the seashore), key 36 the bare cross-reference 'See on Mt 13:10-17' belonging to 4:10-12, key 42 the stony ground of 4:5-6, key 48 the candle of 4:21. Crucially the donor content is NOT verse-aligned here and not even monotonic (key 42 draws from 4:5-6, which precedes what key 36 draws from). So the two halves of the defect behave differently: the mod-6 selection of TARGET keys is stable across three chapters now, while the donor mapping was exactly verse-aligned at 1corinthians 6 and is unordered here. Whatever produces the residue picks its target slots arithmetically and its content some other way. All 207 Jamieson words in this chapter are residue.

Lightfoot is entirely genuine and on-verse in mark 9 -- all five blocks (keys 1, 2, 38, 43, 49) sit on the right verses: the kingdom coming in power, the doubt about Tabor, the exorcist casting out devils in the name, the rabbinic canon on cutting off the hand, and Scaliger on being salted with fire. This is the negative control the acts 12 and 1corinthians 6 cases needed. Lightfoot residue is therefore per-chapter, not a property of the voice, which matches the rule recorded at acts 12: a voice cannot be classified at chapter level, only block by block -- and now also, a voice that carried residue in one chapter cannot be presumed to carry it in the next.

Six-way split on whether the worm and the fire are literal, preserved as a debate: Chrysostom denies a visible worm and makes it conscience, each man his own accuser; Gill presses conscience into detail; Wesley names the gnawings (pride, self-will, desire, malice, envy, shame, sorrow, despair); Barnes supposes no real worm and perhaps no material fire; Augustine weighs the question at length, reporting those who assign both to the soul and read the fire as burning grief, judging pain of body and soul alike more credible, and concluding it is easier to say both belong to the body than that neither does; Bede splits them, the worm accusing inwardly and the fire raging without. Separately Chrysostom, Bede and Wesley all take the hand, foot and eye as intimate friends rather than limbs -- against Gill and Lightfoot, who keep the wider sense and supply the rabbinic canons prescribing amputation.

Robertson states as plain fact that the Valley of Hinnom, desecrated by child sacrifice, was the city rubbish dump 'where worms gnawed and fires burned'. Ellicott allows the same picture only as a possibility and warns explicitly that 'the authorities are hardly definite enough to warrant the positive statement'. Recorded because it is a rare case in this corpus of one commentator flagging the evidentiary weakness of a claim another asserts flatly, and because the garbage-dump gloss is repeated everywhere in modern preaching; the prose gives both and marks which is the guarded one.

The Catena blocks filed under key 38 cover Mark 9:38-42 as a unit, so Gregory's material on the millstone and the depths of the sea sits at key 38 while belonging by sense to verse 42. Under the tiling used here (38-41 | 42-48) that material falls outside the entry it discusses and was deliberately NOT used in entry 42 -- the cross-span borrowing trap recorded at leviticus 5. Worth noting generally: catena sources group several verses under one key, so key number and verse number come apart for the patristic voices in a way they do not for the verse-by-verse commentators, and an entry boundary drawn on verse sense can cut a catena block in half.

CLARKE AND ELLICOTT USE THE SAME CLASSICAL TEXTS AGAINST EACH OTHER, TWICE IN ONE CHAPTER. (a) On the bees in the lion's carcase at v8, Clarke quotes Virgil's fourth Georgic at length on the swarm generated from a dead ox and treats it as evidence that such a thing was not infrequent among the ancients. Ellicott takes the same passage and calls it the vulgar error that has to be cleared away — bees do hate all putrescence — then rescues the narrative by the philology instead, the word rendered carcase meaning a sun-dried skeleton, supported by the head of Onesilus at Amathus which a swarm filled with combs, and by bees building between two skeletons buried at Verona in 1566. Keil reaches the same desiccation mechanism independently but rejects the skeleton reading as too little, since bees would not hive in bare bones. (b) On 'if ye had not plowed with my heifer' at v18, Clarke builds a charge of adultery on a wall of classical euphemism — Theognis, Plautus, Martial, Virgil, all using the ploughing of another man's ground in that sense — and reports the Greek version, the Syriac and Rabbi Levi Ben Gershom on his side. Ellicott dismisses it in one sentence: many commentators follow that rabbi in finding the implication, but there is no sufficient reason for it. Keil calls the proverb one 'whose meaning is perfectly clear' without saying what it is, which between two flatly opposed readings is itself a position. Filed because the pattern is instructive: the same erudition serves as corroboration for one commentator and as the error to be refuted for another, and a corpus scan for shared classical citations would surface pairs like these.

Calvin's exposition of v16 rests on the reading every other commentator here rejects. Ellicott, Clarke, Barnes and Robertson all take tines as interrogative (who provoked? was it not all?), Ellicott noting the oldest MSS carry no accents so the judgment is free, crediting Bengel with recovering it in modern times while an ancient Syriac version and three Greek fathers had it already. Calvin takes the indefinite (some), and builds a positive pastoral point on it: the milder word deliberately softens David's severity, avoids offence, and sets believing fathers before the readers as examples to imitate rather than commanding them to dissent from their fathers wholly. Recorded because the two readings are not a shade of meaning but two different arguments, and because the accent is editorial rather than manuscript evidence -- so this is a case where the corpus preserves a genuine pre-critical reading alongside the modern one.

Duplication watch: Ellicott quotes Bengel for the antithesis 'as Apostle Jesus pleads the cause of God with us; as High Priest He pleads our cause with God', and Wesley's note on the same verse is the same sentence almost verbatim ('The messenger of God, who pleads the cause of God with us. And High Priest - Who pleads our cause with God'). Wesley's Notes are known to follow Bengel closely, so this is one source reaching the page twice, not two agreeing voices -- the genesis 12 Henry/Wesley trap in a different pairing. Prose credits the antithesis to Bengel via Ellicott and gives Wesley only his distinctive compression of both titles into the single word Mediator.

Three separate structural questions in this one chapter turn on where a clause attaches, and the commentators disagree on all three: whether 'Wherefore' in v7 governs 'harden not' in v8 or 'take heed' in v12 (Robertson and Calvin's editors for the first, Ellicott and Calvin himself for the second); whether v15 attaches to v14, to v13, or opens a new paragraph (Ellicott, Robertson, and Calvin's editor canvassing all three, with Stuart and Bloomfield starting a paragraph); and whether the forty years in v9 belongs with what precedes or follows. Worth noting as a chapter-level feature: Hebrews 3 is unusually punctuation-dependent, and the commentators are explicit that the manuscripts give no help, since accents and stops are editorial. Any tiling of this chapter is therefore taking a side by implication; the one used here (1-2 | 3-6 | 7-11 | 12-13 | 14-15 | 16-19) keeps the quotation whole and does not prejudge v15.

THE CHAPTER'S REAL SUBJECT IS HOW PAUL USES SCRIPTURE, AND THE COMMENTATORS FACE IT SQUARELY. Three separate problems, each drawing multiple solutions. (1) At vv.6-8 Paul applies Deuteronomy 30:12-14, spoken of the LAW, to FAITH — and inserts 'that is, to bring Christ down'. Five answers: Calvin states the difficulty without softening it ('it seems to be improperly applied by Paul, and the words are also turned to a different meaning') and unties it by arguing that a law set before the eyes is no easier to keep than one far off, so Moses must have meant more; Ellicott concedes the original 'referred to that very law which the Apostle is depreciating' and calls the use allegorical; ROBERTSON IS CLEANEST — 'He does not quote Moses as saying this or meaning this', the phrases being borrowed for Paul's own conviction; Barnes says Moses nowhere described justification by faith but used language fitly expressing it; Theodoret changes the speaker, 'not Moses himself, but the God of all, through Moses'. (2) At v.7 the Hebrew asks who shall cross the SEA and Paul asks who shall descend into the ABYSS; Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson all note the substitution, Robertson crediting it to 'the orator's instinct'. (3) At vv.20-21 ELLICOTT MAKES TWO ADMISSIONS AGAINST INTEREST: the words applied to the Gentiles 'referred to the apostate Israel', and the following quotation comes from the very next verse of Isaiah, where 'there is no such distinction in the persons to whom it is addressed as the Apostle here draws'. Calvin sees the same adjacency and turns it the other way, showing the two sentences stand connected in the prophet and are reversed in the citation. Worth preserving as a set: this tradition does not hide the difficulty of its own proof-texts.

BARNES REASSIGNS THE SPEAKING PARTS OF THE CHAPTER — a structural reading I have not seen elsewhere. At v.16 he confesses the difficulty openly ('It is not easy to see the connexion... After all the attention which I have been able to give it, I am inclined to regard it as an admission of the apostle'). Then at v.17 he does something more drastic: 'So then faith cometh by hearing... This I take to be clearly the language of the objector.' On his reading the most famous sentence in the chapter is not Paul's own conclusion but the objector turning Isaiah back on Paul — if a report was necessary, men cannot be condemned for not obeying what never reached them. Every other commentator here (Calvin, Ellicott, Theodoret, Clarke) takes v.17 as the apostle's inference. ELLICOTT INDEPENDENTLY SEES THE SAME ROUGHNESS and repairs it differently, by interleaving: 'The argument does not run quite smoothly... He begins to introduce this second topic before he has quite done with the first. Romans 10:17 goes back to and connects logically with Romans 10:15, while Romans 10:16 anticipates Romans 10:19; 10:21.' Two commentators detecting one seam and cutting it in different places. Filed because a reader given only the majority reading would never know the verse was contested, and because the tags' prevalence field currently has no way to record that one voice assigns a verse to a different speaker altogether.

Tiling decision worth recording. Verses 11-12 form a clear pericope by sense (the woman who intervenes in a fight) but only two voices comment substantively -- Calvin 160 words and Gill 168 -- while the 528-word span puts it out of reach of the thin exemption, which requires a source blob of 200 visible words or fewer. Recorded because the gap between the thin exemption's 200-word ceiling and the 350-word floor is a real hole: a span of 200-600 source words with few voices has no honest option except merging, and merging is only available when an adjacent pericope will take it.

Calvin reads 'brethren' in the levirate law as kinsmen rather than actual brothers, and the argument is doctrinal rather than lexical: taking it literally would set the law against the incest prohibition, so that God would contradict himself; and he cites Boaz, who married Ruth as a near kinsman and not as a brother-in-law. Gill holds the literal sense and narrows it further from Maimonides -- brothers on the father's side only, since there is no brotherhood but on the father's side; Keil and Delitzsch keep the brother-in-law and note the verb is denominative, formed from the noun. Preserved as a debate because the two readings give different scopes to the whole law.

Gill reports the rabbinic reading of 'cut off her hand' as a price set upon the hand rather than an amputation (Jarchi), with Aben Ezra comparing the law of retaliation, which the same writers commonly understand of monetary compensation. No other voice in this chapter addresses whether the penalty was ever executed literally, and Calvin argues the opposite way -- that the severity is the point and that the clause forbidding pity exists so judges should not be remiss in inflicting it. Both are in the prose. Noting it because the chapter is a rare case where the corpus preserves a live rabbinic mitigation of a hard text alongside a Reformation reading that insists on its harshness, and a synthesis that reported only one of them would misrepresent the witnesses.

Jamieson residue stream, final refinement of the model. genesis 13 carries NO Jamieson blocks at all. A scan of Genesis 1-20 shows why: where the stream is emitting, the residue lands on a strict stride of 6 target keys (gen 5 at keys 1,7,13,19 - a full stride), but blocks are DROPPED from stride slots where the source stream has nothing to say (gen 10 at 5,11,17,29 with 23 missing; gen 6, 13 and 14 carry none whatever). The command to walk the length and breadth of the land is read in two opposite directions, and the split is not confessional. Gill takes it as survey and seisin and adds the Targum of Jonathan's note that a possession was legally made by walking; Wesley reads it as enter and take possession, the land appearing better than on a distant prospect; Ellicott makes it the ordinary necessity of nomad life and adds the pleasure of knowing the seed will inherit each spot visited. Calvin reads the same command as designed to produce the contrary conviction - that Abram may 'more clearly perceive himself to be a stranger' and, 'exhausted by continual and fruitless disquietude', despair of any stable possession, since he is 'scarcely permitted to drink water' from wells he dug himself. The three take the circuit as an act of ownership; Calvin takes it as the exercise that removes the sense of ownership. A prevalence field counting three against one would misrepresent this: it is not a majority reading with a dissenter but two incompatible construals of the same imperative.

Index Next:'. So there are two independent scraper sources with the same end-of-document failure, of very different severity: Ellicott 100 percent affected at ~930 words each, Gill 9 percent affected at ~25 words each. The Gill case is small enough to be cosmetic; the Ellicott case is not. Both are detectable by fixed markers and could be truncated at ingest in the same pass.

Four-way split on whether this chapter's restoration promise is fulfilled or future, preserved across two entries. Clarke: a dispersion among all nations means a wider captivity than the Babylonian, so the repossession must be other than the return from Chaldea -- yet he also holds that the promise belongs to the days of the Messiah and cannot be fulfilled to the Jews except in their embracing the gospel, making it 'idle and nugatory' to look for a national restoration while unbelief remains. Gill: a future return to Judea is the plain sense, and he places some of the dispersed in Britain and (on Manasseh Ben Israel's belief) America. Ellicott: very difficult to read the words of any land but Palestine, cites Jeremiah for fulfilment in the first restoration, yet notes the curse still stands. Keil and Delitzsch: the promise 'neither points directly to the gathering of Israel from dispersion on its ultimate conversion to Christ, nor furnishes any proof that the Jews will then be brought back to Palestine.' Recorded because Clarke holds two positions that pull against each other and a synthesis that flattened him either way would misreport him.

Clarke and Calvin argue opposite doctrines from the same two verses, and both do it explicitly rather than by implication -- an unusually clean pair. On v15 Clarke builds a full case for free will: were there no such thing, nobody could reconcile these sayings with sincerity or common sense; God made the will free in creation, no power in heaven, earth or hell save God's own can deprive it of its volitions, law and gospel alike are constructed on that ground, accountability follows because a man's actions are his, and liberty is implied in the very idea of volition. On v19 Calvin names that exact move as the enemy's: granting that the law ministers death because no one is found worthy of its reward, he says opponents 'uplift their crests' here 'both to extol free-will and to boast of merits', and answers that Moses also proclaims gratuitous mercy and directs his disciples to Christ. Both are in the prose, in adjacent entries, each stated at its own strength.

Calvin explicitly refuses the reading Gill offers as an option. On 'I call heaven and earth to record', Gill allows either the literal inanimate bodies or, figuratively, their inhabitants -- angels and men. Calvin: the words 'do not address men and angels, as some tamely expound it', but attribute sense to things inanimate by way of amplification. Worth recording as a case where the corpus contains an explicit rebuttal of one witness's alternative by another, which is rarer than simple divergence and is the kind of thing a synthesis should surface rather than average out.

Eight entries tiling all 23 keys, all in window: 1-3 648w, 4-6 633w, 7-9 649w, 10-12 649w, 13-15 650w, 16-18 649w, 19-21 648w, 22-23 649w. Twelve voices carry heads; nine are used (Barnes 23 blocks, Gill 23, Clarke 23, Calvin 22, Robertson 22, Ellicott 20, Wesley 22, Henry 7, Chrysostom 3). Jamieson (4 blocks) is declared as residue, Lightfoot (2) declared as misfiled, Cyril of Jerusalem (3) silenced as florilegium. Every named attribution checked against a head inside its own span. Two traps avoided: Robertson's k12 block quotes Lightfoot by name for the palace-and-mud-hut phrase, but Lightfoot has no head in span 10-12, so the phrase is reported unattributed; Robertson's k13 block cites Ellicott by name for the anti-purgatorial reading, and there Ellicott DOES have heads in the same span, so the citation is reported as made. Every scripture reference in prose is a .ref link.

Jamieson residue: the cleanest lag measurement in the corpus so far, and it confirms the two-stream model at a new point. Four blocks at keys 2, 8, 14, 20 - stride 6 from offset 2, no gap. All four are Jamieson on ACTS 17, in order: k2 the Epicureans and Stoics (17:18), k8 'God that made the world' (17:24), k14 'graven by art and man's device' (17:29), k20 the Greeks and the Resurrection (17:32). Source advances 17:18 to 17:24 to 17:29 to 17:32 across the four slots - about 5 source verses per 6 target keys, the same rate measured at judges 14. LAG: 1corinthians 3 is NT chapter 136 (28+16+24+21+28+16+3); Acts 17 is NT chapter 106; lag = 30. The NT series predicts 0.23 x 136 = 31.3. Measured 30. That is the eleventh contiguous-region confirmation and the closest fit yet, at a position between the romans 10 and galatians 1 anchors.

NEW DEFECT FAMILY: Barnes's chapter-level front and back matter is keyed to the first and last verses of the chapter. The k1 block (1200w) opens 'CHAPTER 3 THE design of this chapter is substantially the same as the former' - that is his chapter introduction, not a note on v1. The k23 block (3246w) carries his verse note and then his whole end-of-chapter 'Remarks' section, a numbered series of practical inferences on the entire chapter, ending '(24.) Christians Should regard themselves as devoted to the Saviour.' Both are genuinely authorial - none of the chrome markers appear ('Copyright Statement', 'public domain', 'This is part N of M Parts', 'Due to space limitations', 'Continuation of Barnes Notes') - so this is NOT the Ellicott chrome family and NOT the Barnes splice family already catalogued. It is a third thing: real commentary at the wrong granularity, chapter-level material presented as verse-level. Consequence: Barnes's first and last keys in every chapter are inflated far above his own median (here ~500w), which corrupts any per-verse length statistic and makes him look like the dominant voice at exactly the two keys where an entry most needs balance.

Lightfoot misfiling, and a probable MECHANISM for it. Two blocks, both at the 200 cap, both wrong. k1 opens 'ADDENDA TO CHAP. XIV.' - his appendix to 1 Corinthians 14 on what Bibles were read in Jewish meetings; wrong chapter. k5 opens 'ver. 5, were saved. For those words achris hou to pleroma ton ethnon eiselthe' - that is ROMANS 11:25, the fulness of the Gentiles; wrong book. Note where it landed: the block's own internal running marker reads 'ver. 5', and it was filed at key 5. That suggests the splitter keys Lightfoot blocks by the 'ver. N' string inside the note rather than by context, which would also explain the 1corinthians 10 case, where a block carrying the running head 'Ch.x.17.' landed on key 11 rather than 17 (the head there names a chapter-and-verse, so a naive scan for the first number would pick up something else). If that is right the fix is cheap and mechanical: parse the running marker properly and re-key, or drop blocks whose marker disagrees with their key. Both blocks here are DECLARED rather than silenced, being identifiable authorial material from elsewhere.

Cyril of Jerusalem is a florilegium here too - THIRD book confirming it, and the second with byte-identical duplicates. Three blocks, all at exactly the 200 cap. k12 and k13 are IDENTICAL, both being Catechetical Lecture 15 on the two comings of Christ, opening '2. And concerning these two comings, Malachi the Prophet says...'. k16 is a different lecture again, on the identity of the Holy Spirit with the Comforter and the Spirit of Truth, which comments on nothing in v16 beyond sharing the word Spirit. Compare ephesians 6, where k1=k3 and k17=k18 were byte-identical, and 1thessalonians 2, where his single block was on 2 Cor 4:4. All three silenced rather than declared, because synthesis_qa.VOICE_LABELS holds the bare 'Cyril' with a regex demanding a colon immediately after the label, so the head 'Cyril of Jerusalem:' cannot be emitted through excluded_voices at all. That prefix bug is now blocking correct declaration in four chapters and should be fixed alongside the Cyril of Jerusalem / Cyril of Alexandria disambiguation.

Attributed borrowing, and a rare case of two commentators disagreeing on a bibliographical fact. (a) Robertson's block at k13 argues the fire is 'a metaphor that must not be understood as purgatorial, but simple testing' and credits Ellicott by name; Ellicott's own block two verses later says the same thing independently in the chapter's own catena, adding that Roman divines evolved purgatory from a literal reading. So the corpus contains both the borrower and the source, with the debt acknowledged - the same shape as Keil citing Calvin at deuteronomy 8, and the opposite of Barnes copying Clarke unattributed at galatians 1 and Ellicott reproducing Keil unattributed at 1samuel 3. (b) At k19 the two men disagree about the New Testament's use of Job. Ellicott says that apart from James 5:11 on the proverbial patience of Job - where the writer says the readers have HEARD, not read - this is the only allusion to the book anywhere in the New Testament. Robertson says Job is quoted in the New Testament only here and at Romans 11:35, both times varying from the Septuagint. They are counting different things (allusions vs quotations) and neither says so, which is exactly the kind of apparent agreement-or-disagreement the prevalence field cannot currently represent.

Two substantial exegetical splits in this chapter, both worth surfacing to readers. (1) At v9 the compound synergoi divides the whole bench four ways, and the split is not confessional. Barnes lays out both senses without choosing - co-workers WITH God in a joint work, or workers BELONGING to God. Clarke argues for the second, rendering it 'fellow labourers of God' with Bishop Pearce, on the ground that the preposition may join the teachers to one another rather than to God. Robertson takes the first boldly: 'God is the major partner in the enterprise of each life, but he lets us work with him.' Calvin takes the first too and makes it the commendation of the ministry, that God who could do the whole himself calls 'puny mortals' to be his coadjutors. Wesley declines to choose and keeps both at once. Five positions on one preposition, from four schools, with the two grammatical-historical voices on opposite sides of it. (2) At v13 Clarke alone refers the whole day-and-fire passage to the approaching destruction of Jerusalem rather than to the last judgment, and says that read so 'all the terms and metaphors will appear clear and consistent'. Everyone else takes it eschatologically. Barnes hedges toward a third reading, that 'day' may simply mean time in general, as we say time will show.

Ellicott end-of-chapter chrome tail, TWELFTH measurement: k23 is 1119 raw words of which only about 137 comment on v23, the remainder being the usual trailer, cut here at the marker '1 Corinthians 1Co 2 1 Corinthians 1Co'. Caps confirmed again per feed: 200 for Gill (five blocks at exactly 200 - k9, k10, k16, k22, k23), 200 for Lightfoot (both blocks), 200 for Cyril of Jerusalem (all three). Two smaller items for the tooling list. Barnes at k4 is an eighteen-word body consisting solely of a cross-reference and a marginal-reference letter code - 'For while one saith, etc. 1 Corinthians 1:12. (c) I am of Paul 1 Corinthians 1:12' - with no comment at all; that is the bare-scripture-reference body already on the owner's list, and it now has a concrete instance to test against. And Robertson's k8 block carries a dateable authorial aside, 'the dreadful drouth of 1930 testifies while these words are written', which is useful as a provenance marker for that feed's edition.

Jamieson residue at keys 6 and 18 -- two members, both congruent to 0 mod 6 and twelve apart. Donor is GENESIS 29: key 6 carries JFB on the well at Haran (the covering not removed until all the flocks are collected in the owner's presence, and the three flocks waiting for Rachel), key 18 on the three days' hospitality among pastoral people and the wages for which Jacob engaged to stay, the hand of Rachel. The donor passages sit about twelve verses apart (roughly 29:3 and 29:15) as the target keys do, so the mapping here looks like a CONSTANT OFFSET of about minus three -- the verse-aligned family again but shifted rather than exact. Only two data points and JFB block boundaries span several verses, so the offset is approximate. Both Jamieson blocks in the chapter are residue: 148 words, none on Genesis 33. Running tally, seven chapters: target-key selection has been mod-6 in every single case, while the donor mapping has been exactly verse-aligned twice, offset-aligned once (here), forward-walked with irregular step twice, unordered once, and constant replication once.

Clarke and Ellicott report the SAME scribal evidence and draw opposite conclusions from it. Both note the extraordinary points the Masoretes set over the word for 'and he kissed him' in Genesis 33:4. Clarke says the rabbis dotted each letter to make the word emphatic, and that they meant thereby to draw attention to the reality of the change in Esau and the sincerity of his welcome. Ellicott says the Masorites are supposed to have signified by the same marks that Esau's kiss was NOT a sign of genuine love, and adds that 'for such an ill-natured supposition there is no warrant whatsoever'. Recorded because it is the clearest case yet in this corpus of two commentators citing one piece of manuscript evidence for contradictory readings of a character; both are in the prose, unreconciled.

Calvin charges Jacob with lying about following Esau to Seir, and stands alone against four. His case: the reasons alleged (tender children, flocks with young) are true but urged under false pretexts, since Jacob afterwards turned his journey in another direction, so he promised what he did not intend; and the principle is pressed hard, that 'truth is so precious to God, that he will not allow us to lie or deceive, even when no injury follows'. Against him: his OWN EDITOR prints a rebuttal beneath the text, that there is no reason to doubt Jacob meant what he said, that he may have had other reasons for avoiding close intercourse with an irreligious man, that it is by no means certain he never went to Seir (though he would have gone without wives and flocks), and that the silence of the sacred writers proves neither that he failed to go nor that he did not intend to, which is all sincerity required. Clarke supposes him perfectly sincere and later prevented; Wesley presumes the visit was made and simply not recorded; Ellicott thinks the purpose lapsed because Esau had not yet settled at Seir. Preserved as a debate rather than harmonised, because Calvin's reading turns on a moral principle he states explicitly and the others do not engage.

Wesley reproduces Henry almost verbatim twice in this chapter, at keys 5 and 16. Key 5: Wesley's 'Eleven or twelve little ones followed Jacob, the eldest of them not fourteen years old: Who are these? saith Esau. Jacob had sent him an account of the increase of his estate, but made no mention of his children, perhaps because he would not expose them to his rage, if he should meet him as an enemy' is Henry's sentence with the clauses barely altered. Key 16: Wesley's paragraph on Succoth ('Having in a friendly manner parted with Esau, who was gone to his own country, he comes to a place, where he rested, set up booths for his cattle...') is again Henry abridged, down to the Deuteronomy 26:5 citation about the Syrian ready to perish. Wesley's OT Notes are known to condense Henry, and this is the third chapter where the duplication has surfaced (genesis 12 first, measured by difflib at 67 percent shared words on one key). Consequence if unnoticed: Henry is puritan-evangelical and Wesley wesleyan-arminian in the school map, so prevalence would report two schools agreeing where there is one source. Prose credits Henry for the shared material and gives Wesley only what is his own.

Five entries tiling all 20 keys, all in window: 1-4 650w, 5-8 648w, 9-12 640w, 13-16 646w, 17-20 647w. Only five voices carry heads in this chapter and all five are used: Ellicott 20 blocks, Gill 20, Clarke 14, Keil 13, Henry 3. No Wesley, no Calvin, no Jamieson anywhere. Nothing is declared or silenced; every block that exists is drawn on. Every named attribution checked against a head inside its own span - Henry is present only at k1, k9 and k18, so entries 5-8 and 13-16 carry four voices and three schools rather than five and four, and no cross-entry reference to him was made. Every scripture reference in prose is a .ref link.

Jamieson residue: judges 15 carries NO blocks at all, and judges 14 immediately before it carries a FULL stride - keys 3, 9 and 15, on Deuteronomy 32:5, 32:10 and 32:15, advancing exactly 5 source verses per 6 target keys. Two adjacent chapters, one saturated and the next empty. That is the sharpest available test of the dropped-slot refinement first noted at genesis 13, and it passes: the stride belongs to the SLOT, not to the content, and blocks are simply absent where the emitting stream has nothing to give. It also rules out any explanation that keys the residue to properties of the target chapter, since judges 14 and 15 are the same book, the same length (20 keys each), the same narrative, and adjacent in the canon. Whatever governs presence or absence lives entirely on the source side.

A fully documented disagreement over a classical parallel, with both parties naming the same third scholar. At v5 Ellicott adduces Ovid's Fasti iv.681-711 - the Roman Cerealia custom of loosing foxes with torches tied to their tails in the circus, in memory of a boy at Carseoli whose burning fox fled into the standing corn - and then says flatly that 'the attempt of Bochart to establish any connection between this custom and the revenge of Samson is quite untenable', allowing only that the incident shows the thing possible. At v20 Clarke reproduces the SAME passage at much greater length, quotes four lines of the Latin, gives the old man of Carseoli's whole story, and reports that 'both Serrarius and Bochart reject this origin of the custom given by Ovid; and insist that the custom took its rise from the burning of the Philistines' corn by Samson's foxes' - siding with them. So within one chapter two commentators cite one classical source and one modern authority and reach opposite conclusions about derivation, each without knowing the other is in the room. This is a fourth kind of relation for the prevalence field, distinct from the three already catalogued (transmission, independent observation, concealed disagreement): shared source, named intermediary, opposite verdict.

Two more clean splits in this chapter, both worth surfacing. (1) THE NAME LEHI, and a commentator contradicting himself across four verses is not the issue - two commentators contradict each other. At v9 Ellicott argues the etymology may run BACKWARDS: the name is used before the incident said to have produced it, exactly as Hormah is used before its own naming; the word for the place and the word for jawbone are not identical; and since 'tooth' is elsewhere the name of an isolated sharp rock, 'jaw' would be a natural name for a range of such rocks - so the place may have been called Lehi already and the pun fitted to it afterwards. He reports honestly that Josephus says the place had no name before. At v16 Keil says the opposite outright: 'This seems to indicate that the name Lechi in Judges 15:9 is used proleptically, and that the place first received its name from this deed of Samson.' Gill sides with Keil in passing at v14. Two grammatical-historical voices, opposite conclusions, neither aware of the other. (2) THE SPRING at v19. Gill gives first the reading that the water came from a tooth-socket in the jawbone and remarks that blood would more naturally have issued from it, then reports the Targum's 'the rock which was in the jaw', and ends undecided, leaning to the rock. Clarke settles it from the text: the fountain is said to be in Lehi 'unto this day', therefore it cannot have been in the bone - 'a most unfortunate rendering'. Ellicott is contemptuous, calling the jawbone-fountain 'one of the childish misinterpretations with which Scripture exegesis is constantly defaced', and explains the spring's name as one more turn of the chapter's punning: once the cliff was called Jawbone, its spring would naturally be called a tooth-socket.

Ellicott end-of-chapter chrome tail, THIRTEENTH measurement, and a near-exact repeat of its neighbour: judges 15 k20 is 1058 raw words of which only about 76 comment on v20, against judges 14 k20 at 1063 words for about 90. Same slot, same size, same feed, adjacent chapters - which is further evidence that the tail is generated per chapter by the same mechanism and not by anything in the text. Caps confirmed again: Keil 12 of 13 blocks at exactly 200, only k19 (at 58) under, the identical 12-of-13 split as judges 14; Gill at exactly 200 twice, k4 and k19. One thing worth flagging for the re-fetch list: Clarke's k4 block runs to 841 words and his k20 to 679, both far above his median here of about 100, and both are genuine authorial content - the k4 block is his full defence of the number of the foxes and the k20 block is the Ovid excursus. So a length-based heuristic for detecting chrome would take two of Clarke's best blocks in this chapter and leave Ellicott's actual chrome untouched, since at 1058 it is only marginally longer. Only the copyright marker discriminates, thirteen for thirteen.

Four entries tiling all 18 keys, all in window: 1-4 649w, 5-8 649w, 9-12 650w, 13-18 617w. Six voices carry heads; five are used (Gill 18 blocks, Ellicott 17, Keil 10, Clarke 9, Henry 3) and Jamieson (2) is declared as residue at entries 1 and 13. FOUR entries rather than five: keys 13-15 carry only about 670 usable source words and 16-18 about 580 once the Ellicott chrome at k18 is cut, so split into separate entries both would have been far too thin to fill the window honestly; merged, 13-18 has about 1,250 words behind 617, which is still the leanest ratio in the chapter and is why that entry runs shortest. Every named attribution checked against a head inside its own span; Henry has heads only at k1, k6 and k10, so entry 13-18 carries four voices and three schools. Every scripture reference in prose is a .ref link.

Jamieson residue: a THIRD Judges measurement, and it interpolates cleanly between the other two. Two blocks, keys 3 and 15 - congruent to 3 mod 6, the SAME offset as judges 14 (keys 3, 9, 15), with key 9 a dropped slot in the middle, exactly the genesis 13 pattern. Source is DEUTERONOMY 29 in order: k3 is Dt 29:2-8 (the appeal to their own memory of the Exodus miracles and of the territory just acquired) and k15 is Dt 29:10-22 (the whole congregation assembled to renew the covenant), the second block citing De 29:12 and De 29:22 by name. LAG: judges 10 is canonical chapter 221 (50+40+27+36+34+24+10), Deuteronomy 29 is 182, so lag 39. Judges 14 gave 225 against Deuteronomy 32 at 185, lag 40. Four chapters apart, lag grows by exactly one, which is the 0.16 OT slope. Three Judges chapters now measured: 10 (lag 39, offset 3, one slot dropped), 14 (lag 40, offset 3, full stride), 15 (no blocks at all). The model holds at every point, and the two neighbours 14 and 15 - same book, same length, adjacent - differing between a full stride and nothing at all remains the strongest evidence that presence is governed entirely on the source side.

Ellicott end-of-chapter chrome tail, FOURTEENTH measurement and the third consecutive Judges chapter at the last key: judges 10 k18 is 1024 raw words of which about 42 comment on v18, against judges 15 k20 at 1058 for about 76 and judges 14 k20 at 1063 for about 90. Three chapters running, same slot, sizes within 40 words of each other while the genuine content varies by a factor of two - which is as clear as this can get that the tail is generated per chapter and is independent of the text it is attached to. Caps: Keil 9 of 10 blocks at exactly 200, only k18 (at 37) under. And that k18 block is the SECOND instance of the structural artefact first recorded at genesis 13 k15: its 37 words are nothing but the reprinted text of v18, with no comment of any kind. Here it did not need silencing because Keil is used elsewhere in the same entry, but a chapter where such a block fell alone in its span would produce a false ghost. Worth teaching the tooling to recognise a block whose body is a verbatim reprint of its own verse.

Three splits in this chapter worth surfacing. (1) HOW THE DIVINE ANSWER CAME, at v11, produces five distinct positions from five voices, which is the widest spread I have met on a single question. Gill lists the candidates (a prophet, as two rabbis hold, whom a third takes for Phinehas though he could not then have been living; a created angel; or the uncreated one in human form). Clarke leaves it open - 'by what means these reproofs were conveyed to the Israelites, we know not'. Henry cannot decide between the angel of ch.2 and the prophet of ch.6. Keil RULES OUT both, from the silence: 'not to be regarded as having been given through an extraordinary manifestation (theophany), or through the medium of a prophet, for that would certainly have been recorded'. Ellicott proposes there was no messenger at all - 'the method of the Divine communication is not specified. A stern experience might have spoken to the national conviction with prophetic voice.' (2) HOW MANY GODS are listed at v6: Keil and Ellicott independently count SEVEN and independently call the count significant, each matching it to the seven nations of vv.11-12 (Keil 'unmistakeable', Ellicott 'obvious symmetry'), neither citing the other - a clean independent-observation case. Clarke numbers FIVE, pairing nation with deity. (3) THE RETRACTED THREAT at v13: 'I will deliver you no more' is reversed three verses later, and the two grammatical-historical voices solve it differently - Ellicott by making the threat conditional as elsewhere in Scripture, Keil by distinguishing God's nature from his attitude, 'the change in the purpose of God does not imply any changeableness in the divine nature'.

Jamieson residue, EIGHTH chapter and a THIRD residue class for the target-key rule. Every affected key here is congruent to 4 mod 6 (4, 10, 16, 22) - four members, the largest set yet after nehemiah 7's seven. Mod-6 selection now holds in eight chapters out of eight with three classes observed: 0 (mark 9, deuteronomy 30, nehemiah 7), 2 (philippians 3, 1corinthians 6, hebrews 3), 4 (deuteronomy 25, ephesians 2). The donor is ROMANS, read as a forward walk that crosses the donor's own chapter boundary: k4 carries JFB on Rom 11:25 (the mystery, blindness in part until the fulness of the Gentiles), k10 on Rom 11:30-31, k16 on Rom 11:34 (who hath known the mind of the Lord), k22 on Rom 12:3 (not to think of himself more highly than he ought). Donor advances about four or five verses per step while the target advances six - the same sub-unit slope recorded at deuteronomy 30 (5/6), and the same boundary crossing recorded at philippians 3. All 362 Jamieson words in the chapter are residue; not one sentence is on Ephesians 2. Declared excluded on the four entries containing those keys (1-3 is the only span with no JFB at all besides 11-13).

The chapter-final key carries TWO independent junk payloads at once, which is the first time I have seen them stacked. (1) Ellicott k22 is 1200 words of which about 230 are genuine comment on v22; the remaining ~970 are the StudyLight page chrome measured corpus-wide earlier today (870 of 870 chapter-final Ellicott blocks carry it, median 926 words, range 926-1227). Fifth hand-confirmation, and the size sits squarely inside the fixed-template range. (2) Barnes k22 is 2434 words of which about 90 are comment on v22; the rest is a REMARKS essay - eleven numbered reflections on the whole chapter, opening 'we were by nature dead in sin, Ephesians 2:1' and walking the argument back through the chapter. This is the Barnes section-overflow pattern, but note the difference from the usual case: it is not commentary displaced from a neighbouring verse, it is a chapter-summary genre parked in the last verse slot. Together the two payloads make k22 5072 raw words, the largest key in the chapter by a factor of 1.7, of which perhaps 1400 are usable. Any word-budget computed from raw key size will badly over-estimate the last span in a chapter that has both.

The v8 pronoun question produces a rare thing: the commentators agree on the grammar and disagree about who disagrees. Barnes, Clarke, Robertson and Wesley all reach the same verdict - the pronoun is neuter, faith is feminine (Robertson adds that grace is feminine too), so the antecedent is the act of being saved by grace. What splits is the doxography. Barnes names 'Doddridge, Beza, Piscator and Chrysostom' among those who refer the pronoun to faith; the editorial note printed with Calvin cites Chrysostom - with Theodoret and Theophylact - for exactly the contrary reading, and quotes Theophylact saying that he does not call faith the gift but being saved by faith. So the same father is enlisted on both sides within one chapter of one catena. Barnes himself defuses it by calling the point theologically small. Worth flagging as a class: where a commentator reports what an earlier writer held rather than quoting him, the report is a claim about a source we do not have in the pool, and two such reports can contradict each other with neither being checkable from inside the catena. I wrote it up as the disagreement it is rather than picking a winner.

The v20 foundation is the sharpest three-way in the chapter. (1) WHICH PROPHETS: Ellicott argues at length that they cannot be the Old Testament prophets - word order, the comparison with 3:5 and 4:11, and the present-against-past emphasis running through the chapter, which he calls decisive 'in spite of much ancient and valuable authority'. Barnes, Gill and Clarke all take them as the Old Testament prophets, Barnes reading the pair as revealed doctrine at large. Three to one, and the one is the only voice that argues the point rather than assuming it. (2) IN WHAT SENSE A FOUNDATION: Ellicott canvasses three readings - the foundation on which apostles and prophets rest, the foundation they laid, the men themselves - dismisses the first two as forced and out of step with the corner-stone clause, and adopts the third with most ancient authorities, noting that modern commentators put it aside from reluctance to give any but Christ that name. Calvin holds the doctrine reading and says Christ alone strictly supports the church. (3) The two also split on v21 'all the building' vs 'each several building', Robertson pressing the missing article and Ellicott defending the received rendering while allowing 'every act of building'.

Tiling a 50,540-word chapter into six. Ephesians 2 is 22 contiguous keys and sits above the ~40k single-chapter-batch threshold, so it was the whole batch. Source words per span came out 11,123 / 5,666 / 5,653 / 6,847 / 10,117 / 10,827 - a 2:1 spread, and deliberately so: the boundaries were set by the argument (dead in sins; but God, rich in mercy; by grace through faith; remember, ye were Gentiles; he is our peace; no more strangers) and then the thin middle sections were widened rather than the fat ends split. The 19-22 span looks heavy at 10,827 raw words but is the lightest in usable terms once the Ellicott chrome and the Barnes REMARKS essay are taken out of k22 - about 4,600. Compression per entry ran 0.06 to 0.11 of raw source, the lowest ratios I have recorded, which is what a 50k chapter distilled to 3,704 words of prose looks like; every entry landed grade A in the 350-650 window with no flags on the first assembly. The lesson for future picks in this size class: budget by USABLE words per span, not raw, or the last span of an epistle chapter will look twice the work it is.

Chrysostom appears in this chapter at three keys only (1, 11, 17; 1,020 words total) and is absent from every other key, which matters for per-entry attribution. Entry 8 (keys 8-10) names Chrysostom in its prose, but only as a figure REPORTED by Barnes and by Calvin's editor in the pronoun dispute - there is no Chrysostom block anywhere in that span. Entry 19 likewise carries 'a remark Ellicott draws from Chrysostom' on the corner-stone binding walls and foundations, again with no block. Because voice grounding is chapter-wide, declaring Chrysostom on either entry would have PASSED the validator while being a false attribution at the pericope level. Declared him only on entries 1 and 11, where he actually speaks. This is the concrete case the loop doc's 'drop, don't launder' rule is aimed at, and it will recur in every chapter where a father is quoted inside a modern commentator: the chapter-wide grounding check cannot see the difference, so the writer has to.

Four entries tiling all 18 keys, all in window: 1-4 648w, 5-8 650w, 9-12 645w, 13-18 634w. Seven voices carry heads; six are used (Gill 18 blocks, Ellicott 12, Clarke 11, Keil 10, Wesley 8, Henry 3) and Jamieson (3) is declared as residue at entries 5, 9 and 13. FOUR entries rather than five, for the same reason as judges 10: keys 16-18 carry only about 550 usable source words once the Ellicott chrome at k18 is cut, far too thin to fill the window alone, so 13-18 is one entry. Two attribution traps avoided: Gill's k13 block cites Lightfoot by name for the scribal marks, and Lightfoot is a voice the corpus knows elsewhere but has no head in this chapter, so the observation is reported as 'one scholar'; Ellicott's k10 block cites Origen on Ruth as the engrafted wild olive, and Origen likewise has no head here, so he is reported as 'an early father'. Every scripture reference in prose is a .ref link.

THE TIGHTEST ATTRIBUTED-BORROWING CASE IN THE CORPUS SO FAR, and both parties are in the same chapter at the same key. At k14 Ellicott writes: 'A sensible man like Boaz knows that we must not only keep a good conscience, but keep a good name; we must avoid not only sin but scandal. (Henry.)' Henry's own block at THE SAME KEY reads: 'We must always take care, not only to keep a good conscience, but to keep a good name... We must avoid not only sin, but scandal.' So the catena contains the source and the borrower side by side, the quotation is verbatim but for the compression, and the debt is acknowledged by name. Compare the four relations already catalogued: unattributed transmission (Barnes copying Clarke at galatians 1; Ellicott reproducing Keil at 1samuel 3), attributed transmission across confessions (Keil citing Calvin at deuteronomy 8; Robertson citing Ellicott at 1corinthians 3), genuine independent observation (Wesley and Ellicott at 1thessalonians 2; Keil and Ellicott on the seven idols at judges 10), and shared-source-opposite-verdict (Ellicott and Clarke over Ovid at judges 15). This is the cleanest specimen of the second kind, and the only one where the quoted text sits at the identical key - which makes it the natural test case if the prevalence field is ever taught to detect transmission automatically.

Jamieson residue: a FOURTH measurement, and the first outside Judges in this run. Three blocks at keys 5, 11 and 17 - stride 6, offset 5, a full stride with no gap. Source is JOSHUA 7, the Achan narrative, in order: k5 is Jos 7:6-9 (the fast and Joshua's prayer after the repulse at Ai), k11 is Jos 7:10-15 (the oracle - not unfaithfulness in Me but sin in the people, the spoil reserved from the doomed city), k17 is Jos 7:16-21 (the lot taken tribe by tribe down to Achan's confession, with Jos 7:19-21 cited in the block). Source advances 7:6 to 7:10 to 7:16, i.e. +4 and +6 verses per 6 target keys, averaging the measured 5-per-6 rate exactly. LAG: ruth 3 is canonical chapter 235 (50+40+27+36+34+24+21+3); Joshua 7 is 194 (50+40+27+36+34+7). Lag = 41. Set against judges 10 at 221/lag 39 and judges 14 at 225/lag 40: fourteen chapters on from judges 10 the lag grows by two, and 14 x 0.16 = 2.24. Four OT points now agree - genesis 28, exodus 39, numbers 1, deuteronomy 8, judges 10, judges 14, 1samuel 3 and ruth 3 - and the model predicts a new book correctly, which it had not previously been tested on.

Two splits worth surfacing. (1) THE FIGURE OF THE WING at v9, where the two grammatical-historical voices take opposite sides and one wesleyan voice argues against his own best evidence. Clarke: 'The wing is the emblem of protection, and is a metaphor taken from the young of fowls, which run under the wings of their mothers, that they may be saved from birds of prey.' Keil flatly denies it: 'the figurative expression is not taken from birds, which spread their wings over their young... but refers, according to Deuteronomy 23:1, 27:20 and Ezekiel 16:8, to the wing, i.e., the corner of the counterpane, referring to the fact that a man spreads this over his wife as well as himself.' Ellicott holds both, illustrating from Ezekiel 16:8 (marriage) and Matthew 23:37 (the bird gathering her brood). What makes this worth recording is that Clarke, arguing for the bird, supplies the decisive evidence for Keil's reading: 'Even to the present day, when a Jew marries a woman, he throws the skirt or end of his talith over her.' (2) A TEXTUAL VARIANT WITH NARRATIVE CONSEQUENCE at v15, raised by Ellicott alone: 'This should be, if we follow the current Hebrew text, HE went. The verb is masculine, and the distinction is shewn in the Targum, which inserts the name Boaz as the nominative. It must be allowed that a fair number of Hebrew MSS., as well as the Peshito and Vulgate, take the verb in the feminine. The LXX. is from the nature of the Greek language unable to mark the distinction.' On the masculine reading Boaz leaves for the city to find the nearer kinsman at once, which changes who is acting in the closing scene. No other voice in the chapter mentions the variant at all.

Ellicott end-of-chapter chrome tail, FIFTEENTH measurement: ruth 3 k18 is 1004 raw words of which about 22 comment on v18. That is the smallest genuine remainder yet recorded behind one of these tails - roughly 2 percent of the block - and it comes in a new book, so the tail is not a Judges artefact. Running series at the last key: judges 14 k20 1063/~90, judges 15 k20 1058/~76, judges 10 k18 1024/~42, ruth 3 k18 1004/~22. Four consecutive chapters across two books, raw sizes within 60 words of each other while the authorial content falls steadily from 90 words to 22 - which is about as direct a demonstration as the data can give that the tail is a fixed per-chapter emission and carries no relation whatever to the text it is appended to. Caps confirmed again: Keil 9 of 10 blocks at exactly 200, only k17 (at 59) under; Gill at exactly 200 twice, k7 and k13.
