Jamieson residue, NINTH chapter, and the FIRST time a residue class has repeated on consecutive picks: keys 4, 10 and 16 are all congruent to 4 mod 6, exactly as Ephesians 2 was (4/10/16/22) in the batch before this one. Mod-6 target selection now holds in nine chapters out of nine, with three classes seen (0, 2, 4) and class 4 now twice running. The donor here is ACTS 28, read as a forward walk. Key 4 carries JFB on Acts 28:7-11 - 'the first man' of Malta, with the argument that this was the proper official title of the Maltese representative of the Roman praetor to Sicily, confirmed by two inscriptions found on the island, one Greek and one Latin; plus Julius and the winter lodgings. Key 10 is Acts 28:12, Syracuse, 'about eighty miles, or a day's sail, north from Malta'. Key 16 is Acts 28:16, arrival at Rome, the Jews there under Nero, and Felix and Festus. Donor advances about 5 then 4 while the target advances 6 each time - the same sub-unit slope recorded at Ephesians 2 (Romans 11:25 -> 12:3) and Deuteronomy 30 (5/6). All 296 Jamieson words are residue; not one is on 2 Corinthians 3. The repeat of both the class and the slope on back-to-back picks is the strongest evidence yet that a single deterministic mis-join produced the whole defect rather than a scatter of independent accidents.

The stacked chapter-final payload seen at Ephesians 2 key 22 recurs here at key 18, one batch later, which makes it a pattern rather than a coincidence. (1) Barnes is 5,030 words, of which 1,502 are comment on v18 and the remaining 3,528 are a REMARKS essay on the whole chapter. (2) Ellicott is 2,160 words, of which 1,244 are genuine and about 916 are the StudyLight page chrome - SIXTH hand-confirmation, and again inside the 926-1227 template range measured corpus-wide. Together they make key 18 9,744 raw words, 2.0x the next largest key in the chapter, of which roughly 5,300 are usable. Two chapters running, both epistles, both last keys, both carrying exactly this pair. The practical rule is now firm: for an epistle chapter, subtract the Barnes REMARKS block and the Ellicott chrome from the final key before budgeting, or the last span will look about twice the work it is. Here the raw figures said 16-17 was 3,931 words against 9,744 for v18 alone, a 2.5x gap; after subtraction it is 3,931 against 5,300, which is what the writing actually felt like.

This chapter carries three of the sharpest splits I have met, and Calvin is the minority in all three. (1) WHAT THE LETTER IS, at v6, is a four-way. Calvin reports Origen's reading - letter as the grammatical sense, spirit as the allegorical - says it 'has got into general circulation' and calls it the source of many evils, since it licensed men to adulterate the plain sense and 'the ancients recklessly played with the sacred word of God as if it had been a ball to be tossed to and fro'. His own reading is outward preaching versus living doctrine, influence and fruit rather than exposition. Ellicott takes 'letter' for the whole written code of Judaism and expressly rejects the literal-versus-mystical sense. Clarke holds the old covenant had both letter and spirit. Henry applies the distinction to the gospel as well. (2) WHO TURNS, at v16: six voices say Israel, Calvin alone says Moses, that is the law, opening with 'this passage has hitherto been badly rendered'. (3) THE MIRROR VERB at v18: Calvin and Ellicott say beholding, Barnes and Clarke work it as reflecting, Robertson reports Philo one way and Plutarch and Chrysostom the other and says either makes good sense. A fourth, smaller split at v15: Clarke asserts an 'evident allusion' to the tallith; Ellicott doubts the usage is that old and adds that even if it were, it covered head and ears but not the face.

A clean case of independent convergence on one image, worth recording because it is the opposite of the usual copying pattern. At vv10-11 four voices reach for the same figure of a lesser light swallowed by a greater, and none cites another. Calvin: 'as the moon and stars, though in themselves they are not merely luminous, but diffuse their light over the whole earth, do, nevertheless, disappear before the brightness of the sun'. Barnes: 'like the splendour of the moon and stars compared with the bright light of the sun'. Robertson: 'the moon makes a dim light after the sun rises... Christ as the Sun of Righteousness has thrown Moses in the shade'. Wesley, compressing: 'the greater light swallows up the less'. Clarke uses it a verse earlier for the glory 'absorbed, as the light of the stars, planets, and moon, is absorbed in the splendour of the sun'. Five voices, three schools, four centuries. Ellicott is the only one who declines it, going instead to the tense of the LXX Exodus and to the transfiguration. When a chapter produces convergence this broad the right move is to report it AS convergence - naming who reaches for it independently - rather than picking one voice and attributing the image to him, which is what the per-verse legacy entries here did.

Chrysostom speaks in this chapter at keys 1 and 7 only (720 words). Entry 18 names him in its prose - Robertson reports that Chrysostom takes the mirror verb in the active, reflecting rather than beholding - but there is no Chrysostom block in key 18. Declared him on entries 1 and 7 and not on 18, for the same reason as at Ephesians 2 last batch: chapter-wide grounding would have passed the declaration while making it false at the pericope level. This is the second consecutive chapter where the trap appeared, and in both cases the vector was identical - a father quoted inside a modern grammatical-historical commentator, in a doxographical aside about who reads a word which way. That is a narrow enough signature to be worth teaching the tooling: if a declared voice's name occurs in the prose only within a clause reporting another commentator's opinion, and that voice has no block in the span, it should be flagged. Also worth noting that entry 1 names Doddridge, entry 4 names Erasmus, Tyndale and Wycliffe, and entry 18 names Macknight, Locke, Philo and Plutarch - none of them declared, all of them reported at second hand, and all correctly attributed in the prose to the commentator who reports them.

Repair of a legacy per-verse chapter: 18 grade-D entries of 353-546 words each replaced by 6 pericope entries of 631-641, tiling 1-3 | 4-6 | 7-11 | 12-15 | 16-17 | 18. The legacy layout had no ranges at all and no excluded_voices anywhere, so the Jamieson residue at keys 4, 10 and 16 had been read as genuine 2 Corinthians commentary in three of the eighteen entries. That is the clearest argument yet for treating per-verse legacy chapters as repairs rather than leaving them: the residue defect is invisible at per-verse granularity because there is no span to declare an exclusion on. Chapter total 43,505 usable source words, over the single-chapter-batch threshold, so it was the whole batch. Every entry graded A on first assembly with no flags, though entries 1, 4 and 18 came in at 648-661 and needed trimming for margin - a consequence of a chapter where nearly every verse carries a live dispute worth reporting. Expansion ratios 0.06 to 0.16 of raw source.

Eight entries tiling all 23 keys, all in window: 1-3 650w, 4-6 650w, 7-9 635w, 10-12 649w, 13-15 650w, 16-18 648w, 19-21 648w, 22-23 650w. Twelve voices carry heads; ten are used (Calvin 23 blocks, Barnes 23, Clarke 23, Gill 23, Theodoret 23, Robertson 23, Ellicott 20, Wesley 14, Henry 5, Chrysostom 2, Cyril 6). Jamieson (3 blocks) declared as residue at entries 4, 16 and 22; Cyril silenced at two keys only, k4 as a byte-identical duplicate of k3 and k19 as a lecture on the state of the soul before it entered the world, which is not what v19 is about - his other four blocks are genuinely on the verse by catchword and are used. Two attribution traps avoided: Ellicott's k2 block cites Lightfoot by name on the force of the aorist, and Lightfoot has no head in this chapter, so the remark is reported as 'a commentator'; Ellicott's k18 block quotes Augustine for 'whose service is perfect freedom', and Augustine likewise has no head here, so it is reported as 'a liturgical phrase'. Every scripture reference in prose is a .ref link.

Jamieson residue: a NT measurement inside a book already anchored, and the blocks are a new size class. Three blocks at keys 4, 16 and 22 - stride 6, offset 4, full stride with no gap - but they are tiny FRAGMENTS of 91, 30 and 13 words rather than the paragraph-sized blocks seen everywhere else. Source is ACTS 9-10, the Cornelius narrative, in order: k4 is Joppa, 'the modern Jaffa, on the Mediterranean... the seaport of Jerusalem' (Acts 9:36 / 10:5-6); k16 is 'three o'clock, the hour of the evening sacrifice. But he had been fasting until that hour', citing Ac 10:30 and Ac 10:9 by name; k22 is 'the flat roof, the chosen place in the East for cool retirement. noon' (Acts 10:9). LAG: romans 6 is NT chapter 123 (28+16+24+21+28+6); Acts 9 is 98 and Acts 10 is 99, so lag 24-25. The decisive comparison is same-book: romans 10 sits at NT chapter 127 with lag 26. Four chapters earlier, the lag is one or two less - the slope holding inside a single book, which is a tighter test than the cross-book fits. Also worth noting the fragment size: these three are marginal-note style snippets, not full paragraphs, which suggests the emitter's block boundaries are set on the SOURCE side and can fall anywhere in a note, not that it always emits whole paragraphs.

Cyril of Jerusalem duplicates for the FOURTH book: k3 and k4 are byte-identical here (138 words each, Catechetical Lecture on baptism as more than remission), after ephesians 6 (k1=k3, k17=k18) and 1corinthians 3 (k12=k13). But romans 6 also shows the OTHER half of the picture, which the earlier chapters did not: his six blocks are sliced out of the Lectures by their internal section numbers - they open '6.', '7.', '13.', '19.', '30.' - and FOUR of the six are genuinely on the verse they landed at. k3 is on baptism being more than remission, which is exactly Rom 6:3; k5 is on Christ suffering in reality and not in appearance, which bears on being planted in the likeness of his death; k12 quotes Rom 6:12 outright inside an exposition of 'Thy kingdom come'; k22 is on life eternal, matching the close of Rom 6:22. Only k4 (the duplicate) and k19 (the soul before it entered the world) are off. So the Cyril feed is not simply noise: it is a florilegium sliced by section number and matched by catchword, and the catchword matching is right about two thirds of the time. That changes what the fix should be - not blanket removal, but de-duplication plus a relevance check, which the section numbers make tractable since they give a stable identifier for each slice. The VOICE_LABELS prefix bug still blocks declaring any of this through excluded_voices, now in five chapters.

Chapter-level front matter keyed to the first verse, SECOND book and now TWO feeds. At romans 6 k1 Barnes opens 'ROMANS Chapter 6 Introduction THE argument commenced in this chapter is continued through the two following' - his chapter introduction, exactly the defect first recorded at 1corinthians 3. But Clarke's k1 block does the same thing independently: it is a running summary of the whole chapter's argument keyed verse by verse ('We must not abuse the boundless goodness of God... Rom 6:1. For, having been baptized into Christ... Rom 6:2-4. And to be planted in the likeness of his resurrection, Rom 6:5...'), with the actual note on v1 following after. So this is not a Barnes-only artefact but a shared convention of at least two feeds: whatever chapter-level apparatus the source edition carried has been swept into the first verse's key. Consequence for any length-based analysis: the first key of a chapter is inflated in BOTH feeds, and at romans 6 Barnes k1 is 367 words against a chapter median near 300 while Clarke k1 is 630 against a median near 150. Henry shows the extreme case in the same chapter, k1 at 5772 words (the full Exposition plus the chapter preface) against k3, k11, k16 and k21 at 152, 258, 170 and 163 - which are the Concise, so this chapter also carries the two-works-at-different-keys mixing, now the seventh instance.

This chapter carries the widest confessional spread I have met, because baptism is the subject and every school is represented. (1) WHAT BAPTISM DOES, at v3-4. Robertson denies instrumentality outright and repeats it three times in the chapter: 'The translation into makes Paul say that the union with Christ was brought to pass by means of baptism, which is not his idea, for Paul was not a sacramentarian'; at v6 'This took place not at baptism, but only pictured there'; at v11 the imperative is 'complete proof that Paul does not mean that baptism makes one dead to sin and alive to God.' Cyril is at the far end: 'Let no one then suppose that Baptism is merely the grace of remission of sins, or further, that of adoption... so also it is the counterpart of the sufferings of Christ.' Calvin sits nearer Cyril than to Robertson - 'it is beyond any question, that we put on Christ in baptism, and that we are baptized for this end, that we may be one with him.' Clarke and Barnes make it profession; Ellicott incorporation into the mystical body; Wesley ingrafting through faith. Seven positions, five schools, one preposition. (2) IMMERSION at v4: Gill, Clarke and Wesley assert it flatly; Barnes concedes 'this is the idea which would strike the great mass of unprejudiced readers' while insisting 'his main scope and intention was not' that - a concession-and-limit found nowhere else. (3) THE OLD MAN at v6 gets three etymologies and a flat contradiction: Gill calls it old as the poison of the old serpent, Wesley as old as the fall, Calvin as old only by relation, 'as the Old Testament is so called with reference to the New'; and where Calvin identifies it with 'the whole nature which we bring from the womb', Theodoret says 'Not our nature, but our evil inclination, is what He here calls the old man.'

Two further things worth recording from romans 6. (1) THEODORET OF CYRRHUS, second appearance in the corpus after romans 10, and this chapter shows what he is for. He has 23 blocks, one at every key, max 200 - a real running commentary, not a florilegium - and he is the only voice who reads the chapter's imagery as ONE sustained figure. At v13 he says that 'having spoken of a reign, in strict keeping herewith, he mentions its artillery also, for the weapons which sin uses against us are our own members'; at v23 he closes the arc, that sin 'formerly reigned, and now tyrannizes, and he had called its weapons our own badly-disposed members, consistently also does he denominate the reward wages, for so he was in the habit of naming the pay of soldiers.' Ellicott reaches the same conclusion from the other end at v13, carrying the military metaphor forward to 'the wages of sin' as a soldier's pay - two voices, two schools, seventeen centuries apart, independently tracing the same figure through the chapter. (2) THEODORET'S SHARPEST SINGLE OBSERVATION, at v12, corrects a conflation the Western voices all make: 'A reign differs from a tyranny in this, that a tyranny is exercised over those who unwillingly submit to it; a reign, over subjects who are consenting thereto. He exhorts us therefore no longer to AGREE to the government of sin.' Clarke at the same verse calls sin 'a king, ruler, or tyrant' without distinguishing them. The distinction changes what the imperative asks for - withdrawal of consent rather than escape from force.

Ellicott end-of-chapter chrome tail, SIXTEENTH measurement: romans 6 k23 is 1038 raw words of which about 56 comment on v23. Caps confirmed again and one is new: 300 for Chrysostom (k5 and k19, both exactly 300 - the fifth measurement of that cap); 200 for Gill (eight blocks at exactly 200 in this chapter alone), for Theodoret (four) and for Cyril. The Gill count is worth flagging on its own: eight of his twenty-three blocks here sit at exactly the cap, which is the highest proportion I have recorded for that feed, and it means a third of Gill's contribution to this chapter is truncated mid-sentence. Any measure of what a voice actually says about a verse has to treat an exact-cap block as a lower bound, not a value.

Jamieson residue, TENTH chapter, a FOURTH residue class, and the first donor of a new kind. Affected keys are 9, 21, 27, 33, 45 and 51 - every one congruent to 3 mod 6. Six members, second only to Nehemiah 7's seven. Mod-6 target selection now holds in ten chapters out of ten, with four classes observed (0, 2, 3, 4). What is new is the DONOR: every previous case borrowed from a different book (Acts, Romans, Numbers, Genesis, 1 Chronicles, Mark, 1 Corinthians, 2 Corinthians). Here the donor is LUKE ITSELF, eleven chapters earlier, walking forward across its own chapter boundary: k9 -> Lk 13:4 (a tower of the city wall near the pool of Siloam, 'of its fall nothing is known'); k21 -> Lk 13:15-16 (the sabbath hypocrisy, citing Mt 12:9-13 and Lk 6:9, 'how the faithful and true Witness tears off the masks which men wear'); k27 -> Lk 13:18-21 (mustard seed and leaven, with the refusal to allegorise the woman as the Church or the three measures as spirit, soul and body); k33 -> Lk 13:24-25 (strive to enter in; the master of the house rising and shutting the door); k45 -> Lk 13:34-35 (O Jerusalem); k51 -> Lk 14:3-6. Both sequences are monotonic, the donor advancing slightly slower than the target (donor steps about 11, 4, 6, 9, 4 against target steps 12, 6, 6, 12, 6), and the donor crosses from Luke 13 into Luke 14 exactly as the target crosses from k45 to k51. Same slope family as Ephesians 2, 2 Corinthians 3 and Deuteronomy 30. I initially guessed Acts 27-28 by analogy with the previous chapter and was wrong; the donor has to be read, not inferred from the last case. All 315 Jamieson words are residue.

THREE laundering traps in one chapter, all the same shape, and the tooling had to be extended to see them. Luke 24 is a Catena Aurea chapter: split_voices recognises Bede, Cyril, Gregory, Augustine, Chrysostom and Tertullian as block labels, but the catena also carries AMBROSE, EUSEBIUS, THEOPHYLACT, CYRIL OF JERUSALEM and GREGORY OF NYSSA mid-block, where their material is silently credited to the host. Concretely: (1) at k1 the remark that the differing hours 'caused great perplexity to many' is AMBROSE inside a Bede block; (2) also at k1 the reconciliation of one angel against two - one seen within the outer enclosure, two afterwards standing - is AUGUSTINE inside that same Ambrose passage, and Augustine's own labelled blocks are at k25 and k36, so declaring him on entry 1 would have passed the chapter-wide grounding check while being false; (3) at k41 the bitter-herbs-versus-honeycomb reading is GREGORY OF NYSSA inside a Cyril block, and the labelled 'Gregory' of this chapter is Gregory the Great at k13, k25 and k45 - two different men behind one surname, which the validator cannot distinguish at all. I extended dump3.py's KNOWN label set with Ambrose, Eusebius, Cyril, Athanasius, Hilary, Isidore, Titus and Epiphanius. That helps but does not solve it: the sub-splitter matches Titlecase-followed-by-colon, and the catena also uses bare uppercase forms (CHRYS., AUG., EUSEBIUS.) which still slip through. In the prose all three are attributed to the catena by name and none of the three is declared. Declared voices per entry were cut accordingly: Augustine dropped from entry 1, Gregory dropped from entry 36.

Two section-shaped source patterns in this chapter, one helpful and one not. (1) HENRY IS SECTION-SHAPED, not verse-shaped. His 15,479 words land at only three keys - k13 (6,844), k36 (4,717) and k50 (1,646) - and each block expounds a whole pericope: k13 covers vv13-35, k36 covers vv36-49, k50 covers vv50-53. This is convenient when the tiling puts a section head at those keys, which mine did, but it creates a trap for any tiling that splits a Henry section: entries 25 (vv25-35) and 44 (vv44-49) have NO Henry block in their spans even though Henry has written at length about those verses. Declaring him there would pass chapter-wide grounding and be false; using his material there would be worse. Both entries were written without him, which is why the puritan school is absent from two of the six. (2) The Ellicott chapter-final chrome recurs at k53: 1,170 words of which 255 are genuine and about 915 are the StudyLight template. SEVENTH hand-confirmation, and the first in a gospel rather than an epistle, which rules out any suspicion that the pattern is epistle-specific. Clarke at k53 is 853 words and is an end-of-gospel essay rather than comment on v53 - the Clarke analogue of the Barnes REMARKS block, and worth watching for at the last key of every gospel. Barnes, unusually, is only 117 words at k53 and carries no REMARKS essay here.

Two things worth surfacing about how these commentators use each other. (1) AN OPEN DEPENDENCY at v50. Clarke's 606-word note on the Bethany-versus-Olivet distance is Lightfoot's argument reproduced whole - the numbered difficulties, the sabbath day's journey against the fifteen furlongs, the Josephus passage about the Egyptian pretender with the Greek quoted - and Clarke credits it openly, 'thus reconciled by Dr. Lightfoot'. That is the cleanest case of acknowledged borrowing I have met in this corpus, and it is the right way to read the many unacknowledged ones: where two voices in a span agree in detail and order, the default assumption should be dependence, not independent confirmation. I reported it as a dependency rather than counting Clarke as a second witness. (2) A FOUR-TO-ONE SPLIT at v30 on whether the breaking of bread was the eucharist. Lightfoot calls it strange that anyone should think so, since Christ meant to disappear in the very distribution and 'the supper was ended before it began', nor does it appear any of them tasted a bit. Clarke says there is 'not the most distant evidence' of it. Barnes says it was not sacramental but a common supper. Calvin reports that Augustine and most other commentators held the opposite, allows it 'might be said with some plausibility' that the Lord was recognised in the mirror of his own supper, and rejects it as resting on no probable grounds - so the majority view of the tradition is preserved only in the report of the man rejecting it. Ellicott alone affirms it, and hedges by anticipating later theological language rather than claiming the rite.

Largest chapter attempted in this run: 64,720 usable source words across 53 contiguous keys, tiled into six pericope entries - 1-12 | 13-24 | 25-35 | 36-43 | 44-49 | 50-53 - at 629-644 words each, all grade A on first assembly (entry 44 came in at 652 and was trimmed). Raw source per span 8,492 / 15,124 / 11,811 / 13,071 / 8,420 / 7,614; expansion ratios 0.04 to 0.08, the lowest recorded. Two things about tiling a chapter this size. First, the pericope boundaries were set by the narrative, not by word count, and the resulting 2x spread was accepted rather than balanced away - splitting the Emmaus road anywhere other than at v25 would have cut the exposition from the recognition. Second, the fat keys are fat for different reasons and the difference matters: k13 (9,922) and k36 (7,816) are large because Henry parked a whole section exposition there, which is real content; k53 (2,201) is large because of scraper chrome, which is not. Budgeting off raw key size treats those identically. The practical rule from this chapter and the two before it: before picking, subtract the Ellicott chapter-final chrome and any Barnes REMARKS or Clarke end-of-book essay from the last key, and check whether the largest interior key is a section-shaped commentator rather than dense verse comment. Ten Catena Aurea and patristic voices appear in the chapter; six are declarable block labels and four are mid-block only.

Six entries tiling all 18 keys, all in window: 1-3 619w, 4-6 647w, 7-9 650w, 10-12 633w, 13-15 628w, 16-18 648w. Eleven voices carry heads; nine are used (Barnes 18 blocks, Ellicott 18, Clarke 18, Robertson 18, Gill 18, Calvin 15, Wesley 14, Henry 3, Chrysostom 2). Jamieson (3 blocks) declared as residue at entries 4, 10 and 16; Cyril of Jerusalem (4 blocks) silenced entirely, none of the four being on the verse. One attribution trap avoided: Wesley's k10 block passes on the traditional description of Paul's person and credits it to Chrysostom by name, but Chrysostom has no head in span 10-12, so the description is reported as coming from 'an early father'. Every scripture reference in prose is a .ref link.

FIRST TRIPLE DUPLICATE in the Cyril feed, and the fifth book showing duplication. Cyril of Jerusalem has four blocks here and k14, k15 and k16 are ALL THREE byte-identical at 172 words each - a passage arguing about the force of the word 'until' in 2 Cor 3:15 (the vail on their heart), which has nothing whatever to do with 10:14-16. The previous cases were all pairs: ephesians 6 (k1=k3, k17=k18), 1corinthians 3 (k12=k13), romans 6 (k3=k4). His remaining block here, k2, is on Psalm 16 and is equally unrelated to 10:2. So this chapter is the first in which the whole Cyril contribution is unusable, and it is silenced entirely rather than per-entry. Note how this cuts against the romans 6 finding, where four of six Cyril blocks were genuinely on the verse by catchword: the feed is not uniformly bad and not uniformly good, which means a blanket rule in either direction is wrong. What the two chapters together suggest is that the duplication and the relevance are separate problems - duplication is mechanical and detectable by hashing, relevance is not - and that de-duplication should be done first, since it is cheap and would have removed two of this chapter's four blocks outright. The VOICE_LABELS prefix bug still blocks declaring any of this through excluded_voices, now in six chapters.

CORRECTION TO MY OWN EARLIER NOTES: the Chrysostom 300-word cap is not real. I recorded it five times (ephesians 6, 1thessalonians 2, romans 6 among them) as a per-feed cap, on the strength of blocks landing at exactly 300. In 2corinthians 10 his two blocks are 626 words (k1) and 347 (k7), both single blocks with one head each. So 300 is not a ceiling on the Chrysostom feed; the repeated exact-300 readings elsewhere must come from something else - most likely a per-chapter or per-fetch truncation that happened to apply in those books and not here. That matters for the re-fetch list: chapters where Chrysostom sits at exactly 300 should be treated as truncated and re-fetched, rather than accepted as complete short blocks, and the same caution should be applied to any cap I have inferred from exact-value repetition alone. The 200 cap for Gill, Keil, Cyril and Theodoret and the 300 for Bede are still supported by many measurements, but they deserve the same test: find one chapter where the feed exceeds the supposed cap and the cap is disproved.

A checkable one-verse misalignment in the Robertson feed. His block at k17 is five words long - the shortest block I have met anywhere in the corpus - and reads in full: 'Paul quotes Pr 27:2.' But v17 is 'he that glorieth, let him glory in the Lord', which is a quotation of Jeremiah 9:24 (as Paul himself uses it at 1 Cor 1:31). Proverbs 27:2 is 'Let another man praise thee, and not thine own mouth' - which is the natural cross-reference for v18, 'not he that commendeth himself is approved', the very next verse. So the note appears to have landed one key early. This is worth recording because it is FALSIFIABLE in a way most of my source-defect notes are not: if the Robertson feed is re-fetched, either his v17 note reads Jer 9:24 (in which case the reference here is corrupted) or his v18 note is missing its Proverbs citation (in which case the block was displaced). Either way the check is cheap. It also suggests a general test for the whole corpus that costs nothing: any block whose body is a bare scripture citation can have that citation checked against the verse it sits on, and a systematic offset would show up immediately.

Jamieson residue: the NT series now has eight points and this one interpolates between two existing anchors. Three blocks at keys 5, 11 and 17 - stride 6, offset 5, full stride, no gap - all on ROMANS 3-4 in order: k5 on the propitiatory sacrifice and the phrase 'faith upon' (Rom 3:25), k11 on whether justification by faith dissolves the obligation of the law (Rom 3:31), k17 on wages against favour against right (Rom 4:4). Source advances 3:25 to 3:31 to 4:4, i.e. +6 and +4 verses per 6 target keys, averaging the measured 5-per-6 rate exactly. LAG: 2corinthians 10 is NT chapter 159 (28+16+24+21+28+16+16+10); Romans 3 is 120. Lag = 39. The series now reads romans 6 at 123/24-25, romans 10 at 127/26, 1corinthians 3 at 136/30, 2corinthians 10 at 159/39, galatians 1 at 163/39, ephesians 6 at 174/42, 1thessalonians 2 at 184/44, revelation 9 at 268/62. This point falls between 1corinthians 3 and galatians 1 and lands where the line predicts, in a book not previously measured. Eight NT points and eight OT points now agree with the same two-stream model.

Two splits worth surfacing, both turning on evidence rather than doctrine. (1) THE TONE OF THE OPENING, v1. Henry hears mildness - the Apostle 'addresses them in a very mild and humble manner' and is 'desirous that no occasion may be given him to use severity' - and Wesley agrees, taking the entreaty as 'copying after the meekness and gentleness of Christ'. Ellicott hears the exact opposite: 'He speaks in the tone of the suppressed indignation which shows itself in a keen incisive irony,' the opening formula being one 'he reserves as emphasising an exceptionally strong emotion.' At v9 Ellicott sharpens it further - 'There is, of course, an implied warning, almost a menace, in the entreaty.' Same words, opposite readings of the voice behind them, and neither side is arguing from anything but the text. (2) WHO SPOKE THE TAUNT AT v10, where two voices reach the same answer by wholly independent routes. Robertson goes to the manuscripts: the reading behind the old Latin gives 'they say', but the critical editors prefer the singular 'says one' - the leader. Gill, with no Greek apparatus, gets there from the versions: 'instead of say they, in which way both the Syriac and Vulgate Latin' read it as singular, and 'the apostle seems to have in view some one particular person, though he does not choose to name him.' A textual critic and a seventeenth-century Baptist converging on one reading from different evidence is the kind of agreement the prevalence field ought to be able to mark as strong, and currently cannot distinguish from two men repeating a commonplace.

Ellicott end-of-chapter chrome tail, SEVENTEENTH measurement: 2corinthians 10 k18 is 1060 raw words of which about 78 comment on v18. And the chapter-level front matter defect appears in a THIRD book with the same two feeds as before: at k1 Barnes opens 'INTRODUCTION to 2nd Corinthians Chapter 10 PAUL, having finished the subject of the duty of alms-giving in the previous chapter, enters in this on a vindication of himself', while Clarke's k1 block is again a verse-by-verse summary of the whole chapter's argument ('The apostle vindicates himself against the aspersions cast on his person by the false apostle... 2Cor 10:1-6. He shows them the impropriety of judging after the outward appearance, 2Cor 10:7...') with the actual note on v1 following after. Three books now - 1corinthians 3, romans 6, 2corinthians 10 - and both feeds every time, which makes it a settled convention of the source edition rather than an occasional accident. The practical consequence is the same each time: k1 and the last key are inflated in both feeds simultaneously, so the two keys where an entry most needs balanced voices are the two where the length signal is least trustworthy.

Jamieson residue, ELEVENTH chapter, and the residue class 2 mod 6 for the FOURTH time (after Philippians 3, 1 Corinthians 6 and Hebrews 3). Keys 2, 8, 14 and 20 - four members at a constant step of 6, and every key in the chapter that is congruent to 2 mod 6 is affected, with no exceptions and no false positives. Mod-6 target selection now holds in eleven chapters out of eleven, across four classes (0, 2, 3, 4). The donor is 2 THESSALONIANS, read as a forward walk crossing the donor's own chapter boundary: k2 -> 2 Th 1:10-12 (reciprocal glorification, the believer's graces redounding to Christ's glory, 'there is but one Greek article to both'); k8 -> 2 Th 2:3-4 (the man of sin, Antiochus as the Old Testament typical Antichrist, the four world kingdoms with their representative heads); k14 -> 2 Th 2:8-9 (the parousia, the energy of Satan against the energy of the Spirit, 'prodigies of falsehood'); k20 -> 2 Th 2:13-14 (the oldest manuscripts read 'us', the obtaining of the glory of our Lord Jesus). Counting 2 Th 1 as twelve verses the donor advances 10 -> 16 -> 20 -> 25, that is +6, +4, +5, against a target advancing +6 each time - the same sub-unit slope recorded at Ephesians 2, 2 Corinthians 3, Luke 24 and Deuteronomy 30. Note also the size: k8 alone carries 1,408 residue words, more than a third of that key's raw total, which would have swamped the shortest entry in the chapter had it been read as genuine. All 1,839 Jamieson words are residue; none is on Revelation 14.

Revelation draws a kind of commentary that the epistles and gospels do not, and this chapter has four clean examples of it. (1) DATABLE IDENTIFICATION at v6: Clarke identifies the flying angel with the British and Foreign Bible Society, founded in his own lifetime, and lists the languages it had already reached; Gill runs through the eighth-century iconoclasts, then Wycliffe, Petrarch and Huss, before settling on ministers still future. Ellicott alone refuses the game, holding that the whole cycle of gospel preaching is in the vision. (2) THE SAME AT v20: Clarke matches the sixteen hundred furlongs to the extent of the papal state from Rome to the Po and calls the coincidence 'surprising and worthy of deep regard', while Robertson quotes Swete that the metaphor is 'worked out with the exuberance of apocalyptic symbolism'. (3) AN INTERPRETATION REPORTED BUT NOT OWNED at v17: Gill relays Brightman's identification of the two vintage angels with Thomas Cromwell and Archbishop Cranmer, and the vintage with the dissolution of the monasteries, calling it 'a strange conceit'. Worth recording as the pattern where a commentator preserves a reading precisely in order to reject it - the same shape as Calvin preserving the majority eucharistic reading of Luke 24:30. (4) A DOCTRINAL FLASH at vv10-11: Wesley breaks off to ask 'is no real anger implied in all this? O what will not even wise men assert, to serve an hypothesis!' and then, one verse later, 'God grant thou and I may never try the strict, literal eternity of this torment'. Barnes on the same verse is scrupulous in the opposite direction, granting that the clause affirms only that the smoke ascends and does not by itself assert that individual sufferings are eternal.

First Revelation chapter in this run, and the voice profile is unlike anything before it. NO CALVIN AT ALL - he wrote no commentary on the Apocalypse - so the reformed school rests on Gill alone in five of six entries and is absent from entry 13 entirely. Barnes supplies 10,355 of the 28,178 words, more than a third, and is the only voice present at every key. Bede appears once, 300 words at k1, and is the chapter's sole patristic voice; there is no catena here, so none of the mid-block laundering traps of Luke 24 arose. The practical effect on tiling: with one dominant voice and no Calvin, the entries lean grammatical-historical (three of six to eight voices in every entry) and the wesleyan-arminian pair of Clarke and Wesley carries most of the interpretive colour, since both write expansively on prophecy where they are terse elsewhere - Clarke's 1,053 words at k13 and 606 at k50-equivalent are far above his usual density. Tiling was 1-5 | 6-7 | 8 | 9-12 | 13 | 14-20, following the three angels exactly; two entries are single verses (8 and 13) and both are strong pericopes in their own right, which is unusual and worth noting as a case where a one-verse span is correct rather than a failure to merge. Source words per span 7,496 / 3,555 / 4,031 / 3,678 / 3,899 / 5,296 - the tightest spread of any chapter in this run. Every entry graded A on first assembly; entries 1, 9 and 13 came in at 655-673 and were trimmed.

JAMIESON RESIDUE -- THE ZERO-LAG CASE, and the strongest confirmation of the model yet. The model built over thirty chapters says the Jamieson feed is one continuous stream per testament, sampled at every sixth target key (the stride belongs to the SLOT, not the content), lagging the chapter it lands in by roughly 0.16 x canonical chapter position in the OT. genesis 2 is canonical chapter 2, so the predicted lag is 0.16 x 2 = 0.3, i.e. ZERO. That is exactly what is found. Two blocks, keys 13 and 25 (both = 1 mod 6, key 19 a dropped slot), and BOTH are Jamieson on genesis 2 itself, merely displaced within it: k13 = 'See on Ge 1:11', which is his note on 2:5, the plant of the field; k25 = the garden as probation and 'in fact a temple in which he worshipped God', which is his note on 2:15, to dress it and to keep it. EMISSION RATE: source v5 at key 13, source v15 at key 25 = +10 source verses per 12 target keys = 5 per 6, EXACTLY the rate measured across books (judges 10, judges 15, ruth 3, romans 6, 1corinthians 3, 2corinthians 10). That the same rate reproduces INSIDE a single chapter rules out the possibility that it is an artefact of cross-book alignment. The mechanism is now characterised well enough to act on. Owner decision still outstanding on re-indexing; note again that a naive re-alignment will duplicate the one-block overlap at each chapter seam.

BORROWING TAXONOMY, type (a) unattributed transmission -- the best specimen in the corpus so far, because both texts sit at the IDENTICAL key and it happens three times in one chapter. At k1 Wesley's block is a near-verbatim abridgement of Henry's block at the same key: Henry 'the creatures made both in heaven and earth are the hosts or armies of them, which denotes them to be numerous, but marshalled, disciplined, and under command'; Wesley 'the creatures made both in heaven and earth, are the hosts or armies of them, which speaks them numerous, but marshalled, disciplined, and under command'. The whole four-point structure (hosts / finished pieces / ceased from creation / rested not as one weary) follows in the same order with the same proof texts. It repeats at k18 (the upper world of angels and lower world of brutes) and again at k21 (the sixth-day placement and 'while he knows no sin, God will take care he shall feel no pain'). Three instances in one chapter, always Wesley shorter. This is a known historical dependence, but the corpus now contains a clean measurable specimen of it: same key, same order, ~35 percent length. Suggest the tags' prevalence field distinguish this from independent agreement -- five relation types are now catalogued (unattributed transmission, attributed transmission, independent observation, shared source with opposite verdict, convergence from independent evidence) and they are being reported identically.

FOUR SOURCE DEFECTS IN THIS CHAPTER. (1) ELLICOTT CHROME TAIL, eighteenth measurement: k25 carries 1102 raw words of which only ~118 are comment, the rest being the boilerplate that begins 'Copyright Statement These files are public domain'. The series across recent chapters -- judges 14 k20 1063/~90, judges 15 k20 1058/~76, judges 10 k18 1024/~42, ruth 3 k18 1004/~22, romans 6 k23 1038/~56, 2corinthians 10 k18 1060/~78, genesis 2 k25 1102/~118 -- shows raw size within 100 words while authorial content varies fivefold. Length and position remain useless as discriminators; only the marker string works. A single removable rule keyed on that string is still the cheapest fix in the tree. (2) KEIL BLOCK GRANULARITY: three of his nine blocks here are the reprinted BIBLICAL TEXT of a multi-verse run plus a comment belonging to a verse outside the key the block sits on. k11 reprints vv.11-15 and comments on v15; k19 reprints vv.19-23 and comments on v23; k24 is 40 words and is PURE reprint with no comment at all. All three silenced by entry. (3) GILL k13, geography: his Gihon block ends by saying the river 'pours itself into the Baltic sea', which fits none of his four candidates (a river near Jerusalem, the Nile, a branch of the Euphrates or Tigris, the Araxes). Almost certainly a corruption -- Caspian is the plausible original, since the Araxes runs into it and Clarke says so at k10. Cheap to check on re-fetch. (4) CAPS, treat as lower bounds not values: Keil 8 of his 9 blocks are at exactly 200 words (only k24, at 40, is under); Gill is at exactly 200 nine times out of 25. Same falsification test as the Chrysostom 300 cap, which this run already disproved -- an exact repeated value is evidence of truncation, not of an author's habit.

FOUR LIVE DISAGREEMENTS WORTH KEEPING, two of them inside a single school. (1) EASTWARD IN EDEN, k8: Keil says the garden 'was to the east, i.e., in the eastern portion' of Eden; Ellicott says flatly 'This does not mean in the eastern portion of Eden, but that Eden itself was to the east of the regions known to the Israelites'. Two grammatical-historical voices, same phrase, incompatible readings. (2) THE PROCESSION OF ANIMALS, k19-20: Calvin has God endue the creatures with a disposition to obedience so that they 'voluntarily offer themselves' to be inspected; Ellicott says 'nor are we to suppose a long procession of beasts and birds passing before the man, and receiving each its title', substituting a naturalist meeting creatures as he works. This is not a nuance -- Clarke's whole rendering of 'this now' at k23 ('this turn, this creature which now passes before me') DEPENDS on the procession Ellicott denies, so the two readings of v23 stand or fall with the two readings of v19. (3) THE STANDING OF THE WOMAN, k21 and k18: Clarke concludes from her being taken out of the man that she has 'equal powers, faculties, and rights'; Ellicott draws from the same words that 'the female is subsequent in order of production to the male, and formed from him'; Henry cites 1 Tim 2:13 and 1 Cor 11:8-9 for submissiveness and then balances it with 1 Cor 11:7, 'if man is the head, she is the crown'. Three schools, one verse, three verdicts, and all three are in the entry. (4) WHO SPEAKS v24: Gill says God (on the strength of Matt 19:5), Ellicott says the narrator moved by the Spirit, Calvin says Moses in his office as teacher, Wesley leaves it uncertain and inclines to Adam speaking in God's name. A genuine four-way with the same proof text cited by three of them.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, genesis 2, eight entries over 25 keys and 43,100 usable source words (over the 40k line, so the whole batch). Word counts: 1-3 616, 4-6 645, 7-9 649, 10-12 645, 13-15 646, 16-18 650, 19-21 648, 22-25 648. All eight in window; all eight required trimming from first draft, four of them three passes or more, and 22-25 needed two full rewrites (974 then 881 then 792 down to 648) because the source is densest at the end. Voice coverage: eight voices in the chapter -- Calvin 18 blocks/14,463w, Henry 7/9,699, Clarke 20/6,269, Ellicott 21/5,268, Gill 25/3,425, Wesley 9/2,038, Keil 9/1,640, Jamieson 2/63. Every entry names every voice that has usable material at its keys. DECLARED: Jamieson as residue at entries 13-15 and 22-25 (see the zero-lag note). SILENCED BY ENTRY: Keil at 10-12, 19-21 and 22-25, all three being reprinted biblical text with either no comment or a comment belonging to a verse in another span (see the source-defect note). Spans are a clean stride of three keys throughout, which the chapter supports: the thinnest span is 13-15 at roughly 1,700 usable words, and no rebalancing was needed. AUTHORITIES CITED BUT NOT NAMED, to avoid claiming a head that is not in the span: Reland, Sayce, Rawlinson, Bar-Hebraeus, Delitzsch's own gloss inside the Keil block, Dathe, Hengstenberg, Jarchi, Aben Ezra, Onkelos, Josephus, Bochart, Parkhurst, Milton. Dathe and Jerome are named where the citing voice is itself sourced in the entry. NOT USED: Clarke's k19 block (22 words, a bare cross-reference to the preceding chapter) carries no content, though he is sourced at k20 in the same entry.

Jamieson residue, TWELFTH chapter, class 3 mod 6 for the second time (Luke 24 was the first). Keys 3, 9 and 15 - three members at a constant step of 6, and every key in this chapter congruent to 3 mod 6 is affected, with no exceptions and no false positives. Mod-6 target selection now holds in twelve chapters out of twelve, across four classes (0, 2, 3, 4), with class 2 seen four times, class 0 three, class 3 twice and class 4 twice. 283 words, all residue. I did not chase the donor this time: the three blocks are 86, 86 and 111 words, too short to fix a donor sequence with any confidence, and the two-point-minimum rule I have been using needs distinctive content rather than merely three data points. Recording the class and the step, and leaving the donor unidentified rather than guessing - the Luke 24 batch showed that extrapolating a donor from the previous chapter's answer produces a wrong one.

Two source artefacts confirmed here, one old and one newly generalised. (1) THE KEIL 200-WORD CAP WITH VERSE-REPRINT BODY. All three Keil blocks in this chapter are exactly 200 words, and each consists of the reprinted KJV text of a run of verses followed by a fragment of real comment cut off mid-sentence: k2 reprints vv2-6 then adds two sentences on Oholiab; k7 reprints vv7-12 then begins a comment on the sabbath; k13 reprints vv13-18 and gets no comment at all before the cap. This is the structural artefact first recorded at genesis 13 k15 and seen again at judges 10 k18, but here it is the RULE for the voice rather than an exception - three of three blocks. A span containing only a Keil block of this kind would produce a declared voice with nothing to declare. (2) THE ELLICOTT CHAPTER-FINAL CHROME at k18: 1,217 words of which 302 are genuine comment and about 915 are the StudyLight template. EIGHTH hand-confirmation and the FIRST in the Pentateuch - previous confirmations were four epistles, one gospel and the corpus-wide scan. That removes any remaining suspicion that the pattern is genre-specific; it tracks the chapter-final position and nothing else.

A THREE-ENTRY chapter, and the reasoning is worth recording because the temptation was to make it five. Exodus 31 is 18 verses in three clear movements - the calling of the craftsmen (1-11), the sabbath command (12-17), the two tables (18) - and the obvious refinement was to split 1-11 into the call (1-6) and the list of works (7-11), and 12-17 into the sign (12-14) and the law (15-17). I dumped keys 7-11 before committing and found them almost entirely list-recitation: Gill's six blocks total 305 words of which most is cross-reference, Clarke's total 144, Keil's 200 is the verse-reprint artefact, and the only genuine interpretive content in the whole run is Ellicott's 187 words on the cloths of service. That is not enough to carry a 350-word entry at grade A without padding, and the span at 805 raw words sits in the dead zone between the thin exemption's 200-word ceiling and the 350-word floor - the same trap that forced the merge at deuteronomy 25 vv11-12. So three entries, at 4,885 / 3,831 / 2,946 raw source words, expansion 0.13 / 0.16 / 0.21. The general rule this confirms: DUMP THE THIN SPAN BEFORE FIXING THE TILING. Raw word counts do not distinguish a run of dense exposition from a run of inventory, and in the Pentateuch the difference is common enough to decide the entry count.

Two splits here, and both turn on how far a text may be pressed. (1) THE WISDOM GIVEN TO THE ALREADY WISE-HEARTED at v6. Calvin names the contradiction outright - if they already excelled in intelligence, what was the object of this new inspiration? - reports the common solution that special grace merely aids natural ability, and rejects it: 'when anything grows in us, and our endowments manifest themselves more conspicuously, our progress is only derived from the continued operation of the Spirit', the prior gift being 'only, as it were, the seed'. Clarke takes precisely the position Calvin rejects, that every man with a natural genius 'had an increase of wisdom by immediate inspiration'. Gill narrows the gift away from grace entirely, to 'ingenuity and skill in manual arts, and mechanical operations'. Wesley states the widest form: 'skill in common employments is the gift of God'. Four voices, four positions, on a verse most readers pass over. (2) HOW LONG THE SIGN LASTS at v17. Gill limits the 'for ever' to the end of the Jewish state at the coming of Christ, listing the land, circumcision, the passover and the atonement fast as parallel cases where the same word is bounded. Clarke argues the opposite from typology: 'the type must continue in force till the antitype come', therefore the observance must be perpetually kept up. Ellicott sidesteps both by pointing past them to 'that final rest which he may be sure remaineth for the people of God'. This is a live confessional disagreement about sabbath continuance being conducted in the margins of an Exodus commentary, and it is worth surfacing as a disagreement rather than resolving.

JAMIESON: FIRST BYTE-IDENTICAL DUPLICATE FOUND IN THIS FEED. The two Jamieson blocks in this chapter sit at keys 2 and 8 -- both = 2 mod 6, so the stride of 6 holds as everywhere -- and they are the SAME 116 words to the byte: the feast of tabernacles closing on the eighth day, Joh 7:37, the offerings fewer than on the preceding days, the spontaneous gifts and vows. Until now mechanical within-chapter duplication had been recorded only for Cyril of Jerusalem (five books, with a triple at 2corinthians 10). This is the first instance in the Jamieson feed and it changes what can be inferred: the k8 slot was filled by RE-EMITTING k2's content rather than being skipped, so no emission rate can be computed from this chapter, and any stride measurement elsewhere that rests on two blocks may rest on one block counted twice. CHEAP CORPUS-WIDE TEST, worth running before the re-indexing decision: hash every Jamieson block and report repeats within a chapter and within a book. That single pass would say how much of the residue-class evidence is independent. Also here: Gill's block at the last key (k19) ends with the navigation string 'Next: Deuteronomy Chapter 27', which the tooling already cuts as chrome. Worth recording that this is a SECOND chrome family, distinct from the Ellicott 'Copyright Statement These files are public domain' block, and that both land at the LAST key of the chapter -- so a rule keyed on last-key position alone would catch both but would also catch genuine end-of-chapter comment, which is exactly the mistake to avoid.

JAMIESON LAG: THE SLOPE RE-FITS TO 0.18, AND THE GENESIS 2 ZERO-LAG CASE IS WHY. deuteronomy 26 is canonical chapter 179. The duplicated Jamieson block here is his note on Numbers 29:35-38 (the eighth day of tabernacles), canonical chapter 146, so the lag is 33. The working fit of lag = 0.16 x position predicts 28.6 -- short. It was short in the same direction at judges 10 (position 221: predicted 35, actual 39) and at ruth 3 (position 235: predicted 37.6, actual 41). One might patch this with an intercept, but the genesis 2 result forbids it: there the lag is exactly ZERO at position 2, so the line must pass through the origin. Re-fitting through the origin gives a slope of about 0.18, which fits all four OT points without an intercept: gen 2 (p=2) 0.4 vs 0; deut 26 (p=179) 33.1 vs 33; judges 10 (p=221) 40.9 vs 39; ruth 3 (p=235) 43.5 vs 41. The residual pattern is now slight OVER-prediction at the high end rather than systematic under-prediction throughout, which is what one expects if the true relation is linear and the reading of each source chapter carries plus or minus a chapter of noise. CAVEAT, and it is not small: this chapter's two blocks are a duplicate (see the source-defect note), so deuteronomy 26 contributes ONE point, not two, and cannot contribute an emission-rate check. The rate of 5 source verses per 6 target keys still rests on genesis 2, where the two blocks are distinct.

FOUR DISAGREEMENTS WORTH PRESERVING. (1) THE ARAMAEAN CRUX at v5, the richest version-catena in the chapter: Clarke lays out six renderings side by side -- Vulgate 'a Syrian persecuted my father', LXX 'my father abandoned Syria', Targum 'Laban the Syrian endeavoured to destroy my father', Syriac 'my father was led out of Syria into Egypt', Arabic 'Laban almost destroyed my father', and Houbigant's 'famine oppressed my father, who went down into Egypt', obtained by detaching the yod from the word for Aramaean and taking the sense of famine from the Arabic cognate. Clarke and Keil independently reach the same verdict against the whole Laban tradition: the Syrian is Jacob, and the participle is intransitive, a perishing Aramaean. (2) WHERE THE TITHE PROTESTATION WAS MADE, v13, three to one: Gill, Wesley and Keil all say NOT at the sanctuary, since the tithe was eaten in the owner's own gates; Henry alone puts it at the next feast before the Lord, and gives a reason the others do not address -- that this tithe was disposed of out of the priests' sight, so the oath supplied the missing supervision. Henry's reason is good even if his location is probably wrong; both should survive. (3) THE VERB AT v17, Keil against everyone: he renders the hiphil causatively, 'thou hast let the Lord say today to be thy God', i.e. hast given him occasion to say it, where Gill, Clarke and Wesley all keep 'avouched, publicly declared'. A grammatical reading with real consequences for who the actor is in the covenant. (4) WHAT 'HIGH ABOVE ALL NATIONS' MEANS, v19, four answers: Gill comparative (Israel higher for having the Lord as King and such laws); Keil reflexive (Israel becomes an object of praise OF GOD among the nations, not of itself); Calvin spiritual and HIDDEN -- the excellency of the Church 'is hidden from the blind, and, since it is spiritual, only obtains its praise before God and the angels'; Clarke national and visible, ending in a direct apostrophe to Britain that neither fleets nor armies but righteousness alone secures permanence. Calvin and Clarke are exact opposites on the same clause.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, deuteronomy 26, four entries over 19 keys and 11,177 usable source words. Word counts: 1-4 629, 5-11 616, 12-15 650, 16-19 650. All four in window; three needed three or more trim passes. Spans follow the chapter's own structure -- the basket brought and set down (1-4), the confession and the command to rejoice (5-11), the third-year tithe with its protestation and prayer (12-15), the mutual avouching (16-19) -- rather than a fixed stride, because the material is very unevenly distributed: k1, k12 and k16 carry Henry's three long blocks (1591, 866, 822 words) and eight keys carry nothing but a Gill note of under thirty words. Voice coverage: seven voices -- Henry 3 blocks/3283w, Calvin 7/2598, Keil 10/1869, Gill 19/1450, Clarke 10/1135, Wesley 10/610, Jamieson 2/232. DECLARED: Jamieson as residue in entries 1-4 and 5-11 (the two blocks are a byte-identical duplicate; see the source-defect note). Entry 5-11 has only four voices and no Henry or Calvin block at all, so puritan-evangelical is not declared there -- correctly, since neither has anything at those keys. TWO THINGS TO FLAG AGAINST MYSELF. First, Keil's comment on the Aramaean of v5 sits in his block at KEY 2, which belongs to entry 1-4, but I reported it in entry 5-11 where the verse itself falls and where Clarke and Wesley discuss the same words; Keil is independently sourced at k6 in that span, so no voice is named without a block, but the material crossed a span boundary and a reader comparing block to entry should know it. His blocks reprint multi-verse runs, which is what makes this happen. Second, HENRY AND WESLEY NEVER SHARE A KEY IN THIS CHAPTER -- Henry has k1, k12, k16 and Wesley has k2, k5, k10, k11, k13, k14, k15, k17, k18 -- so the Wesley-abridging-Henry dependence measured three times over at genesis 2 cannot be measured here at all. That is worth knowing before anyone generalises the genesis 2 result: the co-occurrence rate of those two feeds is itself book-dependent, and where it is zero the transmission is invisible rather than absent. AUTHORITIES CITED BUT NOT NAMED, having no head in the span: Schultz, Houbigant, Maimonides, Jarchi, Aben Ezra, Clericus, Knobel, Riehm.

Jamieson residue, THIRTEENTH chapter, class 4 mod 6 for the third time (Deuteronomy 25, Ephesians 2 and 2 Corinthians 3 were the others). Keys 4, 10 and 16, three members at a constant step of 6, every class-4 key in the chapter affected with no exceptions. Mod-6 target selection now holds in thirteen chapters out of thirteen across four classes. The donor is 2 CORINTHIANS 7-8, read as a forward walk crossing the donor's own chapter boundary: k4 -> 2 Cor 7:8 (the sorrowful letter, 'I do not regret it, though I did regret it', with the note that the Greek words for regret and repent are distinct); k10 -> 2 Cor 7:13 ('we have been comforted... in our comfort we exceedingly the more joyed for the joy of Titus'); k16 -> 2 Cor 8:1 (the collection, the Macedonians' liberality, Paul's engagement in Galatians 2:10). Counting 2 Cor 7 as sixteen verses the donor advances 8 -> 13 -> 17, that is +5 then +4, against a target advancing +6 each time. That is the same sub-unit slope now recorded at Ephesians 2 (Romans 11-12), 2 Corinthians 3 (Acts 28), Luke 24 (Luke 13-14), Revelation 14 (2 Thessalonians 1-2) and Deuteronomy 30. SIX independent donor identifications now share the shape: monotonic forward walk, donor advancing slightly slower than the target, crossing a chapter boundary in the donor when the target crosses one of its own steps. Note also that this chapter's donor is 2 Corinthians, which was itself a residue TARGET two batches ago - the defect is not confined to a fixed set of donor books.

The best-documented translation dispute I have met in this corpus, and the two sides disagree about the TRANSLATORS rather than the text. At v6 all parties agree the received 'if they shall fall away' is wrong: the participle is aorist like the three before it and must be rendered 'and fell away'. What splits them is why the error is there. Clarke quotes Macknight in full: the translators 'following Beza, who without any authority from ancient MSS. has inserted in his version the word si, if, have rendered this clause, If they fall away, that this text might not appear to contradict the doctrine of the perseverance of the saints' - and Clarke adds pointedly that Macknight 'was a Calvinist, and he was a thorough scholar and an honest man; but, professing to give a translation of the epistle, he consulted not his creed but his candour'. Ellicott agrees the rendering is 'altogether incorrect, the Greek admitting of one rendering only', then answers the charge directly: 'the suspicion sometimes expressed that this is one of the (very few) instances in which our translators have been misled by dogmatic bias seems altogether unfounded. On tracing back the translation we find it due, not to the Genevan versions, in which the influence of Calvin and Beza is predominant, but to Erasmus, Luther, and Tyndale.' That is a testable historical claim answering a testable historical accusation, and it is worth recording as a model of what a real disagreement between commentators looks like when both sides are competent. Barnes occupies a third position - concedes on J. P. Wilson's authority that there is no 'if' in the Greek, yet defends the received version as conveying the sense, treating the whole as a supposed case. Wesley denies exactly that: 'Here is not a supposition, but a plain relation of fact.' Gill denies the case can be supposed of true believers at all. Five positions on one participle.

Chapter-final key 20 carries the stacked payload again: Barnes 2,522 words of which only 228 are comment on v20, the remaining 2,294 being a REMARKS essay on the whole chapter; and Ellicott 1,128 words of which 212 are genuine and about 916 are the StudyLight template. That is the NINTH hand-confirmation of the Ellicott chrome and the FOURTH epistle in which the Barnes REMARKS block and the Ellicott chrome sit stacked at the last key (Ephesians 2 k22, 2 Corinthians 3 k18, Hebrews 6 k20; Luke 24 k53 had the chrome with a Clarke end-of-gospel essay instead). Key 20's raw size of 4,723 is the largest in the chapter and would have made the closing span look the heaviest work; its usable content is about 2,400, which put it in line with the rest. The rule now has enough instances behind it to state flatly: in any epistle, subtract the Barnes REMARKS block and the Ellicott chrome from the final key before budgeting or tiling, because between them they routinely account for half that key's raw words.

51,229 usable source words over 20 contiguous keys, tiled 1-3 | 4-6 | 7-8 | 9-12 | 13-15 | 16-20 at 628-645 words each, all grade A. Raw source per span 13,227 / 10,412 / 3,556 / 8,762 / 2,542 / 12,465 - a 5x spread, accepted deliberately because the pericopes are unambiguous and both small spans carry dense content rather than inventory (the reverse of the Exodus 31 case, where a small span had to be merged). Expansion ratios 0.05 to 0.25. What makes this chapter unusual is the DENSITY OF NAMED DISPUTE: v1-2 has a six-way on the plural 'baptisms', v6 a five-way on the conditional, v9-10 a four-way on whether reward implies merit, v15 a three-way on what Abraham obtained, v18 a two-way on the two immutable things with Barnes reporting the rival view before rejecting it. Every one of my six entries had a live crux to organise a paragraph around, which is rare; most chapters yield three or four. Every entry also overran on first assembly (656-677) and needed trimming, which is the signature of a chapter with more to say than the window allows - the opposite failure mode from the thin spans of Exodus 31. Worth noting for whoever picks the remaining Hebrews chapters: budget the writing time by number of live cruxes, not by source words.

CORRECTION TO MY OWN NOTE ON THIS CHAPTER. In the deuteronomy 26 source-defect and build notes I recorded that Keil sits at exactly 203 words nine times of ten and called 203 'a new cap value; elsewhere in the corpus his cap reads 200'. That is wrong and there is no new cap. The 203 was an artefact of my survey script, which counted the voice-name prefix along with the body: 'Keil and Delitzsch:' is three words, so a 200-word capped block measures 203. The same artefact produced the '202' I would have read for Gill, whose prefix 'John Gill:' is two words. Verified directly against exodus 24 and re-verified against deuteronomy 26: every capped Keil block is body-only 200, and every capped Gill block is body-only 200, in both chapters. THE CAP IS 200 IN BOTH FEEDS, as recorded everywhere else in the corpus. The substantive point in the original note stands unchanged and is the one that matters: an exact repeated value is evidence of TRUNCATION, not of an author's habit, and every such chapter belongs on the re-fetch list -- the same test that disproved the supposed Chrysostom 300-word cap. Only the claim of a distinct 203-word cap is withdrawn. Flagging this because the false cap value, left standing, would have looked like evidence that the Keil feed was ingested twice under different settings, which it is not.

JAMIESON: A CLEAN SECOND WITHIN-CHAPTER EMISSION-RATE MEASUREMENT, and a fifth OT lag point. Two blocks, keys 7 and 13 (both = 1 mod 6, the stride of 6 holding), 90w and 89w -- NOT byte-identical, so unlike deuteronomy 26 this chapter yields two independent emissions. Both are Jamieson on EXODUS 12, the passover: k7 is the lamb taken on the tenth day with a kid permitted, and the service domestic because the threatened evil was to every house, which is his run over Ex 12:3-5; k13 is roast and not sodden for expedition, the unleavened bread, and 'bitters' for the affliction in Egypt, which is Ex 12:8-9. LAG: exodus 24 is canonical chapter 74, exodus 12 is canonical 62, so lag = 12. The re-fitted slope of 0.18 predicts 13.3 and the old 0.16 predicts 11.8; actual 12 falls between them. This point therefore CONFIRMS LINEARITY AT LOW POSITION but does not discriminate between the two slopes -- which is worth saying plainly, because at p=74 the two fits are only 1.5 chapters apart and no measurement here could separate them. The discriminating points remain the high-position ones (judges 10 at 221, ruth 3 at 235). EMISSION RATE: source midpoint v4 at key 7 and source midpoint v8.5 at key 13 gives +4.5 source verses per 6 target keys. genesis 2 gave +5 per 6 from two distinct blocks in a single chapter. Two independent within-chapter measurements, in different books at very different canonical positions, agreeing inside the noise. The rate is now the best-supported part of the model.

WESLEY-HENRY TRANSMISSION: THE KEY-CO-OCCURRENCE TEST IS THE WRONG TEST, and this chapter shows why. In my deuteronomy 26 fidelity note I recorded that Henry and Wesley never share a key there, and concluded that the abridgement dependence measured three times at genesis 2 'cannot be measured here at all'. exodus 24 corrects the method. Here Wesley abridges Henry at least five times -- k1 ('Worship ye afar off... enter into God's gates with humble and solemn adorations'), k2 ('a type of Christ, who as the high priest entered alone into the most holy place... typifying the covenant of grace'), k3 (the whole 'he laid before them all the precepts... they had before consented in general' passage), k10 (the entire sapphire-pavement exposition, minus Henry's wisdom-versus-sapphires moral), and k13 (the Joshua passage, including the citation of Bishop Pearson, which Wesley spells 'Peirson'). But Henry has only THREE blocks in this chapter, at k1, k9 and k12, while the Wesley blocks that reproduce them sit at k1, k2, k3, k10, k11 and k13. Only ONE of the five abridgements shares a key with its source. THE REASON is structural: Henry's blocks are long and cover verse RANGES, while Wesley's are short and per-verse, so Wesley's abridgement of a Henry block on vv.1-8 is distributed across keys 1, 2 and 3. Key co-occurrence therefore measures the block granularity of the two feeds, not the dependence between them. CONSEQUENCE: the deuteronomy 26 conclusion should be treated as unproven rather than negative -- Henry's three long blocks there may well be abridged in Wesley's ten short ones without a single shared key. Any corpus-wide measurement of this dependence must match on CONTENT (shingled n-grams over the block bodies, Wesley against every Henry block in the same chapter), never on key equality. The 'Peirson' spelling is a usable fingerprint for spot-checking such a matcher.

FIVE DISAGREEMENTS WORTH PRESERVING. (1) WHAT WAS RECITED, v3: Clarke includes the decalogue outright, with the laws of chs.20-23; Gill excludes it because the people had heard the ten from God themselves, confining the recital to the judicial laws; Keil agrees with Gill and specifies the extent as Ex 20:22-26 plus chs.21-23; Ellicott takes a middle course, an outline of general purport and main heads but not the details, since otherwise reading the book to them afterwards would have been pointless. (2) THE ORIGIN OF WRITING, v4, a flat contradiction: Wesley says God probably taught Moses the use of letters on the mount, and that Moses taught them to Israel 'from whom they afterwards travelled to Greece and other nations'; Ellicott says the familiarity of Moses with writing is presumed throughout the Pentateuch and that one 'learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians' could not well be ignorant of so ordinary an Egyptian accomplishment. (3) WHAT THE TWELVE PILLARS ARE FOR, v4: Clarke and Ellicott make them the second contracting party over against the altar; Calvin gives them a wholly different office -- they stood there so the people would know they were not kept at a distance in token of rejection, being still remembered before God, who 'embraced them all, as it were, by means of these statues'. (4) HEATHEN BLOOD-COVENANTS, v6-8: Keil states that the division of the blood 'had no connection whatever' with the heathen customs adduced by Bahr and Knobel; Ellicott adduces them at length from Homer, Herodotus, Xenophon, Lucian, Pomponius Mela and Tacitus, holding that such rites were felt to add force and sacredness; Calvin sides with Ellicott, that covenants have in all ages and among heathen nations been accompanied with sacrifice. Keil is the outlier and says so explicitly. (5) DID THE ELDERS STAY, v14, a two-against-two with consequences: Keil and Ellicott have them remain in the plain, Ellicott adding that the camp was not to move however long the colloquy lasted; Calvin refuses to take the adverb so precisely and holds they were sent back to their charge, which they could not exercise unless in communication with the people; Clarke agrees they returned, and makes their return the grand cause of the golden calf, since they probably reported Moses lost. NB Clarke gives a SECOND and different cause at v17 -- that the people, seeing the devouring fire and Moses long delayed, supposed he had been consumed by it.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, exodus 24, six entries over 18 keys and 17,921 usable source words. Word counts: 1-2 646, 3-5 645, 6-8 644, 9-11 649, 12-14 650, 15-18 650. All six in window; every one needed three or more trim passes, and 9-11 needed four after a GHOST catch. Spans follow the chapter's structure -- the summons and graded approach (1-2), the recital and the altar (3-5), the blood and the book (6-8), the elders seeing God (9-11), the second summons and the regency (12-14), the cloud and the forty days (15-18). Voice coverage: eight voices -- Calvin 7 blocks/3887w, Henry 3/3423, Ellicott 17/3097, Clarke 14/2715, Gill 18/1703, Keil 8/1624, Wesley 11/1293, Jamieson 2/179. DECLARED: Jamieson as residue in entries 6-8 and 12-14. FLAGS AGAINST MYSELF. (a) GHOST CAUGHT AND FIXED at entry 9-11: my first draft declared grammatical-historical and discussed Keil only in the tags, leaving his k10 block present in the span but unused in the prose. The linter caught it; I added his observation that the representatives went back down with Moses when the meal ended. This is the second GHOST of its kind in the run (the first was 2corinthians 10, Henry at 7-9) and both had the same cause -- a voice whose only contribution is a structural remark that is easy to leave in the tags. (b) Clarke's k1 block is a verse-by-verse CHAPTER ARGUMENT, the chapter-level front-matter defect now seen in five books (1corinthians 3, romans 6, 2corinthians 10, deuteronomy 26 and here). I used none of it as comment, only its content where it duplicates his verse notes. (c) CHROME at k18: Ellicott 1039 raw words of which about 55 are comment -- the nineteenth measurement, at the last key as always. (d) CAPS: Keil 8 of 8 blocks at exactly 200 body words, Gill 3 of 18 at exactly 200; both to be read as truncation, not habit, and note that my survey counter adds the voice-name prefix, which is what produced the spurious '203' I reported at deuteronomy 26 and have now corrected. AUTHORITIES CITED BUT NOT NAMED: Calmet, Schultz, Bahr, Knobel, Abarbanel, Onkelos, Jarchi, Aben Ezra, Willet, Bezaleel's father Hur only as identified. Augustine and Bishop Pearson are named where the citing voice is itself sourced in the entry.

JAMIESON: THREE BLOCKS AT A FULL STRIDE, AND A DOWNWARD REVISION OF THE SLOPE. Keys 3, 9 and 15, all = 3 mod 6, no slot dropped and all three distinct (23w/43w/34w) -- the best case in the run so far. All are Jamieson on NUMBERS 25, the Baal-peor and Phinehas narrative: k3 is Abel-shittim, 'a verdant meadow ... from a grove of acacia trees', his note on Nu 25:1; k9 is the flagitious act occurring while the rulers were deploring the wickedness, his note on Nu 25:6; k15 is the stain of blood confirming him in office and his posterity continuing, his note on Nu 25:13. LAG: deuteronomy 17 is canonical 170, numbers 25 is canonical 142, so lag = 28. This REVISES THE SLOPE DOWN. Fitting through the origin, which the genesis 2 zero-lag case forces, over all six OT points now available -- gen 2 (2, 0), exo 24 (74, 12), deu 17 (170, 28), deu 26 (179, 33), jdg 10 (221, 39), ruth 3 (235, 41) -- gives 0.175, not the 0.18 I recorded at deuteronomy 26. Predictions at 0.175 are 0.4, 13.0, 29.8, 31.3, 38.7, 41.1, with a maximum residual of 1.8 chapters and no systematic sign. deuteronomy 17 is the point that pulls the line down, because at position 170 the 0.18 fit over-predicts by nearly three chapters. EMISSION RATE, and a correction to myself: v1 at k3 and v13 at k15 is 12 source verses across 12 target keys, i.e. 6 per 6. genesis 2 gave 5 per 6 and exodus 24 gave 4.5 per 6. At exodus 24 I called the rate 'the best-supported part of the model' on the strength of two agreeing measurements; with a third in hand the honest statement is that the rate is about 5 source verses per 6 target keys with real scatter, roughly 4.5 to 6. Some of that scatter is unavoidable, since assigning a block to a source verse is itself uncertain by a verse or two at each end -- but it is scatter, and the earlier phrasing overstated the case.

FIVE DISAGREEMENTS, ONE OF THEM INTERNAL TO A SINGLE COMMENTATOR. (1) WHO THE JUDGE IS, v9: Wesley says probably the high priest, named separately because among the priests he especially was to be consulted; Calvin expressly refutes that, since the text distinctly enumerates the priests, the Levites AND the judge, and appeals to 2Ch 19:8 where the high priest was over matters of the Lord and the king's governor over civil causes; Gill prefers the president of the great sanhedrin, since no single ruler such as Othniel or Gideon was always in being. (2) HOW FAR THE COURT BINDS, v11-12, and this is the sharpest: Gill limits it — the court was not to make any new law but to teach the law of God, 'and so far as their sense and opinion of things agreed with that law they were to be regarded'; Wesley denies the limit, holding that people are bound simply to acquiesce in the sentence of their last and highest judge 'or else there would have been no end of strife'. (3) CALVIN AGAINST HIMSELF, v9 against v12, and both belong to his position. At v9 he requires the people to acquiesce in the priests' judgment 'even on the most disagreeable points'. At v12 he says the priests 'were not armed with tyrannical authority, so that it was sinful to reject whatever they might have decreed according to their own fancy', that God 'did not bind men's consciences to obey their ordinances without distinction', that reverence is due to all LAWFUL commands only, and that 'it was often necessary boldly to reject what the priests had commanded'. Reporting either half alone misrepresents him; the entry states both. (4) THE HORSES, v16, opposite directions of travel: Clarke and Wesley fear traffic WITH Egypt, which furnished Canaan with horses, and the idolatry and dependence that would follow; Calvin, taking the particle as 'for the sake of', reads the doubled clause as condemning a large stud because it would tempt a king to march an army INTO Egypt. (5) WHETHER THE CROWN WAS HEREDITARY, v20, three ways: Clarke says it was designed to be, and defends hereditary monarchy on grounds drawn from the experience of nations rather than from the text; Gill, following Jarchi, makes it elective with a standing preference for a fit son; Ellicott says hereditary only so far as Jehovah willed, and adds a dating argument -- that no dynasty but David's lasted more than five generations, and only two more than two, a fact which 'could hardly have escaped notice, if known to the writer of this book'.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, deuteronomy 17, six entries over 20 keys and 16,771 usable source words. Word counts: 1-3 648, 4-7 623, 8-11 647, 12-15 649, 16-18 644, 19-20 495. All six in window. Spans follow the chapter's four sections, splitting the two long ones: the blemished victim and the idolater (1-3), the procedure of trial (4-7), the appeal to the priests and judge (8-11), the penalty for presumption and the permission of a king (12-15), the king's three prohibitions and his copy of the law (16-18), and the reading of it (19-20). Voice coverage: eight voices -- Calvin 12 blocks/5029w, Henry 3/4437, Gill 20/1943, Ellicott 3/1535, Keil 8/1493, Clarke 11/1051, Wesley 16/1017, Jamieson 3/100. DECLARED: Jamieson as residue in entries 1-3, 8-11 and 12-15. SILENCED BY ENTRY: Keil at 19-20, his k19 block being pure reprinted biblical text with no comment at all; grammatical-historical is carried there by Ellicott. NOTE ON A SELF-CORRECTION MADE INSIDE THE PROSE: in the 8-11 entry I first wrote that Calvin 'stands with Wesley, requiring acquiescence even on the most disagreeable points'. That is what he says at v9, but at v12 he says the opposite about the binding of conscience. Rather than drop either, the 8-11 entry now flags that he qualifies it sharply a verse later and the 12-15 entry gives the qualification in full. A reader who saw only one entry would otherwise carry away a false view of his position, and the same risk applies wherever a commentator's blocks straddle a span boundary -- which for Calvin in this chapter they do twelve times. ELLICOTT is unusually sparse here, only three blocks (k1, k18, k20), so grammatical-historical rests mainly on Keil in the middle entries. CHROME at k20: Ellicott 1078 raw words, the twentieth measurement, at the last key as always. Gill's k20 block also ends with the navigation string 'Next: Deuteronomy Chapter 18', the second recorded instance of the Gill chrome family after deuteronomy 26. CAPS: Keil 7 of 8 blocks at exactly 200 body words; Gill 2 of 20 at exactly 200. AUTHORITIES CITED BUT NOT NAMED: Jarchi, Aben Ezra, Maimonides, Knobel, Schultz, the Targum of Jonathan, Urijah. Michal, Solomon, Joash, Jehoshaphat and Josiah are named where the citing voice is itself sourced in the entry.

Jamieson residue, FOURTEENTH chapter, class 2 mod 6 for the fifth time (Philippians 3, 1 Corinthians 6, Hebrews 3, Revelation 14). Keys 2, 8, 14, 20 - four members, constant step 6, every class-2 key in the chapter affected with no exceptions. Mod-6 target selection now holds fourteen out of fourteen. Donor is ACTS 9: k2 -> Acts 9:10-18 (Ananias's 'childlike obedience to the heavenly vision', the note that 'Lord' here means Jesus as almost invariably in the Epistles, the Spirit descending not necessarily after baptism); k8 -> Acts 9:24-25 (the danger at Damascus, 'the governor under Aretas the king kept the city', citing 2 Cor 11:32); k14 -> Acts 9:26-28 ('for fifteen days, lodging with Peter', Gal 1:18); k20 -> Acts 9:32 (Peter 'not now fleeing from persecution, but peacefully visiting the churches', Lydda near Joppa).
