IMPORTANT DIFFERENCE from the last six identifications: the walk is monotonic forward but the STEP IS IRREGULAR - roughly +14, +2, +6 in the donor against a steady +6 in the target - rather than the near-uniform slightly-slower-than-target slope of Ephesians 2, 2 Corinthians 3, Luke 24, Revelation 14 and Hebrews 6. That puts this case in the same sub-family as Nehemiah 7 (forward walk, irregular step) and means the donor mapping has at least two shapes, not one. Worth saying plainly because I have been treating the uniform slope as the signature; it is the common case, not the only one.

TWO patterns in this chapter that the grounding check cannot see. (1) THE CHRYSOSTOM TRAP, fourth instance. Chrysostom has exactly one labelled block in Romans 5, at k12 (300 words). Entry 18 names him in its prose - Robertson reports that 'Chrysostom explains hina here as ekbasis (result)' against Denney's final reading - but there is no Chrysostom block anywhere in keys 18-21. Declared him on entry 12 only. This is now the fourth chapter running where the vector is identical: a father quoted inside a modern grammatical-historical commentator in a doxographical aside about who reads a word which way. (2) A NEW ONE: WESLEY IS A CATENA CARRIER IN ROMANS. His blocks quote THEODORET OF CYRRHUS at length and by name at k3, k9, k10, k13, k15, k16 and k18 - at least seven times in one chapter, each time introduced as 'Theodoret of Cyrrhus:' followed by a paragraph of continuous quotation that often runs longer than Wesley's own comment. At k13 the Theodoret material supplies a reading of 'until the law' (that it means until the END of the law) which no other voice in the chapter offers, so the substance is genuinely valuable - but it is Theodoret's, not Wesley's, and split_voices sees only Wesley. Theodoret is not a recognised block label anywhere in this corpus as far as I have seen, so he can never be declared; the honest handling is to attribute in prose as 'Wesley quotes Theodoret' and declare only Wesley, which is what I did. Worth checking whether the Wesley-plus-Theodoret pattern holds across Romans generally, because if it does then every Romans chapter has a hidden patristic voice that no declaration will ever surface.

Four splits worth surfacing, and three of them are about how a text should be READ rather than what it means. (1) v1, WE HAVE or LET US HAVE peace. Ellicott: manuscript authority 'compels us to read Let us have, though the older reading would seem to make the best sense', and he floats a very early copyist's error later corrected by conjecture. Robertson: the subjunctive is 'the correct text beyond a doubt' and 'it is curious how perverse many real scholars have been on this word and phrase here. Godet, for instance. Vincent says that it is difficult if not impossible to explain it' - then resolves it by tense, the volitive present meaning keep on enjoying peace rather than make peace. (2) v7, RIGHTEOUS versus GOOD. Robertson quotes Lightfoot for 'all the difference in the world', a difference of sympathy. Ellicott grants the distinction and then says 'this distinction is not insisted upon here. The two words are used almost convertibly.' (3) v15, MANY or THE MANY. Ellicott presses the article and quotes Bentley via Lightfoot that 'by this accurate version some hurtful mistakes about partial redemption and absolute reprobation' would have been avoided - a translation point carrying a whole soteriology. Robertson answers that it is 'not necessary to Paul's argument to make the many in each case correspond'. (4) v20, the HINA: final or ecbatic. Robertson lays out both, attributing the result-reading to Chrysostom against Denney's purpose-reading, and declines to decide; Wesley decides flatly - 'the consequence (not the design)'. Also worth recording: Ellicott excuses the chapter's broken syntax by noting the letter was dictated and never revised, quoting Vaughan asking the reader to picture the writer at work - a rare instance of a commentator explaining a difficulty by the physical circumstances of composition rather than by exegesis.

63,536 usable source words over 21 contiguous keys, tiled 1-5 | 6-8 | 9-11 | 12-14 | 15-17 | 18-21 at 623-648 words each, all grade A. Raw per span 12,318 / 10,909 / 3,625 / 15,144 / 7,994 / 13,521; expansion 0.04 to 0.17. Second-largest chapter attempted in this run after Luke 24. The 12-14 span is the heaviest at 15,144 raw words and also the hardest, since Barnes alone puts 4,161 words at k12 and 1,961 at k14, and the passage is the one Barnes himself calls 'usually considered one of the most difficult portions of the New Testament'. Two structural notes for whoever takes the rest of Romans. First, the chapter divides cleanly at 12 because the apostle's own sentence breaks there and is resumed at 18 - the tiling should follow the broken protasis rather than fight it, which is why 12-14 (the interruption) and 15-17 (the contrast) and 18-21 (the resumption) are three entries and not two. Second, ELLICOTT CHROME at k21 is the TENTH confirmation: 1,072 words of which about 175 are genuine comment on v21 and the rest is the StudyLight template. Clarke at the same key is 1,879 words and is an end-of-chapter essay rather than comment on the verse, the same shape as his end-of-gospel essay at Luke 24 k53. So the chapter-final subtraction rule now applies to Clarke as well as to Barnes and Ellicott.

BLOCKED, NOT ATTEMPTED -- needs an owner decision on the source file, like numbers 31. I sized and surveyed exodus 36 (19 source keys, 5,887 usable words) and did not start writing, because the chapter cannot be tiled honestly under the current rules. THE HARD BLOCKER: the source keys are NON-CONTIGUOUS -- 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,14,19,20,26,30,31,32,35,37,38 -- and KEY 26 CONTAINS EXACTLY ONE BLOCK, which is Jamieson on EXODUS 23:14-17 (the three annual festivals), i.e. pure residue. Declared as residue it leaves the entry with zero voices and zero words; silenced it leaves the same. Since coverage_problems flags any span covering a verse absent from the source, key 26 cannot be absorbed into a neighbouring range either (25, 27, 28 and 29 do not exist), so ANY use of ranges in this chapter forces an entry at 26 that cannot be written. THE SOFT BLOCKER: five further keys hold nothing but a bare cross-reference to the parallel construction account -- k19 Ellicott 16w 'This verse corresponds exactly to Exodus 26:14', k20 Clarke 13w 'See Clarke's note on Exo 26:15', k31 Clarke 10w, k32 Ellicott 18w, k37 Clarke 13w. Writing 120 words on any of these is exactly the filler the prose rules forbid, and grouping them is what ranges are for -- but ranges are unavailable while key 26 stands. THE ROOT CAUSE is worth naming: Exodus 36 re-narrates the construction already prescribed in Exodus 26, so the commentators mostly refer back rather than comment, and Clarke says so outright at k38 -- 'There is scarcely any thing particular in this chapter that has not been touched on before.' This is a chapter-shaped instance of the bare-scripture-reference defect already logged at 1corinthians 3 k4. TWO POSSIBLE REMEDIES, both the owner's call: (1) allow a range to span source-key gaps, i.e. let coverage_problems ignore covered verses absent from the source rather than flagging them as extra, which would let 19-20, 26-32 and 37-38 group naturally and is a two-line change; or (2) treat a residue-only key as legitimately omissible and write the chapter with no ranges at all, following the established precedent -- five chapters already omit source keys (numbers 29 omits five of them, 2chronicles 27, numbers 34, galatians 2 and 1corinthians 16 omit one each), and all five declare no ranges, so the validator skips coverage for them. Option 1 is much the better outcome for this chapter and probably for every other partial-scrape chapter in the queue; option 2 costs nothing but leaves six keys unwritten. I picked again rather than land something padded.

JAMIESON: A FOURTH FULL STRIDE, AND THE NT SLOPE IS NOT THE OT SLOPE. Four blocks at keys 1, 7, 13 and 19 -- all = 1 mod 6, no slot dropped, and all four distinct, though again the unusually SMALL fragments characteristic of the NT feed (15w, 32w, 11w, 80w) rather than the paragraph-sized OT blocks. Content: k1 'the first necessity of the sinner, and so the first experienced blessing of the Gospel'; k7 the intervening days spent in further inquiry, the excitement reaching the Gentiles who crowded into the synagogue; k13 'implying some stay in Antioch and missionary activity in its vicinity'; k19 not captured in full. k7 and k13 are plainly ACTS 13 -- the Pisidian Antioch sabbath, where the whole city came together the next sabbath (Ac 13:44) and Paul and Barnabas stayed on. romans 12 is NT chapter 129 (28+16+24+21+28+12); Acts 13 is NT chapter 102 (89+13); lag = 27. THE POINT WORTH RECORDING: the OT slope re-fitted through the origin is 0.175, which would predict a lag of 22.6 here. The NT points give a consistently HIGHER ratio -- romans 6 (123) lag 24-25, romans 12 (129) lag 27, 1corinthians 3 (136) lag 30, 2corinthians 10 (159) lag 39 -- i.e. ratios of 0.20, 0.21, 0.22, 0.245. These do not sit on one line through the origin with the OT points, and within the NT the ratio itself climbs with position, which a single slope cannot produce. Either the NT stream has its own faster drift, or the relation is not linear across the whole canon. The four NT points are now enough to say that plainly, and the honest statement of the model is: stride of 6 on the slot, holding in 4 of 4 chapters measured this window; emission ~5 source verses per 6 target keys with scatter; and a lag that is linear-ish WITHIN each testament but with a materially different coefficient, OT about 0.175 and NT about 0.20 rising. Do not fit one line to both.

FIVE DISAGREEMENTS, AND ONE UNUSUALLY STRONG CONVERGENCE. (1) MINISTRY, v7: Ellicott and Clarke call the word the technical term for the deacon's office; Barnes reviews the whole NT usage and comes down the other way, that the apostle meant those engaged in the ministry of the WORD, not deacons properly so called. (2) OFFICES OR DUTIES, v8: Calvin insists the givers are the deacons dispensing public charity and those who show mercy are the widows appointed to nurse the sick, 'for there were two different offices'; Ellicott holds that at this point the apostle passes from the definite functions of the ministry to what was common to ALL members, so that giving is to be taken widely. (3) IS THE APOSTLE QUOTING THE SERMON ON THE MOUNT, v14: Theodoret says flatly 'this was a law of our Lord's, for the Lord enjoined it to the holy Apostles (Matt. v. 44)'; Ellicott denies it is a quotation and dates the denial -- the compositions that became our gospels began about the time this epistle was written, so the precept reached Paul orally; Robertson independently agrees, 'like Mt 5:44 in spirit, not a quotation, but a reminiscence.' A fifth-century Antiochene and two nineteenth-century critics, and the moderns are the ones denying the citation. (4) HAS THE PRECEPT ANY PAGAN PARALLEL, v21: Barnes makes the largest claim in the chapter -- overcoming evil with good is 'the noble and grand sentiment of the Christian religion. Nothing like this is to be found in the heathen classics; and nothing like it ever existed among pagan nations.' Robertson, glossing the SAME VERSE, cites Seneca for it. Clarke had already cited Seneca at v2 for the sense of 'transformed'. Barnes's claim is refuted from inside his own catena. (5) SPIRITUAL OR PRACTICAL DILIGENCE, v11: Ellicott corrects the English outright -- the word means zeal and refers to the spiritual life, whatever the English reader supposes -- and Gill agrees; Barnes and Clarke make it ordinary industry, Barnes concluding that 'an idle man and a Christian are names which do not harmonize' and Clarke that he who neglects to labour during the week is as culpable as he who works on the Sabbath. THE CONVERGENCE, v13: the variant reading MEMORIALS for NECESSITIES draws four independent treatments -- Clarke reports and dismisses it, Calvin's text calls it a depravation introduced by certain fathers to countenance veneration of the martyrs' sepulchres (objecting that there were then no martyr monuments at Rome), Ellicott diagnoses the same motive and turns the case into a general argument for the purity of the manuscript tradition, and Wesley reaches the identical controversy WITHOUT any appeal to manuscripts, from the apostle's silence: 'treating expressly of the duties flowing from the communion of saints, yet never says one word about the dead.' Four voices, three schools, one target.

THREE DEFECTS, ONE OF THEM THE LARGEST OF ITS KIND YET SEEN. (1) HENRY AT KEY 1 IS 11,654 WORDS -- the whole chapter's exposition dumped onto verse 1. This is the chapter-level front-matter defect at a scale far beyond anything previously logged (the earlier instances, at 1corinthians 3, romans 6, 2corinthians 10, deuteronomy 26, deuteronomy 17 and exodus 24, ran to a few hundred or at most two thousand words). Henry has only four blocks in the chapter -- k1 11,654, k3 214, k9 392, k17 290 -- so 92 percent of his contribution sits on one key and covers all twenty-one verses. Consequence for the work: entries 1 and 2 had to stand alone rather than be grouped, and Henry is unavailable as a puritan-evangelical voice in five of the nine entries even though he certainly comments on those verses; he is simply filed elsewhere. Clarke's k1 block carries his usual chapter argument on top of that. (2) CHRYSOSTOM AT EXACTLY 300 WORDS THREE TIMES (k1, k4, k14), and he has only those three blocks in the chapter. 300 is the value that was wrongly read as an authorial cap until 2corinthians 10 broke it with single blocks of 626 and 347. These are truncations, and romans 12 belongs on the re-fetch list; the k1 block visibly breaks off mid-sentence ('For it was not this, but this...'). Theodoret sits at exactly 200 four times and Gill six times, on the same reading. (3) CHROME at k21: Ellicott 1,055 raw words of which about 73 are comment -- the twenty-first measurement, at the last key as always. NOTE ALSO a probable block-boundary fault: the dump renders Wesley's k1 and several later Wesley blocks as running straight on into Theodoret's text without a break, though the survey parser splits them correctly on the strong tags. Worth a look on re-fetch, since a reader of the raw catena would attribute Theodoret's words to Wesley.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, romans 12, nine entries over 21 keys and 61,055 usable source words -- the largest chapter attempted in this run, half again the size of genesis 2. Word counts: 1 650, 2 648, 3-5 650, 6-8 650, 9-11 647, 12-13 623, 14-16 648, 17-18 649, 19-21 649. All nine in window; every one required trimming, most of them three or more passes. Verses 1 and 2 stand alone because Henry's 11,654-word block sits on key 1 and would otherwise have swamped a grouped entry (see the source-defect note); the rest follow the chapter's own joints. Voice coverage: eleven voices -- Barnes 21 blocks/15,362w, Henry 4/12,550, Calvin 19/11,854, Clarke 21/7,468, Ellicott 21/4,580, Gill 21/2,815, Robertson 20/2,001, Theodoret 19/1,926, Wesley 17/1,094, Chrysostom 3/900, Jamieson 4/138. DECLARED: Jamieson as residue in entries 1, 6-8, 12-13 and 19-21. RATIO: about 5,800 words of prose from 61,055 of source, or 9.5 percent -- the lowest of the run, and unavoidable at this density. That is the honest cost of a chapter this size at nine entries: a great deal of good material was left out, and the entries are selections rather than digests. TWO GHOSTS CAUGHT AND FIXED, both the same failure as at exodus 24: Clarke at entry 1 and Wesley at entry 3-5 were present in the span, discussed in the tags, and missing from the prose. That is now the third and fourth instance of this specific error in the run, always with a voice whose contribution is a single structural or cross-referencing remark. It is worth naming as a standing hazard: when a voice's only content is a chapter argument or a back-reference, it is easy to summarise him in the school description and forget to name him in the prose. Theodoret at entry 14-16 was a third near-miss, caught by the same linter. NAMES USED: Seneca, Thomas Aquinas, William Penn, Griesbach and Keble are named where the citing voice is itself sourced in the entry; Moore, Stuart, Flatt, Theophylact, Jerome, Doddridge, Macknight, Beza, Mede, Erasmus and Alford are cited by the sources but not named in the prose.

SECOND chapter after nehemiah 7 that the Jamieson residue makes unwritable, and the mechanism is identical. Exodus 36 has 19 sparse source keys - 1-9, 14, 19-20, 26, 30-32, 35, 37-38 - with gaps at 10-13, 15-18, 21-25, 27-29, 33-34 and 36. Because a span may not cover a verse absent from the source, the seven contiguous runs ARE the tiling; no merging across a gap is legal, so the entry count is forced at seven. Only one of the seven is writable. Run 1-9 has 4,725 usable words and is fine. Run 26 is 151 words of which ALL are Jamieson, so excluding the residue leaves it DEAD - zero usable words - and it cannot be merged with a neighbour because verses 21-25 and 27-29 are not keys. Runs 19-20 (29 usable words, Ellicott 16 plus Clarke 13) and 30-32 (75 usable after excluding 51 residue words) are far below what any honest distillation can carry; run 35 at 245 usable sits above the thin exemption's 200-word ceiling and so would need 350 output words from 245 of source, which is padding. THE RESIDUE IS REAL: keys 2, 26, 32 and 38, all congruent to 2 mod 6, carry commentary on EXODUS 22-23 - k2 on the pawned garment of Ex 22:26-27 ('the bed of the poor is usually nothing else than a mat'), k26 on the three annual feasts of Ex 23:14-17, k32 on the prohibition against seething a kid in its mother's milk at Ex 23:19, k38 on the concluding promises and warnings of Ex 23:20-33. That is a within-book donor thirteen chapters earlier, the second such case after Luke 24 borrowed from Luke 13-14. Not attempted. Recording so the next offer of this chapter can be skipped on sight.

17,251 usable source words over 18 contiguous keys, tiled 1-3 | 4-5 | 6-11 | 12-14 | 15-18 at 634-643 words each, all grade A. Raw per span 5,809 / 1,874 / 3,666 / 3,041 / 2,924; expansion 0.11 to 0.34. The tiling follows the chapter's own three-case structure, which Ellicott states explicitly at v1 (the false prophet vv1-5, the private individual vv6-11, the city vv12-18) - but I split the first case at 3/4 and the third at 14/15 because each divides cleanly into the offence and the sentence, giving five entries rather than three and keeping the spans between 1,874 and 5,809 raw words. VOICE PROFILE: no Barnes, no Robertson, no Chrysostom anywhere in the chapter; Calvin supplies 7,960 of the 17,251 words, nearly half, and is the only voice at k7. Entry 4 has only four declarable voices (Calvin, Gill, Keil, Wesley) because keys 4-5 carry nothing from Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott or Henry - the thinnest voice roster of any entry I have written, though each of the four had real content. ELLICOTT CHROME at k17 is the ELEVENTH confirmation: 1,053 words of which about 50 are genuine comment on v17 and the rest is the StudyLight template. Also worth noting that Keil's blocks are again all capped at exactly 200 words and consist largely of reprinted verse text, the pattern recorded at Exodus 31 - five of the six Keil blocks here follow it.

This chapter puts the commentators under unusual pressure because the law it expounds commands executions, and two places show how differently they handle that. (1) v5, WHO MAY BE PUT TO DEATH. Calvin sets two explicit limits before defending the penalty: not for 'some particular or trifling error' but only for 'authors of apostasy, who pluck up religion by the roots'; and not at all 'until a positive religion should be established' by public consent and 'sure and indisputable proofs'. He then draws a two-edged conclusion - 'whilst their severity is preposterous who defend superstitions with the sword, so also in a well constituted polity, profane men are by no means to be tolerated' - and mounts an argument from lesser offences to greater (adulterers, poisoners, thieves are punished; shall the corrupters of doctrine go free?). His EDITOR appends a long footnote treating this passage as 'his final apology for the part he took' in the death of Servetus, and quotes M. de Felice's four points in his defence. That footnote is part of the source and I reported its existence rather than passing over it. (2) v15, WHETHER THE INNOCENT DIE TOO. Wesley restricts 'the inhabitants' to 'all that are guilty, not the innocent part, such as disowned this apostacy, who doubtless by choice, at least upon warning, would come out of so wicked a place'. Calvin takes the objection in its hardest form and refuses the escape: 'If any should object that the little children at least were innocent, I reply that, since all are condemned by the judgment of God from the least to the greatest, we contend against Him in vain.' Reported both plainly without adjudicating. (3) A smaller but pleasing case at v11: Keil and Delitzsch quote Calvin BY NAME in order to borrow his phrase 'the utility and fruit of severity' and then guard it, denying that fear of punishment is the principle of the law or the modern deterrent theory. Direct cross-citation between two voices in the same span.

JAMIESON RESIDUE, romans 7 -- THE CHAPTER-SEAM DUPLICATE CONFIRMED BY BYTES, AND THE STRIDE IS PER-CHAPTER. Four residue blocks at keys 4, 10, 16, 22 -- all = 4 mod 6, a full stride with no slot dropped. All four are Acts 10, the Cornelius narrative, in order: k4 = the flat roof, chosen place in the East for cool retirement, noon (Ac 10:9); k10 = 'were inquiring' and the Spirit bidding Peter go with them (Ac 10:17-20); k16 = Cornelius falling at Peter's feet and Peter declining the honour (Ac 10:25-26); k22 = the four-day reckoning of the messengers (Ac 10:30). TWO FINDINGS. (1) romans 6 k22 and romans 7 k4 are BYTE-IDENTICAL: 'the flat roof, the chosen place in the East for cool retirement. noon.' This is the long-flagged one-block overlap at each chapter seam, now proven by bytes rather than inferred. (2) Both chapters sit at offset 4 mod 6. romans 6 has 23 source keys and 23 is not a multiple of 6, so a stride running on a continuous global index WOULD have shifted the offset at the seam. It did not. THE STRIDE IS THEREFORE COMPUTED ON THE VERSE NUMBER WITHIN THE CHAPTER, NOT ON A RUNNING COUNT ACROSS THE CORPUS. Offsets observed to date: genesis 2 = 1, exodus 24 = 1, deuteronomy 17 = 3, deuteronomy 26 = 2, romans 12 = 1, romans 6 = 4, romans 7 = 4. WITHIN-CHAPTER EMISSION RATE DECLINES MONOTONICALLY HERE: k4 to k10 spans Ac 10:9 to 10:17-20, about 9.5 source verses per 6 target keys; k10 to k16 spans 10:17-20 to 10:25-26, about 7; k16 to k22 spans 10:25-26 to 10:30, about 4.5. Earlier within-chapter rates were 4.5 (exodus 24), 5 (genesis 2), 6 (deuteronomy 17). The honest statement remains ~5 per 6 with real scatter, and romans 7 shows the scatter is not noise but a trend inside a single chapter. NT slope still differs from OT slope: romans 6 (123, 24-25), romans 7 (129 approx, same family), romans 12 (129, 27), 1corinthians 3 (136, 30), 2corinthians 10 (159, 39) give ratios climbing with position, which no single origin-line produces. Do not fit one line to both testaments. This is the strongest evidence yet for the re-indexing decision still pending with the owner.

CALVIN EDITORIAL APPARATUS BLEEDING INTO THE COMMENTARY TEXT -- FOUR INSTANCES IN ONE CHAPTER, WITH NO MARKUP TO SEPARATE THEM. The Calvin blocks in this catena carry the 19th-century translator's/editor's footnotes inline, in the same paragraph and the same voice, with nothing to mark the change of hand. Four clear cases here. (1) k13: Calvin argues that the law called the ministration of death in 2 Cor 3 represents not the law's real character but the false opinion of opponents; the very next sentence reads 'This can hardly be admitted. The Apostle in Corinthians evidently states a fact...' -- a flat contradiction of the sentence before it. (2) k15: 'It appears from this, that Calvin did not apply the foregoing words...' -- Calvin referred to in the THIRD PERSON inside his own block, followed by a catalogue of rival schemes he never mentions: Hammond's 'law state' (Stuart's phrase), Locke's Jew living between Abraham and the giving of the law, Vitringa's fiction about the law's effects on Jews and proselytes. (3) k22: a lexical note comparing Macknight's, Stuart's and the common version's renderings of the verb, and pronouncing 'our common version is the best' -- an English translator's judgement, impossible for Calvin. (4) k24: Schleusner cited on the adjective, plus Septuagint parallels at Ps 137:8 and Isa 33:1. CONSEQUENCE FOR SYNTHESIS: a summariser reading these blocks as one voice will attribute to Calvin positions he did not hold and, worse, will report him contradicting himself. I wrote around it in the prose at 9-12 and named the editorial matter explicitly at 15-17, but that is a per-chapter workaround. This is a corpus-wide defect in the Calvin source, not a romans 7 accident -- it was flagged before on the re-fetch list as 'Calvin (editor's apparatus)' and this chapter shows the density: four instances in twenty-five keys. RECOMMENDED: on re-fetch, keep only the Calvin body and drop the apparatus, or wrap the apparatus in a distinguishable tag so build tooling can strip it.

ROMANS 7 TRUNCATION AND CHROME CENSUS -- add to the re-fetch list. EXACT-CAP TRUNCATIONS (body ends mid-sentence at a round number; the cap counts BODY words only, not the voice-name prefix -- see the correction filed against deuteronomy 26). Gill at exactly 200 on SEVEN keys: 5, 9, 13, 15, 22, 24, 25. Theodoret at exactly 200 on FIVE keys: 3, 4, 6, 12, 13. Wesley at exactly 200 on k7 -- FIRST TIME WESLEY HAS HIT THE CAP anywhere in the corpus so far; his blocks are usually far shorter than 200, so this is a genuine truncation of an unusually long note, not a coincidence. Cyril at exactly 200 on k23. Chrysostom at exactly 300 on k14 -- and k14 is Chrysostom's ONLY block in the whole chapter, so the single Chrysostom contribution to romans 7 is a truncated one. Clarke, Barnes, Robertson, Calvin, Ellicott, Henry and Jamieson show no exact-cap blocks here. ELLICOTT CHROME TAIL, 23rd INSTANCE MEASURED: k25 holds 1996 words of which the commentary body is 183 and the remaining 1813 are navigation and copyright chrome, starting at the literal string 'Copyright Statement These files are public domain'. That single removable rule would strip 1813 words from one key in this chapter alone. The second chrome family (Gill's 'Next: <Book> Chapter <n>' navigation string) does not appear in romans 7. HENRY IS TWO DIFFERENT WORKS IN ONE CATENA: five Henry blocks, of which k1 (2282w), k7 (2223w) and k14 (3421w) are the full Exposition -- chapter-level front matter dumped onto the first key of each argument -- while k18 (238w) and k23 (429w) are plainly the Concise commentary, a different register and a different work, with nothing in the markup to distinguish them. Same hazard as the Calvin apparatus: a summariser reading them as one voice will report a single commentator changing his manner mid-chapter.

THE REGENERATE/UNREGENERATE QUESTION IS THE SPINE OF THIS CHAPTER AND THE CATENA SPLITS FIVE WAYS, NOT TWO. (1) Barnes (k14) holds the passage describes a man UNDER THE GOSPEL, after conversion, and gives four numbered reasons: it is the obvious sense to plain men without a theory; making it pre-conversion would repeat settled ground and leave open whether the law can sanctify a believer; the later expressions cannot be said by an impenitent sinner; it accords with parallel descriptions of the Christian's conflict. He rests the whole case at k22 on the verb of delight, which occurs nowhere else in the NT and denotes sensible pleasure rather than intellectual assent -- 'never yet did an impenitent sinner find emotions of pleasure in the contemplation of the pure and spiritual law of God.' (2) Clarke (k14) takes the opposite side with heat: the apostle personates a Jew under the law; by 'I' he cannot mean himself or any believer; and if the words held of a believer they would prove the GOSPEL as insufficient as the law. He says the contrary opinion 'has most pitifully and most shamefully not only lowered the standard of Christianity, but destroyed its influence and disgraced its character.' At k22 he answers Barnes's proof-text directly: every Jew who receives the OT must acknowledge the law's excellence, and 'to say that the inward man means the regenerate part of the soul is supportable by no argument' -- citing Plato and Plotinus via Wetstein, and Yalkut Rubeni on the Jewish side. (3) Calvin (k14, k17) holds the regenerate reading and rests it on the DISOWNING rather than the delight: the man denies being wholly possessed by sin and declares himself exempt from its bondage, which no unrenewed man could say. (4) Theodoret (k14) refers it to the man before the coming of grace. (5) Wesley (k14) REFUSES THE ALTERNATIVE, making the passage the whole process of a man reasoning, groaning, striving and escaping from the legal to the evangelical state, and at k25 keeps it to the end -- the 'I' is 'the person whom I am personating, till this deliverance is wrought.' (6) Henry (k14) alone states the deadlock AS a deadlock and expounds the passage twice over, once each way, without deciding. NOTE that Robertson (k15) sides with the pre-conversion reading on the strength of 'sold under sin' and quotes Denney's formula -- 'the unregenerate man's experience, surviving at least in memory into regenerate days, and read with regenerate eyes' -- which is the only position in the catena that dissolves the dichotomy rather than choosing a side or refusing to.

THREE FURTHER DISAGREEMENTS WORTH KEEPING FROM ROMANS 7. (1) GILL NAMES AND REJECTS TWO POSITIONS HELD BY VOICES IN HIS OWN CATENA (k9). Expounding 'I was alive without the law once' he says it is spoken neither in the person of Adam -- who never lived without law, having the law of nature written on his heart and a positive precept about the fruit, and in whom sin could not be said to REVIVE since it never lived before -- nor in the person of a Jew before Sinai, since the sons of Abraham had circumcision and sacrifices besides the law of nature. THEODORET holds precisely the first (Adam before his transgression, the serpent, Eve, the shared sentence) and CLARKE, quoting Whitby, holds precisely the second (the seed of Abraham, not obnoxious to death for what the law had not yet threatened). Three positions, all inside one chapter's catena, with the refutation printed above the things it refutes. (2) CLARKE'S DEFENCE OF THE WILL (k18-k19) IS A DIRECT ATTACK ON THE REFORMED READING OF THIS VERY CHAPTER. He holds that some faculties suffered less in the Fall because their concurrence is necessary to salvation, and that 'It is not the Will that leads men astray; but the corrupt Passions which oppose and oppress the will. It is truly astonishing into what endless mistakes men have fallen on this point, and what systems of divinity have been built on these mistakes. The will, this almost only friend to God in the human soul, has been slandered as God's worst enemy, and even by those who had the seventh chapter to the Romans before their eyes!' Set against Calvin at k18, who divides the believer into two parts (the relics of the flesh, and grace) and includes under 'flesh' everything a man brings from the womb; and against WESLEY at the same key, whose one-line gloss -- 'The flesh here signifies the whole man as he is by nature' -- contradicts his own school's champion and agrees with Calvin. Wesley against Clarke inside the wesleyan-arminian slot is unusual and worth flagging. (3) THE WORD 'LAW' AT v21 (k21). Ellicott's note lays out the two live readings and states the objection to the majority one -- that taking it as 'rule' or 'habitually-repeated fact' gives the word a sense it bears NOWHERE ELSE in Paul -- then offers Vaughan's alternative, an anacoluthon. Clarke takes 'rule' openly, glossing it with Hesychius as confirmed habit. CALVIN counts FOUR laws in the passage (the law of God, the law of the mind, the law of unrighteousness, the law of the members) where everyone else finds two, defending the third by the observation that even a tyrant's enactments are called laws though not properly. Theodoret sidesteps the whole question by REPUNCTUATING, putting a full stop after the wish to do right.

ROMANS 7: CLASSICAL AND PATRISTIC MATERIAL THE CATENA CARRIES THAT IS WORTH INDEXING SEPARATELY. (a) k20 -- Clarke tells XENOPHON's story from the Cyropaedia of Araspes the Persian nobleman, entrusted with the captive Panthea, confessing to Cyrus 'I am convinced that I have two souls; if I had but one soul, it could not at the same time pant after vice and virtue' -- adduced to explain why ancient philosophers posited two souls in man. (b) k23 -- Robertson lists PLATO, OVID, SENECA and EPICTETUS as describing the same dual struggle between conscience and deeds. Note that this is the same move Robertson made at romans 12:21, where he cited Seneca against Barnes's claim that 'nothing like this is to be found in the heathen classics'; the pattern is consistent enough to be worth a corpus-wide index of Robertson's classical citations. (c) k24 -- Clarke quotes VIRGIL, Aeneid viii.485ff, five lines of Latin on the tyrant Mezentius who bound the living to the dead face to face until the putrefaction killed them, as the image behind 'the body of this death'. He gives both the Latin and an English verse rendering. (d) k22 -- Calvin cites AUGUSTINE, who calls the contest between spirit and flesh 'the Christian struggle'. (e) k23 -- CYRIL of Jerusalem does not expound the verse at all but uses it to argue the INCARNATION: 'The Devil had used the flesh as an instrument against us; and Paul knowing this, saith...' -- therefore God became truly man, that by the very same weapons the victory might be won back. Cyril's other block here (k16) is likewise not exegesis but a guard on FREE WILL, warning the catechumen not to listen to anyone 'perversely interpreting the words, But if I do that which I would not', and answering with Isaiah's 'If ye be willing and hearken unto Me'. BOTH Cyril blocks in this chapter are catechetical excerpts aimed at a doctrine rather than commentary on the verse; that is consistent with his two blocks in every chapter surveyed so far, and supports treating the Cyril source as a doctrinal cross-reference rather than a commentary voice. (f) k21 -- Gill identifies the 'law' the apostle finds with the rabbinic YETZER HARA, and reports that 'evil' is the first of the seven names the rabbis give it.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, romans 7 -- ten entries over 25 contiguous source keys, 59,960 usable source words, 12 voices. Every verse checked against its source blocks before writing and again after each trim pass. WORD COUNTS (window 350-650, no thin exemptions used): 1-3 647w / 9 voices; 4-6 649w / 8 (Jamieson excluded, residue at k4); 7-8 640w / 9; 9-12 648w / 8 (Jamieson excluded, k10); 13 616w / 8; 14 646w / 10 -- the widest voice spread in the chapter, all five schools; 15-17 629w / 9 (Jamieson excluded, k16); 18-20 648w / 8; 21-23 643w / 10 (Jamieson excluded, k22); 24-25 649w / 8. Total 6,415 synthesis words from 59,960 source words = 10.7% expansion ratio. EVERY ENTRY IS ATTRIBUTED: no claim in the prose is made that is not traceable to a named block in that span. GRADE: high confidence on attribution and on the disagreements, which are unusually clean in this chapter because the voices answer each other by name (Gill refuting the readings Theodoret and Clarke hold; Clarke answering Barnes's proof-text at k22; Wesley contradicting Clarke at k18). MEDIUM confidence on two things, both flagged as source defects rather than judgement calls. (1) The Calvin blocks carry editorial apparatus inline with no markup; at 9-12 I wrote around it and at 15-17 I named it as editorial matter rather than attributing it to Calvin, but a reader without the source cannot verify that split. (2) Five Henry blocks come from two different works (full Exposition at k1/k7/k14, Concise at k18/k23); I summarised each in its own register but attributed both to 'Henry', which is what the catena claims. DEGRADATION SIGNAL, unchanged and worsening: EVERY ONE of the ten entries overshot the 650-word ceiling on first draft, by 20-35%, and needed one to six trim passes. I lowered the first-draft target to ~600 words partway through and the overshoot persisted. The expansion ratio here (10.7%) is close to romans 12's 9.5%, the lowest recorded. ROTATION REMAINS THE STANDING FLAG.

Jamieson residue at keys 6, 12, 18 — class 0 mod 6, three members at constant step 6. Fifteenth chapter characterised and the fifteenth mod-6 hit; target-key selection is now mod-6 in fifteen of fifteen cases across four residue classes. Donor is Romans 5 to 6 — the chapter this worker landed one batch earlier, the first time a donor is a chapter the same worker has just written. k6 gives Rom 5:13-14 (until the law sin was in the world), k12 gives Rom 5:18 (resuming the unfinished comparison, the list of interpreters completing the ellipsis each way), k18 gives Rom 6:1 (shall we continue in sin). Counting Rom 5 as 21 verses the donor advances 13, 18, 22 — plus 5 then plus 4 against a target advancing plus 6, the uniform slower-slope family rather than the irregular forward walk. Declared excluded_voices on entries 5, 11 and 14.

The thorn in the flesh is a five-way crux here, and two of the readings are reports about the same father that contradict each other. Clarke lists the older conjectures and assigns headache to Chrysostom; Calvin says Chrysostom inclined rather to refer the thorn to Hymeneus and Alexander and men like them. Both are secondhand — Chrysostom's own blocks in this chapter are at keys 1, 11 and 16 and say nothing of the thorn — so neither report can be checked against the source and Chrysostom was deliberately NOT declared on entry 7. Fifth instance of the laundering trap this session and the same vector every time: a father quoted inside a modern commentator in a doxographical aside. The conflict itself is worth keeping: the corpus contains two mutually exclusive claims about what one father held, and a synthesis that repeated either as fact would be inventing a source.

Clarke does not merely reject the reading that takes 'being crafty, I caught you with guile' as the apostle's own confession — he condemns the doctrine drawn from it. Many suppose the phrase is his own and have concluded from it that guile and deceit are lawful in the service of a religious purpose; Clarke calls that doctrine abominable and holds the words are most evidently those of his detractors. Ellicott reaches the same reading by a different route, reconstructing the sneer in the objectors' voice and noting a modern translator has done well to put the charges in quotation marks. Carried into entry 14 as a debate.

Twelfth confirmation of the Ellicott chapter-final StudyLight boilerplate, here at k21 (~900-1000 junk words). Prior sightings: ephesians 2 k22, 2corinthians 3 k18, luke 24 k53, exodus 31 k18, hebrews 6 k20, romans 5 k21, deuteronomy 13 k17. The practical rule is now firm — before budgeting a final span, subtract the Ellicott chrome, the Barnes REMARKS essay (which stacks with it at the last key in four epistles so far) and Clarke's end-of-book essay where the chapter closes a book.

JAMIESON RESIDUE, luke 16 -- THE PER-CHAPTER STRIDE HOLDS IN A CATENA-AUREA CHAPTER, AND THE DECLINING RATE REPEATS. Three residue blocks at keys 4, 22 and 28 -- all = 4 mod 6, the same offset as romans 6 and romans 7. All three are LUKE 7, in order: k4 = the widow of Nain, 'the Resurrection and the Life in human flesh, with a word of command, bringing back life to the dead body' (Lk 7:14-15); k22 = the people that heard him justified God, having been baptized, while the Pharisees and lawyers rejected the counsel of God against themselves (Lk 7:29-30); k28 = the children in the marketplace who will play neither at weddings nor funerals, that generation rejecting both John and his Master (Lk 7:31-35). RATE: k4 to k22 is 18 target keys across source verses 7:14 to 7:29, i.e. 15 source verses -- EXACTLY 5 per 6 target keys, the corpus-median rate. k22 to k28 is 6 target keys across 7:29 to 7:31, i.e. 2 source verses -- about 2 per 6. So the rate declines monotonically inside the chapter, exactly as it did in romans 7 (9.5, then 7, then 4.5). Two chapters now show a decline rather than a constant, which means the single-slope model is wrong in the tail even within one chapter. SLOTS DROPPED: keys 10 and 16 carry no Jamieson block, so the stride skips two emissions between k4 and k22 without losing the offset -- confirming again that the offset is computed on the verse number within the chapter, not on a running global index. ★ NEW: JAMIESON IS NOT THE ONLY RESIDUE STREAM HERE. Key 22 also carries a CYRIL OF JERUSALEM block (162 words) on ACTS 11 -- Barnabas sent to Antioch, bringing Paul from Tarsus, the disciples first called Christians -- with no connection whatever to Luke 16. It is Cyril's only block in the chapter. A second, independent residue stream in the same chapter has not been seen before and should be surveyed corpus-wide: if Cyril of Jerusalem blocks are being emitted on their own stride, the same re-indexing question applies to them.

CYRIL OF ALEXANDRIA BLOCKS IN luke 16 ARE BARE LECTION TEXT, NOT COMMENTARY -- two of the three are unusable. The catena carries three Cyril of Alexandria blocks. (1) k1, 503 words: opens '15:11-32.' and then prints the parable of the prodigal son VERBATIM from Luke 15 -- the wrong chapter entirely, and no exposition at all. (2) k10, 235 words: opens '16:1-9.' and prints Luke 16:1-9 verbatim -- right chapter, still no exposition. (3) k19, 364 words: opens '16:14-17.' with the lection text and THEN gives real commentary ('THE love of money, my brethren, is a most wicked passion...'). So the pattern is that each Cyril block is prefixed with the pericope's lection, and in two of three cases the block is nothing but the lection. I silenced the k1 and k10 blocks in the build (they carry no expositional content to summarise) and used only the commentary half of k19. CONSEQUENCE: any word-count or coverage measure that treats these blocks as commentary is counting scripture text as source. In this chapter that is 738 of 57,564 usable words -- small here, but if the prefix habit is corpus-wide across every Cyril of Alexandria block it is a systematic inflation of the source-word budget AND a trap for a summariser, who may paraphrase the lection back as though it were a father's comment. RECOMMENDED: on re-fetch, strip the leading verse-reference-plus-lection from Cyril of Alexandria blocks, or at minimum flag blocks whose text is a near-exact match to the scripture of the range they head. A survey of how many Cyril of Alexandria blocks corpus-wide are lection-only would size the problem.

CATENA AUREA NESTED ATTRIBUTIONS: THE BLOCK BOUNDARIES DO NOT MATCH THE CATENA'S OWN ATTRIBUTIONS. luke 16 is a Catena Aurea chapter -- 25 distinct heads, 13 of which the build tooling did not know. Its patristic blocks routinely CONTAIN further attributions in the Catena's own shorthand, inline, with no markup and no <strong> head, so the scrape's block boundaries are wrong. Instances counted in this chapter: k1 Pseudo-Chrysostom's block contains 'BEDE;' and Ambrose's contains 'THEOPHYL.'; k8 Augustine's contains 'AMBROSE.' and 'BASIL;', Origen's contains 'AUG.', Gregory's contains 'AUG.', Theophylact's contains 'AMBROSE;'; k14 Bede's contains 'THEOPHYL.' twice and Eusebius' contains 'AMBROSE;'; k19 Chrysostom's contains 'AMBROSE', 'BEDE', 'GREG.' and a second 'CHRYS.', Gregory's contains 'PSEUDO-CHRYS.'; k22 Gregory's contains 'CHRYS.' and 'AUG.', Pseudo-Basil's contains 'PSEUDO-CHRYS.', Gregory of Nyssa's contains 'CHRYS.', Ambrose's contains 'CHRYS.' and 'GREG.'; k27 Gregory's contains 'AUG.' and 'CHRYS.', Ambrose's contains 'GREG.'. CONSEQUENCE: material the Catena attributes to father X is filed in the data under father Y, and a lint check that only sees <strong> heads cannot detect it. I wrote the prose using outer head names only, which is what the data claims, and avoided naming any nested father who is not also a head in the same span; where a nested attribution carried the best material I either dropped it or used it under the outer name. That is a workaround, not a fix, and it means some attributions in this chapter's synthesis are as accurate as the source and no more. TWO FURTHER PLACEMENT DEFECTS in the same chapter: at k14 the Eusebius block expounds v16 and the Ambrose block expounds v18 -- both printed against v14; and at k1 the Tertullian block expounds vv9-13 (the two masters and mammon). SAME FAMILY as the Calvin editorial-apparatus defect filed against romans 7: a block that is one voice in the markup and several in fact. RECOMMENDED: on re-fetch, split Catena blocks at the internal attribution shorthand (all-caps father name followed by a semicolon or period) and re-head each fragment.

TOOLING GAPS EXPOSED BY luke 16, A CATENA AUREA CHAPTER. (1) THIRTEEN UNKNOWN VOICE HEADS. The build maps carried forward from the Pauline chapters knew twelve voices; luke 16 has twenty-five. The ones that had to be added: Pseudo-Chrysostom, John Lightfoot, Cyril of Alexandria, bare 'Cyril', 'Chrysostom' (no forename, distinct from 'John Chrysostom' elsewhere), Augustine, Gregory, Theophylact, Ambrose, Pseudo-Basil, Eusebius, Gregory of Nyssa, Origen. (2) THE NAME MATCHER NEEDED FIXING. Matching a voice by a bare last-name regex fails here: 'Chrysostom' matches inside 'Pseudo-Chrysostom', 'Gregory' inside 'Gregory of Nyssa', 'Cyril' inside 'Cyril of Alexandria' and 'Cyril of Jerusalem'. I changed the matcher to try labels longest-first and blank each match so shorter labels cannot fire inside longer ones. Any shared tooling that matches voice names by substring has the same bug. (3) THE QA VOICE_LABELS LIST CANNOT DECLARE MOST OF THESE. scripts/synthesis_qa.py VOICE_LABELS holds bare 'Cyril', 'Gregory', 'Basil', 'Chrysostom', 'Lightfoot' and matches with a regex demanding a colon immediately after. So 'Cyril of Alexandria:', 'Cyril of Jerusalem:', 'Gregory of Nyssa:', 'Pseudo-Chrysostom:' and 'Pseudo-Basil:' are all UNDECLARABLE as excluded_voices -- declaring one would fail undeclarable_voices(). This is the same root cause as the Cyril prefix bug already reported. I had to route the k1/k10 Cyril of Alexandria blocks and the k22 Cyril of Jerusalem block through a local silent-list instead of a declared exclusion, which means the residue is invisible to the corpus QA. FIX: make VOICE_LABELS carry the full display labels and match longest-first, as the build matcher now does. (4) THE SCHOOL ENUM HAS NO CAPPADOCIAN SLOT. Gregory of Nyssa and Basil have no natural home among the eight slugs; the corpus is split 11 to 6 between latin-fathers and eastern-alexandrian for Gregory of Nyssa. I followed the dominant assignment (latin-fathers) for coherence, and put Pseudo-Basil there too, but both are plainly wrong on the merits. Theophylact is likewise split 136 eastern-antiochene to 93 latin-fathers corpus-wide; I used eastern-antiochene. Eusebius is filed grammatical-historical 22 times, which is defensible for the historian and is what I used. If the owner ever revises the enum, a cappadocian or a general patristic-greek slug would fix roughly three voices.

luke 16 IS THE MOST OPENLY CONTESTED CHAPTER IN THE CORPUS SO FAR, AND ONE COMMENTATOR SAYS SO IN PRINT. (1) ELLICOTT LISTS THIRTEEN RIVAL EXPOSITIONS OF THE UNJUST STEWARD AT k8, sets his own beside them and invites the reader to judge. In them the steward stands for: the publicans as a class; all Christians; a simple example of temporal prudence; a case where the master did not know of the collusion; nothing but the approach of death; a scheme in which the master is Mammon; Judas Iscariot; Pontius Pilate; our Lord Himself; St Paul; the true penitent; the devil. He concludes that 'the wild diversity of interpretations which this list partially represents should make any commentator more or less distrustful of what seems to him an adequate and complete exposition.' He opens the chapter (k1) by saying there is perhaps no single parable subjected to such various and discordant interpretations. This is the only place in the corpus so far where a voice enumerates its rivals rather than refuting one. (2) PARABLE OR HISTORY, at k19, splits five ways: Gill denies it is history (citing an ancient copy that prefaces it 'he said also another parable'); Lightfoot mocks the friars who show pilgrims the site of a house 'such a one as never had any being, but merely in parable'; Barnes says there is no evidence for a real case; CLARKE REFUSES TO DECIDE -- 'If it be a parable, it is what may be: if it be a history, it is that which has been' -- and notes that some manuscripts even supply the rich man's name; CALVIN comes down for fact, 'as the name occurs in it, I rather consider it to be the narrative of an actual fact'; WESLEY goes furthest and characterises the man, 'very probably a Pharisee... a very honest, as well as honourable gentleman.' (3) THE DOGS, at k21. Ellicott asks whether the licking intensifies the suffering or contrasts brute sympathy with human apathy, and decides for the first on the ground that Eastern feeling made the dog an unclean scavenger; Robertson leaves both open; Calvin takes the second and makes it the crowning proof of cruelty; and CLARKE DENIES THE CRUELTY ALTOGETHER -- the crumbs were likely given, nothing says the beggar was spurned from the gate, and the later request for water 'is a strong intimation that he considered him under some kind of obligation to him; nor does Abraham glance at any such uncharitable conduct.' (4) THE WORD 'SON' at k25: Ellicott hears the same tone of pity the father used to the elder brother in the previous parable; Calvin hears irony, 'as if pain inflicted by a hot iron wounded his mind.' (5) THE FIVE BROTHERS at k28: Ellicott calls the allusions to the five senses and the five books of Moses 'simply fantastic' -- and Gill, in the same catena, attempts a numerical reckoning of exactly that kind. (6) THE MEASURES at k6-7: five voices give five incompatible values for the bath, Barnes declines to settle it because 'the amount is not material', and CLARKE ATTACKS THE ENGLISH for concealing that the two originals stand 'as seven to seventy-five' and says 'the present marginal reading is incorrect.' LIGHTFOOT ALONE notices that the two abatements are of unequal proportion (fifty in a hundred of oil, twenty in a hundred of wheat) and resolves it from the metrology.

FURTHER FINDINGS FROM luke 16 WORTH INDEXING. (a) GILL RUNS A SUSTAINED CHRISTOLOGICAL ALLEGORY OF LAZARUS THAT NOBODY ELSE IN THE CATENA SHARES. At k21 the crumbs 'may express the low condition Christ was in, in his human nature'; at k22 'the death of Christ was not a casual thing... it was agreed unto, and settled in the covenant of grace' -- the beggar's death expounded as the death of Christ at length; at k23 the torment is the state of the scribes and Pharisees and then 'the vengeance of God on the Jews, at the destruction of Jerusalem'. Gill's own k20 note first enumerates and rejects the ordinary identifications (a particular beggar, David, the godly poor, the Gentiles) before arriving at this. It is the most sustained single-voice allegory encountered in the corpus so far and should be flagged if the tags' prevalence field ever distinguishes relation types. (b) LIGHTFOOT AND CLARKE INDEPENDENTLY CITE THE SAME KIMCHI PARABLE at k1 -- the world as a built house, heaven its covering, the stars its candles, the fruits of the earth a table spread, God the owner and man the steward -- Clarke naming 'Rab. Dav. Kimchi's comment on Isaiah, Isa 40:21' and Lightfoot naming Kimchi without the reference. A transmission link between the two, and a second instance of the shingled-content matching problem already flagged for Wesley and Henry: a key-co-occurrence test would catch this one (same key) but not the general case. (c) LIGHTFOOT IS A DISTINCTIVE VOICE IN THIS CHAPTER AND UNDER-USED IN THE CORPUS. Fifteen blocks, 2,614 words, and he alone supplies: the Mishnaic law of letting ground for a share of the produce (k1); the artificer/labourer distinction that answers 'I cannot dig' (k3); the unequal-abatement problem (k6); two proposed renderings of 'mammon of unrighteousness', including 'hurtful mammon' from a legal term for damage to another's estate (k9); the Zacchaeus answer to whether anyone can be faithful in unrighteous mammon (k11); a reading of 'presseth into it' as PERSECUTION rather than eagerness, defended by the method of the Talmudic schools (k16); the Eliezer-of-Damascus suggestion behind the name Lazarus (k20); a rabbinic parallel parable of two wicked men, one repenting, who see each other after death (k23); rabbinic material on the dead conversing (k24); the debate over whether paradise and hell are a handbreadth apart or have a wall between (k26); and the definition of 'the Prophets' as including the historical books, with the Hagiographa excluded because they were not read in synagogue (k29). (d) ELLICOTT DISTINGUISHES HADES FROM GEHENNA at k23 and allows that 'as far as the parable itself is concerned, there is nothing to exclude the thought that the torments might in part have the character of a discipline as well as of retribution' -- the most theologically venturesome sentence encountered in his notes so far, and worth flagging to the owner as a place where the synthesis reports a live position rather than a settled one. (e) ELLICOTT AND ROBERTSON BOTH IDENTIFY THE CLOSING SENTENCE WITH LAZARUS OF BETHANY at k31, Ellicott adding that he 'can hardly believe the coincidence of name and fact' accidental and Robertson citing Alford to the same effect. (f) TRUNCATIONS: Gill at exactly 200 words on SEVEN keys (8, 19, 20, 21, 22, 23, 28). No other voice hits a round cap in this chapter.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, luke 16 -- eleven entries over 31 contiguous source keys, 57,564 usable source words (56,128 after chrome), TWENTY-FIVE distinct voices, the widest voice set met in the corpus so far. Every verse checked against its source blocks before writing and again after each trim pass. WORD COUNTS (window 350-650, no thin exemptions): 1-2 648w / 13 voices; 3-5 620w / 7 (Jamieson excluded, residue at k4); 6-7 631w / 6; 8-9 642w / 13; 10-12 649w / 8; 13-15 645w / 11; 16-18 645w / 9; 19-21 650w / 14; 22-24 648w / 16 -- the largest voice count in any entry written to date, all five modern schools plus latin-fathers and eastern-antiochene; 25-27 646w / 11; 28-31 650w / 8 (Jamieson excluded, residue at k28). Total 7,074 synthesis words from 57,564 source words = 12.3% expansion ratio. ATTRIBUTION: no claim in the prose is untraceable to a named block within its span. GRADE: HIGH confidence on the modern voices and on the disagreements, which are unusually explicit here because the commentators answer each other by name and by position (Ellicott listing thirteen rivals; Clarke denying the cruelty everyone else assumes; Calvin and Ellicott opposed on the single word 'son'). MEDIUM confidence on the patristic attributions, and the reason is a source defect rather than a judgement call: the Catena Aurea blocks carry nested attributions inline with no markup, so material the Catena gives to one father is filed under another. I wrote using outer head names only and avoided naming any nested father not independently a head in the same span, which keeps the synthesis exactly as accurate as the data and no more. Two Cyril of Alexandria blocks (k1, k10) are bare lection text and were silenced; a Cyril of Jerusalem block at k22 is residue on Acts 11 and was likewise silenced. Because the QA VOICE_LABELS list cannot express those labels, none of the three could be declared as excluded_voices, so this chapter's residue is invisible to corpus QA -- flagged separately. DEGRADATION SIGNAL, unchanged: EVERY ONE of the eleven entries overshot the 650-word ceiling on first draft, three of them by more than 25% (10-12 at 835 before trimming, 19-21 at 851, 25-27 at 867), and two needed a full prose rewrite rather than sentence trimming. Six of the eleven took four or more trim passes. ROTATION REMAINS THE STANDING FLAG -- this is the second full chapter of this session and the second consecutive batch in which every single entry needed compression.

Jamieson residue at keys 4, 10, 16 — class 4 mod 6, three members at constant step 6. Sixteenth chapter characterised and the sixteenth mod-6 hit; target-key selection is now mod-6 in sixteen of sixteen cases across five residue classes (0, 2, 3, 4 and now a second class-4 chapter). Donor is Colossians 1: k4 gives Col 1:7 (Epaphras and the 'also' omitted in the oldest manuscripts), k10 gives Col 1:12 (giving thanks unto the Father, who made us meet), k16 gives Col 1:17 (He is before all things). Donor advances 7, 12, 17 — plus 5 then plus 5 against a target advancing plus 6, the uniform slower-slope family. The legacy entries this repair replaces had laundered Jamieson into the voices list at all three keys; the repair moves it to excluded_voices on entries 4, 9 and 12.

NEW TOKENIZER DEFECT, corpus-wide. synthesis_qa._LABEL_RE requires a bare surname from VOICE_LABELS followed immediately by a colon, so any block whose label carries a toponym or epithet is invisible to split_voices and is silently folded into the PRECEDING voice's segment. Confirmed here three times: 'Victorinus of Pettau:' at k1 (183 words, becomes the leading None segment) and 'Cyril of Jerusalem:' at k5 and k13 (each ~200 words, absorbed into the tails of Wesley and Robertson respectively). The same trap must apply to 'Cyril of Alexandria', 'Augustine of Hippo', 'Gregory the Great' and 'Theodoret of Cyrrhus', all of which the corpus already uses as declared voice names (Augustine of Hippo 307 uses, Cyril of Alexandria 122, Cyril of Jerusalem 835). Three consequences: attributions get mis-assigned to whichever modern commentator precedes the block; usable_source_words is inflated because such a block can never be excluded; and undeclarable_voices rejects the long-form name in excluded_voices while ungrounded_voices accepts it in voices, so the two gates disagree. I wrote this chapter with a local dumper using an extended label regex. Worth an owner decision on whether _LABEL_RE should carry the long forms.

Second, independent residue stream in this chapter: the Cyril of Jerusalem blocks are Catechetical Lecture text, selected per key and truncated at ~200 words mid-sentence (same 200-word cap already documented for Gill and Keil). At k13 the block is about the firmament and the waters above the heaven — wholly unrelated to the golden girdle — and is pure filler, so Cyril is NOT declared on the entry covering 12-16. At k5 it happens to be on point: the argument that those who confess one God but deny the Father of Jesus Christ contradict their own prophets, and it breaks off exactly at Ps 88:28 LXX, 'And I will make him my [firstborn, higher than the kings of the earth]' — the very verse Ellicott and Robertson both cite on 'the first begotten of the dead' and 'the prince of the kings of the earth'. So the excerpt was cut to the target verse even though the source is a catechetical lecture. Cyril declared on entry 4 only.

Chrome at BOTH ends of this chapter, a first. At k1 there is a new class: book-preface material at the first key of a book's first chapter — Barnes 3,769 words opening with the scraper line about introductory material being found under Malachi, and Clarke 5,670 words of survey (the four hypotheses of interpretation, the authorship question, Wetstein's synopsis, Bale's commentary) before any verse comment at all, roughly 9,000 words of book-level matter. Much of Clarke's is genuinely usable and I used it, but it must be budgeted separately from verse comment. At k20 the familiar Ellicott chapter-final StudyLight boilerplate appears for the THIRTEENTH confirmed time, and this is the worst instance yet: about 900 words of raw CSS, JavaScript and the site's entire book_data array, plus a navigation fragment. Barnes at k20 by contrast ends in a genuine peroration, not chrome. Rule stands: subtract Ellicott chrome, Barnes REMARKS and Clarke end-of-book essays before budgeting a final span, and now also subtract book-preface matter before budgeting a first span.

The seven spirits are the sharpest five-way division I have met in a single verse, and one commentator names another to his face. Clarke argues for seven angels from Tobit 12:15, the Targum on Gen 11:7 and Pirkey Eliezer, and calls it 'most evident from the place, the number, and the tradition'. Barnes canvasses four opinions in order and lists the angel party as 'Beza, Drusius, Hammond, Wetstein, Rosenmuller, Clarke, Professor Stuart' — naming Clarke explicitly — then decides for the Holy Spirit because angels are nowhere called the Spirits of God. Ellicott calls the angel reading 'plainly untenable'. Wesley argues it from the book's internal usage: the angels are never termed spirits in Revelation, and when all the angels stand and worship the seven spirits neither stand nor worship. Henry takes it as the perfect Spirit in his diversity of gifts, and Victorinus at k1 had already found the sevenfold Spirit in Isaiah. Carried into entry 4 as a five-sided debate.

Two clean head-on collisions in this chapter worth keeping. (1) v7: Gill rules out the fall-of-Jerusalem reading on a date, since on the received dating of Domitian's last years the vision falls twenty-odd years after the event; Clarke asserts the same reading and treats it as presumptive proof the book PREDATES the overthrow of the Jewish state. Same verse, opposite chronologies, neither aware of the other. (2) v8: Gill calls Alpha and Omega 'no small proof of the proper deity of Christ' and Ellicott 'a strong declaration of His divinity', while Barnes — agreeing the language could belong to no one but the true God — refuses to use the verse as a proof-text at all, because the manuscripts now preferred read theos where the received text reads kurios. Robertson resolves it the other way, noting the speaker changes unannounced and that only here and at 21:5f is God himself introduced speaking.

Sixth laundering-trap instance this session, and it stayed clean. At v7 Ellicott reports that Augustine saw in 'the clouds' the emblem of the saints of the Church spreading as a fertilising cloud over the world; Augustine has no labelled block anywhere in this chapter, so the reading is carried in the prose as Ellicott's report and Augustine is not declared. Same discipline applied to the doxography inside Barnes at v4 (Eichhorn, Ewald, Grotius, Heinrichs, Beza, Stuart), inside Robertson at v1 (Hort, Swete, Milligan, Moffatt) and inside Ellicott throughout (Plumptre, Maurice, Wordsworth, Vaughan, Trench, Grotius) — I removed a Hort/Swete debate entry from the tags for this reason and reattributed the position to Robertson, who reports it. Rule unchanged: declare a voice only where it has a labelled block in span.

JAMIESON RESIDUE, colossians 4 -- A THIRD SOURCE BOOK, A CLEAN FULL STRIDE, AND A NEARLY FLAT RATE. Three residue blocks at keys 1, 7 and 13 -- all = 1 mod 6, a full stride with NO slot dropped, three consecutive emissions. All three are 1 CORINTHIANS 7, in order: k1 (32w) = the duty of cohabitation, the oldest manuscripts reading simply 'her due' (1 Cor 7:3-4); k7 (42w) = 'have not continency', burning with the secret flame of lust, the dew of God's grace needed to stifle the flame (1 Cor 7:9); k13 (479w) = the unbelieving husband sanctified by the wife, with a long excursus on infant baptism superseding circumcision and an Anabaptist rebuttal from Archbishop Whately (1 Cor 7:14). RATE: k1 to k7 is 6 target keys across 1 Cor 7:3 to 7:9, six source verses -- 6 per 6 keys. k7 to k13 is 6 target keys across 7:9 to 7:14, five source verses -- 5 per 6 keys. So the rate here is 6 then 5: a mild decline, NOT the steep one seen at romans 7 (9.5, 7, 4.5) or luke 16 (5, then 2). This is an important counter-datum: the in-chapter decline is real but its slope varies a lot, and colossians 4 is close to flat at the corpus median. NEW SOURCE BOOK: previous residue streams traced to Acts 10 (romans 6/7), Luke 7 (luke 16) and Acts 13 (romans 12). 1 Corinthians 7 is a fourth. Note also that the k13 block is 479 words, by far the largest residue block yet measured -- earlier ones ran 27 to 138 -- so residue block SIZE is not a reliable discriminator and length cannot be used to detect it. OFFSETS OBSERVED TO DATE: genesis 2 = 1, exodus 24 = 1, deuteronomy 17 = 3, deuteronomy 26 = 2, romans 12 = 1, romans 6 = 4, romans 7 = 4, luke 16 = 4, colossians 4 = 1. The per-chapter (not global) stride continues to hold in every chapter measured.

TWO DEFECTS IN colossians 4, ONE OF THEM A NEW CHROME FAMILY. (1) TERTULLIAN AT k7 IS THE WRONG EPISTLE, AND CARRIES A CHROME TAIL NOT PREVIOUSLY CATALOGUED. His only block in the chapter (229 words) is not about Colossians at all: it discusses PHILEMON -- 'To this epistle alone did its brevity avail to protect it against the falsifying hands of Marcion' -- and then closes a section of Adversus Marcionem with an address to the reader. Worse, the block ends with a scrape trailer: 'This document (last modified February 03, 1998) from the Christian Classics Electronic Library server, at Wheaton College Verse numbers added from Evans/Kroymann and minor typos fixed for the Tertullian Project, 8th July 2003.' This is a THIRD chrome family, distinct from the two already on the owner's list (Ellicott's 'Copyright Statement These files are public domain' and Gill's 'Next: <Book> Chapter <n>'). It is keyed on 'This document (last modified' and on 'Christian Classics Electronic Library'. A single removable rule would strip it wherever Tertullian blocks appear. I named the block in the prose accurately, as a note on Philemon rather than on this chapter, since Tertullian is a head at k7 and suppressing him would have raised a GHOST. (2) THE CALVIN EDITORIAL APPARATUS, THIRD CHAPTER RUNNING. At k9 Calvin doubts that the Onesimus named here is Philemon's slave; the printed text then supplies, inline and in the same voice, a summary of PALEY's Horae Paulinae and its undesigned-coincidence argument -- a work published more than two centuries after Calvin's death -- concluding against him. At k1 the same apparatus cites Aristotle's definition of proportional equality with a cross-reference to the editor's own page numbering ('See Calvin on the Corinthians, vol. 2, p. 294'). At k15 it does it again ('See Calvin on the Corinthians, vol. 2, p. 78'). At k10 and k16 it supplies the French of the 16th-century translation in parallel. Same defect already filed against romans 7 (four instances) and implicitly against luke 16: a block that is one voice in the markup and two in fact, with no signal of the change of hand. I wrote around it at k9 by naming it explicitly as editorial matter, which is accurate but is a per-chapter workaround. colossians 4: CALVIN DISSENTS ALONE THREE TIMES, AND TWO VOICES ATTACK ROME BY THE SAME ARGUMENT. (1) CALVIN AGAINST THE FIELD, THREE TIMES. (a) At k6, on speech seasoned with salt: Barnes reports that salt among the Greeks was the emblem of wit, Clarke invokes 'Attic salt', Robertson says outright that grace and salt (wit, sense) make an ideal combination. Calvin refuses the whole line -- he grants that classical writers use the term for witticisms but says the apostle does not speak of these; 'as witticisms are insinuating, and for the most part procure favor, he indirectly prohibits believers from the practice and familiar use of them. For he reckons as tasteless everything that does not edify.' A rare case of one voice reading a word in the exactly opposite direction from every other. (b) At k9, on Onesimus: Gill, Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson all identify him with Philemon's runaway. Calvin: 'it can scarcely be believed that this is the slave of Philemon, inasmuch as the name of a thief and a fugitive would have been liable to reproach.' (c) At k14, on Luke: Gill, Barnes, Robertson and Ellicott all take the beloved physician for the evangelist. Calvin: 'I do not agree with those who understand this to be Luke the Evangelist; for I am of opinion that he was too well known to stand in need of such a designation, and he would have been signalized by a more magnificent eulogium... I rather conjecture that he was absent at that time, and that it is another of the same name.' (2) TWO TRADITIONS, ONE ARGUMENT FROM SILENCE, AT k11. Clarke: 'It is evident, therefore, that St. Peter was not now at Rome, else he certainly would have been mentioned in this list... And as it cannot be proved that he ever was bishop or pope of that city, the keystone of the triumphal arch of the pope of Rome is pulled out; this building, therefore, of his supremacy, cannot stand.' Calvin, independently and two centuries earlier: 'But where was Peter at that time? Unquestionably, he has either been shamefully passed over here, and not without injustice, or else those speak falsely who maintain that he was then at Rome.' Reformed and Wesleyan-Arminian reaching the same polemical conclusion from the same verse. (3) THE ARISTARCHUS/EPAPHRAS FELLOW-PRISONER CONTRADICTION AT k10 is admitted by everyone and solved by none. Clarke: 'One of them is wrong, though it is uncertain which; unless both were prisoners.' Ellicott calls the variation 'one of the characteristic marks of independence and genuineness in the Epistles' but concedes 'it can only be accounted for by mere conjecture, such as that of their alternately sharing the Apostle's captivity.' Robertson reports Abbott arguing for literal imprisonment shared by turns. (4) WHETHER THE WORD TO ARCHIPPUS IS A REBUKE, at k17: Gill says he was 'negligent in his office'; Calvin says 'perhaps he was not of such a disposition as to be sufficiently diligent of himself without being stirred up'; Barnes says 'There is no evidence, as has been supposed by some, that he intended to imply... that he had been remiss'; Clarke refutes the rebuke reading BY A DATE, since the same man is called fellow-labourer and fellow-soldier in Philemon written the same year and cannot have been both at Rome and a delinquent at Colosse. (5) THE EPISTLE FROM LAODICEA at k16 splits four ways: Calvin and Wesley say it was written TO the apostle FROM Laodicea; Robertson identifies it with the circular we call Ephesians; Clarke lays out all three standing conjectures and rejects the first as 'forced and far fetched'; Ellicott refers the reader to Lightfoot's excursus and declines to decide.

FURTHER FINDINGS FROM colossians 4. (a) ★ BARNES DATES HIMSELF TWICE, IN AN ANTI-SLAVERY ARGUMENT AIMED AT HIS OWN COUNTRY. At k1 he argues that the apostles 'did not design to make a violent disruption of these bonds, or to lead the slaves to rise and murder their masters', but 'meant to represent slavery as a hard and undesirable condition... to instruct the slaves to embrace the earliest opportunity to be free... and to lay down such principles as would lead masters to emancipate their slaves, and thus ultimately to abolish it.' At k9 he goes further and makes it explicit and contemporary: 'Would a minister of the gospel now in the Northern States, who should send a letter by a runaway slave to a community of masters at the South, say of him that he was one of them? Would it be kindly received, or produce a good impression, if he did?' This is the most openly period-and-place-specific polemic met in any commentary in the corpus so far, and it is doing real exegetical work -- he uses it to argue that Onesimus was not of the rank the modern word denotes. Worth flagging to the owner separately from the ordinary disagreement notes: where a voice argues from the politics of its own decade, the synthesis reports a nineteenth-century American argument as if it were a reading of the text. I attributed it plainly to Barnes and to his own century. (b) THE GENDER OF NYMPHAS IS UNDECIDABLE AT k15, and two voices say so. Ellicott: some manuscripts read 'in his house', some 'in her house', the best 'in their house'; the second would require the feminine form Nympha, 'with which the form of the original hardly agrees'. Robertson lists the witnesses on each side and concludes: 'It is not possible to tell whether it is her or his house here.' A rare instance of the catena leaving a question of fact open rather than resolving it. (c) ELLICOTT DERIVES THE CANON FROM THE EXCHANGE OF LETTERS at k16: 'in the direction to interchange Epistles with the Laodicean Church, we trace the way in which these Epistles became more widely diffused, and recognised as authoritative in the Church at large. Thus it was that they were canonised'; and he adds that the likelihood of public reading 'has an important bearing on the question of the authenticity of some of the books, which were placed among the doubtful by Eusebius', and that the public reading of other books 'was the cause of their being wrongly confused with the books of Holy Scripture.' (d) ELLICOTT FINDS THE GERM OF THE EPISCOPATE TWICE: at k13, in one man's responsibility for three cities, 'we see the link between the apostolate of this period and the episcopacy of the future'; at k17, in the ministry of Archippus, 'it is likely enough that he had that leadership among the presbyters, from which the episcopate was developed at the close of the Apostolic period.' (e) GILL PRESERVES THE GALEN LEGEND at k14: that Luke was a scholar of Galen, or his sister's son, who having heard of Christ's miracles set out with his master for Judea to learn the truth of them, Galen dying on the way while Luke came to Christ and became one of the seventy. (f) TWO TEXTUAL VARIANTS PREFERRED AGAINST THE RECEIVED TEXT: at k8 Clarke and Robertson both prefer 'that ye may know our affairs' to 'that he may know yours'; at k12 Clarke and Ellicott both prefer 'fully persuaded' to 'complete', Clarke noting it is the reading of almost all manuscripts of the Alexandrian recension. (g) TRUNCATIONS: Gill at exactly 200 words on four keys (2, 6, 7, 14). No other voice hits a round cap in this chapter.
