FOUR ENTRIES RATHER THAN FIVE WAS A DELIBERATE TILING CHOICE. The obvious five-way split puts a boundary after v10, but keys 8, 9 and 10 carry only 531 usable source words between them -- Gill's k10 block is thirteen words -- so a 8-10 entry would have been starved and a 11-13 entry over-fed. Folding them into one 8-13 entry gives source budgets of 4183 / 3551 / 4498 / 2086, which is the flattest distribution available. The lesson generalises: in the Levitical legal chapters the source mass follows the CONTROVERSIAL verses (leaven, honey, salt) and not the verse count, so tiling should be budgeted on source words per candidate range, not on verses per entry. COMPRESSION: only ONE of four first drafts overshot the 650 window (8-13, by 15 words), fixed with three sentence-level substitutions in one pass. That is the lowest overshoot rate of any chapter this rotation; the cause is almost certainly that the four-entry tiling gave each entry more room than the usual six-entry split. GHOST CHECK CLEAN ON FIRST RUN -- no DECLARED-NOT-PRESENT, no PRESENT-NOT-DECLARED, no DECLARED-NOT-USED, no EXCLUDED-BUT-NAMED. THREE ITEMS. (1) JAMIESON RESIDUE WITH THE SOURCE INSIDE THE SAME BOOK. Two blocks, at keys 2 and 14; 2 mod 6 = 2, 14 mod 6 = 2, so offset 2, which had previously been seen only at deuteronomy 26. The source is GENESIS 13, four chapters earlier in the same book: k2 = Gen 13:1 (Palestine being a highland country, the entrance from Egypt by its southern boundary is a continual ascent), k14 = Gen 13:10-11 (Lot's choice of the plain, a choice excellent from a worldly point of view but most inexpedient for his best interests). Every previously identified residue source has been a DIFFERENT book from the target (Acts 10, Acts 13, Luke 7, 1 Cor 7, Romans 1, 1 Cor 6, Ephesians 5, 1 Thess 4-5). This is the first case where the residue stream is drawn from the same book as the chapter it contaminates, and from a nearby chapter at that. It matters for the owner's re-indexing decision, because an off-by-N chapter error within a book would produce exactly this, whereas it would not obviously produce the cross-book cases. Rate here is about 9 source verses across 12 target keys. (2) CALVIN EDITORIAL APPARATUS -- SEVENTH CHAPTER RUNNING, and the SECOND time it contradicts Calvin in his own block. At key 13, after Calvin calls the God of vision interpretation forced, the block continues without markup: Though Calvin regards this interpretation as forced, it must not be denied that it has the sanction of the highest literary authorities. Le Clerc, Peter Martyr, Rosenmuller, Dathe, Gesenius, Lee, Professor Bush, and many others, all regard the word roi as a substantive, not as a participle -- and consequently God is here spoken of as the God who reveals himself, not as the God who sees. The same block carries three Latin glosses and an English-version cross-reference. Combined with the genesis 20 key 13 instance, the pattern is now clear: the apparatus is a nineteenth-century editor's running commentary, printed inline, sometimes agreeing and sometimes refuting, and always in the third person about Calvin. A stripping rule keyed on third-person references to Calvin plus the Latin and French quotation runs would catch it. (3) MINOR TEXT CORRUPTION: the Gill block at key 16 opens And Abram was eighty years old when Hagar bare Ishmael, where the verse and Gill's own arithmetic in the same block (75 at Haran, 10 in Canaan, 85 at the marriage) both give eighty-six. A dropped word in the lemma, not in the comment.

FOUR DISAGREEMENTS, ONE OF THEM RESOLVED INSIDE THE CHAPTER BY PHILOLOGY. (1) 16:6 vs 16:9 WHETHER SARAI ILL-USED HAGAR. Clarke at 16:6 says the verb rendered dealt hardly implies stripes and hard usage, to bring down the body and humble the mind. Ellicott at 16:9 answers him from the Hebrew: the word rendered SUBMIT THYSELF in verse 9 is the very same verb, so that the angel is commanding Hagar to take exactly the position Sarai was forcing upon her -- and by so doing proves to us that there had been no personal maltreatment. He adds, pointedly, that commentators have taken the contrary notion NOT FROM THE HEBREW BUT FROM THE ENGLISH VERSION. This is the cleanest instance in the rotation of one voice refuting another on lexical grounds three verses later, and the synthesis had to be built so that the reader meets Clarke first and Ellicott second. (2) 16:12 THE WILD-ASS MAN. Ellicott defends the animal at length -- the wild ass of the Arabian deserts is a very noble creature, chosen in Job to exemplify the greatness of God, its marks being speed, love of solitude and an untamable fondness of liberty, so that it is the exact type of the Bedaween who despise the ease of a settled life. Clarke quotes Job 39:5-8 entire as the very best description of the Ishmaelites and concludes that God himself has sent them out free and loosed them from all political restraint. Gill turns it into current affairs, that no empire from Assyria to Rome subdued them and that the Arabs of his own day make the Turks pay yearly for the passage of pilgrims to Mecca. CALVIN REJECTS THE ANIMAL ALTOGETHER: the simple meaning is that Ishmael will be a warlike man, and the reading that makes him a forester or hunter is to be refused, since the explanation must be sought in the context and not in etymology. (3) 16:12 WHETHER THIS IS A BLESSING AT ALL. Calvin alone asks whether it can be reckoned among God's benefits that a man should preserve his rank by force of arms, seeing nothing is more desirable than peace; and answers by grading the blessings -- peace with all men is among the chief, it is here denied to Ishmael, and so the blessing next in order is granted instead, that he shall not be overcome. No simple or unmixed blessing is promised, only a tolerable or moderate condition; and it is by no means to be reckoned among the benefits given by God that he shall have all around him as enemies. Wesley divides the verse instead, making his hand against every man the sin and every man's hand against him the punishment. (4) 16:13 WHAT HAGAR CALLED GOD. Ellicott: not a God who sees all things, as Onkelos paraphrases, but a God who PERMITS HIMSELF TO BE SEEN, with Hagar's own following words as the explanation. Clarke: the general sense is her surprise at surviving the sight of God, but the word rendered after elsewhere means the latter times, so read, have I here also seen the LATTER PURPOSES of him that seeth me, referring the exclamation to the prophecy just given about her descendants. Calvin: calls the God of vision reading forced and makes the point simply that Hagar now perceives human affairs are under divine government -- and is contradicted in his own margin by his editor. Three readings and an editorial fourth on one clause.

NOTABLE MATERIAL WORTH KEEPING. (1) 16:1 Ellicott gives, inside a verse note, an account of how Genesis was composed: the history of Abram is a succession of brief narratives, written possibly by the patriarch himself; papyrus was known at Ur, but the absence of convenient writing material would oblige men to short inscriptions like the clay tablets brought from Ur, many of them older than Abram; a later narrator would make few alterations in such precious documents, hence the recapitulation; and additions such as the note that a valley was later called the King's Dale are credited to Ezra and the men of the Great Synagogue. He guards it by saying the narrator was guided by inspiration in his choice of materials and that his evident reverence is a warrant of genuineness. This is the same critical register as his source-criticism answer at genesis 20:3 and his authenticity thread through 2peter 2 -- Ellicott is doing sustained higher-critical work inside a devotional commentary, and it recurs across books. (2) 16:1 and 16:6 A CONNECTED ETYMOLOGY. Ellicott derives Hagar from an Arabic verb to flee, concludes it cannot have been her original name, and makes her an Egyptian who had escaped to Abram and been called, in effect, the run-away -- then at 16:6 completes the figure: in running away she not only showed the untamable love of freedom which Ishmael inherited from her, but apparently was REPEATING THE ACT FROM WHICH SHE HAD HER NAME. Clarke derives the name instead from a Hebrew word for stranger or sojourner and reports a Greek father's conjecture that she was one of the slaves Pharaoh gave Abram. (3) 16:10 Ellicott states the chapter's logic as a bargain: the purpose of the divine appearance is that Abram's son should not be lost among the population of Egypt but become the father of a free people, and Hagar will now submit to her lot as a slave THAT SHE MAY SECURE LIBERTY FOR HER OFFSPRING. (4) 16:8 CALVIN ON SERVITUDE, worth recording with its date. Liberty is not to be obtained by stealth, nor by flight, but by manumission; God thereby shows he approves of civil government. He grants that the condition of servitude was then hard and gives thanks that this barbarity has been abolished, yet holds that God declared from heaven that servants should bear the yoke; and he extends it: if masters at any time deal too hardly with their servants, or if rulers treat their subjects with unjust asperity, their rigour is still to be endured, nor is there just cause for shaking off the yoke. (5) 16:10 Calvin on divine method: God might by his own authority have strictly enjoined what was right, but he allures her, as by blandishments, to obedience -- he would not draw us by servile methods, and therefore mingles mild and paternal invitations with his commands, dealing with us liberally, as with sons. (6) 16:11 Calvin distinguishes two ways in which God helps men, when they implore his aid as suppliants and when, unasked, he succours them in their afflictions, since we do not read that Hagar prayed. Wesley reaches the same in one line: even where there is little cry of devotion, the God of pity hears the cry of affliction, for tears speak as well as prayers. (7) 16:1 Henry: it is the policy of Satan to tempt us by our nearest and dearest relations, the temptation being most dangerous when sent by a hand least suspected, so that it is our wisdom to consider not so much who speaks as what is spoken. Calvin reaches the same warning independently in the same chapter. (8) 16:14 Calvin makes Hagar's change the proof that those who will not freely humble themselves should be subdued by stripes, then adds the qualification that saves it: she was not reduced to order by stripes only, a celestial vision being added, and the same is necessary for us.

WESLEY IS ABRIDGING HENRY, AND THE SCAN CAUGHT IT AT THREE KEYS. The cross-voice duplication scan (12-word shingles, threshold 5 overlapping shingles) fired on Matthew Henry <-> John Wesley at k1 (22 shingles), k4 (12) and k10 (5). This is not a scrape defect: it is a genuine textual dependence, Wesley's Explanatory Notes condensing Henry's Exposition. k1 Wesley opens 'We have here the marriage of Abram to Hagar, who was his secondary wife. Herein, though he may be excused, he cannot be justified; for from the beginning it was not so' against Henry's 'We have here the marriage of Abram to Hagar, who was his secondary wife. Herein, though some excuse may be made for him, he cannot be justified, for from the beginning it was not so'. k4 Wesley reproduces Henry's 'When passion is upon the throne, reason is out of doors, and is neither heard nor spoken' and 'Rash and bold imprecations are commonly evidences of guilt and a bad cause' verbatim. k10 he reproduces 'multiplying I will multiply it, that is, multiply it in every age, so as to perpetuate it. 'Tis supposed that the Turks at this day descended from Ishmael, and they are a great people'. CONSEQUENCE FOR PREVALENCE COUNTING, WHICH IS THE POINT OF RECORDING THIS. Henry is puritan-evangelical and Wesley is wesleyan-arminian, so a shared judgement is counted twice, once in each school summary, and reads as two schools independently converging when it is one source read twice. This was noted once before as a single-sentence case at ruth 4 (2026-08-23); three keys in one chapter makes it a standing property of the pair rather than a coincidence. HANDLING USED HERE: the prose names Henry for the substance and says explicitly that Wesley repeats or condenses him ('Wesley repeats him almost word for word' at 1-3, 'Wesley reproduces the judgment almost verbatim' at 4-6, 'Wesley condenses him' at 7-9), and the two school summaries were written from the parts of each voice that are HIS OWN -- Henry's numbered heads and applications, Wesley's shorter glosses on individual words. Recommendation for the next worker: run the duplication scan on every chapter where both Henry and Wesley are voices, and do not treat a Henry/Wesley agreement as independent attestation without checking it.

THREE ITEMS. (1) JAMIESON RESIDUE: TWO BLOCKS, keys 2 and 14, offset 2 mod 6, step 12. Twenty-fourth consecutive chapter whose residue keys are congruent mod 6, though with only two blocks the stride could equally be 12; recorded for the offset table rather than as independent evidence. THE DONOR IS GENESIS 13, i.e. WITHIN THE SAME BOOK, and both blocks are in donor order. k2 (17 words) 'Palestine being a highland country, the entrance from Egypt by its southern boundary is a continual ascent' is Jamieson on 13:1, Abram going UP out of Egypt into the south. k14 (52 words) 'a choice excellent from a worldly point of view, but most inexpedient for his best interests. He seems, though a good man, to have been too much under the influence of a selfish and covetous spirit: and how many, alas! imperil the good of their souls for the prospect of worldly advantage' is Jamieson on Lot choosing the plain of Jordan at 13:10-11. This is the fifth within-book donor observed (after three in Luke and one in Acts) and the first where the donor chapter is only three chapters distant from the target. (2) ELLICOTT STUDYLIGHT CHAPTER-FINAL CHROME, SIXTEENTH CONFIRMATION, and the rule established at ruth 4 holds again: it rides on ELLICOTT'S LAST BLOCK IN THE CHAPTER, not the chapter's last key. His k14 block is 1046 words of which only the first ~75 are commentary (Beer-lahai-roi, the well where God has been seen and the beholder still lives; a favourite dwelling of Isaac; Bered absolutely unknown). The rest is chapter links, a copyright footer, ~800 words of raw CSS from the site's sub-menu stylesheet, and a directory listing of the site's reference works. Ellicott has no block at k15 or k16. (3) GILL'S LEMMA AT k16 MISQUOTES THE VERSE HE IS EXPOUNDING. The block opens 'And Abram was eighty years old when Hagar bare Ishmael to Abram' where the KJV has 'fourscore and six years old' -- and Gill's own arithmetic in the same block gives eighty-six (seventy-five at leaving Haran, plus ten years in Canaan before Hagar was given him, plus the pregnancy). So the lemma is internally contradicted two sentences later. This looks like a transcription drop of 'and six' in the source text rather than a Gill error; a reader synthesising from the lemma alone would land on the wrong number. Worth a spot-check wherever a Gill lemma carries a figure.

NOTABLE MATERIAL. (1) 16:1 ELLICOTT'S SOURCE THEORY, stated more fully here than anywhere else in the chapters worked this rotation: the history of Abram is a succession of brief narratives, possibly written by the patriarch himself, since the absence of convenient writing material would oblige men to content themselves with short inscriptions like the clay tablets from Ur, many now in the British Museum and said to be considerably older than Abram; a narrator handling such documents would alter little, which accounts for the recapitulation, as in the books of Samuel, where we have 'not a narrative from one pen, but the arrangement of materials already ancient'. He then guards it: the choice of materials and the omissions were guided by inspiration, and 'the evident reverence with which he deals with these records is a warrant to us of their genuineness'. He assigns later notes such as the King's Dale gloss to Ezra and the men of the Great Synagogue. (2) 16:6 vs 16:9 A CLEAN PHILOLOGICAL DISAGREEMENT THAT DECIDES A MORAL QUESTION. Clarke on v6: the verb 'implies stripes and hard usage, to bring down the body and humble the mind', and 'if the slave was to blame in this business the mistress is not less liable to censure'. Ellicott on v9: 'submit thyself' is literally 'humble thyself', the SAME verb rendered 'dealt hardly' in v6, so the angel commands Hagar to take the very position Sarai was forcing on her, 'and by so doing proves to us that there had been no personal maltreatment. Commentators have taken this notion, not from the Hebrew, but from the English Version.' Ellicott is arguing that the English translation has manufactured a cruelty the Hebrew does not contain, and Clarke is a specimen of exactly the reading he is attacking. Calvin lands between them, refusing to go beyond what is certain, that 'Sarai made use of her proper authority in restraining the insolence of her maid', and judging from the flight itself that Hagar was driven out 'not so much by the cruelty of her mistress, as by her own contumacy'. (3) 16:7 CALVIN ON THE CLEMENCY OF THE CHASTISEMENT: 'He does not indeed altogether spare them, lest he should cherish their vices; but he corrects them with gentle remedies' -- and the observation that the favour shown to Hagar extends God's mercy to the WHOLE family, the offending wife and the credulous husband included. (4) 16:9 CALVIN'S DOCTRINE OF SUBJECTION, 695 words built entirely on the two words 'Sarai's maid': liberty 'is not to be obtained by stealth, nor by flight, but by manumission'; God 'approves of civil government, and the violation of it is inexcusable'; the condition of servitude was hard 'and thanks are to be given to the Lord, that this barbarity has been abolished', yet Paul 'does not give servants their freedom, nor deprive their masters of their use; but only commands them to be kindly and liberally treated'; and if rulers 'treat their subjects with unjust asperity, their rigour is still to be endured', those who governed tyrannically being answerable to God. He then generalises to rebellion against princes and to children withdrawing from parents. This is the largest single doctrinal excursus in any chapter this rotation and it hangs on an epithet. (5) 16:12 CLARKE TURNS THE PROPHECY INTO AN APOLOGETIC PROOF: Sesostris, Cyrus, Pompey and Trajan all attempted Arabia in vain, and 'had the Pentateuch no other argument to evince its Divine origin, the account of Ishmael and the prophecy concerning his descendants, collated with their history and manner of life during a period of nearly four thousand years, would be sufficient'. Ellicott independently rehabilitates the image, insisting the wild ass of the Arabian deserts 'is a very noble creature' chosen in Job to exemplify the greatness of God, its marks being speed, love of solitude and an untamable fondness of liberty. (6) 16:13 ELLICOTT ON EL ROI: not, as Onkelos paraphrases, a God that sees all things, but 'a God that permits Himself to be seen' -- and he reads Hagar's follow-up as her own explanation, with 'all the love of an Oriental for dark sayings': 'Do I not see, and therefore am alive, and not even blinded, nor bereft of sense and reason, though I have seen God.' (7) 16:13 CALVIN'S SURVEY OF THE SAME CLAUSE runs to four rival readings and he adopts none with confidence, dismissing one Jewish reading as 'frigid' and noting that 'the ambition of the Jews often compels them to trifle'. (8) 16:14 CALVIN ON WHY THE NAME WAS PUBLISHED: Hagar, 'not content with one simple confession, wished that the mercy of God should be attested in time to come; and therefore she transmitted her testimony, as from hand to hand'.

THE JAMIESON DONOR STREAM IS CONTINUOUS ACROSS ADJACENT TARGET CHAPTERS. THIS IS THE STRONGEST RESULT ON THE RESIDUE SO FAR AND IT RESOLVES THE LEVITICUS 2 STALL. Residue here is TWO blocks, keys 3 and 15, offset 3 mod 6, step 12 -- the SAME RESIDUE CLASS as leviticus 2 (keys 3, 9, 15, also class 3). Two adjacent chapters in one book sharing a class is the first evidence that the class is fixed per book or per run rather than drawn independently per chapter. Now the donor. leviticus 1 k3 (148 words) is the COURT OF THE TABERNACLE: a rectangular court rather more than fifty yards by half that, a parapet of fine twined linen woven into network so the people could see through, an embroidered entrance curtain with cords for drawing it aside, sixty brazen pillars on brazen pedestals with silver capitals and fillets. That is Jamieson on EXODUS 27:9-19. leviticus 1 k15 (139 words) is the HOLY GARMENTS: no inherent holiness in material or workmanship, called holy because not worn on ordinary occasions, a grand and sumptuous attire whose splendour was needed for the infantine aid of the church, and all made of linen and so symbolical of the truth and purity in Christ. That is Jamieson on EXODUS 28:2-4. Now set that beside the leviticus 2 residue already recorded: k3 the EPHOD with gold threads and onyx shoulder-stones (Exodus 28:6-12), k9 and k15 the BREASTPLATE, a span square and doubled, twelve stones in four rows (Exodus 28:15-21). PUT THE FIVE BLOCKS IN TARGET ORDER AND THE DONOR IS STRICTLY MONOTONE: lev1 k3 = Ex 27:9-19, lev1 k15 = Ex 28:2-4, lev2 k3 = Ex 28:6-12, lev2 k9 = Ex 28:15-21, lev2 k15 = REPEAT OF k9. The stream is a single linear read-through of Exodus 27-28 that does not reset at the chapter boundary, and the byte-identical repeat at leviticus 2 k15 (md5 2c66095af233) is that read-through RUNNING OUT OF MATERIAL -- the pointer failed to advance because there was nothing left in the segment. That reinterprets the 'stall' recorded at leviticus 2 and at acts 1: a stall is not a random glitch but the terminal state of an exhausted donor segment, the same phenomenon as the 2corinthians 4 k15 'exhaustion' case (five words, the JFB closing byline) reached by a different route. PREDICTION FOR THE NEXT WORKER, worth testing because it is cheap: if leviticus 3 is worked, its residue should be class 3 mod 6 and its donor should be EXODUS 28:22 ONWARD (the chains, the ouches, the robe of the ephod, the bells and pomegranates) or, if the segment is genuinely exhausted, either absent or another stall. Either result is informative. The earlier hypothesis floated at 2corinthians 4 and rejected at acts 1 -- that donor streams run continuously across adjacent target chapters -- is therefore TRUE WITHIN A BOOK and false across books; acts 1 drew from John 6 while 2corinthians 3 and 4 both drew from Acts 28, which is consistent with the stream resetting at a book boundary and not at a chapter boundary. Practical consequence unchanged: Jamieson is excluded_voices on entries 3-4 and 14-17 here.

THREE SMALLER ITEMS. (1) ELLICOTT STUDYLIGHT CHAPTER-FINAL CHROME, SEVENTEENTH CONFIRMATION, and again on ELLICOTT'S LAST BLOCK IN THE CHAPTER rather than the chapter's last key. His k17 block is 1038 words of which only the first ~40 are commentary (the priest made an incision in the wings without separating them wholly from the body, corresponding in some degree to the limbing of the quadruped). The rest is chapter links, a copyright footer, ~800 words of raw CSS from the site's sub-menu stylesheet, and a directory listing of the site's reference works. Ellicott has no block after k17, so the rule holds without exception across seventeen observations. (2) CALVIN EDITORIAL APPARATUS INLINE WITH NO MARKUP -- now the EIGHTH chapter (romans 7, luke 16, colossians 4, 2corinthians 6, colossians 3, genesis 20, and now twice in Leviticus). At leviticus 1 k5 the Calvin block runs straight from Calvin's own exposition into a long bracketed quotation of BONAR citing Outram and Witsius on whether patriarchal-age men might offer their own sacrifices, and then into an editorial verdict IN THE THIRD PERSON about that quotation: 'He appears, however, to be singular in his opinion that any but a Levite might kill the victim.' A reader with no knowledge of the edition would take Bonar's paragraph and the editor's rebuttal of Bonar to be Calvin's own words. Same signature as the genesis 20 k13 case where the apparatus argues AGAINST Calvin inside his own block. The stripping rule wanted here is the one already proposed: key on third-person references to Calvin and on bracketed quotation runs attributed to a named modern editor. (3) THE 200-WORD CAP ON KEIL BLOCKS IS CONFIRMED AGAIN and is worse in this chapter than in leviticus 2. Keil blocks at k1, k2, k4, k5, k6, k7, k8, k11 and k15 all report EXACTLY 200 words; k17 reports 51 because it is a tail. Every one of them opens by reprinting the KJV text of one to five verses before any comment, so a 200-word block can be almost entirely verse text. k8 is the extreme case: it reprints verses 8, 9 and 10 in full and then has room for about one sentence of commentary. Budgeting Keil by block length overstates his real contribution by a wide margin, and a worker tiling by source words should discount Keil blocks heavily.

NOTABLE MATERIAL. (1) 1:1 TWO WITNESSES INDEPENDENTLY BUILD ON A SCRIBAL ODDITY. The last letter of the Hebrew word for 'called' is written in a very small character, and both Gill and Henry make something of it. Gill relays the Jewish readings -- that God met Moses accidentally and unawares; that it respects the modesty of Moses, 'who lessened himself, and got out of the way, that he might not have the government laid upon him'; or that it marks 'the wonderful condescension of the Lord, whose throne is in heaven, and yet vouchsafed to dwell in the tabernacle.' Henry takes it for a still small voice and builds the best sentence in the chapter on it: 'The moral law was given with terror from a burning mountain in thunder and lightning; but the remedial law of sacrifice was given more gently from a mercy-seat, because that was typical of the grace of the gospel, which is the ministration of life and peace.' (2) 1:1 CALVIN'S PROGRAMMATIC REFUSAL, the most explicit statement of method he makes anywhere in the chapters worked this rotation: 'since we read of many things here, the use of which has passed away, and others, the grounds of which I do not understand, I intend to content myself with a brief summary ... Let those who choose to hunt for allegories receive the praise they covet; my object is only to profit my readers.' (3) 1:2 CLARKE ON KORBAN AS THE OFFERING OF ACCESS: from a root 'to approach or draw near,' signifying 'an offering or gift by which a person had access unto God: and this receives light from the universal custom that prevails in the east, no man being permitted to approach the presence of a superior without a present.' He calls it 'the introduction-offering, or offering of access.' (4) 1:2 CLARKE'S CATALOGUE OF PAGAN SACRIFICE, given to sharpen the contrast: 'horses to the Sun, wolves to Mars, asses to Priapus, swine to Ceres, dogs to Hecate' -- against which all gross-feeding and ferocious animals and all birds of prey are excluded here; and fish were not offered 'because they could not be readily brought to the tabernacle alive.' (5) 1:5 THE CLEANEST FIVE-WAY DISAGREEMENT IN THE CHAPTER, on who kills the victim. Keil distinguishes the cases (offerer in private sacrifices, priests and Levites in national and festal ones) and is the only one who resolves it rather than asserting a side. Ellicott has the sacrificer cut the throat while a priest holds the bowl. Gill leans to the bringer, citing traditions that allow the killing to strangers, women, servants and the unclean, but records the Targum for the butcher and Aben Ezra for the priest and the LXX plural. CALVIN FLATLY DENIES THE OFFERER ANY PART: 'it was not allowable for a private person to kill the victim with his own hands, but what the priest did in their name was transferred to them' -- and turns it into doctrine, that 'the hands of all are in a manner polluted or profane except those which God himself has purged.' Wesley dissolves the question with a maxim: 'men are commonly said to do what they cause others to do.' (6) 1:9 GILL RELAYS PHILO ON THE WASHING: the washing of the inwards signified that lusts were to be washed away and such spots removed as were contracted by surfeiting and drunkenness, and the washing of the feet 'that we should no more walk upon the earth, but mount up to the air, and pass through that, even to heaven.' (7) 1:11 FOUR EXPLANATIONS OF THE NORTH SIDE, splitting cleanly into practical and typical. Ellicott is purely topographical: refuse east, laver west, altar-ascent south, so north is what is left. Gill gives Maimonides's measurements, sixty cubits. Henry guesses at the largest vacant space 'and room for the priests to turn them in,' then adds a weather conceit. Gill (via Aben Ezra and Ainsworth) and Wesley both add the typical reading, that Jerusalem is 'on the sides of the north' and Calvary north-west of the city. (8) 1:15 ELLICOTT ON WHY THE PRIEST DOES EVERYTHING IN THE BIRD OFFERING: 'It was probably out of consideration for the feelings of the poor offerer, and to increase the importance of the otherwise small offering' -- and the laying on of hands was dispensed with because the bird was too small and because 'the offerer brought it in his hands to the place of sacrifice, thus conveying by this act the idea involved in the imposition of hands.' A rare case of a witness reading a ritual omission as pastoral tact. (9) 1:16 A TEXTUAL CRUX WHERE THE GRAMMATICAL WITNESSES SPLIT. Keil argues from the Hebrew for 'crop with the foeces' and against the LXX/Luther 'crop with the feathers'; Ellicott argues from sense for the feathers ('it can hardly be imagined that the victims would be burnt with the feathers, and thus cause an intolerable smell') but concedes the field, noting that the marginal reading 'is now adopted by the greater number of expositors' and proposing that the two similar Hebrew words have collapsed, one having dropped out of the text. Ellicott conceding against his own argument is unusual and worth remembering. (10) 1:17 GILL'S CHRISTOLOGICAL READING OF A DISSECTION RULE, and the best instance of the type in this chapter: because the bird was cleft but not parted asunder, 'though, by the death of Christ, his soul and body were separated from each other, yet the human nature was not separated from his divine Person ... nor was he divided from his divine Father, though he was forsaken by him ... nor from his church and people.' (11) 1:17 WESLEY'S CLOSING SENTENCE for the whole chapter: 'yet after all, to love God with all our hearts, and to love our neighbour as ourselves, is better than all burnt-offerings and sacrifices.'

TWO NEGATIVE DATA, BOTH USEFUL. (1) NO JAMIESON RESIDUE AT ALL. This is the first chapter of the rotation with ZERO Jamieson blocks: the tree carries six voices (Gill 17 blocks, Clarke 15, Ellicott 15, Wesley 13, Keil and Delitzsch 10, Henry 5) and no Jamieson head anywhere in the 17 keys. Every previous chapter I have worked has carried one, two or three. This matters for the re-indexing decision because it bounds the emitter: it does not always fire. Genesis 20 had a single block, this has none, most have three. If the emitter placed a block at every key congruent to the offset, a 17-key chapter would carry two or three; that it carries none means either the source stream ran out, or the chapter was never processed by whatever produced the residue, or the offset for this chapter falls outside 1-17 in a way the mod-6 model does not predict. Worth one deliberate check by the owner against the neighbouring 1samuel chapters, since a chapter-level gap in the residue is a much stronger clue to the emitter's boundaries than another positive instance would be. (2) NO CALVIN IN THE TREE EITHER, so the Calvin editorial-apparatus defect, present in the last seven chapters running, did not arise here. Combined with (1), this chapter is the cleanest source I have worked in the rotation: no residue, no apparatus, no chapter front matter from Barnes (Barnes is absent too), no OCR corruption of the Bede kind, and no NAMED BUT NOT SOURCED lint. The only chrome was the familiar Ellicott nav strip at key 17 and a Gill Next: 1 Samuel Chapter footer.

FIVE DISAGREEMENTS, ONE OF THEM A CLEAN GEOGRAPHICAL REVERSAL. (1) 7:16 THE THREE CIRCUIT TOWNS. Clarke spreads them over the whole nation: at Bethel the tribe of Ephraim and all the northern parts could attend him; when at Gilgal, Benjamin and those beyond Jordan had easy access; when at Mizpeh he was within reach of Judah, Simeon and Gad. Ellicott observes that all three lie in the SOUTHERN part of the land, in Benjamin, and draws the opposite conclusion -- that the power of Samuel, if not exclusively, was chiefly exercised among the southern tribes. He then builds a large historical thesis on it: the religion of the Eternal was corrupted at an early date in the north, and the restoration resulting from Samuel's work was so much less marked there that when the strong hand of Solomon was removed a formal secession from the southern league at once took place. Same three place-names, opposite inference, and one of them carries the division of the kingdom on its back. (2) 7:1 WHETHER ELEAZAR WAS A LEVITE. Wesley denies flatly that they made him either Levite or priest, for in Israel persons were not made but born such -- the sanctifying was a setting apart to the work. Clarke agrees the word signifies no more than setting a man apart. Ellicott holds the opposite, that Abinadab was most likely already a Levite, since Eleazar, Uzzah and Ahio are Levitical appellations in that family, and Samuel, unnamed but no doubt directing, would have sought a man of Levi for the trust. (3) 7:2 HOW LONG THE ARK STAYED. Gill says between forty and fifty years; Ellicott says nearly fifty; Clarke says the chapter covers at least twenty and the dates are unknown; Keil says twenty. WESLEY SOLVES IT: the text does not say the twenty years were the whole stay -- the ark remained about forty, but twenty passed before Israel became sensible of their sin. (4) 7:6 WHAT THE POURED WATER MEANT. Clarke admits it is not easy to know, canvasses libation among Greeks and Romans with six classical authorities, then adopts the Aramaic reading that they poured out their hearts in penitence as waters, supported by four scriptural parallels ending with Hannah. Keil and Delitzsch call the same paraphrase correct on the whole and add the confession implied: behold, we are before Thee like water that has been poured out. WESLEY ADDS A SECOND SENSE the others do not have: an external sign testifying their own filthiness and NEED OF WASHING by the grace and Spirit of God and the blood of the covenant. Confession in two, cleansing as well in the third. (5) 7:9 HOW A NON-PRIEST COULD SACRIFICE. Clarke offers a choice -- either Samuel offered it himself, or he had Eleazar offer it and may still be said to have done it, since he who procures a thing done may be said to do it -- and pleads necessity for the irregular place, neither tabernacle nor ark being at hand. Gill reports the Jewish suggestion that he acted through a priest, being only a Levite, but prefers a prophet's extraordinary licence, as with Gideon. AND ELLICOTT AT 7:8 CONCEDES THE POINT OUTRIGHT: Samuel offered with rites SOMEWHAT DIFFERENT FROM THOSE ENJOINED IN THE LAW, for the occasion was indeed a critical one. Three ways of handling one irregularity, and the third simply admits it.

NOTABLE MATERIAL WORTH KEEPING. (1) 7:2 Ellicott reconstructs the twenty silent years as the making of Samuel: there is something very touching in this sad note of time, and we think we read Samuel's own words here, the unwearied toiler having found the twenty years a weary period of waiting. But he insists the hungering of Israel did not begin only when the twenty years were over -- it had been a stern trial time, and taught by the bitter lessons of adversity Samuel saw it was BY NO BOLD STROKE OF A FEW GALLANT PATRIOTS that the nation could be saved, since all such efforts after Aphek would only sink it lower. (2) 7:3 Ellicott alone sees how dangerous the reform was: it was a desperate venture seemingly, to which the prophet summoned unarmed and undisciplined Israel, challenging them to bid defiance to the most cherished institutions of their oppressors; he knew what he urged would at once provoke what appeared a dangerous and most unequal contest. When the images came down, Ellicott counts it an OPEN ACT OF REBELLION against a warlike people who had ruled with an iron rule -- not a religious act only. (3) 7:5 Ellicott's finest suggestion in the chapter: the solemn pouring out of water at Mizpeh may be the origin of the later Temple custom in which the high priest filled the golden vessel with the waters of Siloam and poured it out silently before the Lord -- is it not at least probable that this was the record of one of the holiest memories of the people, their reconciliation with their God-Friend at Mizpeh? (4) 7:6 Clarke coins a phrase for the assembly: it was held for religious, political and military purposes at once. (5) 7:7 Henry: those that seek to do mischief to others will be forward to imagine that others design mischief to them -- and his double moral, that evil sometimes seems to come out of good, since a meeting for repentance brought trouble, but that good is at length brought out of that evil, since Israel could never be threatened more seasonably. Wesley states the first half as a rule: when sinners begin to repent and reform, they must expect Satan will muster all his forces against them. (6) 7:12 Wesley presses HITHERTO as a deliberately guarded word: he hath begun to help us, though not completely to deliver us -- by which wary expression Samuel excites both their thankfulness and their care to please the Lord, that he might deliver them effectually. He also notes what no one else does, that the victory was won in the very place where Israel had suffered their earlier fatal loss. (7) 7:13 Henry: Samuel was a protector and deliverer to Israel, not by dint of sword, as Gideon, nor by strength of arm, as Samson, but by the power of prayer to God and carrying on a work of reformation among the people -- religion and piety are the best securities of a nation. (8) 7:13 Ellicott's constitutional claim: from this victory the pure religion was no longer confided solely to the tribe of Levi, which had shown itself unworthy of the mighty trust; in religious matters THE POWER OF THE PRIESTLY TRIBE WAS NEVER AGAIN SUPREME in the Land of Promise, and from the days of Samuel a new order, that of the Prophets, was acknowledged as the regular medium of communication. (9) 7:15 Clarke: Samuel seems in many respects to have been considered the governor of the people, while Saul was only looked on as the general of the armies. (10) 7:17 Ellicott conjectures that the sacred vessels and furniture were saved from the destruction of Shiloh by Samuel and were very likely in the prophet-judge's keeping at Ramah. (11) 7:12 Ellicott identifies Shen, the Tooth, with the French dent, a favourite name for a peak in districts of the Alps and Pyrenees.

One near-GHOST was pre-empted by hand: Gill has short blocks across 9-13 and 14-17 and was dropped from two late paragraphs during compression, so he is named once per entry rather than repeatedly; that satisfies the lint but the tags record him accurately as a voice throughout. JAMIESON RESIDUE: A TOTAL STALL -- THE CHAPTER'S ENTIRE RESIDUE IS ONE BLOCK EMITTED TWICE. Two blocks, keys 5 and 11, offset 5 mod 6, step 6. They are BYTE-IDENTICAL, 207 words each, md5 fa9cd424a13b. This is the most complete stall observed so far: at acts 1 (k19==k25) and leviticus 2 (k9==k15) the repeated block was one of three or more, with distinct material before it; here there are only two blocks in the whole chapter and they are the same block, so nothing distinct was emitted at all. THE DONOR IS NUMBERS 7, i.e. WITHIN THE SAME BOOK. The block is Jamieson on the princes' offerings at the dedication of the altar: 'This tribe being stationed on the right side of Judah, offered next through its representative; then Zebulun, which was on the left side; and so on in orderly succession, every tribe making the same kind of offering and in the same amount ... a separate notice is given of each, as a separate day was appointed for the presentation, that equal honor might be conferred on each.' That is his note on Numbers 7:24ff. THIS CUTS AGAINST THE 'PREVIOUS BOOK' PATTERN and refines what was recorded at leviticus 1. There the donor for leviticus 1 and 2 was Exodus 27-28, the immediately preceding book, read monotonically across two adjacent target chapters. Here the donor is the SAME book as the target (Numbers 7 -> Numbers 30), which shows the donor is not selected by a fixed offset from the target book. What the two cases have in common is more interesting than what differs: both donors are LONG CEREMONIAL DESCRIPTIVE PASSAGES (the tabernacle court and priestly garments; the twelve identical princely offerings) rather than narrative or epistolary material, and in both cases the stream terminates in a stall. RESIDUE CLASS: 5 mod 6 here, against 3 mod 6 for leviticus 1 and leviticus 2. So the class is NOT fixed per corpus, and the leviticus pair sharing class 3 is now better explained by their sharing a donor stream than by any per-book class rule. Running class tally remains: every class 0-5 attested. Practical consequence: Jamieson is excluded_voices on entries 3-8 and 9-16, which between them contain both residue keys.

TWO ITEMS. (1) ELLICOTT STUDYLIGHT CHAPTER-FINAL CHROME, EIGHTEENTH CONFIRMATION, again on ELLICOTT'S LAST BLOCK IN THE CHAPTER rather than the chapter's last key. His k13 block is 1031 words of which only the first ~40 are commentary ('Reference is again made to the two kinds of vows which are treated of in this chapter -- viz., a vow to do anything, and a vow to abstain from anything'). Everything after that is chapter links, a copyright footer, ~800 words of raw CSS from the site's sub-menu stylesheet, and a directory listing of the site's reference works. Ellicott has no block at k14, k15 or k16, so the rule holds without exception at eighteen observations, and the chapter's usable source total drops from 7505 to about 6515 once the chrome is discounted -- a 13 percent overstatement, which matters a great deal in a chapter this small. A worker tiling by source words on a short chapter should subtract the chrome BEFORE choosing the number of entries; taking 7505 at face value here would have suggested four entries where the material only supports three. (2) A NEW-ISH CALVIN APPARATUS SIGNATURE, worth recording because it differs from the eight cases already logged. At numbers 30 k9 the Calvin block does not merely carry inline third-person editorial comment; it carries an UNRESOLVED TRANSLATOR'S NOTE that admits defeat. After a Hebrew lemma and two rival renderings, the text reads: 'I have translated the latter, not being able to understand the original, nor to reconcile them.' Immediately before it sits a French gloss and a fragmentary sentence ('It may also happen The is, ...') where the apparatus markers have been stripped, leaving Calvin's sentence broken off mid-clause and resumed several lines later. So this chapter shows the defect in its most destructive form: not just unattributed editorial matter inside the block, but a Calvin sentence physically SPLIT by the removed apparatus, so that a reader parsing the block linearly gets a truncated argument. The block also ends with a stray running header, 'Political Supplements to the Third Commandment Leviticus 24'. Any stripping rule keyed only on third-person references to Calvin would miss this instance; it also needs to catch translator's-note first person ('I have translated', 'I am unable') and stray running headers naming a different book and chapter.

NOTABLE MATERIAL. (1) 30:2 HENRY'S DISTINCTION BETWEEN THE TWO BONDS, the best sentence in the chapter: 'A promise to man is a bond upon the estate, but a promise to God is a bond upon the soul.' He then divides the vows a Christian now makes into sacramental vows, 'by which we are bound to no more than what was before our duty, and which neither father nor husband can disannul,' and occasional vows 'concerning that which before was in our own power.' He also relays the rabbinic epigram that vows are 'the hedge of separation, that is, a fence to religion.' (2) 30:2 KEIL ON AN INFORMATIVE SILENCE: 'In what such abstinence consisted is not explained, because it was well understood from traditional customs.' He reads the gap in the text as evidence of a living practice rather than as a defect, and notes the classification is formal rather than material, since the Nazarite's vow is called neder and not issar though it is a vow of abstinence. (3) 30:2 GILL VIA JARCHI ON THE LOGIC OF LAWFUL VOWING: a man 'may forbid himself what is forbidden, and forbid what is free and lawful; but he may not make free or lawful what is forbidden.' A vow can only ever narrow liberty, never widen it -- the cleanest statement of the principle in the chapter. (4) 30:4 CALVIN GENERALISES THE FATHER'S SILENCE INTO A RULE FOR ALL AUTHORITY: 'all those who are possessed of power do not do their duty unless they frankly and discreetly express their opposition whenever anything displeases them; since their connivance is a kind of tacit approbation.' (5) 30:5 CALVIN FINDS A REBUKE INSIDE THE PARDON: the words 'and the Lord shall forgive her' are 'remarkable, whereby Moses gently reproves the foolish thoughtlessness of the girl ... God therefore hints that they are not without blame; but lest they should be tormented by secret remorse, He removes every scruple.' (6) 30:5 WESLEY'S LIMIT ON THE RELEASE, which prevents the whole law from being abused: it holds 'only of vows which could not be performed without invading the father's right; for if one should vow to forbear such, or such a sin, and all occasions or means leading to it, and to perform such, or such duties, when he had opportunity, no father can discharge him from such vows.' (7) 30:9 GILL'S PARADOX OF THE TWO AUTHORITIES, from the Mishnah: for a betrothed woman whose husband dies the power reverts to the father, so 'in this case, greater is the power of a father than of an husband; in others, greater is the power of an husband than of a father, because an husband makes void (the vow of) one at age, but a father does not.' (8) 30:13 WESLEY ON WHY AFFLICTING THE SOUL IS NAMED: to show the husband's power reached 'not only in those vows which concerned himself or his estate, but also in those which might seem only to concern her own person, or body ... because the wife's person or body being the husband's right, she might not do any thing to the injury of her body without his consent.' (9) 30:15 THE GUILT INVERTS. Wesley: if the husband has approved by silence 'from day to day, if after that time he shall hinder it, which he ought not to do: her non-performance of her vow shall be imputed to him, not to her.' A rare case in the Mosaic law of the guilt of a broken obligation being transferred to the person who obstructed it. (10) 30:16 CLARKE'S GENERAL SUSPICION OF VOWING, striking from a commentator on a chapter that regulates it: 'Making vows, in almost any case, is a dangerous business; they seldom do any good, and often much evil. He who does not feel himself bound to do what is fit, right, and just, from the standing testimony of God's word, is not likely to do it from any obligation he may lay upon his own conscience. If God's word lack weight with him, his own will prove lighter than vanity.' He also guesses the law 'rose from the exigency of some particular case that had just then occurred,' as with the succession of the daughters of Zelophehad. (11) 30:16 GILL NAMES THE POLICY BEHIND THE STATUTE: the power of ratifying or disannulling existed 'to prevent imprudent and extravagant vows, and the too frequent use of them, the consequences of which might be bad in families.'

The number of their male children, from ...'. The two blocks are in donor order. THIS REFINES THE LEVITICUS FINDING RECORDED YESTERDAY. There I found that leviticus 1 and leviticus 2 shared a single monotone donor stream through Exodus 27-28 and shared residue class 3, and I suggested the class might be fixed per book. NUMBERS FALSIFIES THE PER-BOOK PART: numbers 30 is class 5 with donor Numbers 7, numbers 25 is class 1 with donor Numbers 3-4. So a donor stream is a property of a RUN OF ADJACENT TARGET CHAPTERS, not of a book; leviticus 1 and 2 shared one because they are adjacent, and numbers 25 and 30 do not because they are five chapters apart. WHAT THE THREE NUMBERS/LEVITICUS DONORS HAVE IN COMMON is more suggestive than the differences: Exodus 27-28 (tabernacle court and priestly garments), Numbers 7 (the twelve identical princely offerings), Numbers 3-4 (the Levite census) are ALL LONG ENUMERATIVE OR CEREMONIAL CATALOGUES. Not one of the Pentateuch donors observed so far is narrative. That is now four observations and worth treating as a real pattern rather than coincidence: whatever produced the residue drew on long catalogue passages, which would also explain why the streams run dry (a catalogue has a definite end) and why exhaustion presents as the stall recorded at numbers 30, leviticus 2 and acts 1. NOTABLE MATERIAL. (1) 25:1 HENRY ON WHY THE SEDUCTION SUCCEEDED WHERE WAR FAILED, the best thing in the chapter: 'If Balak had drawn out his armed men against them to fight them, Israel had bravely resisted, and no doubt had been more than conquerors; but now that he sends his beautiful women among them ... the Israelites basely yield ... those are smitten with his harlots that could not be smitten with his sword.' He generalises it: 'We are more endangered by the charms of a smiling world than by the terrors of a frowning world.' (2) 25:1 CALVIN ON PROSPERITY AS THE HARDER TEST: 'the people were no more able to bear prosperity than adversity. Heretofore, either worn out by fatigue, or rendered impatient by abstinence and famine, they had often rebelled against God; now, when they have entered a habitable land ... they are incited by their more comfortable dwelling-places, and more pleasant mode of life, to lasciviousness.' He also notes the graduated method of the temptation -- 'The Moabitish damsels did not straightway solicit the Israelites to worship their idols, but first invite them to their banquets' -- and reads Satan as creeping upon us by degrees. (3) 25:6 CLARKE ARGUES THAT THIS WAS A MARRIAGE, NOT PROSTITUTION, AND ATTACKS THE VULGATE FOR SAYING OTHERWISE: 'The condition of these two persons plainly proves it to have been a matrimonial alliance, the one was a prince, the other a princess; therefore I must conclude that fornication ... was not practised on this occasion. The matter was bad enough, as the marriage was in flat opposition to the law of God; and we need not make it worse by representing the woman as a common prostitute, as the Vulgate and several others have done.' He cites Josephus that Zimri had married Cozbi. This is a rare instance of a witness defending the dignity of a condemned party against his own tradition. (4) 25:8 THE TENT IS A HAPAX AND EVERY WITNESS REACHES FOR A DIFFERENT PARALLEL. Gill traces an Arabic cognate that gives English 'alcove' and cites the Aruch for a structure 'narrow above and broad below ... a place in which whores were put', used in the Talmud for a brothel. Ellicott gives two options and records that the LXX has kaminos (a furnace) and the Vulgate lupanar (a brothel), and adds the striking suggestion that 'through her belly' may be 'within her tent', the same word standing twice in the verse. (5) 25:8 CLARKE'S WAT TYLER EXCURSUS, the longest historical digression in the chapter: he compares Phinehas to Sir William Walworth, mayor of London, who in 1381 struck down Wat Tyler at Smithfield before Richard II, and concludes it 'was that of a zealot, of essential benefit at the time, and justified only by the pressing exigencies of the case.' (6) 25:8 THE THREE-WAY GUARD AGAINST IMITATION. All three of Clarke, Henry and Calvin insist the act sets no precedent, but by different routes: Clarke by special inspiration, HENRY BY OFFICE (Phinehas was heir-apparent and therefore already one of the judges Moses had commissioned, so 'the civil magistrate is the avenger ... and no private person may take his work out of his hand'), and Calvin by a doctrine of extraordinary calling capped with Christ's rebuke, 'Ye know not what manner of spirit ye are of.' Henry's is the only one that removes the difficulty without appealing to inspiration at all. (7) 25:11 CALVIN GUARDS ATONEMENT AGAINST MERIT: 'let us not imagine that there was a meritorious satisfaction, whereby the Papists feign that their punishments are redeemed before God. For although the just chastisements of sin are sacrifices of sweet savor, they are by no means expiations to reconcile God.' He points out that the psalm ascribes the atonement not to the act but to the prayer of Phinehas. (8) 25:11 KEIL ON THE POSSESSIVE: the Hebrew is 'not zeal for me, but my zeal, the zeal of Jehovah with which Phinehas was filled', so that in acting he 'restrained the working of Jehovah's zeal, which had manifested itself in the plague.' (9) 25:14 CALVIN ON WHY THE WHOLE TRIBE SHARES THE SHAME though not charged with the sin: each is branded 'in order that each one of them may learn severely to correct whomsoever amongst his relatives he may see offending ... for this is the true way to honor one's family and blood.' (10) 25:17 THE FOUR ANSWERS TO WHY MOAB IS SPARED. Gill: for Lot's sake, and (Jarchi) for Ruth's. Wesley: Midian was simply guiltier. ELLICOTT EXPLICITLY REFUTES THE DESCENT ARGUMENT -- 'their exemption ... was probably due, not to their descent from Lot (for the Midianites were descended from Abraham), but to the fact that the measure of their sin was not yet full' -- and notes Moab was punished otherwise, shut out to the tenth generation. Calvin refuses to answer: 'no good reason here appears why God should mercifully bear with the one nation, whilst He hastens speedily to the punishment of the others,' so 'let us learn to regard His judgments with reverence, and not to presume to discuss them further than is lawful.'

SHARPER READ ON THE RESIDUE SOURCE (follows the source-defect note above). The three Jamieson blocks are not merely 'from Colossians' -- they are a MONOTONIC WALK THROUGH THE CANON, crossing a book boundary mid-chapter. k5 comments on Colossians 4:12 (Epaphras labouring fervently in prayers -- 'striving as in the agony of a contest'); k11 comments on Colossians 4:17 (Speak ye to Archippus); k17 comments on 1 Thessalonians 1:2 (Paul, Silvanus and Timotheus, making mention of you in our prayers without ceasing). Colossians 4 has 18 verses, so the walk runs Col 4:12 -> Col 4:17 -> (Col 4:18) -> 1 Thess 1:1 -> 1 Thess 1:2. The residue emitter therefore does NOT re-index within a single chapter or book; it advances through a flat verse stream and steps into the next book when it runs off the end of the current one. That is exactly the behaviour of an off-by-N index into a globally concatenated verse list, and it rules out any explanation local to one book. Compare genesis 16, whose residue came from Genesis 13 (same book, earlier chapter) -- consistent with the same flat-stream model, since Genesis 13 precedes Genesis 16 in the same stream. Recommend the owner treat this as the decisive datum for the re-indexing decision: the fix is a global offset into the source verse list, not a per-book or per-chapter correction.

THE CHAPTER WHERE INTERPRETATION DIVIDES, AND THE COMMENTATORS SAY SO. Barnes opens by declaring that all agreement ends here: up to this point there may be unimportant diversities in the exposition of words, but no material difference as to the writer's meaning; from here begins the divergence toward theories various, discordant, and many of them wild and fantastic. He gives four reasons -- the scene opens into the future, there is no designation of places, no designation of time that is necessarily unambiguous, and nothing in the symbols making it certain they apply to only one class of events. Robertson answers by refusing the whole enterprise: he will make no effort to refer the seals to persons or events past, present or future, but only relate the symbolism to the other symbols of the book. The chapter then proves Barnes right. On the first rider alone the sources give: the gospel (Clarke, Gill), Christ himself (Victorinus, Bede, Henry), victory personified and the reflex of early Christian hope (Ellicott), the emperor Trajan (Wesley), and no identification whatever (Robertson). On the sixth seal: the fall of Jerusalem (rejected by Gill), the barbarian destruction of the empire (rejected by Gill), the conversion of Constantine (Clarke, Gill, Henry), the day of judgment (rejected by Clarke), and God's judgment shown to the wicked departed and perceived by nobody on earth (Wesley, alone). Recorded because it is unusually well documented from inside the sources themselves rather than inferred.

WESLEY'S COMPASS KEY vs BARNES'S EXPLICIT DENIAL, repeated at all four seals. Wesley assigns a quarter of the world to each living creature -- the first looks east (k1), the second west (k3), the third south (k5), the fourth north (k7) -- and gives the rule: at each seal it was necessary to turn toward that quarter of the world which it more immediately concerned. Barnes denies any such significance three separate times, once per seal after the first: at k3, 'it cannot be supposed that there is any special significancy in the fact that the second beast addressed the seer... nor was there any reason in the symbol why this creature rather than another should speak'; at k5, 'it is not apparent why the third beast is represented as taking a particular interest in the opening of this seal, nor is it necessary to show why it was so... the order in which they did this does not seem to be a matter of importance'; at k7, 'there does not appear to have been any particular reason why the fourth of the living creatures should have made this proclamation rather than either of the others... it was poetic and appropriate to represent each one in his turn'. Clarke takes a third position and identifies the creatures by face rather than by compass point (the third is 'that which had the face of a man'). At k9 the disagreement resolves itself: no living creature speaks at the fifth seal, and Barnes, Henry and Clarke all pause to explain the silence, Barnes with the same argument he has used four times -- having shown each in turn, there was no propriety in showing them again.

THE INTERMEDIATE STATE: ELLICOTT AGAINST BARNES AND GILL, ON THE SAME TWO WORDS. At k9 Barnes takes 'the souls of them that were slain' as one of the incidental proofs in the Bible that the soul does not cease to exist at death, and also that it does not cease to be conscious or sleep till the resurrection -- these souls being represented as still in existence, as remembering what had occurred on the earth, as interested in what was taking place, as engaged in prayer. Ellicott, in the same verse, refuses the inference by name: 'The word souls has been made a resting-place for an argument respecting the intermediate state. There is no ground for this: it is quite beside the object of the seal.' He reads souls as the equivalent of lives -- the vision tells that their lives had been sacrificed -- and Robertson's philology backs him ('the lives, for the life is in the blood'). Then at k10 Gill makes the identical inference Ellicott has just refused, and makes it from a different feature: the LOUDNESS of the cry. 'They cried with great ardour and fervency, being very pressing and importunate; and which shows that they were awake, and not asleep, and that the soul does not sleep with the body in the grave.' He repeats it at k11 from the white robe. So the same doctrinal point is drawn three times from three different features of the passage, and denied once as beside the point -- a clean case of the reformed and grammatical-historical schools converging on a doctrine that a grammatical-historical voice rejects on exegetical grounds.

THREE METHODOLOGICAL REMARKS WORTH KEEPING. (1) Barnes at k2 asks what mode of representation the seer experienced -- pictures drawn on successive portions of the volume, a written description he read or heard read, or a scenic representation for which the seal was merely the occasion -- and argues for the pictorial on four grounds, the sharpest being that on the scenic view the breaking of each seal would disclose nothing but a succession of blank portions, so what would be the use of a sealed volume, or of the writing within and without? He returns to it at k12, saying every item of the sixth seal could be painted. This is the clearest statement of his panorama theory anywhere in the chapters worked so far. (2) Robertson at k12 supplies a general warning that applies far beyond this chapter: Peter interpreted Joel's sun-turned-to-darkness and moon-to-blood of the day of Pentecost, and 'Peter's interpretation of Joel should make us cautious about too literal an exegesis of these grand symbols'. (3) Barnes at k15 interrupts his own exposition to say that because this passage does not refer to the end of the world or the day of judgment, the word 'bondman' 'determines nothing as to the question whether slavery is to continue on the earth' -- a nineteenth-century American aside on the text's use in a live controversy, and the only such aside encountered in the corpus so far.

Running total across the loop: 71 of 81 entries have needed compression.
