JAMIESON RESIDUE, offset 0 mod 6 -- second confirmed offset-0 chapter after 2peter 2. Two blocks, at keys 6 and 12 (91 words total), neither discussing its verse. Source identified as ROMANS 9-10: the k6 block comments on Romans 9:33 (Isaiah 28:16, 'shall not make haste' rendered by the Septuagint 'shall not be put to shame', a glorious Messianic passage); the k12 block comments on Romans 10:16 (Isaiah 53:1, 'Lord, who hath believed our report' -- 'the prophet speaks as if next to none would believe: the apostle softens this into They have not all believed'). Note the walk: Rom 9:33 -> Rom 10:16 is a forward step of 18 verses for a key gap of 6, so within this chapter the residue advances through the source stream faster than the target keys advance -- UNLIKE revelation 6, where the walk was Col 4:12 -> Col 4:17 -> 1Th 1:2, roughly 3-5 verses per 6-key step. This is the first chapter where the residue stride is measurably different, and the owner should note it: a single flat global offset predicts a CONSTANT stride, so a variable stride means either the source stream is not a simple concatenation, or the emitter samples rather than walks. Recommend the owner treat the revelation 6 note (monotonic canon walk) and this one together: the direction is consistent, the step size is not. Offset table now: 0 (2peter 2 / Ephesians 5, galatians 6 / Romans 9-10), 1, 2 (genesis 16 / Genesis 13), 3 (colossians 3 / 1 Cor 6), 4 (genesis 20), 5 (exodus 38, revelation 11 / 1 Thess 4-5, revelation 6 / Colossians 4 + 1 Thess 1). Eleven source books now.

CYRIL OF JERUSALEM: OFF-TARGET AND DUPLICATED. Two Cyril of Jerusalem blocks in this chapter, at keys 14 and 18, and they are the IDENTICAL TEXT byte for byte -- a Catechetical Lecture passage on 2 Corinthians 4:4 ('if he blinded the thoughts of them that believe not, he blinded them for a good purpose'), with no bearing on Galatians 6:14 or 6:18. This is the SECOND consecutive chapter in which the whole Cyril of Jerusalem tree is off-target (revelation 6 had three, all Catechetical Lectures, none touching a verse). Two distinct defects are now visible in this voice: (a) the tree is tiled onto verse keys by position rather than by reference, and (b) at least in this chapter the SAME block is emitted at two different keys, which no positional tiling alone would produce. Silenced chapter-wide in the build. Recommend the owner re-fetch the entire Cyril of Jerusalem tree, as was recommended for Tertullian, and add a duplicate-block detector -- an exact-text match across two keys in one chapter is cheap to test for and would have caught this without a human reading either block.

SCANNED-BOOK CORRUPTION IN THE MARTIN LUTHER TREE, AND A PUBLISHER'S CATALOGUE IN THE TEXT. This is the largest single voice in the chapter (17 blocks, 19,576 words -- more than twice the next largest) and it is the dirtiest text encountered in the corpus so far. Three distinct defects. (1) HYPHENATION ARTIFACTS from an uncorrected page scan, throughout: 'doc- trine', 'wil- fully', 'ex- cuse', 'affec- tion', 'cor- rupteth', 'commit- ted', 'main- taining', 'per- fection', 'excommunicate'/'ex- communicate'. (2) RUNNING PAGE HEADERS AND FOLIOS embedded mid-sentence: '644 COMMENTARY ON GALATIANS.', '048 COMMENTARY ON GALATIANS.', 'COMMENTARY ON GALATIANS. 555', '664 COMMENTARY ON GALATIANS.', '574 COMMENTARY ON GALATIANS.', '72 570 COMMENTARY ON GALATIANS.', 'COMMENTARY ON GALATIANS. 563', 'COMMENTARY ON GALATIANS. 573', '71 662 COMMENTARY ON GALATIANS.', '70 664 COMMENTARY ON GALATIANS.' -- at least ten instances. (3) WORST: the k18 block runs 6,159 words, and after Luther's closing doxology it continues into the BACK MATTER OF THE PRINTED VOLUME -- 'THE END. VALUABLE BOOKS RECENTLY ISSUED BY ROBERT CARTER, 58 CANAL STREET, NEW YORK, AND THOMAS CARTER, MARKET ST., PITTSBURG. THE HISTORY OF THE CHURCH OF SCOTLAND... LECTURES ON THE ACTS OF THE APOSTLES; By the Rev. John Dick...' -- a nineteenth-century publisher's advertising catalogue, tiled onto Galatians 6:18 as if it were commentary. Also 'through»the', 'such-Hke', 'offTences', 'sorowful', 'fSared', 'i»eaning', 'agamst', 'boitiful', 'mgratitude', 'crJture', 'hohness', 'qne', 'int5', 'monaeteries'. Recommend: (a) re-fetch or re-OCR the whole Luther tree; (b) add a dehyphenation pass keyed on '- ' at a line end followed by a lowercase continuation; (c) add a detector for running headers of the form '<digits> COMMENTARY ON <BOOK>'; (d) add a hard cut at 'THE END.' followed by all-caps publisher matter, which is the same class of defect as the Christian Classics trailer on Tertullian and the Ellicott copyright strip, but larger by an order of magnitude.

CHAPTER FRONT MATTER AND APPENDED ESSAYS -- both ends of the chapter. (1) Barnes chapter front matter, SIXTH consecutive chapter (colossians 3, 2corinthians 6, 2peter 2, revelation 11, revelation 6, now galatians 6): his key-1 block opens 'GALATIANS Chapter 6 This chapter is composed entirely of affectionate exhortation...' and runs a full verse-by-verse chapter summary before any comment on verse 1. (2) Clarke chapter argument, FOURTH instance (2peter 2, revelation 11, revelation 6, galatians 6): his key-1 block opens with the whole chapter argument, 'The apostle teaches them to be tender and affectionate towards any who...Gal 6:1, Gal 6:2', ahead of the verse notes. (3) NEW SHAPE, at the other end: Barnes's key-18 block is 782 words of which only the first six are comment on the verse ('Brethren, the grace, etc. Rom 16:20'); the remaining 776 are an APPENDED ESSAY, headed 'INGENIOUS CONJECTURE ON PAUL'S THORN IN THE FLESH', which belongs to 2 Corinthians 12 and has been tiled onto the last verse of Galatians. Clarke's key-18 block is 2,548 words and is almost entirely subscription criticism plus a whole-epistle retrospect. So the same two voices carry chapter-level apparatus at BOTH the first and the last verse key, and a detector that only looks at key 1 will miss half of it. Recommend the front-matter/back-matter detector be run against the LAST key of every chapter as well as the first.

NEW VOICE ADDED TO THE MAPS: MARTIN LUTHER, school 'lutheran'. This is the first chapter in the loop to carry Luther, and he is the dominant voice in it -- 17 blocks across 18 keys, 19,576 words, more than Barnes (8,376) and Henry (7,833) and Calvin (7,576) put together. Added to ORDER, LAST ('Luther') and SCH ('lutheran'); the lutheran slot in the school enum had never been used before now. The addition matters beyond this chapter: 'lutheran' was the only school in the enum with no voice mapped to it, so any chapter carrying Luther would previously have failed the school-mismatch lint with no way to satisfy it. Recommend the owner check which other chapters carry a Martin Luther tree -- his commentary is on Galatians only, so the exposure is bounded to galatians 1-6, but five of those six chapters are presumably still unsynthesised and will hit the same map. Note also that dump.py's own NAMES list had to be extended separately from build.py's ORDER: two lists, one omission, and the voice silently vanished from the survey until noticed. Worth collapsing them into one shared list in the scratchpad template.

WHAT 'HOW LARGE A LETTER' MEANS -- the sharpest philological split in the chapter, and the voices divide 5 to 3 with the moderns on the minority side. FOR LARGE CHARACTERS: Robertson ('Certainly not how large a letter') and Ellicott ('Rather, in what large letters: i.e., characters'), both insisting the Greek governs characters of handwriting, not an epistle. Robertson canvasses defective eyesight, ill-formed letters 'like the print letters of children', and Ramsay's placarding theory, preferring the last, and cites Milligan on the papyrus contrast between the scribe's neat hand and the big sprawling hand of the signature; Ellicott prefers emphasis and authority, 'a few bold incisive strokes in his own hand'. FOR LENGTH: Gill ('the length of the epistle, the prolixity of his writing'), Calvin ('this long Epistle'), Wesley ('St Paul had not yet wrote a larger to any church'), Luther ('I never wrote so long an epistle with mine own hand to any other church... he hath respect to the length of the Epistle'), and Clarke, who argues it at length and with heat. REPORTED BUT NOT HELD: Barnes reports the crude-characters reading with its authorities (Doddridge, Whitby, Theodoret, Jerome, Theophylact) and Doddridge's suggestion that it was 'owing to the infirmity or weakness of his nerves'. Clarke's rebuttal is the strongest single argument on either side: to say Paul was unskilled in Greek 'is in my opinion absurd', he being born in Tarsus, 'a city which, according to Strabo, rivaled both Athens and Alexandria'; and as to the writing, 'the uncial character was that which was alone in use in those days, and this character is as easily made as the capitals in the Roman alphabet, which have been taken from it'. Recorded because the split runs cleanly along the line between the two nineteenth-century grammarians and everyone earlier, and because Barnes's own k18 appendix -- that Paul suffered a chronic ophthalmia which made writing painful -- supplies, from inside the same chapter, the physical explanation the large-character reading needs.

THREE FURTHER DISAGREEMENTS WORTH KEEPING. (1) VERSE 2 AGAINST VERSE 5. Bear ye one another's burdens, then every man shall bear his own burden. Ellicott resolves it lexically and contextually at once: the two Greek words differ, 'the distinction would be sufficiently represented if we were to translate in the one case burden, in the other load', but 'the context, however, is quite different' -- there sympathy, here direct answerability to God. Robertson checks the lexical half and weakens it: the second word is 'old word for ship's cargo', and 'Christ calls his phortion light, though he terms those of the Pharisees heavy... The terms are thus not always kept distinct, though Paul does make a distinction here.' A clean case of a grammarian conceding that the distinction is contextual rather than lexical. (2) VERSE 8, WHETHER ETERNAL LIFE IS EARNED. Luther raises it head-on -- 'Here riseth a question, whether we deserve eternal life by good works? For so Paul seemeth to avouch in this place' -- and answers pastorally, that works must follow faith or the faith is no true faith. Calvin meets the same text pre-emptively against the Papists: 'though eternal life is a reward, it does not follow either that we are justified by works, or that works are meritorious of salvation... the undeserved kindness of God appears in the very act of honouring the works which his grace has enabled us to perform.' The two Reformers arrive at the same place from opposite directions, one from the pastoral side and one from the polemical. (3) VERSE 13, WHO 'THEY THEMSELVES WHO ARE CIRCUMCISED' ARE. Calvin restricts it to the teachers and says so against the received text: 'The old version and Erasmus translate thus... But Paul appears to me to refer to teachers only, and for this reason I would prefer to render the words, which would not include all circumcised persons, and thus would avoid ambiguity.' Ellicott takes the Greek to include both those circumcised and those circumcising others; Barnes leaves it open ('the Jewish teachers, or perhaps all Jews'); Robertson notes an actual variant, some manuscripts reading the perfect passive 'they who have been circumcised', and prefers the present as the harder reading. Four positions on one participle.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, galatians 6. 9 entries over 18 contiguous keys, 58,969 usable source words -- the largest chapter worked in this loop, 24 percent larger than 2peter 2 (47,448) and 53 percent larger than revelation 6 (38,613). 12 voices: Luther, Barnes, Henry, Calvin, Clarke, Ellicott, Gill, Robertson, Wesley, Cyril of Jerusalem, John Chrysostom, Jamieson. Spans and counts: k1 alone 649w/10 voices; 2-3 650w/8; 4-5 649w/8; 6-7 648w/9; 8-10 650w/8; 11-13 650w/9; 14-16 648w/9; 17 alone 649w/8; 18 alone 650w/7. Every entry in window, no thin exemptions, tiling exact, all validators pass. Martin Luther added to ORDER/LAST/SCH as 'lutheran' -- first use of that school slot in the corpus. Jamieson residue at k6/k12 excluded; Cyril of Jerusalem silenced chapter-wide as off-target and duplicated; both recorded as source defects. LINT COST: one NAMED-BUT-NOT-SOURCED at entry 11-13 -- 'Theophylact', quoted by name inside Barnes's block among the authorities for the crude-characters reading, replaced with 'others'. That is the SIXTH consecutive instance of this same systematic cost (John Lightfoot at 2peter 2, Augustine at 2peter 2, bare Cyril at colossians 3, Archbishop Trench at revelation 11, St Chrysostom at genesis 16, now Theophylact here), and every one has been a father or a named authority QUOTED INSIDE another voice's block. The rule is doing its job -- it prevents the prose implying a source that is not present -- but the cost is now regular enough to be worth a design decision from the owner: either accept the paraphrase cost permanently, or let the lint carry a per-entry allowlist of names that may be mentioned as quoted-within rather than sourced. COMPRESSION COST: all nine entries needed trimming, first drafts running 779, 914, 827, 865, 966, 922, 958, 862 and 760 words against the 650 ceiling -- a mean overshoot of 34 percent, by far the worst of any chapter in the loop (revelation 6 was 22 percent). Four entries needed a full rewrite rather than clause-level trimming. The cause is straightforward and worth recording for whoever tunes the window: this chapter carries nine or ten voices per entry where the corpus norm is five or six, and 650 words cannot name ten positions and give each a substantive claim. Running total across the loop: 80 of 90 entries have needed compression.

JAMIESON RESIDUE, offset 1 mod 6 -- FIRST offset-1 chapter with an identified source book. Three blocks at keys 1, 7 and 13 (387 words), none discussing its verse, all three drawn from ACTS 17: k1 comments on the visit to Thessalonica and the courage required after the shameful treatment at Philippi (Acts 17:1-2 with 1Th 2:2); k7 comments on Acts 17:5-7, the worthless market people, the raising of a mob, and Jason with whom Paul and Silas lodged, with the note that Jason's name was sometimes used as a Greek form of Joshua; k13 comments on Acts 17:10-15, the converts gathered at Berea, the enemies coming down from Thessalonica, and the Berean brethren escorting Paul as far as the sea. Offset 1 previously had four chapters (genesis 2, exodus 24, romans 12, colossians 4) with no source identified, so this closes the last gap in the offset table: every residue class 0 through 5 now has at least one chapter with a named source book. STRIDE: k1 = Acts 17:2, k7 = Acts 17:5, k13 = Acts 17:11 -- roughly 3 to 6 source verses per 6-key step, and monotonically forward. That is much closer to the revelation 6 stride (3-5 verses per 6 keys) than to the galatians 6 stride (18 verses per 6 keys), which strengthens the case that galatians 6 is the outlier and that the emitter normally advances a small fixed-ish number of source verses per residue key. Recommend the owner add this chapter to the re-indexing evidence set alongside revelation 6 and galatians 6. Twelve source books now: Acts 10, Acts 13, Acts 17, Luke 7, 1 Cor 6, 1 Cor 7, Romans 1, Romans 9-10, Ephesians 5, 1 Thess 1, 1 Thess 4-5, Genesis 13, Colossians 4.

TWO PATRISTIC TREES BEHAVE WELL HERE, AFTER THREE CHAPTERS OF FAILURE -- and the contrast is diagnostic. (1) TERTULLIAN is ON TARGET for the first time in this loop, after three consecutive off-target chapters that produced a standing re-fetch recommendation. His single block in this chapter is from Against Marcion V and expounds 1 Cor 2:6-7 directly: 'By all these statements does he show us what God he means, when he says, We speak the wisdom of God among them that are perfect... This wisdom, he says, once lay hidden in things that were foolish, weak, and lacking in honour; once also was latent under figures, allegories, and enigmatical types.' The defect is now much narrower than 'the Tertullian tree is broken': the block is correct for the CHAPTER but MISPLACED BY FIVE VERSES, sitting at key 1 while commenting on verses 6-7. Excluded from entry 1 and recorded rather than used. (2) CYRIL OF JERUSALEM is mostly on target here, against two consecutive chapters (revelation 6, galatians 6) in which his whole tree was off-target Catechetical Lectures. Six blocks: k4 quotes 2:4 verbatim to prove Paul was full of the Holy Ghost; k9 quotes 2:9 to bound what can be known of God; k10 quotes 2:10 for the Spirit's deity; k12 collects the Spirit's titles; k13 quotes 2:13 as a rule for his own lecturing. Only k8 misses, giving the reasons for the Incarnation with no bearing on 2:8; it alone was excluded. THE PATTERN THIS SUGGESTS: the patristic trees are tiled by SCRIPTURE CITATION, not by position. Where a father happens to quote the verse, the block lands correctly; where he does not, an arbitrary block is attached. That explains both the successes here and the failures at revelation 6 and galatians 6 -- Cyril's Catechetical Lectures quote 1 Corinthians 2 heavily and Revelation and Galatians hardly at all. Recommend the owner test this directly: check whether every correctly-placed patristic block contains a quotation of its verse, and whether every off-target one does not. If it holds, the fix is not to re-fetch the trees but to DROP patristic blocks that do not cite their verse -- a much cheaper and safer remedy than the whole-tree re-fetch recommended for Tertullian earlier in this loop.

THREE DISAGREEMENTS WORTH KEEPING. (1) VERSE 9 IS NOT ABOUT HEAVEN, AND FOUR VOICES SAY SO. The verse is universally quoted at funerals, and every commentator in this chapter refuses that use. Barnes calls the objections 'insuperable' and gives two: the Isaiah passage has no such reference, and 'the object of the apostle is not to describe the future state of the redeemed. It is to prove that those who are Christians have true wisdom.' Clarke: 'These words have been applied to the state of glory in a future world; but they certainly belong to the present state.' Gill grants the future glories are 'indeed invisible, unheard of, and inconceivable' but says 'the context and the reason of their citation abundantly show' the doctrines of grace are meant. Robertson: 'here undoubtedly the dominant idea is the present blessing to those who love God... We do not have to wait for heaven to see them.' A rare case of the whole bench agreeing against the popular reading, and worth flagging for the study desk. (2) WHERE VERSE 9 COMES FROM. It is not in the Old Testament as given. Ellicott states the problem and rules out an apocryphal or lost book, and a reference to historical facts rather than a writing, on the ground that the formula 'it is written' is confined in the apostolic writings to Old Testament quotations; his own answer is memory, phrases from Isaiah joined together. Robertson takes it for a free catena of Isaiah 64:4, 65:17 and 52:15. Barnes notes the sentence appears in the apocryphal books of Elijah and that early writers supposed Paul quoted from them. Calvin is the most troubled: 'two very great difficulties present themselves. The first is, that the words that are here quoted by Paul do not correspond with the words of the Prophet. The second is, that it seems as though Paul had perverted the Prophet's declaration to a purpose quite foreign to his design.' (3) WHAT 'THE NATURAL MAN' IS. Two readings, and the split is not along school lines. DOWNWARD: Barnes -- the word denotes those governed by 'the animal passions and desires', and 'the word sensual would correctly express the idea'; Clarke -- 'the animal man... who lives under the influence of his animal passions'. UPWARD: Calvin explicitly rejects that -- 'By the natural man he does not mean (as is commonly thought) the man that is given up to gross lusts, or, as they say, to his own sensuality, but any man that is endowed with nothing more than the faculties of nature'; Gill agrees and makes it concrete, naming 'the wise philosopher, the Scribe, the disputer of this world, the rationalist, the man of the highest attainments in nature, in whom reason is wrought up to its highest pitch'. So the two reformed voices read the verse as aimed at the intellectual, and the two nineteenth-century expositors read it as aimed at the sensual -- which reverses the usual alignment. Ellicott sidesteps both with a threefold psychology of body, soul and spirit.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, 1corinthians 2. 8 entries over 16 contiguous keys, 43,559 usable source words. 12 voices: Barnes, Calvin, Henry, Clarke, Robertson, Ellicott, Gill, Cyril of Jerusalem, Wesley, John Chrysostom, Jamieson, Tertullian. Spans and counts: 1-2 648w/9 voices; 3-5 649w/8; 6 alone 648w/9; 7-8 649w/7; 9-10 650w/9; 11-12 648w/8; 13-14 649w/8; 15-16 649w/7. Every entry in window, no thin exemptions, tiling exact, all validators pass. Jamieson residue at k1/k7/k13 excluded chapter-wide; Tertullian excluded from entry 1 and Cyril of Jerusalem from entry 7, both per-entry and both recorded as source defects with reasons. LINT COST: two this chapter, and both were the SAME systematic cost as the six before them, though one had a new shape. (a) At entry 3-5 the prose read 'Cyril does not expound the verse' and the name-matcher bound the bare surname to 'Cyril' (Cyril of Alexandria, eastern-alexandrian) rather than to 'Cyril of Jerusalem', producing NAMED BUT NOT SOURCED HERE -- fixed by writing the full name. That is the second occurrence of this exact bare-Cyril trap (colossians 3 was the first), and it is worth a one-line guard in the prose rules: NEVER write a bare surname that is itself a distinct entry in the voice map. (b) At entry 11-13 of the previous chapter and again in drafting here, authorities quoted INSIDE another voice's block had to be paraphrased away -- Theophylact, Origen, John Lightfoot and Chrysostom all appear by name inside Barnes's, Ellicott's, Robertson's and Clarke's blocks in this chapter, and each had to be rendered as 'an early Alexandrian', 'a Greek father', 'one commentator', 'a Hebraist' or 'one bishop'. Running total for that cost is now EIGHT consecutive chapters. The owner decision recommended after galatians 6 stands and is now more urgent: either accept the paraphrase permanently, or give the lint a per-entry allowlist for names that are quoted-within rather than sourced. COMPRESSION COST: all eight entries needed trimming, first drafts running 894, 793, 881, 814, 902, 834, 814 and 783 words against the 650 ceiling -- a mean overshoot of 29 percent. Two entries also needed a Wesley clause added after a GHOST lint, then re-trimmed to fit; that add-then-trim cycle happened twice and is a predictable consequence of drafting to the ceiling before checking voice coverage. Worth changing the procedure: check the voice list against the source heads BEFORE drafting, not after. Running total across the loop: 88 of 98 entries have needed compression.

EXODUS 36 CANNOT BE COMPLETED UNDER THE CURRENT RULES. BLOCKED ON ITS SOURCE FILE, THE SAME CLASS OF PROBLEM AS NUMBERS 31. Nothing was written and the tree was left clean; the emit asserted before any output. THE MECHANISM. The source has 19 keys spread over 38 verses (1-9, 14, 19, 20, 26, 30, 31, 32, 35, 37, 38), so it is SPARSE, not contiguous. QA.coverage_problems forbids an entry from covering a verse absent from the source, which means the tiling cannot bridge the gaps: it is forced to align to the SEVEN CONTIGUOUS RUNS, each of which must be its own entry or be subdivided. Measured usable source per run, after excluding Jamieson residue: 1-9 = 4725 words, 7 voices; 14 = 195, 1 voice; 19-20 = 29, 2 voices; 26 = ZERO, 0 voices; 30-32 = 75, 2 voices; 35 = 245, 3 voices; 37-38 = 200, 1 voice. THE FATAL RUN IS 26. Key 26's entire content is 151 words of JAMIESON RESIDUE, and the residue is demonstrably about EXODUS 23:14-16 -- 'This was the institution of the great religious festivals -- the feast of unleavened bread, or the passover -- the feast of harvest ...' -- and not about Exodus 36:26, which is a board on the north side of the tabernacle and its two sockets. Excluding the residue, as every other chapter this rotation has done, leaves the entry with NO SOURCE AT ALL. The only alternatives are both unacceptable: declare Jamieson a voice and write 350-650 words attributing festival commentary to a verse about tabernacle boards, which would be a fabricated attribution and would very likely pass the mechanical fidelity check (Jamieson IS present in the catena for this book and chapter, so the grounding test would not catch it); or leave key 26 uncovered, which fails the tiling assertion. I did neither. FOUR MORE RUNS ARE TOO THIN even setting key 26 aside: 19-20 offers 29 usable words across two voices, 30-32 offers 75, 37-38 offers 200 from a single voice, and 14 offers 195 from a single voice. A 350-650 word entry from 29 source words is expansion, not distillation, and would breach the prose rules regardless of the tiling. WHAT AN OWNER DECISION WOULD NEED TO SETTLE. Either (a) the residue at key 26 should be stripped from the source and the key dropped, which would leave runs 19-20, 26 gone, 30-32 and make a 1-9 plus 14-38 tiling possible only if the tiling rule is also relaxed to bridge gaps; or (b) coverage_problems should be relaxed so that a range may span verses absent from the source, which would allow a clean two-entry tiling of 1-7 and 8-38 and is what I had drafted before the assertion fired; or (c) the chapter is accepted as unrepairable and removed from the repair queue. Option (b) looks right to me and would probably unblock other sparse chapters too, but it changes a validator and is not mine to decide. NOTE FOR THE PICKER: this chapter is currently at the head of the worst-first repair queue, so it will be offered again to the next worker, who will spend the same effort discovering the same blocker. It should be excluded like numbers 31 until the decision is made.

JAMIESON RESIDUE IN EXODUS 36: FOUR BLOCKS, CLASS 2, DONOR EXODUS 22-23, AND THE FIRST CASE WHERE THE RESIDUE MAKES A CHAPTER UNWRITABLE. Keys 2, 26, 32, 38; offsets 2, 26, 32, 38, all congruent 2 mod 6; four members, distinct md5s, strictly monotone in donor order, no stall. THE DONOR IS THE BOOK OF THE COVENANT, EXODUS 22-23, i.e. WITHIN THE SAME BOOK: k2 is Jamieson on 22:26-27, the pledge of a poor man's raiment ('From the nature of the case, this is the description of a poor man. No Orientals undress, but, merely throwing off their turbans ...'); k26 is on 23:14-16, the three annual feasts; k32 is on 23:19, the prohibition of seething a kid in its mother's milk, referred to Egyptian harvest rites; k38 is on the close of the covenant code, 'The communication of these laws, made to Moses and by him rehearsed to the people, was concluded by the addition of many animating ...'. THIS IS THE FIFTH PENTATEUCHAL DONOR IDENTIFIED AND IT FITS THE PATTERN EXACTLY: Exodus 27-28 (tabernacle court and priestly garments) served leviticus 1 and 2; Numbers 7 (the twelve princely offerings) served numbers 30; Numbers 3-4 (the Levite census) served numbers 25; and now Exodus 22-23 (the covenant code) serves exodus 36. ALL FIVE ARE LONG LEGAL OR CEREMONIAL CATALOGUES. Not one is narrative. Five observations is enough to stop calling this a coincidence. WHY IT MATTERS MORE HERE THAN ELSEWHERE. In every previous chapter the residue merely cost a voice on one or two entries. Here key 26 has NOTHING BUT residue, so the exclusion that has been routine all rotation empties an entry completely and blocks the chapter. See the rejected note on this chapter for the full tiling analysis. THE GENERAL RISK THIS EXPOSES, which the next worker should carry to every chapter: A KEY WHOSE ONLY CONTENT IS RESIDUE IS INVISIBLE TO THE FIDELITY CHECK. The grounding test asks whether a declared voice appears anywhere in the catena for that book and chapter; Jamieson does appear, at these four keys, so declaring him at key 26 and writing festival commentary onto a verse about tabernacle boards would PASS the mechanical check while being a complete fabrication. Any worker who tiles mechanically and writes to fill the window will produce exactly that. The defence is the one used all rotation: read the residue block before excluding it, confirm which chapter it actually belongs to, and never write from a block whose subject does not match the target verse. ALSO IN THIS CHAPTER. (1) GILL CHROME at his last block: k8 ends with 'Next: Exodus Chapter 37 Sacred Texts | Bible << Previous: John Gill's Exposition ...'. Same shape as the Ellicott StudyLight chrome and, like it, it rides on the voice's LAST block in the chapter rather than the chapter's last key. Third confirmation for Gill specifically, after leviticus 2 k16 and genesis 16 k16. (2) NO ELLICOTT CHROME HERE, because Ellicott's last block is k32 and is only 18 words; the chrome appears to need a block of some substance to attach to. (3) HENRY -> WESLEY DEPENDENCE AGAIN, and this time the scan CAUGHT it (k35, 5 shingles) -- but it also MISSED a clearer instance, because Wesley's k2 block reproduces Henry's k1 block nearly verbatim AND PUTS IT IN QUOTATION MARKS ('Even those whom God has qualified for, and inclined to the service of the tabernacle, yet must wait for a call to it ... ability and willingness, with resolution, are the two things to be regarded in the call of ministers'). The scan compares voices WITHIN A KEY ONLY, so a borrowing that crosses keys is invisible to it. That is a second gap in the scan, alongside the sub-threshold-length gap recorded at numbers 25. A cross-key pass over the whole chapter would catch both.

GALATIANS 2 IS ALSO BLOCKED, BY A DIFFERENT SOURCE DEFECT: AN OUT-OF-RANGE VERSE KEY. Nothing was written; the tree was left clean. TWO SEPARATE REASONS, EITHER OF WHICH IS SUFFICIENT. (1) SIZE. 88,977 usable source words across 22 keys. That is more than twice the ~40,000 threshold at which a chapter is supposed to be the whole batch, and it is the largest chapter I have measured this rotation -- larger than luke 12 (65,981 across 59 keys), which I declined earlier and flagged as wanting a fresh window. Density here is 4,044 words per key against luke 12's 1,118, so the shape is more tractable per key, but the raw mass is 35 percent greater. Four individual keys are enormous: k16 is 11,995 words, k20 is 10,643, k1 is 7,531, k19 is 7,052. (2) THE OUT-OF-RANGE KEY, which blocks it outright regardless of size. Galatians 2 has TWENTY-ONE verses in the KJV, but the source file carries a key '29' holding a 169-word MARTIN LUTHER block ('And this is a common evil among men. For such is our misery that when temptation or death cometh, by and by setting Christ aside, we consider our own life past ...'). It is a stray fragment of Luther's Galatians commentary that has been filed against a verse which does not exist. I tested the tiling three ways against QA.coverage_problems. A tiling that omits key 29 fails with 'verses covered by no entry: [29]'. A tiling that absorbs it into the last entry as 19-29 fails with 'entries cover verses absent from the source: [22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28]'. THE ONLY LEGAL TILING IS ONE THAT INCLUDES A STANDALONE '29-29' ENTRY, and that entry is unwritable: it would declare a range 29-29 on a chapter of twenty-one verses, which is nonsense in the rendered data, and it would have to produce a 350-650 word grounded distillation from 167 words of a single voice. THIS IS THE SECOND BLOCKED CHAPTER IN A ROW AT THE HEAD OF THE WORST-FIRST QUEUE, after exodus 36 (see the rejected note there, where the blocker is a key whose only content is Jamieson residue). The two defects are different in kind -- a residue-only key versus an out-of-range key -- but they fail the same way: QA.coverage_problems forces an entry onto a key that has no writable content, and the only ways past it are to fabricate or to skip the key. THE COMMON REMEDY WOULD BE A SINGLE RULE. If coverage_problems allowed a key to be declared UNCOVERABLE, or if the loop dropped keys that are out of range or contain only residue before tiling, both chapters would become workable at once: galatians 2 would tile cleanly over 1-21 and exodus 36 over its two natural halves. That is an owner decision, not mine. PICKER CONSEQUENCE, and this is the practical point: BOTH chapters sit at the head of the repair queue and both will be offered again to the next worker, who will spend the same discovery effort and land nothing. Between them they have cost this batch its whole first half. They should be excluded like numbers 31 until the decision is made, and it would be worth running a cheap pre-flight over the whole repair queue for the same two defects -- a key outside the chapter's verse count, and a key whose only voice is Jamieson -- so the rest are found before a worker starts on them rather than after.

PRE-FLIGHT SCAN OF THE WHOLE COW CORPUS FOR THE TWO BLOCKING SOURCE DEFECTS. Run after exodus 36 and galatians 2 both blocked back to back at the head of the worst-first repair queue. THE TEST. For every chapter in data/commentary/cow, split each key by voice and flag (a) keys numbered above the chapter's KJV verse count, and (b) keys whose only voice is Jamieson, i.e. donor residue and nothing else. Then group the keys into contiguous runs, because QA.coverage_problems forbids an entry from covering a verse absent from the source and therefore forces the tiling to align to runs. A run in which EVERY key is out-of-range or residue-only is a DEAD RUN: it must become its own entry, and that entry has no writable content. THE RESULT. 29 chapters carry one of the defects; of those, SIXTEEN ARE HARD BLOCKED because they contain at least one dead run, and thirteen are benign because the residue key sits inside a run that also has real voices, which is the situation every chapter this rotation has handled by simply excluding Jamieson. HARD BLOCKED (chapter, then the dead runs): 1chronicles 25 [24]; 1chronicles 9 [39]; 1corinthians 16 [55]; 2chronicles 27 [16]; exodus 36 [26]; exodus 37 [23]; exodus 38 [5]; ezra 10 [38]; ezra 2 [13, 49]; ezra 8 [7]; galatians 2 [29]; nehemiah 10 [6, 18, 24]; nehemiah 7 [12, 24, 48, 60]; numbers 29 [22, 28]; NUMBERS 31 [42]; numbers 34 [25]. THREE OF THESE ARE OUT-OF-RANGE KEYS RATHER THAN RESIDUE: 1corinthians 16 has a key 55 in a 24-verse chapter, 2chronicles 27 has a key 16 in a 9-verse chapter, and galatians 2 has a key 29 in a 21-verse chapter. THE MOST IMPORTANT LINE IN THE LIST IS NUMBERS 31, which the standing poke has been telling workers to skip since this rotation began, 'blocked pending an owner decision on its source file'. It is hard blocked by exactly this defect, a dead run at key 42. That is independent confirmation that the defect I hit at exodus 36 and galatians 2 is the SAME defect the owner already knows about in numbers 31, and that it affects fifteen further chapters that nobody has flagged. BENIGN, listed so no one re-investigates them: 1chronicles 1, 1chronicles 6, 1chronicles 7, 1chronicles 8, 1chronicles 14, 1chronicles 15, 1kings 7, deuteronomy 14, exodus 39, exodus 40, leviticus 4, luke 3, numbers 28. These are workable; just exclude Jamieson on the affected entry as usual. WHAT THIS SUGGESTS FOR THE OWNER. A single change unblocks all sixteen: either drop keys that are out of range or residue-only from the source before tiling, or let coverage_problems accept a declared-uncoverable key. Either way it is one decision, not sixteen, and the same decision already pending on numbers 31. NOTE THE SHAPE OF THE LIST: it is dominated by the enumerative books -- Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Numbers, the tabernacle chapters of Exodus. That is the same class of material I identified as the DONOR side of the Jamieson residue (Exodus 22-23, Exodus 27-28, Numbers 3-4, Numbers 7 are all long legal or ceremonial catalogues). Catalogue chapters are apparently both the source of the residue and its most frequent victims, which is what one would expect if the residue is produced by a read-through that mistakes one catalogue for another. THE PRACTICAL ASK: exclude these sixteen from the picker, as numbers 31 already is, or fix the source. Until then the worst-first queue will keep handing them to workers, who will each spend a chapter's worth of discovery and land nothing -- which is what happened to the first half of this batch.

Ellicott alone inverts the Sethite reading of the sons of God. Granting that the Sethite view is the one most accepted in modern times, he asks how the marriage of pious men to women of an inferior race could produce mighty men and men of renown, insists the phrase conveys no idea of piety (the word constantly meaning mighty ones and elsewhere rendered judges), and argues the daughters of men in v2 must be those of v1, who were Sethites. So on his reading the pious are the women and the mighty are the intruders. Keil sets out the three traditional answers; Gill and Calvin both reach the Sethite view by elimination. Recorded because Ellicott's position is held by no other voice in this catena and is easy to flatten into the ordinary Sethite reading.

genesis 6 is the largest chapter attempted this rotation (31,927 usable source words, 22 keys). Tiling 1-2 | 3-4 | 5-8 | 9-12 | 13-16 | 17-22, source budgets 4393 / 5583 / 6186 / 3314 / 7211 / 5022. Foreign-author text inside a voice block. The John Wesley block at k15 (262 words) begins with about 35 words of genuine Wesley and then continues with a long passage of Cyril of Jerusalem's Catechetical Lectures on the baptismal chrism (forehead, ears, nostrils, breast). Only the opening Wesley material was used.

Two more contamination cases in the same chapter. (a) The John Calvin block at k14 carries, mid-paragraph, a verbatim slab of Adam Clarke's description of a Roman triumph, including the Lucius Mummius / Achaicus detail, evidently an editorial footnote flattened into the body text; the same sentences appear in Clarke's own k14 block. (b) The Charles Ellicott block at k17 (1281 words) contains roughly 250 words of real commentary followed by StudyLight site chrome - copyright text, CSS rules, and navigation menus. Combined with the Cyril-inside-Wesley case, this chapter shows that cross-voice contamination is not confined to the Jamieson stream, and that a duplication scan comparing voices only within a key would miss (a) entirely, since Clarke's k14 and Calvin's k14 do sit in the same key but the scan's 12-word shingle would flag them as a genuine agreement rather than as an editorial artefact.

The sharpest split in the chapter is grammatical, not theological. On thriambeuo, Ellicott and Robertson both hold that there is no attested causative use of the verb, so the sense must be 'always leads us in his triumph' and the apostle figures as a captive in the procession; Ellicott adds that it would be out of character for him to cast himself as the victorious commander. Calvin and Barnes take it as causative on the analogy of the Hebrew hiphil, 'maketh us to triumph', Calvin softening the captive image by making him a lieutenant riding beside the general's chariot as a sharer in the honour. Clarke assumes the causative without arguing it. Recorded as a debate on entry 14; the prose gives both readings without adjudicating.

JAMIESON RESIDUE: the walk CONTINUES ACROSS THE CHAPTER BOUNDARY -- the single most decisive datum yet for the re-indexing decision. revelation 7 carries 3 Jamieson blocks at keys 5, 11, 17 (offset 5 mod 6, same class as revelation 6, revelation 11, exodus 38), and the source is 1 Thessalonians: k5 = 1Th 1:7-8, k11 = 1Th 2:1, k17 = 1Th 2:6. revelation 6's three blocks were Col 4:12, Col 4:17, 1Th 1:2. That is not a per-chapter misalignment; it is a single flat global offset into a concatenated Jamieson corpus, read straight through. The offset table is now complete 0-5 with identified source books for every class except offsets 1 and 4. Recommendation to the owner: the re-indexing fix should be modelled as one global pointer, not as per-chapter repair.

CROSS-CHAPTER DUPLICATE BLOCK: Cyril of Jerusalem's single block here (k17, 197 words) is byte-identical to the block that appeared at revelation 6 k6 -- the Catechetical Lecture on the firmament of Genesis 1 ('Let there be a firmament in the midst of the water'). BARNES DEFECTS, three kinds in one chapter. (1) Chapter front matter at k1 -- 7th consecutive chapter. (2) Clarke chapter argument at k1 -- 5th consecutive. (3) Stub blocks: k7 and k8 are the bare two-word string 'Rev 7:5', a cross-reference with no content, and k6 opens 'Continuation of Note from Revelation 7:5'. The standing recommendation for a 'Continuation of Notes on' detector now has a companion case: blocks under ~5 words that consist only of a scripture reference should be dropped as stubs, not carried as content.

Five live disagreements in revelation 7. (1) The four angels: good or evil? Wesley alone says evil -- 'the angels to whom the four winds are committed' are ministers of vengeance -- against Barnes, Gill and Ellicott, who take them as good angels restraining judgement. (2) Angels or kingdoms? Bede reads the four as the four kingdoms, Assyria, Persia, Greece and Rome, against every modern voice. (3) Is the great multitude the same company as the 144,000? Ellicott says yes and reads the two visions as the Passover and the Feast of Tabernacles of one Church; Barnes keeps them distinct, the sealed being a numbered remnant and the multitude the whole assembled host. (4) Where is the scene? Gill refuses heaven and sets the vision in the millennial reign on earth; Barnes takes it as transferred from earth to heaven. (5) Are these martyrs? Barnes says the eye is fixed on the martyrs standing among the host; Wesley denies it flatly, since martyrs are not a multitude no man can number. Add the tribe-list anomaly at k4: Dan is omitted and Manasseh substituted, noticed by Gill, Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott, with no agreed explanation.

Clarke's two outlier readings in revelation 7, both worth preserving because they cut against his own tradition's neighbours. (1) On the white robes at v14 he argues against imputation: the robes cannot be the righteousness of Christ, 'for this cannot be washed and made white in his own blood', but are a righteousness wrought in them by the merit of his blood and the power of his Spirit. Every other voice here reads the washing as cleansing by imputed merit. (2) On 'neither shall the sun light on them' at v16 he alone reads historically rather than heavenly: the sun is the secular rulers, who 'being converted to God, became nursing fathers to the Church', and the heat is persecution. Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Wesley all take the clause as a description of the heavenly state.

PATRISTIC TILING HYPOTHESIS -- third data point, and it holds. The hypothesis formed at 1corinthians 2 was that the patristic trees are tiled by SCRIPTURE CITATION rather than by position: where a father quotes the verse the block lands correctly, where he does not an arbitrary block is attached. revelation 7 confirms it from both sides. Victorinus of Pettau, who wrote an actual commentary on Revelation and cites 7:1-2 directly, lands correctly at k1 and was usable. Bede, likewise a commentator on Revelation, lands correctly at k1. Cyril of Jerusalem, whose Catechetical Lectures barely touch Revelation, gets an arbitrary Genesis-firmament block -- the same one twice, in two chapters. If the hypothesis holds, the remedy is far cheaper than the whole-tree re-fetch recommended earlier for Tertullian: drop any patristic block that does not cite its own verse or an adjacent one. Recommend the owner test this with a citation-match pass over the patristic trees before commissioning any re-fetch.

A clean doctrinal split on whether the verse licenses a doctrine of sanctification by suffering. Wesley enters an explicit caution that what is said of the Lord's being made perfect through sufferings has NO relation to our being saved or sanctified by ours: he was perfect as God and as man before ever he suffered, and by suffering was made a complete sin-offering, which is as far out of our sphere as his ascension; afflictions help only indirectly, as they wean us from sin. Calvin draws the opposite comfort from the same words, that it was necessary for the firstbegotten to be inaugurated into his supremacy by the cross since that is the common lot of the members, and that the faithful may therefore lovingly kiss the cross rather than dread it. Robertson stands aside from both, holding the scruple misplaced because it is the humanity that is under discussion. Recorded as a debate on entry 10; the prose gives Wesley's caution and Calvin's comfort side by side without adjudicating.

A convergence worth recording rather than a defect. At v18 Clarke and Calvin independently reach for the same line of the Aeneid, non ignara mali miseris succurrere disco, to illustrate that a state of suffering disposes men to be compassionate. Clarke gives it with Dryden's rendering and builds his exposition on the maxim; Calvin quotes it as a saying no doubt derived from daily examples among men, and then immediately guards it, since the Son of God needed no experience in order to know the emotions of mercy. Two commentators three centuries and one confession apart reaching for the same pagan poet on the same verse is the kind of agreement the debates field cannot express, so it is noted here.

JAMIESON RESIDUE, offset-4 class, and the source is identified for the first time. acts 25 carries 4 Jamieson blocks at keys 4, 10, 16, 22 -- offset 4 mod 6, the class previously known only from genesis 20, where a single block left the source unidentified. Here the source is ACTS 4: k4 = Ac 4:1-2 (the Sadducees vexed at the preaching of the resurrection), k10 = Ac 4:1-2 AGAIN, byte-identical to k4, k16 = Ac 4:13 (unlearned and ignorant men, they had been with Jesus), k22 = Ac 4:19 (whether it be right to hearken unto you more than unto God). That closes offset 4 in the table; only offset 1 (genesis 2, exodus 24, romans 12, colossians 4) now lacks an identified source. TWO NEW FACTS. (1) The walk here runs BACKWARD within the same book: acts 25 is served from acts 4, twenty-one chapters earlier. Revelation 6 and 7 were likewise served from Colossians and 1 Thessalonians, both earlier in canon than Revelation. Every identified case so far points earlier in a canonically ordered corpus, which is what a single negative global offset into a concatenated tree would produce. (2) The k4/k10 duplicate breaks the monotonic stride seen in revelation 6-7: the pointer emitted the same block twice before advancing. If the pointer model is right, that is a repeat rather than a step, and the re-indexing fix has to tolerate it.

Cyril of Jerusalem off target again (k9): a Catechetical Lecture on Christ going willingly to his passion, attached to Festus asking Paul whether he will go up to Jerusalem. The only visible hook is the phrase 'go up to Jerusalem', which appears in both -- consistent with a crude string match rather than a citation match. Silenced chapter-wide. Cyril has now been off target in revelation 6, revelation 7, galatians 6 and acts 25, and on target only in 1corinthians 2, which his Lectures quote heavily. Also note the duplicate-block pattern recurs here in a different tree: Jamieson's k4 and k10 blocks are byte-identical, as Cyril's galatians 6 k14 and k18 were. A whole-tree duplicate-block detector would catch all of these at once.

PATRISTIC TILING HYPOTHESIS: fourth data point, and the strongest yet. acts 25 has exactly one patristic block, Chrysostom at k23, and it is fully ON TARGET -- a homily on Acts 25:23ff that quotes verses 24-27 verbatim and expounds them. Chrysostom wrote Homilies on Acts and cites the verse; Cyril of Jerusalem, whose Lectures barely touch Acts, gets an arbitrary block at k9. Same chapter, same tree-building process, opposite outcomes, and citation is the only variable that separates them. Combined with revelation 7 (Victorinus and Bede, both actual Revelation commentators, landed correctly; Cyril did not) the hypothesis now has four independent confirmations and no counter-example. Recommend the owner run a citation-match pass over the patristic trees -- drop any patristic block that does not cite its own verse or an adjacent one -- before commissioning any whole-tree re-fetch. Note also that Chrysostom's k23 block runs on past the chapter into Acts 26:27-29, so the citation-match pass should trim at the chapter boundary rather than accept the whole block.

Clarke chapter argument at k1 again -- 6th consecutive chapter. Barnes front matter at k1 is milder here than usual, only the heading 'CHAPTER 25 Verse 1', but present -- 8th consecutive. Two more defect shapes worth a detector each. (1) STUB BLOCKS THAT ARE PURE CROSS-REFERENCE APPARATUS: Barnes at k25 is nothing but the marginal reference string, and several other Barnes blocks in this chapter end in a tail of reference codes in parentheses with letters and symbols. (2) CHROME AT THE TAIL: Ellicott's k26 block ends with the navigation strip 'Acts Act 24 Acts Act Acts Act 26'. Both are already handled by the dump filter in the working scratchpad, but they are in the stored data and will mislead any downstream consumer that does not strip them.

Live disagreements in acts 25. (1) The text of v6: Clarke and Barnes both hold the best manuscripts read 'not more than eight or ten days' against the received 'more than ten days', and Clarke reports a scholar of his day calling the shorter reading indubitably genuine; Gill keeps the longer and explains it as the historian being imprecise. (2) What 'those among you who are able' means at v5: Gill, Calvin and Wesley read it as capacity -- who can spare the time and bear the expense -- while Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson read it as authority, men in office whose character vouches for their testimony. (3) Whether the appeal at v11 was absolute or conditional: Clarke argues it must have been conditional, since Festus could not otherwise have deliberated with his council over granting what he had no power to refuse; Robertson answers that some discretion did exist, an appeal being refusable for a notorious robber or pirate. (4) How to hear Festus's 'unto Caesar shalt thou go': Barnes and Clarke read relief at escaping an impossible trial, Ellicott hears a sneer from a man who knew what kind of judge Paul was appealing to, Calvin suspects indignation and then withdraws the guess as mere conjecture. (5) Whether 'their own superstition' at v19 is an insult: Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson all defend the governor, arguing the word was his own term for religion and that he would not insult a Jewish king to his face; Gill alone lets the harsh rendering stand.

Two convergences worth recording as evidence that the corpus rewards cross-reading. (1) At v16 Barnes and Clarke, working independently, both quote the SAME two ancient authorities for the Roman rule against condemning a man unheard, and then both turn the verse into a patriotic tribute to their own country's courts -- Barnes to American jurisprudence as surpassing all that Rome ever enjoyed, Clarke to English law, twelve honest men, and 'no Bastiles, no lettres de cachet'. Two commentators, one verse, two national anthems. (2) At v23 Clarke and Ellicott independently make the same observation, that the Herodian pair paraded their pomp in the very city where their father had been struck down for his pride and eaten of worms; Clarke draws the moral that the living seldom lay God's judgments to heart, Ellicott that the vice was inherited and the lesson unlearnt. Neither cites the other. These are the kind of agreements that a synthesis surfaces and a single-commentary reading cannot.

Live disagreements in 1timothy 6. (1) What the second noun of v6 means: Barnes and Robertson take it as contentment, a state of mind, from a Greek word meaning self-sufficiency; Clarke takes it as a competency, a bare sufficiency of goods, and defines it as food, raiment and lodging; Henry reports both readings without choosing. (2) How far v8 limits lawful desire: Wesley says food and covering are all a Christian needs and all his religion allows him to desire; Barnes refuses to let the verse forbid a comfortable habitation, the means of knowledge, or conveniences for worship; Ellicott guards it from the other side, against the ascetic error the same letter attacks in chapter 4. (3) Who is rich: Clarke says whoever has more than food and raiment is rich in the apostle's sense -- a far harder line than Gill, who names Abraham and Joseph of Arimathea as rich and good, or Ellicott, who says the term would include many who would hesitate to apply it to themselves. (4) The root of all evil: Clarke would render 'of all these evils' and protests at the popular misquotation; Barnes calls it a popular saying not literally true; Ellicott defends the strong rendering on the grammar of the article; Robertson calls it a proverb of two ancient philosophers. (5) When Timothy made the good confession: Barnes says at his profession or ordination, Wesley and Robertson at his baptism, Clarke at an imprisonment inferred from Hebrews 13:23, Ellicott finds the persecution reading most probable but rejects it on chronology. (6) Whether the falsely named knowledge of v20 is the Gnostic system: Clarke rejects it because the sect may not yet have existed.

Two cross-references between voices worth recording, both of a kind a synthesis surfaces and a single-commentary reading cannot. (1) At v19 Clarke quotes WESLEY BY NAME and adopts his paraphrase of the verse as authoritative -- one voice in this corpus citing another voice in this corpus, approvingly, inside his own commentary. It is the first instance of that I have met in the loop. (2) At v16 Clarke asks whether the apostle, who demonstrably quotes three Greek poets, may also have had the tragedians in his eye when writing the doxology, saying the similarity is so complete that we are almost persuaded of it -- but that if so, he extends the thought infinitely higher by language incomparably more exalted. Alongside these, Robertson at v16 suspects emperor worship behind the word 'alone', one emperor having demanded to be addressed as lord and god, and at v13 he had already noted the same word-field: the Christians claimed 'Lord' for Christ, and it became the test in the Roman persecutions when a martyr refused to say Lord Caesar and insisted on Lord Jesus at the cost of his life.

PATRISTIC TILING HYPOTHESIS: sixth data point, and the first chapter where a father is on target throughout. Augustine of Hippo has 3 blocks (k12, k18, k27) and all three are from his Homilies on the First Epistle of John, so all three are on this text -- the citation rule predicts exactly this. Cyril of Jerusalem has 4 blocks and scores 2 or 3 of 4: k22 and k23 are squarely on target (his Catechetical Lectures expound 'who is the liar but he that denieth that Jesus is the Christ' and 'he that denieth the Son hath not the Father' almost verbatim), k19 on Simon Magus as the inventor of heresy is loosely apt at 'they went out from us', and k15 on walking spiritually is off target. His Lectures quote 1 John 2:22-23 heavily and 2:15 not at all. Six chapters, no counter-example. A REFINEMENT THE EARLIER CHAPTERS DID NOT SHOW: Augustine's k12 and k27 blocks are HOMILY APPARATUS rather than exposition -- k12 is the preface about hearing the Scriptures and guarding against heretics, k27 is the lesson read aloud in church, running from 2:27 straight into 3:8 and closing with 'ye remember, brethren, that yesterday's lesson was brought to a close at...'. So even an on-target patristic tree carries non-expository matter keyed to verses. A citation-match pass should therefore also detect and drop (a) homily prefaces, (b) blocks that are purely the lesson text, and (c) cross-references to a previous day's homily.

Live disagreements in 1john 2, an unusually contested chapter. (1) The extent of the propitiation at v2: Gill restricts 'our sins' to believers who are Jews; Clarke calls any limitation 'a violent outrage against God and his word'; Wesley says as wide as sin extends, the propitiation extends also; and Calvin, remarkably, reports the scholastic sufficient-for-all, efficient-for-the-elect formula, ALLOWS IT TO BE TRUE, and then denies that it suits this passage, since the design was to make the benefit common to the whole Church. (2) Love perfected at v5: Barnes denies the verse says anything about sinless perfection; Wesley, from whom the opposite might be expected, glosses 'perfected' merely as 'perfectly known'. (3) The lust of the eyes at v16: Henry and Clarke take it as covetousness; Wesley takes it as the pleasures of imagination, the internal sense whereby we relish whatever is grand, new or beautiful, and moves covetousness to the third head. (4) The last hour at v18 gets five answers: the last hour of the apostolic age (Gill), the end of the Jewish polity (Henry), a perilous time rather than a chronological last, with the letter written before Jerusalem fell (Clarke), the last dispensation which may run many ages (Barnes), and openly undecided (Robertson). Calvin alone confronts the objection that the centuries since falsify the prophecy. (5) Whether the departure at v19 proves the perseverance of the saints: Barnes makes it a universal proof; Clarke dissents on 'they were not ALL of us', holding that some who went out were sincere. (6) The italicised clause at v23: Barnes and Clarke independently marshal manuscript evidence to restore it. (7) Needing no teacher at v27: Calvin, Clarke and Wesley all independently refuse the enthusiast reading and defend the outward ministry. (8) Whether 'he is righteous' at v29 is the Father or the Son: Gill says Christ; Ellicott and Calvin say the Father, both because the new birth is nowhere ascribed to the Son; Robertson says plainly God despite the adjective.

Independent convergences in 1john 2 worth recording. (1) At v20 Wesley and Robertson, working centuries apart, both suspect that the word 'chrism' was chosen in deliberate opposition to 'antichrist' just used in v18 -- neither cites the other. (2) At v26 Calvin makes driving away wolves as much a pastor's duty as gathering the flock, and Robertson says the same of the writer himself, that he is doing his part to rescue the sheep from the wolves as Paul did. (3) At v28 Henry notes that the apostle includes HIMSELF in 'that WE may have confidence' -- 'let not us be ashamed of you' -- and Clarke independently reads the shame as the minister's over converts who have apostatised and so are not his crown of rejoicing. (4) At v23 Barnes and Clarke each assemble an independent apparatus of manuscripts, versions and fathers to argue the italicised clause back into the text. These are the kind of agreements a synthesis surfaces and a single-commentary reading cannot, and they are accumulating: the same pattern was logged at acts 25 (Barnes and Clarke each turning the Roman legal rule into a patriotic tribute) and 1timothy 6 (Clarke citing Wesley by name).

Source truncation at exactly 200 words, affecting Keil and Delitzsch throughout this chapter and Gill twice. Eight of the 56 voice blocks here are exactly 200 words long, and they break mid-sentence: k1 ends at 'on the one hand to oppose an effectual barrier', k2 at 'after whom they go a whoring). This', k8 at 'the soul which gives life to the flesh) is in the'. Six of the eight are Keil. Two consequences worth recording. Two independent commentators reach for the same modern authority. On 'the life of the flesh is in the blood', Clarke mounts a long defence of the vitality of the blood, citing Harvey's demonstration of the circulation in 1628 and then rehearsing John Hunter's experimental proofs; Gill, quite separately and in his own idiom, cites 'our famous Dr. Harvey, who found out the circulation of the blood' and calls the blood the first that lives and the last that dies. A Puritan-era expositor and a Methodist commentator a century apart both answering a Levitical verse with seventeenth-century anatomy is the kind of convergence the debates field cannot express, so it is noted here. Also recorded: the Henry-to-Wesley dependence fires again at k10, where Wesley reproduces Henry's sentence 'Write that man undone, for ever undone, against whom God sets his face' almost verbatim. The richest interpretive divergence I have met in this rotation, and it is worth recording in full because the entries could only carry part of it. On the seven heads the chapter's voices divide four ways: Robertson and Barnes take the seven mountains as plain Rome, the city known to its own poets as seven-hilled; Ellicott keeps Rome but treats the literalism as the vehicle of a broader symbol, the world-city sitting among the empires that have risen like mountains through history; Wesley narrows to the hills as they stood under the papacy, with the older palace hill deserted; Clarke denies the reference to Rome altogether on the ground that modern Rome does not stand on those hills, and takes mountains figuratively for seven great powers. On the seven kings the split is between kingdoms and men, and Ellicott's argument is the strongest on either side, resting on the verb: the word used of the five that fell is the one employed for political catastrophe, so applied to individuals it would be forced to mean merely that they died. Robertson holds for men and concedes candidly that the identification is one of the puzzles of the book. Recorded as debates on entry 9; the prose gives all four readings of the mountains and both of the kings without adjudicating between them.

PHANTOM KEY BEYOND THE CHAPTER'S VERSE COUNT -- a new defect shape. Galatians 2 has 21 verses, but the source carries a key '29' holding a 169-word Martin Luther fragment that begins mid-sentence and plainly belongs to his verse-20 block (the brazen-serpent passage: turn our eyes wholly to the brazen serpent, Jesus Christ crucified). It carries the usual Luther scan damage -- righ- teousness broken across a line, ofN. conscience. This is NOT the 2 Chronicles 27 shape: ch27 key 16 holds FOREIGN-passage material (Henry on ch28), whereas this key holds material belonging to THIS chapter that simply overflowed its own key. Recommend a whole-tree scan for source keys greater than the chapter's verse count, split by whether the content is foreign (re-index) or overflow (merge back into the preceding key). The eleven entries tile 1-21 and the fragment is not drawn on.

TOOLING: the pericope tiling check contradicted the documented omit-out-of-range-keys rule. coverage_problems demanded an entry for every source key, so a chapter that declares pericope ranges could not omit a phantom key -- galatians 2 failed with 'verses covered by no entry: [29]' and had no legal output: covering 29 by extending the last range makes 22-28 'absent from the source', and a twelfth entry at key 29 would render a verse 29 in a 21-verse chapter to readers. Fixed narrowly: coverage now requires only the contiguous run of keys starting at the lowest, since verses run contiguously and a key past a gap cannot be a verse of the chapter. The 'extra' check still measures against the FULL source key set, so no chapter that used to pass has been narrowed -- verified by a full corpus run of validate-synthesis.py (an earlier shape of the fix broke 10 chapters that legitimately span an interior gap, which is what forced the split between required and want). Loop doc note added under the 2026-07-22 out-of-range entry.

SECOND case of the walk landing on NON-VERSE front matter -- 1john 2 k24 hit a book preface (the essay on the authenticity of Philippians), this one hits a chapter summary. Every identified case now points EARLIER in a canonically ordered corpus -- revelation from Colossians/1 Thessalonians, acts 25 from acts 4, 1timothy 6 from 1 Corinthians 14, 1john 2 from Ephesians 6, galatians 2 from Romans 7-8. Not one points forward. Model it as a single NEGATIVE global pointer into a concatenated tree; any fix must handle non-verse material in the stream (book prefaces, chapter summaries, end-of-book subscriptions, Review-of-book matter).

PATRISTIC TILING -- seventh confirmation, and it RETIRES a standing recommendation. Both patristic blocks in this chapter sit at k1 and both are ON TARGET: Tertullian expounds Gal 2:1-2 directly (against Marcion's edited text -- how great the apostle's desire was to be approved by the very men his adversary wished understood as allies of Judaism), and John Chrysostom expounds the same verses from his Galatians commentary (the objection about running in vain, resolved by the revelation). Both men wrote works ON Galatians. Neither is silenced. This is the seventh confirmation of the hypothesis that patristic trees are tiled by SCRIPTURE CITATION rather than position, and it specifically retires the earlier recommendation of an expensive whole-tree re-fetch for Tertullian: he lands correctly where he cites. The remedy stands as two-stage -- (1) drop patristic blocks citing nothing in the chapter, (2) re-key the survivors by which verse they actually quote -- with the 1john 2 refinement that a citation-match pass must also detect homily apparatus (prefaces, blocks that are purely the lesson read aloud, cross-references to a previous day's homily).

SCAN AND CHROME, recurring shapes. (a) MARTIN LUTHER is the dominant voice here -- 20 blocks, 33,864 words, 38 percent of the chapter -- and carries heavy scan damage throughout: hyphenation broken across lines (righ- teousness, dissimu- lation, COMBfENTART), embedded page headers (COMMENTARY ON GALATIANS. 93 / 97 / 100 / 105 / 111 / 116 / 122 / 129 / 159 / 169 / 183) and running folios dropped mid-sentence, OCR substitutions (hve for live, Uveth for liveth, ndt for not, bour>d for bound, ise for the). (b) ALBERT BARNES chapter front matter -- ELEVENTH consecutive chapter. (c) ADAM CLARKE chapter argument -- NINTH consecutive. (d) CHARLES ELLICOTT navigation chrome at block tails (a bare 'Galatians Gal 1 Galatians Gal Galatians Gal 3' strip at k21). All four are stable, mechanical, and worth a single tree-wide pass rather than per-chapter handling.

The chapter's substantive disagreements, all carried in the prose. (1) CHRONOLOGY: fourteen years from the visit just mentioned (Ellicott, decisive on 'I went up again') vs from the conversion (Clarke's chronologer); Gill makes it seventeen from the conversion, Luther eighteen. (2) WHICH JOURNEY: Calvin DENIES outright that this is the Acts 15 council journey, and his argument is from the rebuke that follows -- Peter would not have dissembled at Antioch if the decree had already been published, so the rebuke, and therefore this visit, must fall earlier. Ellicott, Robertson and Wesley all take it as the Council. (3) WHO IS CEPHAS: Gill and Clarke both report and both reject the ancient dodge that the man rebuked was one of the seventy, not the apostle; Clarke notes the controversy has run more than fifteen hundred years, and that the most learned Catholic writers and popes take it of Peter. (4) WHO IS ADDRESSED from v15: Calvin says the speech to Peter ENDS at v14 (what had Peter to do with this argument?), Barnes says it runs to v21. (5) HOW FAR THE UNION GOES at v20: Robertson says the separate personality is merged into that of Christ; Ellicott denies any actual union of the human and divine and calls the figure metaphor. (6) Luther holds Peter sinned NOT AT ALL in eating with the Gentiles and was reproved only for the dissembling.

CONVERGENCES a synthesis surfaces and single-commentary reading cannot. (a) BARNABAS: five voices independently fasten on his defection -- Clarke calls him the gentle, loving-hearted Barnabas; Wesley says he was borne away as with a torrent; Robertson calls it a solemn moment when Paul saw the Jerusalem victory vanish; Ellicott traces the breach that soon separated the two apostles to this moment; Luther says Paul alone standeth to the truth, for he had lost Barnabas his companion. (b) ANTI-PAPAL INFERENCE from opposite ends: Henry argues from the PLACE (no colour of reason that Peter was bishop of Antioch, else Paul would not have withstood him in his own church), Calvin from the MANNER (an official act in the apostolic character -- another thunderbolt striking the papacy). (c) THE DIVISION OF SPHERES: Barnes, Luther and Calvin each independently raise the same objection (Paul preached in synagogues, Peter to Cornelius) and answer it three different ways -- main business, historical dispersal at the fall of Jerusalem, and a command addressed to the office in general. Calvin adds, drily, that probably not one of the twelve ever passed into Europe and that what is alleged of Peter may for aught he knows be fabulous. (d) TWO THIEVES: Gill denies a literal crucifixion because only the two thieves were crucified with him; Robertson notes the same compound verb is used in the Gospels of the robbers -- the same lexical fact reached from devotional and grammatical ends. (e) CLARKE'S ARGUMENT FROM EMBARRASSMENT at v21: had the apostles acted in concert to impose a forgery, the falling out of the parties would have discovered the cheat, so the quarrel itself is evidence of the truth of the Gospel.

Two further source faults. (1) Gill k34 carries ~30 words of navigation chrome ('Next: Numbers Chapter 3 / Sacred Texts / Previous / Index'). This is the SIXTH consecutive chapter with chrome on the chapter-final key, and the first from a different scrape source (Sacred Texts, not StudyLight) in a different voice (Gill, not Ellicott). The pattern is therefore chapter-final, not voice-specific and not source-specific -- a real refinement of what the previous five notes claimed, and it means the automated pre-flight screen should not be keyed to StudyLight markers alone. It already caught this one because the screen tests for 'Next:' as well. (2) Keil's k19 block reads 'towards the north was the standard of Gad, with Asher and Naphtali': Gad is wrong, the north standard is Dan's, and Gad was in the south camp. The rest of that clause (the handmaids' descent, 157,600, the rearguard) is correct, so this reads as a corruption of a single word rather than an error of Keil's. Not repeated in the entry.

The Henry-to-Wesley dependence has a clear exception here, which is worth recording because the previous six chapters made it look unbroken. At k3 Wesley condenses Henry almost word for word on why Judah led (numbers, but chiefly the Lion of the tribe of Judah descending through Nahshon). But at k2 Wesley's kinship analysis of the four standards -- the three youngest sons of Leah under Judah, Gad added to Reuben in Levi's room, Rachel's posterity forming the third, Bilhah's eldest leading the fourth -- runs parallel to Henry's without being a condensation of it, and Wesley closes with a remark of his own about the wisdom of God in these smaller circumstances. So the dependence is real but not total: where Henry supplies a finished argument Wesley abridges it, and where the material is a list Wesley works it himself.

Clarke's entry on v2 is the largest single block in the chapter (4,358 words) and almost all of it is a translated quotation of Scheuchzer's reconstruction of the camp, down to Reyher's square-cubit allotments per tribe and a total of twelve square miles. What makes it worth recording is the ending: having printed the whole apparatus Clarke withdraws its authority himself, saying the text gives the quarters and no more, that how they were arranged individually cannot be pretended to, and that to claim minute exactness would be absurd. Compare Clarke at revelation 17:1, where he likewise printed the fullest exposition he had met with and told readers they were at liberty to reject it. Same habit in two very different books: print the best available reconstruction in full, then disclaim it in his own voice.

200-word truncation again, and heavier than in any chapter so far: Keil at k1, k2, k3, k4, k5, k9, k10 and k11, and Gill at k12 -- nine blocks cut mid-sentence at exactly 200 words. The Keil blocks are additionally degraded by overlap: k3, k4 and k5 reprint substantially the same run of verse text with the commentary trimmed off the end, so the 800 words counted for Keil across entry 3 contain perhaps 150 words of actual exposition. Two convergences the debates field records only as separate positions. (1) At v9 four voices give four different senses of 'the reproach of Egypt' -- Clarke and Wesley the reproach OF uncircumcision, Keil the reproach PROCEEDING FROM Egypt (reading the genitive as in 'the reproach of Moab'), and Calvin a political charge of desertion and rebellion. This is the cleanest four-way divergence on a single phrase I have met in the corpus, and none of the four cites another. (2) At v12 Clarke and Wesley independently reach the same providential argument for why the manna stopped -- that God will not work miracles where ordinary means suffice -- while disagreeing with Ellicott about the date on which it did stop (the seventeenth against his sixteenth). Agreement on the reasoning, disagreement on the arithmetic.

Ellicott twice does something none of the other voices in this chapter attempt: he computes. At v12 he reckons the manna's whole span from Exodus 16 to Joshua 5 at thirty-nine years and eleven months, notes that it never fell on a Sabbath, and observes that it ceased on the weekday later marked by the resurrection, drawing the conclusion that the risen Christ takes the place of the bread from heaven. At v13 he compares and then contrasts the appearance with the bush at Horeb, resting the comparison on the shared command about the shoe and the contrast on bush-unconsumed against sword-drawn. Both are arguments from structure rather than from doctrine, and both are unique to him here.
