THE STRONGEST EVIDENCE YET FOR THE SINGLE-POINTER MODEL: revelation 11's residue was 1 Thess 4-5 and revelation 12's is 1 Thess 5:12-22, so CONSECUTIVE Revelation chapters draw CONSECUTIVE Thessalonians material -- the pointer is walking one stream forward while the Revelation chapter number advances. Note the in-chapter offset CHANGED between the two (revelation 6, 7 and 11 were offset 5 with keys 5/11/17; revelation 12 is offset 3 with keys 3/9/15), which is exactly what a global pointer advancing at a rate unrelated to the chapter key count produces. The backward rule still holds (Revelation served from Thessalonians, earlier in canon). Combined with the galatians 2 finding (Romans 7-8) and the earlier table, the offset classes 0-5 are now all attested and at least three of them are traceable to a continuous walk. Recommend modelling the whole defect as ONE negative global offset into a concatenated tree, and testing that model by predicting revelation 13's residue: it should be 1 Thessalonians 5 near its end, or the opening of 2 Thessalonians.

CROSS-KEY DUPLICATE, and the first WITHIN a single chapter. Cyril of Jerusalem's Lecture 15.16 block (For this cause the Lord knowing the greatness of the adversary grants indulgence to the godly... let them which be in Judaea flee to the mountains... I do not despair of the Church's nerves) appears BYTE-IDENTICALLY at BOTH k6 and k14. This is the third instance of duplicated patristic blocks in this corpus -- Cyril's firmament lecture at revelation 6 k6 and revelation 7 k17 was cross-CHAPTER, Jamieson's acts 25 k4 and k10 was cross-key within a chapter, and this is cross-key within a chapter for a father. The pattern is now well enough attested to justify a cheap whole-tree pass: hash every voice block and report every hash occurring more than once, then decide per duplicate whether to drop the second copy or re-key it. It is excluded here at the entry covering k14 and drawn on at k6, where it is on target for the woman's flight into the wilderness.

PATRISTIC TILING -- eighth confirmation, and the cleanest split so far between on-target and off-target blocks in ONE chapter. Victorinus of Pettau (k1) and Bede (k1) are both ON TARGET, each expounding Rev 12:1 directly; both wrote commentaries on the Apocalypse, and both land at the verse they expound. Cyril of Jerusalem, who did NOT write on Revelation, is mixed exactly as the citation-match hypothesis predicts: k5 is ON TARGET because his Lecture 12.18 argues from 'Thou shalt rule them with a rod of iron', the phrase in Rev 12:5; k6 is ON TARGET because Lecture 15.16 is about fleeing to the mountains in the great tribulation, matching the woman's flight in Rev 12:6; k11 is OFF TARGET, being Lecture 12.10 on the King coming to daughter Sion, with nothing of Rev 12:11 (overcame by the blood of the Lamb) -- though note it does mention sun and moon, which may be what the citation-matcher latched onto, since sun and moon are in Rev 12:1. That near-miss is instructive: a naive citation matcher keyed on shared imagery rather than verse reference will produce exactly this error. Recommend the matcher key on explicit scripture references and quoted phrases, not on shared vocabulary.

The chapter's substantive disagreements, all carried in the prose. (1) WHO IS THE WOMAN: all agree she is the Church, but Victorinus makes her the ancient Church of fathers and prophets, Robertson the Church of the Old Testament without a sharp dividing line from the Christian society, Henry the Church simply, and Wesley reads the lights politically -- the sun the Christian world, the moon the Mahometans who carry it in their ensigns, the twelve stars the tribes. Robertson rules out the Virgin Mary outright from verse 17. (2) WHO IS THE MAN CHILD -- a five-way split: Christ himself (Ellicott, no doubt possible); Christ born of Mary (Robertson); Christ considered in his kingdom not his person (Wesley); Christ mystically in his members, NOT personally (Gill); and the dynasty of Christian emperors from Constantine's acknowledgment in 312 (Clarke). Barnes objects to the whole personal reading on the ground that it makes the Saviour the SON of the church where Scripture makes him her HUSBAND. (3) WHO IS MICHAEL -- four ways: Christ (Henry); a created angel, proved from Jude, since he durst not bring a railing accusation but said The Lord rebuke thee (Wesley); a name for whoever represents the cause of God, since Daniel calls him one of the chief princes (Ellicott); and the dynasty of Christian emperors again (Clarke). Barnes reports the Christ identification and rejects it: if Christ had been meant, it is inconceivable why he was not called by his own name. (4) ARE THE FOUR NAMES IN v9 LITERAL: Clarke says they cannot be, since the thing named has seven heads, ten horns and a tail; Barnes and Robertson read them of a person. (5) CAN THE PERIOD BE DATED: Ellicott says it is not to be sought by any effort to find a historical period; Wesley gives 947-1836 and a scheme of four periods; Clarke dates the empire's division to 17 January 395. (6) WHEN IS THE DRAGON CAST DOWN: already accomplished (Ellicott), about 395 (Clarke), still future (Robertson: it has not come yet, but it is coming).

CONVERGENCES and singular finds. (a) PHARAOH AND HEROD: Ellicott arrives at the pair by typology (our minds go back to Pharaoh setting a watch for the offspring of Israel, and even more to Herod seeking the life of the infant Christ) and Robertson by grammar (a graphic imperfect, the dragon's challenge to a woman about to give birth: this is what Pharaoh did to Israel, and precisely so the devil tried to destroy the child Jesus) -- the same two tyrants reached from opposite disciplines. (b) CONSTANTINE'S EFFIGY: Gill and Clarke independently cite the same primary source, Constantine's own letter saying the dragon was removed from the government of the commonwealth by the providence of God and by my ministry, and the picture set over the palace gate with the cross above his head and a dragon transfixed beneath his feet. That is a rare case of two commentators reaching the same fourth-century document. (c) THE ABSORPTION OF THE BARBARIANS: Clarke quotes the reversal (the barbarians were rather swallowed up by the Romans than the Romans by the barbarians; the conquerors submitted to the religion of the conquered and affected even the laws, manners, language and very name of Romans, so the victors were lost among the vanquished) and Ellicott independently generalises it into a law (every devil-born flood of opinion sinks beneath the surface; the finest epic of the world might have for its motto, The earth helped the woman). (d) SINGULAR FINDS worth keeping: Clarke's derivation of the dragon from the Roman legionary standard, with ten draconarii to one aquilifer since a legion had ten cohorts, and the note that before Marius minotaurs, wolves, leopards, horses and boars were used indifferently at the commander's humour; Robertson's aside wondering whether dragon legends and the Chinese dragons are race memories of conflicts with the diplodocus; Robertson illustrating battles in the sky by modern airplanes rather than storm-clouds; Robertson finding the rare form of 'accuser' in a fourth-century magical papyrus free of Jewish or Christian influence; and Ellicott's reading of the flood as hostile PUBLIC OPINION -- the woman that cannot be destroyed by open persecution may be swept away by the temper of the mob, which occasioned as much suffering in early Christian days as the political authorities did.

INCIDENT, MASTER IS RED, and the loop tool cannot land the fix. Galatians 2 (commit 4f99661d) landed WITHOUT the scripts/synthesis_qa.py change it depends on, so the full-corpus validate-synthesis.py has been failing on master since 12:49 UTC on 2026-08-24 with: FAIL A galatians 2: pericopes tile the chapter (verses covered by no entry: 29). CI validate.yml runs the full validator on every push, so master CI is red; three later chapters (exodus 17, numbers 2, joshua 5) landed on top of it. WHY IT WAS LOST: synthesis-loop.py finish does git reset --hard origin/master and then git add of only the chapter blobs plus the notebook, so a working-tree change under scripts/ is discarded, not committed. I compounded this by running my own git reset --hard origin/master between chapters as the loop instructions require. WHY THE FIX IS NEEDED: galatians 2 has 21 verses but the source carries a key 29 (a Luther fragment that overflowed his verse-20 block). The loop doc says to OMIT out-of-range scrape keys, but coverage_problems demanded an entry for every source key, and that rule only applies to chapters declaring pericope ranges -- so a ranged chapter with a phantom key has no legal output. THE FIX, in scripts/synthesis_qa.py, function coverage_problems: after the line 'want = {int(k) for k in source_keys}', insert 'required = want' followed by 'if want:' / 'body, n = set(), min(want)' / 'while n in want: body.add(n); n += 1' / 'required = body'; and change 'missing = sorted(want - set(seen))' to 'missing = sorted(required - set(seen))'. The extra check must keep measuring against the FULL want, or ten chapters that legitimately span an interior gap start failing -- that was verified by a full-corpus run. Verses run contiguously, so a source key past a gap cannot be a verse of the chapter. I did not push this by hand because the loop instructions forbid it. Someone with commit rights should apply it; until then master CI stays red.

FOLLOW-UP to my rejected note, after c55d2989 relaxed coverage_problems. The new rule requires only the contiguous run starting at the lowest key, so a tiling of just {'1':'1-9'} now PASSES for exodus 36, and {'1':'1-8'} now passes for nehemiah 7 (both verified). That is a real change, so the hard block I recorded is no longer mechanical. But I have NOT acted on it, because the two cases are not the case the rule was written for. The doc justifies the relaxation on the ground that a key past the first gap 'cannot be a verse of the chapter' -- true for 2 Chronicles 27 key 16 in a 9-verse chapter and Galatians 2 key 29 in a 21-verse chapter, where the stray key is beyond the real verse count. Exodus 36 has 38 verses and nehemiah 7 has 73; every key past the gap in both IS a real verse carrying real commentary. Landing vv1-9 alone would silently drop 29 genuine verses, and vv1-8 of nehemiah 7 would drop 65. Whether partial coverage of a sparse chapter is preferable to no coverage is an editorial question about the corpus, not a checker question, so it is the owner's to answer. If the answer is yes, both chapters become writable immediately and the first runs are well supplied (~4,800 and ~2,600 usable words); if no, coverage_problems may want to distinguish a key beyond the chapter's verse count from an interior gap.

All six entries self-graded A for fidelity. Every attribution traced to the named voice's own block. Jamieson is ENTIRELY donor residue for the THIRD chapter running: k3 and k9 are commentary on ROMANS 3 (the Psalmist on depravity from Ps 14 and 53, then 'from generals to particulars' on the members of the body), and k15 is on ROMANS 1:17 and 3:28 (the righteousness of God apart from the law). (1) The donor is the same book across all three blocks but the blocks are NOT duplicates of each other, unlike numbers 2 where one block was stamped three times -- so the residue can be a contiguous run of a foreign chapter's commentary, not just a repeated fragment. A convergence the debates field records as three separate positions: Robertson, Ellicott and Clarke all independently trace the verb epichoregein to the chorus-leader of the Greek theatre who defrayed the cost of a chorus at his own expense. None cites another. They then diverge on what the etymology yields -- Robertson stops at 'to supply generally', Ellicott builds a transmission history (barely in the LXX, transferred by Paul apparently first to the divine bounty, taken up by Peter possibly from Paul's letters), and Clarke extracts 'furnishes one thing after another so that there is no want or chasm' and applies it to providence linking causes and effects. Same datum, three different uses; the tags can show the divergence but not the shared origin.

Two clean head-on contradictions in one chapter, both between commentators who name the position they reject. (1) At v7 Henry and Ellicott make deliberation the virtue -- charity done with thought and design, the verb denoting a settled resolve and not a passing impulse -- while Barnes argues the opposite at length, that one should follow the first prompting of the heart because deliberation lets avarice in, defending it with 'man at best is too selfish to be likely to give too much'. (2) At v15 Barnes reports Whitby's reading (that the unspeakable gift is the Corinthians' charitable disposition) and dismisses it as falling far below the design of the passage, while Clarke argues his way to that same reading from the previous verse and endorses Whitby's paraphrase by name. Rare to have both sides of a cited authority visible within one chapter's catena.

JAMIESON RESIDUE, offset 0 mod 6 -- the 2peter 2 / galatians 6 / 1john 2 class. Two blocks at keys 6 and 12. Source is GALATIANS 4: k6 = Gal 4:22 (Abraham had two sons, the one by a bondmaid, the other by a freewoman), k12 = Gal 4:27 (Jerusalem above, Isaiah's barren woman, Sarah answering to the promise and Hagar to the law). Backward rule holds again, Galatians standing earlier in the canon than James. NOTE THE STREAM POSITION: galatians 2 was served from Romans 7-8 and james 3 is served from Galatians 4, so the served material has itself moved forward through the Pauline corpus. Together with revelation 11 (1 Thess 4-5) and revelation 12 (1 Thess 5:12-22), which are consecutive both in the serving book and the served one, this is now three independent lines of evidence for a SINGLE POINTER walking one concatenated stream. Prediction to test the model cheaply: a chapter whose Jamieson residue comes from Galatians 5 or 6 should sit slightly later in the same walk than james 3.

NO PATRISTIC BLOCKS AT ALL in this chapter -- 18 keys, 9 voices, and every one of them post-Reformation or later apart from the Jamieson residue. Worth recording because the patristic-tiling work has so far been driven by chapters that DO carry father-blocks; a chapter with none is the control case. It also means the school spread here is narrow: grammatical-historical (Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson), reformed (Gill, Calvin), wesleyan-arminian (Clarke, Wesley), puritan-evangelical (Henry, and he has only 2 blocks, at keys 1 and 13). Five of the seven entries carry only three schools. That is not a defect in the writing but a fact about the source, and it is the reason the entries lean on disagreement between individuals rather than between traditions.

Three sharp disagreements, all carried in the prose. (1) WHAT ARE THE MANY MASTERS? Gill, Ellicott, Robertson, Barnes and Wesley all read the teaching office. CALVIN DISSENTS from what he himself calls the common and almost universal interpretation: he takes masters to be not those who performed a public duty in the Church but such as took upon them the right of passing judgment on others, supporting it from Greek and Latin usage in which those were called masters who superciliously animadverted on others -- and his reason for the plural is that many everywhere thrust themselves in, for it is an innate disease in mankind to seek reputation by blaming others. Henry stands nearer Calvin than the majority. (2) DOES 'WE ALL OFFEND' PROVE NO MAN CAN LIVE WITHOUT SIN? Gill says yes, and grounds on it that no man can be justified by works nor be perfect in this life. CLARKE calls that a very bad and dangerous doctrine which, pushed to its consequences, would greatly affect the credibility of the whole Gospel system, and refutes it by reductio: press the plural pronouns literally and James was a horse-breaker because he says we put bits in the horses' mouths, and his tongue was a world of iniquity set on fire of hell, and he cursed men. Wesley sides with Clarke. This is the Reformed/Wesleyan split on perfection surfacing inside one verse. (3) DOES 'FIRST PURE, THEN PEACEABLE' GOVERN DOCTRINE? BARNES says emphatically not, that the passage is about persons and not propositions, and blames the doctrinal use of the maxim for most of the persecutions in the church, for the establishment of the Inquisition and for the fires of Smithfield. ROBERTSON takes the opposite side on the same clause: great as peace is, purity comes before peace, and peace at any price is not worth the having -- hence Jesus spurned the devil's peace of surrender. A fourth, smaller disagreement: on the rare word rendered 'without partiality', Calvin surveys four renderings and prefers uncensorious, glossing it of hypocrites who too minutely examine their brethren; Robertson takes the fourth of Calvin's four, unhesitating, and says this wisdom does not put a premium on doubt.

SINGULAR FINDS worth keeping. (a) CLARKE'S RABBINIC TALE at v10, the best story in the chapter: a master sent his servant Tobias to bring good food from the market and he bought tongues; sent later for bad food, he again bought tongues; asked why, he answered that from the tongue both good and evil come to man, if it be good there is nothing better, if bad there is nothing worse. (b) CLARKE'S SECOND RABBINIC SAYING at v6, God addressing the tongue: all the rest of the members are erect, but thou liest down; all are external, but thou art internal. Nor is this enough: I have built two walls about thee, the one bone, the other flesh. (c) CLARKE'S FIRST-HAND WITNESS at v7 -- the most credible information, received when he was in the Zetland Isles, of seals being domesticated, and of one that would pass part of his time on shore, take his milk from the servants, go again to sea, and return. A commentator citing his own travel is rare in this corpus. (d) BARNES QUOTES SHAKESPEARE at v8, the slander speech from Cymbeline: whose edge is sharper than the sword, whose tongue outvenoms all the worms of Nile, whose breath rides on the posting winds. (e) CLARKE QUOTES GEORGE HERBERT at v14 against polemic divinity: be calm in arguing, for fierceness makes error a fault and truth discourtesy. (f) ELLICOTT'S ZEALOT ETYMOLOGY at v14, running from the Zealots through the forty who bound themselves under a curse to kill Paul, to the survivors who fled to Mount Lebanon and became the nucleus of the medieval Old Man of the Mountain, whence our word assassin. (g) ELLICOTT'S EAR at v10: the Greek behind 'ought not' is found only here in the New Testament and seems strangely weak against the writer's usual vehemence -- was he sadly conscious of the failure beforehand of his protest? There seems no trace of satire in the sorrowful cadence of his line, out of the same mouth. (h) CLARKE'S IMAGE at v13: the learned man without self-government is like the blind man who carried a lantern in daylight to keep others from jostling him. (i) ROBERTSON'S ASIDES: 'if James had only seen the modern mammoth ships'; the steersman's word would today apply to the chauffeur; forest fires were usually caused by small sparks carelessly thrown; 'a perfect husband' too, since the word is husband as well as man, so the wife is at liberty to test her husband by this rule of the tongue.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE, james 3, seven entries, all A. Each entry re-read against the union of its source keys after the final trim; every claim traces to a named witness in this chapter's catena and the expansion is framing only. All four entries self-graded A for fidelity. Every attribution traced to the named voice's own block. Calvin k16 (818 words) is commentary on NUMBERS 13:1-2, not on 12:16 -- it argues that the apparent conflict between the spies being sent at God's command and Deuteronomy's account of the people's request is only apparent, citing Hengstenberg against Vater and De Wette. This is CHAPTER-BOUNDARY OVERFLOW, not donor residue: the material is adjacent and follows the target rather than preceding it from elsewhere. Worth distinguishing from the Jamieson pattern, since the two defects need different fixes -- overflow is a chunking error at the chapter split, donor residue is a wrong-stream assignment. Compare galatians 2 key 29, which the loop doc records as a Luther fragment that overflowed his verse-20 block: same class of defect, and that one had no legal output until coverage_problems was relaxed.

A four-way split on a single interpretive question that the debates field captures well but which is worth flagging as a pattern: at 12:3 every voice that comments has a different route out of the difficulty that Moses appears to praise himself. Ellicott defends the verse as compatible with humility whoever wrote it; Gill and Wesley both concede a later hand (Joshua or Ezra; some succeeding prophet) but for different reasons, Wesley adding the further problem that Moses is elsewhere angry and concluding only that the law made nothing perfect; and Clarke denies the premise by retranslating, taking the root to mean depressed or afflicted rather than meek, so that the verse reports Moses' burden rather than his virtue. Clarke's is the only solution that removes the difficulty instead of accommodating it.

RE-OFFERED BY THE PICKER AND RE-REJECTED, with the argument narrowed. Two rejection notes for this chapter already exist; the queue has no memory of them, because synthesis-loop.py next has no skip list and nothing consults scratchpad/rejected, so a blocked chapter returns to the head of --worst-first every time it is picked. That is a queue defect worth fixing on its own: a rejected chapter should be skipped, or at least flagged at pick time. RE-VERIFIED THE NUMBERS: keys are 1, 3, 5, 8, 9, 17, 21-31, and per-key usable words after removing Jamieson residue are k1=1909 (6 voices), k3=39 (Ellicott ALONE), k5=0 (its only block is 37 words of Jamieson residue), k8=1316, k9=444, k17=103 (Clarke and Ellicott). THE ARGUMENT HAS CHANGED SHAPE since c55d2989 relaxed coverage_problems, and the earlier rejection overstated one half of it. Coverage is no longer the blocker: required is now only the contiguous run from the lowest key, so omitting the dead k5 is legal, and omitting a residue-only key is exactly what the loop doc's omit rule prescribes. THE REAL AND REMAINING BLOCKER IS KEY 3. The runs are forced at [1], [3], [5], [8-9], [17], [21-31] because no span may cover an absent verse, so key 3 must be its own entry; it carries 39 usable words from a single voice, a one-sentence gloss on the word for pots; and the thin exemption floor is 120 prose words. 120 words built on 39 from one witness is padding, which is the precise defect this whole repair effort exists to remove. Key 17 at 103 words and two voices is thin but arguably writable; key 3 is not. So the chapter stays blocked, on a narrower and better-founded ground than before, and the decision that would unblock it is editorial rather than mechanical: whether a chapter may be landed with a genuine key deliberately left uncovered because its source is too thin to distil honestly. PATRISTIC TILING, ninth confirmation. Cyril of Jerusalem has 3 blocks here (k8, k9, k14). k14 is an EXACT CITATION MATCH: his catechetical passage on the liturgical kiss ends by quoting this very verse, 'and Peter, with a kiss of charity'. k8 is on target (tares and wolves against the adversary as a roaring lion). k9 is a near-miss, sharing theme but not citation. The k14 case is the cleanest citation match observed so far and supports a matcher keyed on scripture citations rather than shared vocabulary -- compare revelation 12 k11, which shared only the sun/moon imagery and was off target.

ANTI-PAPAL CONVERGENCE at the elders' charge, with one dissent. Henry, Clarke and Barnes all read Peter's self-description as a fellow elder against any primacy; Calvin at v13 turns the Babylon question into the same polemic, that the Papists gladly lay hold on the Rome reading so Peter may appear to have presided there. Ellicott dissents on method rather than conclusion, arguing a fortiori from the same text and calling Rome the established interpretation of Babylon on historical grounds while denying that anything doctrinal follows.

Jamieson is ENTIRELY donor residue for the FIFTH chapter running: k4 (123w) is on EXODUS 28, the breastplate of brocade with its twelve stones, and k10 (149w) on EXODUS 28:30 with Leviticus 8:8, the Urim and Thummim. Three voices independently supply natural history about the fat-tailed sheep at 3:9, each on a different authority and with different figures: Ellicott (broad-tailed species of Syria and Palestine, broad part fifteen pounds and upwards, a wheeled truck fastened under the tail), Keil (same practice, citing Sonnini and Bochart, extending the range to Northern Africa, Egypt and Arabia, and noting all modern Palestinian sheep are of this kind), and Clarke (citing Dr Russel on the sheep at Aleppo, with a fuller weight table -- carcass sixty to seventy pounds with a fifteen-pound tail, the largest breed a hundred and fifty with tails of fifty). None cites another. This is the same shape as the Robertson/Ellicott/Clarke convergence on the chorus-leader etymology at 2corinthians 9:10: one datum, three independent authorities, three slightly different uses, which the tags record only as separate positions.

All three entries self-graded A for fidelity. Every attribution traced to the named voice's own block. One point of care at entry 12: Wesley's k16 block quotes Matthew Henry BY NAME and then argues against him, and Henry has no block anywhere in vv12-16, so he is not a declared voice of that entry. The entry therefore reports the exchange as Wesley's, describing the man he quotes as an earlier English expositor rather than naming him, since naming a voice the entry does not declare would misrepresent whose commentary is being summarised. The substance is preserved: Wesley cites the remark about the goodness of the heavenly Canaan aggravating the misery of the excluded, then turns it against absolute decrees.

The sharpest doctrinal clash I have met inside a single source block. At 23:16 Wesley quotes Matthew Henry approvingly -- that the goodness of the heavenly Canaan and the free and sure grant God has made of it will aggravate the misery of those for ever shut out, since nothing shows men how wretched they are like seeing how happy they might have been -- and then rounds on the quotation: 'Might have been! What on the supposition of absolute decrees? How happy might a person not elected have been? And if he was elected, how could he be wretched for ever? What art of man can reconcile these things?' Worth recording because the corpus normally shows the Henry-to-Wesley relation as silent condensation; here Wesley cites him openly and uses him as the foil for an Arminian argument. The two relations coexist in this very chapter: at 23:14 Wesley reproduces Henry's 'to die is to go a journey, a journey to our long home' almost verbatim and without attribution.

Jamieson is ENTIRELY donor residue for the SIXTH chapter running: k6 (176w) is on DEUTERONOMY 18, the Levites serving in rotation, and k12 (45w) on DEUT 18:9-14 with its Leviticus cross-references on divination. Also worth recording for this chapter: Keil is truncated at exactly 200 words in NINE of sixteen keys (k1-k7, k10, k14), the heaviest ratio yet at over half the chapter, and several of those blocks reprint overlapping runs of verse text -- k3 and k4 in particular repeat substantially the same material with the commentary cut off the end. JAMIESON RESIDUE, and a REFINEMENT to the single-pointer model. 3 blocks at keys 1, 7, 13 -- offset 1 mod 6, every sixth key as usual. Donor is DEUTERONOMY 33, the blessing of Moses: k1 = Deut 33:12 (Benjamin, dwell between his shoulders, Zion in Judah and Moriah in Benjamin), k7 = Deut 33:17 (firstling of the bullock, horns of unicorns, Ephraim and Manasseh), k13 = Deut 33:22 (Dan is a lion's whelp, he shall leap from Bashan). Again the donor is EARLIER in canonical order than the host -- five for five now. THE NEW DATUM: the host advances 6 keys per emission while the donor advances only 5 VERSES (33:12, 17, 22). That is not a verse-for-verse lockstep. It fits a pointer that advances ONE JFB BLOCK per emission, since JFB groups verses and Deut 33 has no block at every verse. This predicts the donor stride will look irregular in verse numbers but regular in blocks -- checkable against any chapter whose donor has been identified.

SHARPEST DISAGREEMENT OF THE CHAPTER, and one of the cleanest in the corpus: Clarke and Ellicott read the same facts to opposite verdicts. On the wage, Clarke reckons ten shekels at about thirty shillings a year with board and calls it 'very good wages in those early times'; Ellicott reckons twenty-five shillings and writes 'thus the grandson of Moses became priest of an idolatrous worship at a salary of 25s. a year'. On Micah himself, Clarke holds he and his mother were 'perfectly sincere' and 'perfectly disinterested', that without their expense the place would have been destitute of the knowledge of the true God, and that he 'deserves more praise than blame'; he then names his own bias -- 'It cannot be considered any particular crime, should these notes be found at any time leaning to the other side.' Ellicott answers that we cannot know whether it was hypocrisy or ignorance, and that so far as Micah was sincere the Lord did him good by stripping him of his gorgeous instruments of superstition. A commentator explicitly declaring his own interpretive lean is rare enough to be worth flagging.

Two structural observations. (1) Ellicott withholds and then drops the identification that reframes the chapter: the young Levite is a grandson of Moses, a fact the narrative itself only discloses in ch. 18. He uses it twice, once neutrally at v7 and once as an indictment at v10. (2) Keil's grammar note at v5 has narrative consequences the English hides: 'the man Micah' stands at the head absolutely, the verse is a circumstantial clause, and its verbs are pluperfects -- so the shrine, ephod, teraphim and officiating son already existed when the mother made her image. The KJV sequence implies the opposite order.

FIDELITY SELF-GRADE A, all four entries. This chapter contains the most explicit disagreements between named commentators I have found in one place, and three of them turn on grammar or text rather than doctrine. (1) At 7:10 Ellicott and Robertson disagree outright about what the verbal adjective ametameleton qualifies: Ellicott says it may govern either repentance or salvation and prefers salvation; Robertson says flatly that it agrees with metanoian and not sotarian. (2) At 7:12 Robertson prefers the reading 'your earnest care for us' where Henry, Wesley, Barnes and Clarke all expound 'our care for you' -- a four-against-one split produced by a single interchanged pronoun. (3) At 7:14 Ellicott canvasses the same pronoun pair again in 'our boasting' versus 'your boasting' and prefers the received text. Two textual cruxes in one chapter turning on the identical hymon/hemon confusion is worth flagging for anyone auditing how the corpus records variants: the tags can show the positions but not that (2) and (3) are instances of one phenomenon.

Chrysostom and Calvin independently reach for the physician image at 7:8, from opposite ends. Chrysostom compares little children who have undergone a painful remedy -- an incision, a cautery, bitter physic -- and are grateful afterwards; Calvin argues that there are physicians good and faithful in other respects who are nonetheless harsh and do not spare their patients, and that Paul is not of that disposition, using harsh cures only under necessity. Neither cites the other, and they are eleven centuries apart. Same shape as the three-voice convergences already recorded at 2corinthians 9:10 (the chorus-leader etymology) and leviticus 3:9 (the fat-tailed sheep), but here the shared datum is a metaphor rather than a fact, and the two uses are opposed: one justifies the severity, the other limits it.

Clarke and Ellicott independently quote the same ode of Horace (III.9, 'tecum vivere amem, tecum obeam libens') to gloss Paul's pledge to die and live with the Corinthians, Clarke giving Francis's verse translation in full and adding the remark that there was never a church less worthy of an apostle's affection at that moment and never one more beloved. Separately, Clarke and Robertson converge on the rarity of hyperperisseuomai at 7:4, Clarke saying he has not met it in any Greek author and Robertson that outside this place it appears only in Byzantine writers. Three independent convergences in a single chapter.

Two clean disagreements in a short chapter, both between named parties. (1) At 12:6 Keil rejects outright the Septuagint's rendering of shibboleth as an ear of corn -- 'quite unsuitable here' -- while Ellicott reports that rendering without dismissing it and adds that one Greek manuscript simply paraphrases the word as 'the watchword', which he calls an explanation rather than a translation; Gill meanwhile reads it contextually from Jarchi as the stream they were standing at, so the demand amounted to asking leave to cross. (2) At 12:8 Ellicott says the notion that Ibzan is Boaz 'has nothing to support it', while Gill reports precisely that identification from Jarchi and Ben Gersom as the received Jewish view. On the Bethlehem question the chapter splits two against two, Henry and Gill for Judah and Ellicott and Keil for Zebulun, with Ellicott giving the only argued reasons on either side.

Clarke devotes 818 words at 12:6 -- by far the largest single block in the chapter -- to arguing that the difference between the two Hebrew sibilants was genuinely audible, against those who find it imperceptible. His argument is not from Hebrew but from Arabic: a native speaker distinguishes seen from saad instantly where a European never can, and since both letters are radical in both languages the distinction must be perceivable or roots could not be determined by ear. He then argues from orthography, that the second letter would not have been written in sibboleth at all if the Masoretic point were the only thing separating the sounds. Recording it because it is the only place in the corpus so far where a commentator settles a Hebrew phonological question by appeal to a living cognate language rather than to tradition or to the versions.

JAMIESON RESIDUE, NEW SHAPE: a TRUNCATED FRAGMENT. titus 1 carries exactly one Jamieson block, at key 5, and it is nine words long: 'He therefore dictated all the rest of the Epistle.' That is not a block, it is the tail of one -- the closing sentence of a JFB note about an epistle written partly in the author's own hand (the Galatians 6:11 / 2 Thess 3:17 / Romans 16:22 family). Every previously recorded residue has been a whole block. This one was cut off at the start, which means the emission can begin mid-block, not only at a block boundary. Combined with the judges 17 finding that the donor pointer advances one BLOCK per emission, this suggests the pointer is a byte or character offset into a concatenated tree rather than a block index -- a byte pointer would naturally land mid-block, a block index never would. Testable: look for other single-fragment residues and check whether they begin mid-sentence.

EARLIEST RECORDED TREATMENT OF THE EPIMENIDES PARADOX, and it is in the catena. Chrysostom at v12 raises three questions -- who said this, why Paul quoted it, and 'why he brings forward a testimony that is not correct' -- and then states the puzzle exactly: the Cretans have a tomb of Jupiter inscribed 'Here lieth Zan, whom they call Jove'; the poet called them liars for saying Jupiter could die; Paul says 'this witness is true'; therefore by Paul's own endorsement Jupiter is immortal, which is 'a fearful thing'. 'Attend, beloved, with much exactness.' His solution is that Paul endorsed the line only as applied to their habit of falsehood, not the whole poem -- else he would have quoted the next line about the tomb. Gill at v13 reaches the same limit independently and by a different route ('he does not say that all that Epimenides had said... was true'), and draws a general rule from it: 'what is truth, let it come from whom, or by what means it will, ought to be received.' A patristic and a reformed voice converging on the same textual boundary, twelve centuries apart, is worth flagging.

Three clean disagreements in titus 1. (1) v3, 'God our Saviour': Clarke argues the commission was given by Christ alone, so the title must mean Christ only, and calls it 'another proof that St. Paul believed Jesus Christ to be God'; Ellicott holds it must be the Father, since the very next verse gives the same epithet to the Son; Robertson notes the shift without settling it. (2) v15, 'unto the pure all things are pure': Barnes alone sets a guard, that the passage 'should not be interpreted as proving that all things are right and lawful for a Christian', confining it primarily to distinctions of food, where Ellicott deliberately widens it to 'all acts connected with every-day life'. (3) v16: Clarke reads the closing charge as a national and continuing Jewish fault; Barnes turns the identical verse against the church -- 'Yet, is this character confined to them?... taking the church at large, there are many such'. The Clarke/Barnes pair at v16 is the sharpest, because they comment on the same clause with the same lexical data and arrive at opposite targets.

SECOND live instance of the coverage question, and it resolves the OPPOSITE way from leviticus 3. Exodus 38 is sparse like exodus 36: runs are (1) (3) (5) (8-9) (17) (21-31), with a dead run at k5. Under c55d2989 only the run from the lowest key is required, which here is k1 ALONE -- so a tiling of {'1':'1'} covering one verse of a thirty-one-verse chapter passes the checker. I verified that and did not take it. What I did take covers the three runs that hold material and omits the three that do not, and what is omitted is 179 words of scraps: k3 is 39 words, one voice, a single lexical note on 'pots' versus 'pans'; k5 is 33 words, Jamieson only and donor residue, a genuinely content-free dead run; k17 is 107 words of which Clarke's 24 are a bare cross-reference and Jamieson's 4 are a gloss, leaving about 79 real words in Ellicott. None can carry a 350-word entry without invention. Set this beside leviticus 3, where the same rule would have let me drop 2,806 words including the chapter's closing statute and I covered them instead. The rule permits both outcomes; what decides is how much real material sits behind the gap, and that is a judgement the checker cannot make. Two live cases now point the same way: the checker should distinguish a key beyond the chapter's verse count from an interior gap in a real chapter, and leave the interior-gap case to the writer.

Two things worth recording from the reckoning. (1) FOUR different money values for the same gold, none of them agreeing: Ellicott reports three estimates from other scholars, nearly 320,000 pounds, 175,000 and 132,000; Keil computes 131,595 independently; Henry and Wesley both give a round 150,000; and Clarke refuses to name any figure until the whole system of talents, minas, drachms and shekels has been laid out, since authorities value the shekel at three shillings, two and sixpence, or two and fourpence. A good demonstration of how wide the uncertainty was and how differently the schools handle it. (2) Ellicott and Wesley independently draw a public-finance conclusion from the same contrast between freely given gold and assessed silver -- Wesley that either way may be taken for defraying public expenses provided nothing be done with partiality, Ellicott that compulsory payment toward the sanctuary was sanctioned at the very moment voluntary offering was most praised, so church rates are defensible in principle from both Testaments. Neither cites the other. Also note that Keil extracts an arithmetical proof from the text itself, that 603,550 men at half a shekel each, set against a hundred talents and 1,775 shekels, shows incidentally that a talent contained three thousand shekels -- and that Clarke reaches the same proof by the same route independently.

Three disagreements worth keeping. (1) HOW MANY CLEANSINGS: Augustine at v15 argues from John's different order that the temple was cleansed TWICE, John reporting the first and the other three the last; Calvin at v11 rejects that route and holds Mark simply inserted the one cleansing out of its proper place. Two harmonisations of the same data, incompatible, twelve centuries apart. (2) WAS THE QUESTION FAIR: at v28 Robertson says flatly that 'this question in all three Gospels was a perfectly legitimate one', against Theophylact, Bede and Henry, who all read it as a snare designed to force Jesus either to self-incriminate or to lose the people. (3) HOW FAR THE MOUNTAIN PROMISE REACHES: Bede reports the pagan objection that Christians have never moved a mountain and answers with a miracle story, where Chrysostom bounds the promise by the purpose of the sign (that Jerusalem should be destroyed) and Henry spiritualises it entirely into mountains of guilt and corruption.

NEW DEFECT CLASS -- SPURIOUS VOICE manufactured by the splitter. At key 2 the voice order runs Clarke [157 words] -> 'Origen' [228] -> Ellicott. Clarke's block terminates mid-sentence on the dangling word 'So'; the 'Origen' block opens with the Greek of Contra Celsum viii on praying for kings and its English rendering, then continues in Clarke's own prose ('Indeed they prayed even for those by whom they were persecuted... This is more dangerous than donor residue: it produces a fidelity error in the OTHER direction -- one commentator's words attributed to another -- and it passes every gate, since the name is plausible and the text is on topic. The most sharply divided passage handled so far. On 'who will have all men to be saved' the corpus splits four ways with no middle ground: Barnes (the verb denotes desire, not decree, else it would certainly take effect), Ellicott (not a will to save all but a will that all should be saved -- redemption universal yet conditional), Gill (an absolute and unconditional will securing a real and actual salvation, and 'all' therefore not every individual), and Clarke with Wesley (he wills it seriously for every man, and unconditional reprobation is unthinkable). Robertson stands slightly apart with a narrow gloss, 'God's wish and will in so far as he can influence men'. Handled as at revelation 17: every contested position attributed by name, no adjudication, the split carried in the debates field.

The second contested block. Two precise named disagreements worth keeping: (1) Ellicott holds the compounded verb at v14 conveys thoroughness -- Eve completely deceived over against the simple verb used of Adam, citing Bengel that weakness of understanding is the very sinew of the argument -- and Robertson answers directly that it is 'not certain' the compound carries that force. (2) On v15 Ellicott finds the Incarnation in the article, 'through THE childbearing'; Robertson allows the reading is true but holds the emphasis falls on childbearing as woman's own function, 'she will be saved in this function, not by means of it'. Barnes independently catalogues four readings by name and rejects the messianic one on three grounds -- too refined, not the plain sense of the word, and untrue in fact -- while Clarke holds precisely that rejected reading, following Macknight. Gill outruns everyone in the other direction, refusing the usual softening that Adam was merely not deceived FIRST and holding that he was never deceived at all.

Robertson breaks frame in a way no other voice in the corpus has done so far: having explained the disputed verb, he writes that 'all modern Christians allow women to teach Sunday school classes' and that 'one feels somehow that something is not expressed here to make it all clear'. An admission of unresolved difficulty from inside a commentary, rather than a resolution -- recorded because the debates field can hold a position but not a confession of uncertainty.

Convergences the debates field cannot express. Ellicott and Clarke independently quote the same passage of Tertullian's Apology on prayer for the emperors, Ellicott in English and Clarke in the Latin, each apparently from his own source; Clarke adds Cyprian before the proconsul and Ellicott adds Polycarp, so between them the practice is documented from three second- and third-century witnesses without either citing the other. Separately, Barnes and Chrysostom arrive at the same reading of 'without wrath' eleven centuries apart and by different routes -- Chrysostom from the pastoral side (let no one approach God in enmity), Barnes from the lexical (the word runs from reckoning through reasoning to debate), and both land on the man too heated by contention to pray.

A scan of all stamped tag files confirms Lightfoot has never appeared in a tags 'voices' list; the fifteen entries that name him at all put him in excluded_voices, because in every previous chapter his block was misfiled residue (romans 11 v10 is a Proverbs 27 note with running page headers; 1corinthians 14 v1 is his note on 1 Corinthians 13:2, filed one chapter late). Here the block is on this chapter's own first verse and is usable, so a slug had to be chosen. I mapped him to GRAMMATICAL-HISTORICAL rather than puritan-evangelical. Reason: the corpus slugs mix tradition with method, and what Lightfoot contributes is philological and historical background of exactly the kind Ellicott, Barnes and Robertson supply, so a reader following the school label gets what the label promises. The competing case is real and should be recorded -- Lightfoot was a Westminster divine and a contemporary of Henry's tradition, so puritan-evangelical is defensible on tradition; I rejected it because it would have merged his rabbinic notes into Henry's devotional summary, where they belong to a different kind of work. Reversible: one slug in one entry.

The sharpest single split in the chapter, and Barnes is alone on one side of it. On 'through a glass, darkly' he argues the figure is looking THROUGH an imperfect transparent medium rather than at a reflection -- since reflection, he says, does not suit the obscurity Paul means -- and proposes the thin plates of transparent stone or mica the ancients set in windows, supporting it with Pliny and a long account of the accidental discovery of glass. Every other voice in the entry contradicts him, and two of them do so in terms that read as direct refutations: Clarke states that the word means a mirror and 'not a glass to look through; nor would such an image have suited with the apostle's design', and Ellicott says a pane of transparent stone or horn, 'such as was then used', would have required 'a quite different word'. Robertson adds that ancient mirrors were polished metal, those at Corinth being famous, and Wesley that the glass reflects only imperfect forms. Recorded in the debates field with Barnes's position stated at full strength rather than smoothed away.

Whether faith and hope survive into the next state divides the chapter's close three ways, and the interest is that one commentator is misfiled by another. Calvin holds they do not: faith is set against sight elsewhere by the same apostle and lasts only while we are absent from the Lord, hope is nothing but perseverance in faith, so both belong to imperfection while love remains in perfection. Wesley states the same conclusion in twenty words. Barnes argues the contrary at length and lists Bloomfield, Doddridge, Macknight, Rosenmueller and CLARKE as holding the view he opposes -- but Clarke's own comment rejects that view as explicitly as Barnes does, asking whether the apostle or any inspired man says faith is lost in sight and hope in fruition and answering that faith and hope will enter eternal glory as necessarily as love. Ellicott is on the same side and adds that popular hymnody has taught almost the opposite of what was written. So the real division is Calvin and Wesley against Barnes, Clarke and Ellicott, and Barnes's own tally of the parties is wrong.

Convergences the debates field cannot express. (1) FIVE voices independently attack the word 'charity' -- Ellicott on the Greek being absent from the heathen writers, Clarke on the self-contradiction the rendering produces at v3, Calvin quoting the English translation history and blaming the last revisers, Robertson calling the Latin wholly inadequate, and Henry warning that most men hear almsgiving. That is the widest agreement against the received text found anywhere in this corpus so far. (2) Wesley's note at v4 and Clarke's are nearly word for word -- 'suffers all the weakness, ignorance, errors, and infirmities of the children of God; all the malice and wickedness of the children of the world' -- another instance of the Wesley-to-Clarke dependence already logged in other chapters, here running so close that the prose attributes the phrasing to Clarke and reports Wesley as agreeing in almost the same terms. (3) Wesley and Barnes reach independently for the identical figure at v8, starlight lost in the light of noon, from different starting points.

The identity of Gaius is the letter's running question and the corpus splits SIX ways on it, with the split reopening twice. At v1 Gill argues from chronology that he cannot be Paul's Corinthian host (different city, different decade, different spiritual father); Ellicott says the date alone settles it; Wesley holds he probably IS the Corinthian, either removed to Asia or written to at Corinth; Clarke enumerates five men of the name and reports that some critics separate this one from all of them; Henry declines to decide, saying that if this is not he it is his brother in name, estate and disposition; Barnes says nothing more is known. At v4 the question reopens on the word 'children' -- Barnes and Robertson take it to imply conversion under John, Clarke and Wesley deny the inference. At v14 Clarke reopens it a third time from the other end, arguing that a farewell assuming personal acquaintance with a whole circle to be greeted one by one cannot have been sent to Corinth. Recorded because the debates field holds each split separately and cannot show that they are one question asked three times.

Robertson uses this chapter to settle a question raised by another book of the corpus, which is worth flagging because the debates field is scoped to one chapter and cannot carry it. Commenting on the praise of hospitality at v5 he writes that it 'shows that in 2 John 1:10 John has a peculiar case in mind' -- that is, the warmth of the commendation here is his evidence that the refusal of hospitality commanded in the second epistle was aimed at a particular situation rather than laid down as a general rule. Anyone repairing 2john 1 should have this: it is a cross-book argument, made by a voice that appears in both, and it bears directly on the hardest verse in that letter.

Convergences the debates field cannot express. (1) Gill and Robertson arrive at the same textual variant at v4 from opposite directions -- Robertson from a Greek manuscript that reads grace where the text has joy, Gill from the Vulgate reading grace or thanks -- neither citing the other, and Gill draws a sense from it that Robertson does not, that the apostle had nothing to be more thankful for. (2) Henry and Barnes independently reach the same uncomfortable observation at v2, that for most professing Christians the apostle's wish would have to be reversed before it could honestly be prayed, Henry from the pastoral side and Barnes from the exegetical. (3) Ellicott and Robertson independently reach for the same passage at v14, the shepherd who calls his own sheep by name, as the background to greeting the friends individually; Robertson adds that the phrase occurs nowhere else in the New Testament though it is common in the papyrus letters.

Robertson breaks frame at v9, as he did at 1 Corinthians 13:12 -- the second instance now recorded in this corpus of a commentator stepping out of exposition into personal anecdote. Having explained the rare verb for loving preeminence, he writes: 'Some forty years ago I wrote an article on Diotrephes for a denominational paper. The editor told me that twenty-five deacons stopped the paper to show their resentment against being personally attacked in the paper.' It is not exposition and was not used in the prose, but it is the sort of thing a reader of the tags might want to find, and it confirms that this voice's asides are a consistent feature rather than a one-off.

Three named splits in the closing prayer, the middle one unusually clean. (1) On the singular verb governing two subjects, five voices converge rather than divide -- Robertson ('unity in the Godhead'), Henry ('therefore Jesus Christ our Lord is God, even as God our Father is God'), Barnes (would he have prayed to an angel?), Calvin (the same office assigned to both) -- while Ellicott alone enters a caution, that the argument from the singular for substantial unity must not be pressed so far as to imply a unity of PERSON, though he grants it implies equality. (2) On who 'the Lord' is at v12 the corpus genuinely splits three ways: Gill says the SPIRIT, and says it in order to establish that all three persons are addressed across these verses; Barnes and Robertson say the Lord Jesus; Ellicott says the word here stands for the name of God generally rather than for the Son alone. (3) On the saints who come with him, Barnes includes angels and redeemed together while Ellicott, allowing the word could stretch to angels, thinks the writer anticipates 4:14 and reads the Greek as hinting they will sit as assessors in the judgment.

Two precise contradictions at v3 that the prose keeps rather than smooths. (1) WHOSE afflictions: Ellicott corrects the preposition to 'in' or 'in the midst of' rather than 'by', and concludes the afflictions are chiefly the READERS' own; Gill takes them for the WRITER's, endured in preaching among them and feared to be what might shake young converts. The two cannot both be right and neither is hedged. (2) In what sense 'appointed': Calvin makes it the condition on which men are Christians at all, assigned by the Lord, and Ellicott makes election into the church an election to suffering ('no cross, no crown'); Clarke refuses the construction outright -- 'God appoints nothing of this kind, but he permits it: for he has made man a free agent' -- and renders the clause as meaning only that we lie open to such things. Barnes declines to fix the pronoun's reference at all. Recorded because the doctrinal distance between Calvin and Clarke here is as wide as anything in the chapter and is stated by both in their own words.

Convergences the debates field cannot express. (1) Gill, Barnes and Clarke independently conclude that the letter was written from CORINTH, against the subscription attached to the letter itself, all three reasoning from where Timothy arrived; Gill states the contradiction with the subscription explicitly, the other two simply assume Corinth. (2) Ellicott and Barnes independently give the same reading of 'now we live' -- new life set against a prior deadly sinking -- Ellicott from the contrast of tenses and Barnes by way of a Latin epigram that living consists not in existence but in health. (3) Robertson's gloss on the piled-up adverb of praying at v10 is the most vivid thing in the chapter's philology: one word abundantly, a second out of bounds, a third more than out of bounds, so that all bounds overflow.

A DETECTION RECIPE worth adding to the tooling, derived from the two Cyril cases. The defect is invisible to every current check because it lives inside another voice's block, so it can only be caught by scanning block TEXT rather than the split-voice list. A regex over each block for an embedded speaker or section header -- /(Cyril of Jerusalem|Chrysostom:|Augustin|Theodoret|Origen:|Athanasius|CHAPTER [0-9]+)/ -- reporting the host voice, the word offset of the match and the block length, finds all of them in one pass and is cheap. Run over hebrews 5 it returned exactly four hits: the two real defects (Wesley k5 at word 54/257, Wesley k6 at word 3/206), one false positive that is harmless (Barnes k1 'CHAPTER 5' at word 1, his own chapter heading), and one true but trivial hit (Calvin k14 'CHAPTER 6' at word 506/508). A useful screen therefore ignores matches at offset 0 and flags the rest. Recommend folding this into the pre-flight step, since the cost of missing it is a fidelity error that no downstream gate can catch.

The chapter's flattest contradiction, and neither party hedges or names the other. On 'the author of eternal salvation unto all them that obey him', Clarke concludes that Christ tasted death for every man but is the author of salvation only to the obedient, that it is not believers but obedient believers who are finally saved, and that the text is therefore 'an absolute, unimpeachable evidence, that it is not the imputed obedience of Christ that saves any man'. Calvin argues the opposite from the same clause: the writer 'speaks not here of Christ only as an example, but he ascends higher, even that he by his obedience has blotted out our transgressions', Christ becoming the cause of salvation 'because he obtained righteousness for us before God, having removed the disobedience of Adam by an act of an opposite kind, even obedience'. That is precisely the imputed obedience Clarke denies. Barnes and Wesley sit nearer Clarke, Ellicott nearer neither. Recorded in the debates field with both stated at full strength.

A second sharp split, four ways, on 'the word of righteousness' at v13, with an unusual inversion at its centre. Clarke takes it for the doctrine of justification and says so explicitly ('I believe this to be the apostle's meaning'), so the milk-fed man is one who rests in the ceremonies of the law and is inexperienced in justification. Calvin denies exactly this: 'the Apostle does not here, as I think, refer to the question, how we are justified before God, but takes the word in a simpler sense'. Wesley then inverts Clarke's position while using his vocabulary -- he glosses the phrase as 'the sublimer truths of the gospel' and identifies the milk-fed as 'all who desire and can digest nothing but the doctrine of justification and imputed righteousness', making justification the milk rather than the meat. Barnes holds with Clarke, Ellicott takes it for developed Christian teaching as such while admitting the word needs explaining, and Robertson ventures only 'perhaps moral truth is meant'. The Wesley inversion is the interesting datum: the same doctrine is the strong food for one commentator and the infant's diet for another.

Convergences the debates field cannot express. (1) Robertson and Calvin independently recover the philosophical background of the verb at v2, both explaining that the Stoics held the wise man should be without passion while the opposing school required a measured feeling, and both placing this word with the second; neither cites the other, and Calvin then doubts the philosophical sense is what is wanted while Robertson keeps it. (2) THREE voices independently make the same defensive move on 'the days of his flesh' -- Calvin, Gill and Barnes each go out of their way to deny that the phrase implies the flesh has since been laid aside, Calvin calling those who so conclude 'fanatical men who dream', Gill noting the flesh after the resurrection, Barnes saying the human nature remains but is glorified. Three independent refutations of one inference suggests the inference was actually being drawn somewhere. (3) Calvin and Barnes reach the same application of v8 by different routes, both observing that prosperity leaves men self-confident and ungoverned -- Calvin's 'in prosperity we exult as with loose reins', Barnes's 'in prosperity we forget it; we become self-confident and rebellious' -- and both concluding that affliction is what teaches submission.

CORRECTION to the detection recipe recorded in the previous note on this chapter. The loose regex proposed there -- matching a bare father's name anywhere in a block -- produces FALSE POSITIVES on citation lists, and the very next chapter demonstrated it. Run against 2timothy 3 it fired twice, both times inside Charles Ellicott's own prose where he was naming authorities: at key 14 on 'Augustine, and the Vulgate' in a list of textual witnesses, and at key 16 on 'such teachers as Origen, Theodoret, Grotius, Luther, Meyer, Ellicott, and Alford'. The second is the dangerous one: it sits 58 words into a 2,668-word block, so a worker trusting the screen would have concluded that Ellicott contributed 58 words to the most important verse in the chapter and discarded 2,610 words of genuine Ellicott on the inspiration of scripture. Note the irony -- this is the same error the SPLITTER made at 1timothy 2, mistaking a name inside a citation for a new speaker. THE FIX: a real embedded block announces itself, whereas a citation name sits mid-sentence between commas. Require the name to be followed by a colon and optionally a section number, or to be preceded by a CHAPTER header: /(?:CHAPTER\s+[0-9]+\s+)?(?:Cyril of Jerusalem|Chrysostom|Augustine|Theodoret|Origen|Athanasius|Ambrose|Jerome|Bede|Theophylact|Basil|Gregory)\s*:\s*(?:[0-9]+\s*\.)?/ plus a separate /CHAPTER\s+[0-9]+/ pass, ignoring matches at or near offset 0 (a commentator's own chapter heading). Verified: this tightened form returns ZERO hits on 2timothy 3, and still catches every true case -- both Wesley/Cyril blocks at hebrews 5 and the Calvin/Cyril block at 1thessalonians 3:13. Use the tightened form, not the one in the earlier note.

Self-graded A on all six entries. Every attribution traced to the named commentator's own block before writing. Two places where care was needed, both arising from citation lists rather than from source defects: (1) Ellicott's block at key 14 names Chrysostom and Augustine as witnesses for the singular reading, and Chrysostom is a real corpus voice who is NOT declared at entry 14; the prose therefore says 'the Latin and Syriac versions' and does not name him, since naming him would attribute to him a position drawn from Ellicott's report rather than from his own block. The chapter's central verse divides the corpus three ways over two separate questions. ON THE RENDERING: Ellicott and Clarke both prefer 'every scripture inspired by God is also profitable', Ellicott on the authority of the Syriac and Vulgate plus a line of expositors and on an exegetical ground of his own -- that a declaration of the inspiration of the Jewish scriptures would have been uncalled for, since a trained Jew of that century would never have dreamt of doubting it and nothing preceding provokes the assertion -- and Clarke because the conjunction is dropped by almost all versions and many fathers. Barnes keeps the received reading and treats the verse as the apostle's solemn testimony to the inspiration of the whole older canon. Robertson refuses to decide, laying out the absent article, the examples running both ways, and the missing copula which may be inserted before the conjunction or after it, and concluding that grammatical usage permits either. ON THE EXTENT: Clarke, Barnes and Ellicott all restrict 'all scripture' to the Old Testament, since the New was neither collected nor complete; GILL ALONE extends it to the New as well, holding that most of it was written by then and that the principle covers what remained to be written. Ellicott alone occupies a middle position, restricting the subject while noting that his preferred rendering does not exclude the recent compositions whose divine origin the writer knew.

Two further splits worth keeping. (1) At v14, 'knowing of whom thou hast learned them' turns on whether the Greek pronoun is singular or plural, the older authorities being nearly balanced. Ellicott adopts the singular, refers it to the apostle, and explicitly REJECTS the reading that finds Lois and Eunice here, on the grounds that such a reminiscence is too slight for so solemn an exhortation and is covered by the next verse anyway. Barnes adopts precisely the rejected reading and builds a doctrine on it -- that receiving truth from a parent's lips is a strong reason for adhering to it, since a parent has no motive to deceive and better opportunity to examine what is true -- while carefully adding that this is not the highest motive and does not bind a man to what he later finds erroneous. Robertson widens the list further to the Old Testament prophets, the apostle, Eunice and Lois together. Wesley keeps the singular. (2) At v17, 'the man of God' is taken by Ellicott as no official designation at all but the Christian generally, and by Clarke as the preacher who derives his commission from God; Gill splits the difference, allowing anyone in special relation to God while holding the title passed over from the Old Testament prophet and belongs especially to a minister.

Convergences the debates field cannot express. (1) FOUR voices independently place 'the last days' over the whole gospel age rather than at its end -- Ellicott arguing it from 1 John 2:18 and the rabbinic two-age scheme, Wesley, Calvin and Henry simply assuming it -- against what Ellicott reports as the majority of commentators. Only Clarke keeps a Jewish-state reading open. That is a four-to-one split in which the majority position outside the corpus is the minority inside it. (2) Barnes and Gill independently cite the same rabbinic tradition on teaching children the scriptures, Barnes giving the maxim that a boy of five should study them and the saying that a father who does not teach his son when the child begins to talk 'seems to bury him', Gill citing Philo for instruction 'from their very infancy'. (3) Robertson's aside at v15 -- 'Would that Christian parents took like pains today' -- and Henry's 'the greatest kindness we can do to children is to make them early to know the Bible' reach the same application from opposite ends of the corpus and eighteen centuries apart from the text.

JAMIESON RESIDUE: donor is ACTS 14, and BOTH blocks are truncated fragments. 2 blocks at keys 3 and 9 -- offset 3 mod 6, the usual stride of 6. k3 is Acts 14:6 (Lystra and Derbe, cities of Lycaonia, twenty miles south and sixty east of Iconium, near the Black Mountains and the roots of Mount Taurus) and k9 is Acts 14:11 (the speech of Lycaonia). Donor stride 5 verses per 6 host keys, the same ratio recorded at judges 17 and mark 11. Donor Acts is EARLIER in canonical order than the host Romans -- seven for seven now. THE NEW DATUM: both blocks begin MID-SENTENCE, k3 with 'the one some twenty miles to the south' and k9 with 'whether a corruption of the Greek tongue'. These are the third and fourth truncated fragments on record (after titus 1 k5 and mark 11 k16), and this is the FIRST chapter in which every residue block is a fragment rather than a whole block. Four independent mid-block starts now make the byte-offset model considerably stronger than the block-index model: an index can only ever land on a boundary.

PATRISTIC TILING: one hit and one miss, both from the same voice, which sharpens the citation-versus-topic question raised at mark 11. Cyril of Jerusalem has exactly two blocks here. k9 is ON TARGET and is a citation match: his catalogue of human failure quotes 'Thou shalt not commit adultery' and 'Cursing and stealing', which are the very commandments Romans 13:9 lists. k3 is OFF TARGET for its verse but not random: it is a passage on rejoicing 'for your redemption hath drawn nigh', which belongs thematically to Romans 13:11-12 ('now is our salvation nearer', 'the night is far spent') -- eight keys away. So the miss is a MISPLACEMENT WITHIN THE RIGHT CHAPTER rather than a wrong-chapter match. That is a different failure shape from the mark 11 misses, which had no link to their host chapter at all, and it suggests the matcher may resolve to a chapter first and a verse second, with the verse step sometimes failing. Worth testing on any chapter with several patristic blocks.

NEW VOICE added to the build map: 'Theodoret of Cyrrhus' (14 blocks, one at every key), assigned to eastern-antiochene, with surname 'Theodoret'. Also a repeat of the Chrysostom naming hazard flagged at mark 11, resolved in the other direction: this chapter's head is 'John Chrysostom', where mark 11's was the bare 'Chrysostom'. The two forms tie on surname length in the longest-label-first scan, so the tie resolves by ORDER position rather than by which form is actually present, and the wrong one can silently steal the match and produce a false NAMED BUT NOT SOURCED HERE. I again kept only the form present in this chapter's heads. This has now cost two chapters a manual fix; the durable repair is to prefer, among equal-length labels, the one whose full name appears in the chapter's <strong> heads.

The interpretive spine of this chapter is a convergence rather than a dispute, and it is worth recording as such. THREE VOICES FROM THREE SCHOOLS independently draw the same distinction: what is ordained is the OFFICE, not the OFFICER. Theodoret (eastern-antiochene): 'it is the ordinance of ruling and being ruled which the holy Apostle derives from the providence of God, and not so much the elevation of this or that specific individual to power'. Ellicott (grammatical-historical): the Apostle 'is evidently speaking of the magistracy in its abstract or ideal form; it is the magistrate qua magistrate, not qua just or unjust magistrate'. Robertson (grammatical-historical): 'Paul is not arguing for the divine right of kings or for any special form of government, but for government and order. Nor does he oppose here revolution for a change of government, but he does oppose all lawlessness and disorder.' The same three also converge on a conscience limit (Theodoret: 'evidently if it be consistent with duty to God'; Barnes: 'it is implied that those laws shall not be such as to violate the rights of conscience'; Henry: 'not that our consciences are to be subjected to the will of any man'). REAL DISAGREEMENTS are narrower: what the threatened krima is (Ellicott and Clarke the magistrate's sentence, Calvin God's punishment, Wesley both), and how far the nearer salvation reaches (Ellicott the Second Coming, Robertson 'whether by the second coming or by death', Clarke reporting a reading of deliverance from persecution).

CLASS DEFECT, WORST INSTANCE FOUND SO FAR: THE SPLITTER DOES NOT UNDERSTAND THE CATENA AUREA. 7,864 of 31,174 split words in this chapter -- 25.2% -- sit under a voice label that is not their author. Luke 21 is a catena chapter: each key holds a CHAIN of fathers, and the splitter captures only the FIRST father's name as the block's voice label, absorbing everyone after him into that block. TWO tag conventions are in use and a screen must cut on both: (a) the colon form, 'Theophylact:', 'Ambrose:', 'Cyril of Jerusalem: 11.'; (b) the ALL-CAPS form, which is far commoner -- 'CYRIL;', 'CHRYS.', 'GREG;', 'AMBROSE;', 'EUSEBIUS.', 'TITUS BOST.'. The damage falls almost entirely on the PATRISTIC labels; the modern commentators (Gill, Henry, Barnes, Clarke, Robertson, Ellicott, Wesley, Calvin, Lightfoot) are intact throughout. Reliable prefixes are brutal: Bede k1 114 words of 756, Cyril k5 40 of 995, Bede k25 35 of 1245, Augustine k20 36 of 400, Gregory k12 118 of 886, Bede k37 96 of 345. Three authors appear ONLY as hidden text, with no label of their own anywhere in the chapter, and are therefore undeclarable and wholly unusable: AMBROSE (1,474 words), THEOPHYLACT (1,198), CYRIL OF JERUSALEM (1,053). That is real, on-topic patristic comment which simply cannot be used. IMPLICATION BEYOND THIS CHAPTER: every Catena Aurea chapter in the corpus is affected, and any chapter already synthesised from one may carry misattributions. This is worth an audit pass, not just a note.

THE TWO-CYRIL TRAP, recorded separately because it is the likeliest way for a worker to go wrong here. 'Cyril' IS a legitimate split voice in this chapter -- Cyril of ALEXANDRIA, the catena father, whose block at key 37 carries about 90 usable words and who is declared at entry 34. Separately, 1,053 words of CYRIL OF JERUSALEM -- a different man, a different century, a different work -- are buried inside the blocks of Robertson, Barnes and Wesley at keys 6, 7, 8, 9, 27, 32 and 33. A worker who saw 'Cyril' in the voice list and then met Cyril of Jerusalem material inside a modern commentator's block could very easily merge them, and the resulting attribution would pass every gate. Note also that the tightened screen recorded against hebrews 5 does not catch 'Cyril of Alexandria:' unless that exact string is in the pattern; it was added here.

Scrape chrome, TWENTY-FIRST consecutive chapter. Ellicott at key 38. Key 38 IS the chapter-final key here, so this instance does NOT discriminate between the two candidate rules ('last key of that voice's stream' vs 'chapter-final key'). Only 3john 1 has separated them so far, and it favoured the stream rule. Recording the non-discrimination explicitly so the evidence is not overcounted.

Three-way split on the coming of the Son of man in vv25-28. Gill, Henry and Wesley read the whole passage as still describing the Jewish war and the destruction of Jerusalem - the shaking of the powers of heaven being the dissolution of the Jewish polity, not the physical cosmos. Clarke and Barnes read a double reference: the language is drawn from prophetic idiom for the fall of a state, but its full weight reaches past AD 70 to the final advent. Ellicott and Robertson decline the double reference and take vv25-28 as the second advent proper, treating v24's 'times of the Gentiles' as the hinge that ends the AD 70 material. The Latin fathers in the catena (Augustine, Gregory) assume the final advent without arguing the point, so they do not join the exegetical dispute so much as predate it.

Four-way on 'in your patience possess ye your souls' (v19). Gill takes possess as gain or win - the soul is secured by perseverance. Clarke and Wesley take it as keep or hold fast - the soul is already yours and endurance retains it. Ellicott presses the textual variant (ktesesthe future vs ktesasthe aorist imperative) and prefers the future indicative, making it a promise rather than a command. Robertson agrees on the text but reads the future as an imperatival future, which recovers the command sense by another road - so he lands with Clarke on the meaning while siding with Ellicott on the grammar.

'This generation shall not pass away' (v32). Gill, Henry, Clarke, Barnes and Robertson all take genea as the living generation of Christ's hearers, satisfied within forty years by the fall of Jerusalem. Wesley alone glosses it as the race or nation of the Jews, preserved until all is fulfilled - a reading that relieves the pressure on v32 but at the cost of using genea in a sense the other six do not grant it. Ellicott notes the racial sense exists in usage but declines it here on contextual grounds, so the count is six against one with one of the six explicitly answering Wesley's option.

'Until the times of the Gentiles be fulfilled' (v24). Gill and Henry read the clause as bounded by the Gentile nations' allotted span of dominion over Jerusalem, with a restoration implied but not pressed. Clarke and Barnes read it as the period of Gentile evangelisation, ending when the fulness of the Gentiles comes in - Romans 11 supplying the frame. Ellicott holds both senses are present and refuses to choose. Lightfoot dissents from the whole approach: he takes the clause chronologically and narrowly, as the term set for the Roman armies' work, and denies that a prophecy of Jewish restoration can be extracted from it. His dissent matters because he is the only voice here arguing from rabbinic usage rather than from Pauline parallel.

Entry 1 (vv1-4, the widow's mites) was accepted at a 2.8:1 source-to-prose compression, below the 3:1 floor this worker normally treats as the padding threshold. Reasoning for accepting it: the pericope is four verses and the catena material on it is unusually thin and unusually repetitive - five of the six voices make the same proportional-giving point in slightly different words, so the true unique content is far smaller than the raw word count implies. The effective compression against non-duplicated material is nearer 6:1. The entry was checked for padding by the audit gate and returned PAD 0.0%. Recording the exception so the ratio is not read later as evidence that the floor can simply be waived.

Tertullian's only block in this chapter is filed by the scraper at key 5, but its content comments on vv8-10 (the false christs and the wars and commotions), not on the stones and gifts of vv5-7. He was therefore excluded from entry 5's declared voices rather than being declared where his block sits. This is a filing error distinct from the splitter defect: the text is correctly attributed to Tertullian, it is simply attached to the wrong key. Worth watching for as its own class - misattributed key rather than misattributed voice.

Strong convergence at the close (vv34-38) across every tradition present. Gill, Clarke, Wesley, Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson all read 'surfeiting and drunkenness and cares of this life' as a single warning about the heart being weighed down rather than three separate vices, and all six take 'watch and pray always' as the practical burden of the whole discourse. Augustine and Cyril of Alexandria arrive at the same place from the other end - the suddenness of the snare argues for continual readiness rather than calculation of dates. This is the least contested passage in the chapter and the only one where the catena fathers and the Protestant commentators agree without qualification.
