ELLICOTT CHROME, sixth confirmation, and it corrupts the batch sizer. The block at key 54 measures 1,046 words of which about 63 are commentary; the remaining ~983 are scraped StudyLight page furniture -- CSS rules, nav menus, a list of 144 commentaries, copyright boilerplate. Key 54 is Ellicott's LAST block in the chapter, which is now 6-for-6 on the rule that the chrome attaches to his final block rather than to the chapter's final key (joshua 14 k15, deuteronomy 11 k31 of 32, numbers 36 k11 of 13, joshua 16 k10, exodus 37 k29, luke 11 k54 -- the last two happen to coincide with the chapter end, the first four do not). The operational consequence is the one I flagged at exodus 37 and it matters more here: synthesis-loop.py size reported 63,139 usable words for this chapter, of which ~983 are chrome and a further ~2,000 are Cyril of Jerusalem and Jamieson residue. Real usable content is nearer 60,000. That is a small proportional error here, but on a short chapter it is decisive -- at exodus 37 the same defect inflated a 2,900-word chapter to 4,222. Any batch budgeting that trusts the size number is systematically over-estimating, and the error is largest exactly where it does most harm, on the small chapters where a 1,000-word chrome block can be a quarter of the reported total. Suggest the sizer strip the chrome markers before counting; the markers are stable and easy to match.

THE CALVIN EDITORIAL-INTERPOLATION DEFECT, NOW MEASURED CORPUS-WIDE. I recorded this at hebrews 4 and joshua 20 as an observation; this chapter gave two instances severe enough to justify counting it, so I counted it. METHOD: split every cow file on its HTML voice headings, take the blocks whose host voice is 'John Calvin', and flag those whose body contains the string 'Calvin' -- which Calvin does not write of himself. RESULT: 1,189 files scanned; 11,063 John Calvin blocks totalling 5,803,190 words; 670 blocks flagged, in 288 distinct files, those blocks totalling 611,699 words, or 10.5% of the Calvin corpus by block words. Heaviest books: genesis 90 blocks, romans 82, 2corinthians 63, 1corinthians 57, hebrews 49, jeremiah 43, exodus 31, isaiah 26, ezekiel 22, psalms 21, joshua 19, matthew 18. IMPORTANT CAVEAT, stated because the number invites misreading: 611,699 words is the size of the AFFECTED BLOCKS, not of the editorial matter inside them. The editorial share varies and I have not measured it. In this chapter it was very high -- at key 1, a 1,028-word block whose Calvin content is about 240 words split around an ~830-word editorial excursus on the geography of the Jordan; at key 15, a 911-word block carrying perhaps 250 words of editorial matter. Elsewhere the note may be a single trailing sentence. So 670 blocks and 288 files are the firm numbers; the word figure is an upper bound on exposure, not a measurement of contamination.

The two instances in this chapter are worth describing because they show the defect at its most dangerous, and in two different shapes. AT KEY 1 the insertion is a middle interpolation: Calvin's own text runs about sixty words, then the editor breaks in -- 'This becomes necessary, because Calvin had altogether omitted it, partly... from having unfortunately attached little comparative importance to geographical details' -- and delivers roughly 830 words on the Jordan, including measurements Calvin could not possibly have written: the Sea of Galilee 84 feet below ocean level, the Dead Sea 1,337 feet, a direct course of 175 miles, a stream length of about 200 miles against a direct distance of 65. Calvin then resumes for a further 180 words. A writer treating the block as one voice would attribute nineteenth-century survey data to a sixteenth-century commentator. AT KEY 15 the insertion CORRECTS Calvin: the note observes that the concluding clause of verse 15 'does not literally bear the meaning which Calvin and our English translators have assigned to it', gives his Latin rendering, sets the Hebrew, the Septuagint and Luther against it, and warns that such slight differences have furnished the infidel with grounds for assailing the narrative. That material is genuinely valuable -- it is carried in this chapter as a debate side -- but it must be attributed to the note and not to Calvin, who is the party being corrected. Both were handled that way here.

DETECTION RECIPE FOR THE CALVIN DEFECT, cheap and precise, offered because the measurement above is only useful if a worker can act on it. Within a block whose host voice is John Calvin, search the body for the bare string 'Calvin'. Every hit is either the editor writing about him in the third person or, occasionally, a French or Latin gloss keyed to his rendering; in neither case is it Calvin's own words. Ignore nothing by offset -- unlike the embedded-speaker screen, there is no offset-0 false-positive class here, since Calvin never opens by naming himself. The screen has no false positives that I have found in three chapters of use (hebrews 4, joshua 20, joshua 3). What it does NOT find is editorial matter that never names him, of which there is certainly some -- the geographical excursus here would have been caught, but a note that simply began 'The Jordan, then, by far the most important river of Palestine...' would not. So treat the 670 blocks as a floor, not a ceiling. Recommend folding this into the pre-flight step alongside the embedded-speaker screen.

Henry's Concise commentary appended to his Exposition, THIRD BOOK. At key 14 the 1,151-word block ends with a compressed restatement beginning 'Jordan overflowed all its banks. This magnified the power of God, and his kindness to Israel', repeating in a few sentences what the Exposition has just said at length. Recorded first at exodus 11, confirmed at joshua 20, and now here -- three books, and in every case the tail is the Concise. Also present in this chapter: the 200-word truncation cap on Keil and Delitzsch at keys 1, 2, 6, 8, 10, 12, 13 and 15, EIGHT blocks in a seventeen-key chapter, which equals the highest single-chapter count I have seen (Keil at 1samuel 5). Several of those blocks are bare scripture text with the comment cut off, so Keil's usable contribution here is far smaller than eight blocks suggests; he was declared on the structural note at entry 1-6 and the two genuinely exegetical points at entries 7-13 and 14-17.

Jamieson stride artefact, ELEVENTH confirmation. One block, 52 words at key 5, on the sending of the spies at Moses' assent -- Numbers 13 material, unrelated to the crossing. As at exodus 11 and joshua 20 it is a single block below the 60-word usability threshold, so it yields no within-file gap and never appears in a voice survey. That is now three consecutive Old Testament chapters where the defect is present but invisible to any measurement keyed on usable blocks, which is the point I flagged at exodus 11: the true count of affected FILES must be higher than any survey-based figure.

Chapter shape and screen result. 17 keys, one contiguous run, 16,718 usable source words by the sizer and about 15,575 net. Zero splitter loss on every key. Tiled 1-6 | 7-13 | 14-17, three entries at roughly 5,100 to 6,100 source words each. A four-entry tiling was considered and rejected: the natural break points leave a middle entry near 2,400 words, and the three pericopes here (the preparations, Joshua's speech and the sign, the crossing itself) are self-contained. NO Albert Barnes and NO Jamieson usable blocks anywhere in the chapter, so grammatical-historical rests on Keil with a little Ellicott. The embedded-speaker screen returned ONE hit over 17 keys -- Calvin at key 15, 'CHAPTER 4' at word 909 of 911, the harmless chapter-boundary overflow now seen three times (hebrews 4 key 16, joshua 20 key 7, here). Fourth consecutive clean run.

All three entries fidelity self-graded A. ONE SIGNAL ON THE FIRST READ-BACK AND IT WAS MINE AGAIN: I wrote 'Luther's German' where the source says only 'Luther, whose version is...', and the entity check flagged German as ungroundable. Corrected to 'Luther's' and the re-run came back clean. THIS IS THE THIRD CONSECUTIVE CHAPTER in which the only defect found at the end was introduced by the writer rather than inherited from the scrape -- joshua 20 a stray non-Latin word, titus 3 the coinage 'Epirot', here the unwarranted nationality 'German'. All three are the same failure: supplying a plausible detail the source does not contain. Two of the three were caught by the entity check and one was not (the non-Latin word, which no validator examines). I am recording the pattern rather than the individual slips because three in a row is a trend and not an accident, and because it says something specific about where a tiring writer errs: not in the substance of the attributions, which have held up, but in small ornamental additions around them.

Three residue blocks, and all three are the small-fragment shape rather than whole displaced comments. (a) Jamieson at key 2, 31 words: 'Although I might have confidence even in the flesh... I having, but not using, confidence in the flesh' -- that is PHILIPPIANS 3:4, and it begins mid-sentence with a bare enumerator '4.'. (b) Jamieson at key 8, 276 words: 'be found at His coming again... the righteousness of faith... Paul was transported from legal bondage into Christian freedom at once' -- PHILIPPIANS 3:6-9. So both Jamieson blocks in this two-page epistle come from the SAME donor chapter, Philippians 3, and they advance within it (3:4 then 3:6-9) while the host advances 2 -> 8. Donor-earlier-than-host holds again, twenty for twenty, and the donor-advance-with-host-advance pattern holds in miniature. (c) Cyril of Jerusalem at key 3, 140 words, on 'the book of the generation of Jesus Christ, the Son of David' and the two fatherhoods -- a catechetical lecture on MATTHEW 1:1, collided onto this verse almost certainly by the phrase 'the Son of the Father' in 2 John 3. That is the phrase-collision mechanism of note 2305 operating on a three-word overlap. Worth noting that this is a 13-verse epistle with 9 voice heads and it still carries three foreign blocks; the contamination rate does not fall with chapter size.

VOICE_LABELS prefix bug, hit again and now costing real declarations. The validator rejected excluded_voices naming 'Cyril of Jerusalem' at 2john 1:1 with 'names a block absent from this entry's source', exactly as at 1timothy 3 and 2thessalonians 3. Cause unchanged: synthesis_qa.VOICE_LABELS carries the bare label 'Cyril' and its regex wants the label followed by a colon, so the head 'Cyril of Jerusalem:' is never split out and the declaration cannot be matched. The practical cost is now clear and it is not cosmetic. In this chapter the block IS residue and IS correctly kept out of the prose, but the tags file cannot say so -- a reader of the data has no way to learn that a Cyril of Jerusalem block sits under verse 3 and was deliberately excluded. Every chapter where he appears has the same silent gap, and by the earlier corpus scan that is 241 chapters for Cyril of Jerusalem alone, plus Augustine of Hippo at 174 and C.H. Spurgeon at 150. The fix is small: VOICE_LABELS needs the full head strings, or the matcher needs to accept a label that is a prefix of the head. I have not made it, because synthesis-loop.py finish resets hard to origin/master and commits only chapter blobs plus the notebook, so a scripts/ change cannot ride along with a chapter -- it has to be landed separately by someone who can push a non-chapter commit.

Fidelity self-grade A on all 5 entries; lint 5/5 A with zero UNSOURCED, NOISE, META or SLOT flags. Ratios: vv.1-3 9940w->649w (0.07x); 4-6 3828->650 (0.17x); 7-9 4229->648 (0.15x); 10-11 1907->573 (0.30x); 12-13 4357->588 (0.13x). 13 keys, 9 voice heads, 24,261 words reported by the sizer. ELLICOTT CHROME, seventh confirmation, and this one settles the placement rule cleanly: Ellicott appears at keys 1, 4 and 12 only, and the chrome is on key 12 -- his LAST block -- while the chapter's last key is 13. Every earlier instance either coincided with the chapter end or was ambiguous; here the two come apart and the rule holds unambiguously. The pattern across the three: the sizer's error is roughly a fixed ~1,000 words per chapter wherever Ellicott's last block was scraped this way, so it is negligible on long chapters and severe on short ones. No fabrications caught this time; the entity check was silent on all five entries.

PICKED AND DEFERRED, not abandoned -- no work started, chapter untouched. The picker offered 2peter 3 as the second chapter of a batch that had already landed 2john 1 (24,261 words). It sizes at 49,946 usable words over 18 keys, over the ~40,000 line, and the standing rule is that such a chapter is the WHOLE batch. Adding it to a batch already carrying 24k would put the batch near 74k, roughly double what the rule contemplates for a single-chapter batch, so I stopped instead and am recording the shape here so the next run can start immediately rather than re-profiling. Profile: 18 keys, per-key words 1:3124 2:1129 3:4589 4:2341 5:3331 6:1443 7:1705 8:2028 9:3651 10:3965 11:4834 12:1277 13:2678 14:1022 15:2660 16:4829 17:1029 18:4044 -- unusually EVEN for a chapter this size, with no single key dominating the way luke 11 key 1 (9,347w) did, so the natural pericope tiling should work without the special handling luke 11 needed. Ten voices: Barnes 14,265w across all 18 keys; Henry 9,145 across 6; Ellicott 7,671 across 18; Calvin 5,611 across 17; Clarke 5,227 across 16; Robertson 3,114; Wesley 1,895; Gill 1,856; Jamieson 695 across 3 keys (expect residue); Cyril of Jerusalem 200 at a single key (expect residue, and expect him to be undeclarable -- note 2328). Calvin editorial-interpolation defect, third shape: a citation footnote spliced mid-sentence inside a John Calvin block at k9 (word 60 of 2560), breaking his clause in half. Alongside it, dropped italicised words leave syntactic holes in the same block -- 'the honor of to pictures', 'means properly Hence', 'which the . renders'. Caught by the Calvin-in-Calvin screen, not by any validator.

The cow scrape has NO key 13 for this chapter (32 keys, 1-12 and 14-33). Verse 13 exists in the KJV. A pericope spanning 11-21 therefore fails coverage with 'entries cover verses absent from the source: [13]'. Retiled as 1-5 | 6-12 | 14-21 | 22-27 | 28-33; the 11-12 material (Ellicott on the name, Gill on keep-vs-remember, Wesley's questions) is only 299 usable words and cannot carry an entry of its own, so it was folded into the 6- entry.

Keil and Delitzsch truncated at exactly 200 words at k6 -- the same 200-word cap previously recorded for Keil (1samuel 5, joshua 3), Gill (titus 2, hebrews 4) and Cyril of Jerusalem (titus 2, hebrews 4, titus 3). Fifth voice, sixth book.

Wesley depending near-verbatim on Henry, third confirmed book (after exodus 11 k8 and joshua 20 k2). Dependency is per-block, not per-chapter: Wesley's own catechetical questions at k11-k21 are genuinely his, and he was declared on those. The voices-sourced gate cannot see this.

Sharpest doctrinal collision of the run: Clarke uses 'O that there were such an heart in them' to prove free will ('had man no free will he could neither be punished nor rewarded, being a mere machine'), while Calvin says the verse 'has been ignorantly abused by some, to establish man's free will'. Gill takes a third position through the grammar. Both principals know they are contradicting somebody, so the debate is explicit in the sources rather than constructed.

ALL SIX JAMIESON BLOCKS IN THIS CHAPTER COME FROM ONE DONOR REGION, and that region is not Acts at all: they are John 11-12 and the passion week. Key 4 (23w): 'from any legal uncleanness which would have disqualified them from keeping the feast' -- John 11:55. Key 10 (29w): 'See on Mt 26:6-13... on the sixth day before it; probably after sunset on Friday evening' -- the anointing at Bethany, John 12:1. Key 16 (34w): 'to such a pitch had these chief priests come of diabolical determination to shut out the light... See on Mt 21:1-9 and Lu 19:29-36' -- John 12:10 and the triumphal entry. Key 34 (146w): 'They would see Jesus, would they? ... the middle wall of partition... I, if I be lifted up from the earth, shall draw all men unto Me' -- John 12:21,32. Key 40 (13w): 'some hearing only a sound, others an articulate, but to them unintelligible voice' -- John 12:29. Key 46 (85w): 'the Christ endureth for ever. How can that consist with this uplifting?' -- John 12:34. So the donor advances 11:55 -> 12:1 -> 12:10 -> 12:21 -> 12:29 -> 12:34 while the host advances 4 -> 10 -> 16 -> 34 -> 40 -> 46. Six data points, strictly monotonic on BOTH sides, and the cleanest instance of the donor/host stride relation I have recorded. Donor-earlier-than-host now holds twenty-six for twenty-six. Note the host gaps are 6, 6, 18, 6, 6 -- a period of 6 with one triple skip, which matches the 6-key period measured at judges 17, mark 11, romans 13, deuteronomy 11, numbers 36, 1timothy 3 and 2thessalonians 3. This is the first time I have been able to show the period and the donor advance together from a single chapter with six points.

CYRIL OF JERUSALEM: one block stamped at THREE host keys in a single chapter, the strongest instance yet of the mechanism in note 2305. The block beginning '27. In the power of the same Holy Spirit Peter also, the chief of the Apostles and the bearer of the keys...' appears byte-identical at keys 20, 44 and 45. It is genuinely about Acts -- Aeneas at Lydda, Tabitha at Joppa, and Peter on the housetop in a trance -- so unlike the usual phrase-collision residue it is topically at home in this chapter; but it is still stamped three times, and at keys where it says nothing about the verse. At luke 11 I found the same block at two host keys (13 and 20); here it is three. I used it once, in the entry covering verses 17-22 where the housetop trance is in view, and declared it residue at 44 and 45. His other two blocks in the chapter are genuine and were used: key 36 quotes Acts 10:36 verbatim to establish the lordship of the Son, and key 48 argues from the twofold nature of man that purification must be twofold, water for the body and the Spirit for the soul -- which is exactly to the point at a verse about being commanded to be baptized. So this chapter contains, from one voice, both a genuine placement and a triple mis-stamp, which makes it a good single-file demonstration for anyone deciding whether to repair the tiler.

Fidelity self-grade A on all 10 entries; lint 10/10 A with zero UNSOURCED, NOISE, META or SLOT flags. Ratios: vv.1-4 13825w->646w (0.05x); 5-8 1876->635 (0.34x); 9-12 6640->649 (0.10x); 13-16 3411->645 (0.19x); 17-22 7103->640 (0.09x); 23-29 6935->649 (0.09x); 30-33 2358->650 (0.28x); 34-38 14270->648 (0.05x); 39-43 5293->649 (0.12x); 44-48 8377->643 (0.08x). 48 keys, 11 voice heads, 70,088 words reported by the sizer; ~983 of those are Ellicott chrome at key 48 and ~330 are Jamieson residue, so real usable content is near 68,800. ELLICOTT CHROME, eighth confirmation, and the constant is now firmly established: the chrome block measures ~983 words in every chapter where I have counted it (2john 1, luke 11, acts 10, exodus 37), which means it is a fixed page-furniture payload appended once per chapter rather than anything proportional to the commentary. ONE FABRICATION CAUGHT BEFORE LANDING, and it is a subtler kind than the last two: I wrote 'Judaea' where the source spells the name 'Judea' or 'Judaea' with the ae ligature, and synthesis-fidelity.py flagged it as an ungroundable entity. Nothing was misattributed and no claim changed -- the check is matching orthography, not identity -- but the fix is still the right one, since a reader searching the source for the form I used would not find it. Worth recording that the entity check catches three distinct classes now: a name imported from my own knowledge (Marcion at 1thessalonians 1), an expanded abbreviation the source never spells out (Athanasius at luke 11), and now a spelling variant. Only the first was a real fabrication; the other two are the check being stricter than the fidelity rule requires, and a future worker should not assume every ENTITIES flag means invention.

NEW DEFECT CLASS -- volume-final scripture-index dump inside a commentary block. At k10 the John Calvin block is 752 words, of which 485 (64%) are bare scripture-reference tokens: the entire back-of-book index of his Harmony, appended to the commentary. Corpus sweep (1,189 files, 57,091 blocks of 150+ words): 12 blocks flagged at >=100 ref-tokens and >=30% density, ALL of them John Calvin -- 2corinthians 13, ezekiel 12, acts 13, john 21, john 11, numbers 10, deuteronomy 34, acts 28, leviticus 12, 2thessalonians 3, genesis 50, isaiah 16. 6,162 of 11,232 words in those blocks are index tokens. These sit at Calvin's VOLUME boundaries, not only at book ends. Consequence: synthesis-loop.py size overstates those chapters by up to ~1,000 words, which now matters since batches are budgeted by source words.

Jamieson fixed-stride donor bug, TWELFTH independent confirmation, and the clearest evidence yet that the donor tracks position. Two JFB blocks in this chapter, both alien to their host verse and both drawn from the cities-of-refuge law: k3 (host text: 'and the south, and the plain of the valley of Jericho') carries the manslayer abiding in the city until the death of the high priest; k9 (host text: 'Joshua was full of the spirit of wisdom') carries the law of the blood-avenger as an improvement on Goelism. Six host keys apart, and the donor advances FORWARD through one continuous passage of source. Both excluded from the declared voices.

Chapter-final navigation chrome inside commentary blocks, three voices in one chapter. Gill at k12 ends with 'Next: Joshua Introduction Sacred Texts | Bible << Previous: John Gill's Exposition of the Entire Bible: Deuteronomy: ... Index Next: ...'; Ellicott at k10 ends with 'Deuteronomy Deu 33 Deuteronomy Deu Joshua Jos 1 Footnotes:'; Calvin at k10 ends with the index dump noted separately. All three are book-final artefacts of the scrape, counted as usable source words.

Wesley depending near-verbatim on Henry, FOURTH confirmed book (after exodus 11, joshua 20, deuteronomy 5), and here in three separate blocks: k1 ('When he knew the place of his death he chearfully mounted a steep hill'), k4 ('if his sight had not been miraculously assisted and enlarged'), k5 ('not only as a good man... but as a man eminently useful, who had served God's counsels in bringing Israel out of Egypt') and k12. But at k5 he DIVERGES from his source on the one point that matters: Henry reports the rabbinic kiss and declines it, while Wesley takes it -- 'The Jews say, God sucked his soul out of his body with a kiss. No doubt he died in the embraces of his love.' The dependency is verbal, not doctrinal, and he was declared here on that divergence.

Keil and Delitzsch truncated at exactly 200 words three times in one chapter (k2, k6, k8), and Gill at exactly 200 twice (k5, k10). The Keil blocks are pure verse-quotation overflow: each opens by reprinting the KJV text of the next several verses, so the 200-word cap consumes most of the block before any comment begins. Same cap previously recorded for Keil, Gill and Cyril of Jerusalem across six books.

Ellicott at k4 cites Rashi as 'Raehi' -- an OCR corruption. Avoided naming him in the prose ('One Jewish comment') rather than reproduce a corrupted spelling or silently correct one. Worth a corpus check if anyone wants it: the entity check would flag a corrected spelling as ungrounded, so the corruption is self-enforcing.

Picked by --worst-first and DECLINED on size, not on capacity: 52,369 usable source words over 21 keys. The poke's rule makes a chapter this size the whole batch, and deuteronomy 34 (12,710 words) had already been landed in this one, so starting it would have meant not finishing it. Returned to the queue untouched. This is the fourth chapter deferred on size in this run (acts 20 at 73,251; 1peter 2 at 70,426; jude 1 at 60,425), and the second time the head of the --worst-first queue has offered a 50k+ chapter to a worker that already had one landed.

Jamieson stride, third clean measurement and the one that fixes the ratio. Every Jamieson block in mark 14 is displaced from Mark 7-8: hosts 7, 13, 25, 31, 37, 49 carry donors Mk 7:28, 7:33, 8:5, 8:10, 8:15, 8:24. Monotonic on both sides. Host gaps are 6, 12, 6, 6, 12 (all multiples of 6); donor advances are +5, ~+10, +5, +5, +9. That is five donor verses consumed per six host keys, doubling cleanly where the host skips a period. acts 10 measured the same period 6 on the host side (gaps 6, 6, 18, 6, 6) against John 11-12. Two chapters, two different donor books, same host period: the displacement is a fixed-stride tiling artefact in the JFB source file, not a per-chapter accident. Donor-earlier-than-host now holds 32 for 32.

Cyril of Jerusalem in mark 14 is two separate defects in one voice. (1) Residue: his blocks at keys 9, 18, 30 and 46 are catechetical lecture material with no bearing on the verse they sit under. Key 46 (the arrest) carries an anti-Manichaean passage on Manes claiming to be the Paraclete. All four are excluded from the prose. (2) Duplication inside the chapter: one and the same block, on Christ coming to his passion willingly, is tiled at BOTH key 21 and key 41. I treated 21 as the genuine placement and 41 as displaced. This is the fourth chapter this window where a single block appears at more than one key in the same chapter (luke 11 keys 13 and 20; acts 10 keys 20, 44, 45; mark 14 keys 21 and 41), so intra-chapter duplication is not rare. As at 2john 1, none of this can be declared in excluded_voices: the VOICE_LABELS bug rejects Cyril of Jerusalem there, so the tags file is silent about an exclusion the prose actually makes.

Ellicott chrome, ninth confirmation, and the placement rule holds again. Ellicott's block at key 72 reports 1079 words of which roughly 983 are StudyLight page furniture (sub-menu, copyright statement, BibleSupport credit, contact boilerplate); the real comment is about 96 words on the participle in the last clause. Key 72 is both Ellicott's last block and the chapter's last key, so mark 14 does not discriminate between the two candidate rules the way 2john 1 did, but it is consistent with the rule 2john settled: the chrome rides Ellicott's LAST BLOCK, not the chapter's last verse. Confirmed now at joshua 14, deuteronomy 11, numbers 36, joshua 16, exodus 37, luke 11, 2john 1, acts 10, mark 14. The payload is a fixed constant, so the sizer overstates a chapter by roughly 983 words regardless of length: 2.2 percent here on 44,986 reported words, against 45 percent at exodus 37.

Fidelity self-grade for mark 14, all twelve entries A. Compression ratios prose-to-source: 1-2 0.19x, 3-9 0.15x, 10-11 0.60x, 12-16 0.10x, 17-21 0.35x, 22-25 0.18x, 26-31 0.27x, 32-42 0.09x, 43-52 0.11x, 53-59 0.18x, 60-65 0.27x, 66-72 0.15x. The 10-11 entry at 0.60x is the highest and the only one where the prose approaches the source in bulk, because the betrayal bargain draws only 874 words of catena across two keys; nothing there is invented, the span is simply short. The 32-42 entry at 0.09x is the lowest, 6,947 source words to 648, and it is the entry where selection did the most work: Gethsemane carries nine voices with substantial blocks and the choice of what to omit mattered more than the choice of what to say. Every span was tiled on the catena's own head boundaries rather than on a fixed verse count, which is why the entries range from two verses to eleven. Two entity flags were raised by the checker and both were spelling variants rather than imports: Melchizedek where the source writes Melchizedec, and Galileans where Bede writes Galilaeans. Both corrected to the source's forms. That makes the running tally of ENTITIES classes three, as recorded at acts 10: imported name (real fabrication), expanded abbreviation, spelling variant, of which only the first is invention.

Picked by --worst-first and DECLINED on size: 66,271 usable source words over 38 keys, and it is a catena chapter (Chrysostom, Jerome, Augustine, Gloss, Rabanus, Remigius, Hilary, Origen alongside the moderns). The natural pericopes are 1-8 (12,493), 9-13 (11,131), 14-17 (9,847), 18-26 (14,602), 27-31 (6,336), 32-34 (2,407), 35-38 (7,926). Seven entries would run 14.6:1 average compression, above the ~13:1 point at which most material cannot be represented, so honest tiling needs ~13 entries -- roughly twice the largest chapter landed in this run (hebrews 4, 42,600 words, 8 entries). Deferred rather than started half-finished.

STRUCTURAL, and an owner decision rather than a worker one. Measured the whole remaining frontier: 793 chapters are not yet at the current standard, of which 109 (13%) exceed 40,000 usable source words, totalling 7,141,749 words. The median remaining chapter is 17,323 words, but the head of the tail runs john 1 at 150,785, matthew 26 at 144,865, matthew 5 at 133,177, matthew 27 at 123,014, john 8 at 120,600. At the 5-8:1 compression norm a 150k chapter needs 25-30 entries. Because --worst-first is longest-first, the picker offers exactly these chapters first, so both workers keep drawing from a tail that no single batch can complete: acts 20, 1peter 2, jude 1, 2peter 3, 1john 5 and now matthew 9 have all been declined on size. Deferral cannot clear 109 chapters. The loop needs either a chapter that may span pokes with committed intermediate state, or a --max-words filter on the picker so batches draw from the workable band, or an explicit multi-batch protocol for the tail. Flagging rather than choosing.

Jamieson fixed-stride donor bug, THIRTEENTH independent confirmation and the strongest positional evidence yet: all three JFB blocks in this chapter come from one continuous donor passage in Colossians, and the donor advances monotonically with the host key. k7 carries Col 2:20-22 (touch not, taste not, handle not); k13 carries Col 3:3-4 (ye have died once for all; your life is hid with Christ in God); k19 carries Col 3:7-8 (put away, evil-speaking, foul language). Host keys 7, 13, 19 -- a stride of six -- map to donor verses Col 2:22, 3:3, 3:7. All three excluded from the declared voices.

Pre-flight embedded-speaker screen: one hit, at k13, 'Augustin' at word 85 of a 312-word JFB block. False positive of the known class (host author citing a father mid-argument) -- it is JFB's own bracketed [Augustine] attribution, and it sits inside a donor block from Colossians rather than in Revelation material at all. Screen base rate remains good; this is the sixth consecutive chapter with no genuine embedded-speaker contamination.

Two of the 200-word truncation cap in this chapter, both Gill (k1, k4, k7, k10, k16, k19 -- six blocks at exactly 200). At k1 the truncated block contains no exposition whatever: it is entirely the ecclesiastical succession of Sardis, from Melito in the second century through the councils of Nice and Chalcedon to the eighth-century Nicene synod, cut off mid-sentence. The cap therefore removes the exposition and keeps the antiquarian list.

Long external documents quoted inside commentary blocks, two voices in one chapter. Clarke's k22 block (1,657 words) quotes Wesley's note on the arrangement of the seven letters and then reproduces an entire 1816 letter from a British embassy chaplain at Constantinople on the present state of the seven Asiatic churches. Barnes's k1 block (1,611 words) gives most of its length to travellers' descriptions of the ruins of Sardis, quoting three separate travel writers at length. Both inflate the voice's apparent contribution to a chapter without adding exposition; a writer working from word counts would over-weight them.

Henry's Concise commentary appended to his Exposition again -- SIXTH confirmed book (exodus 11, joshua 20, joshua 3, deuteronomy 5, deuteronomy 34, revelation 3). Here at k1 the last ~330 words of a 2,238-word block repeat the Exposition above them, and the same pattern holds at k7 and k14. Consistent enough now to be treated as a property of the Henry scrape rather than a per-book accident.

Chapter-shaped observation worth keeping: this chapter carries an unusual number of sharp four-way divisions, all explicit in the sources rather than constructed. v.5 -- whether names are blotted out of the book of life (Barnes: security, since none but the keeper has access; Ellicott via Vaughan: a process of erasure is ever going on; Wesley: not blotted out like that of the angel of Sardis, i.e. his was; Henry: divides the enrolment, nominal names erased, overcomers' never). v.10 -- the hour of temptation (Clarke and Wesley: Trajan; Barnes: undeterminable; Gill: still future, on the reformed churches). v.12 -- whether the pillar supports the temple (Ellicott yes; Henry no, heaven needs no props, it is a monument; Robertson both). v.15 -- Wesley draws free will from the wish 'I would thou wert cold or hot', exactly as Clarke did from Deuteronomy 5:29.

Jamieson stride, fourth measurement, and the first where donor and host share a book. Every Jamieson block in numbers 29 is displaced from Numbers 6-7: host 4 carries the completion of the Nazarite vow (Num 6:18-20), host 10 the priestly benediction (6:23-27), host 22 the princes freewill wagons given to the Levites (7:5-9), host 28 the dedication of the altar (7:10-11), host 34 Judah offering first with the platter, bowl and spoon (7:12-14), host 40 Issachar and Zebulun following in order (7:18ff). Six hosts on a perfect 6-periodic grid: 4, 10, 22, 28, 34, 40, with one double period skipped between 10 and 22. Donors strictly monotonic. This is the strongest evidence yet that the defect is a fixed-stride indexing fault in the JFB source file rather than a cross-book mixup, because here the donor text is from the SAME BOOK as the host: nothing was pulled in from elsewhere, the stream was simply re-keyed. Host period 6 now measured on mark 14, acts 10 and numbers 29. Five of the six hosts here are Jamieson-ONLY keys, so declaring the residue emptied them: keys 22 and 28 had no other voice and were omitted entirely.

Keil and Delitzsch is hard-truncated at exactly 200 words in this chapter, and the truncation lands mid-sentence every time. Key 2 stops at 'in addition to the sin-offering of'; key 8 at 'the first of which was to be celebrated with sabbatical'; key 13 stops mid-list of the third day's animals; key 36 mid-quotation of verse 40. Only key 40, whose block is 32 words, is complete. Because each Keil block opens with the bare KJV text of several verses before any comment, a 200-word cap consumes most or all of the verse text and leaves either a fragment of comment or none at all: key 13 is 200 words of pure verse text with no commentary whatsoever. Compounding it, the comment that survives usually addresses the LAST verse the block quotes, not the key it is filed under, so it falls outside the pericope span containing that key. Keil's remark filed at key 2 is about verse 7; the one at key 8 is about verse 12; the one at key 36 is about verse 39. All three were therefore unusable: naming them in the entry that contains the key would attribute the wrong verse, and naming them in the entry that contains the subject would attribute content the fidelity checker cannot find in that span's blob. Keil is consequently silent in three of five entries here and speaks only at key 40.

Ellicott chrome, tenth confirmation, plus a new chrome sighting in Gill and a limit in the residue mechanism. Ellicott's block at key 40 reports 1016 words of which roughly 985 are StudyLight furniture; the real comment is 31 words, that in the Hebrew Bible this verse begins chapter 30. Key 40 is again both Ellicott's last block and the chapter's last key, consistent with the placement rule 2john 1 settled. NEW: Gill's block at the same key ends with navigation chrome of its own, about 35 words of 'Next: Numbers Chapter 30 Sacred Texts Bible Previous: John Gill's Exposition...'. So Ellicott is not the only voice carrying scrape furniture, and a Gill block at a chapter's last key should be read with the same suspicion. The important consequence is structural: excluded_voices operates at BLOCK granularity, so it cannot subtract chrome that sits inside a block whose voice is otherwise genuine. Ellicott's chrome is always appended to a real Ellicott comment, so it is never excludable. Here that inflated the measured source for span 39-40 to roughly 1,276 words against 241 words of real content, which refuses the thin exemption (over 200) while the real content sits below the 350-word floor. That is the same no-legal-output trap the 2026-08-10 residue amendment was written to close, reached by a route the amendment does not cover. This span was writable at 357 words only because the eight surviving claims are genuinely distinct; a chapter with the same chrome and fewer claims would have no legal output at all.

Fidelity self-grade for numbers 29, all five entries A. Reported ratios 0.36x, 0.59x, 0.28x, 0.43x, 0.24x, but those are measured against the raw span source and understate the real compression, because the raw figure includes Jamieson residue, Keil verse text and the Ellicott chrome. Measured against the content I could actually use, the ratios are 0.43x for 1-4, 0.87x for 6-11, 0.31x for 12-13, 0.98x for 34-36 and 1.48x for 39-40. Entry 34-36 and entry 39-40 are therefore the tightest work in the chapter and the two the audit flags as floor-hugging, though it records no padding in either. I let 39-40 stand above 1x because the surviving material carries eight distinct claims, including a real disagreement over where the last verse belongs, Keil closing chapters 28-29 with it against Ellicott reporting that the Hebrew Bible opens chapter 30 with it. Nothing in either entry is invented; the framing is mine and the claims are the witnesses'. One process correction during the writing: I drafted Gill's note that the day's offering did not displace the new moon's into the 1-4 entry, but that note is filed at key 6 and belongs to the 6-11 span. Caught it before the build and moved it. The failure mode is worth naming because it is easy: two adjacent spans discussing the same sacrifices make cross-span attribution feel harmless when it is exactly the error the pericope rules exist to prevent.

Picked and deferred, not attempted. python3 scripts/synthesis-loop.py size 1peter 2 reports 25 source keys and 70,426 usable source words, which is over the ~40,000-word whole-batch threshold and by a wide margin the largest chapter this worker has measured, ahead of 1john 5 at 52,369 and mark 14 at 44,986. The batch had already landed numbers 29, so taking this one would have blown the source-word budget rather than filling it. Leaving it at the queue head for a fresh batch to take as its only unit, which is exactly the case the size rule was written for. Recording the measurement so the next worker does not have to rediscover it: at 25 keys and 70k words the per-key average is about 2,800 words, so the pericope tiling will matter more here than the writing does.

The 200-word truncation is not a Keil defect, it is a harvest defect. numbers 29 showed every Keil block in that chapter cut at exactly 200 words mid-sentence. 1corinthians 5 shows the same cut hitting SIX blocks across THREE different voices: Gill at keys 1, 5, 9 and 10, Lightfoot at key 2, and Cyril of Jerusalem at key 4. Every one ends mid-sentence, and the two blocks near 200 that end cleanly (Calvin at 205, Ellicott at 196 and 198) are natural lengths rather than cuts, which is what makes the pattern legible. So the cap follows the block, not the commentator and not the book: any block that would have run past 200 words is truncated wherever it appears. The practical cost here was moderate because the truncated blocks were Gill's, and Gill is verbose enough that 200 words usually carries his point; at numbers 29 the same cap destroyed Keil entirely, because his blocks open with several verses of bare KJV text and the cap consumed all of it. The rule for a writer is that a block reporting exactly 200 words should be read as incomplete and its final clause discounted.

A block can be PART residue, which excluded_voices cannot express. Two clean cases here first: Jamieson at key 4 is 94 words on Apollos and Alexandria, that is Acts 18:24, and Cyril of Jerusalem at keys 4 and 5 is catechetical lecture material on 2 Corinthians 4:4 and on the word Ecclesia. Both were declared and excluded, Cyril silently because the VOICE_LABELS bug still refuses him in excluded_voices. The new case is Tertullian at key 1. His 347-word block opens with roughly 230 words on 1 Corinthians 4:5 and 4:9, the hidden things of darkness and the spectacle to angels and men, and only then reaches this chapter: the man was an offender who had his father's wife, the sentence to be delivered unto Satan, the destruction of the flesh, and the putting away of the wicked person. So the block is displaced from the previous chapter for two thirds of its length and genuine for the last third. excluded_voices operates on whole blocks by voice name, so it can neither exclude this one nor mark what part of it is sound. Compounding it, the genuine third addresses verses 1, 5 and 13, which fall in three different pericopes, while the block sits at key 1: only the verse 1 material could be used without attributing content the fidelity checker cannot find in the span it would appear in. This is the same block-offset problem recorded at numbers 29 for Keil, now seen in a father rather than a modern and in the New Testament rather than the Old, so it is a property of the harvest and not of any one source.

Ellicott chrome, eleventh confirmation, and the placement rule holds a second time in a row. His block at key 13 reports 1067 words, of which about 103 are real comment (that the best manuscripts read the future, God will judge; that the word therefore is better omitted; that Paul adopts the form in which sentence was pronounced on great criminals, familiar to Jewish converts from Deuteronomy) and about 964 are StudyLight furniture. Key 13 is again both Ellicott's last block and the chapter's last key. Confirmed now at joshua 14, deuteronomy 11, numbers 36, joshua 16, exodus 37, luke 11, 2john 1, acts 10, mark 14, numbers 29 and 1corinthians 5. A practical warning for the writer: my dump helper filters by per-block word cap, and at a cap below the chrome length the real 103 words at the head of the block were invisible, so the block looked like pure chrome. I nearly wrote the entry with Ellicott silent at the last verse. Read the head of a chrome-bearing block directly from the JSON before concluding the voice says nothing.

Fidelity self-grade for 1corinthians 5, all five entries A. Ratios 0.09x, 0.13x, 0.11x, 0.08x and 0.13x against the raw span source, the most compressed chapter this worker has written; 31,201 source words over thirteen verses reduced to five pericope entries of about 650 words each. At this compression the risk is not invention but silent omission, so the tags carry the full account of each voice and the prose carries the disagreements. The chapter is unusually well supplied with real disputes, and I let those set the shape of every entry: whether the father was living (five distinct positions at verses 1-2), whether delivering to Satan is excommunication or an apostolic bodily punishment (Calvin explicitly reversing the older reading, Clarke and Gill denying the excommunication sense outright), whether the letter of verse 9 is lost (Clarke standing almost alone against Calvin, Robertson, Wesley, Gill, Ellicott, Barnes and Henry), whether the command to purge is aimed at the man or at the church's own temper (Ellicott flatly denying what Clarke asserts), and whether verse 12 disclaims a jurisdiction or asks after one (Lightfoot alone rejecting the received rendering because it contradicts the apostle's treatment of Elymas and of Hymeneus and Alexander). One thing I deliberately did not do: Calvin at verse 10 and Robertson at verse 11 both name Chrysostom, who is a declared voice of this chapter at keys 1 and 9, and I let those namings stand in the prose of the 9-11 entry because Chrysostom is sourced within that very span. Where a named third party was NOT a chapter voice, as with Ambrose, Erasmus, Beza, Augustine, Whitby and Selden, I named them as the reporting witness reports them, which the entity check accepted.

Jamieson fixed-stride donor bug, FOURTEENTH confirmation, and the second chapter running in which the stride is exactly six host keys. All three JFB blocks here come from one continuous passage of Ephesians 5, advancing monotonically with the host key: k1 carries Eph 5:16 (redeeming the time), k7 carries Eph 5:21 (submitting in the fear of Christ), k13 carries Eph 5:26 (cleansing with the washing of water by the word). Compare revelation 3, where the same stride of six mapped k7/k13/k19 to Col 2:22, 3:3, 3:7. In both chapters the donor pointer advances about five verses for every six host keys. All three excluded from the declared voices.

Calvin editorial-interpolation defect, TWICE in one chapter, and both times with the authority names dropped. At k6 an editor supplies a reconstructed translation of vv.5-7, canvasses rival views ('according to _ and others', 'as justly stated by _', '_ solves the difficulty by saying'), and proposes a conjectural emendation of the Greek relative -- none of it Calvin's. At k12 the same hand qualifies Calvin by name inside his own block: 'the secondary meaning of earnestly desiring a thing. It is so taken here by , , and ' -- three authorities dropped -- against 'as proposed by Calvin'. This is the correcting shape first recorded at joshua 3 k15, now with the dropped-italics defect on top of it. A writer summarising the block without the screen would attribute the editor's conjectures to Calvin.

BOOK-BOUNDARY OVERFLOW, a new shape. Calvin's k18 block runs past the end of 2 Peter and into the ARGUMENT of Jude: 'END OF THE SECOND EPISTLE OF PETER / THE ARGUMENT / Though there was a dispute among the ancients respecting this Epistle... Jude first shews...' -- roughly 230 words of the next book's preface filed inside 2 Peter 3:18. The trap is specific: the sentence about a dispute among the ancients refers to JUDE, not to 2 Peter, and a writer skimming the block would attribute it to this chapter and produce a plausible falsehood. Related to the chapter-final navigation chrome recorded at deuteronomy 34, but worse, because the overflow is readable commentary rather than obvious junk.

Cyril of Jerusalem filed at k4 (200 words, truncated mid-sentence at 'A time is the one year in...'). The block is Catechetical material on Antichrist and the great tribulation -- thematically adjacent to the last things but not a comment on 'Where is the promise of his coming?' at all. Fifth book in which Cyril's filing has proved to carry no information about the verse it is filed under (luke 9, titus 2, hebrews 4, titus 3, now 2peter 3). Excluded.

The authorship of the epistle is argued INSIDE the chapter, and the alignment is not what a modern reader expects. Ellicott offers four separate notes of genuineness: 'your apostles' as apostolic humility (v.2), three reminiscences of one discourse of Christ that only Peter and three others heard (v.10), 'our beloved brother Paul' as a freedom no second-century imitator could reach (v.15), and the abrupt greetingless ending (v.18). Robertson reports and rejects the 'the forger here allows the mask to slip' inference (v.2). Against them, CALVIN doubts Petrine authorship outright at v.15: 'when I examine all things more narrowly, it seems to me more probable that this Epistle was composed by another according to what Peter communicated, than that it was written by himself, for Peter himself would have never spoken thus.' Captured as a debate at v.14.

Sharpest methodological collision of the run, and it is about method rather than doctrine. At v.10 Calvin refuses to investigate the conflagration at all -- 'it was not his purpose to speak refinedly of fire and storm... Mischievous, then, are those interpreters who consume much labor on refined speculations' -- while Clarke gives the composition of water by weight and volume and an anvil experiment, and Wesley lists three physical provisions for the burning ending with a comet 'two thousand times hotter than a red-hot cannonball'. Both eighteenth-century writers do precisely what the sixteenth-century one calls mischievous, on the same verse.

Henry's Concise appended to his Exposition again -- SEVENTH confirmed book. Also a new variant here: at k5 the Henry block is ENTIRELY Concise (414 words covering vv.5-14 in summary), with no Exposition at all, while k1, k3, k9 and k11 carry Exposition with Concise appended. So the defect is not uniform within a chapter, and a key can yield summary-only Henry.

FABRICATION CAUGHT: Damascus. Writing the 12-13 entry I had Robertson supply the proof that injuring a brother injures Christ from the words spoken to Saul on the road to Damascus. Robertson's block says only that Jesus had said to Saul that he was persecuting him when he persecuted his disciples, citing Acts 9:5. The road, and the city, are mine. Nothing in the chapter's sources names Damascus, and synthesis-fidelity.py flagged it as an ungroundable entity. Removed from both prose and tags. This is the second true import I have made in this stretch of work, after Marcion at 1thessalonians 1, and the two have the same shape: a familiar scene supplied around a bare source reference, in each case a detail so well known that it did not feel like invention while I was writing it. That is precisely why the check is worth more than my confidence. The other flag in this chapter, Athenaeus, was only a spelling variant, since Henry writes Athenaeus with the ligature; the running tally of ENTITIES classes therefore stands at three, imported name, expanded abbreviation and spelling variant, and this chapter produced one of the first class and one of the third in the same run.

Residue and truncation in 1corinthians 8, and a full-block displacement that 1corinthians 5 only half showed. Tertullian at key 1 is 352 words wholly on 1 Corinthians 11:3-10, the head of every man and the woman's power on her head because of the angels, with nothing whatever on this chapter; declared and excluded. That is the clean case of what 1corinthians 5 showed in mixed form, where his block there was two thirds chapter 4 and one third genuine. So Tertullian blocks in this epistle are displaced by a whole chapter or more, sometimes wholly and sometimes partly, and the partial case is the dangerous one because the genuine tail is easy to miss. Cyril of Jerusalem appears at keys 5 and 6 as the SAME 200-word block, his tenth catechetical lecture on the Lordship of the Son. I took key 6 as the genuine placement, since the verse there reads one Lord Jesus Christ, and declared key 5 residue; that is the fifth chapter in which one block sits at two keys. Jamieson is residue at keys 6 and 12, seventeen and thirty-four words from Acts 20 and its neighbourhood, and the host keys are again six apart. The 200-word harvest truncation strikes six blocks here as it did in 1corinthians 5: Gill at 1 and 6, Lightfoot at 4 and 10, Cyril at 5 and 6, every one ending mid-sentence, while Calvin at 203 and Ellicott at 196 end cleanly and are natural lengths.

Ellicott chrome, twelfth confirmation, and the second consecutive chapter where my dump helper nearly hid the real comment. His block at key 13 reports 1219 words, of which about 305 are real and about 914 are StudyLight furniture. Key 13 is again both Ellicott's last block and the chapter's last key, consistent every time since 2john 1 settled the placement rule. Confirmed now at joshua 14, deuteronomy 11, numbers 36, joshua 16, exodus 37, luke 11, 2john 1, acts 10, mark 14, numbers 29, 1corinthians 5 and 1corinthians 8. As at 1corinthians 5, the per-block word cap in my dump tool truncates before the chrome begins and so displays nothing at all for the block, which reads as an absent voice rather than a buried one. I now grep the raw JSON for the chrome marker and slice the block at it before writing any entry that covers a chapter's last key. Worth stating as a standing rule for the loop rather than a note about one chapter: a block whose dump output is empty is not necessarily a silent voice, and a block whose reported length is far above its neighbours should be sliced at the marker before it is judged.

Fidelity self-grade for 1corinthians 8, all five entries A after the Damascus correction. Ratios 0.07x, 0.09x, 0.13x, 0.16x and 0.11x against the raw span source; 31,573 words over thirteen verses reduced to five pericope entries. As at 1corinthians 5, the compression is severe enough that the real risk is omission rather than invention, so the disagreements set the shape of every entry and the tags carry the full account of each voice. The chapter is unusually rich in explicit disagreement between named commentators, which is what made it writable at this ratio: Clarke reports Lightfoot's rendering of an idol is nothing and rejects it, Calvin rejects Erasmus's rendering of the same clause, Ellicott reports and rejects Stanley's sense for not yet, Ellicott prefers a variant reading familiarity against the received conscience while Henry, Barnes, Gill, Clarke and Wesley all expound the received word, Ellicott says the last verse of the 9-11 span is NOT a question while Calvin says expressly that he reads it interrogatively, Clarke says a man for whom Christ died may perish and admits no quibble while Barnes answers that a tendency may be arrested, and Calvin alone calls the closing vow a hyperbole. Two convergences also worth recording as convergences rather than repetition: Clarke names Lightfoot as his authority for the rabbinic material on entering idol temples, and Lightfoot in the same span supplies that material himself, so the two are one witness and a source rather than two witnesses; and Ellicott and Robertson independently adopt the same variant at verse 7.

NEW DEFECT, measured corpus-wide: 'Cyril of Alexandria' blocks in LUKE are not commentary at all but the LECTION TEXT of the sermon -- the Scripture passage reprinted as a heading -- and it is filed one pericope LATE. In this chapter all six of his blocks are pure text: k4 carries the text of Luke 7:36-50, k19 carries 8:4-8, k22 carries 8:19-21, k26 carries 8:22-25, k40 carries 8:26-36, k49 carries 8:40-48. Each is the lection of the pericope that ends shortly BEFORE its host key, so the heading has been attached to the following section. Corpus sweep: 84 of the 108 Cyril of Alexandria blocks in the whole corpus open with a lection reference of the form '8:4-8.', totalling 28,819 words, and ALL 84 are in Luke, spread over 20 chapters (worst: luke 11 with 4,110 words, luke 9 with 3,856, luke 7 with 2,661). Two consequences. (1) A worker weighting voices by word count reads Cyril as a major Lukan voice when he contributes no exposition whatever in those blocks. (2) synthesis-loop.py size counts all 28,819 words as usable source, overstating every affected Luke chapter -- luke 8 by 1,874 words. Worse, the misfiled text is READABLE and apposite-looking: at k4 the block is the story of the woman who was a sinner, which is exactly the passage that fuels the Magdalene confusion discussed at vv.1-3, so a skimming writer would produce a plausible falsehood. All six excluded here.

Calvin editorial-interpolation defect, most extreme instance yet: at k39 the block contains the EDITOR'S ENCOMIUM OF CALVIN, in the third person, inside Calvin's own block. 'Never did those men encounter a more zealous or more formidable opponent than Calvin... He lays down as a general principle, which he endeavors to support by the word of God, that the cures of bodily diseases... It is to this meaning that Calvin, under the word anagoge, borrowing the language, but disavowing the principles, of an ancient school, now proceeds to draw the attention of his reader.' Roughly 180 words of a translator's preface presented as commentary. A writer summarising the block would have Calvin praising himself. The Calvin-in-Calvin screen caught it at two offsets (words 185 and 319 of 515).

GAP IN THE EMBEDDED-SPEAKER TRIM, small but exact and cheap to fix. The catena speaker-tag pattern used by the pre-flight screen and by my dump tool accepts an ALL-CAPS father name followed by a semicolon or a period (CHRYS. / AUG;) but not one followed by a COMMA. At luke 8 k4 the Bede block runs 'the Son of God, Who going forth from His Father's bosom... CHRYS, Now His going, Who is every where, was not local' -- so roughly three quarters of that block is Chrysostom filed under Bede and survives the trim. Corpus sweep over all 141,039 blocks in 1,189 files: exactly 4 blocks contain a CAPS father-name followed by a comma ahead of any current cut point, carrying about 2,764 words of embedded-speaker material that currently survives. Hosts: Bede three times (all in luke), John Calvin once (genesis). Adding a comma to the character class -- [;.] becomes [;.,] -- closes it. Patched in my own tooling; flagging so the same change can be made wherever the shared screen lives.

CORRECTION to the earlier Cyril of Alexandria note in this chapter: I said all six blocks were pure Scripture text, and that is wrong for three of them. Examined end to end, the six blocks are the OPENINGS of Cyril's sermons -- the lection heading followed by however much of the sermon fits before the truncation. k4, k40 and k49 are indeed pure text (their tails are still Scripture); k19, k22 and k26 carry the lection text and then real commentary (k19 ends on Jerusalem killing the prophets, k22 on obedience being better than sacrifice, k26 opening the praise of Christ before the storm). The filing displacement stands and is the operative point: each block belongs to the pericope BEFORE its host key, so Cyril's genuine comment on 8:4-8 sits at k19, his comment on 8:19-21 sits at k22, and his comment on 8:22-25 sits at k26. The usable rule is therefore not 'exclude Cyril' but 'read Cyril one pericope back'. The corpus figure of 84 lection-opening blocks across 20 Luke chapters, 28,819 words, is unaffected, but those words are a mix of duplicated text and displaced commentary rather than text alone.

Jamieson donor bug, FIFTEENTH confirmation, and a new donor relation: the block at k51 is about Elisabeth blessing Mary (Luke 1:42-44), filed at Luke 8:51. Until now every measured donor came from a DIFFERENT book -- Colossians into revelation 3, Ephesians into 2peter 3, the cities-of-refuge law into deuteronomy 34. Here the donor is an earlier chapter of the SAME book. Excluded (it is also below the usable threshold at 99 words).

Cyril of Jerusalem, SIXTH book: the misfiling remains uninformative but is not uniformly so, which is the point worth keeping. Six blocks here, all capped at exactly 200 words except k1 (183). k1 is Catechetical material on the fruits of repentance and John's preaching, k11 on the subsistence of the Holy Ghost, k28 and k40 on Antioch and Barnabas -- none of them about their host verses. But k10 is genuinely apposite: the Archelaus-and-Manes dispute over what sort of God causes blindness, which bears directly on 'that seeing they might not see', and it earned a place in the prose and a debate side. The standing rule holds -- every Cyril block must be read before it is trusted or discarded, and roughly one in six repays the reading.

Chapter-shaped observation. This chapter carries an unusual number of disputes in which the commentators name each other or name a position they are refusing, so the debates are documented rather than constructed. v.2: Clarke's sustained protest that making Mary Magdalene a prostitute is 'a vile slander', with Barnes agreeing and Lightfoot supplying the Talmudic material the tradition feeds on. v.3: Lightfoot derives Chuza from Haman's genealogy as an Idumean name; Gill contests it on the manuscripts, his edition reading Ciza. v.18: Clarke argues from classical usage that 'that which he seemeth to have' is self-contradictory and means simply what he hath, against Ellicott and Robertson who keep the appearance and make self-deception the point. v.20: Calvin names Ambrose and Chrysostom and rejects their charge that Mary acted from ambition. v.33: Clarke calls the rationalising reading -- that the maniac himself drove the swine over the cliff -- 'solemn trifling', warning that on such a plan there is nothing certain in the word of God.

A FOURTH class of ENTITIES flag: silently correcting a corrupt source reading. Barnes at key 8 lists the interpreters who take the fault to lie with the covenant rather than the people, and the source prints the first name as Grottos. That is plainly an OCR corruption of Grotius, and I wrote Grotius without thinking about it. synthesis-fidelity.py flagged it, correctly, because the chapter's sources nowhere contain that string. The three classes recorded so far were imported name (real fabrication, as with Marcion at 1thessalonians 1 and Damascus at 1corinthians 8), expanded abbreviation (Athanasius for Athan at luke 11), and spelling variant (Judaea for Judea at acts 10, Melchizedek for Melchizedec at mark 14). This is none of those. The name I wrote is almost certainly the right one, and writing what the source actually says would put an obvious scanno into published prose. I resolved it by dropping the name and keeping the three that are grounded, which loses nothing of substance since the point is that Barnes names a party of interpreters, not which four they are. Worth stating as a rule: where the source has visibly corrupted a proper name, neither reproduce the corruption nor silently repair it, but write around it.

Residue in hebrews 8, including a placement made by a shared quotation rather than a shared subject. Jamieson is residue at keys 2 and 8, sixty-one and thirty-one words from 2 Corinthians 9 on sowing and reaping and on single-minded liberality; the two host keys are six apart, the same period measured at mark 14, acts 10 and numbers 29. Cyril of Jerusalem appears three times and only one is genuine. At key 1 his lecture on the Son's sitting at the right hand of the Father belongs exactly where the verse puts it, and it is the SAME block that stands at mark 14 key 62, which is also a session text: that is cross-chapter reuse of a relevant patristic block, not a defect, and should be distinguished from the intra-chapter duplication seen at mark 14, luke 11, acts 10, 1corinthians 5 and 1corinthians 8. At key 9 his passage on Paradise, the Fall and the Tree has nothing to do with the covenant made when God took the fathers by the hand. Key 10 is the interesting one. The block is an exhortation to chastity, and nothing in it concerns a law written on the heart; but it ENDS by quoting the promise, I will dwell in them and walk in them and I will be their God, which is also the substance of the host verse. So the block was almost certainly placed here because a phrase at its tail matches a phrase in the verse, not because its subject matches. That is a mechanism for how residue arrives, and it means a block whose last sentence fits the verse should be read from the beginning before it is trusted. Both keys 9 and 10 declared residue; the declaration is silent as usual, since VOICE_LABELS still refuses Cyril in excluded_voices.

Ellicott chrome, thirteenth confirmation, and the 200-word truncation strikes four more blocks. The Ellicott block at key 13 reports 1061 words of which about 147 are real comment and about 914 are StudyLight furniture; key 13 is again both Ellicott's last block and the chapter's last key, consistent at every one of joshua 14, deuteronomy 11, numbers 36, joshua 16, exodus 37, luke 11, 2john 1, acts 10, mark 14, numbers 29, 1corinthians 5, 1corinthians 8 and hebrews 8. The chrome payload has now been measured between about 914 and about 985 words in every instance, which is consistent with a single fixed page template. The 200-word cap hits Cyril at keys 1 and 10 and Gill at keys 4 and 7, all four ending mid-sentence, while Calvin at 202 and 203 end cleanly and are natural lengths; that is the same signature as 1corinthians 5 and 1corinthians 8, and the third consecutive chapter in which the cap lands on more than one voice. Cyril's truncation at key 1 costs something real here, since the block breaks off in the middle of quoting Hebrews 1:3, the last of the testimonies he is assembling.

Fidelity self-grade for hebrews 8, all six entries A after the Grottos correction. Ratios 0.12x, 0.13x, 0.14x, 0.15x, 0.13x and 0.12x against the raw span source, the most even distribution of any chapter this worker has written, which reflects a chapter whose thirteen verses carry roughly equal weight rather than clustering. Six entries rather than five because the closing quotation from Jeremiah divides naturally at the promises, and running verses 10 to 13 as one entry would have buried the argument about the word new under the covenant promises. The chapter is carried by Calvin more than by anyone else, and in a specific way worth recording: three times he states an objection against the argument he is expounding and then answers it. At verse 7 he asks how blame lying in the people can be transferred to God's covenant; at verse 8 he asks whether the apostle has not turned a prophecy about the whole Law to a question about ceremonies; at verse 2 he asks whether calling the heavenly tabernacle true implies that Moses's was false. That habit gave three of the six entries their centre, and it is the reason the prose names him so often. The other structural feature is that this chapter's commentators disagree by counting rather than by contradicting: the promise of pardon is Ellicott's third, Barnes's fourth, and Wesley's first, each numbering the same clause within a different scheme. I have let those stand side by side rather than harmonising them, since the disagreement is real and the schemes are stated openly in each source.

Jamieson block at key 5 (106 usable words) is the introduction to 2 Thessalonians 3 and has nothing to do with Revelation 15:5. Declared as residue and excluded from the span. This is the seventh chapter in this stretch showing the fixed-stride Jamieson displacement (mark 14, acts 10, numbers 29, 1corinthians 8, hebrews 8, revelation 15): host keys sit on a period-6 grid and the donor stream is monotonic. Here only one host key falls inside the chapter because the chapter has just 8 verses.

Cyril of Jerusalem at key 8 (200 words, truncated) is the catechetical passage on the seven Deacons and Stephen, not on Revelation 15:8. It is placed here by a shared TOKEN rather than a shared subject: the host verse speaks of the seven angels and the seven plagues, the block of the seven Deacons. This is the second token-matched placement observed, after hebrews 8 key 10 where Cyril's exhortation to chastity was placed by its closing quotation of 'I will dwell in them and I will be their God'. Standing rule confirmed: a block whose surface tokens fit the verse must be read from its FIRST sentence before it is trusted. Cyril is undeclarable in excluded_voices (VOICE_LABELS gap), so the residue was handled by RESIDUE_BY_KEY.

Victorinus of Pettau and Bede both appear at key 1 and both are GENUINE Apocalypse commentary, not residue - Victorinus 112 usable words, Bede 300. They are worth noting together because Bede's sentence on the number seven reproduces Victorinus almost verbatim: Victorinus writes that the wrath of God always strikes the obstinate people with seven plagues, that is perfectly, as it is said in Leviticus; Bede writes that the wrath of God ever smites the rebellious people with seven plagues, quoting Leviticus in the same breath. The dependence of Bede on Victorinus is visible in the text itself, which is why the synthesis attributes the reason for the number to the two of them jointly rather than to either alone.

Cross-tradition convergence on the identity of the seven angels, reached independently and from opposite ends of the corpus. Bede at key 1 makes the seven the Church, replete with sevenfold grace. Gill at key 6 makes the angels ministers or members of the Gospel churches, and at key 7 makes the four living creatures ministers of the Gospel as well. A patristic Latin allegorical reading and an eighteenth-century Reformed one arrive at the same corporate ecclesial identification while every other voice on the chapter (Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson, Clarke, Wesley) keeps the angels literal. Recorded because the convergence is a real feature of the catena and not an artefact of the tiling.

Two harvest defects, both previously catalogued, confirmed again here. (1) Ellicott chrome: Ellicott's block at key 8, the chapter's last key, measures 1317 words of which roughly 403 are real commentary and roughly 914 are StudyLight page furniture (sub-menu, font-size, Bible Commentaries, Copyright Statement). This is the FOURTEENTH confirmation, and the payload is again in the 914-985 band and again on Ellicott's LAST block. (2) 200-word truncation: Gill at keys 1, 2 and 3 and Cyril at key 8 all stop at exactly 200 words mid-sentence, while blocks at 196/202/203 end cleanly. The defect is in the harvest, not in any one voice.

Fidelity self-grade, revelation 15, all four spans graded A with no ENTITIES, NUMBER or WATCH signals on the final read-back. Expansion ratios: vv.1-2 4627 source words to 649 prose (0.14x), vv.3-4 2382 to 650 (0.27x), vv.5-6 2445 to 634 (0.26x), vv.7-8 3266 to 649 (0.20x). Chapter total 12720 usable source words to 2582 prose, 0.20x, well under the corpus median of 0.84x and nowhere near the 6x alarm. One flag was raised and cleared during drafting: the word Mosaic at vv.3-4, an adjective derived from Moses that appears nowhere in the source; rewritten as 'two songs of Moses'. It was not a fabricated fact, but the vocabulary rule holds regardless.

THE 200-WORD TRUNCATION CAP, MEASURED CORPUS-WIDE AT LAST. I have reported this anecdotally for a dozen chapters (Keil, Gill, Cyril of Jerusalem, five voices, six books); here is the whole picture. Of 141,039 blocks in 1,189 files, 13,799 are exactly 200 words. It is not spread evenly -- it is a property of particular voices: Keil and Delitzsch 9,727 of 10,472 blocks (92%); Cyril of Jerusalem 790 of 1,273 (62%); Leo 18 of 42 (42%); Origen 91 of 279 (32%); John Lightfoot 132 of 1,056 (12%); Theodoret of Cyrrhus 42 of 379 (11%); John Gill 2,894 of 29,682 (9%). Every other voice is at or below 0.1% -- Ellicott 25 of 22,299, Clarke 15 of 20,823, Calvin 14 of 11,063, Barnes 12 of 7,347 -- which fixes the coincidence rate and means roughly ten of Keil's 9,727 are genuine. Heaviest books: psalms 1,029, proverbs 868, isaiah 777, job 620, jeremiah 599, genesis 528. The consequence for this loop: KEIL IS EFFECTIVELY TRUNCATED EVERYWHERE. In nine blocks out of ten his exposition is cut mid-sentence at 200 words, so a synthesis that declares him is quoting an opening paragraph, never an argument, and any voice-weighting by word count silently caps him at 200 per key. In this chapter alone 13 of his blocks are at the cap.

Calvin editorial interpolation, two more instances in one chapter, both of the correcting shape and one of them brutal. At k1 an editor supplies Calvin's Latin, compares the English version and other interpreters, and prefers a different rendering of the Hebrew -- with the authorities' names dropped to bare commas, the familiar dropped-italics defect. At k31 the editor writes, inside Calvin's own block: 'The reasoning of Calvin, besides being in every respect unsatisfactory, is founded on a misquotation of the original. He appears to have put down the words from memory, or else his transcriber has made the mistake for him.' That is the strongest instance of the correcting shape yet found, and it bears directly on the live exegetical question at v.31 -- whether Jacob bowed on the bed's head or leaned on the top of his staff, the Hebrew consonants admitting both under different Masoretic points. A writer summarising the block would attribute the editor's demolition of Calvin to Calvin. The k1 block also carries Hebrew characters, which the non-Latin sweep would flag if copied into prose.

Jamieson donor bug, SIXTEENTH and SEVENTEENTH confirmations, three donor blocks in one chapter and all from the same neighbourhood. k6 carries Genesis 40:12-14 (Joseph interpreting for the butler), k18 carries Genesis 40-41 (the imprisonment and Pharaoh's dreams, with the note on the name Pharaoh and Aphophis), k30 carries Genesis 40:23 / 41:9 (the butler's belated confession). As at luke 8 the donor is an earlier part of the SAME book, and here all three donors sit within two chapters of each other while the host keys are 6, 18 and 30 -- a stride of twelve. Two chapters running with same-book donors after fifteen cross-book ones; the pattern may be that the donor pointer runs over the whole corpus in scrape order, so a host early in a book draws from earlier in that same book. All three excluded.

A fourth Calvin editorial interpolation in this chapter, of the citation kind rather than the correcting kind: at k22 the block carries a long quotation from a nineteenth-century work on the manners and customs of the ancient Egyptians, complete with volume and page reference, and at k5 a Greek quotation of Sophocles is followed by an editor's note discussing which lost play it comes from, citing an 1826 Oxford edition and Langhorne's Plutarch. Publication dates two and a half centuries after Calvin's death, sitting inside his commentary blocks as though he wrote them, are the clearest internal proof of the editorial hand that the corpus offers. Counting k1, k5, k22 and k31, this one chapter carries four.

Chapter-shaped observation: genesis 47 is unusually argumentative, and the arguments are about Joseph's ETHICS rather than the text. Ellicott opens v.20 with 'Joseph has been accused of reducing a free people to slavery by his policy' and all three moderns present feel obliged to answer the charge -- Calvin at length and twice over (vv.16, 20), Clarke with 'for this part of Joseph's conduct he certainly deserves high praise and no censure' (v.16) and then a balanced verdict at v.26 that the conduct 'has been as strongly censured by some as applauded by others' and that a sober reader will 'adore God, applaud the man, and perhaps in some cases censure the minister'. Calvin's defence is notable for conceding the general principle against himself: a man who exploits severe necessity is not excused merely because the sufferer offered the terms. He then turns it on his own readers -- 'let those who are too intent on wealth beware lest they should falsely employ Joseph's example as a pretext' -- and quotes Tiberius on shearing the flock without tearing off the skin against the kings of his own day.

Calvin volume-final scripture-index dump, confirmed in the wild exactly as the corpus sweep predicted. The k4 block is 786 words of which 370 are bare reference tokens -- matching the figure recorded for leviticus 12 in the sweep at genesis 47/deuteronomy 34. Usable Calvin here is about 416 words; synthesis-loop.py size therefore overstates this chapter by 370 words out of 8,679, roughly four per cent. The commentary that survives before the index is substantial and was used.

A four-way disagreement worth keeping, because each party knows what the others say. Why is the term of purification doubled for a daughter? CALVIN canvasses four answers and ranks them: a natural cause (granted in part, but not the ceremony's object); that the mother is more defiled by female offspring because that sex is more disposed to vice ('I know not whether the view is sound'); that the woman began the rebellion, being deceived by the serpent ('more probable, as some think'); and his own choice, that the punishment for males was lightened by circumcision, since God honoured them by engraving his covenant on their flesh. ELLICOTT gives the physiological answer, that the ancients believed the derangement of the system far greater at a girl's birth, with parallels among Greeks, Hindoos and Arabs. CLARKE at v.6 demolishes both of the middle positions: the physicians' claim is 'not justified either by observation or matter of fact', and the appeal to the inferiority of the female sex is 'a miserable reason, and pitifully supported'. HENRY refuses the question entirely -- 'I can assign no reason but the will of the Law-maker' -- and appeals to the abolition of the distinction in Christ. Captured as a debate at v.1 with Clarke's rebuttal at v.6, where his block lives.

Jamieson blocks at keys 3, 9 and 15 are all from 1 Corinthians and none of them touch Colossians. Key 3 is on 1 Corinthians 4:21 (shall I come with a rod, or in love and the spirit of meekness); key 9 is on 1 Corinthians 5:4-5 (to deliver such a one unto Satan); key 15 is on 1 Corinthians 5:9 (rather, in the Epistle: a former one not now extant). The host keys sit on a clean period-6 grid, 3-9-15, and the donor stream is strictly monotonic, 1 Cor 4:21 then 5:4 then 5:9. This is the EIGHTH chapter in this stretch to show the fixed-stride Jamieson displacement, after mark 14, acts 10, numbers 29, 1corinthians 8, hebrews 8, revelation 15 and luke 8. All three declared as residue.

Tertullian at key 1 (352 usable words) is Against Marcion on COLOSSIANS 1, not on Colossians 2:1. It quotes Colossians 1:5 (the hope which is laid up for you in heaven), then Colossians 1:15 (the image of the invisible God) and Colossians 1:15-16 (the first-begotten before every creature). Donor and host share a book, as at numbers 29 with Jamieson: nothing was imported from elsewhere, the stream was simply re-keyed by one chapter. Declared as residue, and note that Tertullian IS declarable in excluded_voices because his catena label is the bare name that VOICE_LABELS carries; Cyril of Jerusalem still is not. The block also contains the word Marcion, which was the fabrication trap at 1thessalonians 1 - here it is genuinely in the source but sits inside residue, so it must not enter the prose either way.

Cyril of Jerusalem appears six times in this chapter and splits three and three, which is the clearest single case yet of how the Catechetical Lectures enter this catena. GENUINE, because the block quotes or expounds the very verse: key 8, which cites many that make spoil through philosophy and vain deceit and then names Greeks, the Circumcision and heretics; key 12, on Abraham's faith and being circumcised by the Holy Spirit through Baptism, not in the foreskin of the body but in the heart; key 15, on the Cross as seal, closing with He triumphed over them in it, having made a shew of them openly. RESIDUE, because the block is placed by topic or token only: key 2, a Trinitarian passage on not separating the Old from the New Testament, attached to a verse that names the Father and Christ but not commenting on it; key 10, the lecture on Golgotha, placed under the head of all principality and power by the pun on Head and the place of a skull; key 20, a 27-word stub that is nothing but a re-quotation of the lemma of verse 8, misfiled twelve verses later.
