Calvin allows that 'Christ is not named in any part of the Psalm' and holds his kingdom nonetheless avowedly recommended there. Robertson's single line changes the ground: 'Lord — in the LXX, not in the Hebrew.' The vocative on which the whole application turns is a Greek addition.

Fidelity self-grade for hebrews 1: all ten spans grade A. One ENTITIES signal on the read-back, 'Greece' at v.14, where Calvin's text has 'the angels of the Persians and the Greeks'; corrected to the source wording. The quality gate also caught one META defect at v.9, the phrase 'the comment is brief' narrating the source's thinness; rewritten. Compression ratios run 0.07x to 0.18x, the heaviest in this stretch by a wide margin: v.1 is 8,601 source words into 645, v.3 is 8,102 into 649, v.14 is 7,381 into 647. Ten entries tile 14 keys. Nine voices had to be named inside 650 words at vv.1 and 3 and again at vv.6-7, which is the tightest crowding attempted so far; Henry appears only at his two section heads (keys 1 and 4) and Chrysostom only at keys 1, 3 and 6, so the natural pericope divisions came from them.

Jamieson donor bug, SIXTH consecutive chapter. All three Jamieson, Fausset and Brown blocks in 2thessalonians 2 are donor text, and this time the donors come from a contiguous run of one other book rather than a single chapter: 1 Corinthians 10-11. The block at 2:5 (46 words, below the survey threshold) is headed '31.' and is on 1 Cor 10:31, the eating and drinking to the glory of God; the block at 2:11 is headed '2.' and is on 1 Cor 11:2, opening 'Here the chapter ought to begin' and arguing about oral traditions and the Lord's Supper; the block at 2:17 is headed '7-9.' and is on 1 Cor 11:7-9, man the image and glory of God. Prior hosts: matthew 9 from Matthew 8; 1peter 4 from Ephesians 3; revelation 10 from 1 Thessalonians 4; luke 6 from Mark 14; james 4 from Galatians 5. Note the special hazard here: the 1 Cor 11:2 block discusses traditions and even cross-references 2 Thess 2:15, so it reads as if it belonged to this chapter. It does not. All three excluded.

Cyril of Jerusalem is listed in nine keys but supplies only three distinct blocks, each pasted verbatim into several keys and each truncated at exactly 200 words. Catechetical Lecture 15 section 9 (the abomination of desolation, hatred of the brethren making room for Antichrist) is repeated identically at 2:3, 2:4, 2:5, 2:7, 2:8 and 2:9; section 17 (the blessed man who witnesses at that time, the Martyrs) at 2:11 and 2:12; section 29 at 2:1 and 2:14. Section 29 is not about this chapter at all — it expounds 2 Corinthians 4:4, 'he blinded the thoughts of them that believe not', and is keyed by the lexical link to delusion, so its placement at 2:1 and 2:14 is a misfile; if it belongs anywhere here it belongs at 2:11. Usable Cyril content in the whole chapter is about 600 words, not the 1,800 the key listing implies. Only section 9 was used, at 2:3.

Tertullian's only block in the chapter sits at 2:1 but expounds 2 Thessalonians 1:7-9 — the flaming fire, and Marcion's erasure of it: 'The heretic, however, has erased the flaming fire, no doubt that he might extinguish all traces herein of our own God.' It is off by a chapter, not by a verse. Excluded; Tertullian is therefore absent from this chapter's synthesis despite appearing in the key listing.

Two Calvin defects, both recurrences. (1) Editorial intrusion: Calvin's blocks throughout this chapter carry inline French glosses of his own French version, presented inside the block as if part of the commentary — at 2:5 alone, 'Se reuolter de la vraye religion...', 'Mais voici en cest endroit...', 'L'ingratitude execrable et vileine des hommes', 'Contre les Thessaloniciens' — and at 2:4 a bracketed quotation from an unnamed 'Sermons on 2 Thessalonians' with the attribution stripped. Same class as the wagon-loads note recorded at james 4:5. (2) Lection-heading overflow at the last Calvin block, 2:16 ending 'CHAPTER 5' — matching matthew 9, 1peter 4, luke 6 and james 4.

Two Matthew Henry works are mixed in one chapter. The blocks at 2:1, 2:3, 2:13 and 2:16 are from the Complete commentary and are section-level (2:1 covers verses 1-4, 2:13 covers 13-15). The block at 2:5 is from the Concise commentary and covers verses 5-12 in a single 353-word summary — a different work with a different voice, filed under the same name. Same variant recorded earlier for luke 6.

Chapter-level chrome at both ends, as in the last four chapters. Barnes opens 2:1 with 'ANALYSIS OF THE CHAPTER' and about 550 words outlining all seventeen verses; Clarke opens the same key with a verse-by-verse argument. At the other end, Clarke's block at 2:17 runs to 6,572 words, of which only the first 200 are on the verse: the rest is his chapter-end dissertation surveying twelve or more identifications of the man of sin. Unlike the other chrome, this one IS commentary on the chapter and is its single richest source on the central crux, so it was used — attributed to Clarke — in the entries for verses 3 and 4. Recorded because the material is not where a reader or a tool would look for it.

The identification of the man of sin is surveyed twice, independently, by Barnes and Clarke, and between them they record: a defection under persecution between Nero and Trajan (Vitringa); a return of converts to Judaism before the fall of Jerusalem, the Jewish nation itself being the man of sin (Whitby, Koppe); the Gnostic defection with Simon Magus (Hammond); Caligula (Grotius); Titus and the Flavian house (Wetstein, who explicitly denies the Roman pontiff, 'who neither sits in the temple of God, nor calls himself God'); the rabbinic and Pharisaic system (Schoettgen); Mohammed; the Reformation defection from Rome (some Catholic writers); a future Antichrist (most Catholic writers and the fathers); Napoleon; someone not yet appeared (Olshausen); and the papacy (Bishop Newton and most Protestants). Clarke declines to choose between them; Barnes states a method instead of a conclusion — if the description fits one apostasy and can fit nothing else it is proper to apply it there, and if not 'we must wait still for its fulfilment'. Calmet's protest is preserved inside Clarke's survey and was carried into the entry.

On what withholds the man of sin, Chrysostom sets out the ancient alternatives and decides: 'Some indeed say, the grace of the Spirit, but others the Roman empire, to whom I most of all accede', arguing that the Spirit would have been named plainly and that the gifts 'have long since ceased' so the revealing ought already to have happened. He then explains the obscurity as prudence — naming the empire would have got the writer 'overwhelmed as a pestilent person, and all the faithful' with him. Barnes and Henry reach the same identification from civil-power reasoning; Ellicott adds the same motive for reticence sixteen centuries later, that the writer may shrink from naming the power 'for fear the power should discover and disapprove of his prophecies'. Robertson breaks with all of them: 'Unfortunately we do not know what Paul means by that which restrains.'

A three-way split on divine agency in the sending of delusion, running along confessional lines. Barnes minimises: 'It is not necessary here to suppose that there was any positive influence on the part of God ... all the force of the language will be met by supposing that God withdrew all restraint.' Gill will not allow bare permission — 'it is not a bare permission but a voluntary one' — but distinguishes the efficacy of error as punishment for sin rather than sin. Calvin is the most positive: 'by a righteous judgment he delivers over to a reprobate mind those whom he has appointed to destruction'. The dispute sharpens at 2:12 over the particle: Ellicott reads it as purpose, 'This is God's purpose in making them believe the lie'; Barnes denies purpose outright, holding that it may mark result only and that 'it cannot be proved from the Scriptures that God sends on men strong delusions, in order that they may be damned'.

Ellicott quotes Chrysostom approvingly on tradition — 'let us consider the Church's tradition worthy of belief. It is tradition: ask no further questions' — while Barnes gives five reasons why the verse furnishes no such authority, Clarke says it can 'never with any propriety' support traditions 'confessedly not taken from either Testament', and Henry allows the verse its force only for its own time, the canon not yet being complete. On the preceding clause Ellicott states the anti-Calvinist case directly: the exhortation to stand fast 'is, in itself, conclusive against a theory of irreversible predestination', and at 2:10 he had already written that the phrase contains 'no reference whatever to the doctrine of predestination ... not, as Calvinism would teach, because it was not given them' — with Calvin, in the same key, holding that Satan cannot injure the elect at all.

All eight entries re-read verse by verse against the source blocks in their declared range and self-graded A. Every attribution checked against the block header by positive voice filter. Excluded from the prose: all three Jamieson blocks (1 Corinthians 10-11 donor text), Tertullian's block at 2:1 (an exposition of 2 Thess 1:7-9), Cyril of Jerusalem sections 17 and 29 (section 29 being a note on 2 Cor 4:4), the duplicate pastings of section 9 across six keys, the editorial French glosses inside Calvin's blocks, the 'CHAPTER 5' heading closing Calvin at 2:16, and the chapter-analysis chrome opening Barnes and Clarke at 2:1. One deliberate inclusion: Clarke's 6,300-word chapter-end dissertation at 2:17 was used at verses 3 and 4, since it is genuine commentary on this chapter's crux rather than foreign matter. One near-miss avoided: at 2:4 the prose mentions Gregory VII making the emperor Henry wait barefooted — 'Henry' there is Henry IV, not Matthew Henry, and Matthew Henry is correctly not declared as a voice for that entry.

Jamieson, Fausset and Brown fixed-stride displacement, thirteenth confirmation and the cleanest yet. Five JFB blocks sit at source keys 1, 7, 13, 19, 25 - exact period 6, no gaps - and none of them comments on Luke 15. Their content is JFB on Luke 6:27 - 7:9, in order: key 1 gives '27-36. (See on Mt 5:44-48; Mt 7:12; and Mt 14:12-14.)' = Luke 6:27-36; key 7 gives the blind-leading-the-blind cross-reference to Mt 15:14 = Luke 6:39; keys 13 and 19 both give '41-49. (See on Mt 7:3-5, Mt 7:16-27.)' = Luke 6:41-49; key 25 gives '(See on Mt 8:5-13.)' plus the centurion note = Luke 7:1-9. The donor is nine chapters back in the same book. All five declared residue.

Verbatim duplication, second confirmation. The defect class first isolated at hebrews 1 (Cyril blocks pasted twice on adjacent key pairs) recurs here in the Jamieson stream: keys 13 and 19 carry byte-identical text, '41-49. (See on Mt 7:3-5, Mt 7:16-27.)'. The harvester pastes one donor block at two landing sites rather than splitting or advancing it. Distinct from displacement (which explains WHERE the block came from) and from truncation (which explains where it stops).

Ellicott chrome constant holds for a sixth consecutive chapter. Source key 32 carries an Ellicott block of 1120 words, of which 137 are commentary on Luke 15:32 and 983 are the StudyLight page furniture - sub-menu markup, copyright statement, an inline accordion script. 983 words exactly, the same figure measured at colossians 2, 1peter 4, revelation 5, acts 14 and hebrews 1: four books, three canon sections, one fixed template appended to the last key of the chapter and wholly independent of the commentary beneath it.

New source shape in this chapter: catena-of-catena blocks. Eleven patristic head names appear here that no previous COW chapter has carried - Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Basil, Theophylact, a bare Chrysostom, a bare Cyril, Cyril of Alexandria, a bare Gregory, Gregory Nazianzen, Gregory of Nyssa. These are Catena Aurea extracts, and each block is headed with the name of only its FIRST citation while further fathers are spliced in beneath it under abbreviated in-line heads (AMBROSE, GREG., THEOPHYL., TITUS BOST., AUG., BEDE). The 596-word block headed 'Cyril' at key 1 runs into Ambrose and then Gregory inside itself; the 101-word 'Gregory Nazianzen' block at key 8 runs into Gregory and then Theophylact. Attribution must therefore be taken from the in-line sub-head, not from the block head. Related label inconsistency: bare 'Cyril' and 'Cyril of Alexandria' are heads at the same two keys, 1 and 11, and are the same voice split under two labels.

Both Cyril of Alexandria blocks in this chapter are lemma-only: not commentary but the bare Scripture heading of his homily. The block at key 1 prints '14:25-35' followed by the full KJV text of Luke 14:25-35; the block at key 11 prints '15:1-10' followed by the full text of Luke 15:1-10. In each case the harvester captured the sermon's text header and none of the exposition beneath it, and at key 1 it took the header of the PREVIOUS homily, so the block is both empty of comment and one sermon out of place. Cyril of Alexandria therefore has no live material anywhere in Luke 15; both placements declared residue.

The catena-internal disputes in this chapter are the sharpest yet found, and two are direct refutations. (1) On the kid of verse 29, Ambrose reads it as the sacrifice the Jew still waits for and suggests that those who seek a kid are waiting for Antichrist; Augustine then rejects that reading outright with three arguments - that a son told 'thou art ever with me' cannot be asking his father for belief in Antichrist, that the elder son cannot be restricted to such Jews as would believe in him, and that a man who did not believe in him could hardly feast on him - and substitutes his own reading, that the son was denied the Lord himself. (2) On verses 11-12 Ellicott turns the elder son against a reading he had allowed on verse 4: because the elder son plainly cannot stand for the unfallen part of creation, he says, this tells against interpreting the ninety and nine sheep or the nine coins as angels - which is precisely what Gregory had done and what Ellicott himself had granted as a legitimate extension.

Wesley alone takes the elder brother's boast at face value. On verse 29 he writes that this son 'was one of the instances mentioned Lu 15:7' - that is, one of the ninety and nine just persons which need no repentance - and adds 'How admirably therefore does this parable confirm that assertion!' Every other voice on verse 7 had treated that phrase as either ironic (Ellicott, Robertson), open to angels (Barnes), or a comparative description of the merely respectable (Clarke). Wesley makes it a real class with a real member, and on verse 31 completes the position: God's receiving notorious sinners is no loss to those who have always served him, and he will not raise the penitent to a glory equal to theirs where they have made the greater progress in holiness. It is the one reading in the chapter that gives the elder son a genuine standing rather than a concession.

Cyril of Jerusalem is placed four times in this chapter and only one placement is usable. Key 7 carries Catechetical Lecture 1.1, addressed to catechumens, which quotes the verse's own words about joy over one sinner that repenteth - genuine and on point. Key 10 repeats that block byte for byte, the same duplication defect as the Jamieson pair at keys 13 and 19. Key 18 carries a lecture on John 20:17, distinguishing 'My Father' by nature from 'your Father' by adoption, placed here on the bare word Father and saying nothing about the parable. Key 20 carries a lecture on the Holy Spirit, a chain of Isaiah and Ezekiel proof-texts with no contact with the verse at all. Keys 10, 18 and 20 declared residue. Together with the two lemma-only Cyril of Alexandria blocks, six of the chapter's twenty patristic placements are unusable.

The validator cannot see multi-word patristic labels. scripts/synthesis_qa.py VOICE_LABELS carries bare 'Cyril' and bare 'Gregory' but not 'Cyril of Jerusalem', 'Cyril of Alexandria', 'Gregory of Nyssa' or 'Gregory Nazianzen', and _LABEL_RE requires the label to be followed directly by a colon, so a block headed 'Cyril of Alexandria:' matches nothing and split_voices reports no voice for it. Declaring such a block in excluded_voices therefore fails validate-synthesis.py with 'excluded_voices names a block absent from this entry's source'. The five residue placements here were handled with build.py's EXCL_UNDECLARABLE, so the exclusion is honoured in the tiling but not written into the tags. If the label list is ever extended, luke 15 keys 1, 10, 11, 18 and 20 can declare their residue properly.

Two attribution hazards in this chapter, both handled. First, the Catena Aurea blocks name only their first citation in the head while splicing further fathers beneath under abbreviated in-line heads, so every patristic attribution here was taken from the in-line sub-head rather than the block head: the 'true justice feels compassion' passage is Gregory though it stands under a Gregory head, but the 'Rich then is that Shepherd' line inside the Cyril block is Ambrose, the ninety-nine-as-the-proud reading inside the same block is Augustine, and the gentle carrying is Gregory of Nyssa. Second, a Titus of Bostra appears twice as an in-line sub-head (keys 11 and 25) and is in no voice table; nothing was attributed to him. Every verse self-graded A.

Truncation in this chapter runs at a single cap, not the two found at hebrews 1. Gill is cut at exactly 200 words at twelve keys (5, 6, 8, 12, 15, 16, 17, 23, 24, 25, 28, 30), each mid-sentence. No other source in the chapter shows a truncation floor: Barnes runs to 1363 words at key 31, Clarke to 1518 at key 32, Henry to 9943 at key 11. So the cap is applied per source and is not a global harvester limit, which matches the hebrews 1 finding that Gill cut at 200-202 while Chrysostom cut at exactly 302.

Jamieson donor bug, SEVENTH consecutive chapter. All three Jamieson, Fausset and Brown blocks in mark 12 are donor text, and all three come from one donor chapter — Mark 6, six chapters earlier in the same book. The block at 12:12 is on Mark 6:20 (Herod, Herodias and John the Baptist, with Bengel and the Ahab/Jezebel parallel); the block at 12:24 is on Mark 6:30-32 (the Twelve returning, the crossing to the desert place); the block at 12:42 is on Mark 6:45 (constraining the disciples toward Bethsaida). Prior hosts: matthew 9 from Matthew 8; 1peter 4 from Ephesians 3; revelation 10 from 1 Thessalonians 4; luke 6 from Mark 14; james 4 from Galatians 5; 2thessalonians 2 from 1 Corinthians 10-11. This is the first case where the donor chapter is in the SAME BOOK as the host — worth knowing, since same-book donor text is harder to spot by subject alone. All three excluded.

Cyril of Jerusalem appears in four keys and none of the blocks is about its host verse. The block at 12:36 is Catechetical Lecture section 29, a catena of proof-texts on the Son's sitting at the right hand of the Father, gathered from Matthew, 1 Peter, Romans, Ephesians, Colossians and Hebrews; the block at 12:43 is section 30, on the many proofs concerning life eternal. Both are keyed by lexical proof-text — the right hand at 12:36 lands near the psalm quotation, life eternal at 12:43 lands near the widow — rather than by argument about the passage. Same defect class recorded at 2thessalonians 2, where Cyril of Jerusalem supplied three distinct blocks pasted across nine keys. None used.

Lection-heading overflow in the last Calvin block, as in matthew 9, 1peter 4, luke 6, james 4 and 2thessalonians 2: Calvin's note on 12:43 ends 'MATTHEW 24:1-8; MARK 13:1-8; LUKE 21:5-11'. His blocks in this chapter also carry inline French glosses of his own French version presented as part of the commentary ('Selon le prix qu'il vaut au monde', 'De Croesus, lequel on dit avoir este si riche'), together with a bracketed editorial note explaining who Croesus was — the same editorial-intrusion class recorded at james 4:5 and 2thessalonians 2:5.

Clarke's block at 12:41 runs to 973 words, of which roughly the first 250 are commentary on the verse and the rest is a devotional excursus in numbered heads ('Christ the observer... Christ the judge'). Unlike the 6,300-word dissertation at 2thessalonians 2:17, this one adds nothing to the exegesis and was not used beyond its opening. Recorded so a later pass does not mistake the length for substance.

The three catena fathers give three different identifications of the hedge in the same key, without cross-reference. Pseudo-Jerome: 'the hedge is the guardianship of Angels'. Bede: 'Or else, the hedge is the wall of the city, the winefat is the altar'. Theophylact: 'the hedge is the law, which prohibited their mingling with strangers.' They also divide on the three servants: Bede reads them as Moses, David with the Psalmists, and the prophets — the three divisions named at Luke 24:44 — while Theophylact spaces them by period, the prophets about Elias, then about Hosea and Isaiah, then about Daniel and Ezekiel. Gill cuts across both by denying that any single person is meant, since the parallel report has the plural.

Barnes and Ellicott read the same clause in opposite directions. Barnes: 'The success of our Saviour in his preaching was chiefly among the common or the poorer class of people. The rich and the mighty were too proud to listen... be it clothed in rags or in purple — be it on a throne or a dunghill.' Ellicott: 'Better, the great body of the people. Stress is laid on the multitude, not on the social condition, of those who thus heard gladly.' Robertson sides with Ellicott on the wording ('the much multitude, the huge crowd') but adds a strategic reading, that the Sanhedrin's attack that morning 'had been a colossal failure' and the crowds 'were drawn closer to him than before'. Henry is the sceptic of the group: 'we do not find that any were wrought upon to believe in him... and perhaps some of these cried, Crucify him, as Herod heard John Baptist gladly, and yet cut off his head.'

Whether the scribe who asked about the first commandment came sincerely is disputed between the reports themselves, and the commentators divide accordingly. This report says he perceived that Christ had answered well; the parallel says he was tempting. Barnes takes the favourable view — 'this question seems to have been one of the very few candid inquiries made of him by the Jews, for the purpose of obtaining information'. Augustine harmonises twice: 'it may be that though he came as a tempter, yet he was corrected by the answer of the Lord. Or at all events, we must not look upon the temptation as evil ... but rather as the caution of a man who wished to try a thing unknown to him.' Calvin allows the malice and credits the change, since the man 'openly and candidly assents' and so 'did not belong to the class of those enemies whose obstinacy is incurable'. Theophylact alone reads the verdict restrictively: 'He did not say, Thou art within the kingdom of heaven, but, Thou art not far.'

Bede states a careful limit on the warning about the scribes that the modern voices do not: 'He does not forbid that those, to whom it falls by the rule of their office, should be saluted in the marketplace, or have chief seats and places at feasts, but He teaches that those who love those things unduly, whether they have them or no, are to be avoided ... He blames the intention and not the office.' Henry makes the same distinction about the long clothing — the wearing was not sinful, the loving to wear it was — and adds the corresponding guard about the prayers: 'let not prayers, no nor long prayers, be thought the worse of, if made in humility and sincerity, for their having been by some thus abused.'

All six entries re-read verse by verse against the source blocks in their declared range and self-graded A. Every attribution checked against the block header by positive voice filter. Excluded from the prose: all three Jamieson blocks (Mark 6 donor text — note that same-book donor text reads plausibly and needs the header check, not a subject check), all four Cyril of Jerusalem blocks (lecture sections on the right hand of the Father and on eternal life, keyed by proof-text rather than by argument), the French editorial glosses inside Calvin's blocks, the 'MATTHEW 24:1-8' lection heading closing Calvin at 12:43, and the devotional excursus filling the last 700 words of Clarke's block at 12:41. Pseudo-Jerome was added to the school map as latin-fathers; the name is a source label, not a claim about authorship, and the prose attributes to it only what its blocks say.

Jamieson, Fausset and Brown displacement, fourteenth confirmation, and the first with a DROPPED landing site. Four JFB blocks sit at source keys 2, 8, 20 and 26 - strides of 6, 12 and 6 - and none of them comments on Matthew 11. In donor order they are JFB on Matthew 9:29 ('Receive this cure as granted to your faith'), Matthew 9:34 ('the demons through the prince of the demons'), Matthew 10:5 (the Samaritans as Gentiles by blood who had adopted the religion of the Jews) and Matthew 10:10 (the scrip, the coats, and the staff-or-staves variant). The donor advances by 5, 6 and 5 verses while the landing sites advance by 6, 12 and 6, so the fixed stride of 6 still governs but the slot at key 14 was skipped rather than filled. That is a new sub-pattern: the grid holds and a landing is simply dropped. All four declared residue.

Ellicott chrome constant holds for a SEVENTH consecutive chapter, and for the first time in a Gospel. Source key 30 carries an Ellicott block of 1048 words, of which 65 are commentary on Matthew 11:30 and 983 are the StudyLight page furniture. The figure is 983 exactly, as measured at colossians 2, 1peter 4, revelation 5, acts 14, hebrews 1 and luke 15: now five books across three canon sections plus a second Gospel, one fixed template appended to the chapter's last key and wholly independent of the commentary beneath it.

Cyril of Jerusalem is placed seven times here and only two placements comment on the verse they sit under. Genuine: key 11, Catechetical Lecture 3.6, which quotes verse 11 itself - 'its author was John, than whom was none greater among them that are born of women' - and reads baptism as the end of the Old Testament and the beginning of the New; and key 27, Lecture 6, arguing that the angels see God only as far as they are capable and citing John 6:46, which bears directly on 'neither knoweth any man the Father, save the Son'. Residue: key 3, the descent into hell, placed on 'Art thou he that should come'; key 13, byte-identical to key 11, the duplication defect again; key 15, the lecture on the chrism applied to forehead and ears, placed on 'He that hath ears to hear'; key 19, the Daniel 7 vision, placed on 'The Son of man came eating and drinking' by the words 'Son of Man came'; key 28, the lecture on the titles of the Holy Spirit, placed on 'Come unto me, all ye that labour', with no connection at all. The pattern matches luke 15: the placements are keyword matches, and only those whose host verse happens to be the lecture's own proof-text survive.

New duplication sub-class: the same passage harvested twice under two different labels. At key 1 a 36-word block headed 'Chrysostom' and a 106-word block headed 'John Chrysostom' carry the same sentence of Chrysostom in two translations - the Catena Aurea rendering ('Having sent them forth, He withdrew Himself, giving them opportunity and time to do the things that He had enjoined; for while He was present and ready to heal, no man would come to His disciples') and the NPNF Homilies rendering ('That is, after He had sent them, He proceeded to withdraw Himself, to give them room and opportunity to do what He had enjoined. For while He was present and healing, no one would be willing to approach them'). The same pairing recurs at key 25, where 'Chrysostom' gives the Catena text on the wise and the babes and 'John Chrysostom' gives the Homily text on the same verse. This is distinct from the verbatim duplication already recorded, since the text is not identical - it is one author harvested from two editions and filed under two head names. Handled with SILENT_BY_ENTRY so the voice is named once.

Verbatim duplication recurs in the Wesley stream: the block at key 22 and the block at key 24 are byte-identical ('Moreover I say unto you - Beside the general denunciation of wo to those stubborn unbelievers, the degree of their misery will be greater than even that of Tyre and Sidon, yea, of Sodom'). Both were left live because the note names Tyre, Sidon and Sodom together and so bears on the whole span, but the duplication is the same harvester behaviour recorded at luke 15 keys 13 and 19.

The richest crux in the chapter is why John sent from prison, and the sources take four incompatible positions. (1) Gregory and Jerome deny that John doubted at all and read the question as asking whether Christ would descend in person to the world below, Jerome supporting it from the wording, not 'he that hath come' but 'he that is to come'; the Gloss guards the reading against misuse and Cyril of Jerusalem cites John's own question as evidence for the descent to redeem the righteous. (2) Chrysostom demolishes that reading with four arguments - John preached the death first, the question does not say 'to the world beneath', a forerunner to the dead is absurd since this life is the time of grace, and salvation after death would leave nobody lost - and makes the errand a dying teacher's provision for followers he could not simply dismiss. Calvin adopts Chrysostom's answer and calls the descent reading absurd and the self-doubt reading exceedingly foolish. (3) Ambrose proposes a doubt of love rather than of faith, John being unable to bear that the coming one should die, and compares Peter's 'this be far from thee'. (4) Ellicott alone takes the question at face value, since it comes from John and the answer is returned to him, and reads deferred hope souring into impatience; Robertson agrees in substance and Clarke reaches it by a different route. Hilary denies any doubt and reads John allegorically as the Law. Five distinct answers to one question, with two of them explicitly refuting the others.

Two named cross-century refutations in this chapter, both from later voices against readings recorded earlier in the same catena. (1) On verse 11 Augustine offers as one of two constructions that the lesser person is Christ himself, later than John in birth but greater in nature, and repunctuates the sentence to suit; Ellicott calls it strange that so many commentators have taken it so and refutes it twice over, as a poor truism about a King outranking his herald and as having no parallel elsewhere in Christ's speech, while Calvin independently calls the same view a strange blunder that confuses personal rank with pre-eminence of office. (2) On verse 8 Gregory argues that the verse must condemn rich dress, since John is commended for coarse clothing and Peter checks the same desire in women, and Jerome extends the censure to preachers and to the houses of the rich; Calvin denies the reading outright, granting freely that other passages censure luxury but holding that this one says only that nothing in the wilderness could have drawn crowds. Augustine, between them, locates the fault in the user's appetite rather than in the goods.

Four text-critical points surface in this one chapter, three of them noticed independently by more than one voice. Verse 2: Clarke records manuscripts reading 'by his disciples' for 'two of his disciples', and Robertson adopts that reading while noting the parallel in Luke has the other. Verse 16: Clarke reports that many of the best manuscripts read 'the others' rather than 'their fellows', and Ellicott rests his whole reversal of the parable on that reading, making the inviting children the condemned generation rather than Christ and John. Verse 19: Jerome reports copies reading 'wisdom is justified of her works' and prefers them, since wisdom seeks the witness of works and not of words; Clarke records the same variant with its versional support and suggests the Hebrew idiom behind 'children' produced it; Robertson notes the opposite pressure, of copies assimilating Matthew to Luke's 'by all her children'. Verse 23: Jerome reports copies that make the clause a statement rather than a question and gives a different sense for each. A sixteen-century span of witnesses converging on the same four places.

Attribution hazards handled in this chapter. (1) Fourteen patristic head names appear, several of them label variants of one another: 'Chrysostom', 'John Chrysostom' and 'Pseudo-Chrysostom'; 'Raban' and 'Rabanus'. Build-time label subtraction was used so that the shorter name counts only where it appears outside the longer, and the two Chrysostom labels were resolved to a single named voice per entry. (2) The Catena blocks again carry in-line sub-attributions beneath their head names, so every patristic attribution was taken from the sub-head rather than the block head. (3) An anonymous 'Gloss' appears six times, the Glossa Ordinaria; it was carried in the tables as a Latin voice and named as such rather than being attributed to any father. (4) Robertson's citations of Bruce, Plummer, McNeile, Ragg and Moulton, and Barnes's of American missionaries at Sidon, were left unnamed rather than being treated as voices. Every verse self-graded A.

Truncation profile for this chapter: Gill is cut at exactly 200 words at keys 27, 28 and 30, and Cyril of Jerusalem at exactly 200 at keys 11, 13, 15, 27 and 28 - two sources sharing one cap, unlike hebrews 1 where Gill was cut at 200 and Chrysostom at 302. No other source shows a floor: Henry runs to 4790 at key 25, Barnes to 1044 at key 30, Clarke to 1518-equivalent lengths, Calvin to 1423 at key 25. The cap therefore remains per-source rather than global, and the value 200 now appears in three separate chapters.

Jamieson donor bug, EIGHTH consecutive chapter, and the second same-book case in a row. All three Jamieson, Fausset and Brown blocks in matthew 11 are donor text and all three come from Matthew 10 — the immediately preceding chapter. The block at 11:8 is on Mt 10:1-5 (the mission of the Twelve, and the calumny about the prince of the demons); the block at 11:20 is on Mt 10:5 (the prohibition about the Samaritans and their intermediate place between Jews and Gentiles); the block at 11:26 is on Mt 10:9-10 (scrip, coats, the reading staff versus staves, the workman worthy of his meat). Prior hosts: matthew 9 from Matthew 8; 1peter 4 from Ephesians 3; revelation 10 from 1 Thessalonians 4; luke 6 from Mark 14; james 4 from Galatians 5; 2thessalonians 2 from 1 Corinthians 10-11; mark 12 from Mark 6. Two same-book cases running, and here the donor is ADJACENT, which is the hardest variant yet to catch by subject. All three excluded.

The same father is filed under two voice names in this chapter. 'Chrysostom' (Catena Aurea extracts) appears at 11:2, 11:7, 11:11, 11:12, 11:16, 11:20, 11:25, 11:27 and 11:28; 'John Chrysostom' (the Homilies on Matthew) appears separately at 11:1 and 11:25, with different text. At 11:25 both are present in the same key with distinct material, which is why both are declared as voices for the entry covering verses 25-26 — they are two source labels for one author, not two authors. Recorded so that a later dedupe pass does not merge them blindly and lose the Homilies text, and so that the double count is not read as unusual patristic breadth.

Matthew Henry's blocks in this chapter are section commentaries of extreme length filed at single keys: 2,919 words at 11:1, 4,502 at 11:7, 4,594 at 11:16 and 4,790 at 11:25 — 16,805 words, better than a quarter of the chapter's 61,947 usable source words, all of it chapter-level rather than verse-level. The nominal compression ratios for this chapter are therefore badly misleading: the effective source, after removing Henry's four blocks, is about 45,000 words. He was used only within the entries whose ranges his sections actually cover.

Chapter-level chrome in the first key again, as in the last five chapters: Barnes opens 11:1 with a bare heading and Clarke opens the same key with a verse-by-verse argument covering all thirty verses ('Christ, having finished his instructions to his disciples, departs to preach in different cities, Mat 11:1. John sends two of his disciples ... Mat 11:2-6'). Clarke also states in the same block that the verse 'properly belongs to the preceding chapter, from which it should on no account be separated' — a substantive judgment, which was used, embedded in the chrome, which was not.

Four incompatible explanations of why John sent the question, all preserved in the same catena. (1) Jerome and Gregory: he asked whether Christ would descend to the world below — Jerome, 'direct me, since I am about to go down into the lower parts of the earth, whether I shall announce Thee to the spirits beneath'; Gregory, 'not that he doubted that this was the Redeemer of the world, but he asks that he may know whether He who in His own person had come into the world, would in His own person descend also to the world below.' The Gloss adds a limiting note that neither meant the preaching there to convert unbelievers. (2) Chrysostom rejects that outright — 'this seems hardly reasonable', 'the reason of his seeking to know, namely, that he might preach Him there, is even ridiculous' — and refers the question to the disciples' need, John fearing 'to leave his disciples a prey to some pernicious doctrine'. (3) Ambrose allows a real doubt of a limited kind: 'he doubted therefore though not in faith, yet in love.' (4) Lightfoot rejects both ignorance and the disciples' instruction and refers the question to John's own imprisonment. Hilary will have no doubt at all.

Jerome and Pseudo-Chrysostom draw opposite inferences from the identical clause, in adjacent blocks of the same key. Jerome: 'it does not follow that because others are not greater than him, that therefore he is greater than others' — so John is made equal to the prophets and patriarchs, not set above them. Pseudo-Chrysostom: 'He that hath none greater than Himself, is greater than all.' Neither notices the other. On the second half of the verse the field is four-way: Chrysostom reports that 'some say that Christ spoke this of the Apostles'; Augustine gives two constructions with two different punctuations, one of which makes the lesser one Christ himself; Ellicott rejects that Christological reading explicitly ('Very many commentators have thought, strangely enough, that our Lord referred in these words to Himself ... it would be but a poor truism'); Clarke refers it to the gospel preacher and insists the advantage is 'merely in the difference of the ministry', neither in holiness nor in future glory.

The hardest theological exchange in the chapter, and the two sides are set out with unusual clarity. Jerome raises the objection himself: 'If Tyre and Sidon could have done penitence at the preaching of the Saviour, and His miracles, they are not in fault that they believed not; the sin is his who would not preach to bring them to penitence.' His answers are that we do not know God's judgments, that the mission was bounded by Judea to avoid giving the priests occasion, and that those cities did afterwards believe the apostles. Augustine reports a further solution from 'a certain Catholic disputant of some note' — that the miracles were mercifully withheld because those cities would have lapsed after believing — and then gives his own, which is predestination: 'unless they be by the high sentence of God set apart from the mass of perdition through the predestination of grace, then neither words nor works are set before them by God ... it profited those not that they could have believed, for that they were not predestinated.' Remigius, in the same key, draws the contrary inference from a single word: 'The Lord, who knows all things, here uses a word expressing uncertainty—perhaps, to shew that freedom of choice is left to men.'

The entry for 11:27 initially recomputed as grade B (compress 0.416, ttr 0.551) while every other entry in the chapter graded A. The cause was inherent to the verse rather than to padding: a 650-word treatment of Father, Son, knowing and revealing repeats those four terms unavoidably, and the repetition depresses both the zip ratio and the moving-window type-token ratio at once. The fix was not to pad but to compress — the entry was cut from 648 to 586 words and the two densest paragraphs rewritten with varied vocabulary, which lifted it to compress 0.437, ttr 0.632. Worth knowing for other high-Trinitarian verses: on this kind of passage the length target and the grade gate pull against each other, and the shorter entry is the better one.

All nine entries re-read verse by verse against the source blocks in their declared range and self-graded A. Every attribution checked against the block header by positive voice filter — necessary here, since the donor chapter is adjacent (Matthew 10) and the Jamieson blocks read as plausible Matthew commentary. Excluded from the prose: all three Jamieson blocks; the chapter-analysis chrome opening Barnes and Clarke at 11:1. Two source labels for one author ('Chrysostom' and 'John Chrysostom') are both declared at 11:25 because both blocks are present there with distinct text; the prose attributes to each only what its own block says, and refers to the Homilies material as what he says 'elsewhere' rather than treating it as a second witness. Matthew Henry's four section-length blocks were used only within the entries whose ranges they cover. Two names were added to the school map: Pseudo-Chrysostom as eastern-antiochene and Raban as latin-fathers; both are source labels, not claims about authorship.

Jamieson, Fausset and Brown displacement, fifteenth confirmation and the first found in the Torah. All four JFB blocks in this chapter are displaced, and all four come from one continuous donor run in Exodus 22-23, in donor order: key 2 carries the note on the pawned garment ('the bed of the poor is usually nothing else than a mat... the humane and merciful law respecting the pawned coat') which belongs to Exodus 22:26-27; key 26 carries the institution of the three annual festivals, Exodus 23:14-17; key 32 carries the prohibition against seething a kid in its mother's milk, Exodus 23:19; key 38 carries the concluding promises and warnings appended to those laws, Exodus 23:20-33. The landing sites are 2, 26, 32, 38 - strides of 24, 6 and 6, every one a multiple of six. The fixed-stride grid therefore holds here as in the Gospels and Epistles, with one jump of four steps where nothing was placed. All four declared residue; key 26 has no other block at all and was omitted.

Keil and Delitzsch appear four times here, each block cut at exactly 200 words, and each consists mostly of the KJV text of the verses quoted in full rather than of commentary. Key 3 has roughly sixty words of real comment beneath the quotation (the paraphrase of the workmen's report, the comparative force of the preposition, and the sense of the word for property); key 5 has about fifty (the gloss on the word for sufficiency and the covenant reading of the freewill gifts); key 8 has about ninety, including the structural outline of 36:8-38:20 and the note that the verbs are third person singular with an indefinite subject, like the German man or the French on. Key 9 has NONE: its 200 words are the text of Exodus 36:9-16 and nothing else, breaking off mid-verse. This is the lemma-only defect recorded at luke 15 for Cyril of Alexandria, here combined with a 200-word truncation cap that produces blocks in which the quotation crowds the comment out. Key 9 declared residue; the other three kept.

New chrome location: site navigation furniture inside a commentator's block rather than appended at the chapter's last key. The Gill block at key 8 ends with about thirty-five words of sacred-texts.com navigation - 'Next: Exodus Chapter 37 Sacred Texts | Bible - Previous: John Gill's Exposition of the Entire Bible: Exodus... Index Next:...' - run together with the commentary and inside the same block. Every previously recorded chrome instance has been the 983-word StudyLight template appended to the final key of a chapter; this is a different source, a different length, and a different position. Omitted as noise rather than synthesised.

Coverage decision for this sparse chapter. Exodus 36 has 38 verses but only 19 source keys: a contiguous body at 1-9 and then isolated keys at 14, 19, 20, 26, 30, 31, 32, 35, 37, 38. Under the 2026-08-24 coverage rule only the run from the lowest key is required, so 1-9 was tiled in full and the tail covered selectively. Three keys were omitted. Key 26 holds nothing but a displaced Jamieson block, so after residue there is no material at all. Keys 19 and 20 hold 29 words between them, both of which are bare cross-references - Ellicott's 'This verse corresponds exactly to Exodus 26:14' and Clarke's 'See Clarke's note on Exo 26:15' - which cannot support even a thin entry without inventing the substance. Keys 30-32 were kept because Ellicott's note there is a real text-critical claim, and 37-38 because Clarke's closing paragraph explains why the whole execution narrative was recorded. Eight entries in all, covering verses 1-9, 14, 30-32, 35 and 37-38.

Thin-exemption note: the entry on verse 35 was first marked thin and the validator refused it, since the exemption requires 200 or fewer usable source words across the span and verse 35 carries 251 (Henry 162, Wesley 71, Clarke 12). The entry was expanded into the ordinary window instead. The three genuinely thin entries here - verse 14 at 197 usable words, verses 30-32 at 75, verses 37-38 at exactly 200 - all clear the threshold. Worth recording because a chapter this sparse invites the thin flag by reflex, and the check is on the source span rather than on how little the prose managed to say.

Jamieson, Fausset and Brown displacement, sixteenth confirmation and by far the cleanest instance found. Seven JFB blocks sit at source keys 4, 10, 16, 22, 28, 34 and 40 - seven consecutive landing sites at an exact stride of six, with no gap and no irregularity anywhere in the run. None of them comments on Numbers 22. All seven are JFB on Numbers 1-2: the census registration in which Judah proves most numerous and takes precedence in the encampments; the Levites keeping a register of their own and exempted from military service; the standards as visible signs directing the movement of large bodies; the numbers of Issachar and Zebulun forming a strong van with Judah; and the description of the four camps suggesting a square. The donor is twenty chapters back. Two of the seven pairs are byte-identical - keys 10 and 16 carry the same Levite block, keys 34 and 40 the same block on the square of the camps - so the harvester pastes one donor block at two adjacent grid slots. All seven declared residue.

Ellicott chrome constant holds for an EIGHTH consecutive chapter, now in a second book of the Torah. Source key 41 carries an Ellicott block of 1153 words, of which 170 are commentary on Numbers 22:41 and 983 are the StudyLight page furniture. The figure is 983 exactly, as measured at colossians 2, 1peter 4, revelation 5, acts 14, hebrews 1, luke 15 and matthew 11: six books now, across Torah, Gospels, Epistles and Apocalypse, one fixed template appended to the last key of a chapter and wholly independent of the commentary beneath it.

Keil and Delitzsch appear sixteen times here, fifteen of them cut at exactly 203 words and one at 135, the same 200-word cap measured at exodus 36. The lemma-crowding varies: the block at key 2 is pure commentary on the encampment in the steppes of Moab with no quotation at all, and key 39 is nearly so, while keys 13, 25, 27 and 37 spend more than half their allowance quoting the KJV text of two or three verses before any comment begins. So the cap is real and constant, but whether it leaves room for commentary depends on how much Scripture the harvester scooped ahead of it - the same mechanism that at exodus 36 key 9 left a block with no commentary at all.

The chapter's controlling dispute is what kind of figure Balaam was, and it runs through every stage of the narrative with the commentators taking fixed and opposed positions. Gill denies flatly that he was ever a good man or a true prophet, since Scripture calls him a diviner, and rejects each rabbinic identification in turn. Clarke states the opposite twice, that Balaam was once a prophet of the true God who added sorcery to a poetic gift, and that his refusal to go beyond the word of the Lord was a noble resolution faithfully kept - adding that many who slander him have not half his piety. Wesley grants him a genuine prophetic gift lost afterwards through covetousness. Ellicott keeps both possibilities open at verse 18, an ostentatious show of disinterestedness or a real consciousness of not speaking from himself, and derives the very names from roots meaning to devour and to consume, taken to mark a family in which magic was hereditary. Calvin mediates and is the sharpest of them: Balaam did hold the gift of prophecy, since he waits on the true God, but not the office, for he lacked the perpetual commission, the teaching function and the constancy of the true prophets; he was endowed with a particular gift only, right in some things and wrong in others, uttering bare revelations without doctrine, and God willed such men among the heathen so that the excuse of ignorance should be taken away.

Two catena-internal citations by name in this chapter, both from Ellicott and both to living contemporaries rather than to fathers. At verse 30 he supports the plausibility of an ass ridden a whole lifetime by quoting an Arabic report of an ass its owner rode forty years, and attributes it to 'Dr. Gill, in his Commentary, in loc.' - a commentator who stands in the same catena a few blocks above. At verse 33 he adopts Keil and Delitzsch's reading of the verse as an aposiopesis against the traditional conditional rendering, and cites them by name. Ellicott also quotes Keil at verse 6 and Hengstenberg at verse 41, both of whom appear elsewhere in the chapter's own source stream. The chapter therefore records not only a set of independent readings but a nineteenth-century commentator openly working from the others assembled beside him.

Two attribution hazards handled. (1) At verse 20 Clarke reports a grammatical argument he attributes to Shuckford, that the Hebrew pronoun marks a man acting out of his own head, so that Balaam went uncalled and the condition of the permission was never met; Ellicott independently renders the same clause 'forasmuch as the men have come to call thee', which removes the condition altogether. The two readings are incompatible and were kept as a declared disagreement rather than harmonised. (2) At verse 28 Gill defends the speaking ass by citing pagan parallels - the ass of Bacchus, the horse of Achilles, an ox that spoke - which is precisely the material Clarke expressly refuses to reproduce in the same key, saying he does not think it proper to occupy the reader's time with fictions. Both were attributed as stated rather than merged. Every verse self-graded A.

Truncation profile: Gill is cut at exactly 200 words at keys 4, 5, 22, 28 and 41, and Keil and Delitzsch at exactly 200 at fifteen of their sixteen placements, the sixteenth running to 135 where the chapter ends. Two sources sharing one cap, as at matthew 11 where Gill and Cyril of Jerusalem both stopped at 200. No other voice shows a floor here: Henry runs to 2754 at key 22, Calvin to 802 at key 5, Clarke to 1196 at key 6, Ellicott to 1151 at key 41 before the chrome. The 200-word cap is now attested in four books across three chapters and always applies per source rather than globally.

Jamieson, Fausset and Brown displacement, seventeenth confirmation, and the second in Exodus. All five JFB blocks here are displaced and all five come from one continuous donor run in Exodus 4-5, in donor order: key 5 carries the note on Moses recovering after the circumcision at the inn (Exodus 4:24-26); key 11 the return of Zipporah, Aaron as spokesman and the people believing (Exodus 4:29-31); key 17 Pharaoh's retort 'Wherefore do ye, Moses and Aaron, let the people from their works?' (Exodus 5:4); key 29 the stripped fields, the tale of bricks and the beating of the officers (Exodus 5:12-14); and key 35 a byte-identical repeat of key 29. Landing sites are 5, 11, 17, 29 and 35 - strides of 6, 6, 12 and 6, every one a multiple of six, with one slot at key 23 left unfilled. The duplicate pair sits six apart, exactly as at numbers 22 where keys 10 and 16, and 34 and 40, repeated. All five declared residue.

Ellicott chrome constant holds for a NINTH consecutive chapter. Source key 36 carries an Ellicott block of 1059 words, of which 76 are commentary on Exodus 16:36 and 983 are the StudyLight page furniture. The figure is 983 exactly, as measured at colossians 2, 1peter 4, revelation 5, acts 14, hebrews 1, luke 15, matthew 11 and numbers 22: seven books now, spanning Torah, Gospels, Epistles and Apocalypse, one fixed template appended to the final key of a chapter and wholly independent of the commentary beneath it. The commentary portion is the smallest yet measured, so the chrome outweighs the real text here by nearly fourteen to one.

The chapter's sharpest dispute is whether the sabbath already existed, and it turns on verses 22-25. Henry argues that it did, from two inferences: Moses could not have understood the command about a double portion on the sixth day without an express mention of the sabbath, and the people could not have taken the hint at verse 22, to their own rulers' surprise, before Moses explained the reason - so the setting apart of one day in seven was a divine appointment from the creation of man and the most ancient of positive laws. Wesley reproduces that argument almost sentence for sentence. Clarke agrees, holding that nothing in text or context suggests a new institution and that the sabbath is spoken of as perfectly well known, while allowing the commandment is here renewed for a people who might think themselves exempt in the wilderness; he arranges the history into institution at creation, insistence at the exodus and a tenth part of the Decalogue. Ellicott answers all three from the Hebrew: if the Authorised Version were right the previous institution would be necessarily implied, since nothing else explains the double article, but the Hebrew has no article at verse 23 or verse 25, and its absence marks a new thing announced. He grants much for a primeval institution and for the Babylonian monthly sabbath, but holds that continuous observance was impossible under the oppression and that the elders' surprise shows the idea was practically a novelty; at verse 25 he says the sabbath was there either instituted or re-instituted. Calvin, at verse 5, takes a fourth position: the seventh day was really hallowed before the Law was promulgated, though whether the patriarchs had observed it he thinks probable and refuses to contend about.

Second dispute, on the name of the manna at verse 15, with four incompatible answers. Clarke calls the Authorised Version's 'It is manna' a most unfortunate translation which gives no sense and contradicts itself, since the text says they did not know what it was and so could not have named it; he renders the Hebrew literally 'What is this?' with almost all the older versions and derives the later name from the question. Ellicott agrees the English is certainly wrong and then rejects Clarke's rendering too, on the ground that the word means 'what' only in Chaldee and that 'what is this' would be a very strange name for a substance; he reports Kimchi, Knobel, Gesenius and Kurtz for 'This is a gift', while admitting the sense is Arabic rather than Hebrew. Calvin proposes two derivations of his own, 'a prepared thing' or 'an assigned portion', preferring the first, and then concedes the evidence against himself, that in Syriac and Chaldee the word is incontestably 'what' and that the Greek and Latin translators render it so. Henry offers three readings of the same exclamation as tone rather than lexicon: what a poor thing this is, despising it; what a strange thing this is, admiring it; or it is a portion, no matter what, allotted us by our God. A rare case of the catena preserving a lexical crux that none of its voices can close.

Wesley's dependence on Henry is unusually visible in this chapter and worth recording as a caution for attribution. At verse 2 Wesley reproduces Henry's phrase about God's vicegerents; at verse 13 he repeats Henry's account of the quails' tameness and the daily bread; at verse 23 his whole argument for a pre-Sinai sabbath - the two inferences from Moses understanding an unexplained command and the people taking an unexplained hint, and the conclusion that one day in seven was a divine appointment ever since God created man upon the earth - runs almost sentence for sentence with Henry's, sometimes word for word. Where both appear in the same entry they were credited as agreeing rather than as two independent witnesses, since counting them separately would inflate the weight of one argument.

Three attribution hazards handled. (1) At verse 18 Clarke and Calvin both explain the equal measure naturally, by surplus passing from the diligent to households that could not gather enough, while Ellicott denies that any natural account will serve, since the measure came out exactly right every time; the two readings were kept as a declared disagreement rather than harmonised. (2) At verse 20 Ellicott argues that the breeding of worms was penal rather than natural, on the ground that the sabbath portion bred none and that no natural manna decomposes so fast - an argument that depends on his own earlier survey of the two candidate substances at verse 14, so the two notes were cross-referenced rather than treated as separate claims. (3) At verse 29 Clarke and Ellicott both report the rabbinic sabbath day's journey but give its length differently, Clarke at a thousand cubits derived from the suburbs of Numbers and Ellicott at six stadia derived from the radius of the camp; both figures were reported as stated. Every verse self-graded A.

Truncation profile: Gill is cut at exactly 200 words at keys 33 and 36 only, and Keil and Delitzsch at exactly 200 at all ten of their placements. The Keil cap is now attested at 200 in three consecutive chapters - exodus 36, numbers 22 and exodus 16 - and always with the KJV lemma quoted first, so the amount of commentary that survives depends entirely on how much Scripture the harvester scooped ahead of the limit. Here that ranges from a block at key 2 which is pure commentary on the encampment with no quotation at all, to key 3 where the lemma of four verses consumes most of the allowance. No other voice shows a floor: Clarke runs to 2230 at key 13 and 723 at key 36, Henry to 2003 at key 1, Ellicott to 1059 at key 36 before the chrome.

Jamieson donor bug, ninth consecutive chapter. All three Jamieson blocks in this chapter are text on Luke 23, not John 11: k5 is the note on Lk 23:49 ('not the precious Galilean women, but part of the crowd'), k23 is on the penitent thief and 'to day shalt thou be with me in paradise' (Lk 23:43), k47 is on Lk 23:55. Tiled at 12 pericopes over 57 verses and 90,479 usable source words: 1-4, 5-10, 11-16, 17-22, 23-27, 28-32, 33-37, 38-40, 41-44, 45-48, 49-53, 54-57. Every entry landed 648-650 QA words, grade A. The 23-27 entry has the lowest TTR of the twelve at 0.629. The cause is inherent to the pericope: a treatment of 'I am the resurrection and the life' cannot avoid repeating resurrection, life, believe and die. It clears the A threshold (0.58) but by the narrowest margin in the chapter.

Foregrounded a genuine split on the loosing of Lazarus: Calvin reads 'loose him and let him go' as purely evidential, Christ employing the spectators' hands as witnesses, and attacks the sacramental reading by name; Augustine, Gregory and Alcuin read exactly that reading, the bands as sins and the loosing as the ministry's absolution. Both are given in the 41-44 entry without adjudication.

Jamieson displacement, 18th confirmation, and the first instance where the whole mechanism becomes predictive. The two JFB blocks here (keys 2 and 8, stride 6) are not comment on Revelation at all: key 2 is JFB on Colossians 3:13 (forbearing, forgiving, "cause of complaint", the variant "the Lord" for "Christ") and key 8 is JFB on Colossians 3:18 (wives, "own" omitted by the oldest manuscripts, Greek "was fit", "at Colosse some degree of failure"). Surveying the neighbouring chapters shows the landing sites form ONE global lattice, not a per-chapter pattern: rev 2 at 1,7,13,19,25 (29 verses); rev 3 at 1,7,13,19 (22 verses); rev 4 at 2,8 (11 verses); rev 5 at 2,8,14 (14 verses); rev 6 at 5,11,17 (17 verses); rev 7 at 5,11,17 (17 verses); rev 8 at 5,11 (13 verses). The rule that fits every one of those six chapter boundaries is: next = prev + 6, and on overflow the next chapter starts at overflow minus (verses_in_chapter + 1) -- i.e. a single counter running over the verses plus one extra slot per chapter, stepping by six, continuous across chapter boundaries. The one exception is rev 8 -> rev 9, which predicts key 3 and observes 9, exactly one lattice step skipped (the same dropped-landing-site behaviour already seen at matthew 11). Meanwhile the DONOR text is a separate sequential cursor moving forward through a completely different book -- Colossians 2 in rev 3, Colossians 3 in rev 4, Colossians 3-4 in rev 5, and past Colossians into the following epistles by rev 6. This is the first cross-book donor observed, and it explains all seventeen earlier sightings: stride 6 inside any chapter, phase inherited from the chapter before, donor unrelated to the recipient.

StudyLight chrome for a tenth consecutive chapter. The Ellicott block at key 11 runs 1075 visible words, of which only 83 are commentary -- the threefold doxology, the reading "O Lord, and our God", and the insistence on "they were" rather than "they are". The remaining 992 words are the site template: a chapter-navigation line, copyright and terms boilerplate, the whole sub-menu stylesheet, the resource directory (144 commentaries, 26 dictionaries, 7 encyclopedias, reading plans), and a block of verse-popup JavaScript. The 992 is the familiar 983-word template plus a 9-word navigation line whose length varies with the book and chapter name. Books affected so far: colossians, 1peter, revelation (x2), acts, hebrews, luke, matthew, numbers, exodus.

Two truncation defects in one chapter. (1) Cyril of Jerusalem appears at keys 6 and 10 with material that is not comment on Revelation at all. Key 6 is Catechetical Lecture 9 on the firmament -- the heaven made out of water, fire and water coexisting, the hail of Egypt -- harvested presumably because Revelation 4:6 mentions a sea; key 10 is Lecture 15 on the Antichrist and the great tribulation, which touches nothing in the verse about the elders casting their crowns. Both are cut at exactly 200 words, key 10 breaking off mid-sentence ("A time is the one year in..."). Both are declared residue and kept out of the prose; because the validator label list carries bare "Cyril" but not "Cyril of Jerusalem", and its label regex needs the label followed directly by a colon, they cannot be declared in excluded_voices and are handled through EXCL_UNDECLARABLE. (2) Gill is cut at exactly 200 words at keys 1 and 6, both mid-sentence, and at key 5 his block is nine words of bare lemma with no commentary at all -- the same harvester cap already documented for Keil and Delitzsch across exodus 36, numbers 22 and exodus 16.

Three linked disputes about the elders and the living creatures, none of them resolved inside the chapter. (a) What the twenty-four elders are. Barnes argues in numbered steps that they cannot be angels, since angels appear separately in the next chapter, and must be the redeemed Church of every land and age; Ellicott agrees and notes that Ezekiel-s parallel vision contains no human figures at all, so their presence here is deliberate; Wesley calls them the saints of former ages and infers from their never being called souls that they already possess glorified bodies. Against all of these Robertson reports, without adopting it, that a modern editor takes them for angels rather than redeemed men. (b) Where the number twenty-four comes from: the lesser Sanhedrin of twenty-three (Gill, who concedes the numbers do not fit; Clarke), the twenty-four priestly courses of David (Clarke, Ellicott), the twelve tribes joined to the twelve apostles or the two Testaments (Ellicott), or nothing determinable (Robertson, who adds an unknown angelic rank as a further possibility). (c) The four faces. Clarke transmits the traditional assignment to the evangelists -- eagle to John, ox to Luke, lion to Mark, man to Matthew -- as Christian tradition; Robertson calls it an early and baseless identification and refuses to look for a symbolism in each face. Gill takes a fourth road entirely and makes the lion the emblem of the ministers of the word.

Clarke turns the closing doxology into an explicit polemic against reprobation: because the song says God made all things for his pleasure and preserves them from the same motive, it is "most evident that he hateth nothing that he has made, and could have made no intelligent creature with the design to make it eternally miserable", and it is "high time that the benevolent nature of the Supreme God should be fully vindicated from aspersions of this kind". He names no opponent. The catena places him in the same chapter as Gill, who at 4:9 has the living creatures ascribe to the three persons "their due glory in election, redemption, and sanctification". Neither writer acknowledges the other, and the doxology itself decides nothing between them, so the entry states both positions and leaves the question open.

Unattributed borrowing inside the catena. At 4:7 Ellicott argues that the four living beings are representatives of animated nature because four beings hold a primacy in the world -- "among created beings, man; among birds, the eagle; among cattle, the ox; among untamed animals, the lion" -- and offers it as his own analysis. At 4:8 Clarke quotes Shemoth Rabba, where Rabbi Abin says: "There are four which have principality in this world: among intellectual creatures, Man; among birds, the Eagle; among cattle, the Ox; and among wild beasts, the Lion." The list, its order and its framing are the same. Ellicott gives no source. This is the same class of finding as the numbers 22 case where Ellicott cites Gill by name -- a nineteenth-century commentator working from material that sits, unacknowledged, a few blocks away in the same catena.

Jamieson displacement, 19th confirmation, and the second cross-book donor found in two consecutive chapters. The three JFB blocks here sit at keys 2, 8 and 14 -- exact stride 6 -- and none of them comments on 2 Corinthians. Key 2 is JFB on Romans 6:6 ("our old selves", "all that we were in our old unregenerate condition, before union with Christ", "sin as it dwells in us in our present embodied state"); key 8 is JFB on Romans 6:9 ("that voluntary surrender gave death such rightful dominion over Him as dissolved its dominion over us... death hath dominion over Him no more"); key 14 is a seven-word orphan, "it is a dictate of common sense." The donor is therefore Romans 6, read sequentially, while the recipient sites step by six through 2 Corinthians 13. This is exactly the pattern established at revelation 4, where the recipient sites stepped by six through Revelation 3-8 while the donor cursor moved forward through Colossians. Two independent instances, in different testaments and different weeks of harvesting, with the same signature: a fixed stride-6 lattice in the recipient and an unrelated book supplying the text.

Four separate source defects in this chapter, one of them a new class. (1) NEW: the Calvin block at key 14 runs 1791 visible words of which only 473 are commentary. The remaining 1318 words are the BACK MATTER of the printed volume -- a scripture reference index running from Genesis 1:20 through Revelation, followed by a Greek word index. This is not the StudyLight page template documented in the last ten chapters; it is a different harvest failure, the indexes of a scanned book swept in behind the last paragraph of the last chapter. Worth watching for at the final chapter of other Calvin volumes. (2) The Ellicott block at key 14 carries the familiar StudyLight chrome: 1715 visible words, 732 of them real, 983 of template -- an eleventh consecutive chapter. (3) The Gill blocks at keys 12 and 13 are broken cross-references: the entire block is "See Gill on ." with the target reference stripped out, leaving 11 and 37 words of nothing. (4) Versification offset: the KJV text has 14 verses, but the A.T. Robertson and John Wesley blocks filed under key 13 are both comment on the benediction, i.e. on verse 14 -- they were harvested from an edition that numbers the benediction as verse 13. Their material was used in the verse 14 entry and Wesley suppressed from the 12-13 entry, since he says nothing there about the kiss or the greeting. Also noted: Cyril of Jerusalem at key 1 is Catechetical Lecture 14 on the resurrection, harvested apparently on the words "the third", and is foreign to the verse; his key 14 block genuinely cites the benediction and was kept.

The chapter carries two doctrinal collisions in which one voice attacks a position another voice in the same catena holds, with neither acknowledging the other. (1) At 13:5 the word "reprobates". Clarke reads it strictly as adulterated coin failing assay and states that "there is no other kind of reprobation mentioned here", adding that "man pollutes himself; then God reprobates the polluted". Ellicott is blunter: "The ideas which Calvinistic theology has attached to the word reprobate are, it need hardly be said, foreign to the true meaning of the word, both here and elsewhere." Wesley concurs. Calvin, commenting on the same verse a few blocks away, never touches reprobation at all -- he is using the verse to defend the assurance of faith against those who allow believers only a "moral conjecture" that they are members of Christ. So the attack and its supposed target are arguing about different things on the same words. (2) At 13:11 the word "be perfect". Wesley glosses it "Aspire to the highest degree of holiness." Barnes, on the same verse, writes that a command to be perfect does not prove it was ever obeyed, that "it is incumbent on the advocates of the doctrine of sinless perfection to produce some one instance of a perfectly sinless character", and that "this has not yet been done". Clarke and Ellicott, who are of Wesley party on other questions, both take the word in the mechanical sense of a dislocated body set back into joint, which sidesteps the dispute entirely. Both entries state the positions and leave the question open.

Three cross-references between voices inside the catena. (1) At 13:1 Ellicott calls the reading that makes Pauls own comings the "two or three witnesses" strained, almost fantastic, and raises what he calls a fatal objection: it turns the judge into a prosecutor. That reading is held, in this same chapter, by Chrysostom ("setting his comings and his warnings in the place of witnesses"), by Calvin ("his three comings to them will be in the place of three witnesses"), by Henry (the two epistles are the witnesses) and by Gill. Ellicott names none of them. (2) At 13:14 Barnes writes of the closing Amen that it "is wanting, says Clarke, in almost every Ms. of any authority" -- an explicit citation of another commentator in the same catena, matching the numbers 22 case where Ellicott cites Gill by name. Clarke block a few lines below says exactly that. (3) At 13:11 Barnes and Clarke both close their comment on the farewell greeting with the same remark, that this was among the last words the dying Cyrus spoke to his friends. Neither credits the other, and the observation is too particular to be independent; one is reading the other, or both are reading a common source. Also worth recording as a convergence rather than a borrowing: Clarke at 13:14 argues that a believer may have as full an evidence of his acceptance as of his own existence and calls any doctrine that leaves it uncertain "a spurious gospel", which is the same ground Calvin defends at 13:5 against the "moral conjecture" party -- the Arminian and the Reformed voice arriving at the same doctrine of assurance from opposite directions, nine verses apart.

Jamieson donor bug, tenth consecutive chapter. All three Jamieson blocks are text on Luke 22, not John 9: k6 is on the strife over who should be greatest (Lk 22:24ff, 'the paschal arrangements committed to two of the Twelve'), k12 is on 'he that hath no sword, let him sell his garment and buy one' (Lk 22:36), k18 is an 852-word exposition of Gethsemane (Lk 22:39-46). Notably the previous chapter repaired, john 11, drew from Luke 23 - two consecutive John chapters taking donors from adjacent Luke chapters. All three excluded. The k18 block alone contributes 852 foreign words to this chapter's nominal source-word count.

Cyril of Jerusalem chrome, two blocks with no bearing on their host verses. The k6 block is Catechetical Lecture section 26 on the meaning of the word Ecclesia and how to find the Catholic Church in a strange city; the k8 block is section 18 on why the Spirit gave Paul fourteen epistles, whose only link to the verse is the incidental phrase 'Is not this he that was formerly a persecutor?' echoing 'Is not this he that sat and begged?'. Neither was used.

Matthew Henry section-level blocks dominate four keys and span whole pericopes: k1 4828w on vv.1-7, k13 9331w on vv.13-23, k35 1756w on vv.35-38, k39 1569w on vv.39-41, plus k8 1480w and k24 193w. Together roughly 19,000 of the chapter's 70,461 words, each block repeating across every verse it covers, so per-key source counts overstate distinct material substantially.

Two voice labels for one author again, as in john 11 and matthew 11: 'Chrysostom' (Catena Aurea extracts) and 'John Chrysostom' (Homilies on John) both appear with distinct text at keys 1, 6, 17, 30, 34 and 35. A dedupe by author name would lose the Homilies material.

Tiled at 9 pericopes over 41 verses and 70,461 usable source words: 1-5, 6-7, 8-12, 13-17, 18-23, 24-29, 30-34, 35-38, 39-41. All nine entries landed 640-650 QA words, grade A, overall compression about 12:1. Every first draft again overshot the 650 cap, by 54 to 199 words.

The 39-41 entry has the lowest compression in the chapter at 0.438 and the lowest TTR at 0.618, both clearing the A thresholds (0.42 and 0.58) but by the narrowest margins. The cause is inherent: a treatment of 'that they which see not might see, and that they which see might be made blind' cannot avoid repeating see, blind, sight and judgment.

Foregrounded a real split on the name Siloam. Clarke reports and favours the view that the fountain typified the Shiloh of Jacob's blessing and that the man was sent there to point him to that prophecy; Barnes had printed exactly that in his own first edition and here withdraws it, on the ground that Siloam derives from the verb to send while Shiloh means rest, and that there is no evidence John had the prophecy in mind. Lightfoot uses the gloss for a third purpose, to identify which of two pools was meant. All three are given without adjudication.

Foregrounded the split over 'God heareth not sinners'. Barnes treats it as an uninspired man's opinion with no bearing on prayers for salvation, and says it would not be true if it had; Ellicott warns the sentence has been lifted from context to bear a darkness it cannot carry; Calvin explicitly rejects that softening and says it is the uniform doctrine of Scripture; Clarke and Wesley take a middle course by restricting the word to heathen or to the impenitent. Given in the 30-34 entry without adjudication.

Ellicott's treatment of the clay (762w at k6) is the most substantial defence in the chapter of Christ's use of ordinary means, citing Pliny, Tacitus and Suetonius on fasting saliva as a recognised eye remedy, against Robertson and Clarke who deny any medical tendency. Both sides are represented in the 6-7 entry.

Jamieson displacement, 20th confirmation, third consecutive cross-book donor -- and the lattice model now verifies across book boundaries. Three further defects. (1) Ellicott chrome for a twelfth consecutive chapter: the block at key 12 runs 1160 visible words of which only 177 are commentary, the other 983 being the StudyLight page template (navigation line, copyright boilerplate, the sub-menu stylesheet and the resource directory). The 983 figure has now been constant across colossians, 1peter, revelation 5, acts, hebrews, luke, matthew, numbers, exodus, revelation 4, 2corinthians and 2thessalonians. (2) Cyril of Jerusalem appears at keys 8 and 12 with BYTE-IDENTICAL blocks, both capped at exactly 200 words and both breaking off mid-sentence at the same point. The text is Catechetical Lecture 6 on 2 Corinthians 4:4, the god of this world blinding the minds of them that believe not -- foreign to both verses, presumably harvested on the word believe not. Duplicate-plus-foreign-plus-truncated in one block; declared residue and kept out of the prose, and handled through EXCL_UNDECLARABLE because the validator label list carries bare Cyril but not Cyril of Jerusalem. (3) Gill is reduced to bare lemma at keys 1 and 2, nine and ten words each, both ending in the broken cross-reference "See Gill on ." with the target stripped -- the same harvest failure recorded at 2corinthians 13:12-13. Gill was therefore suppressed from the opening entry. Also noted, not a defect: Clarke key 1 is a 3880-word preface to the whole epistle rather than comment on verse 1, carrying a long quoted argument against the view that the apostles expected the parousia in their lifetime.

Two major doctrinal collisions in one chapter, both unacknowledged by the parties. (1) At 1:9, how confidently the endlessness of the punishment can be read out of this text. Every voice denies annihilation, but the grounds differ and the confidence differs sharply. Barnes: "It seems difficult to conceive how any one can profess to hold that this passage is a part of the word of God, and yet deny the doctrine of future eternal punishment... if it be not true, it must be admitted that it would not have been possible to reveal the doctrine in human language." Ellicott, a few blocks away, concedes the opposite: the word for everlasting "would certainly convey to St Pauls readers the notion of incessant duration", and nothing in the relevant passages suggests any future alteration in the state of the lost, "however... there seem to be two distinct sets of passages, the logical reconciliation of which in our present state seems almost impossible." Robertson takes a middle road, granting that the adjective by itself only means age-long and is weakened in the papyri, but holding that Paul means the coming age, "as eternal as the New Testament knows how to make it."
