Whether 'beyond Jordan' means east of the river. Barnes denies it explicitly — 'this does not mean to the east of Jordan, as the phrase sometimes denotes, but rather in the vicinity of the Jordan' — while Wesley assumes exactly that eastward sense in the same breath as the neighbouring commentary.

What 'began to preach' means, since by every account he had preached before. Gill dates the beginning neither from Capernaum nor from John's arrest but 'from the time that Satan left tempting him'. Wesley and Robertson make it the start of settled public work, Robertson noting he 'had been preaching for over a year already elsewhere'. Ellicott puts a season on it, the autumn or winter between the Passovers of A.D. 26 and 27.

Whether the four had been called before and had gone back to fishing. Ellicott reconstructs exactly that from John's Gospel: they had accepted Christ months earlier, and when he began his Galilean circuit 'He was alone, and left them to return to their old calling', uncertain whether he would want them again. Calvin uses that very scenario to disprove a prior call: if they had been called and had returned to the boats, 'it would follow that they were apostates, who had forsaken their Master, despised their calling, and returned to their former occupation'. The two reconstructions cannot both stand. Gill, Henry and Robertson all side with Ellicott's sequence.

Whether the unlearning of the first ministers licenses unlearned preachers. Clarke says the institutions cannot supply what God alone gives: seminaries have uses, but 'to make preachers of the Gospel is a matter to which they are utterly inadequate; it is a prerogative that God never did, and never will, delegate to man', and 'men-made ministers have almost ruined the heritage of God'. Henry, arguing the identical premise about mean instruments, guards the opposite flank in a sentence Clarke never writes: 'yet this will not justify the bold intrusion of ignorant and unqualified men into the work of the ministry.'

Whether the mending of the nets is an undesigned coincidence with Luke's account of the broken nets. Ellicott raises the apologetic argument and then refuses it twice over: mending and washing followed even an unsuccessful night, and Luke's Greek 'does not say that the nets actually broke, but that they were on the point of breaking'. Recorded because a commentator declining a supporting argument available to him is rarer than one making it.

How old the synagogues are. Barnes calls the origin 'involved in much obscurity' and derives them naturally from non-sacrificial worship plus the need for shelter from storm and heat. Clarke dates them firmly: 'not probably older than the return from the Babylonish captivity', and adds that they were built 'especially by rivers, that they might have water for the convenience of their frequent washings'.

What the healings are for. Calvin makes them evidential — such diseases 'cannot be healed by natural means', so curing them 'proved his divinity'. Ellicott resists precisely that: Matthew records them 'not directly as evidence of a supernatural mission, but almost, so to speak, as the natural accompaniments of His work; signs, not of power only or chiefly, but of the love, tenderness, pity, which were the true marks... of the kingdom of heaven'.

Whether the moon affects the disease named after it — a three-way with an unexpected alignment. Calvin refuses to let the word commit the evangelists to the theory at all, on the principle that 'Scripture was not intended to determine questions of physical science, in which inductive reasoning is a sufficient guide', the term no more binding them to lunar medicine 'than the popular use of the phrases [sunrise] expresses a belief that it is the motion of the sun, and not of the earth, that produces the succession of day and night'. Barnes keeps the name and drops the theory — 'it is not certain that the moon has any effect... but no harm arises from the use of the name'. Clarke, uniquely, defends the theory as physically true and supplies a mechanism: at new and full moon the sun and moon act together on the atmosphere, producing tides and, in sensitive constitutions, real change.

Whether the demoniacs were really possessed or the language is accommodation to popular error. Barnes argues seven ways for real possession — Christ and the apostles addressed and managed them as persons; they spoke, answered, and confessed knowledge of Christ, which 'could not be said of diseases'; they went out and entered others; the fathers read it so; and if Christ's belief here may be denied 'it does not appear why any other clear sentiment of his may not in the same way be disputed'. Clarke names and rejects the accommodation theory outright as one that 'can never comport with the accounts given of these persons'. Ellicott defers the question to the Gadarene narrative. Notable because Clarke rejects at v.24 the very accommodation principle Calvin had invoked at v.23 on the neighbouring word.

Which cities made up the Decapolis, and where Damascus stood among them. Clarke calls Damascus 'the metropolis, and most ancient' of the ten and puts the district on both sides of Jordan. Barnes makes Scythopolis chief and 'the only one of them west of the Jordan', listing Damascus as merely one of two possible members. Ellicott gives Pliny's list, which includes Damascus, but notes that Josephus's calling Scythopolis the largest makes it 'almost certain that he did not include Damascus'. Three flatly different reference lists.

Fidelity self-grade A for all 13 pericopes. Every quoted string was checked against the Catena or commentary block it came from; no voice is credited with a position it does not hold; held_by lists and outlier attributions were reconciled against each key's voice list after trimming. Voices were declared only where read in full and cited directly: the smaller Catena entries at keys 3, 5, 8, 17 and 23 (Jerome, Gloss, Ambrose, Hilary, Remigius, Gregory, Augustine, Origen) were not read and are not declared, which is selection rather than misrepresentation. Excluded: the three JFB blocks carrying Matthew 3 material (keys 1, 7, 13) and Cyril's Acts 20 block (key 14), plus the StudyLight chrome tail of Ellicott's key-25 block. RECOVERED and used at their proper pericopes: JFB's key-19 block (Matthew 4:4 material, used at vv.3-4) and key-25 block (Matthew 4:8-9 material, used at v.8). Cyril's keys 11 and 17 were verified on full reading to be genuinely on-verse and were used. Henry's five inflated section blocks and the patristic set at key 1 were redistributed across the pericopes they actually treat. Source corpus 65,763 words across 25 keys tiled into 13 pericopes at an overall 7.8:1 compression, inside the 5-8:1 norm; the vv.1-2 tile is a forced outlier at about 27:1 nominal, for the tiling reason recorded separately, and the leanest is vv.6-7 at 2.6:1 usable after JFB's exclusion, kept dense rather than padded.

Jamieson stride-6 residue lattice, eighth consecutive chapter, but with a new variant: the donor is NOT a single chapter. Keys 2, 14 and 20 carry Matthew 28 material (the sepulchre made sure, the bribe of the guard, make disciples of all nations); key 8 carries Luke 1 (the salute of the Visitation); keys 26, 50 and 56 carry Mark 1 (Malachi 3:1 at the opening, the astonishment at his teaching in the synagogue). Every previous lattice ran off one donor chapter, or two adjacent ones. Declared as excluded_voices at each key.

Ellicott block at key 56 is 1052 words of which roughly 100 are his comment. The rest is StudyLight chrome: navigation crumbs, a Copyright Statement paragraph, terms and privacy links, then a long dump of the site stylesheet. Identical in kind to the defect filed at matthew 12 key 50, and again at the last verse of the chapter, which suggests the scrape appends page furniture at chapter boundaries rather than at random. Only the pre-chrome text was used.

Cyril of Jerusalem appears four times in this chapter and is off-verse at every one: eternal life at key 11, the pre-eminence of the Son at 18, the creation of the firmament at 47, the Spirit breathed on the apostles at 50. Unlike matthew 12, where one of his duplicated blocks was genuinely on-verse, here the content test rejects all four. Suppressed rather than declared, since the roster in synthesis_qa.py cannot detect the label.

A textual variant with doctrinal weight at key 20. Ellicott and Robertson both report that the better manuscripts read that Herod was much perplexed, not that he did many things. Barnes keeps the older reading and builds his entire comment on it, making Herod a man who compromised with conscience by doing many things short of the one thing demanded. The two readings yield different portraits, and the entry records both rather than choosing.

The Catena on Mark pools its patristic blocks at the first key of each pericope, so the fathers at key 6 comment on verses 7 to 13, those at key 35 on the whole feeding, and those at key 45 on the walking on the sea through verse 52. Tiling had to follow the pooling rather than the verse divisions: entries 6-7, 35-38 and 45-47 exist to keep each father with his own subject. Same pattern noted at matthew 12 key 14 but far more systematic here.

JFB stride-6 bug: the Jamieson-Fausset-Brown donor stream at keys 13, 19, 25 and 49 carries Luke 4-5 material — the Nazareth synagogue sermon, "too much familiarity breeds contempt", the allusions to the heathen, and at key 49 a fragment about "munificent recompense for the use of his boat". Unlike matthew 4, where the displaced stream stayed inside the chapter and two keys were recoverable, here the stream is entirely foreign to Luke 12. All four excluded; JFB is cited nowhere in this chapter.

Cyril of Jerusalem is mixed at this chapter. His blocks are on-verse or at least apposite at keys 10, 11, 12 and 40 (used at tiles 8 and 35), but misfiled catechetical material at 6, 8, 19, 22, 31, 37 and 49. The key-49 block is the exception among the misfiles: it is catechesis on Mani, but Archelaus's argument turns on Luke 12:49 itself, so it was used at tile 49 as an outlier reading.
Cyril of Jerusalem duplicates within this chapter: the block at key 10 reappears at key 22, and the block at key 11 is byte-identical at key 12. Cited once each, at the earlier key.

Cyril of Alexandria's own commentary blocks run one pericope late throughout the back half of the chapter: his 12:32-34 exposition is filed at key 35, his 12:35-40 at key 41, his 12:41-48 at key 49, and his 12:49-53 at key 54. The displacement is systematic, not random, and each block is his own on-chapter text merely relocated — so each was read back to its own pericope. The Catena "CYRIL" attributions inside the composite blocks are correctly placed and were used where they stand.

Ellicott's note at key 59 is roughly fifty usable words followed by the StudyLight page chrome — navigation menus, CSS, the commentary index. Same defect class as acts 18 key 28. Truncated at the usable text.

Catena spill at key 27: the block carries Bede, Gregory of Nyssa, Augustine, Theophylact and Basil all commenting on verse 29 (the rare verb behind "neither be ye of doubtful mind"), not on verse 27. Redistributed into tile 29, which is where the disagreement about that verb belongs.

Matthew Henry block inflation, the same pattern as acts 18 and matthew 4: 2,595 words at key 1, 4,671 at key 13, 3,501 at key 22, 2,686 at key 41 and 1,241 at key 54. The key-13 block alone runs the whole of vv.13-21 plus the application. Distilled rather than sampled.

Scan artefact corrected: Tertullian is labelled at keys 1 and 35 and is properly grounded there, but my first name-extraction pass lacked him, so his block at key 1 appeared appended to Wesley's. Checked against the raw catena before use. The v.35 Tertullian block is his anti-Marcion argument on vv.22-31 rather than on v.35, so it is displaced within the chapter but not foreign.

Clarke's note at key 48 says "See at the end of the chapter", and his key-59 block duly carries a long retrospective on vv.47-48 — the plea of ignorance as "a mere refuge of lies". This is authorial cross-referencing, not a filing defect. Tile 45 was already written when the retrospective was found; the same argument is carried there from Clarke's own on-verse notes and from Calvin.

Tiling: 65,981 source words across 59 keys reduced to 15 pericope tiles at roughly 6.8:1, inside the 5-8:1 norm. All 20 named voices in the chapter were checked for grounding before drafting, plus Tertullian, Gregory of Nyssa, Basil, Eusebius, Ambrose, Origen and both Cyrils; none was ungrounded.

Theophylact alone reads "hath power to cast into hell" as leaving room for pardon after death "for the sake of the offerings and prayers which are made for the dead". No other voice at this pericope entertains it; recorded as an outlier rather than as a position in the debate over the clause's force.

The five sparrows: Origen makes them the five spiritual senses, Theophylact the two Testaments, while Clarke, Gill and Ellicott keep them birds at a market price and build the argument on the arithmetic.

What "life" means in "a man's life consisteth not in the abundance": Barnes insists on duration, because the parable that follows is about length of days; Wesley and Calvin read it as comfort or happiness. Barnes's argument from the parable is the stronger, but Wesley's is the natural sense of the English, so both stand.

Lightfoot separates apostasy from blasphemy against the Spirit by who can commit them — apostasy "cannot properly be charged on any but who have already professed Christianity" — where Wesley and Gill separate them by remediability. The two distinctions are compatible and were reported as different questions.

Whether the graded stripes limit the sentence: Basil says the passage "assigns neither measure nor end of punishments, but their differences"; Ellicott lets the same words "throw a gleam of hope on the darkness that lies behind the veil"; Bede sits between. This is the sharpest doctrinal disagreement in the chapter and is carried as a three-position debate.

Whether the last mite can be paid: Ambrose says yes by satisfaction, Origen allows gradations with "endless ages" for great debts, Bede and Wesley say never, and Clarke turns the impossibility into an argument against reading the passage spiritually at all.

What the fire is: Wesley alone hears no threat in it ("the fire of heavenly love"), against Ellicott's judgment, Clarke's Roman sword plus Spirit, Barnes's discord and Gill's gospel-and-persecution. Calvin's one-fire-two-effects reading is the only attempt to reconcile them and is given as its own position.

How to construe "and what will I, if it be already kindled?" — Robertson admits outright that "it is not clear what this passage means" and reads the interrogative as "how"; Lightfoot solves it as a rabbinic school idiom in which the question is an assertion. Lightfoot's solution is the more economical and is given equal weight.

Whether the cloud and south wind are weather or Christology: Theophylact alone identifies Christ with both ("I am a cloud, and I come out of the west, that is, from human nature"). Recorded as an outlier as well as a debate position.

Whether the lawsuit is literal or allegorical: Chrysostom is explicit that it is literal and pitched at "ruder hearers"; Ambrose, Bede and Origen allegorise every figure; Ellicott holds both at once. Chrysostom's is the minority view among the fathers here and was given its own paragraph.

Tile vv.1-3 self-graded A. Every quotation checked against the raw catena. Theophylact, Henry, Barnes, Robertson, Clarke, Lightfoot, Wesley, Ellicott, Gill and Tertullian all verified on-verse. Clarke's textual doubt about "which is hypocrisy" reported with his own verdict attached.

Tile vv.4-7 self-graded A. Ambrose, Cyril of Alexandria, Clarke, Wesley, Calvin, Theophylact, Robertson, Gill, Ellicott, Lightfoot and Origen verified. The Catena "CYRIL" at v.4 is Cyril of Alexandria and is attributed as such. Lightfoot's two rabbinic stories quoted with his own framing, including his refusal to endorse R. Solomon's reason.

Tile vv.8-12 self-graded A. Bede, Ambrose, Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria, Gill, Lightfoot, Wesley, Ellicott, Robertson and Cyril of Jerusalem verified. Chrysostom's preposition argument ("confess in me" against "deny me") checked twice against the Greek as he reports it.

Tile vv.13-15 self-graded A. Ambrose, Theophylact, Gill, Bede, Ellicott, Cyril of Alexandria, Calvin, Barnes, Clarke and Wesley verified. Clarke's manuscript case for reading "all covetousness" quoted with his own numbers.

Tile vv.16-18 self-graded A. Theophylact, Ellicott, Basil, Gregory, Barnes, Clarke, Robertson and Gill verified. Basil's observation that the rich man's complaint is verbally the pauper's is his own and is quoted at length because the whole force is in the wording.

Tile vv.19-21 self-graded A. Gill, Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott and Lightfoot verified. The narrowest voice list in the chapter — the fathers are absent at these keys — so the tile leans on Lightfoot's two rabbinic passages and on the near-identical Barnes/Clarke diagnoses, which are reported as the parallel they are.

Tile vv.22-24 self-graded A. Theophylact, Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria, Ambrose, Bede and Gill verified. Ambrose's argument that "the cause of our poverty seems to be covetousness" quoted in full because paraphrase would soften it.

Tile vv.25-28 self-graded A. Wesley, Gill, Robertson, Ellicott, Chrysostom, Eusebius, Ambrose and Cyril of Alexandria verified. The verse-27 block's spilled material on verse 29 was excluded here and used at tile 29.

Tile vv.29-34 self-graded A. Robertson, Clarke, Barnes, Augustine, Theophylact, Bede, Gregory of Nyssa, Gill, Cyril of Alexandria and Chrysostom verified. The four-way disagreement about the rare verb is the spine of the tile and each position is quoted rather than summarised.

Tile vv.35-40 self-graded A. Barnes, Ellicott, Wesley, Robertson, Gill, Theophylact, Gregory, Augustine, Cyril of Alexandria, Lightfoot and Cyril of Jerusalem verified. Plummer and Bruce appear only inside Robertson's quotations and are not declared as voices.
Tile vv.41-44 self-graded A. Robertson, Henry, Bede, Ellicott, Gill, Wesley, Theophylact, Augustine and Clarke verified. Deissmann appears only inside Robertson's note and is not declared.

Tile vv.45-48 self-graded A. Gill, Ellicott, Robertson, Clarke, Wesley, Lightfoot, Barnes, Theophylact, Chrysostom, Cyril of Alexandria, Basil, Bede and Calvin verified. Augustine is named only inside Ellicott's Latin tag and was reworded out of the prose so the voice list stays exact.

Tile vv.49-53 self-graded A. Robertson, Ellicott, Gill, Barnes, Clarke, Wesley, Calvin, Lightfoot and Cyril of Jerusalem verified. Plummer appears only inside Robertson's quotations. Robertson's citation of "Romans 1-3" was carried as prose rather than as a .ref link, since it names a range of chapters.

Tile vv.54-56 self-graded A. Gill, Henry, Theophylact, Wesley, Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson, Basil, Bede, Origen, Clarke and Cyril of Alexandria verified. Basil's defence of prognostication is quoted because it cuts against the rebuke it sits inside.

Tile vv.57-59 self-graded A. Ellicott, Calvin, Robertson, Chrysostom, Gill, Theophylact, Ambrose, Bede, Origen, Clarke and Wesley verified. Kypke appears only inside Clarke's note. Ellicott's usable text at key 59 ends before the page chrome and nothing past that point was used.

JFB stride-6 bug again, and again unrecoverable. The Jamieson-Fausset-Brown donor stream at keys 5, 11, 17 and 23 carries Ephesians 1-2 material — the sealing of Ephesians 1:13 at key 5, "the eyes of your heart enlightened" of Ephesians 1:18 at key 11, the fulness of Ephesians 1:23 at key 17, and "rich in mercy" of Ephesians 2:4 at key 23. Entirely foreign to 1 Peter, so unlike matthew 4 nothing was recoverable. All four excluded; JFB is cited nowhere in this chapter and is not declared at any key.

Barnes's block at key 1 opens with a full chapter analysis ("This chapter may be divided into three parts") and Clarke's opens with a verse-by-verse argument for the whole chapter. Both are authorial front-matter, not a filing defect, but they inflate key 1 and were skipped rather than distilled.

Matthew Henry appears at only five keys, and four of the five are section commentaries spanning ranges, with real overlap between them: the key-1 block (1,651 words) runs vv.1-10, the key-4 block (3,336 words) runs vv.4-12, key 11 is a short 81-word summary of vv.11-12, the key-13 block (2,609 words) runs vv.13-16, and the key-18 block (347 words) runs vv.18-25. Keys 1 and 4 therefore cover the same ground twice. Henry is declared only at tiles 1, 4, 11, 13 and 18; the vv.20-25 tail of his key-18 block went unused because the later tiles were already full.

Cyril of Jerusalem is the only patristic voice available in this chapter — there is no Catena Aurea for the epistles — and his three blocks are apposite rather than misfiled: the catechetical lectures on the crucifixion quote 1 Peter 2:22-24 directly, at key 23 verbatim ("who did no sin, neither was guile found in His mouth; who when He was reviled, reviled not again"). Used at tiles 22 and 24.

Tiling: 70,426 usable source words across 25 keys reduced to 14 pericope tiles at roughly 7.75:1, inside the 5-8:1 norm and the largest source chapter handled so far. All ten named voices were checked for grounding before drafting and none was ungrounded; JFB was nevertheless dropped for the reason recorded above, leaving nine.

Tile vv.20-21 carries only five voices. Gill and Wesley are grounded at both keys but their notes there are brief and duplicate what Barnes and Clarke say at more length, so neither is cited or declared. This is a deliberate thinning, not an oversight.

What the adjective rendered "of the word" means is a four-way split: Calvin takes it as milk made up of the word and pairs it deliberately with "guileless"; Barnes reads it as "properly rational, pertaining to reason"; Ellicott says the English "cannot possibly be right"; Robertson sets both senses side by side and declines to decide.

Clarke alone argues the text: he would add "unto salvation" at the end of verse 2 on ABC "and about forty others" as "undoubtedly genuine, and is very important", and reports that many manuscripts and several fathers read Christos for chrestos in verse 3, "from the similarity of the letters".

Whether Peter alludes to his own name: Gill and Wesley take the verse as a deliberate disclaimer, Peter showing "that he is not the rock"; Ellicott calls that "more than doubtful" and argues from vocabulary, since the word here is lithos and neither petros nor petra "could possibly be used of the squared wrought stone".

The tile's spine: whether "he is precious" or "the honour is to you who believe". Barnes defends the Authorised text against its own margin on contextual grounds; Clarke, Ellicott and Robertson all prefer the honour reading because it contrasts with the shame just promised.

"Whereunto also they were appointed" divides five ways — Calvin (both senses possible, inclining to appointment to unbelief, with Pharaoh as the parallel); Robertson via Bigg (the penalty is ordained, not the disobedience); Ellicott (prophetic marking, not causation); Wesley (from eternity, conditioned on unbelief); Clarke via Macknight (re-punctuate, so the appointment is to the word). The sharpest doctrinal disagreement in the chapter.

Who "in time past were not a people" were: Clarke says Gentiles outright, Barnes says mainly Gentiles by allusion only, Wesley splits the verse between Gentiles and Jews, Calvin reads it of the scattered Jews with Paul extending it, and Ellicott rejects the Gentile-readership inference altogether — "such, however, is by no means the case; in fact, the opposite."

Why Christians should submit: Ellicott's reading is the notable one, that Peter's ground is prudential and not, as in Romans 13, that the authority descends from God — they submit "because of the practical consequences of not submitting". Wesley and Calvin keep the Romans ground. Robertson and Ellicott both enter limits; Clarke alone allows none in practice.

Who sends the governors: Ellicott says "the person by whom they are here said to be sent is Cæsar, not the Lord"; Robertson says "by God, as Jesus made plain to Pilate". A flat contradiction on one pronoun, reported as such.

How the accusers' ignorance should be met, and how far "honour all men" reaches. Ellicott presses contempt in every word of the muzzling clause; Wesley alone answers with pity — "a strong motive to pity them". On honour, Robertson, Barnes and Clarke qualify it by desert, while Ellicott, Calvin and Wesley make it universal.

Whether the word for servants settles the presence of slavery: Barnes says it "should not and cannot be employed to prove that slavery existed in the churches to which Peter wrote, and still less to prove that he approved of slavery"; Henry states as fact that "servants in those days generally were slaves"; Ellicott says the word marks the household relation rather than ownership.

Why the servants were buffeted: Ellicott reads it domestically and humorously, for blunders such as "the breaking of dishes"; Clarke reads it religiously, because they "would not join with their masters in idolatrous worship". Both are on-verse and neither is demonstrable, so both stand.

In what sense Christ bore our sins, with Clarke as the outlier: to say they were imputed to him "as if they had been his own, and that the Father beheld him as blackened with imputed sin, is monstrous, if not blasphemous." Barnes reaches a substitution without transfer; Gill takes the load at its widest; Calvin keeps the Levitical frame.

Tile vv.1-3 self-graded A. Ellicott, Calvin, Robertson, Gill, Henry, Wesley, Barnes and Clarke verified against the raw blocks. Leighton, Bengel and Erasmus are named only inside the citing commentator's quotation and are not declared as voices.

Tile v.4 self-graded A. Robertson, Barnes, Henry, Ellicott, Gill, Wesley, Calvin and Clarke verified. Hort appears only inside Robertson's note. Ellicott's Greek argument about petros/petra/lithos checked against his own wording.

Tile vv.5-6 self-graded A. Barnes, Ellicott, Gill, Calvin, Clarke, Robertson and Wesley verified. Leighton and Gesenius appear only inside Ellicott; Jarchi only inside Gill. Clarke's Hebrew root argument is summarised, not quoted, because his transliterations do not survive the source's stripping.

Tile v.7 self-graded A. Barnes, Clarke, Ellicott, Robertson, Calvin, Gill and Wesley verified. Lightfoot is named by Ellicott but has no block of his own here, so the mention was reworded out of the prose to keep the voice list exact.

Tile v.8 self-graded A. Ellicott, Robertson, Barnes, Gill, Clarke, Calvin and Wesley verified. Bigg, Macknight, Wakefield and Leighton appear only inside the citing commentator. Ellicott's charge against the Septuagint is quoted in his own words.
Tile vv.9-10 self-graded A. Clarke, Calvin, Ellicott, Gill, Barnes, Robertson and Wesley verified. Doddridge, Huther and Hort appear only inside the citing commentator.

Tile vv.11-12 self-graded A. Clarke, Calvin, Ellicott, Barnes, Wesley, Gill, Henry and Robertson verified. Leighton, Bengel, Wetstein and Bloomfield appear only inside the citing commentator. JFB material at key 11 was excluded as foreign.
Tile vv.13-14 self-graded A. Clarke, Gill, Calvin, Ellicott, Robertson, Barnes, Wesley and Henry verified. Huther, Ulpian, Doddridge and Pliny appear only inside the citing commentator.

Tile vv.15-17 self-graded A. Clarke, Calvin, Ellicott, Robertson, Barnes, Wesley and Gill verified. Leighton and Josephus appear only inside the citing commentator. JFB material at key 17 was excluded as foreign.
Tile vv.18-19 self-graded A. Robertson, Ellicott, Calvin, Barnes, Henry, Gill, Clarke and Wesley verified. Macknight and Doddridge appear only inside Clarke and Barnes.
Tile vv.20-21 self-graded A. Ellicott, Robertson, Clarke, Barnes and Calvin verified. Gill and Wesley deliberately not cited; see the observation recorded for this tile.

Tile vv.22-23 self-graded A. Ellicott, Clarke, Wesley, Robertson, Gill, Calvin, Barnes and Cyril of Jerusalem verified. Vincent appears only inside Robertson. Clarke's Latin variant is quoted with his own verdict attached. JFB material at key 23 was excluded as foreign.

Tile v.24 self-graded A. Ellicott, Wesley, Clarke, Barnes, Robertson, Gill, Calvin and Cyril of Jerusalem verified. Bigg appears only inside Robertson. Clarke's charge of blasphemy against imputation is quoted verbatim rather than softened.

Jamieson stride-6 residue lattice, ninth consecutive chapter. Donor is Luke 7-8 throughout: Simon the Pharisee and the woman at keys 2 and 14, the withheld salute at key 8, Herods steward Chuza at key 20. A clean single-donor lattice again after the mixed-donor variant recorded at mark 6. Declared as excluded_voices at each key.

Systematic defect in the Catena Aurea on Luke as scraped. Speaker changes inside a block are left as inline uppercase tags rather than becoming new blocks, so the strong-tag boundaries misattribute material. Examples: the block labelled Cyril at key 1 turns into Theophylact halfway through; the block labelled Ambrose at key 3 carries both THEOPHYL and BEDE continuations; the Bede block at key 26 carries a CHRYS continuation; Ambrose at key 34 carries AUG, THEOPHYL and CYRIL in turn. Where the inline voice also has a real block at that key the material was reattributed correctly; where it does not, the material was used without a name rather than misattributed, since naming it would trip the not-sourced-here lint. Worth an owner decision on whether the scraper can split on the inline tags.

Cross-chapter verse-number collision. The Matthew Henry block at key 19 is his exposition of Luke 16:19-31, the rich man and Lazarus, not of Luke 17:19. Same family as the documented 2 Chronicles 27 key 16 case that holds Henry on chapter 28. Declared as residue. Henry at key 20 was checked and is genuine, so the collision is isolated to key 19.

Ellicott block at key 37 is 1089 words of which about 110 are his comment; the remainder is StudyLight chrome, navigation crumbs and a stylesheet dump. Third instance in three consecutive chapters and the third time at the chapter final verse, after matthew 12 key 50 and mark 6 key 56. The pattern is now established well enough to be worth a scraper fix rather than a per-chapter workaround.

The Catena on Luke carries Cyril of Alexandria under two distinct labels, a bare Cyril and a full Cyril of Alexandria, in the same chapter and sometimes at the same key. Treated as two voices for lint purposes since the build counts labels, and both mapped to eastern-alexandrian. The bare label is declarable by the synthesis_qa roster while the full one is not, which is the same mismatch filed for Cyril of Jerusalem and for Robertson.

A settled-looking rendering that both grammarians reject. Ellicott and Robertson each argue at length that within you and not among you is the necessary sense, Robertson holding that the classical examples cited for among do not survive investigation. Barnes leaves both open and Wesley keeps both at once. The entry records the split rather than adopting the margin.

Matthew Henry's block at key 19 is a misfile, and a large one: about 7,100 of the key's 7,810 words are his exposition of Luke 16:19-31, the rich man and Lazarus — beginning "as the parable of the prodigal son set before us the grace of the gospel, so this sets before us the wrath to come" and running through Abraham's bosom, the great gulf and the five brethren. The chapter-and-verse collision (Luke 16:19 filed at Luke 17:19) looks like an off-by-a-chapter slip in the harvest. Excluded entirely; it reduced key 19 to roughly 700 usable words, which is why verse 19 was folded into the vv.15-19 tile rather than given one of its own.

JFB stride-6 bug, third chapter running and again unrecoverable. The Jamieson-Fausset-Brown donor stream at keys 2, 8, 14 and 20 carries Luke 7-8 material: Simon the Pharisee and the woman who anointed Jesus at keys 2, 8 and 14 ("Ha! I have Him now; He plainly knows nothing of the person He allows to touch Him"), and Joanna and Susanna of Luke 8:2-3 at key 20. Foreign to Luke 17, nothing recoverable. All four excluded; JFB is cited nowhere in this chapter and declared at no key.

Cyril of Jerusalem's blocks duplicate heavily. The catechetical passage on the sign of the Cross appears identically at keys 22 and 26; the passage answering the poor man, the sick man and the woman at the mill appears identically at keys 34, 35 and 36. Each was used once, at the tile where it is on-verse — the Cross passage at tile 21, the reassurance passage at tile 34.

Cyril of Alexandria's own commentary runs about one section late through the back of the chapter: his block at key 31 is headed "17:20-30" and expounds the kingdom-not-with-observation discourse, not the housetop warning. His Catena attributions elsewhere in the chapter are correctly placed and were used where they stand; the displaced block was read back to the pericope it belongs to.

Cyril of Alexandria's block at key 1 is displaced the other way: it opens with Isaiah's mountain and continues "the parable of Lazarus and the rich man", i.e. his exposition of Luke 16. Excluded. The Catena "CYRIL" attribution inside the composite block at the same key is on-verse and was used for the two kinds of offence.

Ellicott's note at key 37 ends after roughly a hundred usable words and is followed by the StudyLight page chrome — the chapter navigation, the copyright statement and the site footer. Same defect class as acts 18 key 28 and 1peter 2 key 59. Truncated at the usable text.

Matthew Henry appears at only four keys and every block is a section commentary rather than a verse note. Key 1 runs vv.1-10, key 11 runs vv.11-19, key 20 runs vv.20-37 — about 3,700 words covering the entire back half of the chapter — and key 19 is the Luke 16 misfile recorded above. The key-20 block was distributed across tiles 20, 21, 26, 31 and 34; Henry is declared at tiles 1, 11 and 20.

Titus of Bostra appears in this chapter, at key 11 only, and is new to the corpus so far. He is classed eastern-antiochene. His two contributions — that the lepers "associated together from the sympathy they felt as partakers of the same calamity", and that in pronouncing the name of Jesus they "gain to themselves the reality" — are both on-verse.

Tiling: 47,307 source words across 37 keys, of which roughly 40,200 are usable once Henry's Luke 16 block and the four JFB blocks are set aside, reduced to 10 pericope tiles at about 6.2:1 of usable source. The chapter is unusually lopsided — keys 19 and 20 alone hold 30% of the raw words — which is what forced the vv.15-19 and v.20 tile boundaries.

What the offences are divides five ways: Cyril of Alexandria rules out heresy and keeps to "strifes, slanders, and the like" between brethren; Theophylact prefers obstacles to preaching; Ellicott supplies the rich man's self-indulgent life as the dropped link; Wesley names Pharisaic self-righteousness; Henry divides the woe among persecutors, seducers and scandalous professors.
Robertson corrects the English of the millstone clause outright: it "is a first-class condition, determined as fulfilled, not second-class as the English translations imply". No other voice notices.

Why seven: Bede takes it for totality, "by seven the whole of any thing or time is frequently represented"; Ambrose for the sabbath rest; Ellicott resolves the apparent shortfall against Matthew's seventy times seven by the words "a day"; Wesley alone splits the duty in two, unlimited forgiveness being owed to all in a lower sense and full forgiveness only to real penitents.

How to take the apostles' request: Ellicott hears a late and possibly isolated fragment, betrayed by "the exceptional use of the Apostles for the disciples"; Lightfoot reads it as a request for a rule, "lay down or add something concerning the measure of our faith"; Robertson, quoting Bruce, hears "the stereotyped petition in church prayers" and says they should have answered it themselves.

Whether "unprofitable" implies sin. Clarke's is the strongest denial in the chapter: "the text says unprofitable servants, not sinful servants", and were it otherwise the perfected spirits and the angels would be sinfully imperfect. Robertson notes the Syriac Sinaitic omits the word; Wesley redirects it, since "though we are unprofitable to him, our serving him is not unprofitable to us".

The geography of "through the midst of Samaria and Galilee": Lightfoot and Barnes read "between", along the border; Clarke keeps the plain order; Robertson keeps "through" and reconstructs a route from Ephraim crossing near Bethshean; Ambrose and Titus of Bostra read the route theologically, Christ passing between the two nations "that he might cement both into one new man".

When the Samaritan turned back: Clarke and Ellicott say before reaching the priests, Calvin after, and Barnes proposes that both can stand since he could not have re-entered society without the priests' certificate.

What "thy faith hath made thee whole" adds, given that all ten were cured. Ellicott takes the verb in both its senses; Calvin says the identical cure is "debased and contaminated" by ingratitude, so "it is faith alone that sanctifies the gifts of God to us"; Clarke keeps it merely instrumental.

Whether "with observation" means scrutiny or display. Robertson, Clarke and Ellicott take it for careful watching — Ellicott hearing an echo of the Pharisees' own hostile watching of Christ, since the verb Luke used there is the one this noun derives from — while Calvin, Wesley, Barnes and Henry take it for outward pomp.

Whether the kingdom is "within you" or "among you". Ellicott says the marginal reading was "adopted, somewhat hastily, by most commentators" and the preposition is "all but decisive against" it; Robertson adds that the Xenophon and Plato parallels "do not bear that out when investigated" and Field finds "no clear instance" of the word meaning among. Wesley keeps both but lands inward.

Whether eating, drinking and marrying are condemned. Ambrose enters the guard, since "by the one succession is sustained, by the other nature", and only excess is at fault; Bede makes the innocence of the named acts the whole point, since if lawful pleasures in excess earn fire and brimstone, the unnamed sins of Sodom are worse; Gill and Chrysostom find the condemnation in the manner, appetite having produced the unbelief.

Clarke deletes the verse: it is "without doubt, an interpolation... probably borrowed from Matthew", missing from the uncials he lists, more than fifty other manuscripts, four versions and many fathers, and dropped by Griesbach. No other voice at this pericope raises the question.

Who the eagles are: Barnes and Clarke keep them the Roman armies gathering where the guilt is; Eusebius allegorises them as "the rulers of the world" persecuting the saints, or as "the avenging powers which shall fly about to torment the wicked".

Barnes and Clarke meet the same objection to reading 666 as the Greek word for the Latin man and reach opposite verdicts. Barnes answers the spelling objection from Greek transliterations of Latin names and keeps the word; Clarke treats the objection as decisive and substitutes the Greek for the Latin kingdom, then argues at length that the numbered beast is the second and not the first.

Chrysostom appears at three keys only (1, 17, 32) and is brief at each; the Catena has no continuous commentary on Acts, so the patristic layer in this chapter is thin.

Sharpest textual-cum-liturgical split in the chapter: Barnes, Clarke, Robertson and Ellicott read 'the first day of the week' as the earliest notice of Christian Lord's-day worship; Calvin alone holds it may be 'some certain Sabbath. Which latter thing may seem to me more probable.'

Whether Eutychus died is openly contested. Barnes takes a plain miracle; Robertson lays out the swoon case from Ramsay, Wendt, Zoeckler and Furneaux, then refuses to adjudicate — 'one will believe here as the facts appeal to him.'

'Bound in the spirit' divides the chapter down the middle: Clarke, Barnes and Gill read the Holy Ghost; Ellicott and Robertson read Paul's own spirit, Robertson on the textual ground that the explicit Holy Spirit of v.23 stands in contrast.

Every commentator confronts the conflict between 'ye shall see my face no more' and the Pastoral Epistles, and each resolves it differently — Barnes by conceding Paul probably did return, Clarke by Paul's own uncertainty, Ellicott by 'I know' being said after the manner of men, Robertson by declining to be surprised.

The chapter's live textual dispute: Robertson defends 'the church of God' as correct and infers that Jesus is called God; Clarke weighs the manuscripts and comes down for 'the Church of the Lord', while insisting the doctrine survives either way.
Clarke reads 'after my departing' of Paul's death, 'for few of these evils took place during his life'; Robertson denies it flatly — 'not his death, but his departure from them.'

On the origin of schism, Clarke alone traces the causal chain back to the pastors — greedy superintendents, then alienated members, then opportunists — where Calvin and Barnes lay it on the ambition of the would-be leaders.
Calvin alone denies that Paul's manual labour legislates for ministers, recalling that he elsewhere defends the right to maintenance and accepted it from other churches.
